Section 1—Introduction 
1.1 IATA—Who We Are; What We Do 
International air transport is one of the most dynamic and fast-changing industries in the world. The 
International Air Transport Association (IATA) is the industry's responsive and forward-looking trade 
association. IATA operates at the highest level of global professional standards. 
Founded in 1945, IATA is the trade association for the world's airlines, representing some 290 airlines or 83% 
of total air traffic. 
IATA airlines recognize that cooperation helps them meet the needs of a rapidly changing aviation industry. 
This cooperation allows airlines to offer a seamless service at the highest possible levels of quality to 
passengers and cargo shippers. Much of this cooperation is expressed through IATA, whose mission is to 
“represent, lead and serve the airline industry”. 
IATA helps to ensure that its members' aircraft can operate safely, securely, efficiently and economically 
under clearly defined and understood rules. Continual efforts by IATA ensure that people, freight and mail can 
move around the intricate global airline network as safely, simply and cost-effectively as possible. 
IATA proactively supports joint industry action essential for the sustainable development of the air transport 
system. IATA's role is to identify issues, help establish industry positions and communicate these to 
governments and other relevant authorities. 
1.2 IATA's Airport Activities 
The Infrastructure and Customer Experience (ICE) section of |ATA's Operations, Safety and Security (OSS) 
division aims to provide planning expertise and the global perspective to ensure that airport projects gain early 
airline community involvement and produce facilities that are demand-led, fit-for-purpose and cost effective to 
develop and operate. The IATA Airport Development Reference Manual (ADRM) provides guidelines and 
recommendations that enhance airport planning and design. Where major airport capital programs are being 
planned or are underway, IATA supports the aviation industry by convening Airport Consultative Committees 
(ACCs). The purpose of ACCs is to help gather airline requirements and recommendations and to centralize 
this input for the benefit of airport operators and owners. IATA also provides specialized commercial airport 
consultancy services worldwide.

1.2.1 Airport Consultative Committees (ACCs) 
Consultation with airport authorities via the Airport Consultative Committee (ACC) mechanism brings together 
the airlines’ airport planning expertise, the IATA secretariat and airport authorities worldwide. ACCs serve as a 
focal point for consultation concerning the planning, delivery and cost-effectiveness of airport expansions, the 
development of new airports or enhancements to the airport experience for both passengers and staff. 
1.2.2 IATA Consulting Services for Airports 
IATA has comprehensive experience in the full array of business challenges facing the aviation sector. 
Serving the airline industry for over 75 years, IATA has developed unrivaled practical experience which we 
bring forth to provide the best solutions to our clients. The full range of IATA’s Consulting services is outlined 
on our website: www.iata.org/consulting 
Regarding airports, IATA Consulting offers comprehensive advisory services to assist in their successful 
development. The airports’ first development stage of their life cycle-the planning and construction phase—is 
of utmost importance as it must be ensured that the initial airport infrastructure meets the future requirements 
of all airport stakeholders from a technical, operational, and financial perspective. 
IATA Consulting offers airport development solutions to facilitate the planning and design of airport 
infrastructure. The primary element of this first phase is the preparation of the Airport Master Plan-see more 
details about IATA’s related services further below. It is important to note that IATA Consulting does not take 
part in construction projects and will not supervise any construction work. 
1.2.2.1 Airport Master Planning Studies 
Many airports lack a visionary blueprint for the future, or their existing Master Plan is flawed or not up to date. 
As a result, their short-term decisions may lead to development projects that are poorly located, 
inappropriately sized or unnecessary, resulting in wasteful expenditures and suboptimal performance. 
To avoid costly mistakes, IATA provides expert guidance to ensure that the future infrastructure development 
meets the expected traffic demand and its requirements in a realistic, cost-effective, and affordable manner. 
IATA Consulting has the specialized tools and extensive experience to prepare or review visionary Master 
Plans for the optimal phased development of new or existing airports.

1.4.1 Introduction to Airports Council International (ACI)

1.5 Purpose of the Airport Development Reference Manual 
The IATA Airport Development Reference Manual (ADRM) is recognized as one of the aviation industry's 
most important guides for airlines, airports, government authorities, architects, engineers and planning 
consultants engaged in planning new airports or extending existing airport infrastructure. The ADRM brings 
together aviation industry best practices with respect to the development of world-class airports through better 
comprehension, briefing and design. Its content represents the consolidated recommendations of world￾renowned industry specialists and organizations seeking to promote the development of sustainable world￾class airport facilities. 
One of the key aspects of this manual is the ability to offer a comprehensive overview of the many complex 
topics that are involved in any airport project, especially at large international airports. However, the 
complexity associated with all airport developments means that the information contained within this manual 
must be carefully considered. As with any complex concept, there are many variables that are subject to 
different interpretations and can lead to significantly different conclusions.

1.6 Emerging Trends 
IATA and ACI are actively exploring and supporting the implementation of new technologies and advanced 
processes to deliver needed Capacity, healthy travel, and enhancements to the entire ground journey within 
their NEXTT (New Experience Travel Technology) initiative. NEXTT challenges current on-ground processes 
to incorporate greater digitalization, automation and customer personalization in an integrated, holistic 
manner. Some aspects within the NEXTT vision are established best practice which are documented within 
this manual. Other aspects require forward-looking airlines, airports and governments to conduct proof of 
concepts and trials such that implementation guidance and standards can be defined. The combination of all 
these aspects shall transform the entire end to end journey for passengers, their bags and cargo customers. 
Considering the benefits that technology improvements and emerging trends can bring to airport 
developments, as defined by NEXTT or elsewhere, is a recommended part of the master planning and design 
process. 
1.7 How to Use the ADRM 
The ADRM should be used by airport planners worldwide as a complementary source of best practice airport 
design guidance. Other key ICAO references include Annex 14 (in particular for airfield and apron design), the 
Airport Planning Manual (Doc 9184), the Aerodrome Design Manual (Doc 9157), and the Airport Services 
Manual (Doc 9137). 
IATA recognizes that international standards will vary from region to region around the world. While the 
ADRM should be the initial source of design guidance for airport development, the airport design professional 
should always seek to clarify national standards and decide appropriately on any potentially conflicting 
requirements. Professional engineering and architectural guidance should be used to assess and resolve 
differences between the ADRM and national standards. 
The ADRM should be used in conjunction with relevant international and national legislation, regulations and 
standards. Examples include, but are not limited to:

Section 2—Key Considerations for Airport Development 
2.1 Introduction 
Airport planning and design requires analyzing the business and operating environment of the airport in order 
to identify requirements and provide the needed inputs for the detailed planning of airport facilities. This 
section explains the essential considerations that planners should take into account in order to inform airport 
design and development plans. 
Key chapter include: 
Traffic Forecasts providing guidance on the basic building blocks of airport planning addressing the critical 
issues of future market demand and airline capacity to determine rationale for expansion. Guidance includes 
the vision, policy, data analysis, common forecasting techniques, types of Traffic Forecasts, and peak period 
analysis 
Master Planning is a critical chapter that explains the importance for airports to have a long-term plan to guide 
future infrastructure and facility developments in a logical, sustainable and cost-efficient manner, in order to 
capture the ultimate development potential of the airport. This includes having a clear, integrated strategy for 
key elements such as the scale and layout of airfields, terminals, support facilities and surface access. 
Airport Environmental Sustainability provides a comprehensive overview of airport environmental sustainability 
and highlights and practices airport can apply to achieve their environmental objectives, linked with airport 
planning and design. Airports and planners should remember to consult closely with stakeholders on the 
economic viability of solutions in parallel. 
Universal Design and Accessibility is an introduction to more detailed guidance in section 3.3.9, reflecting on 
key principles to responsibly promote universal design across all relevant airport activities. This includes 
people with disabilities and those who are ageing and can face physical, sensory, cognitive, cultural and 
attitude barriers within airport built facilities, digital environments, services, operations, evacuation, customer 
service and maintenance. 
Airport Technology has transformed how airports operate over the past 20+ years and continues to feature in 
the ADRM as a method to improve passenger experience and drive efficiencies as part of a broader business 
and operational strategy. The updated chapter reflects on some of the latest trends and considerations for 
planners to take into account. 
Development of a Concept of Operations is a critical part of airport planning that should not be overlooked by 
planners. This new chapter describes the operational outcomes to be achieved from the users perspective as 
an input into the design process of a new airport facility. This should be from an early stage in the 
development process and involve stakeholders requirements. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 9 

===PAGE 29===
ue a 
IATA 4 Airport Development Reference Manual 
Pandemic Resilience and Healthy Buildings explore how airports can incorporate key health principles, well￾being and pandemic resilience in the design and operation of their facilities, that will affect those using the 
facilities and the communities they connect. 
Planning for Construction Delivery is another new chapter and considers how to ensure the smooth, timely 
and efficient delivery of airport projects, including how to minimize their impact to ongoing airport operations. 
Operational Readiness and Airport Transfer (ORAT) describes the methodical preparation required to 
successfully open new airport infrastructure through effective advance planning, governance, trails and 
stakeholder engagement focused on a successful opening day. 
Airport Simulation covers the latest trends throughout all the life cycle phases of an airport in order to fully 
benefit from the many advantages of dynamic simulation modelling, while finally Planning for Collaborative 
Decision Making focused on more efficient ways to make use of existing infrastructure and capacity resulting 
from pressures on airport demand and airspace resources. 
2.1.1 Data Requirements 
In order to use the ADRM for the planning of new airport infrastructure or extending existing airport 
infrastructure, several data sources are required, especially for forecasting of future air traffic volumes, 
determination of current and future peak periods and the usage of capacity equations for passenger terminal 
facility sizing. 
Early collection of accurate and relevant data is critical for the timely and correct analysis of traffic demand 
and hence the appropriate sizing of the new infrastructure. If the data needed for the capacity analysis is not 
currently being tracked or recorded at the relevant level of detail at the airport, it may be necessary to set up a 
data collection process many months in advance of the capacity study. 
This section provides an overview of the data sources needed to follow the ADRM Facility Sizing Process 
from initial annual passenger forecasts, through determining peak hour periods to the final calculation of the 
future facility sizing. For each step, the data requirements and recommended data sources are described, as 
well as alternative data sources if suggested data is not available. The data requirements are described in 
more detail in the relevant sections in the following chapters on forecasting and planning. 
Modern airport technology (e.g., digitalization, self-service, flow sensors and IoT initiatives) can optimize 
current operational performance and improve passenger experience, but in addition provide a new data

===PAGE 30===
IATA + Introduction 
foundation for long-term capacity planning and facility sizing (i.e., automated access gates and passenger 
flow measurement systems). 
See 2.7 Development of a Concept of Operations and 2.6 Airport Technology for a more in-depth discussion 
on the use of airport technology within the airport operation.

2.1.1.2 Annual Forecast 
2.2 Forecasting is devoted to forecasting of future airport activity levels with recommendations on forecasting 
methods and relevant data sources ranging from internal data at the airport in question to general aviation 
industry data and high-level international economic data. 
The collection of data on historical aviation activity is described in detail in 2.2.3.1 Data Collection, highlighting 
that the recommended data source is the airport itself (AODB, FIDS or similar data warehouse). Although 
data on an annual or monthly basis split by passenger segments (Departure/Arrival, Domestic/International 
etc.) is sufficient at this stage, it is recommended to collect this data on a more granular level (preferably flight 
by flight) as it will be needed in future steps for calculation of peak periods and/or design day flight schedules. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 11 

===PAGE 31===
Se & 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.1.1.3 Design Hour Rate (DHR) 
The definition and calculation of the appropriate Design Hour Rate (DHR) is discussed in 2.2.10.1 Selection of 
the Design Rate Definition. It is also described how to forecast the current level to future planning scenarios. 
The calculations require access to a full year of historical traffic schedule. The airport data records (AODB, 
FIDS, Data Warehouse) is the natural preferred data source, alternatively aviation data services (OAG, SRS 
analyzer etc.) may be able to provide schedules, however, they do not provide full coverage of all operations 
and passengers, which will impact the selection of the Design Hour Level. 
For the calculation of the Design Hour Rate, the flight schedule data may easily be aggregated to an hourly 
level, possibly split in various segments (domestic/international, arrival/departure etc.) 
2.1.1.4 Design Day Flight Schedule (DDFS) 
The development of a future Design Day Flight Schedule (DDFS) is relevant in a number of planning studies 
depending on the planning horizon, data availability and required level of granularity (see 2.2.10.3 Design Day 
Flight Schedules). 
The development of a future DDFS builds on a thorough analysis and understanding of the current schedule 
and earlier schedule development, which in turn requires access to historical flight schedules for several years 
(5+ years is recommended). As was the case for the DHR calculations, the airport data records (AODB, FIDS, 
Data Warehouse) is the natural preferred data source, alternatively aviation data services (OAG, SRS 
analyzer etc.) may be able to provide schedules. 
2.1.1.5 Demand Calculation 
Within the ADRM Facility Sizing Process, “demand” is defined as the number of people that undertake a 
specific terminal process over a period of time. 3.3.4.9 Demand-Capacity Assessment provides two 
alternative methods for calculating the demand required for future facility sizing, building on either the future 
Design Hour Level or a future Design Day Flight Schedule. In both situations, the expected passenger 
presentation at the processing facilities must be considered. 
Several data sources may be used to construct presentation profiles (‘when do passengers for flight X show 
up at the back of the line for processor Y?”) which can later be applied to the DDFS to calculate the demand. 
Boarding card scans from existing automated access gates at the processor provide the best possible data 
source as the timestamp and flight number may be combined with additional schedule information from the 
airport flight records to produce detailed presentation profiles for various passenger and time segments 
(domestic/international, weekday/weekend, morning/afternoon) or even on a route-by-route level. Similarly, 
12 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 32===
Ss @- jy | IATA iv Introduction 
passenger flow measurement systems can also provide aggregated presentation profiles that may be used to 
calibrate a smaller set of presentation profiles developed for planning. Finally, manual counts and/or 
passenger surveys (“When did you arrive at the back of the line for processor Y?") can be used to compile a 
set of presentation profiles for planning. 
Passenger surveys may be needed for a detailed segmentation of passengers e.g., group sizes, bags per 
passenger, usage of self-service options etc. See 2.3.6.1.9 Air Passenger Surveys—Scope and Best Practice 
for details on planning and execution of such surveys. 
2.1.1.6 Capacity Calculation 
See 3.3.4.9.2 Capacity Equations for Assessment of Future Facility Requirements for the capacity formulas 
that translate the demand from the previous step into the actual requirements for processing units (counters, 
lanes etc.) and area for dwell and queueing. Critical to the accuracy of the capacity equations are the input 
parameters on expected throughput (or process time), passenger splits (e.g., share using bag drops, kiosks, 
fast-track etc.) and the selected level of service (see 3.3.4.6 Level of Service Concept). 
An analysis of the airport's current operating conditions is naturally a good starting point for selecting the 
future input parameters. For greenfield airports, similar airports in the vicinity may be analyzed instead. Both 
passenger flow measurement systems and data logs from the processor IT systems («ray machines, bag 
drops etc.) are good data sources for throughput rates, process times and passenger splits. Data should be 
thoroughly analyzed to understand distribution, variation, outliers, and significant passenger segments before 
selecting future input parameters. Alternatively, passenger counts, and observations can be used to sample 
current throughputs and splits. 
When deciding input parameters for the capacity equations, it is important to take into account the 
expected impact on throughput and passenger splits of the introduction of additional/new technology (e.g., 
self-service bag drops, biometrics) as well as the proposed concept of operation for the new infrastructure. 
See 2.7 Development of a Concept of Operations and 2.6 Airport Technology for more details. 
2.1.1.7 Simulation 
Simulation studies are useful for all aspects of airport planning, including airspace, runway, apron, baggage, 
and landside access. Specifically, for passenger terminals, simulation studies can be used as a more detailed 
alternative to the static capacity equations, allowing for a more dynamic modelling of pax flows with 
interrelated processes and multiple simulation runs (Monte Carlo simulation). The simulation with a proposed 
future layout supports the “proof of concept” of a planned design under operational conditions to validate 
and/or refine the capacity requirements. 
If a proposed future layout is available, assumptions on the physical flow of passengers through the terminal 
(speed, routes, area per passenger etc.) are required in addition to the data sources needed for the capacity 
equations. Furthermore, input data describing the operational concept and resource allocation are required to 
realistically model passenger flows at the various terminal processors. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 13 

===PAGE 33===
Se [FF IATA pill Airport Development Reference Manual 
Passenger flow measurement systems and infrastructure utilization logs can typically provide insight into the 
current behavior in the terminal, alternatively passenger surveys and manual counts and observations may be 
used to collect data for these assumptions. 
Usually, a simulation uses historic flight schedules for verification and calibration of the model and the used 
input data. For the future situation, Design Day Flight Schedules representing the forecasted peak demand 
and peak structures are used. What-if scenarios on future flight schedules may be recommended for 
sensitivity testing, assuming the same demand level, but alternating the peak structures. See 2.11 Airport 
Simulation for a detailed walk-through of the steps required for a simulation study. 
2.1.1.8 Data Requirements for Other Areas 
For data requirements for areas not covered explicitly by Section 2.2 Forecasting and the terminal capacity 
equations and 3.3.4.6 Level of Service Concept, please see the individual chapters in Section 3 Facilities 
Planning for more details. Such areas include landside forecourt (parking, vehicle flows), baggage systems 
and airfield (stands, gates, taxiways, runways etc.).

2.2.1 Introduction and Definition 
Forecasts of future levels of aviation activity form the basis for effective decisions in airport infrastructure 
planning. Forecasts should provide a plausible and robust guide to future activity levels based upon the latest 
available data. Forecasts should: 
e Use appropriate forecasting techniques 
¢ Be supported by information in the study; and 
¢ Provide an adequate justification for airport planning and development 
The level of effort required to produce a planning forecast will vary significantly from airport to airport and 
project to project. The use of elaborate forecasting tools and techniques may be warranted in the case of 
large airports and more complex projects. The update of an existing forecast may be all that is required for 
simpler projects. Stakeholders should agree on the appropriate level of forecasting effort required in the pre￾planning and scoping phase of the study. 
Aviation activity forecasts used for airport infrastructure planning are typically developed for a 20- to 30-year 
time horizon due to the capital-intensive nature of airport infrastructure projects and their life cycle. Forecasts 
are usually presented in five-year increments. Annual forecasts may be desirable for the first five-to ten-year 
period.

Aviation forecasts provide the basis for: 
¢ Determining the airport's role in the aviation system 
¢ Determining the improvements to the airfield, terminal facilities, apron areas, landside access, car rental, 
and parking facilities needed to accommodate growth in demand 
¢ Estimating the potential environmental effects, such as noise and air quality, of the airport's operation on 
the surrounding community 
e Assessing market risk; and 
¢ Evaluating the financial feasibility of alternative airport development proposals 
This section provides an overview of the information required and approach to developing airport forecasts for 
Passenger volumes, air cargo tonnage, and ATMs. 
The correct approach described in the following chapters provides guidance on how to develop forecasts of 
market-driven aviation demand for air service. These forecasts are considered “unconstrained”. In other 
words, for the purposes of estimating demand, the approach assumes facilities will be provided to meet the 
forecast demand. However, when there are financial, capacity or regulatory constraints, these specific cases 
should be applied to the outcome of the unconstrained Passenger or ATM demand forecast.

Introduction 
Commercial air travel is an industry that is vulnerable to crises coming from such external shocks as 
economic recessions, war, terrorism, and pandemics. Forecasting air traffic demand during and after such 
disruptions is extremely challenging. The effectiveness of the usual drivers of traffic models can be 
significantly reduced during these periods and other factors will need to be considered. Fortunately, there are 
alternative approaches that can be used to help address these issues. 
Pandemics’ Impact on Aviation 
A supply shock is an event that can affect the ability of aviation to provide capacity. For example, an increase 
in fuel prices may cause airlines to pull back on low yield routes or retire less efficient aircraft, thereby 
decreasing the supply of air services. Longer-lasting supply adjustments can come from changes in 
technology. Examples from history include the introduction of jet aircraft and the onset of the Internet. 
Innovations in business models such as the rise of low-cost carriers can cause the cost and price of air 
transport to fall significantly and lead to a higher level of traffic. 
A demand shock is a sudden event that increases or decreases demand for goods or services and is usually 
temporary in nature. Pandemics such as COVID-19 are an example of a demand shock for the air passenger 
market (and a supply shock on the air cargo market). Customers are either reluctant or unable to travel 
because of the risk of an infectious disease or the health controls and border restrictions that are put in place 
to control its spread. Previous demand shocks, such as the 1991 recession, the 2001 terrorist attacks, SARS 
in 2003 and the 2007-2009 global financial crisis (GFC) caused global revenue passenger kilometers (RPKs) 
to fall by 5-20%, but pre-crisis levels were regained after 6-18 months.

The COVID-19 crisis is exceptional in the depth and duration of air traffic decline as a direct result of travel 
restrictions. While the industry should have a near complete rebound in traffic, there could be some longer 
lasting effects on demand from some travel segments, such as business travel due to the widespread 
adoption of videoconferencing, or there could be an impact on supply from the loss of skilled aviation labor. 
Unlike the GFC, COVID-19 is predominantly a travel policy shock rather than a macroeconomic shock as 
many areas of the world, such as North America, experienced a strong economic recovery that outpaced any 
recovery in travel. 
The travel policy shock has, however, caused a deep economic shock to the aviation industry, across airlines 
and airports, resulting in significant increase in debt that is likely to lead to an increase in overall costs to 
passengers and a negative impact on demand due to price elasticity. The duration of this shock has led to 
significant job losses in aviation and associated industries, many of which involved highly skilled staff. The 
ability of airlines, ground handlers, airports and other support industries to rehire and/or train staff to respond 
to any recovery in demand may create a lag in response. 
One also has to consider that the effects of a pandemic will vary according to different types of traffic. 
International travel and tourism have been severely affected by the COVID-19 crisis and its recovery will be 
crucial to the revival of aviation. On the other hand, domestic travel has not been as affected by travel 
restrictions and quarantines as international travel and has, therefore, suffered less of a drop and shown a 
faster recovery.

Another example is air cargo which boomed during COVID-19 as cargo was not a vector for disease and not 
subject to the restrictions placed on air travel. The wider economy experienced a ‘V-shaped’ output recovery 
and, with the demands of global supply chains, generated a strong and growing demand for air cargo services 
(see Exhibit 2.2.1b). Despite the shortage of capacity normally available in the holds of passenger aircraft, 
overall cargo revenues and volume went up as yields hit record highs and air carriers scrambled to find 
capacity.

The pace of the aviation industry's recovery from a pandemic depends upon several factors, all of which need 
to be considered in developing a forecast: 
© Epidemiological trajectory: What course will the pandemic take given the vaccination campaigns in 
place? What health factors will influence passengers’ choice of travel and destination? 
¢ Policy orientation: How will authorities influence the recovery? For how long will health and safety 
measures, including travel restrictions and quarantines, be in place? 
« Macroeconomics: Economic impact (e.g., gross domestic product-GDP). How will the economy sustain 
air travel? 
® Microeconomics: How will air travel spending change? How has COVID impacted the propensity of 
passengers to travel and to which destinations? How will COVID affect airlines and airfares? 
It is important to keep in mind that many travelers are just as concerned about quarantines as they are about 
catching the virus. This was confirmed in several IATA surveys. The latest survey’, undertaken in 11 markets, 
showed that the biggest deterrent to air travel was quarantine measures, with 84% of respondents indicating 
that they will not travel if there is a chance of quarantine at the destination.

The trajectory of the recovery in the forecast will also be affected by the duration and scale of the pandemic. 
In the case of COVID-19, there has been evidence of substantial pent-up demand. Increases in vaccination 
tates and/or relaxation of government travel restrictions have led to air travel surging. The wider ‘V-shaped’ 
economic recovery is boosting incomes and many consumers have accumulated savings during the 
shutdowns, which is likely to fuel a return to air travel once restrictions allow. 
The Usual Drivers of Traffic May Disappear in a Crisis, Temporarily 
Air travel and air cargo volumes are highly sensitive to activity in the wider economy. GDP, or its component 
parts of household and business incomes, is in normal times the main driver of airport air traffic. GDP 
elasticities are usually between 1-2, depending on the stage of development of the economies at each end of 
the route. Air travel, particularly for leisure, is also very sensitive to price, with elasticities of around -1 at the 
level of city-pair markets’, as well as to currency exchange rates. If the demand shock is due to an economic 
crisis, such as a recession or hike in oil prices, then the GDP and price elasticities in air traffic forecasting 
models should do a reasonable job of tracking developments. But if the shock, like COVID-19, triggers 
barriers to traffic outside of the normal model-such as border travel restrictions and health safety measures 
like quarantines—then the normal drivers in air traffic models stop working (see Exhibit 2.2.1c). Traditional 
forecasting approaches are, therefore, not suited for assessing the impact of the COVID crisis

Forecasters and evaluators of forecasts will know something is going wrong when the model predictions begin 
to diverge systematically from the actual data on traffic (i.e., a large ‘residual’ appears). The task of the 
forecaster in the face of a shock-induced breakdown of the model is to either change the model or use off￾model techniques to deal with the problem until more normal market conditions reappear.

Travel demand during COVID-19 is predominantly a highly constrained market and recovery forecasts should 
be built from the bottom up until they meet top-down, largely macroeconomic, forecast drivers. 
¢ Constraints to consider include travel policies, in particular border controls and quarantines that are 
gradually winding down, thereby unlocking demand. 
e Aviation industry constraints, in particular the phased building back of routes and frequencies aligned to 
travel policy changes by reintroducing mothballed aircraft or new aircraft. 
Seasonal constraints depending on when travel policies are unlocked. 
e Broader industry constraints, such are hotel availability, competing markets, healthcare availability, etc. 
e Human resource constraints affected by the above that will add to the latency of the recovery. 
e Capacity constraints for ship- and truck-loaded cargo. 
Macroeconomic forecast drivers include: 
e GDP for both ends of the journey. 
* Journey costs (ticket and at end destination). 
© Changes to reasons for travel (such as fewer in-person meetings). 
¢ Sustainability impacts (such as air/rail substitution for short-haul flights). 
© Impact of e-commerce on demand for rapid delivery services for cargo. 
Usually, it will not be possible to change the model to formally incorporate a new traffic driver, such as travel 
restrictions, into the model. That is because there is no historical data over which changes in the new driver 
will have affected traffic sufficiently for econometric techniques to estimate an efficient and unbiased 
coefficient. So, the task is to use off-model techniques to project the traffic recovery over the short and 
medium term until traffic returns to its 2019 level. 
The forecaster will then search for a relationship between demand recovery and possible variables like travel 
restrictions, the COVID-19 epidemiologic situation, airline plans, and vaccination rates. For example, 
estimates of when vaccination rates will generate herd immunity are likely to influence when governments 
might lower travel restrictions. These assessments will then need to be incorporated judgmentally into the 
profile of the model's ‘residual,’ returning it to more normal levels (1 in a multiplicative equation, 0 in an 
additive equation). At that point, the normal drivers of traffic (GDP and price) take over as the main drivers of 
the forecast traffic profile. 
Demand in the short term (next twelve months) can be derived from published airline schedules (which can be 
quite dynamic during a crisis) and on load factor estimates that consider recent history. 
Trends are more amenable to forecasting, for the most part. The focus of post-crisis/shock forecasting should 
be on the path to the new or previous trend. The forecaster should ask whether there is any reason to expect 
the pre-crisis trend to have changed or if we can expect an almost complete return to pre-crisis trends and 
growth. In the case of COVID-19, it is likely that passenger growth has been lost, ranging from months to 
years depending on the region and market, but the industry will recover and eventually regain its growth 
trajectory. Conversely, the industry has been able to respond to increasing demand for air cargo.

===PAGE 41===
= IATA pi Airport Development Reference Manual 
Transparency of Scenario Assumptions is Vital 
Forecasts developed during and after a shock face extremely high levels of uncertainty. There are factors 
beyond just the risks of reoccurrence of events that have happened in the past and that can be given a 
probability. There are likely to be new developments that cannot be anticipated. 
Scenarios can be usefully employed to quantify a range for the recovery path based on different assumptions. 
The transparency of the assumptions used as well as the forecast model equation residuals is critical to 
enable a proper evaluation and limit the influence of any forecasting bias.

===PAGE 42===

2.2.2 Economic Base for Air Travel 
The intrinsic links between the level of aviation activity and economic growth are well documented. Simply 
put, growth in population, income, and business activity typically lead to increased demand for air travel and 
the shipment of goods by air. The market demand for air travel is often referred to as “underlying demand” or 
“latent demand?” in that it cannot be realized without the presence of air service at a price that results in a 
decision to fly. 
Consequently, one of the first steps in developing an aviation activity forecast is to collect data relating to the 
business, economic, trade, and tourism characteristics of the regions served by the subject airport. These 
help to explain the economic basis for air travel at the airport. In most cases, economy and tourism are the 
primary drivers of air passenger traffic while economy and trade are the main stimulus for air cargo traffic. 
These variables identify historical and/or future trends that can potentially stimulate growth at the airport. Air 
passenger demand depends on the combination of trends in the: 
e Airline industry (airfare in particular) 
* National and international economies (especially at major transfer hubs); and 
e Socioeconomic conditions within the airport catchment area 
A few additional variables may be used for air cargo, including: 
e Regional trade (imports and exports) 
¢ Global trade 
e® Manufacturing activity 
2.2.2.1 Airport Catchment Area 
The airport catchment area is the geographic region where the majority of origin/destination passengers (or 
goods for cargo) begin their journey prior to arriving at the subject airport. When developing an economic 
base, it is essential to determine the catchment area of the airport. Understanding the region where 
passengers originate prior to arriving at the airport will help determine what economic data best describes the 
underlying market potential. Catchment areas range in size depending on the airport, its accessibility and its 
surrounding environment. The passenger and cargo catchment areas of a given airport are often different. 
Cargo activities tend to be more concentrated in the vicinity of the airport, but cargo payloads are often 
transported over long distances to reach the airport. 
One way of identifying the catchment area is through passenger surveys (see 2.3.6.1.9 Air Passenger 
Surveys-Scope and Best Practice). Alternatively, specialized databases (such as Pax|S/AirportlS) provide 
information on where a ticket was issued. This gives a high-level indication of the origin of a passenger's trip. 
Catchment areas also depend on competing airports as well as the geographic and economic characteristics 
of the surrounding region. It should be noted that it is common to find overlapping airport catchment areas, 
particularly in large metro areas served by multiple airports. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 23 

===PAGE 43===
Se GB Ny | . IATA pull Airport Development Reference Manual 
In overlapping catchment areas with more than one choice of airport, passengers typically decide to use a 
specific airport based on: 
e Price 
e Nonstop service 
e Frequency of flights 
e Destinations served; and 
e Proximity to their point of origin or destination 
All other variables being equal, theory dictates that passengers will tend to choose the closest airport. In 
reality, homogeneity in airport choice rarely occurs. As a result, it is important to not assess the subject airport 
in isolation, but to understand the catchment area dynamics of the region as a whole. 
It should also be noted that catchment areas are dynamic and change over time, particularly in multi-airport 
regions. Examples of factors that could cause a catchment area to shift are: 
e Anew model airline initiates service at the subject airport causing a higher proportion of traffic to be 
captured from a neighboring airport due to attractive low fares that outweigh the increased ground travel 
time 
* Anew or expanded ground transportation system results in shorter travel times to a competing airport; 
and 
¢ Urban sprawl puts an increasing proportion of a metropolitan area's population in proximity to the subject 
airport 
2.2.2.2 Socioeconomic Base 
Once the catchment area has been determined and the source markets have been identified (for airports with 
significant inbound traffic), the next step is to collect relevant historical and forecast socioeconomic indicators. 
Socioeconomic historical trends and forecasts are key indicators of air service activity. Examples include: 
«Population 
e Employment 
e Per capita personal income (PCPI) 
e Trade; and 
¢ Gross domestic product/gross regional product (GDP/GRP) 
24 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 44===
. pom 
=e } IATA jal Forecasting 
Growth in population and employment are important indicators of the overall health of the local economy. 
Population and employment changes tend to be closely correlated as people migrate in and out of areas 
largely depending on their ability to find work in the local economy. Income statistics such as PCPI and 
GDP/GRP are broad indicators of the relative earning power and wealth of the region. Thus, inferences can 
be made relative to a resident's ability to purchase air travel. PCPI is calculated by dividing total income by 
total population. Trade and GDP/GRP are important determinants of air cargo activity. 
When working with socioeconomic variables over time, all currency values should be converted to constant, 
or real, units to eliminate any distortions resulting from inflation. The specification of the currency units (US$, 
Euro or local units) is also critical and should be made consistently. 
Sources for socioeconomic data and statistics include: 
¢ Woods & Poole 
e¢ The World Bank 
e The International Monetary Fund 
e IHS Global Insight 
* Moody's economy.com 
* The Economist Intelligence Unit 
e Consensus Economics; and 
e Government agencies 
When choosing a source for socioeconomic data, it is important to check its coverage, both in terms of scope 
and time range (historical and forecast). When organizing the socioeconomic data to serve as input to various 
projections, historical and forecast data should be arranged in compatible formats. 
2.2.2.3 Transfer Traffic 
Unlike origin/destination traffic, transfer traffic has little relevance to the catchment area and its dynamic. The 
factors that influence the number of transfer passengers at an airport will differ from those affecting the 
number of originating/terminating passengers. Therefore, airport forecasters will often analyze and forecast 
these traffic segments separately. Forecasts of transfer passengers at an airport are particularly sensitive to 
the strategies, networks and service densities of the carriers at the airport. 
2.2.2.4 Airline Yields 
Understanding the cost of air travel and its associated affects is part of developing an economic base. Airline 
passenger yields are the aviation industry's measure for average ticket prices. Yield is defined as the average 
revenue an airline obtains from carrying a passenger one mile or one kilometer. It reflects fare, length of haul, 
level of competition, carrier costs, and other factors. Yield is a commonly accepted measure of the price of air 
travel but excludes airport taxes and charges. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 25 

===PAGE 45===
% IATA Hi Airport Development Reference Manual 
If prices decline, passengers can better afford to fly and traffic typically increases. Indeed, potential travelers 
make air travel decisions based primarily on the following factors: 
1. Availability of air service; 
2. Price; 
3. Distance of an airport from point of trip origin/destination; and 
4 Travel time. 
Competitive prices will often cause travelers to select airports that are not necessarily the closest to where 
their trip begins or ends. Yields have a direct impact on the associated level of air travel demand. When data 
is available, understanding historical yield trends and making inferences regarding their future direction is an 
important component in the forecasting process. 
Similarly, businesses looking to ship goods will examine the cost of shipping by air versus other transportation 
modes (i.e., truck, rail, marine) balanced against the required timeframe for shipment delivery. Air freight is 
typically the most expensive form of transportation, but also the most time efficient. Therefore, it will generally 
be used for high-value commodities (per unit weight) or time-sensitive goods such as perishable items or 
fashion apparel. Forecast analysts must understand how the cost of shipping air freight affects air cargo 
volumes at the subject airport versus other airports and other modes of transportation. It is important to note, 
however, that the availability of data makes understanding air cargo shipping costs difficult to evaluate. 
As with socioeconomic data, when working with historical yield and average air fares, all currency values 
should be converted to constant units to eliminate any distortions resulting from inflation. Historical yield 
values should be arranged in the same format as the other socioeconomic variables in order to be compatible 
with various projection techniques. 
2.2.2.5 Tourism 
Airports play a critical role in facilitating tourism. Collecting statistics about tourism trends in the airport 
catchment area is an important part of the forecasting process. Tourism indicators include: 
e¢ Number of visitors to the region 
e Nationality or world region of origin of foreign visitors 
e Number of hotel room nights and average duration of stay; and 
e Seasonality of visitor travel 
26 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 46===
Forecasting 
2.2.2.5.1 Number of Visitors 
Quantifying changes in the number of visitors to a region provides an indication of how attractive the airport 
catchment area is as a place to visit. There are many attractions that bring visitors to a region, such as 
historical/heritage sites, theme parks, prevailing climate. Visitors to airports also drive facility requirements 
such as customs, immigration and border security, car rentals, hotels, restaurants, retail outlets, etc. 
2.2.2.5.2 Nationality/World Region of Foreign Visitors 
When an airport is knowledgeable about the nationality or home region of foreign visitors, the airport will have 
a better understanding of how the world economic climate may affect the airport's traffic volumes. Indeed, 
these trends can be explicitly modeled in aviation forecasts if the visitor data is available by city, country or 
world region. Moreover, the airport can also target emerging markets that have been historically less well 
linked to the airport's surrounding catchment area. 
2.2.2.5.3 Number of Hotel Room Nights and Average Duration of Stay 
To support visitor travel and tourism, hotels and conference facilities are critical for any airport. Understanding 
the number of hotel room nights and the average length of stay of passengers gives airports insight into the 
economic impact of tourism on the region as well as the need for development of new facilities in the future. 
Historical room night capacity should also be considered against historical airport traffic data, as limitations to 
accommodations capacity—particularly in leisure-focused markets—may place constraints on the growth of air 
passenger traffic. 
2.2.2.6 Trade 
Air cargo plays a critical role in the world economy by facilitating trade, especially international trade. As 
previously mentioned, air cargo tends to be oriented toward high-value or time-sensitive goods. Indeed, air 
cargo is estimated to account for less than 10 percent of the world's freight volume, but over a third of the 
value of goods exchanged worldwide. 
The forecast analyst should seek to understand historical trade patterns, estimate future growth in trade, and 
evaluate the implications of trade growth for air cargo volumes at the subject airport. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 27 

===PAGE 47===
we IATA Hi. Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.2.2.7 Intermodal Transportation 
Intermodal transportation involves the use of two or more modes of transport within a given trip, whether it is 
for individuals or freight. The Air Transport Action Group (ATAG) considers intermodal transportation for 
passengers to be a combination of: 
* Access to airports: local transport services between the airport and the neighboring city (e.g., commuter 
train, metro, bus or even boat) 
* Complementary feeder services between the airport and various destinations in the surrounding region 
(mainly provided by train, high-speed rail, bus, or ferry) 
* Competing services between major city centers of neighboring regions (i.e., a passenger uses air 
transport for one leg of the trip and rail or bus for a second leg); and 
¢ Alternative services that fully replace airline feeder services to airports (in general, for trips of less than 
three hours) 
It is clear that other modes of transport have the potential to affect air traffic volumes at the subject airport in 
both complementary and competitive manners. It is incumbent on the forecast analyst to quantitatively or 
qualitatively evaluate whether or not changes in the ground transportation infrastructure and/or multimodal 
offerings are likely to impact air traffic volumes at the subject airport. 
2.2.2.8 Economic.Base Data Analysis 
The final step in developing the economic base is analyzing the key data collected. The forecast analyst 
should: 
¢ Tabulate the key socioeconomic and demographic data in a format compatible with forecast models so 
they can serve as inputs to various projection techniques 
¢ Create compound annual growth rates for each economic category in order to summarize trends over the 
historical period; and 
¢ Document socioeconomic and regional demographic data in a narrative assessment to better explain how 
these variables affect airport activity 
A well-organized collection and analysis of socioeconomic and demographic data will be important when 
developing models for the aviation forecast. 
2.2.3 Historical Aviation Activity 
The past is not always a perfect predictor of the future; however, an analysis of historical data provides the 
opportunity to understand factors that may have caused traffic to increase or decrease and how those factors 
may change in the future. Understanding the historical relationships between the economy (demand) and 
aviation activity (supply) at the subject airport will help form the building blocks of the forecast.

2.2.3.3 Top Domestic and International Destinations 
As mentioned above, the purpose of the historical activity analysis is to build a context for the forecast. It 
answers questions such as what markets are served from the airport and why. It is imperative to research the 
airport's key domestic and international markets to have a better understanding of the current and future 
direction of air service at the airport. This analysis also provides a geographic context for the forecast. The 
mix and range of domestic and international markets will inform what types of aircraft are deployed over the 
forecast period. If feasible and suitable to the scope of the project, this analysis should be conducted on both 
airline capacity as well as Origin/Destination passenger markets. This additional analysis can also provide 
insight into unserved or underserved markets and how those markets have evolved over time.

2.2.3.4 Historical Market Share by Airline 
The analysis of historical market share by passenger airline and/or airline segment provides insight into the 
recent history of the main carriers at the airport, including shifting shares between new model airline (NMA) 
and legacy carrier segments. The allocation of traffic between NMA and legacy segments is an important 
consideration from both a physical planning and financial feasibility perspective. NMAs typically exhibit higher 
utilization, require fewer amenities, and place a significant emphasis on their costs (including airport costs). 
2.2.3.5 Historical Air Cargo Tonnage 
Air cargo is shipped in three ways: 
1. In the cargo compartment, or belly, of passenger aircraft; 
2. On all-cargo aircraft (freighters); and 
3. In “combi” aircraft (where the main deck is shared between passengers and cargo). 
Most passenger airlines accommodate air cargo as a by-product to the primary activity of carrying 
passengers. They fill belly space in their aircraft that would otherwise be empty. The incremental cost of 
carrying cargo in a passenger aircraft is negligible and includes only ground handling expenses and a modest 
increase in fuel consumption. 
Road and sea substitution have become major components in the evolution of air cargo activity in recent 
years. At the continental level, trucks have nearly replaced regional air freight service due to cost savings and 
increased efficiency. Truck services have expanded to provide transport of freight to gateway airports for 
consolidation. A number of air carriers also transport cargo by truck to build their own volumes. Many air 
cargo facilities are operating more and more as truck terminals, yet requirements to report truck-to-truck 
tonnage are rare. At the intercontinental level, improved containerization has allowed sea shipments to 
become more competitive in terms of transportation time and reliability. 
To determine historical trends for cargo tonnage at the subject airport, the forecast analyst should compile 
historical cargo tonnage in a time series, displaying domestic and international cargo for belly and freighter 
tonnage separately. It should be noted that cargo volumes are very different from passenger volumes when it 
comes to directionality. Obviously, cargo does not require return flights. Many airports observe very 
imbalanced import/export cargo flows reflecting the mono-directionality of cargo shipments and the nature of 
the local economy.

Factors that may affect aviation demand need to be addressed when developing the passenger, air cargo and 
ATM forecasts. Forecast impact factors could include, but are not limited to: 
e Economic cycles 
° New aircraft types

e Airport initiatives; and 
e Geopolitics 
Other impact factors to consider include seasonal trends and special events that stimulate air travel. It is

assumptions and accuracy of the aviation forecast. A summary discussion should also be included to describe 
the trends and anticipated changes that may affect the development of projections of aviation activity at the 
airport. 
2.2.4 Review of Existing Forecasts 
Before developing models and assumptions for the passenger forecast, it may be valuable to review prior 
forecasts developed for the airport. This is done in order to obtain an understanding of previous forecasting 
efforts, available data, the assumptions made, and the methodology employed. In particular, comparing the 
actual results with the forecast will show its predictive accuracy and validate the methodology used. 
2.2.5 Common Forecasting Techniques 
There are a number of approaches and techniques to develop aviation forecasts. The most common 
techniques include: 
e Econometric/regression models 
e Time series/trend analysis 
e Consensus forecasts 
e¢ Market share forecasts; and 
These techniques can be used to develop forecasts at the airport level, at the multi-airport level, or at the 
regional level. Each of these techniques has its own set of advantages and drawbacks, and they may be used 
independently or in combination. The following sub chapters demonstrate appropriate forecasting techniques 
for various uses.

2.2.5.1 Econometric/Regression Model 
On a worldwide scale, demand for passenger air travel (or air cargo) is intrinsically linked to the performance 
of the global economy. By comparison, exogenous shocks such as political turmoil, terrorist attacks, weather￾related disruptions (e.g., hurricanes, volcanic ash clouds), and pandemics tend to have a shorter transitory 
impact on air travel demand. Air travel demand typically increases during periods of economic expansion and 
declines during economic contractions. Due to the strong correlation of air travel (or air cargo) demand with 
economic conditions, econometric or regression modeling is one of the most robust and commonly applied 
aviation forecasting techniques. 
The purpose of an econometric or regression model is to quantify the relationship between a single 
dependent variable (e.g., O&D domestic passenger traffic or international air cargo traffic) and one or more 
independent variables (e.g., per capita income and air fares). 
Econometric forecasting is used to demonstrate how predicted changes in the independent variables would 
affect future traffic. The following steps are used when developing an econometric forecast: 
1. Specify the independent variables for testing; 
Select a statistical model; 
Determine the model's ability to accurately predict historical values; 
Evaluate combinations of independent variables in context of historical traffic patterns; 
Use the model to derive forecast traffic values; 
Evaluate the results in the context of historical traffic patterns; 
NO 97 F WO ND 
Introduce adjustments to the forecasts to reflect anticipated changes in the airport environment (e.g., 
regulation, competition, airline strategies); and 
1. Specify Independent Variables 
Prior to selecting a model, the forecaster must determine what combination of independent variables should 
be considered in the forecast. 
Use of airfares or airline yields in econometric models on air passengers or cargo should be handled with 
caution. As these variables represent the price in a market, they are not independent of the regression's 
dependent variable (quantity of passengers/cargo) because they suffer from simultaneity (i.e., price affecting 
quantity demanded and quantity supplied affecting price). Therefore, typical ordinary least squares (OLS) 
regression models may produce inconsistent and misleading results. If a forecasting model with airfares or 
yields is desired, more advanced econometric models such as two-stage least squares may be preferred. 
These econometric techniques can produce unbiased and consistent statistical estimates, but require 
additional data to complete properly and careful understanding of the models to ensure that the results are 
reliable. 
36 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 56===
Se & IATA Pull Forecasting 
2. Select a Statistical Model 
There are many kinds of econometric or regression models. Common types are expressed either in linear or 
log-log format. 
The forecast analyst may develop multiple models to forecast different segments of traffic (e.g. domestic 
versus international, visitor versus resident, length of haul, or world region) in order to apply a targeted set of 
independent variables. 
3. Determine Model's Ability to Accurately Predict Historical Values 
The calculated predicted output of the regression model can be charted against the actual historical values for 
the dependent variable to provide a visual of how well the model predicts actual traffic. There are alsoa 
number of statistical outputs that the forecast analyst should check when developing an econometric model to 
ensure its robustness: 
4. Evaluate Combinations of Independent Variables in Context of Historical Traffic Patterns 
Econometric modeling is an iterative process and a variety of independent variables may need to be tested 
and results reviewed before a model equation is settled upon. The goal is not necessarily to get the model 
with the best statistical fit, but to provide a model that is defensible based on a logical set of input 
assumptions (independent variables) and an overall understanding of the drivers of passenger demand at the 
subject airport. 
5. Use Model to Derive Forecast Traffic Values 
By entering the predicted values for the independent variables into the model (e.g., GDP and fare forecasts), 
the forecaster will derive the forecasted passenger traffic. 
6. Compare with Benchmark Forecasts 
As a final step to ensure the forecasts are reasonable, benchmark or other existing forecasts can be used as 
a comparison to confirm the projected growth is realistic. 
7. Introduce Adjustments to the Forecasts to Reflect Anticipated Changes in the Airport 
Environment 
The airport forecaster should critically review the ability of the forecasting model to reflect anticipated changes 
in the airport business environment. Regulation, airline strategies, airport competition and modal competition 
are a few of the many changes that may affect the airport future traffic. For instance, open-skies 
implementation or high-speed rail construction are likely not reflected in any forecasting model based on 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 37 

===PAGE 57===
ye @- [lh IATA al Airport Development Reference Manual 
historical observations. The forecast analysis should consider both short-term and long-term factors for 
adjustment. 
Therefore, the airport forecaster will identify and characterize changes that are not factored in the baseline 
traffic projections and study their potential impact in terms of traffic gain or loss compared to the baseline. 
2.2.5.2 Consensus Forecasts 
This approach involves applying aggregate aviation market growth rates developed by a third party (or third 
parties) to the subject airports traffic base. This approach is often used when there is a lack of historical 
information for the subject airport. It is also useful to provide a context or cross-check to validate a subject 
airport's forecast that has been developed using more airport-specific techniques. 
Governments, aviation authorities, non-governmental organizations and aircraft manufactures publish their 
own national and/or regional forecasts for aviation activity, including growth rates for a defined period of time. 
While these forecasts are typically not developed at the airport level, they may provide a consensus outlook 
for aviation activity as a whole for the region where the subject airport is located. 
The U.S. FAA, for example, publishes an annual aerospace forecast that contains forecasts for passengers, 
air cargo, and ATMs for the U.S. as a whole over a twenty-year horizon. The growth rates promulgated in the 
annual forecasts are often used by planners, particularly at small U.S. airports where general aviation is a 
higher percentage of the activity, to provide a guide as to how activity might change at the subject airport. 
Similarly, ACI, Boeing and Airbus publish twenty-year market outlooks for passenger and cargo volumes by 
world region. The growth rates published in these forecasts can be used as a guide as to how aviation 
demand may develop at the subject airport given its location and traffic mix. 
It is important to be prudent when developing a forecast using the consensus forecast method. Industry 
forecasts may be predicting higher growth than is reasonable for the subject airport. The forecast analyst 
should adjust the industry growth rates accordingly when there is a disconnect between industry forecasts 
and historical activity at the airport. 
The Delphi Method is a specific type of consensus forecast whereby a panel of experts is requested to 
provide their views on the future market growth through structured questionnaires. Several rounds of 
questionnaires are sent out. Responses are aggregated and shared anonymously with the panel after each 
round. The experts are invited to adjust their answers in subsequent rounds based on the answers from the 
panel. The Delphi Method seeks to reach the “correct” response through consensus. 
2.2.5.3 Market Share Forecasts 
Market share forecasts project airport activity as a percentage of a larger aggregate forecast (i.e., national-, 
state- or regional-level forecasts). This approach is used when the forecast for the larger market is more 
readily available or easy to produce than for the airport itself. This includes the case of large metropolitan 
areas with multiple airports. 
38 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 58===
B= IATA Forecasting 
The market share for a specific airport can be calculated by taking the historical dataset for a specific period 
and dividing it by the amount of the total market over the same period. If the share of the subject airport has 
exhibited relatively little variation over the historical period, extrapolating this share into the future is a 
reasonable and relatively efficient way of developing a forecast for the subject airport. Equally, if the share 
analysis indicates increasing or decreasing shares of the larger benchmark that are readily explainable, the 
forecast analyst can estimate future changes in market share and apply these to the aggregate level forecast. 
Forecast impact factors, industry trends, and market outlooks should be considered when developing the 
market share forecast. 
2.2.5.4 Trend/Time Series 
Time series analysis projects historical trends into the future using time as the independent variable. As time 
series forecasts are “one-variable” models, they require only the data for the variable to be forecast. 
In general, time series data can be described by trends, seasonal effects and cyclical effects. The first step in 
putting together a time series forecast is to analyze a time series of historical data for the specific market in 
order to determine the growth trend. The easiest procedure for isolating the trend in a time series is to plot the 
historical data in graphic form, on an x and y axis. The traffic data is plotted on the vertical (y) axis. Time, the 
independent variable, is plotted on the horizontal (x) axis. Then a best-fit curve is obtained by minimizing the 
sum of the errors squared. Different curves may be tried to find the best fit, such as linear or exponential. In 
simple forecasts, it is possible to extend this line into the future to estimate future traffic. Growth rates, 
positive or negative, can be calculated from the slope of the line. 
The time series technique is useful for the following situations: 
e When detailed data is not available 
¢ When the financial and technical resources required for a more rigorous forecast are not available 
© When the anticipated growth is expected to be relatively stable; and 
¢ When the operating and economic environment is expected to be relatively stable 
Time series analysis is a relatively expedient forecasting technique and, as such, is commonly used. 
However, one of the major limitations of a time series forecast is that there may be factors that can 
reasonably be expected to affect aviation activity at the subject airport in the future that are not reflected in the 
historical time series. 
2.2.6 Passenger Activity Segmentation and Scenarios 
Once the methodology of the forecast is decided, the assumptions and key findings of the forecast model 
should be described in narrative and tabular formats. For long-term forecasts, the forecaster should use the 
most recent year reported as the base year and focus the report on planning level years, usually in five-year 
increments until the end of the forecast period. For short-term forecasts (less than five years), a forecast 
should be developed for each year.

¢ Domestic O&D 
¢ Domestic transfer 
¢ International O&D 
¢ International transfer; and 
* Other segments relevant to the airport (e.g., transit, regional variations, etc.)

Overlaps/dependencies between segments should be closely studied when summing up the traffic of each 
individual segment. Typically, a strong growth of O&D demand may result in fewer seats for transfer

When analyzing the results of the passenger activity forecast, the airport forecaster should incorporate:

e Market shares for each passenger activity segment

These factors will help explain the outcomes of the forecast and determine which Passenger segments are

2.2.6.2 Passenger Activity Alternative Scenarios 
All forecasts are subject to uncertainty, especially long-term forecasts. Consequently, it is prudent to develop 
alternative scenarios that define the likely upper and lower ranges of potential demand at the subject airport. 
This approach brings flexibility to the planning process and allows stakeholders to assess a range of 
outcomes for an infrastructure program should demand be realized sooner or later than anticipated. 
Assumptions commonly used for optimistic scenarios include: 
e Faster than anticipated economic growth 
e The airport captures increasing market share 
e An airline expands hub service; and 
¢ Lower oil prices result in a decline in air fares stimulating traffic 
The inverse of these assumptions can be used for a low-end scenario. Scenarios that consider a material 
change in the character of the traffic base at the subject airport, such as the transition from an O&D airport to 
a transfer hub, should be developed in a manner that allows planners to evaluate the implications of shifts in 
40 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 60===
Psy 
No IATA * Forecasting 
the individual market segments. Evolving aircraft types is another example of material change that requires 
detailed attention as there may be implications on runway capacity requirements as well as the size and 
number of parking stands. 
Other approaches may be used to reflect uncertainty in airport demand forecasting. The simplest ones are 
“what-if analysis” and “sensitivity analysis”. These approaches estimate the impact of a single event or 
modified assumptions on the baseline traffic projection. More sophisticated methodologies can be used to 
incorporate uncertainties. The main ones are: 
e Prediction intervals 
¢ Distribution fitting and Monte Carlo simulation; and 
e xtrapolation of empirical errors 
2.2.7 Baggage Forecast 
Not all airports process the same amount of baggage per passenger. Checked baggage tends to increase 
when passengers are traveling internationally or for longer periods of time. Leisure travelers tend to check 
more bags than business travelers, even for trips of a similar duration. As a result, the air service and type of 
passenger at the subject airport will have a large effect on total baggage per passenger. The baggage 
forecast should be developed on a case-by-case basis dependent on the airport, its respective air service, 
and the profile of the typical passenger. The amount of checked baggage has decreased over recent years 
due to additional security requirements as well as fees on checked baggage. The amount of checked 
baggage per passenger also tends to vary by world region based on cultural factors. 
Average bags per passenger ratios are most often determined based on final destination. The baggage 
forecast will be developed by multiplying the forecast passenger volumes by the forecast passenger bag 
ratios for the various categories of passenger (i.e., international, domestic, transfer). 
Like determining a catchment area for an airport, using data collected from the airport baggage system, where 
all bag tags are scanned for sortation is the best way to determine the average bags per passenger at the 
airport. And for carry-on baggage, data from x-ray machines at security checks can be used. This may be 
complemented by passenger surveys when necessary. 
Common questions used on passenger surveys to determine passenger bag ratios include: “How many bags 
did you carry on?” and “How many bags did you check?” The results of a passenger survey can be 
segmented by final destination and applied to all passengers at the airport. 
An alternative source for determining average bags per passenger is the ground handlers. Airport planners 
can also use pre-determined bag ratios. These ratios are only suggested to be used for a first draft of the 
baggage forecast when survey data or historical baggage information at the airport is not readily available. 
Exhibit 2.2.7 displays the bag-to-passenger ratios to be used for high-level forecasting purposes.

2.2.8 Air Cargo Activity Forecast 
As discussed in the historical activity chapter, cargo traffic may by carried three ways: 
1. On all-cargo aircraft (freighters) 
2. In “combi” aircraft (in which the main deck is shared between cargo and passengers) 
3. In the belly hold of passenger aircraft 
It is essential to forecast cargo tonnage and cargo aircraft movements to determine the need for physical 
cargo handling facilities as well as aircraft ramp space. 
Like passenger forecasting, when developing a cargo activity forecast, underlying market forces must be 
considered. Elements such as market assessments and economic theory as well the airport's physical 
capabilities and limitations are items to consider during the cargo activity forecasting process. While historical 
air cargo volumes play a key role in defining the economic relationships that will be used to predict future 
growth, broader industry trends, economic analysis, and review of peer forecasts such as those published by 
Boeing, Airbus, IATA, ICAO, and the FAA will also play a role in forecasting future activity. 
The future levels of air cargo traffic and related activity for a particular airport will be affected by various 
supply and demand elements over a specified forecast period. An air cargo activity forecast requires an 
understanding of how these factors have determined activity levels in the past and how changes in those 
factors may affect the future. The forecaster needs to be mindful of how supply and demand characteristics 
produce an aggregate level of cargo and aircraft traffic. The following sub chapter will give insight into what 
elements to consider when developing an air cargo activity forecast. 
2.2.8.1 Air Cargo Supply and Demand 
The demand for air cargo services is driven by the highly diverse needs of shippers and consignees. 
Examples include: 
e The overnight delivery of a document 
* The transport of donor organs to hospitals; and 
¢ The managed distribution of components and products for multi-national high-tech manufacturers 
42 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 62===
ray v 
Se IATA Bull Forecasting 
Some key characteristics that determine air cargo demand are: 
¢ Origin/destination 
e Commodity type and price 
¢ Desired level of service; and 
© Overall shipment size 
Cargo demand for an airport is primarily determined by the location and volume of air commodity production, 
consumption and/or distribution within that airport's catchment area (or market vicinity). The demand for any 
particular airport is also affected by the location, accessibility and competitiveness of alternative airports or 
modes of transport. Economic growth, regional and world trade (imports and exports) and manufacturing 
activity will be the main macro-level drivers for the air cargo demand. 
Factors that have affected the air cargo industry over the past several decades include road and sea 
substitution, e-commerce, manufacturing changes, aircraft technology, and belly cargo capacity. 
2.2.8.2 Cargo Data Analysis 
Airport forecasters should start by determining the historical trends and activity levels associated with 
dedicated freighter and belly traffic individually. During this process, the forecasters consider the supply and 
demand of cargo that affects the airport. Then they determine the forecast method to use by testing several 
different models to get the most accurate results. Once several methods have been evaluated, they compare 
the results with reliable market forecasts. 
2.2.8.3 Cargo Market Forecast Benchmarking 
Cargo activity forecast assumptions should consider broader industry trends, economic analysis, and review 
of peer forecasts such as those published by the FAA, Boeing, and Airbus. A review of cargo industry trends, 
regional market data, and historical shipping patterns will increase the reliability of the results of a cargo 
activity forecast. Several cargo market outlooks can be used for benchmark analysis, including the FAA 
Aerospace Forecast, Boeing Current Market Outlook and Airbus Global Market Forecast, as they are 
reasonable industry forecasts. 
2.2.8.3.1 International Market Forecasts (Boeing/Airbus/Other) 
For airports globally, industry manufacturer forecasts can be used as valuable benchmarking tools. At a 
macro level, manufacturer forecasts such as those made by Boeing and Airbus are helpful in considering 
international volume growth. However, they should only be applied as a means of comparison to airport￾specific forecasts, rather than used as a source for growth rates. The Boeing Current Market Outlook and the 
Airbus Global Market Forecast can be consulted for their assumptions and freighter fleet growth projections. 
These consensus forecasts cargo growth rates and an outlook of future aircraft orders can be used as a 
metric to better understand the potential growth of cargo operations in the future. Regional forecasts are also
