included in the Boeing and Airbus forecasts, projecting cargo growth for specific areas of the world over the 
forecast horizon. On a cautionary note, all industry manufacturer forecasts include an inherent bias towards 
future aircraft demand. 
2.2.8.3.2 Additional Forecasts and Research 
For a near-term global benchmark, IATA develops an annual cargo industry forecast that can be used to 
analyze the latest freight traffic growth expectations for over 3,000 country pairs. This data source includes 
individual assessments of global and regional economic conditions, detailed rankings, and annual projections 
for the next five years. Also included are five-year forecasts for international cargo traffic by region, sub￾region, and country.

¢ Changes in national air cargo security regulations

The results of the cargo forecast should be evaluated to determine whether there are any gaps between the 
airport's historical trends, the cargo forecast assumptions, and the information used for benchmarking 
purposes. When analyzing these variables, it is important to consider the nature of cargo and the potential 
impact factors of the industry. For the purposes of evaluating dedicated cargo facilities and apron areas, the 
total air cargo forecast should be allocated between the cargo handled in dedicated freighter aircraft versus 
the cargo shipped in the belly hold of Passenger aircraft. 
A new regional manufacturing facility or logistics center may also drive growth in air cargo. The opposite of 
these factors would be considered for a low-end scenario. 
The results of the cargo tonnage forecast are used as a basis for total cargo ATMs for an aviation forecast. A 
narrative summary should also be provided detailing the cargo tonnage forecast assumptions and 
methodology. To ensure consistency, the results of a cargo tonnage forecast should be organized on the 
same planning levels as the passenger forecast.

2.2.9 Air Transport Movement Forecast 
The volume (frequency) and type of air transport movements (ATMs) are key drivers of airfield, taxiway, 
apron, and stand requirements at an airport. An ATM is defined as either an aircraft arrival or departure. Total 
ATMs at a given airport are typically defined as the sum of all aircraft arrivals and departures that use the 
airport's runways’. 
Generally, in both the passenger and cargo markets, an increase in aircraft gauge (size) is observed over 
time. The deployment of larger airliners and freighters is a driver for industry cost savings. Therefore, it is 
often observed that ATMs increase at a slower pace than passenger and cargo volumes. 
2.2.9.1 ATM Segments 
In order to provide an ATM forecast that readily facilitates the evaluation of existing and future airport facility 
requirements, it is recommended that the ATM forecast be developed by key operational category: 
e Commercial Passenger 
e¢ Commercial Freighter or All-cargo 
e General Aviation; and 
e Military 
e Total 
ATM forecasts will be developed separately for each segment; therefore, historical trends will need to be 
analyzed in the same manner. A time series should be developed for historical ATM volumes in each 
category. 
2.2.9.2 Passenger ATMs 
Passenger ATM forecasts are typically derived from the passenger forecast. Indeed, the aggregate number of 
commercial passenger movements at an airport depends on three factors: 
e Total passengers 
e Average aircraft size 
° Average load factor (percent of seats occupied)® 
Total ATMs reported by an airport operator may include overflights and helicopter traffic that use the airport's airspace but do not use 
the airport's runway or taxiway infrastructure. Care should be taken to exclude these traffic components as necessary when evaluating 
existing or future airfield requirements. 
° 
While airfines measure load factors as a function of revenue passenger miles (RPMs) and available seat miles (ASMs), for airport 
planning a ratio of actual passengers to actual capacity load factor is preferred as it provides a more accurate measure of throughput 
through the airport's facilities. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 45 

===PAGE 65===
aS 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
The relationship is shown in the following equation: 
Total Passengers 
Average Load Factor * Average Aircraft Size 
ATMs = 
This equation permits a multitude of combinations of load factors and average aircraft size to accommodate a 
given number of passengers. These varying combinations may be developed across different traffic sectors 
(domestic vs. international), travel segments (long-haul vs. short-haul) or by airline or airline grouping to meet 
the needs of the forecast. 
In the absence of load factor and average aircraft size information, the forecast analyst can use passenger 
per movement assumptions to derive an ATM forecast from the passenger volume forecast. This is essentially 
a one-step approach that combines the load factor and aircraft size assumptions in one metric. 
2.2.9.2.1 Key Passenger ATM Segments 
The basic approach to deriving the passenger movements forecast is essentially the same at all airports. The 
underlying assumptions at each airport, however, are inherently different due to the differences in how airlines 
choose to serve the demand for air travel to, from, and over each airport. These differences may result, for 
example, from: 
¢ Astrategic focus on unit revenue versus unit costs 
* An emphasis on a hub-and-spoke system versus a point-to-point operation 
¢ The business model (new model versus network airline); and 
* The airport's geographic location relative to other markets 
Further segmentation of the passenger ATM forecasts is recommended in order to provide a more refined 
ATM forecast and associated fleet mix. The segments to be analyzed will need to be determined by the 
forecast analyst on a case-by-case basis. The following segments provide an example of the potential ATM 
segments an analyst may consider as part of developing a passenger ATM forecast. 
Domestic versus International ATMs 
In most aviation markets the domestic segment tends to be made up of a higher percentage of narrow-body 
and regional aircraft while the international segment tends to have a higher concentration of wide-body 
aircraft. A relatively straightforward division of ATMs into domestic and international segments will allow an 
analyst to consider growth expectations at the segment level and develop the associated average aircraft size 
and load factor assumptions. 
46 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 66===
ae } IATA Forecasting 
Length of Haul/Geographic Region 
This is an extension of the domestic and international segmentation. The distance of down-line markets from 
the subject airport are one of the determining factors in the type of aircraft deployed. By segmenting ATMs by 
length of haul or by geographic region, the results may show greater consistency in the fleet mix that may 
otherwise be masked by a less disaggregated approach. For example, in the United States, there has been a 
significant reduction in domestic short-haul flights (less than 500 miles). These markets have typically been 
served by small regional jets (35-50 seats) and turboprop aircraft. By allocating less activity to the short-haul 
segment, the forecast can naturally de-emphasize these aircraft types and drive a higher overall average 
aircraft size. There are always interesting exceptions to many broad rules. For example, the Sydney￾Melbourne market is less than 450 miles apart, however, the significant passenger demand in the market 
results in high-frequency wide-body aircraft being deployed on the route. 
Network Carrier versus New Model Airline 
Network carriers tend to have more diverse fleet mixes than new model airlines (NMAs) which historically 
have operated relatively homogenous narrow-body jet fleets. The growth in NMA activity has been a critical 
driver of activity at airports around the globe, particularly in the last decade. From a forecasting perspective, 
segmentation by airline business model allows for more targeted assumptions to be made based on the 
segment of activity that is expected to drive growth in the future. From a facility planning perspective, NMAs 
may need more basic terminal facilities and fewer terminal amenities than their network counterparts. NMAs 
may also make higher utilization of their stands than network carriers which may have slower aircraft turn 
times. NMAs may also time flights to meet banks at down-line hubs. 
Average Aircraft Size and Passenger Load Factor Assumptions 
Once the key passenger ATM segments have been identified, there are a number of micro and macro 
sources that can assist in the development of average seats per flight assumptions at a given airport. 
Third-Party Aircraft Databases 
There are a number of companies that maintain aircraft inventory databases including aircraft orders and 
retirements. These can be expensive, so the cost must be balanced against the needs of the project. 
General Considerations 
Understanding historical and potential future air service and aircraft trends at an airport is critical to 
developing defensible measures of average seats per passenger flight as inputs to the passenger ATM 
forecast. 
The second step in developing the passenger ATM forecast is to develop load factor assumptions for each of 
the passenger ATM segments. Load factors in the past five or six years have generally trended upwards as 
airlines have made better use of their aircraft assets. The forecast should try to reflect load factor trends for 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 47 

===PAGE 67===
= 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
the subject airport and the key markets it serves. The forecast must consider if there is potential for further 
growth in load factors prior to airlines either adding frequency or increasing average aircraft size. 
Once the average aircraft size and load factor assumptions have been developed, the passenger ATM 
forecast can be derived based on the formula shown in 2.2.9.2 Passenger ATMs. 
2.2.9.2.2 Passenger Aircraft Fleet Mix 
For purposes of physical planning at an airport, the passenger ATM forecast can be further disaggregated into 
fleet mix categories. A typical requirement is to develop the ATM forecast by aircraft groups. Airports outside 
of the United States typically group aircraft based on ICAO categories. U.S. airports group aircraft by Airplane 
Design Group (ADG) per FAA standards. 
More detailed planning forecast exercises, environmental forecasts, or forecasts that have a simulation 
component may require ATM forecasts down to the level of aircraft make and model. 
A top-down approach should be employed to allocate the results of the movements forecast to the defined 
fleet mix categories. The fleet mix should be developed to match the aggregate average aircraft size and load 
factor targets. 
2.2.9.3 Freighter ATM Forecast 
The freighter ATM forecast is typically derived from the associated freighter tonnage forecast based on 
tonnage per movement assumptions. The freighter tonnage per movement implicitly reflects both the size of 
the aircraft and the associated load factor. 
Similar to the passenger ATM forecast, the freighter ATM forecast should be developed based on a blend of: 
* Historical analysis to understand the mix of freighter airlines at the subject airport 
e Freighter business models 
© Aircraft fleet mix 
¢ Forward looking aircraft orders; and 
¢ Cargo industry trends 
Cargo load factors can be estimated based on specific aircraft or the average payload of freighter movements 
anticipated at a given airport. Cargo load factors can be a useful statistic when determining how much 
additional cargo the freighter aircraft at a given airport can accommodate before adding frequency or 
increasing average aircraft size. However, cargo load factors should be used with caution for the following 
Teasons: 
¢ The capacity of a freighter aircraft is dictated not only by weight, but also by volume. For example, a 
freighter aircraft full of flowers will result in a significantly different tonnage per flight metric than a freighter 
full of steel ball bearings. Consequently, weight-based load factors can be misleading

===PAGE 68===
ray 
Se_i—Ci* A 
IATA Forecasting 
¢ Cargo flows are often imbalanced. For example, a 65 percent cargo load factor on a route between 
Shanghai and the United States may represent full freighter flights from Shanghai to the United States, 
but half empty flights on the way back 
e Awide-body aircraft may only unload a portion of its total load at a given airport before heading to another 
destination. This type of routing results in a relatively low tonnage per flight metric at the subject airport 
and may lead the forecast analyst to defer adding frequencies if the multi-segment routing is not 
understood 
Once the tonnage per freighter movement assumptions have been developed, they can be applied to the all￾cargo tonnage forecast to derive all-cargo ATMs. A top-down approach can be used to determine a more 
detailed aircraft fleet mix. Similar to the passenger ATM forecast, grouping the fleet mix into FAA or ICAO 
design groups is recommended as a minimum step for physical planning studies. 
2.2.9.4 General Aviation ATM Forecast 
Expert judgment often goes into making general aviation (GA) forecasts due to reliance on national trends, 
forecasts and, to the extent such are available, local historical records. GA activity typically includes all ATMs 
that are not included in commercial passenger, commercial freighter, or military/government movements. GA 
activity includes diverse uses that can range from: 
e Fractional jet operators 
¢ WIP (very, very important person) aircraft 
¢ On-demand air taxi flights 
e Recreational flying 
e Flight training activities 
¢ Business travel 
e News reporting 
¢ Traffic observation 
e Police patrol 
« Emergency medical flights; and 
e Crop dusting 
Understanding the history and current state of the GA industry can help predict future aviation demand. The 
following sub-chapters discuss how to develop a general aviation forecast while considering nationwide 
historical, emerging, and forecast trends.

2.2.9.4.1_ Emerging Trends 
When developing movement forecasts, it is essential to consider historical, national, and emerging trends in 
the general aviation market. Similar to the aviation activity from the passenger and cargo segments, GA is 
influenced by the overall health of the economy. The forecaster should consider the influence of local 
business, tourism, and other economic activity on general aviation activity as well as the influence of various 
socioeconomic and demographic characteristics. 
Changes in fuel prices impact the economic relationships between modes of transportation and the price 
differentials between different segments of the aviation market. Although fuel prices are a major problem for 
the commercial airlines, corporate GA users are less sensitive to changes in fuel prices. Given the cost to 
own and operate a corporate aircraft or to charter a business jet, the incremental cost of fuel is typically a 
secondary consideration. 
The concept of fractional ownership in general aviation aircraft has significantly contributed to the revitalization 
of the GA manufacturing industry in the 21st century. This concept of purchasing hours of jet time has 
encouraged more general aviation activity, allowing more people to have access to GA aircraft. 
Regions that are sparsely populated, isolated and/or poorly served by surface modes will tend to have higher 
GA activity. 
2.2.9.4.2 GA Forecast 
Historical GA activity data should be reviewed and organized to identify significant characteristics, the local 
and itinerant mix, and the fleet mix of airport-based aircraft over the Planning period. For all airports, the GA 
forecast should be further guided by discussions from the fixed-base operators (FBOs), flight training 
academies and other factors at the subject airport that may impact GA activity. 
The first step in developing a GA forecast is to organize the historical data in tabular format by distributing the 
total general aviation movements into aircraft segments (i.e., turbo jet, turbo prop, piston, helicopter, etc.) if 
available. This distribution will display historical trends and set-up the groundwork for the GA fleet mix. 
The next step is to select a forecasting approach that makes the most sense for the airport (i.e., econometric, 
trend, or market share). Once the methodology has been developed, the forecaster should apply the forecast 
results over a time series. Based on research of historical, national, and emerging GA trends, the next step is 
to develop the fleet mix based on this analysis. Explanations should be provided if major changes from 
historic trends are expected in the future. 
The projections of GA activity should be prepared for the forecast planning horizons along with projections of 
the airport-based aircraft fleet mix for the same horizons. To determine the activity level required between 
these planning horizons, interpolate the data as needed.

2.2.9.4.3 VVIP Aircraft Activity 
It is important to remember that not all airports are the same when developing a general aviation forecast. A 
key segment that may affect some airports is often called VVIP, or “very, very important person” activity. 
WIPs are most commonly royalty or political figures. Airports with VVIP activity often have a private apron 
and/or an exclusive FBO associated with this traffic. Although VVIP service is not common at most airports, it 
is significant to keep this type of activity in mind when developing a general aviation forecast. 
2.2.9.5 Military/Government ATM Forecast 
Historical military/government aviation activity should be identified using airport statistics. Work with airport 
management and staff who are in contact with representatives of the military to have a better understanding 
of the expected future levels of military and government activity. Often, military movements are limited and/or 
secretive, and therefore hard to forecast. 
2.2.9.6 Total ATM Forecast 
The total movements forecast should be derived by adding all the ATM forecasts described above. An overall 
tabular format of total movements should be created displaying each category as well as total movements, 
including compound annual growth rates. The results from each segment of the movements forecast will be 
used for the peak period analysis described in detail in the next chapter. 
2.2.10 Peak Period Forecast 
Traffic demand at an airport is subject to seasonal, monthly, daily, and hourly variations. These variations 
result in peak periods when the greatest amount of demand is placed upon facilities required to accommodate 
passenger and aircraft movements. Peaking characteristics are critical in the assessment of existing and 
planned facilities to determine their ability to accommodate forecast increases in passenger and operational 
activity throughout the study period. The objective of developing peak period forecasts is to ensure planned 
facilities are neither underutilized nor overcrowded too often. Exhibit 2.2.10 illustrates a distribution of active 
hours at a specific airport ranked from busiest to quietest over a period of one year. Typically, the selected 
design hour will not be the absolute busiest hour, but rather some measure of a typical peak that covers most 
of the year while excluding the extreme busy periods. The outcome of a peak period selection will result on a 
design rate and not a specific period of time. Therefore, the use of design rate is used to represent that traffic 
level. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 51 

===PAGE 71===

IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
Exhibit 2.2.10: Hourly Passenger Demand Ranked in Decreasing Order Over the Year 
iest Hour 
Typical Busy Hour 
Source: Airport Research Center 
Passenger peak period forecasts will usually cover the design rates for total, arriving, and departing 
Passengers, as well as other elements of traffic mix (e.g., domestic, international, transfer). This is necessary 
because of the different facility requirements associated with each of these traffic elements. The different 
design rates should be analyzed separately in accordance with the methodology described in the following 
subsection for each specific traffic segment. Therefore, ranking of the hours of the year should be conducted 
for each of the traffic segments that will be required as part of the planning exercise. 
To determine the current representative design rate, it is necessary to evaluate historical design rate activity 
for each required segment. Historical data should be obtained covering the annual traffic and the traffic during 
the representative design rate. It is recommended that the dataset has several data points from multiple years 
and all the passenger segments driving facilities’ requirements. 
The departure design rate determines requirements for facilities such as check-in, security screening, and 
gate hold rooms. Arriving peaks drive functional elements such as immigration, baggage claim, and greeter 
requirements. The total peak may drive overall circulation, concessions, and restroom requirements. It is 
important to note that these peaks can be distinct, occurring at different times of the day as a function of 
airline scheduling practices, the role of the airport in the regional or national system, and geography. 
Depending on the airport and scope of the forecast, further disaggregation of peak hour activity may be 
required: 
e By multiple terminals 
¢ Per individual subsystems 
ATM peak period forecasts will focus on total, arrivals, departures, international, domestic and possibly other 
service types. In addition, planners may also require forecasts for maximum number of aircraft on the ground 
for stand and gate planning.

The following sections provide guidance and recommendations to obtain the necessary traffic information 
airport planners will need during facility requirements planning stages, focusing on how to: 
e Analyze and select the design rate 
e Forecast the historical design rates into the future 
e Develop design day flight schedules 
2.2.10.1 Selection of the Design Rate Definition 
The following subsections provide an overview of the most common ways to measure peak traffic. These 
methods form the basis of forecasting future peak demand (See 2.2.10.2 Deriving Design Rate Forecasts 
from Annual Forecasts). Some of the approaches are used and/or imposed by the local civil aviation 
authorities. These are also presented for reference. Critical to any of the measures of peak traffic is to select 
a peak rate that is not necessarily the absolute peak traffic volume in a year, but rather a peak rate that is 
representative of busy periods rarely exceeded throughout the year. Planning for the absolute peak could 
result in infrastructure that is impractically designed and oversized to meet a level of traffic that is rarely 
observed. 
From the 12" edition of the ADRM, IATA has decided to change its recommendation on the peak demand 
definition. This change has been made following an in-depth analysis of the peak structures of more than 400 
airports globally. The main finding from the study was, given its very nature, the previous |ATA Busy Day 
definition was resulting in some inconsistencies when applied at airports with different demand distributions 
(or even at the same airport in different years). While the previous definition has been in use for many years 
in a wide range of airport projects, the new recommendation would result in a more consistent set of results 
and easier to understand decision-making by airports, authorities, regulatory agencies and any other relevant 
stakeholders involved in airport planning activities. 
2.2.10.1.1 Design Hour Rate (IATA Recommendation) 
The Design Hour Rate (DHR) is the new definition proposed and recommended by IATA as the primary 
methodology for selecting the relevant design peak demand. It ensures there is greater certainty in the ratio of 
passengers that the facilities will be able to accommodate at an optimum level of service (or higher). 
In general terms, IATA recommends facilities be designed to ensure a predefined percentage of passengers 
using the facility will experience the selected level of service. IATA recommends using a rate that ensures the 
passenger flow during the DHR is higher than the traffic flow during hours adding up to 97-99% of total annual 
passengers. 
The proposed 97-99% range is a recommendation and could be adjusted by the forecaster to accommodate 
specific airport circumstances and business requirements. In general terms, when the traffic segments 
analyzed have annual volumes larger than 10 million passengers (MPAX), selecting a percentage value in the 
upper end of the proposed range may be more appropriate. For very large traffic segments (>40 MPAX), 
forecasters may want to consider analyzing values above the proposed range. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 53 

===PAGE 73===
ue Se 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
To determine the DHR, the hourly data must be ranked in order of passenger volume. Starting with the hour 
with the least volume, the traffic numbers should be added until the cumulative figure reaches X% of the 
annual traffic. The passenger volume of that particular hour is the DHR that should be used for further 
forecasting of future peak levels. This analysis is conducted on the scheduled time of operation using clock 
hours. 
The cumulative approach described above must be undertaken separately for each of the traffic segments 
that need to be forecasted (i.e., departures, arrivals, transfer, international, domestic, etc.). 
While it is recommended each airport conduct specific analysis to understand the suitability of the specific 
percentage recommendation, the following table provides an indication of average equivalence between the 
hour ranking and the percentage for different airport sizes. The table below has been produced with the 
findings from a study conducted by IATA analyzing the traffic patterns and distribution of 500 airports. 
Exhibit 2.2.10.1.1: Hour Ranking Equivalence with Percentage Figure 
0 to 1 MPAX per year 10 21 32 
1 to 2 MPAX per year 13 28 44 
2 to 5 MPAX per year 22 46 72 
5 to 10 MPAX per year 25 53 80 
10 to 40 MPAX per year 35 73 96

2.2.10.1.2 Other Design Definitions 
While IATA recommends using the DHR definition for the selection of the relevant hourly peak periods, it must 
be noted that other standards have been applied in the industry that may still be relevant in some jurisdictions 
and planning exercises. The methodologies described below are conceptually very similar to the proposed 
approach but focus on different elements. 
(a) Definitions Based on Hour Ranking 
The definitions based on hour ranking can be calculated differently based on airport operator requirements. 
The more common use approaches use either the 30" or the 40" highest hour of passenger flow. To 
determine the hour ranking, the hourly data must be ranked in order of magnitude. The Xth busiest hour is 
then identified as the design hour. 
54 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 74===
ae | ; 
IATA * Forecasting 
(b) Definitions Based on Selecting a Design Day 
While IATA recommends the DHR to be used for the selection of the design rate, it must be noted, in some 
instances (i.e., developing DDFS and day scenarios/measurements), there might be a need to choose a 
specific day of the year to be used as the basis for future projections. The two methodologies listed below are 
the two most widely used to provide guidance that could be used when there is a need to choose a specific 
design day. 
It should be noted that the use of these definitions will have its limitations and require a thorough review of all 
historical data. The analysis of the peak structures and patterns using the previously described methodology 
will need to be reflected in a design day. The selected design day should be a good representation of the 
typical peak hour structures for the different traffic segments. Multiple design days may need to be considered 
for detailed planning stages. 
Busy Day 
This methodology defines the design day, or busy day, as the second busiest day in an average week during 
the peak month. To determine the average week, the monthly passengers or movements are divided by the 
number of weeks in the peak month, or are divided by the number of days of the month and multiplied by 
seven. The seven-day period (Monday through Sunday) that is closest to an average week is selected and 
the second busiest day of the week during that period is identified. 
While this methodology has been observed to produce widely inconsistent results when used to select peak 
hours, it can be useful in selecting a design day. 
Average Day of the Peak Month 
FAA guidance suggests using the peak hour of the average day in the peak month for purposes of physical 
planning; typically referred to as the average day of the peak month (ADPM). The FAA recommends three to 
five years of historical data be analyzed to determine the typical peak month at the subject airport. The peak 
month to be selected is the month representing the highest percentage of total annual activity. The average 
day is determined by dividing the peak month's activity by the total number of days in that month. The ADPM 
is the day that most closely represents the average day in the peak month. 
2.2.10.2 Deriving Design Rate Forecasts from Annual Forecasts 
Once the historical design rate has been determined, forecasters will inevitably have to determine how the 
design rate for each relevant traffic segment is going to evolve in the future and establish a clear design rate 
forecast. 
It is very common that forecasts of design rate passengers and aircraft movements are derived in some 
manner from annual forecasts. This often involves the application of some sort of methodology to convert 
annual passenger and ATM forecasts into forecasts of busy period traffic. Depending on the requirements of 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 55 

===PAGE 75===
ray 
Se | IATA pu Airport Development Reference Manual 
the project and availability of data, all the necessary flows and segments (e.g., departure, arrivals, domestic, 
international, by terminal) can be analyzed and forecast in this manner. 
A useful too! for this analysis is the application of the design ratio, defined as the ratio of design hour traffic to 
annual traffic. This can be developed by analyzing current and historical annual and design rate traffic, and 
then this ratio can be forecast into the future. 
A commonly observed finding is that the peak ratio declines as annual traffic volumes increase (see 
Exhibit 2.2.10.2) using historical data. As annual traffic volumes increase, the ratio declines rapidly at first, but 
slows as the airport gets larger. This is reflective of peak spreading as traffic at the airport develops. 
Exhibit 2.2.10.2: Peak Hour Ratio as a Function of Annual Passenger Volumes 
Peak Hour Ratio (Peak Hour Passengers / (Average Day Passengers) 
Millions 
Source: ADP Ingénierie 
This peak spreading can be explained as follows: 
* Atsmaller airports, the daily demand profile can be concentrated around a few peak times (at a minimum, 
one for arrival and one for departure), with long periods with very limited or even no demand. Peaks will 
occur at times that are most convenient and attractive for passengers (depending on several factors, 
including type of traffic and geographical position), such as at the beginning and end of day for business 
travel. Therefore, the design hour ratio for these “peaky” daily profiles will be rather high, as most of their 
average daily traffic happens around the peaks. 
* Atlarger airports, or as traffic grows, the daily demand profile can become more evenly distributed, 
usually with multiple arrival/departure peaks during the day, preceded and followed by “shoulder” periods, 
where demand tends to increase/decrease gradually to/from the peaks, and can achieve almost the same 
56 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 76===
IATA * Forecasting 
traffic levels. Peak periods could last for multiple consecutive hours, depending on the nature of traffic, 
and could come in multiple waves (arrival peaks followed by departure peaks). Periods with very limited to 
no demand tend to be rarer at larger airports, as the natural demand tends to spread along the day. Less 
convenient times tend to fill in as the catchment area served by the airport grows in its attractiveness and 
the peaks possibly arrive at capacity, generating longer peaks with even longer shoulders. The design 
hour ratio for these daily profiles will, therefore, be lower than in smaller airports. 
Therefore, the relationship between the design rate and annual traffic can provide an indication as to how 
future peak period traffic may evolve once the annual traffic forecast has been established. However, it should 
be noted that other important factors besides the size of the airport may impact the development of design 
rate traffic and need to be accounted for. A non-exhaustive list of some of the most important factors is as 
follows: 
© Specificity of airline operations: The different types of traffic that an airport is welcoming (e-g., transfer 
vs. O&D, low-cost carrier (LCC) vs. full-service carrier (FSC), hub operations for a large carrier vs. 
multiple carriers sharing similar portions of the market) will have an important impact on the design rate 
development. An airport's traffic type could generate different peak ratios than those of other airports of 
similar size but different traffic nature. 
* Airport operating hours: Airport working hours could have an impact on the peak periods, as well as the 
less busy period, depending on the type of traffic welcomed at the airport. Operating hours or curfews of 
key destinations/markets can also have an impact on the peak structure for some airports. 
¢ Constrained capacity : Airports with constrained capacities (e.g., slot-controlled airports) could impose a 
maximum hourly number of operations/passengers during peak periods, changing the shape of the daily 
demand and potentially filling the shoulders more rapidly than at airports of similar size. Similarly, a 
constrained airport that receives new capacity can see its peaks change in ways that historic data does 
not capture (e.g., peaks rise rapidly to fill the new capacity). 
e Environmental constraints: Similar to capacity constraints, environmental restrictions (e.g., noise 
restrictions) could limit hourly capacity during certain hours of the day, including curfews where certain 
movements could be prohibited. 
¢ Seasonality of demand for a particular destination: Airports in certain regions may be subject to high 
levels of seasonality concentrating large parts of the annual traffic during specific weeks or months of the 
year, resulting in larger than expected hour-to-annual ratios. 
For these reasons, it is recommended to run a detailed analysis of the recent historical data, where possible, 
which will allow the planner to better understand the traffic behavior and confirm the different relationships 
between peak hour demand and annual demand for each relevant traffic segment, and what trends or factors 
have the largest influence in those ratios. It is important to also consider factors and traffic drivers in the future 
that may impact the development of design rate traffic that are not reflected in the historical data. 
2.2.10.2.1 Methodological Approaches 
The discussion above illustrates the complexity of forecasting design rate traffic from forecasts of annual 
traffic. There is no single approach that works for all airports. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 57 

===PAGE 77===
Be 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
The following subsection discusses general approaches and good practice for the development of design rate 
forecasts. 
(a) Modeling the Relationship with Annual Traffic 
As described above, there is a commonly observed relationship between annual traffic and the design rate 
ratio. This can be analyzed for the individual airport using historical data, if available. With sufficient data, a 
mathematical relationship between annual traffic and the design rate ratio can be estimated using line fitting 
software available in most spreadsheets and statistical packages. However, this approach may not be 
possible for a number of reasons: 
¢ Insufficient data was collected in previous years to conduct statistical analysis. 
¢ The analysis is for a greenfield airport, so no data is available. In some cases, however, data from the 
airport it is replacing or augmenting can be used. 
¢ The airport has experienced limited growth (e.g., it is capacity constrained); therefore, there is little 
variation in the data. 
One workaround for these factors is to also analyze data from benchmark airports that share similar 
characteristics as the study airport. For example, airports of similar size, traffic mix, and geographic location 
(although some variation in size is needed to establish the relationship). 
As noted, while the analysis of the relationship with annual traffic is useful, it is important to consider other 
factors and future drivers of traffic and make appropriate adjustments to the forecasts. The forecaster may 
include adjustments if changes are foreseen to impact the future traffic pattern. Examples of impactful 
changes include: 
* Sudden evolution in the airline mix (LCC/FSC) 
¢ Change in the connecting banks by the based carrier 
¢ Increase in the capacity of the airport 
58 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 78===
we 
IATA Forecasting 
In instances when extensive historical data is not available or not appropriate to use, a reasoned approach to 
forecasting the development of the design rate ratio can be applied. For example, this could involve breaking 
the ratio down as follows: 
Peak Month x Peak Day x Peak Hour 
Annual Peak Month Peak Dayr Design Rate Ratio = 
Each of these component ratios can be considered in turn to generate the final peak period ratio. For 
example, the peak month/year ratio could decline if the airport in question serves a highly seasonal tourist 
destination that is investing in developing an out-of-season product. An airport that has high traffic only on 
certain days (e.g., weekend traffic) may be seeking to develop traffic on other days, lowering the peak 
day/month ratio, and so on. Applications of these ratios will result in forecast peak period traffic that 
incorporates various assumptions about traffic development at the airport. 
(b) Bottom-Up Approaches 
An alternative, or supplementary, approach to ratio modeling is a bottom-up approach considering which 
flights may be added at peak periods. This can involve examining the flights and passenger flows operating in 
the current identified peaks and assessing which flights might be expected to be added to this period given 
the outlook from the annual forecasts. For example, for a tourist airport where peaks are generated by 
seasonal charter flights, the forecaster might want to consider if the additional traffic forecasts for the airport 
will be of a similar nature with similar time of day requirements or whether the traffic will be from other time 
zones or carrier types (e.g., network carriers) that may prefer other times of day. Similarly, are carriers likely 
to up-gauge their aircraft in the peak periods? 
This approach is easiest for smaller airports dealing with relatively few flights in the peak period. For larger 
airports, the number of flights can be considerable, adding to the complexity of the analysis. Nevertheless, 
this approach can be an instructive method for generating or validating realistic and reasoned forecasts of 
peak traffic. 
(c) Traffic Segmentation 
As noted previously, forecast of design rate traffic for different segments may be required (e.g., arrivals and 
departures, domestic and international, O&D, connecting). In some instances, it may be possible to model 
each segment separately by analyzing the relationship between the design rate ratio and annual traffic for 
each segment (¢.g., the relationship between the domestic peak and domestic annual traffic). However, this 
may not always be possible or even desirable. An alternative approach is to consider the relationship between 
different peaks, for example, the ratio between the arrivals peak and the two-way total peak, or between the 
O&D peak and the total peak. Consideration can be given to how this ratio might change over the forecast 
period. Will it remain the same or change as traffic develops? 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 59 

===PAGE 79===
=e IATA piu Airport Development Reference Manual 
(d) Aircraft Movement and Passenger Flows 
Typically, forecasts are required for peak aircraft operations and peak passengers flow to quantify different 
facility design requirements. While these peaks sometimes occur at the same time, this is not always the case 
since passenger peaks can be driven by use of large aircraft and/or aircraft with high load factors and/or large 
numbers of smaller aircraft. Therefore, if forecasts for both peak aircraft operations and peak passengers flow 
are required, analysis and forecasting may need to be carried out for each separately always keeping in mind 
there is a close relationship. 
(e) Cross-Checking and Sensitivity Tests 
In developing the design rate forecasts, especially when a large number of separate segments are required, 
care needs to be taken to ensure the resulting forecasts are consistent and logical; examples include: 
Is the forecast design rate ratio more than or equal to 1/365 x 1/operating hours per day? A value lower 
than this, which can happen with some modeling approaches, would result in a peak hour lower than the 
average hour in the day. 
ls the relationship between passenger and aircraft movement peaks logical? If the two peaks occur at the 
same time, it would be expected that they rise in a similar manner (allowing for higher passenger loads). If 
they occur at separate times, is there a plausible logic to how these peaks grow relative to each other? Is 
there a historical trend between passengers and ATMs that can be identified? Does it match the known 
airline fleet modernization plans? 
Is the relationship between various segment peaks logical and consistent? For example, how do the 
peaks for O&D and connecting traffic compare? Are they consistent with anticipated air carrier 
development and the growth in overall peaks? 
Benchmarking the peaks against other comparable airports. In this context, a comparable airport would 
be an airport located in the same region, with an annual traffic volume comparable to the considered 
planning activity level of the airport to forecast and a traffic mix (domestic/international, FSC/LCC, 
O&D/transfer) similar to the airport to forecast. If the actual peak hour traffic is not available for the 
comparable airport(s), the forecaster will use the airline schedules (available in commercial datasets) to 
estimate the peak hour seats and apply an estimated load factor to derive passengers. 
To what extent do certain assumptions significantly change the peak forecasts and do these need to be 
further validated. 
2.2.10.3 Design Day Flight Schedules (DDFS) 
2.2.10.3.1 Introduction 
The most common result of a traffic forecast usually provides expected annual, daily, and peak hour demand 
figures for aircraft and passengers serving as main input parameters for many airport planning tasks. Traffic 
peaks, often expressed in peak hour figures, are one of the main driving forces for airport capacity and related 
60 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 80===
SS By IATA a Forecasting 
facility requirements for planning and dimensioning. Therefore, peak hour figures are widely used in airport 
capacity calculations and formulas. 
For certain planning tasks, if required, it may be recommended to further refine or define the demand figures 
and develop detailed flight schedules for one or multiple design days. These are often referred to as DDFS. 
Typical use cases of DDFS include: 
In-depth facility requirement studies (strategic, tactical and pre-operational), where timely process 
sequences and dwell times of aircraft and passengers play a significant role (e.g., disposition-dependent 
resources and inter-dependencies of resources). 
¢ Simulations supporting design studies as a “proof of concept” of a planned design under operational 
conditions (design of new facilities and extension or re-organization of existing ones), capacity 
enhancement studies on different types of facilities (airside, terminal and landside) and/or changes in 
operational procedures. 
© Verification and refinement of facility requirements derived from aggregated formulas. In this case, not just 
the peak hour volume is relevant, but also how it is composed according to markets (e.g., LCC, FSC) and 
timely occurrence of traffic levels before/after the peak hour used for dimensioning (check risks for 
accumulation of delay for longer peak periods). 
© Refinement of master plans requiring in-depth facility requirements to test and validate planning 
assumptions. 
© Operational planning and resources allocation strategies. 
e Stand/gate requirements analysis. 
e Capacity saturation studies. 
© Declared capacity for slot coordinated airports. 
© Detailed noise reduction, fuel emissions and other environmental studies. 
2.2.10.3.2 Typical DDFS Attributes and Characteristics 
DDFS aim to provide a detailed view of the traffic forecast regarding the future growth of traffic segments, the 
mix of markets, aircraft fleet mix, and the expected evolution of the hourly operational profile of the airport. 
Alternate versions can be produced to test “what-if” scenarios regarding traffic and peak patterns and support 
sensitivity analyses. 
Flight schedules can be developed on a portion of the day, an entire day, or even longer periods (e.g., full 
design day schedule, two/three-day schedule, one-week schedule, busy period/season schedule, 4-6hr peak 
periods), depending on the studies’ objectives and framework. 
The future flight schedule typically considers several flight attributes for each listed flight. The use case will 
drive the needed attributes to be included on the future schedule. For instance, passenger process 
requirement studies may focus on passenger numbers and types (O&D and transfer) associated with each 
flight, whereas an airside study would typically include flight types (passenger, cargo, general aviation, 
military, positioning and maintenance) and linked ATM (arrival and departure). 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 61 

===PAGE 81===
IATA wull Airport Development Reference Manual 
As a minimum requirement, a DDFS will typically contain the attributes listed below. Depending on the level of 
detail required for the DDFS, more general placeholders might be used for certain attributes as explained in 
later sections of this chapter. 
¢ Airline name (or placeholder for category of airline, such as LCC, FSC) 
e Flight number or another identifier 
° Aircraft type (e.g., B737 or B737-800 or placeholder for aircraft category, such as code or seat capacity) 
e Flight direction (arrival/departure) 
¢ Airport codes of O&D flights (or placeholder for region/market) 
¢ Arrival/Departure time and date (on-block/off-block) 
Additional attributes relevant to airside studies may include: 
¢ Aircraft registration (or identifier if registration is unavailable) to link arrival/departure of ATM 
¢ Flight type (passenger, cargo, GA, military, scheduled/non-scheduled), including specific flights that are 
linked to the scope of the project (e.g., cargo flights for cargo apron planning) 
¢ On-board cargo (for cargo facility planning as well as ground handling operations and facility planning) 
Additional attributes relevant to terminal studies may include: 
° Aircraft seat configuration (seats and load factor to derive a passenger count) 
* On-board passengers split into O&D (local) and transfer 
Additional attributes relevant for baggage handling system (BHS) studies 
e Number of O&D and transfer bags 
2.2.10.3.3 Time Horizons and Areas of Application for a DDFS 
One or several alternate DDFS might be developed for different planning tasks and time horizons (strategic, 
tactical, next-season, pre-operational). 
Typical time horizons for DDFS can be categorized as follows: 
° Short-term (pre-operational or next season): The current schedule is a good and reliable basis to test 
the impact of additional flights or changed load factors on airport capacity and delay. DDFS for short-term 
planning might be used, for instance, in the context of declared capacity to assess resource demand and 
staffing requirements or for testing changed operational procedures to optimize airport capacity. 
¢ Mid-term tactical planning (1-5-year time horizon): DDFS might be used for detailed facility 
requirement analysis for different traffic segments and detailed terminal design/re-organization, allocation 
strategies and other planning and design tasks. 
62 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 82===
Se &, IATA pull Forecasting 
¢ Long-term strategic master planning (>5/10/20/40-year time horizon): Further out, the future 
schedules will include a high degree of uncertainty; therefore, the level of granularity of the schedule 
should be questioned. It must be kept in mind that a DDFS is just one potential scenario for the future 
traffic situation under consideration. The further the forecast reaches into the future; the more 
uncertainties are involved. Therefore, long-term forecast schedules may include less detail and more 
aggregated placeholders (e.g., airline types, market groups). Additional sensitivity analyses are 
recommended on the key parameters to respond to the main uncertainties. 
2.2.10.3.4 Main Challenges and Limitations of DDFS 
Developing a consistent DDFS is often a complex and time-consuming task. It requires the planner to 
consider many detailed assumptions on a flight-by-flight level of detail as well as the intelligence of potential 
new routes and growth strategies of the airlines. While a DDFS gives a more detailed picture on a flight level 
of a possible future scenario, it does not necessarily mean the prediction of the peak level is more accurate 
compared to simple aggregated peak level considerations. Adding and timely positioning specific aircraft 
movements in a flight schedule opens-up a large variety of possible scenarios. 
The planner requires a broad knowledge of airline strategies, aircraft fleet usage concepts, trends in aircraft 
fleets and their modernization, growth markets, flight ranges/flight times/operating windows at O&D airports, 
and more. Furthermore, the planner requires a thorough understanding of traffic characteristics and peaking 
patterns of the airport in question. In combination with the information provided with the market forecast, the 
planner needs to elaborate a consistent and logical assumption model that can be well understood by airport 
stakeholders. 
Compared to simple and aggregated forecast peak hour figures, a DDFS is the most granular and, therefore, 
the most flexible to use for planning purposes. 
2.2.10.3.5 General Considerations for Future DDFS Development 
There is no single recommended method or prescriptive step-by-step approach to developing a DDFS. 
Aviation experts apply different methods that best fit their use cases. Consequently, this section does not aim 
to give a prescriptive method, but rather sketch certain boundaries, guidelines and general steps to consider 
when developing a DDFS. 
The most common input for a DDFS usually comes from a forecast that defined a target traffic volume in 
terms of annual, daily or hourly demand figures for passengers and/or ATMs as well as a description and 
prediction of the market segments contributing to the traffic growth. 
It is recommended, as a first step, a planner gets acquainted and understands the airport's current traffic 
structures and peaking patterns by analyzing current and historic flight schedules. Comparing the evolution 
and features of the current traffic structure helps to understand the possible evolution over time. This analysis 
will help establish trends to project into the future. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 63 

===PAGE 83===
ie 
IATA Biull Airport Development Reference Manual 
Based on the forecast and discussions with airport stakeholders, the planner elaborates and formulates a 
logical assumption model. When developing a DDFS, the decisions taken shall be consistent and further 
refined based on that logical assumption model. 
Depending on the planning horizon, assumptions shall be checked on a regular basis to see if they would 
change fundamentally over time, which can trigger a re-evaluation of planning assumptions. A review of a 
master plan is recommended on a recurring basis, which shall consider the assumption model the planning 
and design was based on. 
General Steps 
1. Preliminary steps to define boundary conditions 
Limiting boundary conditions: Assess any conditions that limit the growth of peak levels (e.g., 
runway capacity, terminal capacity) and time restrictions (e.g., curfew, noise limitations). On some 
occasions an unconstrained DDFS may also be developed without consideration for known boundary 
constraints. 
Planning horizon: Target capacity associated with one or more years/milestones/planning activity 
levels. 
Traffic type: Depending on the objectives of the study, DDFS may be prepared for a Passenger 
design day or an ATM design day. 
Airport scope: Focus on the whole airport or a particular terminal, subsystem or facility. 
Time period: Depending on the scope of the project and the type of traffic welcomed at the airport 
different timespans could be of interest for the study. For instance, at very seasonal airports with 
traffic changing every day of the week, it could be important to develop future DDFS for a whole 
week, while at airports with busy overnight operations it could be useful to look at two- or three-day 
schedules. If the traffic structure varies considerably for different weekdays, it is recommended to 
consider more than one day. For some use cases, it might be feasible to not develop a complete flight 
schedule, but instead apply a simplified approach and consider a selection of peak periods. For 
example, this could be used to elaborate stress tests of the runway system or an arrival immigration 
area. Also, the period shall cover more than one or two hours to consider fluctuation of demand, 
possible accumulation of delays and interdependencies of airport subsystems. A limited peak period 
consideration would not be suitable for analysis requiring a consistent flight schedule covering one or 
more days (e.g., gate/stand demand planning). 
Type of design day: Different types of schedules could be defined for the future specific weekday(s) 
and/or peak periods (e.g., busy day, weekday busy day, weekend busy day, worst-case scenario, 
average day, low-traffic-season day) consistent with the scope of the project and the traffic nature at 
the airport. 
2. Selection of a design day schedule as a baseline to develop the future DDFS 
64 
Selecting reference design day(s): Understanding the current traffic structures and peaks is 
important when selecting reference design day(s). This design day should be carefully chosen for its 
features being in line with the timespan, traffic type, scope and DDFS type identified as targets for the 
future DDFS. In fact, the design day (its characteristics and profiles) will be used as an important 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 84===
Se By IATA pull Forecasting 
source of information to extract parameters and ratios helpful to building the new DDFS. It will also be 
used as a means of comparison with the newly created DDFS once it is built to double-check the 
projected evolution of traffic. Different methodologies exist for selecting the current design day. The 
most applicable one should be chosen based on the exact scope of the study and type of traffic. 
Operational feedback from the airport should be welcomed to confirm that the analyzed and selected 
day(s) match the planner's understanding of the specifics that are being considered. 
° Several approaches might be applied to identify a suitable reference design day to be used as a 
baseline to develop the DDFS: 
= Accurrent design day usually refers to a “typical busy day” that should not be an extreme day 
(unless planning for extreme situations). 
= The DHR approach could help select days based on segments and types of traffic of interest 
for a particular study. 
= A thorough analysis of the last traffic year-data (flight schedule data log) is recommended to 
understand seasonal and weekday-related traffic and peak hour patterns. 
= For the selection of the current design day, usually different traffic segments (arrivals, 
departures, international, domestic, or any other relevant criteria relevant to the use case) are 
ranked (see 2.2.10.1.2 Other Design Definitions). 
In certain cases, multiple days could be selected for the same time horizon, depending on the 
nature of traffic (e.g., one day for arrivals and one for departures; one day for international 
passengers and one for domestic; one day for passengers and one for cargo). These multiple 
days (or portions thereof, related to the segments of interest) could be combined to create a 
fictitious single current design day schedule, or could be used separately, depending on the 
scope of the project. 
© Definition of the granularity of the future DDFS: Depending on the scope of the project, future 
DDFS may contain fewer details than current and historical flight schedules. In particular for DDFS 
considering a planning horizon of more than three or five years, it is recommended to use generalized 
flight characteristics (e.g., airline groups, aircraft groups, geographical areas or markets, flight types). 
This action will reduce complexity and better manage risks of errors by grouping operations in a 
convenient manner to simplify the DDFS creation task. Each grouping should be tailored to the use 
that will be made of the DDFS. A few examples of groupings are provided below: 
° Airlines could be grouped in different ways, including alliances, codeshares, main carrier vs. all 
others, FSC vs. LCC, domestic carriers vs. international carriers. Airline names/groupings could 
be omitted for certain types of studies. 
Aircraft are typically consolidated by families (e.g., A320 family, B737 family) or sizes (e.g., 
narrowbody vs. widebody, ICAO aircraft reference code, wake turbulence group). 
O&D could be omitted for certain types of studies or could be grouped in different manners, 
including by country or geographical area (e.g., IATA regions), type of O&D (e.g., domestic, 
international, Schengen, precleared). 
Arrival and departure times could be grouped as well (¢.g., for simulation studies to reflect 
fluctuations in time and delays) when it could be helpful to provide less detail.

3. Development of DDFS 
e Based on forecast and in accordance with the assumption model, set targets for how the schedule to 
grow (e.g., how many additional flights will be added to the day; how will the peaks grow; which 
markets will be affected). 
¢ Build up the schedule by adding additional flights or modifying existing flights (e.g., aircraft) based on 
clear rules set according to the assumption model and general airline scheduling guidelines (e.g., 
turnaround times, operating window at O&D airports). 
¢ Ensure iterative consistency checks and discussions with airport stakeholders. 
¢ Run potential sensitivity scenarios to reflect changes in the assumption model (e.g., other aircraft 
mixes) having an impact on peaking patterns. 
2.2.10.3.6 DDFS Development Methodology and Consistency Checks 
Building a future DDFS is a challenging and complex task. Different methodologies exist when creating a 
future DDFS, depending on the scope of the project and the data available. A variety of boundary conditions 
and assumptions have to be considered to elaborate a logical and consistent DDFS. Consistency checks 
performed during and after the elaboration of the DDFS could help planners move forward from one step to 
another. The different approaches and their applicability could also change materially depending on the type 
of schedule and scope of the DDFS. The main considerations include: 
° Fixed system boundaries: Maximum peak hour movements (runway system) total and time of day (e.g., 
due to curfew limitations) and ensuring the DDFS does not contain higher ATM peaks than 
possible/allowed technically or by regulation. 
* Traffic growth rates: Traffic growth rates between the reference year and the forecast year could be 
applied, segment by segment, to determine the volume of operations and passengers of the future DDFS. 
¢ Aircraft maximum ranges: Destinations being serviced by different aircraft should within the allowable 
ranges. 
* Fleet mix: Airline fleets should be double-checked and consistent with annual forecasts. 
* Schedule segments: The detailed characteristics of each segment in the schedules (e.g., international, 
domestic, arrival, departure) are estimated based on relationships between the annual traffic and the 
traffic in the design day. This is because the peak day volumes for ATMs and passengers in relation to 
annual passenger volumes usually stays relatively stable (busy day ratios). For instance, for a busy day 
schedule, the future DDFS is built from an historical one. Existing flights might be modified (e.g., update 
aircraft type, LF), and new flights to be added to each segment of relevance for the study, according to 
historical trends, future annual traffic and future predicted evolutions of busy day ratios. For a worst-case￾scenario schedule, the future DDFS is built from multiple historical ones (or a combination of them) to 
extract the busiest periods for each segment and keep adding onto them, according to historical trends 
and future predicted evolutions. 
* Peak periods: The peak periods are predetermined with the use of ratio-based approaches. For instance, 
for a busy day schedule, the future DDFS is built from an historical one, adding flights on the peak 
periods to reach the busy hour targets, and distributing additional traffic in the less busy periods. 
66 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 86===
=e IATA al Forecasting 
e Schedule patterns: Considerations of anticipated changes in the schedule pattern may include the 
development of new routes, the introduction of new aircraft or phasing out of old ones, the development 
by airlines of new connecting banks, etc. These potential changes will be identified after analysis and 
interviews with the main carriers. Note that fundamental changes in traffic patterns at an airport (e.g., a 
new airline introducing hub-and-spoke traffic at a traditional O8D airport) might trigger a revision of peak 
structures/ratios and impact the assumption model for the DDFS. 
e Load factors: Considerations about increases/decreases in load factors should not be underestimated. 
Passenger flights should keep consistent load factors, in line with historical and future predicted trends. 
The same considerations must be made about belly cargo and general cargo aircraft. 
* Flight schedules: When creating a flight schedule for a hub airport with a high volume of transfer 
passengers, it should be cross-checked that passenger volumes and ratios of arriving/departing 
wavelbank structures make sense, considering typical and minimum connecting times for passengers and 
bags. 
¢ Adding flights: As long as the general flight schedule structure stays the same, the attractive peak 
periods when passengers want to fly and the existing established destinations usually stay stable. 
Assumptions for new flight rotations (arriving and departing flights) to new O&Ds are derived from the 
market forecast and placed at preferred peak flight times as long as possible before adding them to less 
busy periods. When adding flights, it has to be ensured that times at O&D airports are within their typical 
operating time windows. For instance, flights from Europe typically arrive on the US East Coast in the 
afternoon or evening, while flights from South-East Asia typically get to Western Europe in the early 
morning. 
¢ Turnaround times: Arrivals and departures should be paired in a logical way and with a realistic 
turnaround time that allows ground handling operations, including consideration of realistic ground times 
(e.g., LCCs aim for the shortest ground times; FSC's wide-body aircraft require longer turnaround times to 
complete all ground handling activities). 
e Scenarios and sensitivity analyses: Creating a future DDFS, regardless of the methodology, requires a 
fair number of decision-making milestones to determine how to translate demand into a DDFS format. In 
this scope, it is important to keep track and document the line of reasoning based on the logical 
assumption model for the schedule development. For each of the approaches described above, for each 
planning horizon, multiple DDFS could be developed to reflect multiple scenarios representing different 
possible outcomes of the main decision points. This approach could help for comparing results through 
sensitivity analyses and making more informed decisions on the outcomes. However, developing multiple 
DDFS for multiple scenarios can quickly become very time-consuming and will deliver a larger result 
range from which to draw conclusions. Therefore, it could be decided, for instance, to limit sensitivity 
analyses and DDFS scenarios just to specific items that need in-depth discussions with the stakeholders. 
Similarly, depending on the time horizon, the scope of the project and its uncertainty level, the planner 
could define just one main scenario and build sensitivity analyses to predict possible changes in 
requirements. Typically, sensitivity scenarios may be less required for pre-operational schedules and 
planning, where the level of uncertainty is lower compared to longer-term planning.

fie pe 
lata al Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.3. Master Planning 
Vision 
All airports should develop a master plan in order to guide future infrastructure and facility development 
programs in a logical, consistent, sustainable and cost-efficient manner. The transport of passengers, 
baggage and cargo will benefit from the latest technology developments to improve the customer experience, 
reliability and efficiency. This vision is in line with the NEXTT vision. 
Policy 
It is recommended that all airports ensure that: 
¢ All airport capacity enhancement programs are closely tied to an airport master plan 
¢ The master plan is prepared by independent consultants with global experience and a proven history of 
delivering plans that enable all stakeholders to expand their operations and undertake profitable business 
¢ Airlines, their representative associations, and airport stakeholders are fully involved in the creation, 
development and review of the master plan 
¢ Infrastructure is designed to be as cost efficient as Possible (facilities should not be “gold plated”) 
¢ The master plan allows for unfettered incremental expansion of all facilities until the ultimate capacity of 
the site is attained 
¢ No development proceeds until a master plan is in place

COVID-19 Master Planning Impacts 
See 1.8 COVID19 Green Pages for additional explanation on how to interpret the Green Pages 
Introduction 
The unprecedented impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on the aviation industry have resulted in ongoing, 
substantial uncertainty for airport planners regarding capacity enhancing investments, phasing strategies and 
the development of airport master plans. While short-term delays and cancellations of major capital 
investments have been the inevitable result of government policies to close borders to contain the disease, 
there is also the potential for long-term master plans and their phasing strategies to be significantly impacted. 
There is a substantial risk that decisions taken in the short term could result in some investments and facilities 
being poorly located or inappropriately sized, resulting in wasteful expenditures or restrictions on an airport's 
overall capacity or performance in the medium to longer term. While some airports have taken the opportunity 
to complete projects in the construction and delivery phase during the traffic downturn, in most cases the 
timing of master plan developments will need to be carefully reviewed. 
Consultation with users and particularly the airline community to review and agree upon the master plan 
strategy is highly recommended as part of an airport's restart strategy. 
Possible Master Plan Impacts 
Structural changes in the industry resulting from COVID-19 could impact airports’ and airlines’ business plans, 
which are closely reflected in long-term master plans. In particular, recovery may not reflect previous traffic 
distributions or structures that could impact facilities requirements, which should be carefully reflected upon. 
Short-term recovery profiles vary globally with some airports exceeding 2019 levels in 2021 while others have 
only experienced a small percentage of 2019 traffic. The pace of recovery could impact phasing strategies 
(see Section 2.2.1 COVID-19 Traffic Forecasting for additional guidance). 
COVID-19 impacts have added an additional layer of uncertainty and complexity to predicting airport traffic 
forecast scenarios within a reasonable tolerance. The factors to consider that could result in irreversible 
changes include: 
Supply and demand considerations: 
¢ Airline bankruptcies will impact capacity with no guarantee the void may be filled at that specific airport. 
¢ Downsizing fleets, such as retiring older aircraft types, could shrink airline routes and networks. 
¢ Changes in fleet compositions could affect peak structures at airports in some cases requiring new or 
more flexible facilities. 
e Accelerated trends to change fleets of some passenger aircraft could impact networks and transfer traffic 
e.g. older, less fuel efficient aircraft, fewer orders for wide body aircraft. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 69 

===PAGE 89===
a iii Sea 
IATA 4 Airport Development Reference Manual 
Viability of some pre-COVID routes and networks may be under threat given the huge financial impact of 
the crisis, which may also have longer-term effects in areas such as attracting airport staff, as well as on 
airport efficiency and capacity. 
Traffic pattern changes 
Traffic patterns and structures may have changed; for example, international travel restrictions have 
resulted in the growth of domestic markets, which may remain in the longer term and have major impacts 
on airport master plans. This trend has materialized in markets such as. the US, Canada and China. 
Affordability and Prioritization of investments 
The severe economic impact of the pandemic has resulted in significant additional cost sensitivities 
regarding capital investments and, in particular, capacity enhancements, even where demand exists or is 
recovering. Investments that were planned pre-pandemic may no longer be feasible in the short to 
medium term. 
“Fail safe” or “break points” should be incorporated into large development projects in order to Pause or 
stop development or delivery works resulting from unexpected events, crisis, or economic downturn 
affecting the viability of capital investments. 
Consultation with stakeholders is important to identify their ability to accommodate investment costs and 
review the case for investment in the context of master plan developments. 
The application of technology and digital solutions accelerated by Covid-19 impacts can help to support 
efficient use of existing facilities and future investment business cases. 
Passenger trends 
Passenger demographics during COVID have resulted in some population shifts from cities to more rural 
areas as trends to work from home have accelerated. The impact of these changes on business and 
leisure demand for air travel is currently unclear and could result in shifting airport catchment areas and 
demand for surface access modes. 
Impacts on travel behaviors, such as accelerated use of technology and digitization, will support the 
efficient use of infrastructure and mitigate capacity impacts, where applied effectively. 
While there is strong pent-up passenger demand, government-mandated quarantines remain in place 
across many international borders. Therefore, Passengers are avoiding all but essential travel. This, in 
turn, could impact airport master plan phasing strategies, noting medium-term projects can take several 
years to plan, design and procure, providing time to accommodate market shifts prior to construction 
commencement. 
Cargo developments 
70 
Cargo volumes have grown substantially and been an essential part of global supply chains during the 
pandemic. This trend may continue for some time with an upside demand for additional cargo facilities. 
Planners should carefully consider their development strategies to accommodate additional cargo 
facilities, such as stands and ramp space, noting flexibility should be maintained to ensure efficient 
development of the passenger terminal. Additional cargo facilities require evaluation and possible 
upgrades to access roadways and utilities.

Land use 
e Strategic master planning should be built around safeguarding of land for future use to ensure the efficient 
development and use of the airport's real estate. 
© Changes in the pace of demand recovery may result in delays or the acceleration of new developments. 
Changing the future land use, given the current uncertainty of future demand, should be avoided unless 
there is flexibility to convert to previously identified use. 
* Planners should be aware of possible longer term impacts of increasing local community sensitivities to 
noise resulting from low traffic volumes during Covid-19. 
Summary 
If traffic profiles change, this could have a major impact on sizing facilities, from demand day schedules to 
peak hour planning assumptions, resulting in unnecessary, wasted investments or the need to accommodate 
changing fleet requirements. 
While the impact of COVID-19 on airport master plans is still unclear, it could be substantial. Until we have 
greater insights into key factors driving demand and supply, we recommend a cautious approach be taken to 
committing prematurely to master plans and their phasing strategies.
