2.4.2 Local Environmental Issues 
An airport and its associated activities can have a significant impact on the local environment; therefore, 
airports have had a long-standing focus on issues that affect the surrounding community. Such concerns as 
air quality, noise, water management, biodiversity, and protection of local resources have been a prime 
concern and are also often subject to regulatory compliance. 
Maximizing the potential benefits that an airport provides to its local community and region, while minimizing 
any adverse impacts, is an important consideration in airport planning, design, and management. Many 
airports understand the value of addressing local environmental concerns and proactively implement 
strategies that enable them to operate in harmony with their local neighbors while also meeting regulatory 
requirements designed to safeguard everyone's interests. This section examines some of the technical 
solutions and operational practices that can be used as part of airport planning and design to reduce the local 
environmental impact and risk that may come from airport development and operations. 
2.4.2.1 Air Quality 
Airport-related sources of emissions emit pollutants that can contribute to the degradation of air quality in 
nearby communities. The impact of airports on air quality primarily arises from aircraft engine emissions 
during the aircraft Landing and Takeoff cycle (LTO) and from the use of aircraft auxiliary power units (APU) 
during ground operations when aircraft are parked at contact or remote stands. Airport emissions also come 
from other airport-related activities. These include: 
e Airside handling operations 
e Ground support equipment (GSE) and vehicles 
e Landside airport ground access systems 
° Cargo operations 
Local air quality at an airport, therefore, is a function of many factors, including aircraft and surface transport 
traffic levels, congestion, and local meteorological conditions. 
In the airport surroundings, monitoring systems can provide data that is used to build and manage models to 
identify the contribution of airport activities to outdoor pollutant concentration, with special regard to nitrogen 
oxides (NOx), volatile organic compounds (VOCs), hydrocarbons (HC), particulate matter (PM), and carbon 
monoxide (CO). Airports are subject to local, national, and international air quality standards and must 
operate accordingly. Regulations vary by country and the ability to conform to these national guidelines and 
regulations is dependent on local variables, including meteorological conditions, local topography, population 
density, background concentrations, and the available emission control technologies. Guidance on the 
regulatory framework and local measures can be found in ICAO's Doc 9889 Airport Air Quality Manual. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 167 

===PAGE 187===
= IATA wa Airport Development Reference Manual 
Many of the measures that airports can take to improve local air quality can also reduce carbon emissions. 
These include: 
e Airfield layouts that facilitate efficient aircraft movements 
e Assisted aircraft taxiing 
¢ Fixed electrical ground power and preconditioned air at aircraft gates 
¢ Transition of airport vehicles and GSE to electric power 
e Airport surface access strategies. 
Ultrafine Particles 
Ultrafine particles (UFP) are PM with a diameter of less than 0.1 micrometers (100 nanometers), also called 
PMO.1. They are generated at very high temperatures, such as those that occur during aircraft engine 
combustion. As far as health impacts of UFP are concerned, while there is a growing understanding that 
Particulate air pollution (covering different sizes of PM) in urban environments may lead to an increased risk of 
respiratory and cardiovascular disease, the knowledge base on UFPs specifically is still limited. To better 
understand and address the impact that airport-related activities can have on UFP concentrations, ACI 
EUROPE commissioned a study (ACI, 2018) Ultrafine Particles at Airports (see link below), which provides 
useful guidance on the monitoring and measurement of local air quality. 
According to ACI EUROPE, the most likely particle sources at airports are generated from: 
e Aircraft: main engines, APUs, brakes, and tires 
e Airside operations: GSE, vehicle engine combustion and tires 
¢ Landside traffic access: vehicle engine combustion and tires as well as rail services (diesel engines, 
brakes and rails). 
* Other: diesel smoke from combustion processes, VOCs from paints, pollen from landscaping. 
Reference Documents 
¢ ACI (2018) Ultrafine Particles at Airports 
Ultra-Fine Particles at Airports.pdf (aci-europe.org) 
e ICAO (2020) Airport Air Quality Manual 2" Edition 
www.icao.int/publications/Documents/9889_cons_en.pdf 
2.4.2.2 Noise 
Aircraft noise is one of the long-standing community challenges that airports face. Concerns about the noise 
impact of aviation date back to the 1950s and 1960s as jet engine technology became more commonplace 
and the number of flights increased significantly. Aviation noise can not only annoy surrounding communities, 
but prolonged exposure to noise, particularly at night, can cause long-term health issues. 
168 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 188===
we 
IATA Airport Environmental Sustainability 
Although aircraft have become quieter, the relationship between airport operations and nearby communities is 
still an important issue that can affect an airport's social license to operate and grow. The degree to which 
aircraft noise is a material issue is airport-specific; consequently, no single solution will be appropriate for all 
airports. The local rules and decibel limits for noise are a key input for airport planning, including the airport's 
master plan, and for securing the necessary environmental permits. The ICAO has established a 
comprehensive approach to managing aircraft noise known as the Balanced Approach that requires the 
involvement of all stakeholders and is centered on four pillars: 
¢ Reduction of noise at source through technology 
* Managing land uses around airports 
* Adapting operational noise abatement procedures to reduce the noise impact on the ground 
¢ Using operating restrictions on aircraft if the other three pillars are exhausted 
Many airports worldwide have developed long-term noise management strategies and noise action plans in 
line with the four pillars of the ICAO's Balanced Approach. 
Some airports have started to incorporate a fifth pillar into their noise management strategies and plans, 
“Working with Communities”. The driver behind the inclusion of a new pillar at some airports has been the 
recognition given to the importance of open and constructive dialogue with local communities affected by 
aircraft noise. By committing to engaging closely with local communities, an airport increases its 
understanding of their concerns and can be better placed to identify and implement the right sort of noise 
management measures in response. This of course requires building trust and making relevant information 
accessible for an on-going and transparent dialogue. 
2.4.2.2.1 Noise Barriers 
Sound barriers can be employed near runways or at airport boundaries to mitigate noise from aircraft taxiing, 
landing, and taking off. These barriers are high noise-insulating walls that deflect sound waves away from 
noise-sensitive areas. They need to be installed carefully to not create an airspace obstruction. 
One example of their use is found at the south-western corner of London Heathrow Airport. A wavy concrete 
wall, approximately 7 meters in height, 1,200 meters in length was constructed to provide a noise barrier for 
residents living in nearby communities. The distinctive wave design has been proven to be most efficient at 
reflecting noise from runway O9R; however, noise propagation paths still find their ways to nearby residents 
when the airport is on easterly operations which is about 30% of the time. 
2.4.2.2.2_ Engine Test Enclosures 
Engine testing is often carried out at airports as part of aircraft maintenance, repair, and overhaul operations 
(MRO); however, these test run-ups can cause ground noise pollution and impact surrounding communities. 
Noise barriers in the form of test run walls, noise protection hangars or run-up enclosures provide acoustic 
and blast protection and can reduce the noise impact of engine testing. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 169 

===PAGE 189===
Se By Vee | IATA yl Airport Development Reference Manual 
The size and type of engine test enclosure depends upon the number and type of aircraft that use the airport 
and the scale and type of maintenance activities that are carried out there. A noise protection hangar is 
typically open to let in the large volumes of air necessary for run-up tests without generating turbulence with a 
closed back design reduces noise levels by up to 30 db. These hangers are also often equipped with jet blast 
deflectors, which directs the exhaust from the aircraft engines upward and out of the rear of the hall. 
2.4.2.2.3, Building Soundproofing 
Building soundproofing methods include incorporating acoustic design during the architectural planning 
process and using noise-insulating materials during construction. Soundproofing essentially involves either 
noise absorption, reflection, or deflection of sound waves through noise dampening materials such as floor 
underlayment (subfloor material), in-wall equipment like rails and pads, and double-glazed windows. 
2.4.2.2.4 Airfield Design Noise Considerations 
For greenfield airport projects, airside and airfield design must consider runway, taxiway, and apron locations 
to optimize aircraft taxiing times and maximize runway throughput. Reducing taxiing times not only reduces 
emissions, but also benefits noise abatement. Comprehensive airport master planning should look to provide 
direct, unconstrained taxiway capacities capable of handling forecast ATMs and fleet mixes. 
In cases where an airport has two or more runways, noise preferential runways (NPRs) where aircraft follow 
pre-defined routes can be used effectively to mitigate and distribute noise impact to less noise-sensitive 
Zones. Often, the runways to be used will depend on the time of day and the day of the week, or when certain 
conditions are met. Weather, in particular wind, is a major parameter in selecting a runway configuration. For 
example, when tailwinds or crosswinds exceed certain thresholds, aircraft may not be able to takeoff or land 
on the preferred runway for safety reasons. NPRs are being effectively used at many airports around the 
world, including Sydney, Brussels, Boston, and London Heathrow. 
2.4.2.2.5 Land Use Management 
Land use planning and management around airports focuses on ensuring activities around the vicinity of an 
airport, which fall under the calculated noise contour levels, are compatible with aircraft and aeronautical 
safety requirements. Aviation-compatible activities include industrial and commercial sites, while non￾compatible activities include residential and other sensitive uses such as hospitals, schools, places of worship 
and aged-care facilities. 
For greenfield sites, this can be achieved by comprehensive planning and locating the airport away from 
settlements, while for existing airports, solutions such as land-use zoning, development control requirements, 
and building codes may be used to prevent additional residential development and/or encroachment. For 
existing airports that are already constrained by urban development, land use planning is much more difficult 
and may not be very flexible. 
170 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 190===
aay 
Seo IATA Airport Environmental Sustainability 
ICAO's Balanced Approach and its associated documents describe the most comprehensive methods of land 
use planning and management for noise mitigation around airports. 
Each airport will need to find the mix of solutions that best fit its circumstances. One such example, involving 
the use of landscape design, can be found in the vicinity of Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport at the Buitenschot 
Land Art Park. After a new runway was built, it was found that mitigation measures were required for a nearby 
residential area. A park area consisting of a series of three-meter ridges and trenches was placed in a field 
perpendicular to the runway and angled to reflect soundwaves upwards. This has not only reduced ambient 
decibel to within required noise limits but has provided a recreational facility with bike paths, jogging tracks 
and a sports field for the local community. 
Reference Documents 
* ICAO (2008) Guidance on the Balanced Approach to Aircraft Noise Management 
Aircraft Noise (icao.int) 
2.4.2.2.6 Noise Measurement and Monitoring 
To measure and quantify aircraft noise impact, airports often deploy either mobile or permanent noise 
monitoring systems (NOMS) or noise monitoring terminals (NMT) at various locations around the airport. 
These sensors record ambient noise and noise events related to aircraft movements. This recorded data also 
provides input to software that can combine ATM data such as time of day, altitude, flight path, etc. to support 
users in understanding operational adherence to noise management plans. 
NOMS systems are good for measuring single event data but are not as effective for assessing cumulative 
noise exposure over the course of a year. 
2.4.2.3. Water and Soil Protection 
Another important environmental consideration is protecting soil and water. Aviation related activities such as 
fuel storage, fuel distribution, land filling and use of firefighting equipment and foam can contaminate the soil. 
Airports should have a monitoring and remediation plan in place to protect soil. 
Safeguarding water quality requires a holistic approach to stormwater management as well as targeted 
strategies for potential airport-specific pollutants and for construction activities. Airports have focused on 
methods to decrease pollutant levels in airport wastewater. Wastewater may be treated on site or sent to a 
nearby municipal treatment system. Local water quality regulations may set limits on the quantity of 
wastewater or require pretreatment of wastewater before it can be discharged into a municipal system. 
For stormwater, the objective is on-site management of precipitation runoff. Management of airport-specific 
operations, such as fuel handling, aviation fuel storage, aircraft deicing and firefighting exercises, requires 
land use planning and infrastructure design as well as operational approached and training to ensure water 
quality standards are maintained. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 171 

===PAGE 191===
== 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.4.2.3.1 Stormwater Management 
Managing stormwater quality and quantity are especially challenging tasks for airports. Airports need to 
design runoff systems with enough capacity to handle predicted rainfall events. This will help the airport avoid 
flooding events and will reduce pollution of local water resources. Sustainable stormwater management 
strategies should consider the nature and quantity of discharges into water bodies or treatment facilities, flood 
management and mitigation, precipitation changes associated with climate change, and the creation of 
resilient systems. 
Large, paved areas in airports, such as runways taxiways and aprons, require the best management practices 
for drainage systems and stormwater management to mitigate the impact of runoff water and prevent flooding. 
A comprehensive approach for all airport facilities and infrastructure is required to collect stormwater runoff, 
along with the pollutants contained therein, for conveyance to a treatment facility. Green infrastructure is also 
very effective with managing stormwater runoff, depending on soil type. There are also nature-based solutions 
(e.g., bioswales, retention basins, semi-permeable surfaces) to manage pollutants, conserve and reuse water 
and recharge groundwater in addition to mitigating the risk from floods. Surface water runoff from buildings, 
toads, flight operation areas and other developed surfaces that collects over large areas or in drainage can be 
filtered near the surface with sand and gravel to ensure the protection of groundwater. 
2.4.2.3.2 Airport-Specific Contaminants Management 
Stormwater runoff from the airport runways, taxiways and aprons may contain contaminants from aircraft 
activities, which can pose a risk to surrounding water supplies. Water contaminants at airports include: 
¢ Ethylene or propylene glycols from de-icing and anti-icing of aircraft 
¢ Fuel from spills during refueling and leaks from pipes or tanks 
¢ Fire suppressant chemicals and fuels dispersed during firefighting exercises 
¢ Dust, dirt and hydrocarbons from paved surfaces and engine leaks 
e Herbicides and pesticides 
Most airports have established water management programs and procedures to comply with local water 
regulations and contain potential contaminants. Solutions may include the use of water retention and isolation 
basins to contain pollution. Airports can operate treatment plants and combine gray water infrastructure and 
nature-based solutions to reduce discharges into the environment. These facilities can have water tested for 
compliance before release. In addition to sampling surface runoff, groundwater sampling should be conducted 
at key locations to better understand water quality issues. Decisions on which processes to include in a water 
management program will be influenced by the airport's operating, physical and regulatory environment. 
(a) Hazardous Liquids Runoff Management 
Many airports that experience colder climate during at least part of the year require de-icing operations to be 
carried out during winter conditions. De-icing and anti-icing fluids are applied to aircraft and, in some cases, 
anti-icing fluids are also applied directly to airport surfaces to keep them free from ice. These chemical fluids 
172 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 192===
Se RY IATA wal Airport Environmental Sustainability 
can contaminate water resources and their use is subject to local regulation; therefore, most airports will track 
the amounts and types of fluids used annually as well as the amount of waste generated. 
To the greatest extent possible, any spent de-icing fluids should be collected after use. Airport plans will 
depend upon specific circumstances; however, they may include the use of glycol recovery vehicles to 
vacuum the glycol when de-icing is performed at the aircraft stand, as is done at many airports. Another 
option is purpose-built permanent aircraft de-icing pads located near the runway and collection systems such 
as pipes and lagoons. 
This approach aims to reduce the glycol contamination associated with aircraft de-icing from reaching the 
main surface water drainage collection system. Spent glycol can be collected, separated from other water, 
and recycled. The recovered glycol can be transferred to a dedicated recovery and distillation unit, from which 
high-grade glycol can be produced for reuse. Soft water, which is a by-product of glycol recovery, can be 
used in aircraft and window washing, thus reducing the demand on the water supply. It should be noted, in 
recent years, more environmentally friendly de-icing fluids have been introduced to replace glycol-based fluids 
and these are much less toxic. 
Over the past several years, there has been a surge in regulatory interest in many countries on addressing 
the public health and environmental risks from releases of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), 
including use of aqueous film-forming foams (AFFF) for firefighting or training. Firefighting foams have been a 
significant source of PFAS contamination as it can seep into the ground to contaminate soil and ground water. 
The use of PFAS-based foam is highly regulated, and requirements vary around the world, but airports are 
increasingly expected to test soil and water and have spill management and clean-up plans in place. Best 
practice in containment of firefighting foams is evolving quickly and new, less hazardous foams are currently 
being developed and introduced. 
Vertical reedbeds are another nature-based solution used to treat many types of water contamination. Flows 
percolate vertically through the gravel and the treated effluent is collected at the base of the bed for 
discharge. In the case of aerated beds, air is fed to the gravel through a network of air distribution pipes. This 
encourages the development and sustenance of a population of bacteria that feed upon the organics and 
nutrients in the polluted water, making aerated beds smaller and more efficient than unaerated ones. 
2.4.2.3.3 Conservation and Restoration of Natural Water Bodies 
Safeguarding water resources (e.g., wetlands, river systems) within the airport and its surroundings is an 
important objective of local environmental protection. There are several different options that can be used for 
the design approach: 
© No-build: Identify critical water resources on-site in the master plan as no-build zones 
© Restoration: Restore degraded on-site wetlands for water quality and stormwater control 
* No-impact: Conduct hydrological studies to monitor the impact of airport activities on adjacent off-site 
water bodies 
© Compensation: Where wetland destruction is unavoidable due to aeronautical infrastructure constraints, 
implement compensatory restoration of proximate off-site wetlands 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 173 

===PAGE 193===
IAT: aul Airport Development Reference Manual 
Whatever strategies are used, the threat of wildlife hazards to airport operations and aircraft (e.g., bird strikes) 
needs to be considered. Airport operators should be aware of the conditions that attract birds and other 
animals and take appropriate steps to avoid or mitigate the risk. 
2.4.2.4 Indoor Environmental Quality 
Indoor environmental quality, including air quality as well as thermal, visual, and acoustic comfort, are 
important for the well-being of airport workers, passengers, and other visitors. 
2.4.2.4.1 Indoor Air Quality 
Indoor air quality (IAQ) assessment is a key element of the environmental quality evaluation of airport 
terminals. Airport terminal buildings are complex environments comprising large expansive areas that can 
accommodate many functions, occupant densities, activity levels, and time spent by travelers. The passenger 
flow in airport terminals varies significantly during the day and throughout the year. Continuous air quality 
monitoring systems, working on short time intervals, can identify possible repetitive patterns of contamination 
and support air quality management. 
All airport buildings should aim to establish good practice standards for IAQ. Design teams should ensure 
adequate specification and integration of: 
e Sensors 
¢ Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) systems 
¢ Materials and finishes selection 
Key IAQ strategies include the following: 
¢ Adequate ventilation of all spaces that meets or exceeds international, national, and local guidance 
* Monitoring of hazardous air pollutants such as PM2.5, PM10, VOCs, CO,, O3, and radon 
¢ Particle filtration through media filters in the ventilation system 
¢ Ultraviolet treatment of heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) surfaces to reduce the 
transmission of pathogens 
¢ Where natural ventilation is used (e.g., open windows), measure outdoor air quality 
° Negatively pressurize bathrooms, kitchens, storage rooms for cleaning and chemical supplies, rooms with 
high-volume printers and copiers, and high humidity areas 
¢ Select building materials and cleaning/operational materials that emit low levels of VOCs (reducing 
concentrations of chemical contaminants) 
Other strategies include: 
* Construction-related pollution mitigation strategies such as recycling of construction waste 
¢ Green cleaning products to help reduce exposure to pathogens, allergens, and hazardous chemicals 
174 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 194===
IATA Airport Environmental Sustainability 
2.4.2.4.2 Thermal Comfort 
Thermal comfort is defined as “the condition of mind that expresses satisfaction with the thermal environment 
and is assessed by subjective evaluation” (ANSI/ASHRAE Standard 55). The most-used indicator of thermal 
comfort is air temperature; however, it should be considered in relation to other factors such as radiant 
temperature, air velocity, and humidity. Airport buildings should aim to provide a maximum level of thermal 
comfort for all building users through improved HVAC system design and control. 
Design teams should incorporate HVAC systems and the building envelope to meet the requirements of local 
or national standards such as the ASHRAE Standard 55-2010, Thermal Comfort Conditions for Human 
Occupancy that is used in the United States. To verify performance, thermal comfort indices (e.g., dry-bulb 
temperature, relative humidity) can be monitored in key spaces and supported by occupant surveys. 
Depending on the climate, location and occupant expectations, design teams may carefully consider relaxing 
the comfort criteria in some transient zones to save energy and adjust comfort conditions seasonally. 
2.4.2.5 Outdoor Comfort and Urban Heat Island Effect 
The comfort of the outdoor experience can affect visitors’ perception of the airport. Outdoor walkways and car 
parking areas should provide protection from the harsh elements, especially direct sun, rain, and high winds. 
By replacing open spaces and vegetation with structures built of materials that absorb and retain heat, a 
phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect occurs. The most prominent feature of an urban heat 
island is a sustained elevated temperature when compared to the surrounding undeveloped areas. 
Various strategies can be used to mitigate urban heat island effects and improve outdoor thermal comfort. 
These methods focus on either cooling the area or reflecting solar radiation, and may include adding 
vegetation, providing shading structures, introducing water features, and roof technologies that boast high 
surface reflective index ratings. 
2.4.2.5.1 Vegetation 
The use of trees or vegetation facilitates evapotranspiration and provides shade, contributing to lower surface 
and air temperatures. Other benefits of introducing vegetation and green spaces include improved air quality 
and water quality (via stormwater management). 
Trees should be selected and distributed in a way that provides sufficient shading from direct sun. Trees with 
a larger crown provide more shade, but can also attract roosting birds; therefore, the risk of bird strikes needs 
to be assessed. In addition, when selecting trees, priority should be given to native and drought-tolerant 
plants that, once established, generally require little or no irrigation. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 175 

===PAGE 195===
ray 
Se IATA pit Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.4.2.5.2 Outdoor Canopies 
Shelter canopies help block solar radiation and provide relief of thermal stress in extreme temperatures. A 
shaded surface can be up to 25°C [45°F] cooler than the peak temperature of a nearby unshaded surface. 
Further reductions of surface temperatures of sidewalks, roadways and parking lots can be achieved with 
paving materials that reflect light and absorb less heat. The shading canopies can integrate solar photovoltaic 
(PV) panels and provide renewable electricity. 
The canopies should also be sized to provide protection from the rain. Attention should be paid to the angle of 
inclination of the canopy to block solar rays and protect from rain. Additionally, the tilt can help block 
prevailing winds that can bring rain in at a shallow angle in some locations. 
2.4.2.5.3 Evaporative Cooling 
Bodies of water can have a positive effect on microclimates by moderating extreme temperatures. Small 
water bodies, such as fountains or shallow pools, can regulate temperature fluctuations and help improve 
thermal comfort during days of extreme heat. Air temperatures around water bodies can be lower compared 
to surrounding areas. In hot and dry climates, the outdoor “felt” temperature can be improved using 
evaporative cooling and misting systems if available supplies of water permit. 
2.4.2.5.4 Pedestrian Wind Comfort 
In high wind speed environments, analyses should be used to confirm that pedestrian wind comfort and safety 
has been achieved. Pedestrian wind comfort studies combine statistical meteorological data with wind flow 
conditions around buildings. The results are compared to wind comfort criteria (such as Lawson's criteria), 
which set the threshold wind speeds and frequency ranges for different pedestrian activities. Consideration 
also needs to be given to any challenges with accessing buildings (i.e., opening doors) in windy conditions. 
2.4.2.5.5 Design Tools 
Outdoor comfort conditions can be estimated using indices such as Physiologically Equivalent Temperature 
(PET) or Universal Thermal Climate index (UTCI). These are used to predict the felt temperature, and to 
measure the impact of selected strategies (shading, wind control or evaporative cooling). Computational fluid 
dynamics modelling, or wind tunnel testing, can be used to predict the likelihood of wind movement. The 
effectiveness of shading devices or vegetation can be assessed through solar access analyses.

===PAGE 196===
IATA Airport Environmental Sustainability 
2.4.2.6 Enhanced Access to Nature 
Humans are increasingly living in environments where they have insufficient exposure to nature. Natural 
elements, such as plants, water, and daylight, have been linked with health-promoting benefits, including: 
¢ Decreased levels of depression and anxiety 
Increased attention levels, productivity, morale and satisfaction on the job 
e Increased overall psychological well-being 
Incorporating elements, materials and art that reflect the local culture can help celebrate a project's unique 
identity and further enrich the space for employees and travelers. Where feasible, projects can incorporate 
plants, water, natural materials, and patterns, as well as elements that celebrate local culture and provide a 
sense of place (local architecture, materials, flora, art, surrounding community). 
Example: Jewel Changi Airport 
Jewel Changi Airport is a nature-themed entertainment and retail complex linked to three of Singapore 
Changi's terminals. At the heart of its glass roof is an oculus five stories up that showers water through a 
primary multi-story garden to the forest-valley garden at ground level. 
The rain vortex is the world's tallest indoor waterfall and transforms into a light and sound show in the 
evening. During the region's frequent and powerful thunderstorms, recirculated natural rainwater flows at more 
than 40,000 liters per minute, which helps provide cooling and airflow in the landscape environment, collecting 
significant rainwater to be reused in the building. 
Conceived to serve both the people of Singapore and travelers, the building is directly connected to the 
Changi Bus Terminal and the airport's Terminal 1. It is also accessible from Terminals 2 and 3 via pedestrian 
bridges. The interterminal train crosses through the gardens, giving visitors with limited time a glimpse into the 
‘forest valley’ below.

2.4.3, Community and Social 
Airports have a significant social and economic impact on their surrounding community and region. Planning, 
designing, and developing sustainable airports must incorporate ideas that promote and maintain a healthy 
and sustainable relationship with the peopele who live and work around the airport. 
Airport sustainability requires an integrated approach to balance operational requirements with the need for 
economic stability, environmental sustainability, and social responsibility. How an airport engages with its 
region and local community will help determine its success in achieving an optimal balance. 
As such, airport development may benefit from an “outside-in” approach to understanding the local constraints 
and opportunities of their region, and then using that knowledge to develop sustainable strategies for airport 
growth and to promote health and well-being for local communities.

2.4.3.1 Engagement with Local Stakeholders in Airport Development Plans 
Airport activity and its accompanying noise and emissions can affect not only the immediate area, but also 
human health and the ecology of surrounding areas. Therefore, it is crucial to engage local municipalities, 
communities, and others at an early stage of any airport development plans. 
A proactive approach will be seen positively and should be ongoing to develop and maintain a constructive 
relationship. Regular and effective consultation is crucial for understanding opportunities and constraints that 
can reduce time and costs while providing benefits to the people who live and work in the area surrounding 
the airport. 
By building relationships with, and supporting the local municipalities around the airport, the surrounding 
communities’ views and concerns can be better understood. With that knowledge in hand, airports should be 
in a better position to mitigate potential negative effects, deliver social/environmental enhancements to the 
surrounding areas, and maximize economic opportunities related to jobs, apprenticeships, and (airport￾related) businesses. 
2.4.3.1.1 Consider Local Values and Culture 
Airports are gateways to countries, regions and cities, and can play an important role in shaping passenger 
perceptions by creating unique arrival and departure experiences through architectural, interior design, and 
service elements. The local characteristics and environment can be incorporated into the building design by

Integrating local values, culture, art, and other elements can help connect an airport and its local community

2.4.3.1.2_ Continuous and Long-Term Engagement 
Community engagement should be regarded as a continuous process, with regular interactions building 
toward a long-term vision. Regular engagement allows for the delivery of wider benefits beyond the 
development period. It is important that the planning process and reporting of accumulated goals are 
communicated and reviewed periodically by all stakeholders. Effective consultation can speed up the 
development process and create stronger trust. Airport designers should recognize the opportunity to deliver a 
positive legacy for passengers and local communities. Failure to consult with local communities can 
undermine a project and event lead to its cancellation. 
2.4.3.2 Sustainable Land Utilization 
Land use by airports and surface access networks are among the problems requiring attention to mitigate 
impacts on surrounding communities. Utilization of land by airports for the purpose of building and expanding 
facilities and infrastructure is often affected by changes in the surrounding community. Careful planning for 
efficient design solutions and future needs, including assessing land requirements for surface access, should 
be part of every airport master plan update. 
Land use plans, developed in collaboration with local stakeholders, play a critical role in limiting any negative 
effects on the local environment and community. The protection of land for future development is critical to 
ensuring the airport's sustainable growth. 
Airports are at times situated on land with significant meaning in a historical sense, for archeological reasons 
or related to Indigenous peoples’ heritage. Using this land for airport activities, or for the purpose of building 
an airport, will need to be carefully considered and discussed with local communities. Social and economic 
benefits of the airport for the region must be weighed carefully against disturbances to the area; often, win-win 
solutions can be found with good proactive engagement. 
In finding communal solutions, the goal must be to incorporate and respect historical ties, which will bring an 
airport more relevance and connection to the land and region it serves by: 
© Reserving time and space for archeological sites to coexist or be properly excavated 
¢ Respecting and honoring Indigenous peoples’ land and cultural heritage, which will bring an airport more 
relevance and connection to the land and region it serves. 
Due to airports’ tendency to grow, the local planning engagement must include not just the immediate land 
use, but also the land use (or land acquisition) required for future needs, including surface access. 
Land use plans, developed in collaboration with local stakeholders, play a critical role in limiting any negative 
effects from airport operations on the local environment and community. The allocation of land for future 
airport development is critical to ensuring the airport's sustainable development and economic growth as well 
as continued social benefits. 
Expanding the site area of an airport can be a long-term infrastructure project, subject to many jurisdictional 
requirements, which will benefit from well-developed planning and community consensus. When site areas

2.4.3.4 Communicating Social and Economic Impacts of Airports 
Air service contributes to the local and regional economy, especially in business sectors that are reliant upon 
air transport as an element of their operations. Nonetheless, in the planning and design of airport expansions, 
it can be important to measure and communicate these contributions to local parties. Economic impact 
studies detail these contributions to employment and identify opportunities to grow the number of supply 
chains and businesses that are related to the airport, or dependent on aviation, particularly in neighboring 
communities. Leveraging economic and social impact studies creates greater awareness of the role aviation 
plays in the region and can bring about synergies and partnerships that can benefit the planning and design 
of airport expansions. 
Research has identified statistical relationships between air service and economic activity. Aviation’s link to 
the tourism and hospitality industry is well established. There are also the benefits that the business of 
running an airport brings to the local economy in terms of employment and economic activity. Finally, the 
connectivity from air services also contributes to the local or regional economy by opening access to markets 
and generating economic growth. Airports are a key interface between a wide range of aviation and non￾aviation stakeholders, providing essential connectivity services to their communities. Understanding that 
linkage is a critical step in facilitating broad support for aviation. 
2.4.3.5 Ensuring Seamless Local and Regional Transport Links 
Airports require efficient surface access for passengers, employees, freight, and deliveries. Surface access, 
whether by road, rail, or other means needs to be convenient, fast, reliable, and affordable. In addition, there 
are increasing expectations that surface access to and from the airport should be sustainable. Surface access 
modes with internal combustion engines (ICE) contribute to GHG emissions. Governments and other policy 
makers have been encouraging a shift to more sustainable modes of travel. In some jurisdictions, this has 
included putting policies and targets in place to encourage greater use of public transport. 
Airports do not have direct control over many aspects of surface access and, therefore, need to collaborate 
with local, regional, and national stakeholders. For each airport, the best solutions may be different; however, 
from an environmental perspective, promoting the use of efficient transport modes with a lower emissions 
footprint can help reduce the overall climate impact of air passenger journeys. Ensuring seamless intermodal 
regional connectivity is critical to supporting sustainable growth and the optimal utilization of the airport. Some 
strategies being used include: 
° Integrating efficient mass transit options that are convenient to the local community 
e Enhancing intermodal transport by taking steps to ensure simple and seamless connections between the 
airport and local and regional rail and bus services 
e Establishing infrastructure such as recharging and refueling points to support zero emissions vehicle use 
e Facilitating new mobility options (e.g., on-demand transport) 
© Maintaining a resilient and free-flowing road network to reduce delays and congestion 
¢ Complementing public transport with walking/cycling lanes that do not conflict with roadways.

It is important to keep track of planned improvements in local transportation infrastructure and airport access 
to ensure future investments are aligned with airport access strategies. Development in areas surrounding the 
airport can alter traffic patterns and utilization and should be monitored to anticipate future access needs.

2.4.4 Energy and Carbon 
Airport planning and design decisions related to energy use and carbon emissions can have a significant 
impact on the environment, particularly the GHG emissions that contribute to climate change. Airport buildings 
can have an impact on the environment in their construction as well as operational aspects. Environmental 
considerations should, therefore, be part of the planning process and evaluation criteria. 
The United Nation's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), which is the UN body for assessing 
the science related to climate change, has established that for the necessary GHG emissions reduction to be 
achieved by 2030, buildings and infrastructure would need to achieve near net zero energy operations and 
reduce their embodied carbon. Current green building rating systems can help achieve this goal by focusing 
on energy efficiency, cost efficiency, health and well-being, waste management, and, in some cases, 
embodied carbon reductions. 
Around the world, there are several green building and infrastructure certification programs with frameworks 
that vary depending on the project type and scope. One of the most widely recognized is the LEED, which, 
based on the project type, can be divided into the following sub-categories: 
* Building Design and Construction (BD+C) 
¢ Interior Design and Construction (ID+C) 
* Building Operations and Maintenance (O+M)

===PAGE 204===

IATA Airport Environmental Sustainability 
° Neighborhood Development (ND) 
¢ Homes 
© Cities and Communities 
In addition to the above, the LEED frameworks differ for new or existing buildings and can take a campus 
approach for projects sharing a site under a single entity's control. 
Green rating systems can support sustainability goals while also generating significant savings on operating 
costs, These systems are limited by their lack of custom criteria for airport buildings, especially terminals. 
Awhole life carbon assessment can be very useful in helping an airport understand the scale and sources of 
its carbon emissions and to develop strategies to drive reductions. Two areas that have a significant impact 
on CO, emissions are the embodied carbon associated with materials and construction as well as the 
operational carbon resulting from the airport's activities over its life cycle. 
2.4.4.1 Minimize Embodied Carbon 
Development plans should make the best use of existing facilities and adopt an infrastructure lifecycle 
approach that considers design, construction, and operations. Embodied carbon is associated with materials 
and construction processes throughout the whole lifecycle of the infrastructure, including emissions 
associated with the extraction, production and transport of materials and products, and their repair, 
replacement, disassembly, and disposal. Some of the strategies to reduce embodied carbon include: 
* Adopting green procurement practices that minimize the use of high-embodied carbon materials such as 
concrete and steel 
© Optimize the structural scheme to minimize material use, e.g., column grids and roof spans 
e Using a lower window-to-wall ratio (as glass can have a higher embodied carbon per m? than solid 
materials 
© Procurement of low-carbon materials (e.g., use of recycled concrete aggregate in concrete or use of low 
cement content in concrete) 
e Reduce material use in general and use bio-based carbon storing building materials 
The adoption of a green building certification system such as LEED or BREEAM can provide tools and 
methods to assess the environmental performance.

2.4.4.1.1 Circularity: Materials and Equipment Reuse 
Airport operators should strive to minimize use of virgin materials and increase the opportunities for value 
creation in both construction and operation of airport facilities. A circular economy approach can reduce 
embodied carbon through material efficiency, eliminating waste, employing leaner design solutions that use 
less material, and keeping materials in use either as a product or as. components or raw materials. 
Reuse and recycling of existing steel and concrete components in new structures can cut waste as well as 
reduce carbon emissions associated with the manufacturing of new products. Consideration of circular 
economy principles should be given throughout a structure's entire lifecycle, from concept to demolition. New 
designs should ensure the materials used in components will be suitable for reuse and recycling when the 
structure reaches the end of its life. 
Reference Documents 
¢ Ellen Macarthur Foundation 
Circular economy principle: Circulate products and materials (ellenmacarthurfoundation.org) 
Example: South Terminal Pier 1-Gatwick Airport, London 
One example of reuse and recycling is found in the replacement of airport aprons at London Gatwick Airport. 
The project required the removal of the existing concrete aprons, some of which had been in place for over 50 
years. The old apron concrete was crushed and delivered back to the site for reuse as type 1 sub-base for the 
project. This removed the costly requirement to dispose of the material offsite and contributed to the overall 
sustainability of the project. A pavement assessment also identified 8,500m? of existing concrete apron to be 
retained as part of the works. 
(a) Maintenance over Lifecycle 
As pavements and other structures reach their end of life, rather than planning to replace them, less extensive 
solutions can be considered, such as providing a flexible overlay on top of an existing concrete pavement 
instead of reconstructing the concrete. Carrying out routine inspections and maintenance throughout the 
lifecycle of a structure can reduce the rate of deterioration and limit the onset of major defects that result in 
carbon-intensive repair works, End-of-life maintenance works will also likely have lower embodied carbon and 
a lower associated cost.

2.4.4.1.2 Low Embodied Carbon Design Solutions 
The design process can be guided using tools that integrate the design options with embodied carbon 
analysis, thereby informing the performance of the different design options. The model of a building can be 
used together with an updated material palette and an interactive analysis. In this way, the design team can 
test different material options to better understand and compare the impact of the material choices. These 
integrated analysis tools help to better visualize where the carbon is located.

Example: Low Embodied Carbon Design Solutions and Tools—Marseille Airport, France 
The extension of the Marseille Airport passenger terminal followed a low-carbon design approach and took 
advantage of technology to inform the design. Several opportunities to minimize the embodied carbon were 
created during the design phase, from site optimization and refurbishment of the existing structure to the use 
of low embodied carbon materials. 
Some site optimization and refurbishment strategies included demolishing only where necessary, excavation 
works were avoided by not altering the foundations, and the roof designs were optimized to minimize material. 
These strategies saved around 60% of the carbon when compared to a scenario of demolition and rebuild. 
Materials such as steel and aluminum with high recycled content, concrete with a high percentage of cement 
replacement, and renewable timber from certified sources was used. The design team also explored the 
sourcing of the materials since, in some cases, a locally sourced material can have more embodied carbon 
than one brought from a more remote location, even when considering transport-related carbon. A process￾based analysis reduced the project's embodied carbon by one-third through the adoption of low-carbon 
materials. 
An embodied carbon analysis visualization tool was developed and adopted during the project's design stage 
to highlight the most significant carbon impacts and verify compliance with rating systems.

(a) Low-embodied carbon design solutions—timber roofs 
Efficient design and engineering can have a huge impact on carbon emissions without changing the 
architecture or construction materials and methods that are used. The dimensions of the grid of columns that 
support concourse floors is a key driver of CO,. Smaller grids use less material and lead to lower emissions of 
CO, but may have less flexibility especially around planning airport equipment like baggage handling systems, 
security lanes and check-in positions. Roof geometry is another key area. A roof shape that is naturally 
vaulted can be designed using a much smaller amount of material and can save thousands of tons of CO). 
Timber roof structure can be very light and efficient as well as beautiful. The timber itself is a relatively low￾carbon option in construction and its use can lead to the replanting of forests, which will sequester carbon 
over the coming decades as they grow to maturity.

The project's goal is to increase the flexibility and resilience of Portland International Airport's core terminal, 
through a rebuild and expansion project that will improve the user experience and sustainability by 
incorporating natural materials. An arrangement of plywood panels is being used to create one of the largest 
roofs made entirely of mass timber. The use of locally sourced and responsibly harvested wood instead of 
steel for the roof structure results in 7% embodied carbon savings and analysis also indicates that if timber is 
sourced from a sustainably managed forest there would be a saving of up to 17% of embodied carbon. 
Example: Terminal 2, Oslo Airport 
The project involved the extension of the main terminal and the new construction of a pier. Timber was used 
for the roof to meet environmental requirements, and to align the design with the existing terminal's 
Scandinavian design elements and allow natural lighting. As a result, Oslo Airport is one of the world's first 
airports to be ranked as “excellent” under the BREEAM environmental certification scheme, and the extension 
is considered one of the world's greenest terminals with carbon emissions reduced by 35 percent while 
doubling the airport's capacity. 
(b) Low-carbon solutions—earthworks 
In large-scale infrastructure projects, earthworks are often a major contributor to carbon emissions due to the 
large volume of material that needs to be excavated, transported and recompacted. This can be reduced by 
considering earthworks movements during design and developing solutions that balance the cut and fill 
volumes on site and minimize the amount of material moved both within and to and from the site.

IATA Airport Environmental Sustainability 
Example: Second Runway-Sabiha Gékcen Airport, Istanbul 
Advanced 3D modelling software was used to calculate cut and fill works, as well as tunnel alignment plans 
and slope stability calculations. Engineers could then determine the most economical and sustainable option 
for the site. The fill requirements were reduced by approximately 50% by proposing a lower runway elevation 
and staggering the runway, while the total earthworks cost was reduced by approximately 25%. 
2.4.4.1.3. Embodied Carbon in Mechanical, Electrical and Plumbing Systems 
Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) systems can have significant embodied carbon—the emissions 
associated with the extraction, production and transport of materials and products, and their repair, 
replacement, disassembly, and disposal. MEP components are often made with metal, which can have a high 
embodied carbon. The metal supply chain can also be complex and involve many manufacturing processes 
and long transport distances. 
Environmental product declarations (EPDs) are a standard way of expressing embodied carbon and other 
environmental impacts throughout the lifecycle of a product. There is a lack of easily accessible embodied 
carbon emissions data associated with MEP products. Very few manufacturers have published EPDs, due to 
the complexity of the manufacturing processes, but also because incentives from the market and regulators 
are absent. 
The Charted Institution of Building Services Engineers (CIBSE), based in London, has published guidance 
(TM65 for engineers and consultants) on how to calculate and cut down the embodied carbon associated with 
MEP systems in buildings. 
Embodied carbon emissions associated with building services design can be lowered by implementing simple 
design strategies. The most effective way to reduce the embodied carbon of MEP systems is to “design them 
out”, or at least reduce the use and weight of the equipment. Once this has been done, the embodied carbon 
of MEP plant can be further reduced by specifying equipment with: 
¢ Low global warming potential (GWP) refrigerant and leakage rates 
° Long lifetimes 
e Materials with low embodied carbon 
e Products and components that can be demounted and reused 
e Products that can be disassembled, and whose materials can be recycled. 
e MEP systems should be easily accessible for inspection, maintenance, and replacement. 
Reference Documents 
CIBSE (2020). CIBSE TM65. Embodied Carbon of Building Services Equipment 
CIBSE-Building Services Knowledge

2.4.4.2 Energy Sources and Conservation 
One of the biggest sources of airport emissions is from the energy generated to operate the airport. Airport 
facilities are intensively used and, therefore, have a high energy footprint. Not only do airports operate 
around-the-clock throughout the year, but they have many types of energy uses that are typically not found in 
other types of infrastructure, such as: 
e Airport landside (passenger terminals): lighting, heating, cooling, baggage handling systems (BHSs), 
moving walkways, elevators, and escalators 
e Airport airside: airfield lighting, fixed electrical ground power, pre-conditioned air at aircraft stands, GSE 
and other vehicle charging, maintenance hangars and firefighting services 
An energy audit can help an airport operator understand energy usage and make strategic choices about 
energy sources and efficiency technologies. 
Airports can reduce GHG emissions by shifting to renewable sources. The energy needs of most airports are 
met by purchasing energy from the local utility. The utilities may offer the option to purchase clean power, 
such as wind power, as is done by Dallas Fort Worth International Airport. In addition, airports may choose to 
develop onsite renewable energy through solar (PV panels and solar hot water), biomass, small scale hydro 
and geothermal. Their applicability depends on the airport's local climatic conditions. 
Solar PV have been widely used at airports. The generated electricity can be used on site to reduce cost and 
reliance on the electricity grid, while excess electricity may be able to be fed back to the local grid. One of the 
advantages of solar is its modular construction, allowing the solar panels to be integrated into the airport 
landscape, either on building rooftops, in larger farms over unused airfield land, or elevated on canopy 
structures above surface car parking areas. It is recommended that engineering surveys be conducted to 
ensure that existing buildings can support additional wind and weight loads from such installations. 
Solar facilities can, however, infringe on protected airspace if located too close to runways or block radar 
signals when located near such facilities. In addition, the smooth surface of solar panels can produce glare 
that can hamper control towers and aircraft when landing. There have been improvements in finishes that 
reduce glare from PV installations, however, early-stage simulations will ensure the correct locations, 
arrangements, and tilt of the proposed systems meets requirements. Safety risk assessments should be 
performed, and operational impacts should be assessed before installation of any renewable energy source. 
Wind turbines are not commonly used in airport projects due to potential interference with aircraft operations 
and communication systems due to their height. Wind turbine installations need to be assessed on an 
individual basis regarding both their power potential and compatibility with aeronautical operations. 
Biomass could be a viable renewable energy solution depending on the availability of feedstock supply. 
Biomass boilers usually provide heat that is used in the airport for space and water heating and can also be 
coupled with absorption chillers to provide cooling. 
192 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 212===
ray 
ae i 
IATA Airport Environmental Sustainability 
Geothermal systems can provide both heating and cooling. In certain locations, deep geothermal can reach 
higher temperatures that can be used to drive a turbine and produce electricity. For heating and cooling 
applications, most of the system is underground and will not interfere with any aircraft operations. When used 
in cooling mode, the system can inject heat in the ground and negate the need for cooling towers, which will 
lead to energy and water savings. Desktop studies and test bore holes will need to be made pre-construction 
to ensure the geological conditions are suitable, and the ground can provide the heating and cooling required 
for the airport. 
Stockholm Arlanda Airport has used such an aquifer thermal energy system to help cool facilities in the 
summer and heat them in the winter. The airport has been able to reduce its annual energy use by 19 
gigawatt-hours (GWh), which is equivalent to the energy used by 2,000 single-family homes.

Example: Renewable Energy—Cochin International Airport, India 
In 2005, Cochin Airport became the first airport to be powered solely from solar energy. Cochin installed a 
12 MWp solar PV plant in an area of approximately 45 acres near the international cargo complex. This 
system was added to an existing 1 MWp capacity that was installed earlier, partly on the roof and partly on 
the ground near the hangar. A further 5.1 MWp was installed on the car parking area with plans to install 
more on top of the irrigation canal. The systems operate without any battery storage and are connected to the 
grid to sell surplus electricity not consumed on site, and to buy electricity as needed, especially at night. 
Example: Renewable Energy—Kuwait International Airport, Kuwait 
A new terminal at the Kuwait International Airport is being developed with many sustainability features. In 
addition to roof lights designed to bring light deep into the terminal, much of the roof is covered with PV 
panels. The airport is expected to have the largest single rooftop PV installation with a nominal capacity of 
29 MWp. Kuwait International Airport is targeting LEED Gold certification.

Example: Solar PV panels—Abu Dhabi International Airport 
Another example can be found at Abu Dhabi International Airport where a 3 MWp solar array comprising 
7,542 solar PV panels is shading the short-term car park at Midfield Terminal. Apart from providing shading,

sections of the airport, saving 5,300 metric tons of CO, per year. 
2.4.4.2.1 Energy Storage and Resilience 
Energy storage systems can provide a storage medium for excess energy generation that can then be used 
when needed. This leads to significant environmental benefits by reducing distribution losses, and financial 
benefits by utilizing the generated energy when tariffs offered by utilities are high during peak demand. 
A common energy storage medium for renewably generated electricity is electrochemical batteries. 
Electrochemical batteries (e.g., lithium-ion—Li-ion) are a proven and stable technology. Costs associated with 
energy storage systems are gradually decreasing. 
194 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 214===
Se RY p IATA a Airport Environmental Sustainability 
Thermal energy storage for building operations has been around longer and is more cost-effective than 
batteries for airports that have a significant heating and cooling load. Generating chilled water at night when 
electricity is usually less expensive and storing it until the next day can provide operating cost savings and 
allow for a smaller electrical service overall, offering construction cost savings when planning a new system. 
The sizing of the energy storage system should be based on the size of the generation system and the 
airport's energy demand. Energy/cost analyses should be performed at design stages to ensure the energy 
storage system is optimally sized to increase utilization and reduce cost. 
Designers should consider the modularity of the system to ensure uninterrupted operation during 
maintenance. Additionally, potential future expansion of the energy storage system may be required to cater 
to the possible future electrification of traditionally fossil fuel-based airport systems. 
Energy storage systems can also be utilized for emergency services. Airports are generally required by local 
building codes to have an emergency power system to supply critical life safety systems such as fire pumps 
and fire lighting. Traditionally, most airports use diesel generators that, apart from the environmental impacts 
of burning fossil fuels, require several seconds to come online. The use of microgrids coupled with alternative 
forms of energy storage, such as batteries, can reliably and instantaneously provide back-up power. 
2.4.4.2.2. Energy Management through Smart Microgrid Systems 
A microgrid is a local airport energy system that can operate either in parallel with or separately from the utility 
supplier, providing their own energy production and load balancing to achieve stable operations. Microgrids 
include energy generation systems and energy storage systems to allow for flexibility in peak conditions and 
optimum energy and cost efficiency in normal operation. Smart grids provide advanced infrastructure and two￾way communication to ensure an economically efficient, sustainable power system with low losses and high 
levels of quality, plus security of supply and safety. 
Renewable energy generation can be more efficiently utilized by smart grid networks, where most of the 
generated energy is used on site, by managing local distribution. Such a system increases energy security in 
case of storms or other events that may affect the reliability of electricity supply. Data collection from smart 
grids can be used for optimizing energy distribution and smooth operation.

2.4.4.3 Operational Energy Verification and Optimization 
There are various guides and methodologies available that provide information on how to evaluate operational 
energy more fully and accurately at the design stage. These types of tools can be used to estimate the 
operational energy demands of a building and the approximate costs. 
Allowances should be made for all anticipated energy consumption in the building, including process load. 
Benchmark values for unknown components can be used until more detailed information is available. 
Normalized values can be utilized on either a million passengers per annum (MPPA) basis or by area, 
whichever is more applicable to the value that is being estimated. For example, building heating and cooling 
should be based on area, but a BHS-benchmarked value should be on MPPA.

e CIBSE (2022). TM54: Evaluating Operational Energy Performance of Buildings at the Design Stage

2.4.4.3.1 Plan for Post-occupancy Evaluation 
To enable successful project delivery, the client and the design team should establish clear goals and key 
performance indicators (KPIs) that will be assessed during the post-occupancy phase. KPIs can include 
environmental parameters (energy or water use), indoor environmental quality or occupant satisfaction. During 
the design, the team should clearly define what data will be collected, at what frequency, and how it will be 
used to improve the building's performance. During the construction and pre-handover phase, the team 
should review quantitative performance targets, check commissioning records, train future operators, and 
compile guides for end-users and facilities management teams. During the initial operating period, members 
of the design team should be on site to ensure information and support are provided to the end users and 
initial “teething” issues are addressed quickly. 
2.4.4.3.2 Post-Occupancy Evaluation 
Many buildings do not perform as planned, either in terms of running costs, staff and client satisfaction, 
health, safety, or comfort. Post-occupancy evaluation (POE) is the process of obtaining feedback on a 
building's in-use performance. It is typically tailored around three main topics: operational performance, indoor 
environmental quality, and occupant satisfaction. 
196 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 216===
IATA Airport Environmental Sustainability 
The value of POEs is being increasingly recognized and is becoming mandatory on many public projects. 
Energy use can be analyzed through: 
e Utility invoices and meter readings 
e Analysis of metering and controls strategy 
e Equipment surveys 
e Ventilation, heating, cooling, and lighting strategy 
Best practices include the “initial aftercare”, where design team representatives are present on site, carry out 
walkabouts, communicate with end users, provide support to the facilities team and record lessons learned. 
POEs are suggested to last for three years. In Year 1, problems are identified, training provided and systems 
fine-tuned, with regular reviews. In years 2 and 3, performance is reviewed and post-occupancy surveys 
carried out, but with reviews becoming less frequent.

2.4.4.4 Minimizing Operational Energy Demand at the Terminal Design Stage 
There are some basic principles that can enhance the environmental performance of a passenger terminal 
design. Firstly, a terminal should be planned with resilience and flexibility in mind. It is recommended to use a 
modular approach so infrastructure can be quickly altered or converted depending on the actual traffic 
development. Secondly, how a terminal will be operated (concept of operations) and the level of automation 
that will be used will be an important determinant of the building's utilization, efficiency, and ultimately its 
required size and design. 
Another consideration is the terminal's layout and location. The physical distances between areas should be 
reduced to the extent possible. The terminal's location should minimize taxi distances from the gate or stand 
to runways and taxiways to reduce fuel consumption and emissions of taxiing aircraft. 
The orientation, layout and location of a passenger terminal will influence the solar gains and heat losses. 
Westerly and easterly exposures are usually associated with excess solar heat gains and glare issues due to 
the angle of the sun. These orientations might require vertical or horizontal shading elements to reduce solar 
gains and help mitigate glare issues. The facade glazing ratio should be rationalized to provide a balance 
between daylight, views, glare potential and heat gains/losses. 
Facades can be easily shaded by overhangs that can also provide rain protection while still allowing natural 
light into the terminal. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 197 

===PAGE 217===
ay 7 
Se IATA a Airport Development Reference Manual 
Energy modelling at the design stage can provide a balanced solution and optimize the use of glass on the 
facades. Larger expanses of glass can be shaded to protect from excessive heat gains and the use of solar 
control glass can provide even further protection. In cooler climates, the use of low-e glass can protect from 
heat loss and help mitigate local discomfort and downdraft issues from exposed glass. 
Airport buildings tend to have deep floor areas. To further enhance daylighting potential, the use of skylights 
can help bring natural light into the building and provide a visually comfortable space. Skylights can also be 
utilized in smoke extraction strategies. Skylights, however, can lead to excessive solar heat gains, so 
daylighting calculations should be performed at the design stage to optimize the location and number of 
skylights provided. 
Thermal mass can help regulate interior temperatures by providing a buffer for heat to be absorbed, retained, 
and released at a slower rate. Thermal mass can help reduce peak demand for both heating and cooling and 
creates a more comfortable environment. Nighttime cooling can help recharge the thermal mass in hotter 
climates, either naturally or mechanically, with limited energy input. In climates where more heating is 
required, thermal mass should be preheated to reduce peak heating demand and provide extra comfort. 
Depending on the climate, natural ventilation can provide significant energy savings. Careful consideration of 
the air inlets to avoid lower air quality should be considered. The use of stack effect (chimney effect) can take 
advantage of airports’ typically high floor/ceiling heights to drive the natural movement of air through the 
terminal, picking up heat and naturally exhausting it. 
A building's form can greatly influence the need for heating and cooling. Highly compact buildings are easier 
to heat and condition. Compact buildings have reduced surface areas in contact with excess heat, cold and 
air infiltration. Compact buildings also provide benefits in air pressurization requirements as lower volumes are 
easier to control using mechanical systems. 
Airport buildings have large roof areas compared to the treated floor area. Heat gains and losses from the 
roof will play a significant role in the environmental loads that the building will need to deal with using 
mechanical systems, so reducing both heat gains and losses will result in improved thermal and energy 
performance. Sufficient insulation will need to be installed to avoid excess heat losses and gains through 
conduction. Further improvements can be realized by providing roof finishes that reflect heat gains from the 
sun and radiate any solar gains to the sky (high solar reflectance/high emissivity). This will not only 
significantly reduce cooling demand and strain on the mechanical systems, but also help mitigate potential 
heat island effect issues and improve the outdoor thermal comfort of the adjacent airport spaces. A green 
roof, with a vegetative layer grown on the rooftop can also lower heat absorption and the heat island effect.

Source: Foster + Partners 
A careful selection of solar control glazing coupled with a deep overhang provides natural light and views to 
the outside, while reducing solar gains and the need for mechanical cooling. The daylighting strategy is 
coupled with openings in the roof that have been strategically located to allow daylight to penetrate the 
furthest reaches of the building. Skylights provide optimum daylight uniformity when their number has been 
rationalized to reduce unnecessary solar gains in the space. 
Amman's climate experiences high diurnal temperatures, with summer temperatures that vary markedly 
between daytime and nighttime. The building is constructed entirely from concrete. The high thermal mass of 
the material provides passive environmental control, allowing the mass of building to act as a thermal battery 
and absorb heat throughout the day when the ambient temperatures are high and release it at night when the 
temperatures drop significantly. This saves energy and produces a better indoor environment for users.
