2.4.4.5 Active Strategies to Minimize Terminal Energy Demand 
Energy consumption needs to be understood to manage its use. Simple tools such as “sub-metering” allow an 
airport to identify, track and address areas of high energy use and thus correct inefficiencies. Computer￾controlled “smart building” technologies will automatically track energy uses and adjust temperature or lighting 
controls as needed. Older buildings often lack meters and must undertake retrofit projects to gain this 
important data. 
Frequently, the most expedient and economically feasible way for an airport to make an impact on reducing 
energy related GHG emissions is through the implementation of energy conservation measures. These 
include the choice of an appropriate temperature setpoint, maximum utilization of natural ventilation, usage of 
heating/cooling strategies, proper thermal insulation, and HVAC management systems. 
HVAC systems are generally responsible for a large share of the energy consumed in an airport building. 
Careful system selection can help optimize and reduce the amount of energy consumed. Local climatic 
conditions should be investigated at early design stages to understand the impact that energy efficiency 
measures (EEM) will have on operational energy demand. 
200 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 220===
=e 
IATA Airport Environmental Sustainability 
2.4.4.5.1 HVAC System Selection 
Efforts to reduce energy use and the associated emissions that come from it will often focus on improving 
HVAC system efficiency. Airport buildings have several distinguishing characteristics when compared to other 
commercial buildings. HVAC system selection should take these parameters into consideration. 
Airport buildings are characterized by high floor-to-ceiling heights and rarely have more than a couple of 
levels above the ground floor. To ensure optimal energy efficiency, an HVAC system should be selected that 
provides comfortable conditions to the occupied volume without having to treat the whole volume of the 
building. Low-level supply systems, such as displacement ventilation and under-floor air distribution systems, 
provide comfortable conditions without needing to treat all the air. 
In cases where these systems are not applicable, well-designed high-velocity jet diffuser systems can be 
utilized. Energy and air flow simulations should be performed at the design stages to ensure optimum energy 
efficiency and comfortable occupied level conditions. The locations and arrangement of the inlets and outlets 
need to be carefully designed to ensure optimal use of treated air. 
Airport buildings are also characterized by high occupancy density, which leads to high sensible and latent 
loads (high humidity and heat). Treatment of these loads, especially the latent loads, relies on dehumidified 
air in large quantities. HVAC systems should be able to provide treated air efficiently and turn down the 
volume of air when loads are lower. 
2.4.4.5.2 Economizers (Free Cooling) 
Air-side economizers (ASE) work by allowing more outside air into the building instead of recirculating the 
reconditioned air when external ambient conditions are favorable. During full economizer mode, the chiller can 
completely switch off. ASE can lead to substantial energy savings, especially in temperate and dry climates. 
Water-side economizers (WSE) use cooled water to indirectly cool indoor space. Waterside economizers 
have advantages over airside economizers as they are not directly subject to outdoor air conditions, waterside 
economizers can provide longer operating hours and better humidity control. 
2.4.4.5.3 Heat Recovery 
Given the large amount of air that needs to be treated for conditioning of an airport, heat recovery can be 
used for building heat or hot water and lower energy use. Heat recovery is the process of collecting and re￾using heat that is generated from any process where the heat would otherwise be lost. Opportunities for heat 
recovery should be considered in the building design. 
2.4.4.5.4 Demand-Controlled Ventilation 
Demand-controlled ventilation automatically adjusts the ventilation rate provided to a space in response to 
changes in conditions, such as occupant number or indoor pollutant concentration. This can lead to 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 201 

===PAGE 221===
IATA sul Airport Development Reference Manual 
substantial energy savings as the amount of treated air that is supplied to the space fluctuates based on 
demand. The control of the system usually relies on CO, or occupancy sensors. For larger spaces, CO, 
sensors are required to ensure good environmental air quality. 
2.4.4.5.5 Displacement Ventilation 
Air is introduced closer to the floor in multiple locations and the fresh air pushes the warm air up, creating a 
layer of cool air near the ground for people to move around in, while the upper layer of air can remain warm. 
The benefits include reduced energy requirements and improved air quality. 
Example: Displacement Ventilation-Norman Mineta San Jose International Airport, US 
A displacement ventilation system was selected for Norman Mineta San Jose International Airport. Air is 
provided at low levels through small binnacles and from underneath the seats, removing the need for floor 
diffusers. The low velocity and temperature system avoids drafts and local discomfort issues while also being 
energy efficient compared to an overhead mixing system. The airport is LEED certified (Silver). 
2.4.4.5.6 Temperature Settings 
Significant energy savings can be made by changing temperature setpoints while still providing comfortable 
conditions in the buildings. The transient use of several space typologies allows for more flexible setpoints. 
Consideration should be given to the system design in the early stages to ensure the system will run 
efficiently when relaxed setpoints are used, as some systems do not perform optimally at lower loads than 
their design conditions. The HVAC system should be sized to meet the peak demand and consider capacity 
requirements for a booster mode. 
2.4.4.5.7 Artificial Lighting Optimization 
Optimizing lighting design, operation and controls can yield significant savings in electricity consumption. 
Additionally, it can reduce the heat gains in the space, resulting in further energy savings. 
Efficient lighting luminaires and fittings can reduce energy consumption without sacrificing the visual quality of 
the space. Pale-colored surfaces will reflect light more efficiently and make the space appear to be better lit. 
Staff and operational areas can have task lighting installed, which will provide sufficient illumination levels for 
tasks while maintaining minimum required light levels in the rest of the areas. Individual task lighting control, 
either automatic or manual, can further reduce electricity consumption. 
Daylighting sensors can reduce the lighting power consumption in areas where there is access to daylight. 
Timers and automatic control can eliminate instantaneous changes in daylight levels and provide comfort. 
202 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 222===
=e IATA al Airport Environmental Sustainability 
Presence detection systems in specific areas, such as bathrooms and corridors, and automated lighting 
control systems linked to operations, such as flight schedules, can further reduce lighting energy by switching 
off or dimming spaces with no occupancy. 
2.4.4.5.8 Efficient Equipment Selection 
Process loads in airports are a significant energy consumption contributor. These are typically high-power 
machines that are in frequent use throughout operational hours, so design and efficient operation have a 
significant impact on an airport's energy performance. 
(a) Escalators and Travelators 
Horizontal and vertical transportation systems should be optimized for energy efficiency. Most of the energy 
consumed in escalators and travelators are for their motors. Consider several measures from design and 
during operation to reduce energy requirements. High-efficiency motors can run with lower consumption and 
less generated heat. Most motors are installed to serve peak capacity and run inefficiently at lower volumes. 
Secondary motors can match lower load. Motor efficiency controllers (MEC) also improve part-load efficiency. 
Regenerative drives can also recover some of the energy in downward movements (escalators). Intermitted 
drives will reduce speed when passengers are not present bringing further energy reductions. 
(b) Apron Lighting 
Apron lighting provides lighting for several operations, such as fueling, baggage loading/unloading, pre-flight 
checks and maintenance, all of which require high illumination levels. There are also challenges specific to 
apron lighting, such as luminaire locations which are usually one sided and long throw. There are now light￾emitting diode (LED) solutions that can be used instead of the high-intensity discharge (HID) systems that 
have been traditionally used. Current efficiency levels of LEDs surpass the HID systems and offer longer life, 
reducing the cost of replacement and maintenance time. Careful luminaire selection can also provide reduced 
light spillage to adjacent areas, glare control and good uniformity. Lighting simulations and calculations should 
be performed at early stages to ensure the solution is optimal. Large-scale mock-ups can also provide further 
information on the lighting design performance. 
Example: Apron Lighting—London Gatwick Airport, London, UK 
London Gatwick handles approximately 46 MPPA using a single runway. In 2017, the airport changed its 
existing sodium apron lighting system to an LED floodlights system. This resulted not only in energy savings 
of 40%, but also 50% increased lighting levels and better uniformity. In total, 867 sodium projectors were 
replaced by 561 LED floodlight projectors. 
(c) Baggage Handling System 
Baggage handling systems BHSs may consume a significant amount of the energy used at airports. It is, 
therefore, very important that these systems function as efficiently as possible. Unlike a conventional BHS 
that uses continuous conveyor belts, an individual carrier system (ICS) which are often used at larger airports. 
An ICS can split the BHS into 2.5m-long segments, each with its own motor. This means that if only one 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 203 

===PAGE 223===
=e | IATA al Airport Development Reference Manual 
baggage item is being carried by the BHS, instead of the entire conveyor belt having to move all the time to 
circulate that one object, only the individual segments move as and when the baggage item reaches them. No 
wasted energy from anything moving that doesn’t need to move. Carts and tracks can be added as required. 
New motor technologies, such as linear synchronous motors (LSM), reduce contact between moving parts 
and enhance efficiency. Tilt-tray sorters that make use of all available space and reduce the system size can 
efficiently run at different volumes of baggage. 
BHSs are designed to handle a specific peak volume of baggage. Measures should be taken to ensure 
energy is reduced when the volume is lower. These measures include the use of enhanced drives that can 
regulate the use of the BHS (start/stop) according to demand. A BHS-integrated screening systems can 
further optimize the baggage handling operation and increase efficiency. 
Example: Baggage Handling System—Helsinki International Airport, Finland 
Helsinki International Airport handles 350 departures per day serving 15 MPPA. During the expansion to 
Terminal 2 and renovation of Terminal 1, the BHS has been redesigned to include smart and energy-efficient 
measures, such as tilt-tray sorters, high-velocity totes-based systems with in-tote screening, and automatic 
intelligent control, which only engages the motor when baggage is approaching the belt. The system is served 
by LSMs that can save up to 75% of energy use compared to that of a traditional standard motor. 
2.4.4.6 Refrigerant Selection and Management 
Most airports will require the installation of cooling equipment, such as chillers and heat pumps, which rely on 
the use of refrigerants to provide cooling and/or heating. Refrigerants play a crucial role in ozone depletion 
and climate change. While ozone-depleting coolants called chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) have been phased 
out, their replacement, hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) have since been found to be thousands as times more 
potent than CO, in warming the planet. An international agreement (2016 Kigali Amendment to the Montreal 
Protocol) is now being implemented by many states to curb the production of HFCs, which are still widely 
used in air conditioners and refrigerators. Selection of equipment should ensure climate-friendly alternatives to 
HFC refrigerants are used. 
Designers should specify equipment that relies on refrigerants with low GWP. Higher GWP refrigerants will 
not only contribute more to climate change when leaks occur, but also procuring top-up refrigerant for the 
system will become increasingly difficult as refrigerants with higher GWP are phased out. Equipment should 
be periodically tested to ensure leak tightness is as prescribed. 
2.4.4.7 Reducing Carbon from Operational Energy Use—Airfield 
Airfield operational activities are another significant source of CO, emissions. Making improvements in this 
area can reduce utility costs, maintenance costs and emissions as well as improve asset performance. Airport 
planning decisions on operational infrastructure and measures can have an impact on the emissions of the 
airport and its users. 
204 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 224===
Se By IATA aa Airport Environmental Sustainability 
2.4.4.7.1 Airfield Design 
The design of an airport airfield has influence on aircraft CO, emissions. An efficient layout can optimize 
capacity and operational performance, while also reducing aircraft fuel burn and emissions. One kilogram of 
fuel burned results in 3.16 kg of CO,, so the efficiency of airfield operations has a significant impact on aircraft 
fuel burn and emissions. Aircraft ground operations can be expedited by: 
e — Siting runways, taxiways, and taxi lanes to facilitate shorter taxi and turnaround times 
e Using RETs and staggered departures to reduce runway occupancy times and decrease congestion 
e Using runway holding bays and bypass taxiways to facilitate aircraft flow and sequencing 
The design and features of the airfield will depend on the airport's size, type, traffic volumes as well as user 
expectations regarding optimal taxi and holding times. The size and shape of the airfield should be aligned 
with development plans for the terminal area. The airfield should not be designed in such a way that it 
constrains the future growth of the terminal area. 
2.4.4.7.2 Aircraft Fuel Systems 
An airport's fuel infrastructure also has a role to play in sustainability. Fuel hydrant systems can reduce the 
need for fuel trucks and the emissions they generate. However, these systems also require a significant 
investment and are best suited for larger airports with sufficient traffic movements and a need for efficient 
aircraft turnarounds. Where fuel trucks are used, alternative fuels such as biodiesel can be considered. 
Airports may also need to consider recent and future trends in aviation fuel. Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) 
is currently regarded as one of the most effective solutions for decarbonizing aircraft emissions and its use is 
being encouraged. The primary challenges for Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), scaling up feedstocks and 
production, will require industry collaboration and supportive government policies to bolster the supply chain. 
One of the positive aspects of SAF is that it is a drop-in fuel that meets the same technical standards as 
kerosene and can be incorporated into existing airport fuel systems without any significant changes to airport 
infrastructure. 
Research is being conducted on how to produce a viable form of SAF that is a power-to-liquid fuels. These 
fuels, known as e-fuels, can be synthesized from hydrogen (generated from green energy) and CO, taken 
from industrial, biomass or direct-air capture and are carbon neutral-the CO, emitted by combustion is the 
same amount captured and used in production of the fuel. E-fuels can be used in any existing aircraft via the 
existing jet-fuel infrastructure, but it will require massive amounts of renewable energy to produce the 
hydrogen, capture the CO, and convert them to liquid fuel. 
Intensive research is also under way on the development of next generation aircraft and engines that can 
provide zero-carbon solutions in the medium to long term. Small electric planes are already flying, but more 
research is needed to make the technology viable for most commercial flight. The challenge for passenger 
planes is creating electric batteries that are energy dense, yet light enough to be carried on board. Electric 
aircraft may eventually be used for regional commercial flights; therefore, airports will need to be aware of 
possible future electrical infrastructure requirements to support those operations. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 205 

===PAGE 225===
IATA pull Airport Development Reference Manual 
Hydrogen-powered propulsion for aircraft is a promising but longer-term prospect that needs to overcome 
many challenges before it can play an appreciable role in reducing aviation's carbon footprint. There are 
several ways that hydrogen may potentially be used in commercial aviation ranging from pressurized 
hydrogen and fuel cells in smaller, shorter-range commuter aircraft to liquid hydrogen and fuel cells for longer 
range regional aircraft. 
Hydrogen is difficult to handle and its use would necessitate new aircraft fleets and substantial infrastructure 
for its production, transport, storage, and distribution. This would require a significant amount of coordination 
among fuel companies, airlines, aircraft manufacturers, and airports to ensure infrastructure development and 
the introduction of these new aircraft types are synchronized. Any move to hydrogen will also require early 
planning at the airport level and several research projects are already underway to test concepts on the 
production, storage, transport, and distribution of hydrogen. 
For example, ACI World, in partnership with the Aerospace Technology Institute (ATI), is developing a study 
to help airports better understand the implications of hosting hydrogen aircraft including understanding the 
supply chain options for bringing hydrogen into and distributing around an airport. The study will highlight the 
safety, electrical energy, space, and infrastructure requirements of each option, and provides an initial 
assessment to bridge the gap between aviation and hydrogen/energy providers to try to better understand the 
challenges and solutions of zero-carbon emission aircraft at airports. 
2.4.4.7.3 Aircraft Parking Stand Electrification 
Aircraft parking stand systems can reduce airport noise and air pollution, including carbon emissions, from the 
use of aircraft APUs and diesel-powered ground power units (GPUs). 
The provision of fixed electrical ground power (FEGP) during pre-flight operations, boarding and maintenance 
is an alternative to using APUs and GPUs, which are noisy and generate significant levels of emissions, 
including particulates, that affect local air quality. In addition, pre-conditioned air (PCA) systems can cool, 
ventilate, and heat the cabin of parked aircraft. The combination of 400Hz FEGP and PCA eliminate the need 
to run the APU during an aircraft turnaround. 
Alternative systems for ground power and pre-conditioned air are available in various configurations: 
e Fixed-Installed on the apron next to the aircraft or inside a gatehouse 
e Bridge-mounted-Installed underneath a passenger boarding bridge 
e In-ground systems—Pop-up pits typically used at remote stands 
e¢ Mobile—Mounted on a self-propelled vehicle 
GPUs can be powered by fossil fuel engines or by electricity. Fossil fuel-driven units offer a good amount of 
flexibility to the airport, particularly for less frequently used remote stands. These units are much more 
efficient than APUs but still pollute. Battery-powered mobile electric GPUs offer a good alternative for remote 
stands. If PCA is required at the remote stands, electrical infrastructure needs to be installed to power a 
mobile electrically driven PCA unit. 
206 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 226===
Pay 
Se 
IATA Airport Environmental Sustainability 
A tool that can be used to measure and plan the infrastructure required to provide electricity to aircraft on the 
ground is the Aircraft Ground Energy System (AGES) Simulator. AGES-S evaluates both environmental and 
economic benefits of substituting the use of APUs by AGES by calculating the reduction of fuel consumption. 
It provides a snapshot of fuel savings and associated GHG emissions reduction, along with expected financial 
savings for aircraft and airport operators, based on a selected scenario and using the advanced APU 
emissions calculations in ICAO's Doc 9889 Airport Air Quality Manual (based on aircraft type, turnaround 
cycle and capacity, PCA needs, and others). 
2.4.4.7.4 Assisted Aircraft Taxiing 
The use of semi-autonomous, pilot-controlled, towbar-less tractors can reduce the need for aircraft to use 
their engines for ground movements around the airfield. These types of tractors are currently available in 
hybrid diesel-electric and pure electric versions. The employment of such vehicles reduces the amount of time 
that airplane engines need to be used during taxi operations, significantly reducing aircraft fuel usage and the 
risk of foreign object damage. It is important to keep in mind that aircraft still need to run engines 3-5 minutes 
prior to takeoff to warm up and on the inbound taxi journey 2-3 minutes is needed to thermally stabilize before 
switching off and connecting to such a device. 
To operate this service, minimal or no changes need to be made to the aircraft itself. However, there could be 
airport design and planning implications as additional taxi lanes and extra space close to the runway may be 
needed to position the tractors and enable them to connect with the aircraft before moving on to the gate. 
Example: Amsterdam Schiphol Airport 
Schiphol Airport carried out a trial of semi-robotic towbar-less tractors in March and August 2020 with Boeing 
737s (700 and 800). Results confirmed that fuel savings were about 50-65% compared to standard taxiing 
procedures and that local emissions of UFP and noise were greatly reduced. CO, and NOx emissions were 
also measured as 50% to 65% lower. Schiphol plans to be operating with fully sustainable taxiing by 2030. 
Reference Documents 
e Schiphol | Sustainable taxiing: Taxibot trial 
2.4.4.7.5 Airside Vehicle Fleet Decarbonization 
Another strategy to reduce environmental impact is to transition airport light-duty fleets and GSE to hybrid, 
100% electric or hydrogen fuel -cells with a progressive switch of heavy-duty vehicles/GSE to biofuels and 
eventually to electric or hydrogen-powered variants. 
For airside electrification, it is important to keep in mind that a reliable and continuous supply of electricity is 
critical to the smooth running of ground operations. This includes ensuring the required infrastructure, such as 
charging points, are put in the right places and connectors are standardized. The cost benefit analysis should 
consider the required infrastructure, maintenance, electricity as well as the operational impact such as the 
time to recharge. It is also important to understand whether and how the energy source is sustainable. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 207 

===PAGE 227===
=e | Tara a Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.4.5 Green Mobility 
Surface access is an essential part of an airport's operations; however, passenger and employee journeys as 
well as the transport of goods and freight can also contribute to local air pollution and CO, emissions. Airports 
need to consider strategies to mitigate the environmental effects of surface transport to and from the airport. 
This will likely include managing and integrating different modes of transport. 
2.4.5.1 Rail 
Rail transport is a low-carbon and high-capacity transport option for connecting airports to their direct markets, 
specifically where it serves city centers and significant passenger demand is concentrated. Rail connections 
to airports range from dedicated high-speed links, metro lines and extensions, light rail, and last-mile links 
such as automated people movers. The success of an airport rail link relies on a range of service factors: 
regional coverage, frequency, journey time, and hours of operation are all key factors driving passenger use. 
Air-Rail stations should be planned to be as close as possible to the terminals; in many cases, this is 
achieved using a tunnel to provide a station box under or adjacent to the main terminal or, where this is not 
possible, by providing accessible walkways or travellators to access terminal buildings from stations. Stations 
need to be adequately designed for airport passengers and easily identified and signposted. Where possible, 
best practice is to provide elevator capacity as this is the safest form of vertical transport for passengers with 
heavy luggage. Stations should be designed with clear information for passengers and a higher-than-normal 
number of ticketing facilities to cater to inbound visitors who need to purchase tickets. 
Example: Stockholm Arlanda Express, Sweden 
Arlanda Station at the airport serves the Arlanda Express to central Stockholm and regional rail services, with 
nearly 40% of passengers travelling by rail to and from the airport. Other notable examples of air-rail systems 
in Scandinavia can be found at Oslo and Copenhagen airports.

Example: Amsterdam Schiphol Airport, Netherlands 
Schiphol Station has direct services to most Dutch cities in addition to regional rail and a proposed metro 
extension. It is located under the main terminal building. Schiphol Station has 25 million users per year, 
making it the 6" busiest station in the Netherlands in 2019.

2.4.5.2. Bus and Coach 
Bus and coach transport represents a significant share of public transport at medium-sized airports and 
provides many regional links at larger airports. With a high level of energy efficiency and increasing levels of 
electrification, they can play a role in reducing air pollution and GHG emissions at the airport. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 209 

===PAGE 229===
iil Se 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
When compared to cars, buses and coaches can provide low-carbon transport for a range of journey 
purposes, providing connections to local communities and regions without the capital investment required for 
rail links. For airports without rail links, they can also provide high-capacity connections to city centers. 
Buses can also play an important role in encouraging airport workers to travel by public transport. Design for 
bus facilities needs to balance access to the road network and passenger access to the terminal with serving 
areas outside the main passenger terminals in the wider airport zone. 
Appropriate design will depend on the type of services offered. For high-frequency services, traditional island 
or perimeter bay bus stops may be the most appropriate, allowing buses to reduce dwell time and use less 
space. For longer distance coaches, where luggage needs to be unloaded from vehicles, reversing bays with 
waiting areas provided for passengers are more appropriate. These can be designed with secure pedestrian 
areas, meaning bus users are protected from the active highway. Where multiple routes are operating, 
providing passengers with realistic journey times and stand information will improve the passenger perception 
of bus and coach travel. 
2.4.5.3 Walking and Cycling 
Active modes of transport have the lowest carbon impact and can provide health and well-being 
improvements to airport workers, passengers, and neighbors. Traditionally not a mode associated with 
airports, many have begun to design safe access for pedestrians and cyclists and integrate these into local 
networks. 
Many cities have begun prioritizing walking, cycling and micro mobility (e.g., electric scooters) as a simple 
method of both decarbonizing transport and improving health outcomes. Airports are similarly beginning to 
see the benefits of improving non-motorized accessibility options. 
These improvements can, however, face significant barriers, with airports dealing with high levels of road 
traffic and many complex internal road layouts. Passengers also tend to have luggage, especially when 
travelling relatively long distances. Nevertheless, airports are increasingly seeing opportunities to encourage 
active travel for employees, lowering demand for car parking and reducing local traffic impacts. For these 
purposes, it is important to combine safe access to the airport on dedicated off-road walkways or cycle tracks 
with facilities for showering and securing of bicycles, etc. 
For passengers, airports can provide cycle hire and storage facilities to support those travelling by bicycle. 
Airports are also utilizing active travel to promote the wider use of the airport as a leisure facility with 
perimeter tracks and leisure cycling facilities supporting their commercial diversification. 
2.4.5.4 Mode Share Management 
With better data collection and active management of surface access, airports can play an active role in 
reducing their environmental and local impacts. Targets can be set and data provided to support investment 
and better understanding. 
210 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 230===
B— | IATA al Airport Environmental Sustainability 
Operators often have a very good understanding of the behavior of their customers once they have arrived at 
the airport, but a far more limited picture of the steps they took to get there. As well as working with local 
transport providers and other stakeholders to ensure high-quality, high-capacity public transport connections 
for passengers and staff, airports can optimize their surface access impacts and strategically grow their 
catchments through active monitoring and management of travel behavior and preferences. 
Meaningful targets, coupled with effective governance, can greatly reassure stakeholders and the public about 
other adverse impacts of airport operations (e.g., noise, air quality, GHG emissions). This means that 
monitoring and processing data, including from new sources such as mobile phones, will be a fundamental 
component of the management of airport assets, including car parking. The setting up of such systems is 
crucial to maximizing opportunities for sustainable travel in the medium to long term. 
Example: London Heathrow Airport 
In the context of its plans for a third runway, London's Heathrow Airport proposed a target of 50% of 
passengers arriving by public transport by 2030 and 55% by 2040. A substantial increase in data collection 
capability was planned to provide a granular understanding of the factors influencing mode choice, enabling 
targeted improvements in public transport provision and insights that support commercial planning. 
The UK government set Heathrow a target to demonstrate it could achieve a higher share of public transport 
use for both passengers and employees to reduce car trips of those driving to the airport. As part of this work, 
they conducted a perimeter test of how many vehicles entered the airport utilizing vehicle number plate data. 
Heathrow now produces a travel report that records how passengers travel to the airport and its progress 
towards surface access targets. 
2.4.5.5 Traffic Management 
The movement of passengers and goods by road can generate high levels of vehicle trips and congestion, 
which creates air pollution and carbon emissions. This can be mitigated by smoothing the traffic flows on the 
road network at and around the airport. 
In addition, positioning related infrastructure adjacent to the airport, close to the strategic road network, and 
instituting policies to manage this generally uncontrolled activity can significantly mitigate the negative impact 
of these essential journeys. The following traffic-related elements should also be considered. 
2.4.5.5.1. Managing Forecourts 
Forecourt design and operations can have a direct impact on vehicle flows and emissions. Forecourt access 
fees and commercial ground transportation contracts can be used to encourage the use of low-emission 
vehicles and/or discourage inefficient operations. While terminal forecourts reflect the dimensions of the 
terminal they serve, airport planners have several tools that can be used to encourage sustainable forecourt 
operations. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 211 

===PAGE 231===
See IATA wa Airport Development Reference Manual 
Configurations—Forecourts with four or more lanes can provide smoother flow and higher average speeds 
because they can better accommodate surges in demand (and the resulting double-parking) at key locations, 
such as doorways and curbside luggage check positions. Another design element that can improve vehicle 
speeds is to provide pedestrian bridges across forecourts. Where that is not possible, vehicle flow can be 
improved by minimizing the number of crosswalks and using crossing signals or control officers to gather 
pedestrians into groups that cross at one time. 
Allocation-Airports can improve the attractiveness of low-emission and/or higher occupancy access services 
by allocating them preferred forecourt curb space (e.g., space that minimizes walking distances to the 
terminal). However, such allocation may reduce the overall efficiency of the forecourt by impeding traffic flow. 
Contracts—Service agreements with transportation providers can be used to encourage the use of low- or 
zero-emissions vehicles (i.e., offering reduced access or parking fees), discourage excessive waiting and/or 
trips (i.e., excess dwell time and excessive trip fees), and discourage “dead-head” trips to or from the airport 
(.e., incentivize operators to both drop off and pick up passengers during a single trip to the airport). 
2.4.5.5.2 Car Parking 
When planning car parking, it can be beneficial to consider the ways in which car ownership trends and use 
may evolve, and design accordingly. In some locations an increasing number of passengers and staff are 
arriving at airports by public transport. Nevertheless, airport may still need to plan and develop additional 
parking if overall passenger growth more than offsets the shift toward public transport services. The growing 
adoption of electric vehicles means that a network of electric vehicle charging stations should be considered. 
In the future, the uptake of connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) might mean that even passengers 
with their own vehicles do not need to keep them at the airport when they travel, but CAVs will still need a 
place to unload or load passengers and the volumes may exceed the capacity of existing curbside facilities. 
Many airports now use terminal-adjacent structured car parking garages or surface lots for the loading and/or 
unloading of commercial ground transportation services, such as travel network companies (TNCs) and 
courtesy vans. Some airport car parking garages have ground floors designed to serve TNCs, hotel courtesy 
shuttles, and over-height vehicles, such as public transit buses. 
2.4.5.5.3 Freight 
The term “freight” is generally associated with air cargo, but also includes mail, in-flight catering, retail goods, 
food and drink, waste, maintenance suppliers, and construction materials. Movement of these at airports can 
generate a significant number of vehicle trips and associated emissions. The negative impacts of these 
vehicle movements can be mitigated via a variety of best practice solutions. 
Cargo- and mail-related facilities should be positioned at locations that facilitate an unhindered flow of goods 
between the airfield and landside. Retail goods and construction- or maintenance-related materials can be 
routed via consolidation centers that also provide off-site storage, generally reducing vehicle trips by up to 
80%. Security screening should start upstream and be integrated into the supply chain so no additional steps 
212 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 232===
&, 
Se IATA ull Airport Environmental Sustainability 
or touchpoints are required. In-flight catering service providers can be co-located to enable the sharing of 
resources. During peak times, freight vehicle flow can be managed by using truck parking lots and mandatory 
slot bookings. Airports should encourage and support digital infrastructure to facilitate e-Freight which is an 
industry-wide initiative to build an end-to-end paperless process for air cargo through a regulatory framework, 
electronic messages and high data quality. 
2.4.5.6 Zero Emission Vehicles 
Zero-emission vehicles are now a credible alternative to ICE vehicles, provided that their electricity or other 
fuel source used to power the vehicle is generated from renewable or clean sources such as wind, solar, 
hydroelectric, or nuclear. Both battery electric and hydrogen fuel cell vehicles can be adopted for airside and 
landside operations 
2.4.5.6.1 Introducing Zero-emission Vehicles into an Airport Environment 
The key to the successful adoption of a zero-emission vehicle is first to fully understand the duty cycle of the 
vehicle that is being replaced. The duty cycle incorporates factors such as the mileage between charging 
opportunities and the ambient temperature as well as the vehicle speed of operation, together with any 
additional power demands, such as hydraulic pumps or air conditioning. Once this has been established, in 
the case of a battery electric vehicle (EV), the required battery capacity and charging regime as well as the 
impact of charging on the airport's primary power supply can be determined. Battery electric alternatives are 
now available across most vehicle classes. Recent declines in the cost of battery packs have made the total 
cost of ownership of a battery EV comparable to or better than an ICE equivalent. 
Reference Documents 
The Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET) Code of Practice: Electrical Vehicle Charging Equipment 
Installation, 4" Edition 
e |ET Codes and Guidance (theiet.org) 
2.4.5.6.2 Enablers and Technologies 
The choice available for zero-emission vehicles is growing steadily as more manufacturers bring products to 
market and increase competition. It is important to keep in mind that a reliable and continuous supply of 
electricity is critical if recharging points are to be provided. 
Other enablers of this technology are also important. Battery technology has developed to the point where an 
EV battery can be substantially recharged in under 30 minutes using rapid charging stations. 
Another enabler is the provision of hydrogen fueling stations. These service hydrogen fuel cell powered EVs, 
which also have zero emissions. This technology is attractive as the vehicle tank may be charged with 
hydrogen in three to four minutes, enabling a journey of up to 400 miles. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 213 

===PAGE 233===
we IATA i Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.4.5.6.3 Designing for Landside User Groups 
In addition to airside vehicles for airport operations, landside users will increasingly require facilities to support 
the charging of their own EVs. The provision of EV charging needs to be tailored to the user group to be most 
effective. Broadly, there are five landside user groups: passengers, workers, taxis, buses, and freight. 
Passengers, employees, and taxis present the greatest opportunity for surface access carbon savings due to 
the higher levels of emissions they generate. 
Airport workers’ vehicles present a substantial opportunity for carbon savings. Airports have utilized 
discounted pricing and the supply of dedicated EV charging facilities at employee car parking lots to 
encourage their use. Taxis present a similar opportunity for charging with vehicles frequently using the airport 
queuing systems and staging lots. Airports can provide dedicated fast charging to support taxi operations, 
particularly in staging lots. 
Airports can design car parking with future trends in mind and develop parking models that support EVs. With 
power management systems, multiple spaces can be electrified and charging can be efficiently/smartly 
managed for a relatively affordable cost assuming that the user bears the cost and not the airport. 
Cumulatively, however, the supporting electrical infrastructure can be costly and should be considered early 
on in planning, to ensure local switchgear/substations are appropriately sized. 
For public transport and freight, airport facilities will need to be developed in coordination with transport 
providers to ensure these are integrated into long-term proposals for vehicle design. For freight, the options 
are likely to be more diverse, with hydrogen potentially playing a greater role for larger vehicles. 
2.4.5.7 Future Proofing Mobility 
Future proofing the provision of mobility at airports requires consideration of the changing context within which 
airports will operate, which will be quite different from today. This transition has already begun and may 
include: 
¢ Greater emphasis on public transport 
¢ Sustainable transport technologies such as electric and hydrogen-powered vehicles 
¢ Increased focus on recovery from disruptions including those caused by climate change 
Passengers’ expectations will continue to change with access to the latest mobility options, and with 
expectations of better integration between modes, designs that better integrate single journeys between 
ground transport and aviation may need to be considered. Increasingly, carbon emissions will become more 
important in consumer choices and airports will need to provide clearly sustainable options. 
COVID-19 has also demonstrated that greater flexibility may be needed in a more unstable future, with 
facilities that can be adapted as they are required to respond to new trends and requirements.

2.4.5.7.1_ Future Proofing Mobility for Automation 
CAVs and EVs will present some challenging implications for operations within the airport environment as well 
as some significant opportunities. These types of vehicles are already in operation at many airports 
worldwide. As their capabilities and rate of adoption develop, they will have a considerable impact on the 
airside and landside environment of airports, and on airport investment programs and business models. With 
electric powertrains, these vehicles will be used to transport people and goods and to service aircraft. 
The crucial difference between the airside and landside environments is that the adoption of autonomy airside 
will be subject to the control of the airport operator, while landside autonomy will happen with or without the 
airport's involvement. It can be expected that autonomous vehicles will enter airside service much more 
rapidly than landside as the airside is a controlled, self-contained environment. 
2.4.6 Resources Management 
The conservation and protection of natural resources is another important element of airport sustainability. 
Resource management ranges from the conservation of the local environment and natural resources such as 
water and land, to the reduction, reuse, and recycling of waste. 
2.4.6.1 Water 
Airports rely on the local availability of water for their own activities, including: 
© Cleaning and maintenance of infrastructure and equipment 
e Irrigation of grassed areas and landscapes 
° Hospitality facilities for passengers, staff and tenants 
e Operation of utilities 
e Firefighting services and systems 
Water is a finite resource and many parts of the world suffer from water scarcity. The effects of climate 
change have exacerbated the problem; therefore, water use must be considered carefully. Water 
management must be approached from a local perspective, considering aspects like the climate, the 
watershed where the airport is located, sharing between different users, and other aspects that can vary 
depending on the airport context. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 215 

===PAGE 235===
Se 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
The ICAO Eco-Airport Toolkit e-publication on water management (reference below) explores how airports 
can consider water in three primary ways: supply, handling capacity, and disposal. It also includes several 
examples of actions implemented by airports. 
2.4.6.1.1 Build a Water Strategy 
The development of a water management strategy will allow airport operators to identify the water uses and 
users to create a water footprint baseline and establish the most appropriate goals to be achieved through the 
implementation of different measures. The strategy will also assess the suitability of the potential measures 
identified to reach the defined goals and provide a draft action plan for their implementation. 
The first step in developing a water management strategy is to generate the airport water footprint baseline; in 
summary, how much, where, when, and how water is used. Even airports located in regions where water use 
is not constrained are encouraged to undertake this type of water audit so they will be ready to respond more 
effectively to any change in current water availability and conditions that could emerge from, for example, new 
water policies or regulations, or climate change effects. 
Regarding different airport facilities, as some are not under the airport's control, it is crucial to involve all the 
airport stakeholders, tenants and third parties, not only to generate the most comprehensive baseline, but 
also to involve them in definition of the targets to be pursued, the subsequent measures to be undertaken, 
and the associated action plan. 
Water management measures should be considered early in the airport design and development process. 
Consideration should be given to the geographic location and vulnerability to potential flooding or rising sea 
levels. Water infrastructure, such as drains and culverts, can be incorporated into the airport or airfield to 
protect against flooding, while many features can be put in place to reduce consumption of water, such as 
harvesting rainwater and using low-flow fixtures. 
KPIs should be defined early in the process as this will allow the airport operator to quantify and monitor 
specific parameters and the performance of the strategy. Examples of KPls for water use include: 
e Water consumption by facility area 
¢ Per capita water consumption by passenger, employee, tenant 
¢ Water consumption reduction target per annum

2.4.6.1.2 Reduce Water Consumption 
Water is consumed at airports for different purposes at terminal buildings, airport offices, airport tenants’ 
facilities as well as for maintenance activities and various aviation support services. Apart from the cost of the 
large amount of water an airport uses, there is a considerable consumption of energy associated with its 
distribution, treatment, and disposal. Thus, reducing water consumption, apart from conserving this invaluable 
natural resource, will help airports lower costs and reduce their energy and CO, footprint. 
A potential first step would be to identify the water wasted by the airport. This can be undertaken when the 
airport is generating its water footprint baseline, by installing water meters at high water use elements or, 
independently, through a specific audit and the use of detection systems to find leaks and reduce water 
losses. 
Once the existing leaks have been fixed, the second step would be to increase the water-efficiency of fixtures, 
systems, and equipment, especially those involved in high-consumption uses. Some solutions that can be 
implemented across different airport water usage areas are: 
e Landscape—Drought-tolerant and native plantations, drip irrigation systems, weather-based irrigation 
control sensors 
e Restrooms and kitchens—Low-flush toilets and urinals, low-flow pre-rinse spray valves, faucets with 
motion sensors and aerators 
© Utilities and maintenance—Water-efficient cooling towers, high-efficiency water pumps, increased 
number of valves in the fire suppression piping system 
Another way to reduce water consumption, complementary to the technical solutions considered above, is to 
change how water is used at the airport, for example: 
© Airport operations—Less frequent vehicle fleet washing, aircraft dry-wash and zonal cleaning, capture 
water used during fire suppression tests 
e User behavior—Water use educational programs for airport staff and partners, campaigns for passengers 
to increase water-saving awareness and to report leaks to maintenance staff, free water audits for 
stakeholders, promotion of contests, visits and other events related to water conservation 
In addition, on-going monitoring is key to ensure a system or element, existing or new, is working as 
expected, allowing the airport operator to identify high water demand processes and detect leaks and any 
mistakes during installation, as well as any degradation over time during operation. An asset management 
tracking system will help monitor the condition of a fixture and its deterioration rate and will also help to 
forecast when replacement is required.

2.4.6.1.3. Recycle, Reclaim and Reuse Wastewater 
In general, wastewater is divided into black or gray water, depending on whether it has been in contact with 
fecal matter (black) or not (gray). In the airport sector, and in addition to black and gray water, blue water 
refers to sanitary wastewater generated by commercial aircraft. 
Regardless of the types of wastewater, recycling, reclaiming and reusing it is a further step in the 
conservation of water resources, as a disposable waste is converted into a resource, reducing both airport 
costs and waste burdens. Depending on the wastewater characteristics, appropriate treatment is needed prior 
to providing airports with an alternative to conventional water supply for a range of uses. At this point, it is 
essential to engage with the relevant authorities to ensure compliance with regulations. 
Although there is some hesitancy among some to the reuse of wastewater, it is important to note that water is 
continuously reused through its own natural cycle, and the reality is that an increasing number of different 
users around the world are using reclaimed water as an alternative source to conventional water supplies for 
a range of applications, integrating reclaimed water for non-potable uses (in most cases). Wastewater can be 
used for potable purposes. However, the requirements and processes will be much more stringent and 
expensive than for other uses; therefore, airports must assess carefully from a financial, environmental, and 
social perspective, along with regulatory compliance, the potential water reuse options before making any 
decision. 
Some of the potential reuse applications to be considered by airports are the following: 
¢ Landscape-For irrigation, decorative fountains, and lagoons 
e Sanitary—For flushing toilets 
e — Industrial-For cooling towers and boiler processes 
¢ Operational and maintenance-For aircraft, ground vehicle and equipment washing; for pavement and 
building cleaning; for firefighting activities 
Water from a range of activities may be reused, beyond just gray water, stormwater and treated effluents 
(e.g., water condensed from A/C units, spent rinse water in utilities, or water used in firefighting tests).

2.4.6.1.4 Harvest Rainwater 
Opportunities exist throughout the airport for the harvesting of rainwater, a potentially significant source for 
use in building systems and landscape irrigation (see the above section for possible uses). On-site harvesting 
and storage can strengthen the autonomy of the airport in water resources and reduce its dependence on off￾site sources. 
The practice of rainwater collection from roofs and storage in subsurface cisterns has long been a necessity in 
arid climates and island environments where sources of fresh water are limited or non-existent. This 
experience and knowledgebase can be extended to airport buildings in all climates, from small-scale facilities 
up to large passenger terminals. However, there must be space for storage tanks, and treatment. 
The principle of harvesting can also be applied to site infrastructure (e.g., roadways, parking, airfield 
pavements and shoulders) for collection and reuse. Filtering by vegetation and appropriate soils allows reuse 
in landscape irrigation; further treatment may allow certain types of domestic use. 
Design approach: 
© —Buildings—Collection of rainwater from roofs for storage in cisterns and reuse in building systems or 
landscape irrigation 
© Site infrastructure—Collection of stormwater from landside and airside pavement for surface storage 
(eg., in planted retention basins) or aquifer storage for reuse in landscape irrigation 
2.4.6.2 Materials 
How to reduce the use of materials and planning for their reuse and recycling should be considered. 
2.4.6.2.1 Resource Reduction 
In airport infrastructure construction, large amounts of raw materials are used. In raw material extraction and 
production of building materials, fossil energy sources are often used. The production of building materials, 
therefore, accounts for a significant part of the environmental impact of a structure. In the design phase, there 
are many opportunities for sustainable use of materials. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 219 

===PAGE 239===
Se ae IATA Biull Airport Development Reference Manual 
Resource reduction appears at the top of the waste hierarchy because it minimizes environmental impact 
throughout a material's lifecycle. Resource reduction encourages the use of innovative construction 
techniques, such as prefabrication, resulting in minimized material cutoffs and inefficiencies. For example, a 
building can be designed based on functional requirements, such as load-bearing capacity, that result in less 
use of materials, but construction duration still needs to be considered. 
Some recommendations to reduce resource usage at the design and planning stages include: 
¢ Determine whether renovation is possible instead of new construction. 
¢ Build multifunctional facilities. Check whether some functions can be combined to increase the usage of 
spaces if possible. Look for an optimal use of space. 
¢ — Limit the structural weight. For instance, consider wood or metal frame construction. A hollow-core slab 
floor weighs less than a solid floor. 
¢ If possible, choose prefabricated components. As these are manufactured in a controlled environment, 
most of the wastage can be captured and recycled easily. 
e Align the dimensions of the construction plan to standard sizes. 
¢ Provide a design in such a way that no “difficult” connection details are required. For instance, try to avoid 
fancy shapes unless a flexible material is used. 
¢ Optimize the design to minimize the pipe lengths required for heating, ventilation, cooling, and potable 
water supply. 
¢ Apply building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) solar solutions. These can save materials; for example, 
integrated solar panels will replace roof tiles. 
* Choose materials that are made from a hybrid product. For instance, slabs that are made from steel 
beams and a thin layer of concrete can give material savings of up to 20%; however, they can be harder 
to disassemble, reuse and recycle. 
¢ Concrete is one of the most carbon-intense materials in the construction industry, where it is mainly used 
for its durability, flexibility, affordability, and capacity to handle high compression loads. Consider designs 
that minimize concrete use such as by limiting it to the foundations, where it is most needed to carry the 
loads of the building. 
2.4,.6.2.2. Reuse Materials 
Reusing building materials, or entire buildings through renovation, is the next most effective strategy to reduce 
the environmental burden of the manufacturing process. In the future waste can be prevented by providing 
materials with a material “passport” that includes information about the user, location, and reuse method. 
Another aspect is to consider use of mechanical joints that help to ease disassembly. Also, if possible, make 
use of “clean” materials that do not require paints or adhesives for assembly. 
220 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 240===
Be fai ; : ae 
IATA 4 Airport Environmental Sustainability 
Some recommendations to consider at the design and planning stages are: 
e Use standard profiles and prefabricated parts that can be reused. 
* Do not reinforce pipes or channels with concrete. 
e Assess the specifications, dimensions, quantity, and availability of recycled materials before suggesting 
them as part of the design, even at the preliminary design phase. 
2.4.6.2.3 Recycle Materials 
Recycling is an important method to reduce materials going to landfills. Innovations in recycling technology 
improve sorting and processing to supply raw material to secondary markets. If the quality of the recycled 
material is reduced, it is called “downcycling”. If waste is used to create new products of higher value, it is 
called “upcycling”. Additionally, recycled resources should be used in consecutive lifecycles, thereby reducing 
costs, and increasing the predictability and productivity of the supply chain. 
2.4.6.2.4 Materials Adaptability for Circularity 
Circularity involves a lifecycle approach to design, construction, and operation of new and existing buildings 
and provides an opportunity to reduce waste and pollution. In the case of materials, this can involve keeping 
valuable resources in use or by increasing the lifecycle of the building. 
Recommendations for material choice in design and planning: 
* Select materials with properties that can be reused 
¢ Decide on pure materials as much as possible, which can be recycled with ease 
e Choose materials of a high quality that have longer lifecycles 
e Use non-toxic materials to provide a healthy environment 
e Ensure the supporting structure can cater to future needs 
«Make sure installations such as ventilation are replaceable and modifiable 
2.4.6.3 Waste 
Waste is generated from different locations and during most of the activities that take place at an airport. The 
following types of waste can be found: 
© Municipal solid waste-Includes common inorganic and compostable waste, both food and green waste, 
including vegetation debris arising from landscape maintenance. 
e Construction waste-Non-hazardous waste generated during construction activities. 
© Deplaned waste-Any waste coming from aircraft passengers and crew; generally divided into national and 
international, as the latter requires specific management.

¢ Lavatory waste-Hazardous waste that is removed from aircraft lavatory tanks.

2.4.6.3.1 Waste Reduction and Reuse 
The most preferred approach to waste management is to not create it in the first place. Minimizing waste 
generation reduces the amount of waste that ultimately needs to be handled which can generate both 
environmental benefits and cost savings. Waste reduction practices that can be easily implemented at airports 
include: 
e Avoid disposable or single-use goods 
© Appropriate bins, bags and associated labels and signage 
* Replacing paper documents with electronic ones as much as possible 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 223 

===PAGE 243===
Ps . 
Se IATA ii Airport Development Reference Manual 
Donation programs are an indirect yet very effective way of reducing waste, because in addition to leaving the 
waste stream, they also bring valuable environmental and social benefits. Donating food to vulnerable people 
must be accompanied by the provision of appropriate means, such as refrigerators, storage areas and 
transport vehicles. Many airports also donate unclaimed lost items, electronic equipment, and luggage. 
Another way of reducing volumes in the waste stream is by preparing materials for reuse, either for the 
original purpose or for a new one. Furniture, dishes, mugs, pallets, cardboard boxes, office and maintenance 
supplies, and construction materials are examples of elements that can be reused. 
It is not only the quantity of waste to be managed that is important, but also its quality. For example, many 
airports have implemented liquid collection points that, apart from improving water conservation, remove 
water from the waste stream, making all the downstream stages more effective and efficient. 
Example: JetBlue Terminal 5 Rooftop Farm-JFK Airport 
This example encompasses multiple sustainable concepts and practices, such as circularity, composting, 
educational outreach and promoting surrounding communities. The T5 Farm is more than a new green space; 
it Serves as an agricultural and educational resource for the community. Food grown at the T5 Farm 
completes the full cycle of food production. JetBlue Airways takes many leftovers from restaurants in T5 and 
hauls food waste each day for composting. The nutrient-rich organic soil is then transported to the T5 Farm to 
grow potatoes and other produce. In three months alone, the farm produced almost 1,000 Ibs. of food that 
was donated to local food banks. 
2.4,.6.3.2 Waste Recycling 
Recycling is the process that takes used materials and Preprocesses them into substances, materials, or new 
Products. Currently, airports, airlines, and other stakeholders and third parties are carrying out recycling 
programs and receiving the associated environmental, financial, and social benefits. 
A global sector such as aviation poses some inherent barriers to maximizing the benefits of recycling; for 
example, the different languages and cultures of Passengers can limit the separation of materials, or even the 
existence of different programs and regulations at airports across an airline route. To address this, airports 
must take a holistic view and look for potential synergies between the different recycling strategies. 
Recycling is commonly used at airports for both municipal solid and construction waste; however, other types 
of waste should not be discarded from recycling programs. For example, the de-icing products used during 
winter can be converted into anti-freeze or lavatory fluids, or into coolants, coatings, and paints. 
224 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 244===
Se Ry IATA al Airport Environmental Sustainability 
2.4.6.3.3 Waste to Compost 
Composting is defined as the method of turning organic materials (e.g., leftover food, garden trimmings) into a 
nutrient-rich soil fertilizer called compost through the natural process of decomposition. At airports, organic 
waste is generally generated in the form of food waste from airport restaurants, cafeterias and catering 
facilities, and green waste from landscaping or gardening activities. 
Green waste and pre-consumer food waste (i.e., food waste generated during meal preparation stages) is the 
easiest to compost due to the simplicity of separating the organic material at source. Post-consumer food 
waste (i.e., table scraps and food refuse) is more challenging and requires an additional stage for separating 
the organic material from the non-compostable waste stream to ensure it is not contaminated. This can be 
facilitated by using separate bins for organic waste in kitchens and cafeterias, increasing awareness among 
staff and/or passengers, and having composting policies in place. 
Apart from the environmental benefits, composting also provides potential for cost savings (diversion of waste 
from landfills), revenue generation (resale of compost) and community engagement (edible food recovery and 
donation, cooperation with local farmers and landscapers for compost uptake, etc.). 
2.4.6.3.4 Waste to Energy 
Waste to energy is defined as any waste treatment process that creates energy (electricity, heat, power) from 
a waste source. The most common technologies include incineration, combined heat and power (CHP) plants, 
and biogas reactors. These can be applied to several waste types (municipal solid waste (MSW), sludge, 
organic wastes, etc.). 
Biogas reactors, or digestors, use a process called anaerobic digestion which breaks down organic matter to 
generate biogas which can be used for electricity or converted into biomethane which is a renewable form of 
natural gas. In this way, organic waste that would otherwise emit harmful GHG in a landfill or through 
incineration are instead recycled into a sustainable source of energy. 
Example: Kansai International Airport, Japan 
At Kansai International Airport, combustible waste (including kitchen waste, wood waste, non-recyclable 
paper, rags, etc.) is incinerated at the airport's onsite incineration powerplant. The airport also has a Clean 
Centre to process the various types of incoming waste streams and act as a critical interface point between 
different stakeholders and waste management activities. Waste heat from incineration is used as a source of 
heat for the incineration plant as well as for hot water and air conditioning at the Clean Centre. 
2.4.6.3.5 Waste Disposal—-Temporary and Residual 
Waste is collected at different airport locations after it is generated. Even after implementing best practices, a 
residual part of the waste must be disposed of if it cannot be reused, recycled, repurposed, donated, etc. 
Although this fraction has been reduced progressively in recent years through innovation and research, 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 225 

===PAGE 245===
C3 |p 
TATA pull Airport Development Reference Manual 
implementing new technologies and procedures, and changing people's culture and behavior, temporary and 
final collection points must be planned and designed in a proper manner. 
For example, lack of space is a common issue that airport tenants mention as a barrier to improving waste 
management. Food and beverage areas are usually designed to maximize revenues through the space 
available to passengers and other customers, while back-of-house space is minimized, making it difficult to 
locate recycling bins or compactors. 
A sustainable design must incorporate these needs and consider the “big picture”. If a new airport is being 
planned or designed, the travel distances and times from waste generation points to final collection facilities, 
as well as the waste management logistics and procedures to be put in place, must be jointly considered. 
A iurther step that airports can take to improve waste management is to provide on-site processing facilities, 
optimizing their efficiency, and reducing the associated emissions. However, even for simple collection 
centers, any potential risk to aviation safety must be mitigated, including wildlife attraction. 
Regarding construction waste, a solution widely and successfully implemented at airports around the world is 
the provision of a construction logistics consolidation center, especially when large construction projects are 
underway. Apart from reducing waste volumes by efficiently reusing, recycling, and transforming, its reverse 
logistics also reduce ground traffic, GHG emissions and Noise, while improving productivity and program 
reliability, and saving costs. 
2.4.6.4 Land Use Planning 
Airport master planning is often limited to the rigorous application of aeronautical design standards. Although 
this remains the absolute priority, it is often to the exclusion of a more comprehensive land planning approach 
to airport development. An airport's natural environmental as well as its cultural context should be integrated 
into the airport's planning and design, including its master plan. 
An amplified role for land use Planning will integrate nature-based solutions to protect and augment airport 
natural resources. A balance between aviation-based planning and sustainable land use planning can be 
achieved by a thorough analysis of the airport site, which will enable planners to better understand the 
Opportunities and constraints. Geographic information systems (GIS) provide tools for these studies, with 
analysis of spatial location and mapping techniques to evaluate suitability and capability. 
For existing airports, a design-with-nature planning approach can facilitate the designation of specific zones 
for various uses, such as preservation, habitat restoration, landscape integration and working landscapes. 
Zones reserved for long-term development could be used for these uses until needed. 
226 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 246===
IATA Airport Environmental Sustainability 
2.4.6.4.1_ Land Preservation 
Protect key natural areas by dedicating zones within the airport and its surroundings to ensure ecosystem and 
resources preservation. Design approach to master planning: 
© Site-specific—identify and set aside natural areas that are vital to local resources or cultural context, then 
integrate these areas into the master planning process 
¢ Comprehensive-For the entire airport site and its surroundings, identify specific zones outside of airport 
facilities for the dedicate purpose of habitat improvement, preservation, or compensatory measures. 
2.4.6.4.2 Habitat Restoration and Biodiversity Protection 
As a controlled area with restricted access, an airport has the potential to be a large-scale natural reserve, 
protecting endangered species. Some airports may harbor flora and fauna in great quantity to counter 
declines in animal populations. Because of its limited access, nature is often preserved on airport sites, and 
for the most part sheltered from urban development. This biodiversity deserves to be evaluated, monitored, 
and improved, and can contribute to the well-being of all. 
The overriding risk is aeronautical safety, such as bird strikes and other wildlife intrusions. Birds, for example, 
may be attracted by plants near the runway for the purposes of roosting or feeding. Airport planning plays an 
important role in bird strike hazard reduction. Proper planning of an airport can help to recognize land uses 
and plant types on or near the airport site that can potentially attract wildlife. By controlling these land uses, 
bird strike hazard can be reduced. 
The strategies used will depend upon the local circumstances. A French study of airports found that a 
balanced natural ecosystem, such as an airside prairie, presents fewer hazards than can occur with 
conventional landscape management (i.e., frequent mowing and grass cut flush). Bird populations, in 
particular flocks of smaller birds and their predators, are attracted to areas of low-height vegetation, but 
deterred by higher prairie vegetation.® It is important to keep in mind that local assessments should be done. 
Simple practices can be put in place for airside landscapes, on a case-by-case basis, to enrich biodiversity 
without impacting safety. Several government agencies and trade organizations have issued guidance on how 
to implement an active wildlife hazard plan. ACI, for example, provides guidance in its Wildlife Hazard 
Management Handbook-2” Edition, on how to develop habitat management plans and what operational 
practices can be used to monitor and control wildlife hazards.

access, as well as alternative management of rainwater and photovoltaic energy.
