2.4.7 Airport Environmental Resiliency 
Airport environmental resilience is an important issue, as air transport is often subject to external shocks. 
Some of the challenges that airports face, such as economic downturns, can be intermittent, while others, 
such as risks brought about by climate change, require longer-term solutions. How an airport is affected by a 
crisis, such as a climate event, and how quickly it recovers, is driven by its design and the robustness of 
systems, infrastructure, and processes Actions should be based on individual airports risk assessments as 
there is no ‘one fits all’ solution. This includes the ability to improve financial stability, plan for physical 
impacts, respond to operational disruptions and adapt to future innovations. This section touches upon each 
of these key resiliency goals as they can all influence airport planning and design. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 229 

===PAGE 249===
& B= 
IATA - Airport Development Reference Manual 
Goals Objectives 
Enhance Business Continuity Airport ability to continue to generate income in the face of disruption. 
Similarly, building in flexibility to cater to different airline models and 
non-passenger revenue sources would reduce risk to the airport's 
cashflow position when faced with change. 
Enhance Operational Resiliency Airport facilities to maintain operations in the wake of unforeseen 
events. Critical infrastructure needs to be supported by plans for 
resilient energy sources. Flexible infrastructure is also essential for 
operational resiliency. Examples include swing gates and other 
infrastructure that can be adapted to other uses. 
Enhance Climate Resiliency Climate change needs to be addressed in terms of existing airport 
facilities and future planning. Investment now can avoid higher future 
costs. 
Accommodate Future Innovations Flexible airport systems and IT-platform capabilities that are the and Trends backbone for the increasing dependency on technology will avoid the 
need for major overhauls of systems in the future. 
2.4.7.1 Enhance Business Continuity 
The key goal of enhancing business continuity is to incorporate income diversification into the strategy of the 
airport, and thus into its design. Airport master plans that include non-passenger income-generating areas 
allow airports to diversify their business. Similarly, building in flexibility to cater to different airline products as 
well as non-aeronautical activities can reduce risk to the airport's financial position when faced with a crisis. 
2.4.7.1.1_ Non-Passenger Activities 
At the same time, there is an Opportunity to diversify airport activities to reduce both volatility and the negative 
effects of drops in passenger traffic, downturns in the economy, or other unexpected (shock) events. Cargo 
operations, commercial real estate and other non-passenger-related activities are less sensitive to direct 
changes in passenger numbers and will increase airport resilience. 
Influence on Design and Planning 
Incorporating non-passenger activities, such as cargo-related activities or real estate, means that in the 
master planning phase, sufficient land area is reserved for their development. Cargo operations come with 
facilities and access not just for cargo airlines, but also for freight forwarders, parcels and mail, warehousing, 
industry and manufacturing opportunities, trade zones, and many more. 
Examples of real estate activities are those derived from either the direct operations of real estate (e.g., hotel 
operations) or the leasing out of real estate and land. 
More importantly, commercial real estate generally has a different economic cycle than the wider aviation 
industry, which is mostly influenced by passenger numbers. As has recently been seen, passenger numbers 
can drop overnight, but real estate contracts usually have a much longer duration. 
230 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 250===
IATA Airport Environmental Sustainability 
Diversification also provides airport leadership with additional time to handle unexpected events and crises 
that impact the passenger-based activities. 
2.4.7.1.2 Phased and Flexible Infrastructure Projects 
Resiliency priorities should inform planning efforts. Airport operators can build in resilience through 
redundancy, flexibility, and technology. Flexible planning solutions are important so spaces can be quickly 
altered or converted to other uses in a crisis. Similarly, being able to incorporate flexibility in infrastructure 
projects by, for example, designing a terminal expansion so it can be phased and adjusted allows for 
responses to changes in financial conditions. 
Influence on Design and Planning 
When planning new or expanded infrastructure projects, an increasingly common practice is to incorporate 
some form of phasing of the construction project. Not only does this allow for some flexibility during the 
construction by, for example, being able to make last-minute updates to the design, it will also constitute a 
phased financial burden for the airport. If part of an infrastructure project can be put on hold or even cancelled 
when an unexpected decrease in passenger demand or economic downturn occurs, there is a smaller risk of 
creating overcapacity or financial loss. 
An option for phasing construction projects is to utilize modular design principles, which essentially means 
breaking down the construction project into smaller partitions, or modular elements, which are standalone and 
scalable, thus creating flexibility. Further, the infrastructure design can be such that it allows for flexibility 
inside a more standalone outer shell. An example of this concept is a large open hall in which walls and floors 
can be put in without interfering with the supporting structural elements, something that is typically very hard 
to accomplish with closely spaced columns. 
2.4.7.2 Enhancing Operational Resiliency 
The key goal of enhancing operational resiliency is to incorporate design guidelines for both facility and 
process flexibility. This can be achieved by addressing design and planning processes to incorporate common 
use systems, integrate sustainable aviation technologies, enable stakeholder collaboration, and avoid 
operational disruptions. 
2.4.7.2.1. Common Use Systems and Infrastructure 
Airports increasingly utilize common use systems and shared terminal equipment for efficiency and ease of 
use for both employees and passengers. These systems involve using the same equipment regardless of 
airline, whereas historically each airline would have their own designated systems. 
A robust asset management program is also important to ensure the viability of critical operating 
infrastructure, helps understand the total cost of ownership, and informs senior management for 
maintenance/repair priorities. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 231 

===PAGE 251===
== i IATA a Airport Development Reference Manual 
Influence on Design and Planning 
Passenger-processing platforms, such as Common User Terminal Equipment (CUTE), Common User 
Passenger Processing System (CUPPS) and Common User Self-Service (CUSS) provide shared passenger 
processing platforms. These solutions can increase asset optimization, provide flexibility, offer resiliency for 
operators, and provide opportunities for future growth in airports, potentially preventing or delaying the need 
for facilities expansion and reducing the footprint required. Design strategies, such as swing gates and, swing 
processing facilities, MARS stands, and others, can also be planned to provide operational resiliency. 
2.4.7.2.2, Energy Resilience 
Energy resilience is about ensuring a reliable source of power for critical infrastructure and operations 
whereby failure would result in major impacts to operations. An energy resilience plan should be developed to 
respond to serious incidents that may cause power disruptions such as from natural disasters. An energy 
resiliency plan must consider the capacity and reliability of the local power grid and microgrids onsite. and the 
type of risks that the airport may experience (e.g., frequent power outages, natural disasters). The energy 
resilience plan should be able to address current power needs as well as prepare for what may be required in 
the future. 
Influence on Design and Planning 
Energy resilience should be key consideration in any airport master plan or a climate change risk assessment 
and adaptation plan. It should also be a part of infrastructure requirements and facilities design. 
2.4.7.2.3 Flexibility 
Airport designs need to be adaptable to climate change and fluctuations in passenger demand and be flexible 
enough to accommodate new technologies such as alternative aviation fuels or autonomous ground transport. 
Influence on Design and Planning 
For any introduction of sustainable technology, there will be implications on airport design and planning. 
These can include the type or location of infrastructure or changes in handling processes. Flexible planning 
solutions are important so spaces can be quickly altered or converted to other uses in a crisis. Space may 
need to be safeguarded for new types of technology and facilities as part of the master planning process. 
For example, electrification initiatives, whether of aircraft gates and airside vehicles or the introduction of 
electric aircraft, will require a reliable and continuous supply of electricity. The power supply network must be 
able to meet this increased demand. This includes minimizing the risk of power supply shutdowns that can 
disrupt air operations and ensure the necessary infrastructure, such as charging points, are in the right 
places. Environmental mitigation measures, such as elevating critical assets to avoid high water, should also 
be included in the design and planning.

2.4.7.2.4 Stakeholder Collaboration 
To enhance stakeholder collaboration and facilitate short communication lines in cases of disruption, the 
provision of a centralized airport operation control center (AOCC or APOC) which provides all parties involved 
in airport operations with the same information to manage day-to-day activities. The result: improved overall 
situational awareness and decision-making quality. 
AOCCs serve as a single point of contact for all airport stakeholders and have played a pivotal role to ensure 
business continuity during the COVID-19 pandemic. 
Influence on Design and Planning 
With today's technology, an AOCC or APOC does not need to be placed at a central location; however, site 
selection should consider future airport expansion and incident response functions. The area should be 
carefully planned with considerations to: 
¢ Allow enough space for expansion of the AOCC to accommodate future needs, stakeholders, and 
technologies. 
e Include multiple stakeholders and their workspace requirements. 
Incorporate current technology (e.g., desks, screens, video walls, meeting rooms, fiber optics, WI-FI) and 
anticipate future technology needs to the extent possible. 
e Plan for resiliency equipment such as an independent secondary power supply and an alternate/back-up 
location. 
This secured and centralized facility alleviates the need for multiple smaller control centers. The AOCC should 
not be confused with the Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) which is a facility to provide strategic 
coordination during major emergencies and disruptive events. 
2.4.7.2.5 Operational Disruption 
Disruption to operations because of natural and human-induced disasters is an unavoidable risk that confronts 
every airport. Maintaining operational resilience is important for airport operations, as well as for airlines, 
passengers, and other partners at the airports. 
Influence on Design and Planning 
Airports recognize that incidents can and will happen and must try to anticipate, absorb, and adapt to 
disruptive events. The design approach includes: 
* During the initial design phase, evaluate multiple scenarios for optimal decisions and focus on reducing 
the probability that unforeseen events will adversely impact operations, users and passengers, and 
upgrade the design requirements, including the recovery time objective (RTO), accordingly. 
° Build redundancy and reliability into systems.

¢ Design should enable innovation and technology to boost business continuity during the operational 
phase. 
° Provide strategic flexibility and adaptability in the design to reduce the probability of facilities failure and 
ensure emergency response can be activated in a prompt manner. 
* Put contingency plans in place to react appropriately when events impact facilities, ensure passengers 
receive the best outcome possible given the circumstances, and enable recovery from incidents as 
quickly as possible.

2.4.7.3 Enhance Climate Resiliency 
More extreme weather and climate-related events are expected as the climate continues to change. The 
increasing frequency, intensity, and duration of extreme weather events as well as the gradual socio￾economic effects of climate change will have an impact on airports. Many will be vulnerable as the risks of 
flooding, flight disruptions and cancellations become more likely. Airports need to understand the risks and 
initiate adaptation measures, for both existing and new infrastructure, as well as manage critical operations so 
they become more resilient to the changing climate. 
A climate-resilient airport takes steps to prepare for the challenges that climate change and extreme weather 
events might bring. Airport planning should consider the risks and impacts associated with climate change 
and actively plan for future climate conditions. 
Airports should conduct “climate stress tests” and risk assessments, develop mitigation measures and 
communication channels, and take climate resilience and adaptation into consideration for their master plans. 
ICAO has established the following short list of the type of climate hazards that may have to be planned for: 
¢ Changing climatic conditions (temperature change, precipitation, storm intensity) 
¢ Sea level rise 
° Desertification 
Example: Flood Resilient Schiphol Airport, the Netherlands 
To implement Schiphol's long-term adaptation strategy (Water Vision 2030), a flood risk assessment was 
carried out to identify vulnerable assets and operations and to quantify flood risks. Following the results of this 
assessment Schiphol's management team initiated the ‘Flood resilient Schipho? program. The goal of this 
program is to adapt existing infrastructure and mitigate flood risk effects on operations. 
In 2020, a more detailed financial risk evaluation was done, which resulted in the Strategic Water Investment 
Plan 2020-2030. A distinction was made between already planned projects and additional measures required 
to meet the “flood resilient Schiphol” ambition. A geo-based management tool was developed to benchmark

===PAGE 254===

ww WiAirport Environmental Sustainability 
and report on climate risks and airport developments. Every year, the Strategic Water Investment Plan is 
being recalibrated and updated. 
Example: Icing Conditions at Iqaluit Airport, Nunavut in Northern Canada 
As a result of climate change, the Iqaluit International Airport is becoming more susceptible to permafrost 
thaw, increasing the likelihood of sinkholes and other instabilities that can affect infrastructure and runway 
safety. Through the Northern Transportation Adaptation Initiative, Transport Canada is funding a study of the 
current state of permafrost at the airport and identifying specific locations that are at risk of damage from a 
changing climate. The results of this study are informing decisions on the $300-million Iqaluit International 
Airport Improvement Project that includes a new terminal and an upgraded runway. This will minimize the risk 
of costly repairs over the life of the airport.

2.4.7.3.1 Climate Stress Test 
An airport climate stress test identifies the potential impact on operations and the vulnerabilities of critical 
infrastructure to such climate threats as floods and heat stress. It collects and creates information about the 
effects of climate change in the present and in the future and assesses different scenarios. 
This information is combined with data about the climate sensitivity of various installations and functions in the 
airport area. Research conducted during the test shows when and where potential bottlenecks will appear and 
is useful for developing climate change adaptation measures. 
Although climate stress tests typically focus on the physical infrastructure and operations of an airport, stress 
tests on the airport organization and its stakeholders may also be considered.

2.4.7.3.2 Climate Resilience Strategy 
Adapting airports to climate change means reducing the vulnerability of airport infrastructure, operations, and 
organizations to climatic extremes. Developing an adaptation plan or climate resilience strategy sets out the 
airport's long-term ambitions and implementation plans for coping with the effects of climate change. Such a 
strategy can include the following three parts: 
The airport climate resilience strategy, including CAPEX and OPEX plans, should be integrated with the 
airport's master plan as it will influence the planning and design of airport infrastructure. Besides physical 
infrastructure and operations, it is important to note that the resilience strategy is also about organization of 
the adaptation process and climate-adaptive actions. 
2.4.7.3.3. Early Warning and Monitoring Systems 
To give airport operational personnel the ability to respond to extreme weather events, early warning and 
monitoring systems are indispensable. Different types of systems exist: 
Nowcasting of extreme weather This involves high spatial and temporal resolution forecasts of weather 
events developments for the next few minutes and up to a maximum of six 
hours ahead. (e.g., predict thunderstorms, hail, and heavy rainfall). 
Forecasting of extreme weather This involves forecasts of weather development for the next few days 
events and up to a maximum of two weeks ahead. (e.g., predict hurricanes, 
typhoons, heat stress). 
Monitoring and evaluation Data collection of weather developments and analysis of extreme values 
as well as the effect on infrastructure and operations (e.g., flood alert 
monitoring systems). 
A combination of these systems is recommended. They also demand a certain resilience in future airport 
design and planning. This can take the form of flexible or multi-functional infrastructure, a calamity plan 
(script) or even a disaster recovery plan. 
2.4.7.3.4 Virtual Test Environments 
A digital twin is an interactive representation of a physical airport and its operations that allows the analysis of 
data and monitoring of systems before problems occur. This can be useful for predictive maintenance or for 
modelling different scenarios to better understand the operational impacts of new technologies, facilities, or 
processes. Digital twins can also be used to analyze the resilience of airport systems and their 
interdependencies, by simulating scenarios that include the impact of hazards, risks, and vulnerabilities. In 
existing facilities sensors can be installed at relevant locations to measure flows, throughput, conditions, etc. 
for passenger and other traffic to quantify the performance of facilities.

Influence on Design and Planning

help mitigate risk and issues in advance. During the operational phase, they improve predictions of asset 
failure and ensure better understanding of passenger flow levels and the passenger experience. 
2.4.8 Airport Sustainability Performance Management 
This section focuses on performance management and covers some activities that can be used to support 
this in the context of sustainability. 
2.4.8.1 Measuring, Monitoring and Reporting 
Airports should measure and monitor their sustainability activities to plan for the long term, manage progress 
over time, identify gaps and impacts, and implement corrective actions. Sustainability reporting can raise 
awareness, support stakeholder engagement, demonstrate progress over time, and attract investment. 
2.4.8.1.1_ Common Topics Measured and Reported at the Global Level 
Airports report on sustainability topics that are most relevant to them in terms of the greatest impact or 
influence (social, environmental, economic). There are common sustainability topics identified at the global 
level, such as climate change, that airports may prefer to report on in a harmonized fashion across regions, 
but local activity on sustainability matters should not be ignored. 
2.4.8.1.2 Implementing a Measuring, Monitoring and Reporting System 
A sustainability business model requires regular measuring, monitoring and reporting of environmental, social 
and economic matters that allow an airport operator to manage performance. The benefits of measuring, 
monitoring, and providing regular reports to public forums include increased transparency, greater 
accountability, improved stakeholder relationships, and the ability to benchmark. Assessment of the relevant 
topics and collection of stakeholder feedback should also be reflected in the report. 
Some examples of topics that may be covered include: 
* Location of the airport to avoid sensitive areas 
¢ Land use planning to protect existing biodiversity 
¢ — Airport layouts (airside and landside) to facilitate process and efficiency 
e Energy consumption and GHG emissions

2.4.8.1.3. Performance Targets and Benchmarks 
Measuring progress against sustainability targets is an essential feature of performance management. 
Developing a roadmap and benchmarking progress against peer airports can be useful tools to ensure 
progress is made. Targets can be set or adjusted with the input from stakeholders. 
For carbon emissions, the only institutionally endorsed, global carbon management certification program for 
airports is ACI's Airport Carbon Accreditation (ACA). The program independently assesses and recognizes 
the efforts of airports to manage and reduce their carbon emissions through six progressively ambitious levels 
of accreditation: Mapping, Reduction, Optimisation, Neutrality, Transformation, and Transition. With this step￾by-step process, ACA acknowledges that airports are at different stages in their journey toward 
comprehensive carbon management. It is a program for airports of all sizes with scheduled passenger traffic, 
extending beyond hubs and regional airports to include general aviation and freight-focused airports. 
While ACA does not prescribe specific emissions reduction measures, airport design is one of the areas 
through which reductions can be achieved. ACA is also site-specific, allowing flexibility to take account of 
national or local legal requirements, while also ensuring that the methodology used is robust. 
For other sustainability matters, ACI has identified common topics at the global level that airports generally 
report on. Each airport, however, will have their own priorities and will focus on the most relevant and 
impactful areas for them.

2.5 Universal Design and Accessibility 
2.5.1 Introduction 
Universal Design is a set of principles and processes whereby infrastructure, environment, facilities, products, 
services, information, communications and technology, may be accessed, understood and used to the 
greatest practicable extent by all people regardless of age, disability, or other factors. Airports should be 
accessible in the most independent and natural manner possible, in the widest possible range of situations 
and without the need for adaptation, modification, assistive devices or specialised solutions, by persons of 
any age or size or having any particular physical, sensory, mental health or intellectual ability or disability. 
The Aviation sector plays a major role in connecting people in the global economy. For the 15% of the world's 
population who live with some form of disability and people with access requirements, travelling can be a 
challenging process or sometimes even impossible. 
The proportion of the world population aged 65 and over is projected to increase from 9% in 2019 to 16% in 
2050. A further reason why universal design should be incorporated into all practices and operations and 
guided by accessibility standards. 
People with disabilities and those who are ageing can face physical, sensory, cognitive, cultural and attitude 
barriers within Airport built facilities, digital environments, services, operations, evacuation, customer service 
240 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 260===
= | IATA ull Universal Design and Accessibility 
and maintenance. It is very difficult and, in some cases, impossible to find clear and accurate information on 
the accessibility of airport facilities, products, services, support aids and technology. 
The Aviation sector has an opportunity and responsibility to promote universal design across all of its 
activities, driven by leadership and an inclusive culture from CEOs and boards of directors. As one example, 
airports should establish procedures requiring Universal Design in public procurement tenders and when 
awarding contracts for infrastructure, buildings, transportation and equipment. In this way planners, designers, 
manufacturers and suppliers will be encouraged to create accessible and inclusive airports and experiences, 
thus bringing benefits to users and businesses. 
It is important to understand the terms and definitions from the outset, especially the difference between the 
barriers that disable people and the solutions and processes that enable every person to participate to the 
greatest extent possible. 
2.5.1.1. Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 
The Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities is a binding human rights treaty. It adopts a broad 
categorization of persons with disabilities and reaffirms that all persons with all types of disabilities must enjoy 
all human rights and fundamental freedoms. 
Specifically, Article 9 states: “To enable persons with disabilities to live independently and participate fully 
in all aspects of life, States Parties shall take appropriate measures to ensure to persons with disabilities 
access, on an equal basis with others, to the physical environment, to transportation, to information and 
communications, including information and communications technologies and systems, and to other facilities 
and services open or provided to the public, both in urban and in rural areas. These measures shall include 
the identification and elimination of obstacles and barriers to accessibility.” 
Article 4 states: “To ensure and promote the full realization of all human rights and fundamental freedoms for 
all persons with disabilities without discrimination of any kind on the basis of disability. To undertake or 
promote research and development of universally designed goods, services, equipment and facilities, and to 
promote universal design in the development of standards and guidelines”. 
The core philosophy of Universal Design implies that all users should be provided with equitable use of 
products, services and environments, regardless of their age, size, ability or disability. 
2.5.1.2 Definitions 
This section provides definitions on the common terms used in describing the concept of Universal Design 
and Accessibility. These definitions will be used in this section and in other parts of this manual. 
Disability 
Physical, mental, intellectual or sensory impairments which in interaction with various barriers can hinder a 
person's full and effective participation in society on an equal basis with others. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 241 

===PAGE 261===
== pti 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
Impairment 
Limitation in body function or structure such as a significant deviation or loss which can be temporary or 
permanent, slight or severe and can fluctuate over time. 
Reasonable adjustment 
Necessary and appropriate modification and adjustments not imposing a disproportionate or undue burden, 
where needed in a particular case, to ensure that persons with disabilities enjoy or exercise on an equal basis 
with others all human rights and fundamental freedoms. 
Accessibility 
The extent to which products, systems, services, environments and facilities can be used by people from a 
Population with the widest range of user needs, characteristics and capabilities to achieve identified goals in 
identified contexts of use. Context of use includes direct use or use supported by assistive technologies. 
Universal Design 
Design of products, environments, programmes and services to be usable by all people, to the greatest extent 
Possible, without the need for adaptation or specialized design. 
2.5.2 Universal Design 
Universal Design is a fundamental condition of good design. If an environment is accessible, usable, 
convenient and a pleasure to use, evéryone benefits. By considering the diverse needs and abilities of all 
throughout the design process, universal design meets all peoples’ needs to the greatest practicable extent. 
Universal Design is a human centred approach that makes projects more sustainable, durable and more 
valuable. It results in more innovative, more marketable and more usable designs. It delivers on independent 
use, social participation, human performance, health and wellness, increases safety and reduces risk. 
Note: Universal design shall not exclude assistive devices for particular groups or persons with disabilities 
where these are needed. 
Aviation providers should adopt a holistic approach ensuring that all touchpoints of the employee and user 
journey apply Universal Design principles in their processes to ensure they are inclusive and accessible for 
all. This includes the initiation phase involving users looking for Airport information, to booking or reservation 
processes to the preparation and execution of the journey, the design and organization of services offered at 
the airport, the overall management of customer relations and the return journey of the user. 
Airport infrastructure, environment, facilities, products, services, communication, information and technology 
provision should be designed in accordance with the Universal Design principles and goals. 
Note: Terms such as Universal Design, accessible design, design for all, barrier-free design, inclusive 
design and transgenerational design are often used interchangeably with the same meaning

2.5.2.1 Universal Design Principles 
The Seven Principles of Universal Design were developed in 1997 by a working group of architects, product 
designers, engineers and environmental design researchers, led by Ronald Mace, at North Carolina State 
University. The following principles guide the design of environments, products, services and communications: 
Principle 1: Equitable Use 
The design is useful and marketable to people with diverse abilities. 
Guidelines: 
4a. Provide the same means of use for all users: identical whenever possible; equivalent when not. 
1b. Avoid segregating or stigmatizing any users. 
1c. Provisions for privacy, security, and safety should be equally available to all users. 
4d. Make the design appealing to all users. 
Principle 2: Flexibility in Use 
The design accommodates a wide range of individual preferences and abilities. 
Guidelines: 
2a. Provide choice in methods of use. 
2b. Accommodate right or left-handed access and use. 
2c. Facilitate the user's accuracy and precision. 
2d. Provide adaptability to the user's pace. 
Principle 3: Simple and Intuitive Use 
Use of the design is easy to understand, regardless of the user's experience, knowledge, language skills or 
current concentration level. 
Guidelines: 
3a. Eliminate unnecessary complexity. 
3b. Be consistent with user expectations and intuition. 
3c. Accommodate a wide range of literacy and language skills. 
3d. Arrange information consistent with its importance. 
3e. Provide effective prompting and feedback during and after task completion. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 243, 

===PAGE 263===
aS S- Sa IT IATA Bull Airport Development Reference Manual 
Principle 4: Perceptible Information 
The design communicates necessary information effectively to the user, regardless of the ambient conditions 
or the user's sensory abilities. 
Guidelines: 
4a. Use different modes (pictorial, verbal, tactile) for redundant presentation of essential information. 
4b. Provide adequate contrast between essential information and its surroundings. 
4c. Maximize “legibility” of essential information. 
4d. Differentiate elements in ways that can be described (i.e., make it easy to give instructions). 
4e. Provide compatibility with a variety of techniques or devices used by people with sensory limitations. 
Principle 5: Tolerance for Error 
The design minimizes hazards and the adverse consequences of accidental or unintended actions. 
Guidelines: 
5a. Arrange elements to minimize hazards and errors: most used elements, most accessible; hazardous 
elements eliminated, isolated, or shielded. 
5b. Provide warnings of hazards and errors. 
5c. Provide fail safe features. 
5d. Discourage unconscious action in tasks that require vigilance. 
Principle 6: Low Physical Effort 
The design can be used efficiently and comfortably and with a minimum of fatigue. 
Guidelines: 
6a. Allow user to maintain a neutral body position. 
6b. Use reasonable operating forces. 
6c. Minimize repetitive actions. 
6d. Minimize sustained physical effort. 
Principle 7: Size and Space for Approach and Use 
Appropriate size and space is provided for approach, reach, manipulation, and use regardless of user's body 
size, posture, or mobility. 
244 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 264===
a | 
Be IATA al Universal Design and Accessibility 
Guidelines: 
7a. Provide a clear line of sight to important elements for any seated or standing user. 
7b. Make reach to all components comfortable for any seated or standing user. 
7c. Accommodate variations in hand and grip size. 
7d. Provide adequate space for the use of assistive devices or personal assistance. 
2.5.2.2 Goals of Universal Design 
Along with the seven principles, Universal Design has eight goals devised in 2012 by the Center for Inclusive 
Design and Environmental Access at the University at Buffalo (Steinfeld and Maisel). These are an expanded 
definition of the principles of universal design to include social participation and health and wellness. Rooted 
in evidence-based design, the eight goals of universal design were also developed to apply universal design 
and measure outcomes. They cover functional, social and emotional dimensions. Each goal is supported by 
an interdisciplinary knowledge base e.g., anthropometrics, biomechanics, perception, cognition, safety, health 
promotion, and social interaction. The following are the eight goals of Universal Design: 
¢ Body Fit-Accommodating a wide range of body sizes and abilities 
© Comfort-Keeping demands within desirable limits of body function and perception 
e Awareness—Ensuring that critical information for use is easily perceived 
¢ Understanding—Making methods of operation and use intuitive, clear and unambiguous 
¢ Wellness—Contributing to health promotion and protection from hazards 
© Social Integration—Treating all groups with dignity and respect 
© Personalization—Incorporating opportunities for choice and the expression of individual preferences 
¢ Cultural Appropriateness—Respecting and reinforcing cultural values, and the social and environmental 
context of any design project 
2.5.2.3 Universal Design in Digital Accessibility 
Digital accessibility means that websites, tools, and technologies are designed and developed so that people 
with disabilities can use them. 
2.5.2.3.1 Connecting Universal Design with Digital Accessibility 
Universal Design principles also support the functionality of digital communications: 
¢ Equitable Use means everyone uses the same website, without a separate “accessible” site or an 
“accessibility mode.” 
¢ Flexibility in Use means people can operate websites using different input methods, such as touch, 
speech, gaze, a mouse, or a keyboard. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 245 

===PAGE 265===
i Be |i a TAT: al Airport Development Reference Manual 
¢ Simple and Intuitive Use means websites are straightforward, with clean layouts, consistent interaction, 
and clear information. 
¢ Perceptible Information means content is provided in text as well as visually or audibly, so that the 
information is accessible using different senses. 
* Tolerance for Error means interactions are designed to promote success and minimize risks, for 
example, by providing confirmations and feedback. 
* Low Physical Effort means people can efficiently operate websites using their preferred input device 
(such as a keyboard). 
¢ Size and Space for Approach and Use means the necessary tools to operate a website interface are 
visible and readily available. 
Similar to accessibility standards in the physical world, digital accessibility standards support universal design 
principles. WCAG (World Content Accessibility Guidelines) is the recognized standard used globally to ensure 
digital accessibility. 
2.5.3 Social and Legal Drivers 
The case for making airports more universally usable to all is a compelling one on many fronts. Universal 
Design proposes a progressive and evolving approach to the development of inclusive environments that can 
be accessed, understood and used to the greatest extent possible. Not only does Universal Design make 
good business sense, but it also has many compelling social and legal drivers: 
¢ Benefits to Individuals 
e Benefits to Society 
¢ Business Benefits 
e Legislation 
2.5.3.1 Benefits to Individuals 
Universal Design is a human-centred approach that is user-friendly and convenient, but also respectful of user 
dignity, rights and privacy. 
The degree of difficulty that people experience when using a product, service or environment can vary, and 
the degree of personal benefit will vary accordingly. Therefore, if a product, service or environment is well 
designed, with accessibility and usability in mind, all people will benefit. 
The age-distribution of the world's population is changing dramatically. People are living longer as a result of 
medical developments in the last century and healthier lifestyle changes. Therefore, the number of people 
living with physical, sensory, mental health or intellectual impairments is increasing, as is the life expectancy 
of people with particularly severe or multiple impairments. 
246 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 266===
Yo By IATA pruly Universal Design and Accessibility 
Independent Living 
Universal Design creates inclusive design solutions and promotes accessibility and usability, allowing people 
with all levels of ability to live independently. The ability of a person to remain as independent as possible can 
be influenced by how accessible and usable products, services and environments are. 
Ability as a Continuum 
Universal Design assumes that the range of human ability is ordinary, not special (Elaine Ostroff, 2001). No 
two people are the same and no two people have exactly the same ability. The considerable variation that 
exists between people can be influenced by both external and internal factors. Ability can vary according to 
the type of activity in which a person is participating or the environment in which that person is carrying out 
the activity. 
Every person experiences reduced functioning at some stage during his or her lifetime. For example: 
e Noisy environments impair a person's hearing 
¢ —Dimly lit rooms impair a person's vision 
¢ Getting the flu reduces a person's stamina. 
A Universal Design approach therefore requires an appreciation of the varied abilities of every person and to 
design in such a way that the resulting product, service or environment can be used by everyone regardless 
of age, size, ability or disability. 
2.5.3.2 Benefits to Society 
In this technological age, the skills required to participate in society are becoming increasingly complex. As 
each technological innovation becomes mainstream, people who do not adopt it are being excluded from 
accessing a whole range of financial, state, social or cultural services or amenity improvements. 
In order to facilitate people with differing abilities, of differing ages and sizes within society, systems and 
buildings must be designed with the user (and different users’ ability, input, feedback and testing) at the 
centre of the design process. A universally designed environment promotes equality and makes life easier 
and safer for everyone. 
2.5.3.3 Business Benefits 
The benefits to business of adopting a universal design approach vary from cost reduction to increased 
customer satisfaction. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 247 

===PAGE 267===
ay TL He ff IATA Bll Airport Development Reference Manual 
Reduced need and cost of assistance services 
An important implication is that an airport that enables customers to function independently will see a 
reduction in the need to provide assistance services and therefore, a reduction in the cost associated with 
these. 
Increased Market Reach 
Universal design should lead to an increase in market reach. A product, service or environment can become 
available to a wider range of customers. 
Enhanced Customer Satisfaction and Retention 
A satisfied customer will tell other people about the airport and airline product, increasing awareness and 
potentially introducing new customers. 
Market Crossover Success 
Products that are aimed at a specific target group can sometimes generate interest and demand from 
unforeseen markets. 
Positive Public Brand Image 
A business that positively contributes to society by incorporating a universal design approach is likely to 
Teceive a reputation for having a high level of corporate social tresponsibility. 
Increased Consumer Expectations 
In recent decades, the voice of the general public has become more Prominent and more influential. People 
are more confident to speak up when they have a complaint, and information and communication 
technologies have made this increasingly easy to do. Direct pressure from consumer groups as well as direct 
engagement with their customers have encouraged many companies to evolve their design processes and 
improve their customer services to accommodate a wider range of people.

2.6 Airport Technology 
2.6.1 Introduction 
Technology has fundamentally changed many aspects of an airport's operation over recent decades, and 
offers considerably more change in the years to come. All levels of airport planning, from the development of 
the master plan to ongoing operational improvements are most likely to involve technology components. 
Before any new technology is considered, it is important to carefully examine and evaluate current processes 
and to perform continuous process improvements. All airports should seek to increase capacity of existing 
facilities and maximize the level of service by improving existing processes or introducing new processes 
before employing a technology solution. Utilizing proven process improvement methodologies has yielded 
significant improvements in existing airport processes reducing the need to expand existing space, or employ 
technology solutions to achieve the same results. 
Once a rigorous process improvement methodology has been applied and targeted processes have been 
improved, it is then appropriate to consider the use of technology to further enhance the operation, optimize 
the passenger experience and reduce the need for additional infrastructure. 
For technology to be effective, it must be aligned with the strategic objectives of the airport. While technology￾enabled business change can offer considerable efficiency, cost and service benefits, as with other airport 
developments it is critical that airline partners are engaged early and regularly in the planning, implementation 
and support of key systems. Similarly, other stakeholders such as government and ground handling agents 
should be consulted, as the industry works together to drive improvements to enhance operational efficiency. 
There are two key business aspects that technology should be viewed from: 
¢ The “push” of technology-airport and airline customers expect technology to efficiently deliver an optimum 
level of service at a reasonable cost. The application of technology, for example the use of passenger￾held mobile devices, presents the opportunity to enhance the passenger experience and drive efficiency 
even further. 
© The “pull” of technology-technology that is available and could improve the business, which is not yet 
utilized by the airport and/or airline partners (e.g., biometric passenger processing). 
Technology has been a key contributor in driving many changes that have been taking place in the industry 
over the last decade, and which can be categorized into three major trends. These global trends are visible 
across the largest and most successful airports. The trends are strongly supported by new technology: 
e Passenger Centricity —Airports are striving to meet the expectations of the individual traveler, most of 
whom now have access to the Internet and social media through their mobile phones and are familiar with 
self-service technology through banks, transport systems and supermarkets. 
Mobile phones are becoming the front-door of businesses, and airports and airlines are transforming their 
business models to ensure their service design starts with the customer at the center, and their preferred 
mode of engagement. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 249 

===PAGE 269===
Se S- IATA wa Airport Development Reference Manual 
A challenge for airports and airlines is to satisfy technology-aware passengers with high-quality and 
appropriate services, while also supporting less technology-capable passengers (that do not use modern 
technology) through relevant services, generally provided through on-airport signage and airline/airport 
staff support. 
* Control —some airports are moving from the role of a landlord or infrastructure provider to that of a 
business and process manager. This requires a cultural change from a more traditional approach and is 
not a straightforward transition. Airlines and stakeholders should be closely consulted on any changes 
that impact passengers, their operations or contractual agreements. 
¢ Collaboration -leading technology airports act as the coordinator and consolidator for the concentration 
and exchange of relevant data in the interests of the airport community. This requires a different approach 
for the technology service provider at an airport that needs to look beyond the needs of the internal airport 
departments. 
Most airports are developing in the same general direction regarding the application of technology. However, 
a technology strategy needs to be specific to a particular airport since the starting position, business priorities, 
customer expectations and specific challenges will be different. 
2.6.2 Future Technology Goals and Objectives 
Airports need to have confidence in the abilities of new technology to perform the desired operational 
functionality. To achieve this confidence, technology should accomplish the following goals: 
e Improve the airport experience 
¢ Cope with increased traffic 
° Meet airport business imperatives 
In meeting these goals, any proposed technology must accomplish the following objectives: 
° Be effective. 
e Be reliable. 
¢ Not adversely affect the operation. 
¢ Be accepted by its users. 
¢ Be safe and secure for its use. 
¢ Be fit for purpose. 
e Be commercially viable. 
250 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 270===
IATA Pull Airport Technology 
Airports and airlines should achieve these objectives through prudent implementation of newer technology. A 
philosophy of proving the value of technology via operational trials, within the appropriate environments 
should be adopted. See 2.6.7.2 Transition From Future Technology to Viable Current Technology on the use 
of testing facilities and eventually live operational airport locations. 
2.6.2.1 Improve the Airport Experience 
At the core of any customer-centric airport strategy is an understanding of what the customer wants. It is 
important to recognize airlines are airport customers, and a good understanding of their requirements and 
expected service will shape the overall airport experience. In addition, key to improving the airport experience 
is the understanding of passenger preferences to capture and build profiles. Understanding patterns and 
behaviors of passengers can create a more personalized experience. 
A lack of coordination in sharing information among stakeholders (i.e., airports, airlines, ground handlers, 
government agencies) means repetition of processes (e.g., presentation of the boarding pass and travel 
document) at different touchpoints of the passenger journey, which may have a negative impact on the 
passenger experience. Therefore, all stakeholders should attempt to share information and have a 
coordinated approach to provide a truly seamless journey. 
2.6.2.2 Cope with Increased Air Traffic 
Technology presents an opportunity to use infrastructure capacity more efficiently by improving passenger 
throughput while maintaining customer levels of service. As a result, technology can support a reduction in 
operational costs and potentially reduce the size of building footprints in processing areas and/or defer capital 
construction. 
Most airports are physically constrained, which means airports and airlines need to make the most of the 
available infrastructure and still provide a high level of service. Technology plays an important role in 
expanding the physical boundary and extending it digitally by enabling self-service, off-airport check-in and in 
some cases bag drop (i.e., taking some of the processes off the airport premises). Other applications include 
automated resource allocation and scheduling for gates, stands, airline zones/desks along with other 
technologies such as business intelligence supporting the efficient use of infrastructure. 
2.6.2.3, Meet Airport Business Imperatives 
Most airports are dealing with three business imperatives and technology can play a key role in helping 
airports achieve them: 
e |mprove Passenger Satisfaction 
© Optimize Operational Processes 
e Improve Financial Performance

SS IATA yl Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.6.2.3.1_ Improve Passenger Satisfaction 
As passengers migrate more of their daily lives to mobile interactions, airports and airlines need to rethink and 
redesign their processes and services, such as providing information and payment services so that they are 
more intuitive for mobile using passengers. 
Creating a passenger-centric airport should be focused on enabling the digital traveler, given most 
passengers now carry smartphones and have a preferences to use their device to store tickets and make 
payments. Smartphones can also be used to digitally store passport details, and as a safe, secure platform to 
demonstrate vaccination credentials, enabling an efficient biometric process through the airport with minimal 
physical interventions and touch points. Planners should consider where relevant biometric equipment should 
be installed to optimize passenger processing, and take into account processing time and the required level of 
service for each sub-processor as part of the overall passenger experience strategy. 
Most airport Information and Communications Technology/infrastructure has historically been designed for 
airport staff interactions rather than for passengers. Despite this, there is a growing focus on passengers 
recognizing their needs for connectivity. 
It is equally important to equip airport staff with up-to-date information as passengers can have access to 
better information and tools than the staff serving them leading to passenger frustration and dissatisfaction. 
Equipping and enabling airport staff with access to real-time information on mobile devices enables them to 
be more efficient, and in turn provide a better service to passengers. Due to the highly technical nature of 
these solutions it is important this evaluation is managed in partnership between airport technology staff and 
airline head office specialists in data processing, communications, terminal planning and handling procedures. 
2.6.2.3.2 Optimize Operational Processes 
Airports are tasked to deliver safe and secure operations, as well as ensure a high standard of level of service 
and customer satisfaction, which means ensuring key stakeholders (e.g., airports, airlines, ground handlers, 
and government agencies) can operate and deliver on their services effectively and efficiently. Technology 
should serve to support these stakeholders as they provide their respective services across the airport 
campus. Many airport stakeholders will have their own technology and cybersecurity requirements and it is 
incumbent on the airport to understand and coordinate these disparate technologies into a unified working 
solution at the airport. 
2.6.2.3.3. Improve Financial Performance 
More and more airports are deploying technology to maximize asset utilization to make the most of their fixed 
assets (e.g., gates, stands, taxiways, runways) and other resources. This reduces overall operational costs 
which improves financial performance. In addition, technology is also being used to generate additional non￾aeronautical revenues (e.g., airport car parking, retail and food & beverage) further improving financial 
252 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 272===
IATA Airport Technology 
performance. Personalization creates opportunities for passengers to spend more while enhancing the 
passenger experience at the same time. The creation of personalized offerings using passenger data requires 
close collaboration between the airport and the airlines, to ensure that issues of data ownership and privacy 
are identified and appropriately addressed. 
2.6.3 Establish a Unifying Technology Strategy 
It is highly recommended that the airport establishes a unifying technology strategy that supports business 
and planning activities for the coming five years, with a focus on the shorter term to accommodate rapid 
changes in technology. An airport's unifying technology strategy should address: 
¢ Base technical infrastructure (e.g., communications integration platform) 
e Airline enabling systems to support passenger, baggage, cargo and aircraft handling 
¢ Airport Operations systems (e.g., Flight Information Display Systems, Apron Management) 
e Financial and administration systems (e.g., airline billing) 
e Engineering systems (e.g., asset and maintenance management) 
* Control Centers (e.g., operations control) 
¢ Interfacing services to the airport community (e.g., departure control systems—DCS, Air Traffic Control) 
2.6.4 Airport Digital Transformation 
The airport digital transformation is acknowledged by the airport industry as an important success element as 
it harnesses the power of data and technology to support growth ambitions through the transformation of key 
processes. Ultimately, the objective is to leverage the capabilities of technology and its increasing penetration 
to drive business improvement in the areas of efficiency, financial performance, and passenger experience, 
while ensuring the core functions of safety and security are paramount. 
2.6.4.1 Defining Digital Transformation 
Digital Transformation is a continuous evolution of business activities, processes, competencies, and models 
that utilizes innovative solutions and digital technologies, improving the business’ abilities to drive growth by 
rethinking its strategy, organization capabilities, and culture to sustain long-term performance. Digital 
Transformation provides a unique opportunity for all stakeholders to collaborate and co-innovate to improve 
the core business and transform the business. The fundamental point is that business strategy (i.e., business 
imperatives) drives Digital Transformation and not technology.

2.6.4.3 A Foundation of Mutual Trust and Agreed Standards 
Ultimately, many of the technology components are already understood and even proven in isolation, 
however, the challenge is integrating the various components together in a harmonious manner across all 
stakeholders. Collaboration between stakeholders is required based on trust and willingness to share 
information to deliver mutual benefits for all parties. Each stakeholder should be aware of the success of other 
stakeholders as much as their own. The isolated self-interest of any single stakeholder will slow and even 
potentially halt the ability for meaningful end-to-end change. 
Further, this sharing of data is going to need standards being agreed and adhered to such as IATA's One ID 
initiative are seeking to identify and facilitate the development of such standards. The aviation community has 
a long history of working together to create standards such as operational message formats. The airport 
digital transformation journey that is now being envisaged is going to need faster and tighter collaboration in 
the development of such standards. 
Underpinning this need for business collaboration will be an understanding of the data that enables it; 
therefore, the IATA Architecture and Technology Strategy Board (ATSB) standards and the IATA Aviation 
Industry Data Model (AIDM) are key. As much as airport planning needs to consider operational industry 
standards, given that airlines need to be able to operate as consistently as possible from multiple airports, it is 
critical that technology planning leverages standards. 
In addition, through the cooperation of various stakeholders, Airport Community Recommended Information 
Services (ACRIS) is focused on setting the standard for data exchange in the aviation community. 
2.6.4.4 Airport Digital Readiness 
Digital transformation is described by ACI in its Airport Digital Transformation handbook as evolving 
processes and services to deliver a better experience to all passengers and customers, by adopting and 
implementing new technologies and integrating them with existing ones. The handbook indicates three levels 
regarding digital readiness: 
¢ Digitally Enabled Airport —have the basics in order, such as infrastructure and cyber resilience, to be 
able to become a digital airport to reach a customer 
¢ Fully Digital —have all options implemented that provide a fully digital airport based on mainstream and 
commonly available technologies 
¢ Next Gen Digital —have implemented all advanced digital concepts that are not commonly available and 
tested in the aviation industry, such as seamless travel with single token biometric (IATA One ID) 
touchpoints, new business models based on digital services such as block chain, and personal and 
context aware services 
An updated version of ACI's Digital Transformation handbook (second Edition, 2021) highlights this is not just 
about deployment of new technologies, but instead business sustainability in the long-term “will come from 
transforming the business of airports, adapting to customers, staff, community and cultures while leveraging 
existing and new technologies to meet strategic objectives and goals”.

2.6.4.5.2 Operational Processes 
ConOps translates into operational processes and procedures (i.e. standard operating procedures “SOP”) that 
are unique to that airport and incorporate the required safety, security, and general operating procedures 
(both in normal and irregular operations scenarios). These operational processes have developed over time, 
as have the technology systems that underpin those processes. Of note, many of those systems will have 
been developed with a specific set of functions in mind, where the principals of digital transformation need the 
collation of data from multiple systems to each enable the other to be enriched. Data from multiple operational 
systems needs to be harnessed in order to achieve the intended overarching outcomes and efficiencies. 
The key for the airport is to focus on a holistic technology approach across the entire airport campus; one that 
will avoid “silos” of technology wherein the data, systems, and outputs from one technology system act in 
isolation and do not interface with other technology systems.

2.6.4.5.3 Digital Capabilities 
Digital transformation provides airport development direction and solutions based on stakeholder engagement 
and data analytics; however, transformation can move faster than adaptability of stakeholders and 
passengers using advanced technologies. Airports need to balance digital capability and users’ adaptability in 
order to optimize benefits of digital transformation (McKinsey, 2017). 
2.6.4.5.4 Passenger Experience 
The digital transformation of the passenger experience is underway; however, this change has been much 
slower than many on the technology side of the business had expected. While all the technology components 
exist, and in most cases are proven operationally in a stand-alone fashion, there are two key factors that need 
addressing for the change to be embraced: 
Stakeholder collaboration—While technology presents huge potential to enable a significantly improved 
passenger experience, this can only be achieved with airports and airlines leading their business 
stakeholders (i.e., government agencies, ground handling agents) through a business change process 
Data sharing and standards—Business change needs data sharing, and data sharing needs to be based 
on agreed and adopted standards, as well as on industry data models for consistency of definitions and 
format 
Therefore, it is the regulatory and stakeholder collaboration elements that limit technology potential. 
Technology initiatives have the potential to deliver solutions that either currently exist for use today or are 
under development, such as the following: 
A passenger authenticates their biometric identity off-airport and creates their biometric token in the 
process. The passenger also prepares their own bag tags (home printed or electronic)-they are airport 
ready. 
A shared use platform provides the opportunity for any passenger to use any on-airport infrastructure 
device. This has the potential to deliver efficiency across the airport terminal and simplify the passenger 
experience while reducing the need for significant cross terminal passenger movement. It is of note, of 
course, that this is an extreme potential, and that an airport with their airline stakeholders will agree to a 
model of airport use that is efficient, yet delivers specific airline needs such as branding and operational 
requirements. 
Passengers with bags may proceed directly to any self-service bag drop. Trials are currently underway for 
passengers to establish their identity with their biometric token, so their pre-tagged bags are injected into 
the baggage system.

2.6.5 Airport IT Trends 
2.6.5.1 IT Best Practices and Principles 
The capability of IT has changed over the last two decades from providing relatively isolated and localized 
systems and services to communicating with passengers and delivering broadly integrated services across 
the airport community. This new capability opens new opportunities to improve the contribution of IT to the 
airport vision. The new IT world, however, needs a solid framework that will enable continuing change in the 
future to meet evolving business needs at a reasonable and justified cost. 
Best practices in IT have improved over the decades based on two fundamental principles: 
* IT systems require continual updates to meet changing business needs-they are not like most plant and 
equipment where the function does not change significantly during its lifetime. 
¢ IT systems and services deliver optimal benefits when business processes change to take advantage of 
new capabilities—implementing IT systems that mimic manual processes creates cost and rigidity. 
The most important best practice elements in IT for airports and other organizations include: 
* The use Commercially-available Off-the-Shelf (COTS) products developed to open industry standards 
with minimal change, rather than developing in-house solutions to meet supposedly unique user needs. 
The economic case is very strong and the reduction of risk is overwhelming, if products are chosen and 
installed intelligently. The selection and use of COTS products should be universal, unless there is a 
unique competitive advantage expected from an in-house development. 
* Keep close to core business objectives when developing IT solutions, and then implement containable 
and targeted releases, so benefits are realized as soon as possible, and business engagement is 
sustained and maximized. Significant investment can be lost when technology spend gets ahead of 
proven business need. 
2.6.5.2 Technology Adoption 
Airports and airlines continue to invest in technology to both enhance and protect their business. The 
following information is the result of research conducted by AC! and SITA. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 259 

===PAGE 279===
we IATA 4 Wi Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.6.5.2.1 Airport Trends 
The pandemic has significantly accelerated the digital transformation of the industry and the adoption of new 
solutions and technology. The results of research suggest that airports are eager to invest in technology in 
higher proportions than in previous years to leverage technology benefits despite the drop in revenues. 
Due to the increasing dependence on technology, digital services, and remote work patterns, it is no surprise 
to observe cybersecurity initiatives as one of the airport's top investment priorities, followed by cloud services, 
and inhouse virtual and remote IT services as high priorities for airports over the coming years. As the 
industry enters the recovery phase, airports are also placing new technology services at the forefront as they 
focus on offering seamless health and safety solutions to enhance the passenger experience, while optimizing 
resources and infrastructure. 
Investments in self-service initiatives continued to increase, with the following areas being significantly 
impacted (source of statistics SITA 2021 Air Transport IT Insights): 
° 71% of airports have implemented bag tag printing via kiosks. 
° 42% of airports have implemented automated boarding gates, and airports are expected to continue to 
increase the automation of the boarding process. 
° Self-service bag drop uptake has increased, with 68% of airports having implemented assisted services, 
and 52% of airports now having implemented unassisted services. Three-quarter of airports surveyed 
expect to increase the number of unassisted bag drops. 
Supplementing this, Internet of Things initiatives are seeing significant investment, aimed at smoothing the 
passenger journey through the airport via beacons or sensors powering wayfinding solutions as well as 
personalized messages regarding facilities, baggage, and more. 
As sustainability and reducing carbon emissions reduction efforts are prioritized, airports are looking to 
technology to support their initiatives. The majority of airports have implemented sustainability programs 
including building airport infrastructure (green spaces, use of natural light, renewable energy), widely available 
recycling points, and smart building technology and automation. Technology should underpin and support any 
sustainability and carbon reduction initiatives similar to the airport business plan and ConOps, in close with 
airlines and other airport stakeholders. 
2.6.5.2.2 Airline Trends 
Airline spend on technology is expected to reduce in coming years however research shows that industry is 
cautiously optimistic and technology continues to be a critical investment area for airlines. 
Similar to airports, cybersecurity is the key IT priority for airlines, followed by cloud services, which are a focus 
for a growing proportion of airlines over the coming years. The other areas of investment are mobile 
applications for passenger services such as purchase of tickets and services, check-in and boarding. 
Investment in airline self-service such as mobile, web-based and automated services continue to grow and 
dominate how passengers engage with airlines and pass through the airport. Through check-in, bag drop,

oz lil Se 
IATA 4 Airport Technology 
boarding, and baggage reclaim, increasing numbers of airlines now offer self-service options supported by 
real-time data: 
¢ Implementation of unassisted bag drop is increasing and is a trend that will continue. 
¢ Over a third of airlines (35%) have implemented automated boarding gates, with 65% planning to do so. 
¢ Self-service solutions to help airlines face irregular operations remained the top priority. 91% of the airline 
respondents expect a significant increase in major investment programs. 
¢ More passengers are receiving real-time information sent to their mobile about their bags, with 25% of 
airlines now offering this service. 69% of airlines expect to offer this by 2026. 
Data centers play a key role in airline digitalization, which has accelerated throughout the pandemic, as 
airlines turn their focus to maximizing agility and scalability. Sustainability has become an important 
consideration, with 52% of airlines planning to implement selection criteria for external data center providers 
that favor carbon neutrality, renewable energy sourcing, or other environmental considerations. 49% plan a 
data center shift from dedicated infrastructure to an energy efficient cloud or other large-scale infrastructure. 
Other IT services are rising significantly in priority, with the majority of airlines investing in major programs for 
aircraft maintenance (86%), business intelligence (85%), and mobile applications for pilot services (85%). 
Again, this reflects the strong trend towards digitalization to drive efficiencies. 
Technology trends supports the NEXTT vision of biometric-powered Identity Management with Self-boarding 
remaining a fundamental part of future airline strategy around passenger identity management, and the use of 
“biometric only” gates has seen a significant increase and set to increase. 
2.6.5.2.3. Passenger Technology Insights 
Passengers are demanding faster, automated journeys and more sustainable approaches to air travel as key 
takeaways from latest Passenger IT Insights®. 
The report also indicates passengers want technology that helps them automate their entire journey and 
enables a more fluid travel experience, with the increased use of mobile phones to facilitate each step of the 
Journey. This trend falls into line with the industry's COVID-19 response, helping to ease congestion at the 
airport and reducing the interaction points between staff and passengers through contactless touchpoints. 
Overall passengers are satisfied, however, the satisfaction rate is significantly higher when passengers use 
technology at various stages of their journey.

2.6.6 Best Practice 
It is of note there is considerable variation in the way that many airports make use of technology, although 
most are moving in a similar direction. 
Key to the implementation of new technologies that underpin digital transformation will be the following 
characteristics that have more to do with a way of working rather than just the technology: 
e Business change is the focus, and only fully enabled when there is quality engagement across all 
stakeholders 
* Trust among stakeholders to share data so that it is applied to mutually agreed processes for the benefit 
of all 
¢ Standards that apply globally, so stakeholders can “invest once, deploy everywhere”

With the forecast growth in passenger numbers, further pursuing the capabilities enabled by digital 
transformation is mandatory. It is neither feasible nor sensible to expand airports and continue with a number 
of processes that history will look back on as unnecessary and resistant to change. 
Some examples of the best practice processes that are expected to emerge are: 
e True end-to-end self-service, where passengers can make a relatively unimpeded trip through the airport 
enabled through the use of a biometric token 
e Predictive systems that can alert, well ahead of time, about disruptions so out-of-schedule operations can 
be optimally planned 
e Simplification in the use of airport space, where every device is shared use, not just technically, but in its 
business use

2.6.6.1.1 Planning the Journey 
From a planning perspective, passengers have a wide range of alternatives to plan and purchase a ticket. The 
airlines provide passengers with different channels to check-in, such as the web or mobile applications, which 
means passengers can print their boarding pass at home or store it on their mobile phone. 
Some airlines also allow passengers to print baggage tags at home and place the printed baggage tag into 
special plastic sleeves that are then attached to the bag at the airport. In this case, the airport working with 
airlines should make provisions to facilitate passenger journeys; for instance, to collect the plastic sleeves and 
drop the bags at either assisted (i.e., with help of a check-in or bag-drop agent) or automated bag drops. 
2.6.6.1.2 Passenger Check-In

A. Common Use Passenger Processing Systems 
Common use passenger systems have been an essential element of airport technology for many years: 
¢ For airports seeking to optimize the utilization of core assets, in particular the existing footprint of the 
airport building, CUPPS enables different airlines to use the same IT equipment at different times of the 
day, rather than needing dedicated IT equipment and space. 
¢ Airlines seeking to deliver a consistent quality service globally should employ a “build once, deploy 
everywhere” strategy. 
There are three key standards to comply with: 
1. CUPPS-IATA RP1797 for agent-facing solutions 
2. CUSS-IATA RP1706 for passenger-facing solutions such as kiosks and self-service bag drops 
3. Web services-IATA RP1741 utilizing IATA Passenger Airport Data Interchange Standards (PADIS) and 
Airline Industry Data Model (AIDM) 
CUSS enables passenger and baggage processing by connecting to an airline's Departure Control System 
(DCS) host systems. 
A CUPPS platform allows a workstation to run several different airline applications using the same hardware, 
providing a user-friendly interface. The solution ensures that when a user swaps between applications, any 
peripherals associated with the application also swap, instantly. This means that there is no need for the user 
to wait while a printer is reloaded with the parameters for the new session, thereby resulting in increased
