2.6.6.1.3 Baggage Management 
The Baggage Handling System (BHS) is a critical system, and as such it is vital that during the planning of a 
new terminal, the BHS is properly defined to meet the airport's needs and those of its passengers. 
The baggage management process is supported by an integrated BHS system that moves the baggage 
accepted at check-in to the baggage make-up area used in preparation to be loaded on an aircraft. 
Baggage management at airports is evolving with self bag drop becoming more accepted where the 
passenger can check-in their hold baggage quickly and safely without agent assistance. As a result, airports 
and airlines can offer a better passenger experience by reducing queues and faster processing. 
Airports have the flexibility to introduce self bag drop in two ways: 
(a) utilizing the existing infrastructure to maximize terminal capacity, which does not require any costly 
modifications to the current check-in desks or conveyor belts. It can be installed quickly and easily with 
minimum disruption to daily operations; 
(b) a new fit for airports building a new terminal or refurbishing an existing one. 
Airports can also future-proof their self bag drop technology by ensuring that the technology can be easily 
integrated with passport identification and biometrics recognition that will create automated, secure and 
seamless baggage management processes. 
2.6.6.1.4 Security Screening 
Today's passenger and cabin baggage security screening is delivered at some cost to the aviation industry, 
control authorities, and passengers, whether financial or in the passenger experience. Technology presents 
the opportunity to help address these issues, given the predicted growth in air travel, continuously evolving 
threats, and the potential for longer passenger queues and intrusive measures. 
States and stakeholders are introducing concepts such as risk-based differentiation, new technologies, 
automation and process improvements as options for airports and their stakeholders to address challenges, 
all of which require special consideration from a digital transformation perspective. They come with increasing 
connectivity, facilitation and business intelligence opportunities, and at the same time, have additional 
computing power and data transfer needs, as well as carry with them greater risks in terms of cybersecurity 
and system failure. Therefore, they need to be considered as part of the wider airport system planning 
process. Such technologies and processes include: 
e Advanced technologies such as passenger security scanners, explosive detection systems, and 
Computed Tomography (CT), which, in addition to their own power and data requirements, may need to 
be integrated into the wider checkpoint management system 
e Centralized Image Processing (or multiplexing), which uses network connectivity to send the next image 
to the next available operator, regardless of where the officer is located 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 267 

===PAGE 287===
IATA paul Airport Development Reference Manual 
e Automated access control (potentially with biometric capabilities) and automated handling of trays. 
Particularly in the case of the latter, integration with both the checkpoint technologies and the checkpoint 
management system is critical 
e Checkpoint management systems, which collect and analyze data from across the checkpoint, providing 
security managers and officers with both historic and real-time information. These systems can also 
integrate and support the wider airport management and security systems 
Risk-based passenger differentiation, where permitted by regulatory authorities, may require a means to 
communicate between airport/regulatory systems and the checkpoint in order to adjust the screening process 
applied to individual passengers in real time. 
2.6.6.1.5 Border Security/Immigration 
Technology plays an important role in the modernization of border security through optimized interactions with 
travelers. There are now many automated border solutions across the globe, with their implementation being 
evidence of ongoing collaboration between airports and government agencies with responsibility for the 
security of the airport (e.g., immigration, customs and law enforcement). 
Typically, these solutions have moved on from the original Registered Travel Programs (28) to the dynamic 
alignment of a passenger's biometric data (mostly facial recognition) to that same passenger's passport chip 
details. 
2.6.6.1.6 Biometrics 
The convergence of requirements for the improved efficiency, effective use of airport infrastructure, increased 
security, and enhanced passenger experience lead to smarter solutions. The deployment of biometric 
technology facilitates a secure, fully self-service passenger flow, from the time of booking to boarding. 
Passenger identity is confirmed as early as possible in the process, and the passenger's biometric details are 
captured. Biometric recognition can be used for identity verification throughout the various process steps 
which may include self-bag drop, secure area access, security screening, border control and boarding. This 
solution can be realized providing there is substantial collaboration and information sharing between 
stakeholders on a need-to-know/authorized-to-know basis. Biometrics remove the need to present travel 
documents (e.g., boarding pass or passport), speed up the passenger journey, and improve operational 
efficiency for airports and airlines. 
The implications of introducing new solutions and technologies are the need to retrofit existing facilities (e.g., 
check-in devices with cameras to capture the facial scan) or redesign the processing areas with devices that 
are biometric enabled. 
Therefore, a robust and pragmatic framework must be considered because of the different level of maturity 
regarding the adoption of biometric technology. Border Control/Immigration is a relatively mature environment 
for biometrics, however for other aspects of the passenger journey, the framework must help key stakeholders

involved in the passenger journey understand the benefits of biometric technology and how it can be 
integrated into their existing infrastructure. 
Technology for face recognition is not new, and currently it's being used in most of the global hubs for i.e. 
Passport controls, access through boarding gates, etc. The use of this system has dramatically improved 
passenger experience, mainly through the reduction of waiting times in the queue for passport controls. 
In the future, the addition of different data layers to this systems, as for example the share of data between 
the airlines, public authorities, or even the passenger; would allow to improve further the passenger 
experience through concepts like oriented retail offer, higher seamless passenger travel, only touchless 
processes and further developments. Data storage and protection laws, which vary between countries, have 
to be respected. 
2.6.6.2 Airport Operations Management-Technology Elements 
The following subsection is an introduction to key airport systems used by airports that directly impact 
passengers for planner's general awareness. 
2.6.6.2.1 Airport Operational Database 
An Airport Operational Database (AODB) is the central repository where all operational information is 
managed and made available to other systems for further processing. Aircraft movement information for the 
airport is recorded through automated interfaces or by manual capture, utilizing tracking screens with user￾friendly graphical interfaces. All major activities (e.g., configuration, scheduling, tracking, aeronautical billing 
run, archiving, reporting) will ideally interact with this central repository. 
2.6.6.2.2 Flight Information Display System 
A Flight Information Display System (FIDS) is utilized for the management and presentation of flight timing 
information to correspondent aeronautical audiences, such as general flight information for passengers, visual 
messaging and media advertisements. 
Increasingly, FIDS solutions are capable of using evolving technologies, such as media-rich displays, that 
incorporate the use of text, graphics and video. 
FIDS ideally have a two-way automated interaction with the airlines; for example, to receive the latest flight 
status from airlines and to communicate information (e.g., assigned gates to airlines).

2.6.6.2.3 Resource Management System 
The objective of an RMS is to maximize the usage of resources. RMS are used to perform real-time and 
planning allocations of airport fixed resources (e.g., parking stands, baggage carousels, remote gates, 
counters), optimizing the utilization of airport resources across all flights. RMS software also helps airports to 
predict staff resource levels required to efficiently and effectively serve this moving flow of passengers at a 
specified time. 
In addition, a RMS also typically provides the capability to manage mobile resources, such as personnel and 
vehicles, and in doing so deliver an optimized planning, rostering and staff management outcome.

2.6.6.2.4 Closed-Circuit Television 
A dedicated closed-circuit television (CCTV) security surveillance system composed of cameras and monitors 
should cover most of the airport, such as the terminal building, apron, and perimeter. CCTV provides access 
to images from various cameras securely dedicated to one or more security personnel end-users according to 
the selection and control of the users. Monitoring will be performed onsite by CCTV operators at workstations 
located in the Security Control Room. The CCTV control system also provides the facility for CCTV feeds to 
be provided to other locations within the airport, such as the Operations Control Center.

e Ensure appropriate lighting, particularly in the apron or perimeter areas

2.6.6.2.5 Building Management Solution 
The Building Management Solution (BMS) is a computer system that controls and monitors the airport's 
temperature, lighting and power systems. The system calculates the preset requirements of the building and 
controls the connected plant to meet those needs. The level of control via the BMS is dependent upon the 
information received from its sensors and the way in which its programs tell it to respond to that information. 
As well as offering a precise degree of control of its environment, it can be made to trigger alarms or warn of 
individual failure items. 
Occupancy times for different areas of the terminal are programmed into the BMS, such that the system 
automatically switches on and off to meet the set requirements. 
The BMS core functionality keeps the building climate within a specified range, provides lighting based on an 
occupancy schedule, and monitors system performance, device failures, and provides notifications to building 
engineering staff. The BMS functionality reduces building energy and maintenance costs when compared to a 
non-controlled building, thus resulting in a more cost-efficient passenger terminal building. 
2.6.6.2.6 Artifical Intelligence for Efficiency 
Predictive modelling through algorithms and machine learning (ML) are key elements for the improvement of 
the efficiency in the operation of the airport. The forecast of capacity issues like bottlenecks or over capacity 
situations, are one of the main uses for ML at the airport. In tandem, the following characteristics allow the 
airport system to be a good example for ML processes: 
¢ The availability of reference data, through data sharing and different acquisition methods like video, 
Bluetooth, wi-fi connections, and loT sensors. 
* Repetitive actual real scenarios: more easily for middle and big size airports, the periodic repetition of 
flight schedules allow to have solid comparisons, which are the base for the convergent ML processes. 
¢ Good contrast with new situations, which allow to check the performance of the ML against new traffic 
situations. 
* — Setting-up a “digital-twin” model of an airport linked to all kind of airport information systems (e.g. AODB 
for continuous flight updates), enables stakeholders to predict potential bottlenecks even on the day of 
operations and to conduct what-if scenarios on the effects of mitigation measures (e.g. shifting staff's 
break times, redistribute staff, re-allocation of resources for a better and balanced resource usage). 
Balancing demand and capacity. Ongoing calibration of model can be realized based on ML algorithms 
comparing forecasts of demand and operational performance with actual operations. Rolling updates and 
verification enable a continuous improvement of such a digital twin model. 
As a summary, the airport is a good place for the ML, to initially learn and balance the algorithms for capacity 
situations, and later check the behaviour of the forecast with refreshed new data.

2.6.6.3 Technology Infrastructure 
This subsection describes systems and services that support the airport and other stakeholders. It is divided 
into the following categories: 
¢ Network and Communication—the fundamental IT infrastructure for communications 
e Voice and Unified Communication-the group of services specifically associated with voice communication 
* Common Services—comprising services that are made available for use by all authorized systems and 
users at the airport, including the data centers, integration services, and IT security. These services are 
generic rather than associated with particular users 
2.6.6.3.1_ Network and Communications Infrastructure 
Key to the airport's operational performance is the availability of a robust, secure and reliable network and 
communications infrastructure. 
When selecting technologies sustainable solutions should be considered. Such as converged multi-service 
networks that eliminate duplicate infrastructure and systems, and fiber-optic-based networks that require 
much less space, power and cabling than conventional copper-based technologies. 
The key components of an airport's network and communications infrastructure are described below: 
(a) Passive Communications Infrastructure—Cable Plant 
Passive communications infrastructure, or cable plant is a common structured data cabling system for all 
users, which provides the physical media that allow the interconnection of all airport-wide communications 
systems. This is the first element to consider in the design and construction phase. 
When planning and designing the airports cable plan, consider elements such as 99.99% system availability, 
telecommunications resilience, appropriate cabling types such as fiber (or copper), provision for in-building 
wireless and Near Field Communications (NFC) support, accessibility through ceilings and floors, and the 
design of cabling trays and conduits. 
(b) Local Area Network 
The Local Area Network (LAN) comprises the active infrastructure components that provide the bandwidth 
over which various communications systems distribute and share data. Some applications, like video and 
voice transmission, require dedicated amounts of bandwidth over the entire network. Airports are moving 
towards an integrated infrastructure with a common data Campus Area Network (CAN) for the terminal 
system platforms and tenant users, where all systems would use the CAN managed by the airport operator, 
unless by specific law or government policy that requires government agencies (e.g., airport police, 
immigration, customs) to have their own dedicated network. 
The demand for bandwidth and guaranteed Quality of Service (QOS) continues to increase rapidly, and new 
applications and hardware are being developed with the assumption of high bandwidth availability. Examples 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 273 

===PAGE 293===
ray 
Se IATA Biull Airport Development Reference Manual 
of applicable hardware/software systems could include video conferencing, document management, common 
databases, remote file access, video-based training, broadcast TV, and video/data-conferencing. Therefore, 
scalability is an important element of the design. 
Similarly to the design considerations of the cable plant, during planning and design of the terminal, 
implementation can be optimized with participation of IT professionals. 
(c) Wide Area Network (WAN) 
This component of the network and communications infrastructure provides connectivity to remote systems 
such as an airline DCS, remote maintenance support from the airframe manufacturer, or other various 
systems or service providers that distribute and share data. 
Airports benefit from deploying an airport-wide shared connectivity platform that provides airlines and ground 
handlers with reliable, flexible and cost-effective communication services within the airport. One of the key 
benefits of an airport in providing a shared connectivity platform is that it saves the airport community from the 
complexity and cost of dedicated WAN and LAN solutions. 
(d) Wireless Infrastructure (Wi-Fi) 
Awireless access point (WAP or AP) is a device that connects wireless communication devices together to 
form a wireless network. The WAP usually connects to a wired network and can relay data between wireless 
devices and wired devices. Several WAPs can link together to form a larger network that allows roaming. 
Wireless usually covers one or more of four different technologies: telephony, 802.x, Bluetooth, and satellite. 
Wireless is an access media for networking that will support a multiplicity of different data transmission 
speeds, depending on distance and power. Wireless is the medium through which the signal is expected to 
travel. The uses of wireless include all airport users on the ramp, support for all airport tenants, RFID, and 
many others. Wireless brings great flexibility; however, it also brings security challenges. Airports and airlines 
need to have detailed IT and Internet Protocol (IP) security policies where wireless is deployed, as well as 
suitable wired policies that specify and control who actually has the right to deliver which wireless service in 
any given location. 
In addition to accommodating the needs of their stakeholders, airports must accommodate the growing needs 
of passengers, which means improving their current infrastructure (i.e., 4G and Long-Term Evolution (LTE) 
networks) to support the needs for higher bandwidth. The evolution to a faster network (e.g., 5G) and its 
impact on airport operations should be considered as part of a Technology Master Plan: 
¢ Airport infrastructure readiness (e.g., neutral host technology to support multiple networks without 
increasing the networking equipment) 
¢ Airport construction (e.g., provide flexibility to devices that were previously wired that may now be 
wireless such as kiosks) 
¢ Emerging technologies (e.g., with faster data speed and low-latency, increased bandwidth may see a 
proliferation of new solutions such as autonomous vehicles, smart facilities using loT devices) 
274 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 294===
IATA Airport Technology 
Because airports are becoming centers of excellence for technology management and support, cities 
increasingly consider them as critical elements of their emergency response capability. To support this, an 
airport campus may need to integrate with a wider, Metropolitan Area Network (MAN). In this way, emergency 
response centers using airport knowledge and capability can be established as a broader user in the local 
community. 
Large numbers of passengers now have an expectation to have free Wi-Fi Internet access across the airport. 
Critical to the digitalization of processes is a technology infrastructure (wired and wireless) that supports the 
airport and its stakeholders to introduce new capabilities leveraging new technologies. 
(e) Network Management 
Network Management Systems (NMS) are critical and used for managing only network equipment: routers, 
switches, modems (DSL and other), Wi-Fi controllers, and access ports. NMS does not manage any servers 
or data center equipment. 
NMS can be “proactive” or “reactive.” Reactive presupposes a user reports a fault and then a technician is 
dispatched to fix it. Proactive means that the IT asset is monitored (for which bandwidth needs to be 
allocated), and the watching agent intervenes without a user calling in the fault. This requires the definition of 
an operations support model with links to customer and vendor service levels. 
2.6.6.3.2 Voice and Unified Communications 
Telephony and voice communications are critical for day-to-day business needs, with IP communication and 
collaboration platforms quickly replacing obsolete Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM) telephony systems that 
can reduce telecom and infrastructure management costs. 
Voice and unified communications allows for more effective interactions between employees, customers and 
partners, improving the overall efficiency and responsiveness of each organization. Key components are 
described below: 
(a) Voice Services 
Unified communications provide the integration of real-time communication services (e.g., instant messaging 
(chat), presence information, voice (IP telephony), audio, web and video conferencing, desktop sharing, 
document sharing) with non-real-time communication services such as unified messaging (e.g., voicemail, 
email, fax). Airports and the industry as a whole are taking advantage of IP communications and collaboration 
platforms to increase competitiveness and improve global workforce productivity. 
(b) Trunked Radio System/Professional Mobile Radio System 
In today's airport environment, reliable communication is increasingly important for the effectiveness of 
ground-based operations. The more demand that is placed on communication systems, the more critical those 
communication systems become. Professional Mobile Radio (PMR), or Land Mobile Radio (LMR) as it is 
EDITION 42 - MAY 2022 275 

===PAGE 295===
we 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
referred to in North America, offers the reliable, secure and robust connectivity that is the foundation of many 
air transport processes. The PMR solution is based on the Terrestrial Trunked Radio (TETRA) technology 
designed for providing mission-critical mobile communication in built up areas like airports and must be a 
dedicated, secure, robust and reliable radio system. 
2.6.6.3.3. Common Services 
Common services covers specialized systems, technologies and services used by airports and their tenants. 
Several of those services are by nature not visible to the end user (e.g., integration platform), others are used 
daily (e.g., office automation tools), and some have a mission-critical scope (e.g., IT security). The description 
of key systems and services are provided below. 
(a) Data Center and Systems Management 
A data center is a facility used to house computer systems and associated components, such as 
telecommunications and storage systems. It generally includes redundant or backup power supplies, 
redundant data communications connections, environmental controls (e.g., air conditioning, fire suppression) 
and various security devices. 
A data center houses all computer systems and associated components. The planning and design of a data 
center, especially one located at the airport, must carefully consider space requirements, power, and cooling 
requirements; layouts and cabling; backup electrical power; and physical security and access control in 
relation to other critical airport systems and utilities. 
Advances in cloud computing are enabling the optimization of IT infrastructure through data center 
virtualization, which means virtualizing physical servers in the data center facility (e.g., storage, networking 
equipment and devices) to deliver benefits such as cost reductions, faster redeployment, and easier backups. 
The introduction and adoption of new technologies (e.g. server virtualization, edge computing, ultra-efficient 
cooling systems) will enable airports to implement more sustainable data centers (i.e., green data centers) 
that minimizes its environmental impact due to design, energy utilization and reduction in CO, emissions. 
System management provides the capability of centralized monitoring and management of the entire IT 
environment. It includes all components from servers to workstations as well as network and storage devices. 
(b) Enterprise Services Bus 
Enterprise Services Bus (ESB) allows systems at the airport to work cooperatively by providing a 
standardized interfacing mechanism based on messaging middleware. It should be the foundation for the 
messaging between systems for the airport. In other words, the ESB is the integration platform for the airport 
systems providing a single source of truth. 
A major challenge real-time integrated IT systems is data updates that are accepted in one logical system are 
rejected by another, so systems essential to airport operations lose synchronization and the confidence of 
users. In an evolving legacy airport environment, there will be data replication across systems and there 
276 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 296===
=e 
IATA Airport Technology 
needs to be active master data management and consistency of validation rules across systems, that is a 
significant and continuing task. 
(c) IT Security 
IT security, also known as computer security or cybersecurity, is security applied to computing devices (e.9., 
computers and smartphones) and company computer networks, as well as the whole Internet. The field 
includes all the processes and mechanisms by which digital equipment, information and services are 
protected from unintended or unauthorized access, change or destruction. IT security is of growing 
importance due to the increasing reliance on computer systems, and the increasingly sophisticated threats 
from ill-intentioned individuals and groups. It includes physical security to prevent theft of equipment and 
information security to protect the data on that equipment. 
Cybersecurity is the process of applying security measures to ensure the confidentiality, integrity and 
availability of data. Cybersecurity attempts to assure the protection of assets, which includes data, desktops, 
servers, buildings, and most importantly, humans. The goal of cybersecurity is to protect data both in transit 
and at rest. Countermeasures can be put in place in order to increase the security of data. Some of these 
measures in the airport environment include access control, awareness training, audit and accountability, risk 
assessment, penetration testing, vulnerability management, and security assessment and authorization. 
Due to increasing cybersecurity threats, airports should consider the implementation of a focused security 
framework that includes audits to identify threats; detection of incidents; response to attacks; and protection of 
company assets, as well as compliance with emerging regulations and standards (e.g., ISO 27001 Information 
Security and EU GDPR). 
(d) Master Clock 
The master clock is a precision clock that provides timing signals to synchronize slave clocks as part of a 
clock network. It provides the master time signal for all systems, typically based on a GPS signal. In simple 
terms, it is a network time synchronization system that provides time and date information for LAN and LAN￾connected devices. For example, the synchronized time will be displayed publicly on the FIDS displays 
throughout the airport. The synchronized time will also be displayed on digital or analogue clocks throughout 
the terminal building. 
2.6.6.3.4 Key Considerations 
(a) Future-proof by focusing on the future usage of technology, which means to have continued value in the 
distant future. This does not mean an item will last forever, but that it will not quickly become obsolete or 
unable to support the changes in the business. They will likely wear out before advancements in 
technology make them obsolete. Therefore, the approach to future-proof technology is based on three 
critical points: (1) follow industry standards because technologies that have a large community of 
stakeholders tend to progress over time and remain useful for longer; (2) scalability that will help adapt 
the infrastructure both when there is growth but also when there is contraction; (3) flexible technology that 
enables the introduction of new technologies as and when the business is ready (e.g. biometric-enabled 
gates that can be switched on when needed or retrofit to enable this capability).

2.6.7 Developing and Adopting Future Technology 
2.6.7.1. Developing New Technologies for New Challenges 
The airport and airline industry must work with technology developers to ensure that new technology is 
developed to support their business. The private and public sectors offer a range of technology development 
options or avenues. These will allow the airport and airline industry to explore the boundaries of technologies 
and the options available to improve efficiency, safety and the environment associated with the aviation 
sector. 
Airports and airlines and their technology partners or vendors should facilitate the development and 
application of newer technologies in collaboration with: 
e Respected universities or Research Institutes. 
e Industry forums/peer review groups IATA/ACI/ICAO/ECAC/TRB-ACRP. 
e Airport authority/airline research and development teams. 
« National or independent pioneering engineering consultants (e.g., DERA, etc.). 
Airports and airlines need to have regular dialogue with these types of organizations, explain the challenges 
and help lead new technological advances for the industry through technology development sponsorship 
programs. 
2.6.7.2 Transition From Future Technology to Viable Current Technology 
A challenge for airports and airlines is make the transition to incorporate unproven technology to replace older 
equipment or services, or to address operational issues given the risks and costs involved. The process steps 
defined below can help airports and airlines to develop confidence in newer technologies: 
Step 1-Establish the type of technology that may be applied. 
Step 2-Co-development to prove through proof-of-concepts or trials that the technology can be applied to the 
industry effectively. 
Step 3-Fail-Fast: test the technology through a limited exposure live airport operational trial. 
Step 3a—Repeat Step 3 test but at a separate airport operation, again with limited exposure/risk. 
Step 4—Obtain independent verification of the test results collated from the tests in steps 3 and 3a, verifying 
that the technology meets the operational objectives and the criteria. 
Once these steps have been achieved, the technology is where appropriate be incorporated into airports and 
airline operations.

===PAGE 299===
se i IATA ja Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.6.8 Future Technologies—Impact Consultation 
It is essential that certain groups are consulted when new technology is proposed to be implemented. 
The objectives are to ensure that the technology is: 
¢ Suitable for the local environment. 
e Can be used or managed by either local or specialist staff alike. 
e Provides confidence to stakeholders the technology is to support them. 
When change is involved, if an airport developer asks a local consultant group's opinion. about the proposed 
change, the group and the individuals involved will generally feel a sense of being part of the solution. They 
may not agree with the final decision, but they believe they were heard in the discussion phase. Implementing 
future technology is no different. Making certain groups of people part of the decision-making process almost 
always ensures a smoother transition of the technology. 
There are a set of best practices to follow when looking at future technology and how to make consultation 
groups function effectively, these can include: 
¢ Form a group of those affected by the proposed technology. Not everyone affected by the technology 
needs to be a member, but they must have some form of representation. 
¢ Give the group power to decide carefully through a formalized process. 
e Ensure the group is fully informed. Give them access to all and any appropriate information about. 
e Have the group enumerate the impact on their lives of the proposed technology. 
e Require that the group arrive at a decision within a reasonable timeframe. 
e Require that the group create a technology implementation timetable (project delivery program; and if 
required develop a change management program to speed up adoption specially when automating a 
manual process). 
e Ask the group to answer questions such as: How does this technology fit with the existing processes? 
How will it be used? What metrics determine if it is used effectively? What training is required? 
Once the airport developer has consulted certain interested groups, the implementation of the technology 
becomes then a more straightforward matter of following the project delivery program. As technology then 
gets implemented the airport developer has the confidence that the new technology project can be evaluated 
on its true technical merits. .

2.7 Development of a Concept of Operations 
2.7.1 Introduction 
The purpose of this section is to describe the importance of understanding, defining and agreeing to the 
proposed Concept of Operations (ConOps) for the development and operation of airport infrastructure and 
provide guidance on the contents of the ConOps. This section is not intended to cover every aspect of an 
airport ConOps or dictate a preferred ConOps, rather it serves to highlight issues that need to be considered, 
among other drivers, when planning infrastructure development. 
2.7.1.1 What Is a Concept of Operations? 
AConOps is a document that describes the operational outcomes to be achieved from the perspective of the 
user of the system in question. It should be developed for all parts of an operational process and document all 
operational assumptions and characteristics of the proposed infrastructure. Planners should note ConOps is 
an important input into the design process of a new airport facility (e.g., Terminal building) from an early stage 
in the development process. Further, airport ConOps should take account of stakeholders and airport users' 
requirements. 
A ConOps can be developed in many ways, but usually includes: 
e A statement of the goals and objectives of the proposed infrastructure. 
¢ Operational processes for how to use the infrastructure and deliver the required outcomes. 
e Key assumptions that help to describe the operation. 
¢ How technology is proposed to be applied to help deliver the outcomes. 
* Acclear split of responsibilities between users of the infrastructure and stakeholders. 
© Definitions of interfaces between users, stakeholders and other infrastructure/systems. 
A ConOps should not detail the proposed solutions. Its focus should be on defining and agreeing to the 
outcomes that a solution will need to deliver. 
2.7.1.2 Why Is a Concept of Operations Important? 
Airports are comprised of numerous complex but inter-related systems that must operate together to enable 
an airport to function effectively and reliably in both the existing state and future state. Developing and 
implementing ConOps for each of those systems individually and collectively is essential. Without a clear 
understanding of the required operational outcomes, a project cannot be assured that it is delivering the right 
infrastructure or systems for its users and stakeholders. Conversely, having a clear understanding of how the 
infrastructure will be operated from the beginning of the project allows the user to document the operational 
outcomes that are expected to be delivered. This creates a link between operations and the planning and 
design of infrastructure, generating an auditable trail and clear link between outcomes, requirements and 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 281 

===PAGE 301===
=H 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
design activity (see Exhibit 2.7.1.2). This helps ensure all design activity is focused on delivering infrastructure 
that will provide the expected operational outcomes. It should be noted that this ultimately extends to the 
benefits that the project is expected to deliver, however, that is outside the scope of this section.

A ConOps should be underpinned by the relevant operational assumptions as to how the proposed 
infrastructure is to be used, which will then inform the facility assessment and design at key touchpoints within 
the airport. 
How a facility is to be operated can drive different levels of utilization within the proposed infrastructure. It is 
important to be clear on these points from the beginning. On one hand, this can mean additional demand can 
be accommodated by working differently, or it could mean additional infrastructure is required, which means 
additional cost. 
It is therefore in the interest of all parties, when developing the ConOps, to consider how the expected 
operational outcomes will impact either the utilization of the infrastructure or the scale of infrastructure 
required to deliver the agreed product and service requirements of users, particularly airlines, that the 
infrastructure serves. 2.7.1.3 Future Concept of Operations. below expands on Levels of Service and the 
assessment of facility requirements. It should be noted that commercial models and many other factors will 
also drive these decisions; however, infrastructure utilization is an important factor to include. 
Using the ConOps to define a clear split of responsibilities between stakeholders provides early and ongoing 
clarity that is required in a work program so each stakeholder knows what is expected from them to operate

IATA 4 Development of a Concept of Operations 
the infrastructure. It allows the right stakeholders to be consulted and engaged throughout the program, and 
their requirements to be considered and incorporated into the infrastructure design. 
In addition, the ConOps highlights where interfaces with other systems will exist and allows specific actions to 
be taken to manage those interfaces and reduce the risk of them impacting the success of the operation. 
2.7.1.3. Future Concept of Operations 
While documenting the existing ConOps (at brownfield airports) can form a robust base, the design of future 
infrastructure and systems needs to consider how the ConOps will evolve. Given the length of time needed to 
bring infrastructure into service, current processes, technology and operating practices will change. There is a 
clear risk that designing future infrastructure based on current operations will result in infrastructure that is not 
fit for purpose. A good example is the rollout of biometrically enabled processes. 
Hence, there are choices to be made when developing the ConOps. A conservative approach might be taken 
based on an existing, but well-understood ConOps, with the clear risks associated with this approach. 
Alternatively, and preferably, the ConOps can be developed to represent the anticipated future operation. This 
can be informed by reviewing operational trends and anticipating how they will further develop, as well as 
benchmarking best practices from other appropriate airports. The reader should carefully consider these 
options as they will have a material impact on the infrastructure being designed. 
2.7.1.4 Stakeholder Consultation and Approval of the Concept of Operations 
Early stakeholder consultation is critical for any airport project where multiple stakeholders operate in the 
same environment. Stakeholders should be identified at the earliest opportunity, their degree of influence 
assessed, and plans developed that clarify: 
e Who will be consulted and engaged with throughout? 
e How they will be engaged? 
¢ How often they will be engaged? 
o Emphasis on regular consultation throughout the design and development process. 
e What input and output is required from the stakeholders? 
o To understand their requirements 
o To agree on the operational outcomes to be delivered 
o To keep them informed on progress 
e What are the interdependencies between the different stakeholders?

passengers, bags, staff, aircraft, vehicles, goods or waste (i.e., anyone or anything that moves through the 
airport).

uses of infrastructure as a means to prompt the reader to think about the implications of choosing a particular 
ConOps and illustrate, for example, how technology can support the operation. These scenarios are not 
provided to suggest a preferred option and it is recognized that many other factors will need to be considered 
by the user when developing the ConOps, such as branding, wayfinding, technology strategy, customer 
products, and Level of Service.

2.7.2.1 Passenger Types 
In developing the ConOps for the passenger journey, the different types of passengers need to be 
considered. For example, if there are likely to be a significant number of premium passengers at the airport, 
think through the operational outcomes they will experience. Premium check-in and security facilities will offer 
a short queue time and allow passengers to access airside facilities faster, while premium passenger lounges 
will offer places to work and relax before boarding and, in some cases, on arrival. 
Facilities will need to accommodate the needs of passengers with (and without) reduced mobility. There may 
be specific equipment that needs to be provided for some passengers, and wayfinding needs to be accessible 
and intuitive to all. See 2.5 Universal Design and Accessibility for more detail on accessibility. It should be 
agreed who will be using the facilities before developing the ConOps and put in place plans to understand the 
operational outcomes expected by all passengers (e.g., international, domestic, Schengen, non-Schengen, 
direct, transfer passengers).

2.7.3 The Bag Journey 
The ConOps guidance for the bag journey is focused on the Initial ConOps as per Section 1.4. In the next 
stages (Preliminary ConOps and Final ConOps), a deeper level of detail needs to be added. 
¢ While initial facility sizing will be carried out as part of the Initial ConOps, different functionalities should be 
assessed, such as path redundancies, response to contingencies, security levels, volume of out-of-gauge 
baggage and special items, other health screening or local requirements, and parameters to consider for 
improving energy efficiency. 
¢ The location of the baggage system should be considered in relation to the Passenger and aircraft 
handling processes, including consideration for the sizing of the building, impact on passenger processing 
facilities, commercial/retail space, and ease of access to ramp areas. 
In the following sections, the different stages of the standard bag journey are described as well as two 
additional sections for out-of-gauge baggage and live animals or special items. 
2.7.3.1 Travel to the Airport 
It should be noted, while travel to the airport is not covered in Section 2 The Passenger Journey (see 3.4 
Landside Access Systems) it is considered in this section as there are specific baggage issues to address. 
The following is a list of questions the reader should consider when determining the operational outcomes for 
the travel of baggage to the airport. This is not an exhaustive list, and the reader should determine which 
questions are relevant to their airport. 
* How will passengers and bags arrive at the airport (e.g., rail, road, boat, helicopter, air)? 
¢ Will the airport serve different modes of transportation differently? 
¢ Will there be a centralized check-in facility or distributed to serve different modes of transportation (e.g., 
curbside baggage drop-off point, train/subway station check-in counters, boat/ferry terminal check-in or 
baggage receiving point)? 
Is the airport located near the city/town? How far is it from the intended Passenger groups? If the airport is 
far from the main population, passengers and bags may arrive earlier than the one closer to the city. 
¢ Will the baggage arrive at the airport closer to the departure time or long before? 
* How will baggage arrive at the airport (i.e., carried by the Passenger, by the airline or by a dedicated 
company)? 
* If carried by the airline or a dedicated company, where will the baggage entry point be located (i.e., 
airside or landside)? 
¢ How will the different passenger segment types influence the turn-up profiles and the number of bags per 
Passenger impacting baggage storage and systems?

2.7.4 The Staff Journey 
2.7.4.1 Introduction 
To determine the required staff flows and the desired ConOps, the first step is to identify all stakeholders with 
personnel that will work within the Passenger Terminal Building (PTB) or in its vicinity. The purpose is to 
identify as early in the process as possible all staff that may need access to the PTB and involve those 
stakeholder groups in the development of the ConOps. 
The specific staff flows for each stakeholder group should be determined to analyze the need for dedicated 
paths for specific employees. The earlier this is done in the PTB design, the better. A distinction must be 
made between employees on the landside and the ones on the airside. 
2.7.4.2 List of Potential Stakeholders 
The following list of stakeholder categories is given as an example to be included in the development of the 
Staff ConOps. This should not be considered as an exhaustive list and should be developed to be specific to 
the project being considered.

e Airline staff and crew 
e Third-party operations (e.g., ground and baggage handlers, catering)

Department of Transport, Civil Aviation Authority) 
e Retailers (e.g., duty free, food and beverage) 
e Delivery and logistics services

2.7.5 Planning for Irregular Operations (Operational Resilience) 
2.7.5.1 Introduction 
While the baseline for facility planning and development of the ConOps is the “normal day,” almost all airports 
experience irregular operations that place additional pressures on service providers. Part of the development 
of facilities and related ConOps is the need to plan for irregular operations to deliver reasonable operational 
resilience. Such planning and ConOps will help identify the infrastructure and systems needed, both on and 
off airport to deliver resilience. 
The ability to maintain service during irregular operations relies on good planning and operational practices. 
Such events can be broken down by duration and predictability of the ability to plan and respond. In addition, 
each event should have its own risk matrix of likelihood, severity, and ability to mitigate as part of normal risk 
management. The diagram below includes some of the more common risks for the purpose of illustration:

Development of ConOps considering irregular operations during the planning process is highly recommended 
to mitigate the impact on the facilities and their operations that may or may not be correctable later in 
operations. 
While providing operational resilience for all risks may not be affordable, a ConOps play book for foreseeable 
risks is essential. Such ConOps need to be supported by effective means of communication, through the 
Airport Operations Center (AOC), with stakeholders and the travelling public. 
To ensure facilities are planned well at the outset, it is important to develop a ConOps to address irregular 
operations. It is about documenting the “what ifs?” and developing a play book. For example, in 2019, 
planning for pandemics would be unusual for a design brief; however, in 2022, it would be unusual if it were 
not in the brief. Of course, the predictability and duration of pandemics remains challenging. 
2.7.5.2 What Should Be Considered in ConOps for Irregular Operations 
ConOps for irregular operations should be established at an early stage of the development cycle, in 
particular where they have the potential to impact on the spatial planning. Such facilities could include:

2.7.5.3 ConOps Scenarios for Irregular Operations 
The section below sets out examples of irregular operations and some of the impacts that should be 
considered in the planning and design of airport facilities. 
2.7.5.3.1 Predictable Short-lmpact Events 
On-airport system failure/outage 
System outages and failures is the area of irregular operations where the airport and airlines have the 
greatest control of outcomes. A well-designed and operated airport should aim to experience a minimal 
number of system outages that have a negative impact on operations. 
The ConOps should describe how a service can be maintained if a system or component fails or is 
undergoing maintenance and is not available (known as an N-1 test). For instance, if a single elevator is not 
available, where is the nearest alternative and will it be able to meet all passenger needs (e.g., PRM) or 
operational levels of service and capacity? 
Typical on-airport system failures/outages may include: 
e Energy distribution system (loss of power) 
¢ Mechanical passenger transportation (elevators, escalators, and travelators) 
« Baggage systems 
* Communications and security systems 
° Access controls 
e Fire/life safety systems 
¢ Pumps (to drain rainwater) 
e Road accidents 
e Boarding bridge outages 
e¢ Pavement maintenance (airside and landside) 
e Airline systems failure (could be off-site) 
e ATC tower or area control center outage 
e Threat of drone interference 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 317 

===PAGE 337===
Se IATA all Airport Development Reference Manual 
While design and operations should reduce the risk of on-airport system failures, they are unlikely to be fully 
avoidable. The ConOps should consider the risk of system failure to ascertain alternative operations or 
additional system resilience at an affordable cost. Additional resilience can be provided through the provision 
of redundant systems, such as additional escalators and emergency power supplies. However, full 
tedundancy may not be possible or affordable (e.g., additional/auxiliary runway, uninterruptable power supply 
for all services, or additional contact gates). In such circumstances, there will be a broader impact and the 
ConOps needs to include plans that mitigate the impact as much as possible. 
Regular weather events 
Electrical storms—Create “ground stops” on aircraft servicing, leading to delays due to extended aircraft 
turnarounds and in the terminals due to delays to departing passengers and potential missed connections. 
¢ Some airports, such as Singapore Changi, have electrical storms as year-round threats and build in 
buffers to gate operations and passenger spaces. 
¢ Inthe US, summer electrical storms can create an extended ground stop at a major hub airport, creating 
not just a local, but network-wide, impact. The ability for airlines to quickly re-gate aircraft and reschedule 
Passengers onto later flights or through other hubs is critical to overcoming the event as well as having 
contingent hotel space and buffer time in gate operations. 
Low visibility-Even airports that have invested heavily in navigational aids will have occasions when the 
operating minima will be insufficient for either landing or ground movement. The impact is usually a reduction 
in runway capacity with consequential delays and the need, at busy airports, to cancel flights. 
¢ Where low visibility is a regular event at busy airports, the need to reschedule is normally done through a 
collaborative decision-making process between airlines, ATC and the airport. 
e Low-visibility events may occur during the off-peak season. 
* Low-visibility events can occasionally affect a wide geography with numerous airports. 
Snow-Airports that are exposed to snow and freezing conditions will normally have a snow plan that will have 
detailed operational, and facility needs for both airfield and landside snow clearance. 
¢ The snow removal plan should identify facilities that need to be taken out of normal operations for snow 
management (e.g., apron areas for snow melt, forward operating ramp space for snow clearing 
equipment). 
* Snowstorms can also disrupt landside journeys, making it difficult for staff to get to work. 
* De-icing as part of normal winter operations would not be considered an irregular operation.

Tropical storms/hurricanes/typhoons/cyclones—These events can include a combination of high wind, intense

Predictable short-term weather events, where operations can recover relatively quickly, are likely to create 
schedule disruptions to several operational requirements to handle aircraft, passengers, baggage, and cargo.

e How can the airport handle stranded passengers, in particular for connecting international passengers

© What contingent airside and landside space for additional equipment, snow storage, or flood relief can

Sports and other events 
Major sporting events that are not at a fixed location, such as the Olympics, Super Bowl, FIFA World Cup and 
UEFA Champions League, involve a significant influx of visitors for a short period of time and will often place 
additional requirements on the airport facilities. The suitability of the venue will often be subject to the capacity 
of the transport infrastructure and the provision of additional, often temporary, facilities. 
Particular issues commonly encountered include additional: 
* Access to and from the airport (see 3.4 Landside Access Systems for further guidance) 
e Aircraft parking, including charter and GA operations 
e Processing capacity, in particular security and border control 
¢ Out-of-gauge luggage for sporting equipment 
e Protocol facilities for certain groups of passengers requiring separate handling 
Critical to the success of such events is the pre-planning, trials, systems resilience, and availability of 
temporary facilities. There is also extensive experience around the world to draw from. 
Major events alone are unlikely to justify significant investment, however, they are often a trigger for new 
gateway projects as part of the regional showpiece.

Holiday and pilgrimage peaks 
While affordable design should provide an optimum Level of Service for the design busy hour/day, there will 
be days where peak demand exceeds the design capacity. Designers need to understand what this may look 
like so they can be handled without excessive delay or reduction of service. Pilgrimages, such as the Hajj, 
may have particular facility requirements and may or may not coincide with peak holiday periods. Regular 
holiday and pilgrimage peaks would not normally be classed as an irregular operation. 
Labor and other disputes 
Labor disputes are more prevalent in certain parts of the world than others. They often result in flight delays 
and cancellations, missed connections, the need for rebooking, and potentially stranded passengers. Such 
events usually come with some warning and are resolved with close collaboration with the affected airlines. 
2.7.5.3.2 Predictable Long-Ilmpact Events 
These events are more about when, rather than if, a service disruption will occur, requiring a strategic level of 
input. While not exhaustive, the events listed here should be part of strategic planning scenarios. 
Climate change events 
This is probably the major issue facing the industry, including how we plan infrastructure accordingly. Due to 
the uncertainty of the level of impact of climate change, ConOps should consider impacts both within design 
parameters and outside design parameters. 
The impacts of climate change on the airport could include: 
¢ Sea water and ground water level rise, requiring flood prevention planning: 
o Consider moving vulnerable equipment above a level of inundation 
o Where this is not possible, put infrastructure in place, such as flood barriers, drainage, etc. 
© If transportation or utilities infrastructure or equipment, on or off-airport, are vulnerable to inundation 
or damage, consider how the airport would remain operational. 
¢ Increasing extremes of weather, both in terms of frequency and intensity: 
o Extreme cold can lead to waterpipe bursts and flooding. Consider risks in critical operational areas. 
o Extreme heat can lead to the building overheating, affecting not just people but also electronic 
systems, leading to system failure.

Cyberattacks are now part of the regular threats that airport operators and their stakeholders should consider

down due to cyberattacks should be considered, as well as strategies for protecting airport systems. 
Denial of service, terrorism threats and fire events will throw additional challenges to airport operators. These 
can potentially result in disruption to operations, emergency evacuation, stranded passengers, re-check of 
passengers and baggage, and ground stops with increased off-gate operations. Some of the ConOps, such 
as fire evacuation, will be part of the fire/life safety design compliance with national codes, while irregular 
operations are part of basic design.

Earthquakes and volcanic eruptions 
Airports located in high-risk areas for seismic and volcanic activity may have a low probability of occurrence 
but a potentially extreme outcome. The airport will often play a critical role in disaster relief following such 
events as it is likely the communities that the airport serves will be harder hit due to lower building and 
infrastructure construction quality. Airports are often the primary gateway for relief flights and the importance 
of the airport being able to restart essential operations as soon as possible cannot be understated. It is likely 
passenger operations will be significantly reduced, but cargo services carrying aid could increase. 
Seismic events—Major seismic events are likely to affect buildings (including control towers), utilities and 
transport infrastructure (landslides and bridge failures). The ConOps should consider how services can be 
maintained, such as access to airside ramp that avoids unsafe buildings, resilience of the CNS services for 
ATC, space for temporary shelter, aviation fuel reserves and energy resilience. 
Volcanic events—The main risk to aviation is ash, both in the air and on the ground at the airport, with 
secondary risks of lahar and lava flows disrupting access. Eruptions will create no-fly zones due to the risk of 
ash resulting in aircraft positioning away from the airport or being ground-stopped and sealed at the airport. 
Heavy ash and rock falls can lead to building collapse. Following the eruption, ash clean-up and removal, in 
particular in areas of jet blast, will be critical. The ConOps should consider taxiing routes that minimize jet 
blast onto grass areas that are hard to clean. 
2.7.5.3.4 Difficult to Predict Long-Impact Events 
Security/terrorism 
Security threats have had an incremental influence on the design and operation of airports. With some 
exceptions, this has increased facility requirements. Mitigation of many threats are implemented on a global, 
regional, and country basis (e.g., through ICAO, European Commission (EC), and country regulators such as 
civil aviation authorities), although the interpretation can differ depending on the national security agency and 
other local mitigations. 
The ConOps needs to consider the range of managing threats currently prescribed by ICAO and the country's 
security agency, and should consider emerging threats, in particular mitigation to threats that have been 
encountered in other airports and elements of operation, such as passenger evacuation preserving the 
security sterile line. An example is the 30m/100ft offset from curb to fagade applied in a number of countries. 
Pandemics 
Pandemics of infectious disease, affecting a significant part of the world, or epidemics, which are more local, 
can result in restrictions imposed on the travel industry to reduce the spread of the disease. Until a pandemic 
is fully resolved into a stabilized condition, the restrictions are usually applied by sovereign states and 
guidance is provided by health and trade organizations, such as World Health Organization (WHO), ICAO, 
IATA and ACI. The application of restrictions during this period is likely to be varied but may result in a 
significant or absolute reduction in demand and increase in border controls. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 323 

===PAGE 343===
Se IATA Bull Airport Development Reference Manual 
Each infectious disease will have particular pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical interventions that can be 
applied to reduce the risk of cross-contamination and infection. These interventions will be part of a protocol, 
often subject to agreement with the state. For COVID-19, the main pharmaceutical intervention has been 
inoculation, while non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) have been social distancing, facial coverings, 
barriers, hand washing, and sanitation of remaining touchpoints. 
Airborne infectious disease can also be further spread by ineffective ventilation, and this can negate the 
benefits of the NPls. See 2.8 Pandemic Resilience and Healthy Buildings that sets out several principals that 
are recommended for consideration in the planning and design of healthy buildings to reduce the risk of 
transmission of infection. 
Most airports will have some operational procedures for pandemics. These should be summarized into the 
ConOps and used as part of the design. It is recommended that the ConOps for pandemic operations 
includes: 
¢ Realistic target capacity of the facility during a pandemic given various NPls and other procedures 
¢ Passenger routes to minimize cross-contamination of low and high-risk passengers 
*¢ Staff routes and facilities that minimize interaction with passengers 
* Capacity and facilities for additional health and document checks for both inbound and outbound 
passengers and staff at the earliest point of entry to buildings 
* Reduced facilities to minimize risk of close proximity and contact with alternative routes 
¢ Ventilation system settings that reduce the risk of cross-contamination of passengers through high fresh 
air content, filter requirements and reduced velocities 
* Ventilation segregation between high-risk passenger areas and staff areas 
Political change 
For the purpose of irregular operations and ConOps in the ADRM, most political change is likely to impact 
border controls. Changes, such as joining an existing common border enabling the free movement of people 
and goods such as in the European Union or UK Brexit can significantly change the number of Passengers 
being classed as international or domestic or with special exemptions either positively or negatively. The 
impacts could include changes to demand for border control, security, reallocation of departure areas for 
international and domestic passengers (if segregated), and additional process for transfer passengers. 
ConOps should consider whether this is a likely risk and how the facility can operate under certain scenarios 
of change so that an assessment of the cost, if any, of political change can be easily accommodated.

2.8 Pandemic Resilience and Healthy Buildings 
2.8.1 Introduction 
Airports are the front door to many countries and communities and act as a critical gateway in controlling the 
flow of people and goods as well as what they bring with them. The planning, design, construction and 
operation of airports will affect the health of those using the facilities as well as the communities they connect 
to, both in normal operations and as experienced during disease, pandemics, epidemics and outbreaks, such 
as SARS (2002), H1N1 (2009), MERS (2012), Ebola (2014), Zika (2015), SARS-CoV-2 (2019), etc. 
The COVID-19 pandemic has provided focus on the resilience of building assets, and the opportunity to 
provide places that genuinely enable health, well-being and productivity. Future design needs to consider the 
resilience, not just to COVID-19, but broader infectious disease control. following the principles of WHO 
Infection Prevention Control. 
While it is difficult to completely eliminate the risk of spreading pathogens, such as SARS-CoV-2, in buildings, 
much can be done to substantially reduce airborne concentration and general risk through appropriate best 
practice design and innovation, technology, operations and maintenance. Implementing the key principles of 
healthy buildings, as described below, will reduce the risk of viral transmission, while creating a more pleasant 
indoor environment and increasing passenger satisfaction. 
In a post-pandemic world, airport buildings especially should be measured with respect to how they can 
approach disease prevention, preparedness, resilience and recovery. Buildings generally play a role in 
supporting our health and well-being, as well as our collective ability to prepare for and respond to global 
health challenges. 
In this section, the major attributes of pandemic resilience and healthy building design are discussed. This 
includes details relating to the concept of ‘Circles of Protection’ when addressing general resilience, 
architectural and interior design, building services, digital innovation and technology. These follow guidelines 
from the WHO, CDC and other national/international sources. Designers should refer to guidance prepared by 
IATA, ACI, ICAO and other organizations to apply infection prevention control. 
2.8.1.1 Principles of Pandemic Resilience 
The ‘new normal’, post-pandemic, further emphasizes the importance of adapting the operation and design of 
airports to better withstand uncertainties—such as lockdowns and new disease threats. 
Resilience of airport buildings and operations can be understood as the ability to retain control over their 
primary objectives and functions when challenged by external threats and stresses. In doing so, an airport 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 325 

===PAGE 345===
ue''| Se 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
building's design and operation should allow for a response that is aligned with three key dimensions of 
pandemic resilience: 
e Absorb-To be more resistant to pathogen transmission 
¢ Adapt-To be more responsive to changing needs, such as pre-planning and local lockdowns 
¢ Transform-To be more versatile and allow change from usual functions 
This understanding can be applied to both sudden crises and long-term stresses. Resilience involves actively 
understanding the risk landscape and determining where those risks are best owned and managed. 
Strengthening these components can reduce potential economic losses when a crisis occurs. 
Pandemic response management is essential for decreasing the spread of a pathogen and its associated 
disruption. The over-arching theme in responding to a pandemic situation is to map out all identified safety 
issues and to ensure there is a well-functioning management system and operational procedures in place, 
which ensures that risks can be identified and managed effectively. 
Utilization of epidemiological evidence and data-driven tools is important, as they help disentangle and 
interpret the linkages between risk, capacity and economic activity. Interventions required to address these 
risks may include assessing the operation of the building, changes to building services and systems, 
identifying and managing the introduction of technologies to reduce face-to-face interactions, as well as 
leveraging opportunities for digital innovation and new technologies for pandemic resilience. 
2.8.1.2 Particular Issues for Airports 
While airports have many similarities with other types of public facilities with a significant number of people 
gathering together, there are some issues that need special consideration. In particular, airports: 
* Are primary cross-border entry points for people entering countries and regions, with the accompanying 
tisk of introduction of infectious diseases that can harm the local population. 
¢ Bring together flights from various origins under one roof, increasing the risk of cross-contamination. 
* Support a significant number of transactions and processes (e.g., immigration, customs, security, 
boarding pass check, baggage drop) that have to continue during a pandemic. 
* Have processes and features that encourage common-use facilities, common snake queuing, high footfall 
commercial routes, and multiple touchpoints. 
¢ Depend on non-automated processes that can be impacted by labor shortages due to staff sickness, 
need for isolation, and impact of a pandemic on dependents (e.g., check-in, government services, ground 
handling, airline operations). 
* Bring people together in long queues, which may involve longer processing times during a pandemic, 
increasing the chance of infection due to being in a crowded place for extended periods. 
° Are generally not designed to reduce the risk of cross-contamination by containment of air handling to 
Particular zones, such as no landside/airside staff/public segregation as found for, say, security. 
326 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 346===
ray Win 
Se IATA al Pandemic Resilience and Healthy Buildings 
e Need simple, consistent, easy-to-implement communications and wayfinding for passengers that have 
various language and visual needs and are likely to be infrequent users of the facilities. 
Changing human behaviors to reduce the risk of transmission of an invisible pathogen, such as a virus, is 
particularly challenging, even at airports. Changes need to be simple, logical and easy to implement and use. 
2.8.1.3 Healthy Building Design 
A healthy building is one whose design actively looks to enhance the health and well-being of those 
occupying it as well as the environment surrounding it. Typically, we spend up to 90% of our lifetime inside 
buildings, which emphasizes the importance of creating indoor spaces that are nurturing rather than 
debilitating. 
Historically, buildings that are particularly poorly designed, operated incorrectly or in poor condition, have the 
capacity to cause discomfort, irritation, tiredness and a reduction in the general productivity of their occupants 
through poor indoor environmental quality. In severe cases, a condition some refer to as ‘sick building 
syndrome’ can arise, where the indoor environment of the building can actively cause symptoms of illness. 
The evidence around healthy buildings is as relevant to aviation as it is to any other sector. In the context of 
airport terminals, passengers may be under additional health strains and risks due to long- or short-haul travel 
and associated-potentially long-transits through an airport terminal building. This might include symptoms of 
jet lag, dehydration, general stress and risk of serious physical conditions such as deep vein thrombosis. 
Airport buildings should, therefore, aim to prioritize the creation of environments that cater to passenger and 
staff health and well-being needs accordingly. 
2.8.1.3.1. Summary of Key Principles 
A healthy building should include strategies that aim to achieve positive human health outcomes by 
enhancing the indoor environment. Strategies should address a wide range of performance parameters and 
issues connected to building operations, architectural design, interior design, and building services. The 
fundamental principles of healthy buildings cover the following: 
e Air quality 
¢ Thermal comfort 
e Visual comfort 
* Acoustic comfort 
e Water quality 
e Mental health 
e Access to nourishment 
e Ability to maintain physical fitness. 
e Cleanliness 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 327 

===PAGE 347===
IATA a Airport Development Reference Manual 
These can be addressed in various ways through the design, construction, operation and maintenance 
phases of a building's lifecycle, but are also determined by occupant behaviors and activities. Addressing 
health and well-being criteria in a project and determining their importance from a business perspective can 
have the most impact on the health, well-being, and productivity of people. 
2.8.1.3.2 Healthy Building Standards 
To support the development of healthier building environments, there are a variety of healthy building 
certifications and standards to assist designers and facilities managers, such as LEED IAQ, WELL, Fitwel, 
RESET and others. These building certifications and standards, along with other best practice guidance and 
research, provide a framework to achieving health, wellness, and sustainability goals for various building 
types, including airport buildings. It should be noted that as of the time of publication these listed standards 
and guidelines are in the process of evolution to account for pandemic resilience. 
2.8.2 Circles of Protection for Pandemic Resilience 
The transmission of disease through the air is an important public health concern. Respiratory viruses spread 
mainly via droplet and aerosol transmission. Virus-containing droplets from infected individuals are passed via 
exhalation, speaking, coughs and sneezes, and infect others by landing in the mouth, nose or eyes. Larger 
droplets remain in the air for a relatively short period of time and fall to the ground within a few meters, 
whereas aerosols are smaller particles that remain airborne for minutes to hours and can travel longer 
distances on air currents. 
Touch points that can transmit infection from one person to another are known as fomites. Fomite 
transmission occurs by touching contaminated surfaces or objects and then touching the mouth, nose or 
eyes, allowing the virus to enter the body. The prevalence of fomite transmission during the COVID-19 
pandemic is considered minor but is active for other viruses such as norovirus. 
Airports and aircraft provide opportunities for disease transmission due to close human contact, sharing of 
communal spaces and a high number of touched surfaces. In addition, airports present the unique challenge 
of managing the interactions of large numbers of individuals from diverse regions with varying endemic 
diseases. 
The successful spread of infectious diseases relies on sustained transmission to new hosts. In the absence of 
new hosts to infect, the outbreak will be self-limiting. While factors such as host susceptibility and vaccination 
status play a role in disease transmission, limiting the contact between infectious and susceptible individuals 
is a key factor in the management of an outbreak.
