Following infection prevention control principles of multi-level circles of protection can be used to guide 
considerations during the design, construction, operation and maintenance. This approach includes four key 
elements as follows: 
1. Minimize access: Allow access only to those fit to fly and those needed to enable flying 
2. Minimize time: The less time in the terminal, the less risk of transmission 
3. Minimize contact: Reduce, where possible, close proximity and touchpoints for transmission, such as 
face-to-face transactions 
4. Optimize hygiene: Optimize hygiene and sanitation 
2.8.2.1. Non-Pharmaceutical Interventions 
Key elements in the successful risk reduction of diseases are through pharmaceutical interventions, such as 
vaccines, and non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), such as cleaning, testing, social distancing, and fresh 
air, which are in the area of control or influence of an airport. 
The circles of protection help guide the use of NPls, aimed to minimize the risk of transmission. Key NPIs, 
which should be considered for airports to help incorporate pandemic resilience, should include the following: 
* ConOps: Develop a ConOps to introduce NPIs and include all key stakeholders in core evidence-based 
decision-making during the early stages of planning as well as during an outbreak to manage different 
levels of demand and intervention (see 2.7 Development of a Concept of Operations). 
e Communications and wayfinding: To support the ConOps and keep people informed so they can play 
their part through behavior change, communication strategies to improve compliance and confidence 
should be developed. Note, staff may not be available to assist. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 329 

===PAGE 349===
IATA 4 Airport Development Reference Manual 
e Enable space for additional controls and services: Either through repurposing space due to reduced 
demand or using contingent space for testing, quarantining, storage, etc. 
e Reduce exposure risk through reducing density: Decrease the density of people in certain areas, 
especially queues, and, where appropriate, minimize the time people spend in close proximity to one 
another in such areas and in the building. 
¢ Re-engineer passenger flows: Examine and adapt how people circulate to encourage social distancing. 
Consider introducing one-way flows to reduce contact. 
e Provide clean air: Consider the design of air handling operations that can provide fresh or cleaned air to 
everyone and avoid cross-contamination between people in the same area or different parts of the 
building. Consider that HVAC should provide high air changes and filtration, with supplemental air 
cleaning in areas of dense occupancy used to eat and interact. 
¢ Minimize close personal contact: Examine how people interact in the facility and adapt processes to 
reduce close contact, in particular through introduction of technologies. 
e Minimize touch points: Minimize contact with fomites by removing non-essential surfaces and 
redesigning processes, using digital contactless solutions where possible. 
e Focus contact for those who need or expect it: Examine provision of dedicated channels for 
passenger groups, such as disabled, elderly and young families, where contactless solutions are difficult 
to implement. 
* Improve sanitation and maintenance: Design facilities to improve the performance of cleaning, 
disinfection, and maintenance of building services and adapt where needed for added protection. 
¢ Encourage individual protection: Consider hand sanitizer, face coverings and personal protective 
equipment (PPE). 
In addition to incorporating best practices learned during the COVID-19 pandemic, the longer-term strategy for 
pandemic-resilient airports involves integrating procedures for pandemic events. This should be 
mainstreamed alongside existing procedures for weather events and changes in security levels, helping to 
create a more prepared and resilient system. Furthermore, airports have for many years been control points 
for the regional and international spread of communicable disease. An integrated approach should be 
developed among agencies, tenants, and stakeholders to include security, immigration and customs to best 
manage any risk of disease importation and to safeguard a healthy environment and building. 
2.8.2.2 Risk Assessment 
Risk assessment using properly reviewed data will help to focus the areas of intervention. Risk assessments 
would normally be weighted by population density and risk reduction due to certain interventions, such as 
social distancing, face coverings, barriers and cleaning.

2.8.2.3. Operational Design Considerations 
Airport operation during a pandemic is likely to demand flexibility in the use of facilities and space. The impact 
on a terminal building will depend on the level of peak demand, which, if subdued, may help manage some of 
the issues. New or enhanced processes can dramatically reduce the terminal capacity and lead to the airport 
being unable to handle relatively low flows compared to normal operations. Designers should consider 
implications on the ability of the airport to function in various scenarios of demand and intervention. 
The primary issues are likely to include: 
* Increases in process times: Additional documentation to be checked (both departure and arrival) 
* New processes: Checks before entering the building (either landside or airside) 
* Segregation: Separating passengers from different risk areas and staff from passengers 
* Flight schedules: Frequent changes to flight schedules and international/domestic mix 
* Fewer operational positions: Due to physical distancing or staff availability (sickness or isolation) 
e Reduced contact routes: Conflicting routes of passenger flows 
« Less “common use” facilities: To reduce the risk of cross-contamination 
* Reduced densities: Impacts on static occupation and passenger flows depend on allowed distancing 
e Additional signage and barriers: Implement required changes

For airborne infectious disease, such as COVID-19, the most likely area of transmission risk is in queuing

passengers and staff at the earliest point of entry to buildings. 
¢ Where queuing is unavoidable, airports should carefully plan where queuing will be located, given 
consideration for the building to provide a low-transmission environment (e.g., in an area with enhanced 
ventilation). Queue reservation systems or virtual queuing can be considered as strategies to minimize 
queuing on site. 
¢ Ventilation system settings that reduce the risk of cross-contamination of passengers through high fresh 
air content, filter requirement and reduced velocities. 
¢ Ventilation systems that reduce the risk of cross-contamination between different functional areas, (e.g., 
air from arriving passenger areas being circulated into staff areas). 
Until procedures and facilities introduced for infection control become mandated by authorities for long-term 
use, in the same way that security has been mandated, optimum Level of Service may not be achievable or 
designed for in the areas affected. However, as passenger demand during a pandemic is likely to be 
significantly reduced during times of peak transmission risk, traffic in the building facilities may also be 
reduced, which will mitigate some of the impact. 
2.8.3 Key Design Considerations for Healthy and Pandemic-Resilient 
Buildings 
2.8.3.1 Introduction 
The influence that architects, interior designers and engineers can have on the development of a pandemic￾resilient and healthy airport building is huge. The building form, interior design, services and control strategies 
can dictate the indoor environmental quality and the likelihood of spread of infectious diseases. 
While it is not to be considered exhaustive, the following section details some of the key principles that should 
be considered when aiming to create healthy and resilient indoor airport environments. Green and healthy 
building design frameworks, such as the WELL Building Standard and LEED, provide more background 
information along with best practice performance criteria.

2.8.3.2 Role of Building Management Systems 
A Building Management System (BMS) can provide significant information to improve the operations of an 
airport building and maintain an indoor environment that is healthy and pandemic resilient. The future of 
building automation revolves around Jess reliance on human intervention to execute repetitive or routine tasks. 
Automated BMS solutions help to deliver consistent indoor environmental quality, which is critical to health 
and well-being, and reducing the transmission of pathogens. Importantly, this includes close control of the 
following, as discussed in further detail in this section: 
e Air refresh rates and general air quality 
e Humidity 
e Indoor temperature 
Automation also improves reliability, programmability, remote/targeted intervention, and seamless operations. 
This can be achieved through the use of Internet of Things (loT) technology, including loT sensors and 
instrumentation that are able to monitor indoor environmental quality across the building at high resolution. 
Implementation of Artificial Intelligence (Al)-driven digital control platforms will enable analysis of real-time 
data and provide systemwide transparency and a centralized view of building operations, indicating where 
systems are failing to maintain healthy indoor conditions. This technology has the potential to create a more 
resilient building, unlock high levels of efficiency and reduce long-term operational costs. 
2.8.3.3 Ventilation and Air Quality 
Indoor air quality can be degraded by external pollutant sources, as well as by off-gassing from building 
materials, indoor combustion sources and water leaks. Poor ventilation strategies can fail to address these 
sources, exposing occupants to VOCs, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and microbial pathogens 
(such as airborne viruses), which can linger in still air. 
An indirect way in which poor airflow may impact health is via surfaces, which can accumulate airborne germs 
if they do not disperse on air currents and if the surfaces are not regularly cleaned. All of these contaminants 
contribute to a range of negative health outcomes such as asthma, allergies and other upper respiratory 
illnesses. Maintaining low levels of CO, in indoor spaces to internationally recognized standards (ideally 
450-600 parts per million-ppm) is important for concentration, productivity, and a general sense of well-being. 
Airport terminals are highly relevant for pathogen transmission owing to the high number of passengers from 
across the world coming together in enclosed spaces. Aside from close contact and commonly touched 
surfaces, we can be exposed to viruses through airborne respiratory droplets when someone nearby sneezes, 
coughs or speaks. These droplets vary in size, and smaller droplets can be carried on air currents and inhaled 
by people at greater distances. Measures to reduce the potential airborne route of infection are of primary 
importance when tackling respiratory communicable diseases such as COVID-19. While interventions such as 
face coverings and social distancing help to reduce risk, air quality has a large influence on infection and does 
not require individual compliance. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 333 

===PAGE 353===
Se S. ih IATA yi Airport Development Reference Manual 
The mitigation of risk from respiratory communicable diseases within the airport is achieved in a similar 
manner as on aircraft-through the ventilation and air filtration systems. Building HVAC systems provide a 
mechanism for diluting and filtering airborne contaminants. Recommendations to minimize the potential 
airborne route of infection are largely based on increasing the ventilation rate and enhancing air cleaning as 
much as technically, environmentally and economically feasible. The airport terminal has many different 
micro-environments, each of which has its own exposure and risk profile. It is recommended that design of the 
HVAC system for an airport terminal be split into different ventilation zones to lessen the transmission 
potential of pathogens. These zones could include: 
e Arriving passenger areas (in particular international arrivals) 
¢ Departing passenger areas 
e Landside public spaces 
e Frontline staff areas 
e Back-of-house operations 
Further principles that should be considered regarding ventilation strategy during a pandemic are as follows: 
¢ Pre-occupancy ventilation: Operate building/zones ventilation and filtration systems prior to operations 
to provide a clean air environment as needed. 
¢ Increase fresh air supply and exhaust ventilation: Supplying fresh air at as high a rate as possible 
given physical and climatic constraints. 
¢ No (or minimal) recirculation: If full closing of the recirculation air is not possible for adequate comfort, 
the recirculation air should be kept at a minimum level. Direct Outdoor Air Systems (DOAS) should be 
considered where feasible and appropriate (e.g., no significant energy penalty) to avoid recirculation. For 
smaller buildings in temperate climates, this can include natural air circulation through open windows and 
using natural air convection. 
¢ Separate systems for airside and landside: To avoid the potential risk of transit passengers infected 
with COVID-19 or other communicable diseases transmitting pathogens outside of the airport, landside 
and airside areas should be served by completely separate air distribution systems where feasible. 
e Enhance air cleaning: High-efficiency media-based filters appropriate to the targeted pathogen should 
be installed and operated in the air handling units (AHUs), where outdoor air supply is constrained. 
Consideration for use ultraviolet germicidal irradiation (UVGI) to increase during pandemic 
¢ Portable air cleaners (PACs): For larger indoor spaces, the number of PACs deployed should be based 
on the performance and space volume. Units with proven efficiency and certification are to be considered. 
It is important to ensure PACs don't interrupt existing HVAC flows negating the positive effects. 
¢ Airflow pathway: Occupancy layout for social distancing should take into consideration airflow patterns. 
¢ Room air cleaners: Useful in specific situations, such as toilets. It is important to ensure air cleaners 
don't interrupt existing HVAC flows negating the positive effects.

2.8.3.3.1 Materials 
Various chemicals are still used in the manufacture of common building materials, despite known or 
suspected health hazards. This includes chemicals found in furnishings, floor coverings, paints, ceiling panels, 
wall coverings and common adhesives. Invariably, these chemicals make their way into the air within a 
building through off-gassing over time. During design stages, materials should be selected in line with best 
practice guidelines and restrictions, covering the following: 
e Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) 
e Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs) 
e Perfluorinated Compounds (PFCs) 
e Halogenated Flame Retardants 
e Phthalate (Plasticizers) 
e lsocyanate-Based Polyurethane 
e Urea-Formaldehyde 
The WELL Building Standard provides detailed guidance and criteria for healthy materials specification, which 
should be considered at the design stage. 
2.8.3.3.2 Air Cleaning Technology 
Air cleaners include a variety of technologies and should be considered for high-risk areas in airport terminal 
enclosed spaces, such as toilets. Some air cleaners remove pathogens by filtration, while others render 
pathogens biologically inactive. Any technology deployed should be certified by an agency with the 
appropriate jurisdictional authority. A single device could contain one or more of the technologies listed below: 
e High-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter or other mechanical filters 
e Ultra-violet (UV) germicidal irradiation 
e Thermal or photocatalytic oxidation 
e Electrostatic precipitation 
e Other ‘novel’ proprietary technologies 
Air ventilation system design should consider airport-specific pollutants such as volatile organic compounds 
from jet fuel combustion (see 2.8.3.3.1 Materials). Mitigation includes. among others, preventing 
contamination from communicable diseases through specific features or design criteria of HVAC systems, and 
increased air inflow and the installation of active processes (e.g., bipolar ionization).

2.8.3.4 Temperature, Humidity and Thermal Comfort 
2.8.3.4.1 Introduction 
The indoor thermal comfort of building occupants is dependent on the indoor environmental conditions 
created and maintained by the HVAC systems, and the architecture of the building, including the fagade. 
These conditions are defined by the following: 
e Air temperature 
e Radiant temperature 
e Relative humidity (RH) 
e Air velocity 
Indoor thermal comfort will also be determined by an individual's metabolic rate and their choice of clothing. 
Temperature and humidity control is important in tackling the spread of pathogens and creating pleasant and 
healthy indoor environments within airport buildings. For the design of HVAC systems, including their control 
systems, close consideration should be given to the sensitivity of temperature and humidity on virus half-life, 
both in relation to airborne droplets and on surfaces. Systems should be designed to ensure appropriate 
conditions can be maintained such that the risk of viral transmission is minimized as much as possible.

The climate zone an airport building is in will also play a role in relation to what internal temperatures are 
considered acceptable. Generally, for hotter climates, indoor temperature setpoints can be higher than those 
in cooler climates. For a naturally ventilated space, the adaptive comfort model is typically adopted; whereas, 
for fully enclosed conditioned spaces, the Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) or Percentage People Dissatisfied 
(PMD) assessment approach should be adopted. The internationally recognized ASHRAE 55 standard 
provides the performance criteria for each of these approaches. 
The concept of ‘thermal alliesthesia’ goes beyond these approaches, proposing that the hedonic qualities of 
the thermal environment (qualities of pleasantness or unpleasantness, or ‘the pleasure principle’) are 
determined as much by the general thermal state of the subject as by the environment itself. In its simplest 
form, cold stimuli will be perceived as pleasant by someone who is warm, while warm stimuli will be 
experienced as pleasant by someone who is cold. This concept should be explored at the design stage, 
especially for airports located in warm or tropical climates. 
2.8.3.4.2 Air Temperature 
Air distribution systems have the capacity to create temperature asymmetry within a space, which can cause 
significant thermal discomfort, especially for cooling systems, where the supply temperature of an air 
conditioning system is below 15°C. Steps should be taken to create a uniform air distribution in the spaces 
being conditioned. 
Ambient air temperature can also have an influence on the activity and spread of viruses within airport 
buildings. For example, viruses that cause respiratory infections often break out in the winter months. There 
are indications that this is partially due to a reduced resistance of the mucous membranes in the nose when 
cold air is inhaled. To counter this, it is recommended to ensure spaces in the building are not overcooled. 
With social distancing in place, there will be a lower heat load, so some air systems may need rebalancing to 
account for this. 
Air temperature is known to influence the risk of passing on disease. Studies"' on COVID-19 indicate that the 
lifespan of the virus is significantly reduced with increased humidity and temperature as well as UV exposure. 
However, risks such as food-based toxins, increase significantly with increased humidity and temperature. 
Displacement ventilation should be explored for large open spaces commonly found in airport terminal 
departure lounges, for example, as these can create a more uniform air distribution as well as saving energy 
by requiring less air volume to be moved. 
2.8.3.4.3 Radiant Temperature 
The temperature of a person's surroundings, including surfaces, heat generating equipment, sun and sky, 
define radiant temperature. This is generally expressed as mean radiant temperature (MRT), a weighted 
average of the temperatures surrounding a person. In airport buildings, the main consideration with respect to 
radiant temperature is the fagade. It is common to have large areas of glazed facade in airport terminal 
"1 Probabilistic Analysis for National Threats Hazards and Risks (PANTHR), https://www.dhs. gov/science-and-technology/panthr 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 337 

===PAGE 357===
fie 1 
Se | IATA wal Airport Development Reference Manual 
buildings, which can have a significant impact on the thermal comfort of the occupants. In hotter climates, 
discomfort caused by thermal asymmetry can be addressed with a glass curtain wall equipped with radiant 
glass (RG) technology. The thermal performance of an RG curtain wall can be adapted according to occupant 
requirements and should be considered along with external solar shading devices. In colder climates, thermal 
discomfort caused by a ‘cold’ fagade should also be a consideration, with appropriate positioning of perimeter 
heating to counteract cold drafts. 
2.8.3.4.4 Relative Humidity 
While relative humidity (RH) is a consideration for indoor thermal comfort, importantly it is also a key 
parameter to consider in the growth and transmission of pathogens within an airport building. Extremely low 
humidity can lead to dryness and irritation of the skin, eyes, throat and mucous membranes. Conversely, high 
humidity may promote the accumulation and growth of certain viruses and other microbial pathogens, 
including bacteria and fungi, which can lead to odors and cause respiratory irritation and allergies in sensitive 
individuals. Additionally, higher humidity levels can lead to increased off-gassing; for example, an increase in 
relative humidity above 35% can increase the emissions of formaldehyde. 
Relative humidity plays a key role in the lifespan and size of respiratory droplets in the air and on surfaces. It 
also impacts human sensitivity to infections. 
It is recommended that the design of airport facilities, in particular terminal buildings, includes systems that 
keep relative humidity within an appropriate range for general pathogen control and thermal comfort. The type 
of systems would depend on the local climate and prevailing regulations. 
2.8.3.4.5 Air Velocity 
The velocity of air supplies into a space is important when it comes into contact with a person. The faster the 
air is moving, the greater the exchange of heat between the person and the air. For air-conditioned spaces, it 
is typically cold supply air that creates a draft and makes people feel cold, so air flow patterns within spaces 
should be considered, not just for thermal comfort, but also for the removal of pathogens from a space. High 
air velocities that can unnecessarily spread pathogens between people should be avoided. Displacement 
ventilation should be considered as this reduces air velocity relying on natural convection. 
2.8.3.5 Surfaces, Cleaning and Touch-Free Access 
People come into contact with common objects at a high rate, which means people are likely to get germs on 
their hands far more frequently than they wash them. Touch points that can transmit infection from one person 
to another are known as fomites. The contribution of fomites to transmission of disease will vary.

Hot spots are considered as points or sites within an environment where the risk of disease transmission is at 
least transiently increased due to favorable conditions for transmission, including human behavior. Many 
microbes survive on surfaces for periods long enough to allow transmission, in some cases up to several 
days. This is particularly the case for non-porous and water-resistant materials, such as steel and plastics, 
meaning surface contamination within an airport should be considered a risk. 
Hot spots are formed by a high density of passengers and frequently touched surfaces. The risk of surface 
contamination can be minimized with adequate cleaning and disinfection regimes in place, and by offering 
hand sanitization before and after identified hot spots. The respiratory nature of certain viruses, such as 
SARS-CoV-2, means surfaces can quickly become contaminated again if infectious individuals are nearby. 
The following initiatives could be considered: 
* Changing processes to reduce the need for contact: Including passenger and staff operations, journey 
routes, transaction points, and objects to touch. 
¢ Antimicrobial surfaces: Touch points that have high levels of use, such as elevator control panels and 
push panels on doors. 
e Automated cleaning: Handrails on escalators and moving walkways that are needed for safety.

¢ Touch-free access and activation: Using biometric recognition, motion and proximity sensors. 
e Personal hygiene support: Hand sanitization prior to contact. 
¢ Enhanced cleaning regimes: Focused on high-contact areas, driven by data. 
2.8.3.6 Natural Daylighting and Visual Comfort 
Light influences the human body in non-visual ways. Humans have internal clocks that synchronize 
physiological functions on roughly a 24-hour cycle called the circadian rhythm. Exposure to appropriate 
amounts of natural light reinforces the alignment of circadian rhythms and reduces dependence on electricity 
for artificial lighting. Excessive daylight, however, can cause glare and unwanted visual contrast. 
Daylight, and specifically UV levels, within a space has also been shown to significantly reduce the lifespan of 
pathogens, both on interior surfaces and attached to airborne particles. While daylight in a building can 
reduce artificial lighting loads, it should be noted that daylight penetration also needs to be balanced with 
associated heat gains and cooling loads to ensure energy performance targets can be achieved. When 
designing for natural daylight in airport buildings, the following principles and performance criteria should be 
considered. 
2.8.3.6.1 Levels of Illuminance 
Consideration should be given to introducing useful levels of daylight into an indoor space that are appropriate 
to the function of the space. Two of the most common ways to measure daylight levels include Spatial 
Daylight Autonomy (SDA) and Useful Daylight Illuminance (UDI). sDA generally requires indoor spaces to 
receive a minimum level of daylight while UDI provides a range for the majority of operating hours each year. 
2.8.3.6.2 Control of Glare 
Daylight light levels beyond a certain threshold have the ability to cause visual discomfort to passengers and 
staff. Appropriate control measures should be implemented to avoid excessive indoor solar exposure, 
including external shading devices, solar control glazing, and installation of glass at levels above the occupied 
Zone of the terminal to create indirect sunlight. A key performance metric that should be considered for 
relevant spaces, especially passenger terminals, is Annual Sunlight Exposure (ASE), which gauges how long 
a surface within a space receives daylight above a certain threshold deemed to be uncomfortable to the 
majority of occupants. 
2.8.3.7 Acoustics 
Electronics, HVAC systems, mechanical equipment and other noise-emitting devices, as well as occupants 
themselves, can be sources of indoor noise. External noise break-in is also a key consideration, especially in 
an airport context. Noise can lead to decreased productivity, annoyance and stress, especially in open-plan 
spaces that might require close work or periods of concentration to take place. This would include areas such 
340 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 360===
Le S- it IATA a Pandemic Resilience and Healthy Buildings 
as departure halls and security checkpoints, where aural distractions and interruptions can be frequent. 
Additionally, studies show that exposure to noise generated within the building can lead to reduced 
concentration and mental performance, as well as increased distraction and reduced speech privacy. 
Designers should follow best practice guidance appropriate to airports for acoustic design, relating to: 
e External noise break-in and fagade performance 
e Mechanical equipment sounds levels within spaces and building harmonics 
* Reverberation times and sound absorption 
¢ Sound insulation between different spaces 
2.8.4 Digital Technology 
2.8.4.1 Using digital Technology for Pandemic Resilience 
Digital transformation should not just be about technology, but also about transforming people and processes. 
In the context of global health challenges, understanding the relationships between people and the use of 
spaces within airports is critical to minimizing the spread of infectious diseases. For example, investigating 
passenger flow to help identify the highest risk points for close contact and how it may affect airflow and virus 
diffusion patterns. It is important that digital thinking is engaged with at the earliest possible stages to best 
understand the potential risks and mitigations. With pandemic resilience in mind, some potential areas of 
application for digital solutions have been described: 
e Airport operations: Leverage the loT and web-service platforms to provide more comprehensive 
solutions that optimize HVAC, power management and control! of VoC's and provide Epidemic mode for 
emergencies. By connecting passenger data, ground support resource capacity can be utilized more 
effectively, helping to improve customer service and minimize contact between passengers and staff. 
e Passenger monitoring: Camera systems that show where people are in a space by providing broad 
coverage from above. This allows observation of queuing, crowding, and etc., as well as the provision of 
wait times, equipment outages, and other real-time information. 
*¢ Global health security: Leverage Al (predictive and prescriptive analytics) coupled with video 
infrastructure to allow for the adaptation of airports to become primary monitoring points to prevent the 
tegional and international spread of communicable disease. Take advantage of global health data 
regarding outbreaks in countries of origin. 
*° Capacity management: Leverage a deep understanding and monitoring of passenger flow to help 
optimize airport infrastructure capacity, promoting better use of space. 
¢ Contactless touchpoints: Replacement or adjustment of self-service touchpoints with facial recognition 
(e.g., check-in kiosks, boarding pass check, immigration) as well as contactless payments and pre￾authorization to fly before travel. 
e Building services and asset management: To monitor and control air handling, vertical transportation 
should adapt to reduce the risks of infection.

e Wayfinding and signage: To communicate information effectively with passengers on new directions,

2.8.4.2 Digital Twins 
Access to a digital twin can allow for simulations on new operating conditions, indicating issues to address as 
well as potential savings in time or money. Digital twins can provide further capabilities in improving pandemic 
resilience and better understand the impacts of changing demand and capacity. Some of these applications 
are as follows: 
* Social distancing: Simulate passenger flows and queues in a virtual environment to allow airports to 
effectively monitor physical distancing and inform passengers of safe airport navigation procedures. 
¢ Propagation and exposure: Simulate the spread of a virus to highlight potential cross-infection areas in 
the airport and related impacts on passengers and their surroundings. 
e Virus diffusion: Simulate airflow and virus diffusion patterns. Airport operations managers can 
communicate effectively with all stakeholders and increase passenger confidence by creating high￾rendering videos. 
2.9 Planning for Construction Delivery 
2.9.1 Overview 
Airports require large amounts of infrastructure for their operations, and the construction of airport projects is 
complex. It often involves a multitude of parties and resources, requiring time and significant amounts of 
coordination between all involved. Successful project delivery must be an imperative for airports since there 
are significant financial and reputational risks if things go wrong. 
All airport infrastructure projects, once planned and designed must be constructed, delivered, and placed into 
operation. This section provides guidance on key construction delivery elements and logistics to evaluate and 
consider; and, where appropriate, incorporate into the planning and design process to facilitate a smooth, 
timely and efficient construction delivery phase with a focus on minimizing impacts to existing operations while 
maintaining airport capacity and levels of service. 
2.9.1.1. Planning for Construction Delivery 
Most airport planning efforts typically focus only on creating an optimal end-state operating plan without 
consideration for how that plan will be constructed, or how the construction may impact existing facilities or 
operations. While some interim phasing diagrams may be developed by the planning and design teams, these 
tend to only illustrate areas that must remain in service as the construction advances but do not truly plan for 
342 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 362===
Pay 
Se 
IATA Planning for Construction Delivery 
construction. As a result, it is often left to the construction contractor to prepare a construction 
phasing/delivery strategy based on the completed design that minimizes not only the impacts to ongoing 
airport operations, but also the total construction cost, time and effort required. 
In most cases, the construction contractor will focus on minimizing cost, time, and level of effort over impacts 
to ongoing airport operations. At brownfield sites while zero operational disruption for airlines and airport 
users is difficult to achieve in live operational environments, acceptable passenger and airline level of service 
should be agreed and committed to by all parties as an input into the construction delivery plan. A balance 
ultimately needs to be agreed considering a finite construction period to maximize the end-state operating 
plan without severely impacting operations to the detriment of airport customers. Trade-off's need to be 
identified between the additional time and budget that yield both compromised operations during construction 
and end-state operating plans. These potentially unanticipated conditions can and should be identified, 
planned, and optimized prior to commencement of the construction phase, by carefully evaluating a range of 
standard construction delivery elements and planning for the optimum construction delivery phasing and 
logistics approach for each project during the planning and design phases. 
Considerate construction delivery planning minimizes impacts to existing facilities and operations, maintains 
capacity and levels of service, saves construction time and resources required, decreases environmental 
impacts, and ultimately reduces the project cost and risk. 
2.9.1.1.1. Procurement 
At the outset of planning for construction delivery, it is important that appropriate focus is given to the 
procurement approach and the delivery method to be used for the development of both professional services 
and construction activities. Setting a clear strategy at the outset will ensure the various parties brought 
together for the development and project delivery are able to interact and integrate in the most efficient way. 
The procurement strategy that is most appropriate for a particular project depends on a number of criteria: 
e The client's ability to manage risk 
e The project type, complexity, and size 
e The time available and any interim milestones that must be achieved 
e The cost and schedule certainty required 
e Where responsibility for design and quality will be held 
These criteria will often conflict with one another and the most suitable procurement strategy will, therefore, 
represent a balance between them. A structured approach to developing the procurement strategy, 
considering the airport's objectives for the development set against the above criteria, will assist in assessing 
alternative procurement options and result in development of a robust procurement strategy. 
As part of the procurement strategy, the type or form of contract that will be utilized should be considered. 
There are numerous forms of construction contracts in use globally, with each responding in different ways to 
the above criteria. It is advisable to seek early expert advice to assist in the selection of the most appropriate 
form of contract. Further, the airport should have in-house capabilities to administer contracts or outsource 
these capabilities. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 343 

===PAGE 363===
= lil Se 
IATA - Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.9.1.1.2 Master Schedule 
When planning for construction, the timing of delivery is often a key success factor. Delivery dates may be 
driven by new regulatory compliance dates, predicted increased demand past known capacity, or 
commitments to airlines/tenants, or investors. 
The early preparation of a master schedule that identifies all the key activities and major milestones, with 
appropriate links between them will assist in understanding the likely duration of the overall schedule and 
affords the ability to test various delivery scenarios compared against any required operational needs. It will 
also assist in identifying the timing of significant investment decisions. 
At this early stage of the master schedule development process, there are likely to be some activities and 
durations that are beyond the direct control of the airport; these can include public consultations, permits and 
approvals from local or national authorities, interfaces with other construction works and/or construction 
projects, or the provision of new and/or the diversion of existing utilities to service the development. It is 
imperative that adequate time is allowed in the master schedule to cover these potential events. 
2.9.1.2 Airport Types 
Whether planning for an existing “brownfield” or a new “greenfield” airport, all projects can benefit from a 
thorough assessment of a range of standard construction delivery elements during the initial planning and 
design phases. This chapter provides examples of those aspects that are uniquely associated with each type 
of airport. 
2.9.1.2.1 Existing “Brownfield” Airports 
Construction at existing “brownfield” airports pose potential impacts to existing operations. Because 
disruptions to any ongoing operations are likely to degrade the passenger experience, reduce capacity, 
compromise functionality, reduce revenue, or diminish the desired levels of service, it is important to consider 
and carefully weigh those potential impacts against the benefits of the new construction projects. 
As further described later in this section, it is recommended that a range of standard construction delivery 
elements of a project be integrated into the planning and design of the facilities from the outset to avoid or 
344 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 364===
dil Se 
IATA Planning for Construction Delivery 
reduce those potential impacts. If left to chance, they pose a significant risk to achieving the following key 
targets of existing operations: 
e Passenger Experience and Customer Service 
° Capacity 
e Functionality and Operability 
e Levels of Service 
e Safety and Security 
¢ Commercial Revenue 
e Emergency Egress 
e Airside and Landside Traffic Volumes 
¢ Utilities and Life Safety Systems 
Through close examination of project phasing, utilities, logistics, scheduling, and zoning early in the planning 
and design process, many of the potential impacts during construction can be mitigated, reducing the risk to 
the overall operation and business. 
2.9.1.2.2 New “Greenfield” Airports 
While the construction of “greenfield” airports does not present potential impacts to existing airport operations, 
there are several other aspects about construction project delivery that should be taken into consideration 
during the planning and design phases. For example, since many new “greenfield” airports are often located 
in relatively remote settings, the existing roads in the region are not typically designed to handle the type and 
volume of construction traffic that is likely to occur during construction of the new airport. As a result, 
upgrading these routes to accommodate construction traffic should be considered during the planning and 
design phases and incorporated into the overall construction delivery plan. Similarly, the capacity of off-airport 
site utilities may need to be upgraded to accommodate new construction loads. As a result of new 
construction activities, requests for new restrictions may need to be put in place. 
2.9.1.3 Initial Construction Impact Assessments 
Planning for construction delivery should include initial construction impact assessments. Many construction 
projects will occur in a live operational environment, which poses significant challenges and risks. 
Construction impacts should be evaluated against the airport's current operations plan, safety and security 
protocols, and the environmental/sustainable management program, which all serve as the airport's baseline. 
The goal is to identify potential impacts and then, during planning, design, and/or construction, define 
mitigation measures. The identified impacts should also be communicated and discussed with the various 
stakeholders for feedback. While detailed impact assessments will be the responsibility of the prime 
construction contractor, planners and designers should begin to develop preliminary construction impact 
assessments during the planning and design phases for the key areas represented. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 345 

===PAGE 365===
= iil Se 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
See 2.7 Development of a Concept of Operations to provide a comprehensive overview of airport operational 
matters that may serve as a guide to help identify how construction projects might impact the airport. 
2.9.1.3.1 Operational Impact Assessment 
An operational impact assessment addresses the impacts to existing operations that are foreseen during 
construction. This assessment includes the anticipated reduction in throughput capacity (if any) of operational 
areas affected by construction (e.g., reduced number of aircraft stands, gates, check-in areas, parking 
spaces, available curbside frontage), hours of work, duration of impacts, proposed mitigation measures, and 
other relevant operational impact analyses. The airport should continue to monitor the passenger experience 
and perform level of service assessment surveys to inform any revisions that may be necessary to maintain 
the level of service during construction. 
2.9.1.3.2. Safety Impact Assessment 
A safety impact assessment addresses the safety impacts from the planned construction works. The safety 
impact assessment aligns with the existing airport safety program and identifies areas where impacts to the 
safety of people, facilities, equipment, and systems may be affected during construction. The assessment can 
also be subject to change once all trades have been procured with the full working knowledge of equipment, 
materials, workforce, activity durations and travel paths. 
2.9.1.3.3. Security Impact Assessment 
A security impact assessment defines how the construction works will comply with the existing airport security 
protocols. It defines planned construction contractor access and egress points; the screening of workers, 
materials, and equipment; and how the airside/landside boundary will be maintained during construction. 
2.9.1.3.4 Environmental and Community Impact Assessment 
An environmental and community impact assessment forecasts construction impacts (e.g., noise, air quality, 
waste, carbon footprint, surface transport, consumables) and identifies mitigation measures to ensure 
alignment with the airport's environmental/sustainability program and community engagement goals.

2.9.2 Project Execution Plan 
How the project will be planned, designed, engineered, procured, contracted, constructed, tested, 
commissioned, and handed over is fundamental to success. Developing a Project Execution Plan (PEP) to 
address all the project development activities is critical to a project's success. 
The PEP is a dynamic document that is initially developed in outline form at the outset of a project. As the 
project advances, the PEP will be updated and developed in more detail as information and plans become 
more mature and finalized. The PEP is used frequently by the project team for guidance. It serves as a 
roadmap for the team and each subsequent team member's contributions to project delivery. PEPs should be 
developed for all projects. Smaller, less complicated projects may have an abbreviated PEP. 
The PEP outlines the basics of project delivery as outlined below: 
e Who: defines who (what entities) will participate 
¢ What: defines what duties each participant will perform 
e Where: defines where the participants will perform their duties 
e¢ When: defines when the participants will perform their duties 
* How: defines how the participants will perform their duties 
PEPs require the project team to define how the project will be delivered early in the formation phase, 
highlighting roles and responsibilities, key issues and risks, and developing strategies for mitigation prior to 
encountering these issues in the field. 
The key elements of a comprehensive PEP include the following: 
e Business Goals and Objectives 
e Project Scope Definition 
e Project Team Members and Stakeholder Management Plan 
e Environmental, Safety and Health (ES&H) Management Plan 
¢ Quality Management Plan 
e Risk Management Plan 
e¢ Communication Plan 
e Project Controls and Documentation Plan 
¢ Contracting and Procurement Plan 
e Design Management Plan 
e Construction Execution Plan 
e Testing and Commissioning Plan 
° Operational Readiness and Airport Transition (ORAT) Plan 
e Project Closeout Plan

which focus on the construction delivery aspects of the PEP. 
2.9.3 Construction Execution Plan 
The Construction Execution Plan (CEP) is at the heart of the PEP. Addressing the key elements listed below, 
early in the planning and design phases, will provide benefits downstream in construction. 
The key elements of a comprehensive CEP include the following: 
e¢ Approvals and Permitting

project delivery planning process.

2.9.3.1 Approvals and Permitting 
Depending on the scale, size, and nature of the project, advance planning of the construction activities may 
be required during the planning application phase to secure the requisite approvals and consents to proceed 
with the project. Each jurisdiction will have their own specific guidelines and requirements for submission and 
approval. It is recommended that each proposer research and identify what the exact requirements are for 
planning application submission early in the project development phase. The proposer should then develop a 
plan of work to ensure all requisite data is developed, analyzed, and presented to conform with the planning 
application submission requirements. Specialty consultants/partners may be required depending on the 
planning application requirements. 
For large airport expansion projects, it is common to identify a wide range of activities and their corresponding 
volumes with proposed mitigation measures for review and approval, which are discussed below. 
A focus for large project planning application submissions entail defining what construction activities will be 
performed, the level of construction activities, the times of day, and other such information to help 
communicate the level of impacts to the surrounding communities during construction. These requirements 
and data are different from the final total impacts of the project, once in operation. Different studies may need 
to be performed for specific construction activities to understand the associated impacts (e.g., demolition). 
A non-exhaustive list provided below begins to define the types of data that may be required for a planning 
application submission and any mitigation measures that the proposer may wish to employ to further reduce 
impacts either to the environment or to the surrounding communities during construction: 
e Proposed Work Shifts 
¢ Volume of Earthworks/Cut and Fill 
¢ Proposed Construction Haul Routes/Type and Volume of Vehicles 
e Planned Construction Workforce Transport/Type and Volume of Vehicles 
* Construction Workforce Lodging 
¢ Construction Waste 
e Anticipated Noise Volumes 
e Air Quality Management 
e Impacts to Aircraft Protected Surfaces and Navigational Aids 
e Environmental and Community Impacts Mitigation Plan 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 349 

===PAGE 369===
Be IATA yl Airport Development Reference Manual 
Many of the above elements are common to most construction projects. Planning to accommodate 
requirements for these elements early in the project planning application phase will require input from experts. 
A list of assumptions should be logged to help define the methods and data used in the assessments. As part 
of the planning application process, the authorities having jurisdiction and the local communities need to 
understand the impacts of the construction activities and the proposed measures that will be taken to mitigate 
or reduce impacts. A brief discussion about key requirements is provided below. 
2.9.3.1.1_ Proposed Construction Haul Routes/Type and Volume of Vehicles 
The location of both on- and off-airport construction haul routes along with the vehicle types, sizes, volumes, 
and time(s) of day expected to occur, may be required in detail to provide the necessary data for the planning 
application submission. Competent construction partners should be consulted for large, complicated projects 
to help develop and define these data. Safety and congestion may require the involvement of the police and 
other public safety agencies, engaged as necessary during the planning phase. 
2.9.3.1.2 Planned Construction Workforce Transport/Type and Volume of Vehicles 
Most planning applications require the volume of construction activity and, in particular, the volume of 
construction workforce and their associated transport vehicle operations. Typical questions that must be 
addressed include: 
e Where is the construction workforce coming from (i.e., local commute, longer distance, citizenship)? 
e What are the volumes of the construction workforce (i.e., is the volume generally stable or are there 
peaks and valleys during the different phases of construction)? 
¢ How will the construction workforce be transported to site (i.e., private vehicles, public transportation, 
dedicated busses)? 
¢ Over what routes are the construction workforce transport vehicles anticipated to travel? 
e What are the volumes of vehicles anticipated for construction workforce transportation? 
e At what times during the day are the construction workforce transport vehicles intended to operate? Are 
there multiple work shifts? 
e Where are the construction workforce transport vehicles intended to park?

===PAGE 370===
GS 7 
Se IATA al Planning for Construction Delivery 
2.9.3.1.3. Construction Workforce Lodging 
If the intent is to use local existing lodging to accommodate the construction workforce during construction, 
this element may not require much thought. However, if existing local lodging is insufficient to support the 
needs or projected volumes of the project, alternate lodging must be planned. The impacts on the surrounding 
community and site must be identified and submitted for any new or temporary construction of lodging 
facilities, including environmental impacts. 
2.9.3.1.4 Anticipated Noise Volumes 
The noise levels of construction plant and machinery, and the nature of the construction works may also be 
requested to be analyzed as part of a planning application submission. Each corresponding work task will 
have a noise level associated with it and/or assumptions can be made to define levels. The hours of operation 
and the activity must also be taken under consideration (i.e., the noise from an activity permitted during the 
day may not be permitted at night). Methods to reduce and/or mitigate the noise levels and/or when they 
occur should be examined to optimize the construction works and the impacts to the surrounding 
communities. Noise monitoring devices will most probably be required to be installed and up to one year's 
data collected to establish a seasonal baseline prior to planning application submission. A comparison of pre￾construction works noise levels, planned construction works noise levels against actual construction works 
noise levels, may be required as part of the planning permission consent. 
2.9.3.1.5 Air Quality Management 
Similar to noise volumes, the impact on the air quality from construction plant and machinery, and the nature 
of the construction works, may also be requested to be analyzed as part of a planning application submission. 
Each corresponding work task must be examined to determine and define the potential for air pollutants 
and/or assumptions can be made to define levels. Methods to reduce and/or mitigate the amount of air 
pollutants should be examined to optimize the construction works and the impacts to the surrounding 
communities. Air quality monitoring devices will most probably be required to be installed and up to one year's 
data collected to establish a seasonal baseline prior to planning application submission. A comparison of pre￾construction works air quality levels, and planned, and actual construction works air quality may be required 
as part of the planning permission consent. 
2.9.3.1.6 Impacts to Aircraft Protected Surfaces and Navigational Aids 
One area of key importance for safety is the management and effect of the construction works on airspace 
and navigational aids (NAVAIDS). Equipment, especially cranes heights may violate aircraft protected surface 
areas requiring the means and methods of delivering the construction works to be re-examined, or perhaps 
temporary waivers may be granted and obtained. In addition, temporary structures, plant and machinery, 
materials storage, and construction stockpiles may affect NAVAIDS, communications, and/or lines of sight 
that require careful planning, design, and modelling to demonstrate compliance with applicable airport and 
airspace requirements.

===PAGE 371===
se IATA al Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.9.3.1.7 Environmental and Community Impacts Mitigation Plan 
Creating an Environmental and Community Impacts Mitigation Plan is critical to obtaining required approvals 
and permits. Proper management and mitigation planning ensures adverse effects from the construction 
phase of the proposed development on the environment and the local communities are minimized. 
Following are several key methods to minimize environmental and community impacts during construction 
that should be included in the Environmental and Community Impacts Mitigation Plan. 
Limit Fuel Usage: Typically, the greatest environmental impacts produced by construction are caused by 
burning fossil fuels, such as gasoline and diesel. These emissions generate significant amounts of carbon 
dioxide, methane and other waste products that pollute the air and contribute to global warming. Suggestions 
to limit fuel usage include the following: 
¢ Minimize haul distances 
¢ Introduce consolidated distribution centers 
* Reduce vehicle idling time 
e Use green (sustainable, renewable) alternative fuels 
e Use hybrid electric equipment 
e Utilize clean electricity to power hybrid electric equipment 
Reduce Noise: Construction noise is a major source of overall noise pollution in the environment. The 
majority of construction noise is generated by machinery during site preparation, demolition, and landscaping. 
Since many airport sites are located near residences and businesses, noise can be a nuisance to their 
occupants. When planning for construction, it is important to understand the regulations restricting noise and 
to comply with local construction time restrictions. 
Properly Dispose of and Recycle Waste Material: Most construction waste material is disposed of in 
landfills or is incinerated, both of which are extremely harmful to the environment. To minimize impacts, it is 
recommended to develop a plan to salvage, reuse and recycle existing materials as much as practicable. 
Hardware, appliances, and fixtures can be recycled or reused. For example, concrete waste can be recycled 
and used as fill or underlayment, and wood and metals are valuable commodities that can be easily recycled. 
Select Construction Materials High in Recycled Content: Resource-efficient construction should make 
best use of materials, water, and energy. Making use of recyclable materials decreases natural resource 
consumption, reduces greenhouse gases from manufacturing processes, reduces landfill waste and can cut 
costs from hauling, disposal fees, and purchasing raw materials. Any new construction project should aim to 
use high percentages of materials high in recycled content. 
Locally Source Construction Materials: Utilizing materials that are available locally can significantly reduce 
energy consumption and pollution, especially for heavy materials such as concrete. 
Use Construction Materials Low in Embodied Carbon: The carbon emissions generated through 
production, transport, use, and disposal of a material are known as Embodied Carbon (EC). Strategies to 
reduce EC in construction materials can include the specification of concrete mixes, limiting the use of 
352 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 372===
=e a 
IATA + Planning for Construction Delivery 
carbon-intensive materials, choosing lower-carbon alternatives, minimizing the need for new material through 
efficient planning and value engineering, as well as minimizing construction waste. 
Avoid Single-Use Plastics: The biggest contributors to single-use plastic waste in construction are: 
e Plastic packaging (which accounts for 25% of packaging waste in construction) 
e Unused materials from over-ordering and off-cuts 
e Improper storage and handling 
¢ Construction workforce food packaging and utensils 
Possible measures to avoid single-use plastics include use of recyclable packaging, ordering materials in bulk 
to reduce the amount of packaging needed, storing materials in reusable plastic boxes, large plastic sheet 
packaging as weather protection, and sending plastic that cannot be recycled to a licensed contractor for 
waste management. Adopting a more sustainable approach to plastic use not only helps to reduce waste but 
can also have financial benefits. 
Modular and offsite construction: The use of modular and offsite construction offers great opportunities to 
change the way materials are used and reduces the waste generated during construction. Further benefits 
include safer working environments, higher quality and reduced activity onsite. 
Reuse/Reconfigure Existing Facilities to the Greatest Extent Possible: Before adding new facilities, 
consider if an existing space can be reused/reconfigured instead. Identify opportunities to convert 
underperforming existing assets into high-performing capacity or commercial assets during the planning and 
design phases to minimize the need for new construction. 
See 2.4 Airport Environmental Sustainability for further discussion of related sustainability factors. 
2.9.3.2 Construction Phasing 
When planning expansion projects at existing airports, planners should always consider construction phasing 
alternatives that minimize the impact to existing operations. For example, phased expansion alternatives 
should seek to avoid the need to cross active passenger or aircraft movement areas for the delivery of 
materials to construction sites. To the extent possible, new expansion areas should be phased to occur in 
areas isolated from existing operations so each subsequent expansion zone is a natural extension of the 
existing facilities. These conflicts can be avoided either by modifying the physical layouts without 
compromising the optimum end-state conditions or by conducting construction activities during off-peak hours. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 353 

===PAGE 373===
iil Se 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.9.3.2.1 Capacity, Functionality and Levels of Service 
Construction activity at an airport should be as imperceptible to passengers as possible. This is not always 
achievable, however, since it may be necessary to close existing facilities to construct or reconstruct a project. 
To achieve the greatest passenger experience and maintain required capacity, functionality, and levels of 
service during construction, projects should be phased in relatively small increments, conducted sequentially 
until all portions of the entire project are completed. Since minimizing the size of each increment typically 
increases the overall project duration, it is important for airport owners to understand the trade-offs in time and 
impact to existing capacity, functionality, levels of service and their associated costs to arrive at the optimal 
size of each phased increment of construction. 
In addition, phasing of temporary construction works should seek to minimize passenger walking distances or 
additional aircraft taxiing distances around active construction zones. Planners should carefully consider these 
conditions and plan for an acceptable interim concept of operations plan during construction and the 
associated temporary facilities that meet minimum passenger experience and aircraft circulation goals as 
defined in airport guidelines developed for this purpose. More and more airport owners have now begun to 
develop their own unique planning standards and guidelines that airport planners and designers must follow 
to avoid any unexpected circumstances during construction. 
2.9.3.2.2 Construction Phasing Principles 
The following items represent general principles, recommendations and best practices that can assist in 
Preparing and carrying out construction work with minimal disruption to the airport's existing operations. Every 
construction project requires a detailed assessment of its risks, and individual construction guidelines should 
be informed by such an assessment. History has demonstrated that planning the phasing of the construction 
works early in the project helps identify obstacles the project team can resolve prior to construction. 
Health, Safety and Wellbeing: The health, safety and wellbeing of all passengers, staff and workers is of 
paramount importance to any construction undertaking within a live operational environment. Construction 
sites should be physically separated from any public spaces to the greatest extent possible to minimize 
impacts to air and noise quality. 
Airport Security: Any construction project must ensure the integrity of the airport security boundaries at all 
times. Temporary security boundaries must follow boundary guidelines as set out by the relevant security 
agency or agencies and must be reviewed by them well before implementation. Particular attention is needed 
for staff, equipment and materials site entry and exit points. The importance of efficient layouts and operation 
of construction site access checkpoints should not be underestimated. 
354 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 374===
GS ; 
Se IATA vl Planning for Construction Delivery 
Prior to returning the completed construction area back to airport operations, airport security will need to 
perform a review and perhaps a full sweep of the construction area to ensure prohibited items do not remain 
in the secured area. 
Unhindered Operations: Construction projects can represent significant challenges to live operations due to 
their intrusive nature. As a first consideration, any planning of the construction works is to ensure 
operationally required areas are accessible at all times. Where an intervention blocks or inhibits the 
accessibility of an operationally required facility or route, alternatives must be provided, and should be 
discussed and coordinated with the airport and relevant stakeholders. Any such alternative solution must be in 
place and fit-for-purpose before accessibility to the existing facility or route is removed. Ideally, construction 
worker access is segregated from airport staff and passenger access to minimize the impact on passenger 
experience and flows. Similar thought should also be given to the delivery of construction materials and 
removal of waste. The creation of an external site access can minimize traffic impact on the landside road 
access system, as well as on the terminal's forecourt facilities. 
Throughput Capacity and Levels of Service: While it might not always be possible, construction work at 
airports should always aim to maintain the passenger throughput capacity and levels of service at all times. 
To this end, it is often required to create decant capacity in advance, so portions or all of an existing process 
can be relocated to free up the site in question for the construction works. Maintaining minimum levels of 
capacity should always go hand-in-hand with maintaining a terminal's target Level of Service to ensure 
sufficient passenger processing and queuing areas are available and the risks of passenger congestion are 
minimized. Furthermore, a minimum standard for circulation widths for temporary works during construction 
shall be set and maintained throughout. 
Passenger Experience and Comfort: To maintain high levels of passenger comfort and experience, it is 
recommended to maintain the terminal's look and feel, as well as its sense of place, around the construction 
site. Unhindered, intuitive passenger flows shall be ensured around or past construction sites. Solid barriers 
between the site and public areas can assist in minimizing any noise, dirt, or visual impact on the existing 
public areas. These barriers can also serve as carriers for wayfinding, signage, and other passenger 
information. Intuitive and unimpeded access to existing services, conveniences and facilities is to be 
maintained. Temporary seating areas, concessions and other amenities can be provided to compensate for 
the impacts of construction interventions. 
Clear and Intuitive Signage and Wayfinding: To the maximum extent possible, existing passenger 
circulation routes shall be maintained and construction sites shall avoid any disruption to these 
well-established routes. Where construction sites intrude into existing circulation routes, alternative routes 
shall aim to remain as close to existing ones as possible and remain as intuitive as possible for passengers. 
Clear wayfinding and statutory signage is to be provided at all temporary decision points. Additionally, 
passenger informational signage to existing or temporarily displaced services, conveniences and facilities is to 
be provided. Where required, existing signage is to be modified to reflect the temporary conditions. 
Appropriate lighting shall also be provided to ensure adequate levels of illumination along the passenger 
journey. Temporary modified passenger routes resulting from construction activities (e.g., diverted passenger 
circulation routes, modified passenger processing) should be conveyed via the airport's website and airport 
app. This will afford passengers and stakeholders the ability to review and be aware of changes in advance of 
their travel to/from the airport. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 355 

===PAGE 375===
, 3 
Be IATA ull Airport Development Reference Manual 
Expedient and Efficient Construction: The general aim of any construction project must be to carry out 
construction works as quickly, safely and efficiently as possible to minimize disruption to the operations and 
airport business. Construction works should be carried out during off-peak times as much as possible. To 
expedite construction works and minimize the need for additional security checks, construction sites should be 
planned with a landside, non-security-restricted access approach to the greatest extent possible. Agreement 
will need to be obtained from the airport as to the size of areas taken over for construction at any time. Larger 
phases are generally more efficient for the construction contractors delivering the construction works, but 
conversely create greater impact on the passenger and airport operation. 
Revenue Generation: The commercial performance of the terminal's facilities is to be preserved to greatest 
extent possible during construction. Impacts on commercial outlets is to be minimized. Where existing 
commercial outlets are impacted, providing temporary alternatives is advisable. Coordination with the airport 
commercial team to identify potential opportunities to prioritize construction works and/or re-phasing of the 
works may minimize impacts to revenue generation.

phasing examples that minimize impacts to existing operations and the environment, while maintaining 
capacity, functionality, desired levels of service and emergency egress during temporary, enabling, and 
permanent construction works.

2.9.3.3 Enabling Works 
All major airport construction projects usually require the project sites to be cleared from existing constraints 
or facilities to prepare for the anticipated main construction works. Such preparatory pre-construction works 
can take the form of dedicated enabling works. 
Enabling works are often major undertakings that are important to ensure the airport retains operational 
readiness at all times and the main construction works can be initiated without delay or unforeseen impacts. 
Enabling works can include, but are not limited to, the following: 
* Creation of utilities connectivity, or utilities relocations, in advance of the main construction works 
e Removal or relocation of existing facilities (from the airport and/or other stakeholders) 
e The creation of any new facility that needs to be in place prior to the commencement of the main 
construction works 
* Carrying out of any types of surveys and preconstructions data monitoring required for the main 
construction works 
¢ Potentially, the creation of central plant areas (e.g., batch plants for concrete or asphalt), construction 
contractor marshalling/laydown areas, or construction workforce facilities. 
2.9.3.4 Project Logistics 
Project Logistics deals with a wide array of logistical issues for projects, including labor force access to/from 
the project site, project equipment and vehicle access, plant and materials, site offices, construction workforce 
facilities, and the maintenance of the airside/landside boundary in a secure manner. In addition, for some 
projects, fabrication yards, construction workforce lodging, and other project requirements may also need to 
be considered when planning and designing airport infrastructure projects. 
Each project has unique transportation, access, and logistics requirements. In most cases, projects are not 
typically organized or contracted with logistics in mind. Each project and airport site is unique and careful 
thought should be given to the specific requirements of the project as it applies to logistical requirements and 
planning at a given airport: “one size does not fit all’. As with other design elements and factors, a balance 
must be struck between the need for the optimal location of the above construction facilities and the 
maintenance of existing airport operations and commercial business revenue generation. 
Incorporating project logistics early in the planning and design process with key stakeholder participation will 
serve to identify issues and solutions that will influence the design, construction methods, cost, and schedule 
of the project. Project stakeholders typically do not have visibility into logistics/transportation issues until there 
is a problem-which is too late.

===PAGE 380===
