2.9.3.4.1 Site Logistics 
Site logistics planning should address all passenger, public, airport, and project safety parameters. It should 
also incorporate all physical location constraints of the specific project. Further, it should identify and manage 
how traffic flows through and around the project site (pedestrian, vehicular, materials, equipment, and 
aircraft-if applicable), with defined access points. The project site boundaries should be identified with fence, 
barricade, or hoarding locations (see 2.9.3.4.8 Construction Hoarding for more information). Airport 
operational, commercial and local community concerns should also be addressed. 
Other considerations include planning how the project is accessed for materials and equipment (Goods￾In/Waste-Out); defining project laydown areas and pre-assembly work areas; identifying how any crane height 
and hoisting for the project will be accomplished; identifying and planning how the site is utilized for material 
handling/staging/storage; and identifying and planning how property is used for offices, trailers, and 
trade/craftsman parking. 
Site logistics planning involves the following basic processes: Identify the site characteristics; this 
includes topography, existing site usage (operations, commercial, other), existing utilities, and transportation 
routes (if any). 
Determine the size and other constraints of any work areas and facilities: As referenced above, this 
includes adequate sizing of marshalling and laydown areas, work compounds, plant and material 
requirements, and other related elements evaluated against site-specific constraints. Too small a site will lead 
to poor productivity, schedule slippage and increased costs. Too large a site may negatively affect airport 
operations and commercial business operations. 
Establish the inter-relationships between the site work areas and the facilities: Understanding how the 
work will be performed, as well as where site facilities will be located versus material storage and fabrication 
areas, will have a big impact on productivity. A general understanding with some preliminary planning should 
be performed to better prepare for the construction works early in the design phase. 
Optimize the layout of the site work areas and facilities: The construction contractors are ultimately 
responsible for “means and methods” of construction, and they will optimize the layout of their site compounds 
to best suit their needs. Ensuring that adequate space, access, and utilities are planned early in the project 
will benefit all parties. 
2.9.3.4.2 Project Site Offices 
The location and size of project site offices must be identified early in the planning and design process. 
Following are the key factors to identify and evaluate in developing the site office requirements and solutions. 
Size and Number of Project Site Offices: !dentifying the number of different prime construction contractors, 
sub-contractors, testing laboratories, architect/engineering (A/E) consultants, owner's representative, 
authorities having jurisdiction (AHJ), and other key stakeholders requiring project site offices must be 
evaluated. Defining this number can be assisted by understanding the planned number of work packages for 
the project; a single design-build approach, multiple trade packages, or other combination will help define 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 361 

===PAGE 381===
Se TATA pill Airport Development Reference Manual 
those parties requiring a project site office. In addition to determining the number, the size of the construction 
contractor project site offices must be estimated and should take into account general office requirements 
such as meeting rooms, private offices, general work areas, layout areas, office storage, hand tools storage, 
PPE storage, computer/telecommunication rooms, and other essential office space requirements for the field. 
Such construction contractor site offices are often referred to as the “site office complex’. 
Location of Project Site Offices: Construction contractors want their site offices as close to their project site 
as possible (preferably within the project boundaries), Depending on the nature of the project, the construction 
contractor's site offices may reside within the project boundaries. However, if the project boundaries are tight 
and/or limited, alternate locations may need to be identified. A balance between access to the site offices and 
travel distances to/from the project boundaries and marshalling/laydown areas must be maintained. 
Construction Workforce Vehicle Parking: Each day, a large construction workforce will arrive at the 
construction site and require ample parking for their vehicles. Ideally, there is ample space on the project site 
to accommodate construction workforce vehicle parking; however, this tends to be the exception. In some 
cases, airports may have sufficient parking at their remote parking facilities and offer shuttle bus services to 
the project sites. For those projects and airports that do not have sufficient spare car parking capacity, 
alternate construction workforce vehicle parking will be required. Security for the car parking facilities and 
transportation to/from the project site must be incorporated into the final construction parking solution. 
2.9.3.4.3 Construction Workforce Facilities 
The provision of project site offices also includes the provision of construction workforce facilities. Depending 
on the site requirements, logistics, and the scope of the work, the following construction workforce facility 
elements may need to be planned and accommodated within the site office complex: 
e Toilet and Hygiene Facilities 
e Clothing and PPE Storage 
e First Aid Facilities and Equipment/Supplies Storage 
e Canteen 
e Lodging 
The above facilities may not be applicable to all projects; however, a further discussion about each 
requirement is listed below. 
Toilet and Hygiene Facilities: The provision of construction workforce toilet facilities is a requirement on the 
job site. The appropriate amount and location of portable toilet facilities throughout the job site provides for 
convenience and helps to maintain productivity levels. A more robust facility may be required for larger or 
more complex projects, depending on the scale and nature of the works. Adequate toilet and hygiene 
facilities, including showers, may be required for specific types of work, large-scale projects, or projects that 
are remote and dictate long travel distances each day. Thought should be given to shift work, the type of work 
to be performed, and the size of construction contractor work crews to help size the facilities. If there are 
insufficient facilities, the construction workforce will use the airport's own facilities designated for use by 
362 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 382===
ray 
IATA Pull Planning for Construction Delivery 
passengers, which can have a detrimental impact on the customer experience. Further, it could lead to 
reduced construction productivity levels, depending on the location of and access to the facilities. 
Clothing and PPE Storage: A companion of the construction workforce hygiene facilities is the provision of 
construction workforce clothing and PPE storage (e.g., hard hat, protective eyewear, ear protection, gloves, 
boots, high-visibility vest/jackets). Routine construction work dictates the use of PPE by the construction 
workforce. Depending on the nature of the works, the construction workforce may require specific PPE (other 
than the normal PPE listed above) that dictates the daily storage (in lockers) of worker clothing and PPE. The 
provision of PPE storage facilities is good industry practice and should be incorporated into the site office 
planning requirements. 
First Aid Facilities and Equipment/Supplies Storage: The provision of adequate construction workforce 
first aid provisions, equipment and supplies is a legal requirement and good industry practice. For some types 
of construction work that may be deemed high-risk, additional first aid facilities may be required. Providing 
suitable space and the requisite facilities, as required for each specific job, is fundamental to proving 
appropriate first aid. Planning for the size of adequate first aid facilities should include an evaluation of the 
type and nature of the works to help decide what types of equipment and facilities may be required, and these 
requirements should be planned as part of the overall site offices complex. 
Canteen: Most airport construction projects occur at existing airports that have good public transportation to 
city and suburban areas. This established transportation network affords adequate construction workforce 
food delivery options; however, the size, work shifts, and location (predominately for new “greenfield” 
airports), may dictate the provision of a construction workforce canteen. Traditionally, a third-party food 
service provider will enter into an agreement with the construction contractor(s) or airport operator for the 
provision of an employee food service. The requirements of food storage, preparation, consumption, and food 
waste must be addressed and planned within the construction contractor site office complex. 
Lodging: Some airport projects require the construction workforce to commute long distances, thereby 
necessitating local lodging. The most logical and easiest provision of lodging is local hotel/motel 
accommodations. Some airport projects may not have local lodging that is practical. For those airport projects 
that require on-site or near-site lodging for the construction workforce (even for brief periods), the sizing and 
associated requirements must be evaluated and planned. Vehicle parking, food service, maintenance, and 
recreation facilities must also be included in this planning subject. 
2.9.3.4.4 Airside/Landside Security Border 
The maintenance of the airside/landside security boundary is fundamental to all airport construction projects. 
Planning for maintenance of this security boundary during the construction phase requires some thought and 
evaluation, as referenced within this section. Key to consider in planning is the access/egress of the 
construction workforce, tools and equipment, materials, and goods in/waste out. Specific dedicated routes 
must be planned, coordinated, and agreed with the airport and key stakeholders (e.g., airport operations, 
airport police, airport fire and rescue, airlines, retail operators, and others as may be applicable). As the 
construction advances, the different construction phasing requirements may dictate changes to these 
dedicated security routes. Planning for these modifications will help promote a smooth transition from one 
construction phase to another. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 363 

===PAGE 383===
may 
Seo IATA paul Airport Development Reference Manual 
If construction work is currently located on the airside, it is recommended, if possible, to temporarily relocate 
the airside/landside boundary so the construction site activities may be performed in a landside environment. 
This approach eliminates the need for construction workers to gain access to what was previously a secured 
airside zone, thus minimizing security risks and reducing the overall project schedule and costs. 
2.9.3.4.5 Construction Site Access Checkpoints 
Identifying construction site access checkpoints to/from the airport project jobsite requires a holistic planning 
exercise with many planning inputs. These planning inputs include the location(s) of the existing airport 
access points, construction project site office complex, construction workforce facilities, construction 
marshalling/laydown areas, and construction contractor haul routes. Ideally, there are multiple existing airport 
airside/landside security access checkpoints that help determine the location and number of potential 
construction site access checkpoints. Some airports will have sufficient capacity at existing airside/landside 
security checkpoints to facilitate the volume of traffic and type of screening required for construction activity. 
However, planning and coordination with the airport operator should convene early in the planning process to 
ensure assumptions and plans are aligned with the airport. 
There are three types of construction site access checkpoints: 
e Passenger Terminal Building Security Access Checkpoints 
e Airfield Security Access Checkpoints 
* Non-Secured Access Checkpoints 
Each type will have unique requirements that must be addressed as follows. 
Passenger Terminal Building Security Access Checkpoints: The passenger terminal building construction 
site access is geared towards those construction projects within the passenger terminal complex. This 
security access point generally includes access for construction workers, hand tools, some light equipment, 
and goods in/waste out activities. 
Airfield Security Access Checkpoints: The airfield construction site access is geared towards those 
construction projects requiring access to/from the airfield. This security access point generally includes all of 
the activities for the passenger terminal building listed above, plus the provision for heavy plant 
machinery/equipment and bulk materials. Depending on the volumes, the existing airport airfield security 
access checkpoint(s) may not be sufficient to accommodate the volumes of construction activity, requiring 
new standalone airfield construction site access checkpoints. 
Non-Secured Access Checkpoints: Some construction project sites may not require access to secured 
areas (e.g., traversing the airside/landside boundary). These types of projects generally include landside 
projects, roadway projects, utility upgrades, and other non-secured area projects. Nonetheless, planning to 
ensure a measured, controlled, and holistic approach to the protection of the works is required across the 
airport. For these non-secured access projects, coordination and planning must also address the same types 
of planning considerations and activities as the secured access checkpoints. A key planning focus is the 
maintenance of traffic (pedestrian and vehicular) for these types of projects.

2.9.3.4.6 Construction Marshalling/Laydown Areas 
A construction marshalling yard is a place where material and equipment are stored for consolidation and a 
construction laydown area is a space of ground or pavement located near or at the construction site that is for 
the receipt, storage and partial assembly of the project equipment and materials to be installed or constructed. 
Careful thought should be given to the planning of these facilities on a construction site so it is located in 
close proximity to the work being performed to minimize unnecessary vehicular movement on the site and to 
ensure adequate sizing to accommodate the project's bulk material and equipment storage requirements. 
Marshalling and laydown areas accommodate the following: 
e Bulk Materials Storage 
e Plant and Machinery 
e Recycled Equipment and Materials Storage 
¢ Construction Waste 
Most of the above requirements are common to most construction projects. Planning to accommodate these 
requirements early in the project planning and design phases will help provide efficient construction phase 
delivery. Suitably sized areas, access (both worker and vehicular), security, temporary utilities, and other 
considerations form part of the planning for these requirements. A brief discussion about each requirement is 
listed below. 
Bulk Materials Storage: Adequate storage of bulk materials is a key planning consideration. Bulk materials 
storage can either be for materials used to create other products, such as concrete aggregates (sand, gravel, 
potash, portland cement), asphalt materials (bituminous materials, emulsions, binders), soil, steel (structural 
members or rebar), or it may include the storage of equipment to be installed (e.g., passenger loading bridges 
or air handling units). Depending on the type and quantity of bulk materials to be stored, weather protection 
may be required and should be adequately planned during the design phase. 
Plant and Machinery: Plant and machinery is defined as all temporary equipment, machinery, tools, and the 
like necessary to fabricate, assemble, erect, install, and construct the project that do not form part of the 
permanent works. Examples of plant and machinery include (but are not limited to) cranes, rebar bending 
facilities, heavy civil equipment (e.g., bulldozers, graders, tractors, haul vehicles) carpenter shops, concrete 
and asphalt batching plants, formworks, and other such required for the prosecution of the construction works. 
Recycled Equipment and Materials Storage: On many construction projects, demolition of some of the 
existing facilities (buildings, pavement, etc.) is required and generates both equipment and materials that can 
be recycled. A key for an effective equipment and materials recycling program is the ability to separate 
recyclable items from waste items on site. Examples of recyclable equipment include passenger loading 
bridges, HVAC units, flight information display system/baggage information display system (FIDS/BIDS) 
monitors, baggage handling system (BHS) conveyors, seating, etc. Examples of recyclable materials include 
concrete, asphalt, steel, etc. Adequate space to store the items identified as recycled equipment and 
materials should be incorporated during the planning phase. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 365 

===PAGE 385===
an . 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
Construction Waste: The waste management hierarchy is 1) Reduce; 2) Reuse; 3) Recycle; and 4) Dispose. 
A goal should be to eliminate the disposal of any construction waste, which requires the temporary storage of 
construction waste until such time as the materials can be recycled. However, not all construction waste can 
be recycled, and accommodating the waste that cannot be recycled must also be planned. In most cases, 
large construction dumpsters or skips are used to temporarily store the waste before being moved off site to 
the appropriate facilities. It is important to identify the composition of the construction debris to determine if it 
includes any contamination from lead, asbestos, petroleum or other hazardous materials. Hazardous 
materials must be disposed of separately. As a result, separate and specially designed storage facilities may 
be required. 
2.9.3.4.7 Construction Haul Routes 
Identifying adequate haul routes for construction vehicles is also a careful consideration that should be 
incorporated into the planning and design process. The local roads that lead into the airport must be analyzed 
to determine their adequacy for handling large construction vehicles. Further, the volume of construction 
vehicles and at what time of the day they are in use must also be forecasted (as some construction works 
may occur at off hours). Construction vehicles includes all construction worker vehicles and their commute 
to/from the job site, worker busses and other forms of transport, construction haul vehicles (materials, 
equipment, waste), construction worker food service providers, and any other related vehicles to support the 
construction work activities. Depending on the location of the airport, small, isolated country roads may create 
problems for large vehicles, or large volumes of vehicles, and should be identified and addressed early in the 
design phase. 
On-airport haul routes should also be identified and planned. Coordination with Airport 
Operations/Commercial to ensure visibility among key stakeholders, early in the planning process, is 
recommended. This will avoid any last-minute surprises. 
2.9.3.4.8 Construction Hoarding 
Construction hoarding is a temporary structure erected around the perimeter of a construction site to protect 
the public from the construction works and debris. It also prevents unauthorized access to the job site (or 
conversely prevents unauthorized construction worker access to a secured portion of the airport) and acts to 
support a comprehensive project site security system. Depending on the nature of the works, the airport's 
policies, and other factors such as weather conditions, the hoarding may also shield the view of the 
construction works from the passengers and public. Construction hoarding, both public and passenger facing, 
plays an important role in safely segregating the public from construction areas. Construction hoarding affords 
an excellent opportunity to display communication about the project, assist in wayfinding, and improve the 
level of service during construction. Temporary structures can include concrete barricades, wood fencing, 
chain-link with scrim fencing and reusable modular partitions. 
Most airports will have defined standards on the size and type of hoarding, and for any graphics that are 
permitted within the various terminal facilities and exterior construction site locations. Construction hoarding 
plays a significant role in helping airport operations maintain adequate levels of service for passengers during 
construction and provides clear paths for means of egress during an emergency. Construction hoarding is 
366 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 386===
x il Se 
IATA Planning for Construction Delivery 
linked directly to the construction phasing plan and consideration must be given during each phase of 
construction for maintaining utility service, clear passenger flows (including assistance vehicles), appropriate 
air flow, containment for fire and life safety purposes, adequate lighting, sufficient wayfinding information, and 
the provision of project key personnel contact information for emergencies and deliveries. 
2.9.3.4.9 Airside and Landside Traffic Diversions 
Whether airside or landside, diversions to vehicle traffic circulation paths and volumes to facilitate construction 
activities can be extremely inconvenient or potentially unsafe if not addressed well in advance, preferably 
during the planning and design process. Traffic diversions necessary to construct the project should seek to 
avoid impacts to existing operations without undue compromise to developing and achieving an optimum end￾state solution. Coordination with the local community and the authorities having jurisdiction to reach a 
consensus on any traffic diversions in advance of the construction works is recommended. 
In addition, it is recommended that any temporary roads required to accommodate traffic diversions not be 
located where future permanent facilities will be located to avoid the need to relocate temporary roads 
multiple times as construction progresses. Similarly, it is recommended that the planning and design of 
permanent roads not be located in the same place as existing roads to avoid conflicts with existing traffic. 
2.9.3.4.10 Utilities and Life Safety Systems 
Construction work requires the use of temporary utilities for equipment, tools, and energization of installed 
equipment and systems. Many airport construction projects expand and/or upgrade existing utility services at 
the airport or at least for the areas directly affected by the project. For many projects, the delivery of the 
expanded/upgraded utility service is only realized once the construction works are completed. Ensuring 
adequate temporary supply and capacity of all required utilities (power, water, drainage, Wi-Fi, other) during 
the construction works phase must be considered and may require temporary utility service. Planning 
application submissions may require a definitive demonstration of sufficient utility capacity during the 
execution of the construction works, which would include engineering of such utilities. The location of 
temporary utilities and the impact on local communities is of interest and must be examined and planned to 
provide a minimal footprint. 
It is essential to maintain uninterrupted utilities service and life safety systems to existing operational areas 
during construction to ensure the safety of passengers and staff. When planning for these conditions, airport 
planners must understand the critical utilities and life safety systems necessary to provide uninterrupted 
service by creating a phasing plan that efficiently addresses the existing systems so as not to be disrupted. 
Often, the utility supply for the passenger/public areas emanates from the construction work areas. Further, in 
the construction work areas, these utilities are often taken out of service to be relocated or upgraded. 
Advance knowledge and planning of how passenger/public areas will be served by the required utilities is 
paramount to maintaining adequate fire and life safety measures as well as the desired levels of service 
during construction.

2.9.3.5 Disruptive Events 
Pandemics, volcanic eruptions, strikes, and other similar events have a disruptive effect on aviation. 
Construction works are not immune to these disruptive events, and consideration should be given during the 
planning and design stages to account for such disruptive events. Key considerations should include: 
2.9.3.5.1 Availability of Resources 
Disruptive events may limit the amount of materials or construction workforce availability. Other projects in the 
region may further strain limited resources as multiple projects compete within the same supply chain. 
Planning for the stockpile of materials should be a consideration. Identification of the construction workforce 
and their locale in relation to the airport should also be forecasted. These considerations may affect the work 
packaging and delivery strategy of the project. 
2.9.3.5.2 Separation of the Construction Workforce 
During pandemic events, keeping the construction workforce safe and healthy are priorities. Assuming 
transportation to/from the airport jobsite is achievable, maintaining proper construction workforce separation 
(as defined by public health officials) should be considered. The separation requirements may influence the 
design and location of the construction workforce facilities and jobsite access/egress routes. In addition, 
separation of the construction workforce will reduce worker productivity rates, which will likely increase the 
project schedule and costs. 
2.9.3.5.3 Accelerated Construction Works 
Disruptive events, by their nature, reduce the volume of airport operations. Reduced operations provide an 
ideal “window” for construction works to advance at an accelerated pace that may not be achievable under 
normal operations. The work plan and the availability of resources should be examined to identify areas 
where the construction works could be accelerated if possible. The ability to accelerate the construction works 
during a period of reduced operations serves to mitigate the time lost as a result of the reduced productivity 
rates noted previously. 
In planning for disruptive events and the considerations outlined above, it is recommended that the 
planner/designer also review and identify the construction impacts (see 2.9.1.3 Initial Construction Impact 
Assessments).

2.9.3.6 4D Simulation Modeling 
4D simulation is a process that combines a 3D model with the project schedule allowing all stakeholders to 
visualize the construction phasing in a virtual environment. The use of 4D simulation modelling during the 
planning stage of the development process provides the project delivery team with the ability to create, review 
and modify in real-time complex project elements to enhance the project delivery process. 4D modeling 
should be adopted and implemented throughout every phase of the project. Parties should be familiar with the 
platforms and software proposed, and the applications needed in the early stages of the project. 
The 4D tool can link 3D Building Information Modeling (BIM) models of existing and proposed conditions with 
the project development schedule to logically synchronize the construction phasing, detailed work breakdown 
structure, construction methodology, costs, resources, and supply chain logistics to create a virtual simulation 
of the project delivery process. 
The 4D simulation model is used to understand and test multiple construction staging, phasing, and logistics 
alternatives during the planning stage. The results of these tests inform changes to the layouts required to 
avoid conflicts between existing conditions, permanent design works and temporary construction logistics 
elements, such as marshalling/laydown areas, site offices and construction haul routes. Avoiding these 
conflicts minimizes disruptions to existing operations, diminishes the need for unnecessary temporary 
construction works and reduces environmental impacts during construction. 
As an added benefit, the multiple animations of the construction sequencing can be used to visually 
demonstrate the critical aspects of project development to key stakeholders to help them better understand 
the physical relationships and delivery timing of all projects permanent and temporary construction works. 
See 2.11 Airport Simulation for further discussion of related simulation factors. 
2.9.4 Testing and Commissioning Plan 
The testing and commissioning of equipment, systems, and facilities to ensure they are safe, meet applicable 
code and fire/life safety requirements, and perform to project specifications is a requirement of any project. 
The Testing and Commissioning (T&C) Plan should be tailored for each specific project. The T&C Plan should 
encourage planning with the end in mind; however, it should also address any interim milestones or specific 
construction phases of delivery.

2.9.4.1 Role of Key Stakeholders 
Active involvement of key stakeholders is encouraged during the project planning process leading to the 
testing and commissioning program. An examination of the affected stakeholders for each project must be 
performed. This examination should expand outside of the airport authority/operator. For many airport 
projects, the stakeholders will provide equipment and/or systems for operational use (such as governmental 
agencies or airlines) and having them on-board early to understand their scope, the schedule of activities, and 
what they will have responsibility for delivering (e.g., dedicated data and communication networks). Their 
participation in the testing and commissioning program will further ensure success and avoid surprises. 
Who is best placed to manage stakeholder relationships and lead the interactions requires detailed 
consideration. In many instances, the airport's relationships with stakeholders are long-term and strategic in 
nature. The secondment of the airport's own personnel into the construction team to lead the management of 
stakeholders should be considered, as they are often best placed to do so. 
2.9.4.2 Required Information 
The T&C Plan will require a wide range of information, the majority of which should be part of the construction 
contract documents. The technical information in the form of plans and technical specifications will serve as 
the foundation for the testing and commissioning program. These documents will define the layout and 
performance requirements of the facilities, equipment, and systems. 
In addition to the contract documents, the additional testing and commissioning information that is required is 
listed below: 
e Testing and commissioning schedule 
e Identification of parties with roles and responsibilities 
e List of consumables required 
e List of special equipment required (if any) 
* Training requirements and training plan 
¢ Definition of testing criteria (defines how the test will be performed and, more importantly, what constitutes 
a pass/fail of the test) 
e Equipment/system testing plan (equipment must first be tested and then progressively tested outwards 
until the system as a whole is tested—such as power distribution) 
¢ Related systems testing (such as fire and life safety-when the alarm is activated what related systems 
must go into activation (e.g., HVAC, security doors, public address)

===PAGE 391===
& IATA wi Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.9.4.3 Integration with Operational Readiness and Airport Transfer 
Upon successful completion of the T&C Plan phase, the project enters into ORAT. The ORAT Plan identifies 
how the project team will organize within the airport (and with any applicable stakeholders) the requirements 
and schedule for conducting the ORAT. Activities include familiarizing, training staff, performing a series of 
operational modules (“dry runs”) of actual operational scenarios to gain confidence and identify any 
shortcomings that must be addressed prior to placing the facilities and/or systems into operation. The 
operational modules are developed so they can be repeated to accommodate multi-shift training and 
familiarization. Further, the operational modules are developed in such a manner that they can be linked 
together to simulate actual operational conditions (e.g., check-in/bag drop, security screening). 
For Construction Delivery, the ORAT Plan is focused on the major elements listed below: 
e Airport Operations 
e Airport Facilities Maintenance 
e Airport Operations Manual 
e Airport/Owner Procurement Program 
e Tenant Fit-Out Construction 
¢ Airport-Wide Testing and Commissioning 
e Airport Trial Operations Program 
e Airport Certification and Licensing 
e Airport Relocation Program 
e° Stakeholder Management 
Not all elements may be applicable to a given project; however, the project team should perform an analysis 
to determine the applicability as each project will require some aspect of each of the nine elements to be 
effective and deemed safe and ready to be placed into service. The ORAT Plan should also be developed for 
interim construction phasing to ensure safe and functioning facilities, equipment, and systems. It should also 
be noted that ORAT program planning should commence early in the project development phase and 
progress in maturity leading to implementation. 
2.9.4.3.1 ORAT Scope 
Define what the scope of the ORAT Plan is and, more importantly, what it is not. 
e Familiarization and Training—Classroom, factory, or online training sessions should be included in the 
scope definition and identify any pre-training requirements such as certifications and/or prior experience 
necessary for participation. 
*¢ Operational Trials—Define what trial operational scenarios must be developed and implemented. Most 
airports develop these trials in a modular format to allow simulation of discrete tasks that can be trialed 
over and over again to accommodate multiple staff worker shifts or to re-run the trial based on lessons 
learned (e.g., passenger ticket check-in process). Further, by developing the operational trails in a 
372 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 392===
Se i p IATA Mi Planning for Construction Delivery 
modular format, it affords the operator the opportunity to link individual modules together (e.g., passenger 
ticket check-in, passenger bag tagging, passenger bag drop). 
2.9.4.3.2 ORAT Schedule 
Similar to the T&C Plan, an ORAT schedule should be developed that is resource loaded, identifies the 
activities (their durations and sequence), and utilizes the project WBS. 
e Predecessor activities—Defines what previous facilities, elements, equipment, and systems must be 
completed and deemed safe to operate prior to commencement of ORAT trials. 
e Training requirements—Should be included in the schedule and identify any training required prior to full 
participation in the ORAT Plan. 
e Trial operations modules—All trial operations modules should be listed in the schedule, with their 
frequency and required attendees. 
2.9.4.3.3, ORAT Participants 
The list of participants for each activity and trial operations module should be identified and communicated 
well in advance so the personnel can schedule their work accordingly and ensure participation. Public 
volunteers are often recruited as some trials require a large number of people (i.¢., to simulate the boarding 
process of a Code-F aircraft). 
2.9.4.3.4 ORAT Requirements 
The ORAT requirements should be clearly identified, highlighting which entity will provide what items. The 
requirements should include a list of the following: 
* Construction contractor supplied staff, tools, equipment, etc. 
e What consumables are required, and which entity will provide them. 
e All special equipment (e.g., aircraft, ground handling equipment, trace detection items for security) or 
special tools, and which entity will provide them. 
e People to simulate the various passenger processing elements. 
* Stakeholder participation to ensure all affected stakeholders participate and are fully trained and 
competent in the use of the new equipment/systems and facilities. 
2.9.4.3.5 ORAT Performance Objectives 
Similar to the T&C Plan, a list of ORAT performance objectives should be developed, implemented, and 
communicated to all participants. The performance objectives should then be monitored to ensure progress is 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 373 

===PAGE 393===
Be IATA i Airport Development Reference Manual 
being made against the pass/failure rate of the trial modules, and to identify shortcomings with the ORAT Plan 
and corrective measures that should be implemented. 
See 2.10 Planning for Operational Readiness and Airport Transfer for a more complete description and 
overview of this subject. 
2.9.5 Demobilization 
Upon the successful completion of the contract requirements, including the punch list or snagging list from the 
T&C phase and the ORAT, and prior to placing the facility, equipment, and systems into operation, the 
construction contractor must demobilize and relocate from the affected areas. Construction contractor 
demobilization is a critical step prior to operation. The construction contractor must vacate the operational 
areas and leave the space clean and safe. If there is adjacent plant and equipment, machinery, materials, 
etc., measures should be taken to ensure they will not negatively affect the areas that are soon to be placed 
into operation. Utility service is always a concern. Some of the construction contractor's temporary work areas 
may supply the operational areas and care should be given to ensure disconnecting any utility service or fire 
and life safety systems (including travel distances and means of egress) are not disrupting the operational 
area. 
2.9.6 Other Industry Guidance 
While significant effort has gone into the development of this section, it is important to recognize that there are 
a number of other industry manuals and guides available that explore the process of planning for construction 
delivery in more granular detail or simply from other perspectives. 
Upon reviewing this section, the reader may consider it worthwhile to seek further views on specific areas of 
interest from these other sources, which are widely available. For example, ACI published the ‘Managing 
Operations During Construction Handbook’ and national regulators such as the UK CAA and US FAA issue 
specific guidance related to operations during construction activity, which can assist in the planning for 
construction delivery. In addition, the reader may consider the advice and recommendations included in the 
‘Airport Owner's Guide to Project Delivery Systems’ published by a joint committee of ACI-North America 
(ACI-NA), ACC and the Associated General Contractors of America (AGC). Finally, it is recommended that a 
review of the Advanced Work Packaging (AWP) process documented by a number of sources, including the 
Construction Industry Institute (Cll), be conducted to reinforce and further delineate many of the concepts 
outlined in this section.

2.10 Planning for Operational Readiness and Airport Transfer 
2.10.1 Overview 
The purpose of an Operational Readiness and Airport Transfer (ORAT) program is to ensure the safe and 
successful operation of a new airport facility from Day 1 and beyond. The increasing sophistication of airport 
systems and technology has made opening an airport facility a complex endeavor; therefore, methodical 
preparation is necessary before operations get underway. Not only do systems have to work, but new 
standard operating procedures have to be in place and staff have to be trained in their use. A well-planned 
ORAT project simplifies all preparation activities and monitors their progress through effective real-time 
information-sharing among all stakeholders. 
This can only be achieved through the implementation of a governance structure similar to Airport 
Collaborative Decision-Making (A-CDM), in which stakeholders are completely engaged in working towards a 
common goal. The concept also involves implementing a set of operational procedures, automated 
processes, mechanisms and tools. 
Although there are a variety of methods to implement an ORAT program, key considerations common to all 
include: understanding the interactions between all projects and processes as well as engaging and managing 
stakeholders at the right moment. 
2.10.1.1 Scope 
This chapter of the ADRM captures and synthesizes lessons learned from opening new airport facilities (e.g., 
terminals, aprons or BHS) and complete airports, and provides guidance on the associated ORAT challenges. 
Note: The ADRM does not provide a definitive guide on how to approach an ORAT process and it is not 
intended to be used in this manner. 
2.10.1.2 Benefits of ORAT 
Opening a large, new greenfield airport or existing airport expansion presents unique challenges when 
compared to other types of facilities: 
e Airport openings are very high profile, and problems can become widely known and have an enduring 
impact on an airport's reputation 
e New airport facility openings are infrequent, so there is a limited pool of expertise and sources of 
information to guide the process 
* Openings often include complex new systems and processes, plus a wide variety of new individuals with 
diverse interests, all required to work together as if they had been doing so for years 
¢ Openings often involve the integration of existing and new systems and processes 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 375 

===PAGE 395===
Soe IATA pill Airport Development Reference Manual 
There is often a long period of time between the initiation and completion of airport facility projects. During 
this period, staff, business processes and technologies will often change 
Implementing an effective ORAT methodology will mitigate surprises on the opening day. A well-defined 
ORAT program should: 
Set a firm governance foundation for senior airport management, regulatory bodies, the airline community 
and other key stakeholders 
Create an atmosphere of transparency and collaboration among all stakeholders and facilitate the 
integration of plans 
Review the design of new infrastructure to assess its suitability to meet operational and maintenance 
objectives, as well as international and national standards and regulations. Prior to construction, the 
ORAT methodology should identify and assist in the resolution of any design issues that may have a 
negative impact on the facility's maintenance processes 
Confirm that the contractor has delivered its obligations and the new facility is fit-for-purpose and is fully 
commissioned in accordance with contract requirements 
Track progress to make sure that the airport authority, airlines and other stakeholders have the 
processes, staff, skills, training, and tools necessary to effectively operate the new facility 
Provide an operational vision and plans encompassing all aspects of the new facility 
Prepare operational plans that address normal, irregular and emergency conditions, and review or assist 
in the development and implementation of contingency plans to manage any identified operational risks 
prior to the introduction of new infrastructure or services 
Developing and executing effective recruitment, training and familiarization programs specific to the 
individual needs of the airport authority, airlines and other stakeholders 
Developing a well-communicated change management program 
Confirm that new infrastructure maintenance practices are operationally validated, where practical, 
through testing of operational interfaces between facilities, systems, procedures and human resources 
within a given timeframe 
Ensure that operational validation testing includes all relevant stakeholders, both internal and external 
Oversee or assist in the development of transition planning to ensure a smooth transition of new 
maintenance-related infrastructure or services 
Manage media and public relations so that expectations are controlled and that accurate timely 
information is shared 
Prepare the airport for a robust and sustainable outcome 
376 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 396===
we i IATA Planning for Operational Readiness and Airport Transfer 
2.10.1.3 Applicability 
The complexity of an airport operational readiness project depends on the systems and equipment employed, 
the number of stakeholders involved and the time available for preparation, rather than its physical 
dimensions. ORAT is critical to realizing a new facility's operational goals. 
ORAT involves all airport stakeholders in the airport readiness preparation process, and enables systems, 
facilities, procedures and personnel to be tested under real operational conditions. This allows fora 
comprehensive analysis of potential problems well in advance of opening day. The aim of ORAT must also be 
to create a sustainable outcome. Airport facilities often provide the vehicle for regional economic growth, 
employment opportunities and other wider benefits. Delivering these benefits requires not only mitigating 
ORAT challenges, but also educating the airport and its personnel to cope with future difficulties as well as 
identify opportunities and systems to ensure continuous improvement. 
2.10.2 Program Structure 
2.10.2.1 Stakeholders 
2.10.2.1.1 Overview 
Stakeholders are parties with an interest in the successful launch and future operation of an airport facility. 
The number of stakeholders will vary, depending on the extent and complexity of the project. However, in all 
cases, to achieve success, stakeholder engagement in the project must be achieved at the right level and at 
an appropriate stage of the process. 
An initial analysis of all stakeholders involved in the project must be completed at the beginning of the ORAT 
process and a systematic approach must be taken from the outset so that: 
e Stakeholders are engaged throughout the process and effectively managed by the ORAT team to 
minimize the risk of surprises 
¢ Stakeholders with different roles and interests are familiar with each other during the whole process. This 
helps to maintain a common culture of transparency and of working together as a team to achieve a 
common goal 
e Stakeholders are involved appropriately to support and enhance the outcomes of the ORAT process 
¢ Stakeholders are engaged and communicated with at the right time, using the appropriate media, so they 
all feel involved in the ORAT process and responsible for its success 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 377

IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.10.2.1.2 Stakeholder Groups 
Irrespective of project size, there are always multiple stakeholders involved in an ORAT process, with the size 
and makeup of involved parties increasing as the project progresses. The approach described here is based 
on a large project and can be scaled as appropriate for smaller ORAT efforts. 
The approach presented in this chapter classifies stakeholders according to their role and final interest in the 
overall process. A diagram illustrating the main groups is presented in Exhibit 2.10.2.1.2 below: 
378 
Construction Stakeholders are parties working on the design and construction of the airport facility. 
These are normally the first stakeholders involved in the ORAT project and their involvement remains until 
the Airport Opening Date (AOD), as they must deliver a complete facility for other stakeholders to convert 
into an operative facility. The impact of construction stakeholders in the airport's opening day varies 
according to their role in the construction 
Airport Operation Stakeholders are those involved in the final operation of the airport. Airlines are the 
primary users and customers of airports and should be included as a specific stakeholder group in all 
cases. Ground handling companies are also an extremely important stakeholder group to be consulted. 
The earlier these groups of stakeholders are involved in the process, and the more open the 
communication between the Construction Group and the Operations Group, the easier it will be to achieve 
a successful, sustainable launch. For major projects, operational stakeholders must have the opportunity 
to guide the Construction Group to develop the project in a manner to best serve their operational needs; 
for instance, to ensure construction phasing minimizes disruption of airline operators 
Regulatory and Government Stakeholders must certify the facility according to standards, so it is 
recommended to engage them from the outset in order to stay compliant

2.10.2.1.3 Engagement Model 
As stakeholders are such a key determinant to success, the ORAT team should consult with them from the 
beginning to identify their requirements and integrate them into the process at the right stage. This may 
include consultation methods and techniques such as running focus groups, workshops and structured or 
semi-structured interviews. The success of these methods is highly influenced by local conditions such as the 
airports location, so they must be tailored to the context of each project. 
At the beginning of the ORAT process, ideally in the planning stage, the ORAT team must meet with each 
stakeholder independently to assess their involvement in the various stages of the program. Stakeholders 
should be involved from an early stage and their engagement should be retained throughout the whole 
process. The ORAT team works to promote the ORAT concept to the wider airport community and increase 
understanding of the importance of continued participation throughout the ORAT process.

2.10.2.2 Program Governance 
The formality and complexity of ORAT program governance will be determined by the size and complexity of 
the project. ORAT programs of small and repetitive projects require less formal governance and less 
involvement of senior management, while ORAT programs of larger, more complex or exceptional projects 
tequire more formal and structured governance, as projects of this nature typically include multiple 
organizations with different cultures, goals, objectives and governance. This subsection reviews the 
governance used to manage relatively large and complex projects. 
2.10.2.2.1 Program Office 
The objective of ORAT governance is to encourage and ensure the diverse project participants to operate as 
one team with common goals based on their agreement following consultation. 
To achieve this, an ORAT team, including representatives of all stakeholders and project participants, is 
established. The ORAT team is led and directed by an ORAT Executive Steering Committee (ESC). 
In addition to the ORAT ESC, the ORAT team must be reinforced by a flexible governance structure of 
committees, commissions and working groups that guarantee the engagement of all stakeholders. This will 
lead to a structure with: 
¢ Quick decision-making capability 
* Flexibility to adapt to the necessities in each phase of the project 
* Ability to ensure total coordination between all parties by facilitating open communication and the 
multidirectional flow of information 
e Ability to capture all parties’ experiences

members; major stakeholders are normally permanent members, including primary constructors and

2.10.2.2.2 Schedule 
The ORAT Governance Structure must be defined from the beginning of the project at the planning stage, 
when the ORAT team and the ORAT ESC are composed. 
The first activity of the ORAT ESC is to define the ORAT “Mission Statement”, which must encompass the 
focus of the ORAT team and be limited to the scope of what can be controlled by the ORAT team and 
processes. 
Beyond commissioning, ORAT is the process of moving from the construction phase to full operation of a 
facility. ORAT is ultimately the responsibility of either the owner or operator of the facility. In any case, the 
early involvement of the ORAT team reduces resources and timescales in the later stages of the process and 
has the following benefits: 
¢ An ORAT team that fully understand project and design decisions can apply lessons learned from 
previous projects from the beginning and can justify change management 
¢ Early identification of key stakeholders and setting accountabilities 
e The ability to prepare robust plans, schedules and resources for ORAT 
¢ Improved and strengthened relations between the ORAT team and all stakeholders, through an adequate 
governance structure 
e Better and earlier understanding of end users’ needs leads to fewer changes later. The ability to change 
decisions is higher in early stages of the project, which means less cost and lower impact to the schedule 
* Understanding passenger flows and commercial offerings (e.g., retail and food & beverage) allows traffic 
flow optimization to maximize efficiency and revenue 
* Accommodation of phasing through small ORAT projects 
e Great starts lead to great finishes

contingency measures to realign the deviations with the schedule. An adequate monitoring of the overall 
process is mandatory to achieve success. 
2.10.2.2.3 Phasing 
Major construction projects are normally phased to enable the infrastructure to become operational as soon 
as the minimum required readiness is achieved, while all supplementary facilities and systems that are not 
crucial to operations are introduced after the AOD. Phasing more commonly means that, at AOD, only 
infrastructure required to supply sufficient demand is opened, and the next phases will provide capacity for 
future demands. In such cases, each phase is normally treated as a separate project, part of the wider airport 
construction program. Each phase has a different AOD target and a specific ORAT project. 
As indicated in Exhibit 2.10.2.2.3 below, all ORAT projects follow a similar schedule, although timings might 
vary. Once the ORAT methodology is in place, the governance structure is implemented, the key stakeholders 
are on board, and a path of work is organized, some stages’ timings (Planning and Readiness) can potentially 
be reduced. The stakeholders would already have experience in working together for ensuring the successful 
opening and, for them, the second ORAT project would merely be a continuation of already existing 
processes. 
The ORAT projects for the phases after the first one will use the applicable documents, manuals and plans 
prepared for the initial ORAT project, which will only need to be adjusted to meet the particularities of the 
airport expansion. It can also safely be assumed that the risk will be reduced, especially in the case of the first 
phase development of a new Greenfield airport or when adding new terminals and runways to an existing 
operation within a few years after the initial AOD. 
In the case of construction phasing of key airport infrastructure, there should be a separate ORAT project for 
each phase.

2.10.2.2.4 Risk Management System 
In addition to the ORAT mission statement, the key objective of the ORAT ESC is to mitigate surprises on the 
AOD. This can only be achieved through a Risk Management System (RMS), which allows the identification, 
analysis and resolution of issues before AOD. It must be noted that the complete elimination of risk will never 
be viable; however, the airport must be able to analyze the acceptability of risks and propose contingency 
measures to manage them toward acceptable levels. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 387 

===PAGE 407===
oz li Se 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
Due to the complexity of programs, an Initial Risk Identification (IRI) is desirable, which will include a complete 
analysis of risks and corresponding contingency measures. Ideally, the ORAT ESC, which includes 
representation of main stakeholders, must approve it and the RMS. 
After the approval of the IRI and RMS, new risks will continue appearing as the project advances and will be 
analyzed according to the approved system. Risks of varying acceptability can be identified by different 
stakeholders in all levels of the chain of command. 
The definition of an adequate RMS, which is transparent and objective for all the stakeholders, is a vital 
component of a successful launch. 
2.10.2.2.5 Reporting 
Reporting must be made according to the Issue Resolution Ladder (IRL). 
Ideally, issues are resolved at an operational level and do not need to be escalated to the ORAT ESC. 
However, some issues may require escalation through a procedure such as the following: 
e Level 1: Any party identified at an operational level can raise an issue and seek counterparts to find 
resolutions. if this is not possible in the prescribed timescale, or if issues are determined to need input 
from the next level of the IRL, the issues are escalated 
° Level 2: Issues involving contract interpretation, issuance of instructions or change orders, significant 
operational changes, or intervention by Level 2 individuals are escalated to Level 2 for resolution 
e Level 3: Where issues involve resolution between parties that cannot be addressed at Level 2 and involve 
input by the ORAT team or stakeholder SPOC, they are escalated to Level 3 for resolution 
¢ Level 4: This is the highest level of resolution, reserved for issues that cannot be resolved at Level 3 or 
involve executive decisions to implement

To achieve the goal of opening without surprises, transparent accurate information about the real-time status 
of construction and preparedness of all stakeholders is necessary. Depending on the size and complexity of 
the project, it may be appropriate to use automated tools and services to facilitate the sharing of accurate, 
transparent information between all stakeholders and to manage the timely resolution of issues. Implementing 
an integrated tool is not easy due to the number of different stakeholders involved in an ORAT process. 
2.10.2.2.6 Interfaces 
The ORAT process consists of a complex array of interfaces between a large number of stakeholders, all 
taking place within a local context and subject to timing constraints. The stages of the ORAT process are 
often managed by different teams and corporations, meaning that open communication, effective coordination 
and stakeholder engagement is vital for a successful launch. Ensuring that all stakeholders work together to 
achieve this common goal is a vital component in the bigger ORAT picture. 
Managing the interfaces and dependencies between the stakeholders is the key task of the ORAT project. 
Stakeholders must be engaged at the right moment and their involvement retained until the AOD. The 
implementation of an integrated ORAT schedule, including main stakeholder milestones and the ORAT ESC, 
has the aim of facilitating the coordination between all parties. Managing different interests toward a common 
goal is critical to achieving a successful launch. The ORAT ESC defines a governance structure to achieve 
the involvement of all stakeholders in the appropriate timing. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 389 

===PAGE 409===
we IATA Wi Airport Development Reference Manual 
Stakeholder participation in working groups and focus groups, as well as representation in the ORAT ESC, 
helps achieve stakeholder commitment. This achieves a shared responsibility between all stakeholders with 
the intended outcome of having the airport open successfully on the planned AOD. As the ORAT team raises 
the awareness of dependencies between the individual stakeholders, this increases the level ownership that 
each stakeholder has over their project deliverables.

2.10.2.2.7 Timing 
Independent of ORAT methodology, timing can be defined by three milestones that divide the ORAT stages. 
The involvement of different stakeholders varies at each of the stages described below: 
e Start of ORAT Activity. The start of ORAT is dedicated to reaching the Operational Availability of the 
new facility and is normally divided into Planning and Readiness stages. Theoretically, the Readiness 
phase coincides with the construction commissioning of the new facility. In practice, delays in design and 
construction are common, resulting in a period in which the Readiness phase of ORAT runs in parallel 
with construction. This brings additional risk to be managed by the ORAT team 
© Operational Availability. When the ORAT process reaches this second milestone, the new facility and its 
operator and stakeholders are considered ready to begin operations. The Activation phase consists of 
certification and trials, while the Transition stage is dedicated to the airport transfer 
e Launch-Beginning Operations. In an adequate ORAT process, the Transition stage continues after the 
opening day to guarantee the creation of a sustainable outcome 
All stakeholders are normally committed to a clear deadline, with the ORAT period defined as a number of 
months or days before the AOD. The beginning of the last two stages of the ORAT project (Activation and 
Transition) is dependent on the readiness of the four ORAT prerequisites (Facilities, Information, Systems, 
and Human Resources). Delays in the construction stakeholder's deadlines (i.e., providing facilities or 
installing, testing and commissioning systems) or the airport operator's deadlines (i.¢., delivering information 
or providing resources) will have an impact on ORAT timing. If the AOD is fixed, delays in the readiness of the 
four ORAT prerequisites reduces the Activation and Transition stages. 
Ideally, the opening day is fixed when there is certainty that facilities will be 100% complete and 
commissioned, and when stakeholders are familiar with the new facility and trained on normal, irregular, and 
emergency operations. When it is necessary to fix an AOD early in the process, the potential impact on ORAT 
of construction delays can be mitigated by including sufficient float in the construction schedule, plus 
allocating additional funds in the budget to accelerate construction, if necessary, in order to protect an 
adequate ORAT period. 
2.10.2.2.8 Communications 
As the size of a project increases, the number of stakeholders increases and information flows can become 
increasingly difficult to manage, with meetings and forums becoming unnecessarily overcrowded and 
ineffectual. An initial definition of stakeholder roles and a clear delimitation of responsibilities is essential for a 
successful launch. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 391 

===PAGE 411===
Hy Be i 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
For smaller projects, stakeholders may assume multiple roles, resulting in streamlined and simplified 
information flows. On large projects, to facilitate the communications between various departments and 
government agencies, a SPOC and a back-up deputy from each major stakeholder group is assigned to 
support the ORAT team. 
To ensure a seamless transition into operations, each SPOC supports a direct reporting structure within its 
home department or division, although they functionally report to the airport ORAT team. This method 
encourages constant dialogue and transparent communication between each department and the airport 
ORAT team. 
Management, airport stakeholders and construction stakeholders have various dedicated forums at which 
information is transferred, project status tracked, and issues raised. Based on the governance structure 
described above, key meetings can be established. 
Due to the complexities of major airport projects, and the number of different stakeholders directly and 
indirectly affected by the changes that the airport project will bring, communications must be carefully 
managed, both internally and externally. 
An Airport ORAT Communications Management Plan, which should be developed in conjunction with the 
airport authority and other key stakeholders, details how both internal and external communications are 
managed. The communications management plan ensures that communications with parties are bidirectional 
and that stakeholders and other organizations are informed and consulted at prearranged stages of the 
project. This facilitates consistent and timely release and receipt of information by all participants in the 
project. 
2.10.3 ORAT Stages 
The ORAT schedule is divided into four stages. At each stage, the aim of the ORAT project is different and 
main stakeholders also change. The first two stages of the ORAT process (Planning and Readiness) are 
aimed at achieving the operational availability of the new facility, while the other two stages (Activation and 
Transition) are focused on achieving a successful launch and a sustainable outcome. The Transition stage is 
divided into two phases: 
° Preopening day transition stage 
e Post-opening day transition stage 
Each stage of the ORAT process is explained in detail below.

2.10.3.1 Planning 
Depending on the project being undertaken, an ORAT project will often start at the same time as the 
construction of the new facility or airport. The intensity of ORAT will increase as the project gets closer to the 
AOD. 
The Planning phase sets the tone for the ORAT project. The key items to plan are: 
(a) People who will comprise the ORAT team. 
(b) Stakeholders involved in the project and the SPOC within each organization. 
(c) ORAT Governance Structure definition. 
(d) ORAT Mission Statement. 
(e) ORAT project scope and timeline, including integration with key construction milestones, such as: 
1. Mandatory certification milestones, including the timing and requirements for regulatory submission 
and approval of any new or amended airport license. 
2. Operational plans, including the concept of operations, recruitment and training plans, airport manual 
and standards, irregular and emergency operating procedures. 
3. Milestones for the inspection by regulatory authorities. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 393 

===PAGE 413===
& IATA Gi Airport Development Reference Manual 
4. Milestones for the agreement of operational interfaces with key stakeholders, including airlines, 
ground handlers, air navigation service provider, state control authorities, immigration, customs, police 
and security services. In cases where fire, crash and rescue is provided by the state or a third party, 
suitable performance agreement milestones will need to be agreed upon. 
5. Milestones for the development of service level agreements with the identified stakeholders. 
(f) Integrated program, recommended to guarantee the success of the launch (may be dependent on the 
number of stakeholders involved). 
(g) Risk Management System and the process for escalating key issues that would have the potential to 
impact the AOD (the Issue Resolution Ladder Structure). 
(h) Airport Opening Scenario. There are many factors that impact the Airport Opening Scenario (AOS). The 
ORAT ESC should determine the AOS, although there may be political opinions to be taken into account. 
The ORAT ESC must be flexible and able to adequately navigate ORAT planning through these 
decisions. Moreover, despite that the AOS should be theoretically fixed at the Planning stage, it normally 
does not occur then, resulting is an initial period in which the planning is based on assumptions about the 
AOD. 
2.10.3.2 Readiness 
This stage of the ORAT process has the aim of achieving operational readiness. It comes after the Planning 
stage and includes all the activities necessary to guarantee the readiness of the four ORAT prerequisites: 
Facilities, Information, Systems and Human Resources. 
2.10.3.2.1 Readiness Management 
The ORAT team should monitor the readiness prerequisites on a regular basis, typically monthly, and more 
regularly as the AOD approaches. This requires open and transparent communication with the main 
stakeholders to determine what is achievable, if the engagement model is adequate and to ensure the 
stakeholders are profoundly involved in the project. As with any major project activities, a common platform is 
established to monitor progress and stakeholder readiness. 
For each of the prerequisites, all adequate ORAT processes must verify the following aspects, as a minimum: 
(a) Facilities 
1. Follow up on the provision of facilities with respect to time, quality and quantity. 
2. State the necessary operational conditions for rooms or equipment. 
3. Alignment of requirements with available facilities. 
4. Development of space requirements.

In addition to monitoring the stakeholders to achieve readiness, the ORAT team should update the critical 
path and records of expected issues to feed the Activation stage. A first list of trials and required testing 
scenarios might be advanced at this stage and presented to the ORAT ESC for analysis and approval. 
Tracking stakeholder progress on a monthly basis will enable the ORAT team to prepare accordingly, and 
advise when there are risks of delays in the program that will have an effect on the AOD and require 
mitigation measures. The more proactive the ORAT team is, the easier it will be to align stakeholder progress 
with the initial schedule.

2.10.3.2.2 Testing and Commissioning 
The Testing and Commissioning phase is a standard stage of the construction project. It must not be 
confused with the ORAT operational trials, although it is considered within the ORAT timescale due of its 
importance. It aims to establish and certify that the item (i.e., facility, zone and/or system) is safe and ready 
for use by members of the public. 
2.10.3.3 Activation 
The Activation ORAT stage begins just after the Operations Availability milestone. It includes all activities 
aiming to achieve the certification of the airport and the trials of the facility. 
2.10.3.3.1 Certification 
Before beginning operations, an airport must be certified by the national Civil Aviation Authority (CAA). Other 
licenses might be required depending on the new facility. 
The certification of the airport is the responsibility of the airport operator. It is issued for each infrastructure 
and operator, so it must be renewed any time either the infrastructure or the operator changes. Whether or 
not the airport operator has experience with the certification process, informal agreement and approval of 
critical items with the CAA is recommended to avoid surprises. Documentation must be formally sent to the 
CAA at an established time prior to the beginning of operation, but by that stage both the airport operator and 
the ORAT team must be confident about the certification of the airport. Even if the ORAT team does not have 
responsibility for the airport certification, the process to obtain the certificate is complex and must be carefully 
monitored due to its impact on the AOD. 
The process of acceptance handover and occupancy certification must be ready for the beginning of ORAT 
trials, including the testing and commissioning required and the level of service the assets must provide. 
Delays in construction lead to the overlap of the Readiness and Activation stages. Insurance must be in place 
to guarantee the Activation phase is covered independently of the owner and that members of the public can 
safely enter the premises of the airport in order to take part in the ORAT operational trials. 
2.10.3.3.2 Trials 
The ORAT operational trials are one of the main activities of the ORAT project and simulate the real operation 
of different airport processes. The aim of the operational trials is to ensure that: 
© The integration of all airport systems is working correctly 
e Staff are knowledgeable and experienced in the standard operating procedures related to their role 
e Passenger, bag and aircraft flow processes are adequate 
¢ All contingency procedures are planned realistically and achievable. They are used by the ORAT team to 
verify the airport is ready for operation as part of the Activation phase 
396 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 416===
an 
ae 
IATA Planning for Operational Readiness and Airport Transfer 
Ideally, the ORAT operational trials take place after the acceptance handover and after the certification of the 
facility, although trials sometimes begin before the facility is certified. Insurance must be modified to cover all 
participants, with training and resourcing adapted accordingly. If trials begin within the construction phase, 
initial Health & Safety training and PPE are mandatory for all people involved. 
A period of three to six months is reserved to complete the trials and must always be finished before the 
Transition stage and the AOD. 
2.10.3.4 Transition 
The Transition stage is critical within the ORAT process, covering at least the transfer management and 
strategy for the AOD. A best practice ORAT process will go further to extend the Transition stage beyond the 
AOD to guarantee the creation of a sustainable outcome. 
Although operational readiness is always managed by the ORAT team, the airport transfer can be led by 
another party (e.g., the airport owner or a local authority). When this happens, open communication between 
both teams is mandatory to achieve a successful launch. 
The airport transfer is normally managed within a short period of time, and involves a high number of 
stakeholders. Detailed transfer and transition strategies must be developed for all stakeholders, including: 
e Equipment and systems available for transfer and transition 
© Logistics for transfer and transition 
e Analysis of any possible early opportunities for transfer and transition 
¢ Asset dependencies for IT, systems, equipment, facilities and staffing 
e Timing sequence 
¢ Monitoring methodology to be proactive in the detection of any risk with an impact on the AOD 
In a similar fashion to the rest of the ORAT process, working groups and focus groups are developed to help 
the stakeholders in producing these plans. 
These plans are consolidated and a countdown-to-operations checklist is compiled, including a detailed list of 
all issues to be addressed to achieve a successful launch. The list will identify the status of each issue, along 
with the individual responsible and the scheduled date for a resolution. 
The status of each issue is normally highlighted through a color-coding system (e.g., a red—amber—green 
traffic light). The checklists are based on the number of days to AOD and facilitate a detailed review of the 
status of readiness moving toward AOD. A formal checklist review is normally settled monthly. Issues that are 
not closed according to plan can be escalated and managed to avoid affecting the AOD.
