===PAGE 417===
Se By IATA pull Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.10.3.4.1 Relocation/Move Management 
Planning for the physical relocation of facilities is always challenging and requires significant planning and 
coordination. However, there are key strategic considerations to determine as the AOD approaches: 
(a) Project type and complexity: Greenfield airport vs. airport facility. 
(b) Continuity of operations of the existing airport/facility. 
(c) Benefits of each opening strategy (“Big Bang’/“Hard” opening vs. “Phased”/“Soft” opening). The analysis 
must include at least the following: 
1. Cost impact. 
2. Political pressure. 
3. Commercial/contractual considerations. 
4. Capacity constraints in the old airport/facility. 
5. Seasonality of the traffic. 
(d Airline assessments, including at least overall passenger volume of each airline, number of ground 
handlers, proportion of domestic and international traffic, and transfer mix. 
(e Sourcing of staff and equipment: percentage of new staff/equipment and percentage of staff/equipment to 
be transferred from the closing airport. 
(f) Facility and systems readiness, including physical infrastructure and systems, support facilities, power 
stability as well as certification and licenses. 
(g) People readiness, including training, process development, familiarization and cultural change. 
(h) Previous ORAT experience. 
There are two main opening strategies. A “hard” opening benefits from the cost savings of not operating two 
big pieces of infrastructure (airports) simultaneously, but requires strong stakeholder engagement and 
significant coordination to ensure the transition takes place during the established period of time (generally 
overnight). The large scope of this logistical task has led to this approach also being named a “big bang” 
opening, and is selected by some airports when the old and new airports are owned and operated by different 
organizations. It should be noted there are significant risks in selecting a hard opening. IATA strongly 
recommends a phased opening and relocation plan to minimize operational risks of disruption, unless there is 
a compelling reason to do so otherwise. 
The alternative to a hard opening is a phased approach, also known as a “soft” opening. This method allows 
for a gradual transition between the two pieces of infrastructure. It is, however, most commonly practiced for 
airport facility expansions rather than for new Greenfield airports. The phased opening can take place over 
several weeks or months and is most commonly organized on an airline-by-airline basis, or one ground￾handler at a time. 
Once all the stakeholders have completed their plans for transfer and transition, the ORAT ESC decides the 
overall transfer strategy. 
398 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 418===
IATA Planning for Operational Readiness and Airport Transfer 
A successful relocation process depends on the proper planning of the following: 
¢ Determination of the Relocation Route, which must be carefully analyzed to guarantee that all 
equipment and systems can be transferred within the planned timeframe. Alternative routes are studied 
as contingencies 
e Equipment and Staffing required to initiate the operation. A complete analysis and compilation of 
stakeholder transfer and transition plans is required at this step. The flight schedule for the AOD 
determines the operational procedures. Ground handlers must confirm the availability of equipment, 
vehicles and staffing required for the operation, and are asked to move forward within approved plans to 
avoid risks to their commitments to airlines 
e Logistics for Transfer and Transition—determination of moving method and logistics platform. The 
transfer and transition logistics must be carefully analyzed to guarantee that equipment and vehicles are 
available according to the operations plan. Simulation tools are used to guarantee timings are achieved. 
The analysis will include: 
© Time required to transport equipment through a single route, or using several routes; 
o Number of trucks required to move non-motorized vehicles; 
© Arrival points and security procedures for equipment entering the new airport; 
o Parking areas within the new airport; 
© Procedures for the transfer of all vehicles to the final locations; 
© Offload and installation of non-motorized vehicles from the parking area. 
An analysis of any possible early opportunity for transfer and transition, and asset dependencies, is 
recommended at this step. 
¢ Clear Definition of Stakeholder Responsibilities. In order to ensure a seamless transfer process, inter￾stakeholder coordination must be enabled. Tables including key stakeholder roles to successfully execute 
the operation are shared and approved 
¢ A Monitoring Methodology should be defined in order to detect any risk that could have an impact on 
the AOD. A list of issues to achieve a successful relocation should be developed and tracked on a 
periodical basis. Issues not resolved according to the program should be escalated for quick resolution 
2.10.3.4.2 Airport Opening Day 
The time required for the ORAT Transition stage (relocation and preopening day transition) depends on the 
size and the complexity of the project. Three months is often dedicated to this stage for major projects, but 
this can be potentially reduced for smaller, simpler or repetitive projects. 
When best practice ORAT planning is in place, additional buffer time is recommended to ensure the timing 
required is protected, in case there are delays in the previous stages. All stakeholders work through and 
report on their progress in completing the countdown checklists. New issues are monitored, reported, 
escalated and managed in line with their importance and status to fully complete the checklist. Issues with 
potential to impact the AOD are assessed and contingency measures proposed in the event of not being 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 399 

===PAGE 419===
aie . 
IATA 4 Airport Development Reference Manual 
possible to resolve them before the AOD. Contingency measures are analyzed, tested and incorporated into 
the operations process. Less critical issues can be resolved after the AOD. 
Mitigation strategies include the following: 
e Accelerate construction progress, if it is behind schedule, by increasing working hours and resourcing 
¢ Modify the program to open only what is finished 
¢ Develop contingency plans for systems that are not working as expected 
Stakeholders will make the transition to their new facilities at the optimal moment according to the approved 
countdown list, as well as transfer and transition plans. As progress is made and the opening day 
approaches, it is important that checks are made at regular milestone intervals to confirm the feasibility of 
achieving a successful AOD. The Go/No-Go decision is normally defined as a milestone some time before the 
AOD. From that moment, this decision must be confirmed by the ORAT ESC at all milestones. Each project 
has its own critical issues, although in all cases the following aspects must be fully studied: 
e Is the construction progress on track, including general construction, systems and equipment installation 
and integration, commissioning, handover and training? 
e Are stakeholders prepared? Are the main aspects of staff readiness (i.e., progress of recruitment, training 
and familiarization against approved plans), acceptance of facilities’ progress, and plans of operation 
readiness complete? 
« Are critical issues raised during the trials resolved? 
e Have mandatory certifications been achieved? 
During the final month countdown, the following activities should be completed: 
e Handover of the facilities and systems to end users (i.e., owners, operators and maintainers) 
¢ Creation of an AOCC as a centralized reporting hub for the AOD and post-opening transition period. This 
central command and control center monitors, manages and resolves all issues 
e Implementation of a set of operational procedures and automated processes. The ORAT project works 
toward a successful opening on Day 1, but also toward operating perfectly on Day 2 and beyond. It aims 
to improve the operational efficiency of all stakeholders involved by reducing delays, increasing the 
predictability of events, and optimizing the utilization of resources during the ORAT process. This aim is to 
be achieved via improved real-time information sharing between all stakeholders 
e Relay of all communications to external interest groups who will be involved in the AOD. This includes 
arrangements required to manage the media and public expectations 
The final countdown to opening is the most critical period for the ORAT team toward the AOD. It has the most 
intense activity and involves the largest number of relocations and moves. Stakeholder engagement and the 
establishment of an AOCC are critical for a successful launch.

2.10.3.4.3 Post-Opening Day 
An effective ORAT process will also consider the post-opening day transition period, during which much 
ORAT-related activity occurs. 
The ORAT team will review and monitor many activities and processes to facilitate successful ongoing 
operations of the facilities and teams, including: 
e Handover of all ORAT documentation and facilities 
¢ Familiarization and training of some stakeholders (e.g., airlines, ground handlers, in-terminal 
concessionaires) who may join the airport's operations at a later stage 
¢ Coordination of any remedial works. Minor issues that were not made available for the AOD are resolved 
at this stage, with construction continuing on less critical elements. Each of these needs to be trialed and 
accepted prior to their integration into daily operations 
e Review of warranties and maintenance contracts, and confirmation that spare parts are handed over 
Finally, the ORAT team develops a lessons-learned report for the ORAT process. This report is shared with 
all stakeholders, with alternative methodologies analyzed. A thorough analysis is especially important to 
phased projects in order to avoid making similar mistakes during subsequent delivery phases. 
2.10.4 ORAT Workstreams 
2.10.4.1 Process 
2.10.4.1.1 Concept of Operations 
As the aim of the ORAT process is to ensure that any new airport infrastructure project functions well from 
Day 1 onwards, a clear “Concept of Operations” must be developed. This should include a clear and complete 
set of operational plans that the facility will use following the AOD, covering standard, irregular, and 
emergency operating procedures for the new airport facilities. 
Plans of operations are developed for each key aspect of the airport that will be affected by the new airport 
facilities. The plans must be developed by the end users, normally within a working group, and revised and 
approved by all stakeholders concerned. 
An airport's functions can typically be divided into 11 core processes, which are necessary for the operation of 
a major international airport: 
e Airport Access 
e Passenger/Crew Handling 
e Baggage Handling 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 401 

===PAGE 421===
Ze IATA pi Airport Development Reference Manual 
¢ Cargo Handling 
e Ground Handling 
e Aircraft Control 
e Administration and Management 
e Facility/System Maintenance 
e Airport Security 
e Customer Service 
e Environment 
These 11 core processes can be divided into main functions and further into subfunctions. These main and 
subfunctions represent packages that must be planned and implemented in terms of scheduling, quality, and 
quantity, ahead of the trial operation. As per the ORAT schedule, each main function and subfunction will 
require consideration of Facilities, Information, Systems and Human Resources (see 2.10.2 Program 
Structure, particularly 2.10.2.2 Program Governance). 
It is important that end users define from the outset the level of service they want to offer to internal and 
external clients. This decision cannot be made in isolation by each stakeholder, because all functions 
contribute to the global positioning of the facility. The level of service agreed upon is clearly linked to the 
Concept of Operations guiding individual stakeholder plans, but all must be aligned with a centrally made 
decision. Depending on the level of service standards agreed upon, resourcing the functions will vary and, 
consequently, the Operating Expenses (OPEX), Capital Expenses (CAPEX) and Replacement Expenses 
(REPEX). This will have a significant impact on the sustainability of the future airport. 
For projects involving the renewal of existing facilities or the construction of new infrastructure with an impact 
on preexisting facilities, a review of the current airport operating plans should be undertaken. This will assess 
whether the plans can be applied to the new facilities with no changes, with minor or major changes, or need 
to be completely rewritten to cover the processes and procedures suited for the new facility. It must be 
highlighted that it is sometimes more difficult to modify the existing Concept of Operations for an area or 
facility of an airport than to completely change the operation's concept. The renewed facility is part of the 
overall airport and its Concept of Operations must be integrated with that of the rest of the airport. This is not 
always easy due to the different systems and technologies in place. 
Working groups are established to review and develop plans of operations for new facilities. The Concept of 
Operations must address regular, irregular, and emergency operations, and includes the following: 
e Roles and responsibilities of all stakeholders involved in the plan 
* General descriptions of systems, equipment, and standard operating procedures 
© Detailed diagrams of passenger and employee flows, as well as the flow of goods and waste disposal 
e General passenger processing, including check-in, gate, and boarding processes 
© Customer service amenities 
e Irregular operations equipment, facilities, and processes 
402 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 422===
Planning for Operational Readiness and Airport Transfer 
¢ Terminal evacuation plan 
¢ Communication and coordination strategies, such as briefings and emergency centers 
e Staffing and monitoring schedules 
¢ Terminal irregular operations, such as weather, air traffic, life safety, building flow, air carriers, uncleared 
baggage, building mechanical, and IT 
e Labor disruption plan 
e Default, bankruptcy, or termination of service plan 
e Overview of Emergency Management Program and Incident Management System 
e Definition of airport operational levels, including normal, irregular, emergency, and disaster operations 
e Description of emergencies: aircraft-related, non-aircraft-related, and medical 
e¢ Command and control flowcharts for each emergency type 
e Emergency checklists 
e Emergency contact information for all stakeholders 
Each ORAT working group will delegate responsibility for developing aspects of the various plans of operation 
to focus groups. Each plan is fully developed through discussions with working group members and owners of 
processes, systems and equipment to document and confirm: 
¢ Roles and responsibilities 
e Processes, systems and equipment 
¢ Requirements for contingency and mitigation plans to support operations during irregular or emergency 
operations 
As plans are developed and finalized, they are reviewed and approved by associated stakeholders and, when 
appropriate, by the entire ORAT working group. The aim of this revision process is to ensure accuracy, 
including grammar, style, consistency and format. It is important that the stakeholders actively engage in this 
process because they are ultimately responsible for implementing the procedures set down. Upon thorough 
review by the owner and working group, the document is finalized and published. The working group must 
then develop the required training material and organize the testing of operational plans. 
The ConOps includes the structure of the SOPs, Irregular Operating Procedures (IOP) and Emergency 
Operating Procedures (EOP). The sum of all operating procedures should be considered carefully to address 
all the instructions required, and not to lead to a breakdown of operating systems. 
The resulting set of operating plans and procedures is treated as a live document to be regularly updated to 
reflect changes and enhancements made during the life of the new airport facility. Each of the plans contain 
references to the SOPs implemented by staff.

2.10.4.1.2 Management Systems 
Due to the significant financial impact (OPEX, CAPEX, and REPEX), all airports must develop an Asset 
Strategy (AS) and an Asset Management System (AMS), defining: 
e Whatis considered to be a critical asset, in terms of operations, money, number of impacted 
stakeholders, level of service, and other attributes 
¢ Arisk management system for critical assets, which determines the critical path 
¢ Acclear definition of all critical assets, their tolerability and contingency plans 
Airports have hundreds of systems and pieces of equipment that must be managed to peak efficiency, with 
each item having unique resourcing and maintenance needs. The implementation of an effective AMS allows 
the operator to concentrate on the critical path and target investment most required. The operator normally 
develops individual maintenance plans; compilation of these into an integrated AMS permits a reduction in 
OPEX through better use of assets. In parallel, it improves the service life of assets and reduces CAPEX and 
REPEX. 
2.10.4.1.3 Operational Procedures 
Operating procedures (SOPs IOPs, EOPs) are detailed written instructions to achieve uniformity of the 
performance of a specific function within the ConOps. They help ensure safety and operational efficiency for 
all airport functions. The structure of each SOP must be carefully analyzed to comply with standards and to 
facilitate user application of the instructions. As a result, they should be the basis of everyday work of every 
employee, as well as the foundational base for their training programs. 
SOPs must be considered live documents that should be frequently updated to ensure they reflect real-world 
conditions and working practices. 
2.10.4.1.4 Organization 
Human resources planning is an essential prerequisite to implement a successful ORAT. Stakeholder needs 
for recruitment and training are identified and planned early in the ORAT process. Sufficient, properly-trained 
staff are fundamental to a successful launch and in creating a sustainable operational environment from Day 
1 onwards. 
The ORAT team confirms that a thorough review of each stakeholder human resource plan has been made to 
ensure the adequate number of staff is available to cope with the operational goals of the new facility. 
Stakeholder human resource plans are ideally integrated into the ORAT program. Milestones are defined to 
monitor progress and main resource issues are included in the countdown checklist. Stakeholder readiness is 
a key consideration in confirming the AOD.

2.10.4.1.5 Recruitment 
Each stakeholder should be encouraged to create a staff report as the basis for the recruitment process. This 
will identify the skilis and competencies of existing staff, with the goal of developing them to their potential 
through a training plan, plus defining the recruitment necessary to fill shortfalls. This can then provide a 
framework for managers responsible for preparing, conducting and promoting familiarization and training 
sessions among members of the airport working community. 
Once each organization has mapped their vacant positions, the next task is to put together job descriptions for 
each position. Job descriptions are very important as they are the basis to determine the prerequisite 
education, experience and skills candidates require, in addition to providing contracts for new members of 
staff, and the starting point to determine training and familiarization requirements. Line managers must be 
involved, together with the Operations Director and Human Resources team performing the recruitment 
processes. Recruitment tasks will include publishing the job vacancies, reviewing applications, conducting 
interviews and selecting candidates. Managing negotiations, contracts and the supporting documentation to 
add the hired staff to payroll will also require that the Enterprise Resource Planning System be available at an 
early stage—ideally six months before the AOD. This is particularly important for Greenfield airports. 
The recruitment process is critically important for the launch of Greenfield airports when the existing airport 
continues operations. Competition for staff will become strong between the new and existing airports, and 
stakeholders might find it difficult to find the right competencies for key positions. Important familiarization and 
training processes need to be defined to cope with this weakness and guarantee a well-prepared team. 
2.10.4.1.6 Training 
Training and familiarization are two activities included in the readiness stage of an ORAT process, although in 
most cases, it will continue during the next two stages (Activation and Transition). 
Training refers to all mandatory and standard corporate trainings, which new members of staff are required to 
receive upon starting a new job. Familiarization focuses on practical sessions that help staff get acquainted 
with their day-to-day working environment (see 2.10.4.1.7 Familiarization). 
While each stakeholder is undertaking and managing their recruitment and training processes, the ORAT 
team focuses on the overall familiarization strategy. The ORAT team requires stakeholder input to define a 
useful strategy that guarantees all staff are accustomed to working in the new environment on the AOD. 
Stakeholders have a choice between two strategic approaches when planning their training and familiarization 
program, and may use a combination of the two for different roles. 
e All staff are trained directly by the stakeholder—this is often used for familiarization 
¢ “Train the trainers”-this is often used for more complex, specialized training that is sometimes outsourced 
to professional agencies. Trainers must be familiar with the airport environment, processes and roles 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 405 

===PAGE 425===
IATA al Airport Development Reference Manual 
Even when staff training and familiarization processes are outsourced, the airport operator remains the owner 
of this activity. The airport operator's Human Resources department oversees preparation for the training and 
familiarization sessions, which includes: 
e Compiling training and familiarization materials 
e Listing stakeholder participants and trainers 
e¢ Communicating with the trainers, stakeholders, airport operator and contractors to facilitate the 
organization of the training and familiarization sessions 
e Scheduling training and familiarization sessions and site visits 
¢ Organizing the debriefing from training sessions and site visits, and tracking attendance 
The development of a stakeholder training matrix can support the organization of the training and 
familiarization processes. This is a tool that can be used to map stakeholder training needs for the multiple 
systems being installed. It provides all stakeholders with a comprehensive list of the systems being installed 
and a snapshot of the types of training staff that are nominated for each system. The matrix identifies which 
stakeholders are operators, maintainers and users of each system; this information will influence the type of 
training each stakeholder requires. 
The ORAT team prepares a training schedule for staff that must then be formally approved by all 
stakeholders. Training is a fundamental prerequisite for the commencement of the familiarization stage. The 
ORAT team tracks that all staff have undergone the training sessions allocated for them prior to the 
commencement of their work. As most of the staff of the future airport facility are not directly contracted by the 
operator, this becomes a key dependency for the AOD. 
2.10.4.1.7 Familiarization 
The familiarization stage aims to provide staff with practical sessions to acquaint them with their new 
workspace. Tools and materials to manage familiarization include guidebooks, virtual visits and classroom 
sessions tailored according to training requirements. A site visit or airport walkthrough is normally mandatory. 
More advanced tools are used in major projects, such as simulators that virtually introduce staff to their future 
work environment. 
The ORAT team is normally in charge of the familiarization process, and base it on the requirements identified 
in the staff plans. Most sessions are tailored for different groups, according to their role and the area of the 
airport where they will work. The ORAT team prepares the materials for the familiarization sessions, involving 
leaders of key departments within the airport operator, including terminal operations, security, safety, airside 
management, IT and systems, technical services, commercial developments, marketing, corporate 
communications, and strategic planning. Classroom sessions take place according to the familiarization 
strategic plan developed at the beginning of the ORAT project. 
Following the classroom sessions, it is of great benefit for staff to see their working environment; putting first￾hand experience together with theoretical familiarization is proven to enhance the process. If construction has 
not concluded at this stage, insurance arrangements must be made to cover these walkthrough sessions, and 
construction safety measures and training must be assumed as part of the process.

Familiarization sessions are vital when most of the staff do not come from an airport environment and are not 
accustomed to mandatory security and safety measures and tools. The ORAT team must track the progress 
of the familiarization program and complete a lessons-learned report for subsequent openings. 
2.10.4.2 Trials 
The Activation stage of an ORAT process ideally begins once construction is finished and the facility is fully 
operational. Trials are planned to test whether the performance of the facility is adequate to meet the desired 
level of quality, to test if systems are fully integrated, and to evaluate the training of staff. Trials should 
reproduce the main operative processes of the future operation of the airport in order to detect anomalies 
before the AOD and to implement corrective measures in time. 
The trial's objectives can only be achieved if real operations are reproduced as closely as possible. The 
ORAT team must work to achieve the following required conditions: 
e Ensuring appropriate participation and involvement of the airport's operative staff and stakeholders, such 
as airlines, ground handlers, immigration and other regulatory bodies. Stakeholders must be engaged in 
advance so that they can organize their resourcing for the execution of the trials 
¢ Organizing the availability of participants acting as passengers (with their corresponding baggage), as 
well as real aircraft, handling equipment and other elements involved in the airport process required for a 
realistic trial 
° Creating a logistics and operations team for the management of the trials, responsible for managing 
volunteers and their baggage, organizing support staff, and monitoring the trials 
e Recruiting complementary services, such as security, cleaning, transportation, catering and/or information 
Construction delays may result in pressure for the ORAT period is reduced, with the testing and 
commissioning period (Readiness stage) overlapping with the trials period (Activation stage). However, both 
activities must never be confused, as they refer to different processes with different goals. While the systems 
and equipment testing and commissioning period is focused on verifying their correct installation and 
operation, the trials period simulates complete operative processes when the four ORAT prerequisites are 
available. 
Trials must not be initiated until the milestone of “operational availability” is reached, which implies: 
e Facilities are available-completed, tested, secure and accessible, with equipment acquired, installed and 
tested 
e Information is ready—new procedures are defined and approved 
e Systems are available—fully installed, integrated and tested 
e Human resources are prepared-new staff are hired, trained and familiarized with the new infrastructure

Depending on their scope and content, trials are classified in two groups: 
e Basic trials are dedicated to specific functions or subfunctions within the airport processes. Their main 
objective is to verify the proper function of the installations 
e Advanced or global trials reproduce the overall airport process, including the simulation of a real flight 
schedule, typical issues and contingency procedures 
Other trials are included to recreate failures or emergency situations: 
e Fall-back trials of contingency programs to address the failure of systems, equipment or standard 
operating procedures 
e Emergency trials to test emergency operating procedures as well as command, control and 
communications

2.10.4.2.2 Trials Management 
The ORAT team will carefully monitor the execution of the trials. The coordinator of each area collects from 
observers any anomalies or dysfunctions detected during the trials and creates a list of issues. 
An evaluation meeting takes place after the trials with all stakeholders involved and coordinators from each 
area will share the list of issues. Issues are evaluated and classified according to their impact on the AOD: 
e High impact-Issues that will impact the planned airport operation 
e¢ Medium impact—Depending on their number and criticality, these have the potential to impact the AOD 
e Low impact-Issues that do not or will not have a bearing on the planned operation 
It is important to have this meeting as soon as possible after the execution of the trials to ensure that 
stakeholders have a clear memory of all the processes. If no major issues are detected and the evaluation is 
positive, the process continues as scheduled. When important issues arise, contingency measures are 
defined and trials are repeated to guarantee a successful launch. These measures, including individuals 
responsible and timing, are included in a final report and follow up until the repetition of the trial.

A good description of a trial scenario must include a definition of the logistics required for its execution. With

2.11 Airport Simulation 
2.11.1 Introduction 
The concept of simulation means different things to different audiences, contexts and industries. In the airport 
environment, there is a wide variety of applications in use for different planning stages. A few examples of 
simulation applications in use at airports are: 
e 2D and 3D deterministic design simulations, such as those that allow operators and planners to set the 
aircraft path on the airfield, mapping out wing tips and undercarriage to ensure safety clearances are 
maintained. 
¢ 3D design simulations used for simulating GSE and boarding bridge movements to ensure clearances are 
maintained. 
e Deterministic and stochastic simulations with a lesser visual component, but which reflect future 
conditions of an airport or airspace system and allow the evaluation of resources needed for a forecast 
demand as well as the cost-benefit analysis at a high level of aggregation. The numerical results of these 
types of analyses are often presented in graphics and tables. 
¢ Discrete event simulations in which almost all variables are stochastic, i.e. vary randomly over time and 
space. Dynamic flows of aircraft, vehicles, passengers and baggage can be modelled in abstract process 
flow models or highly visual within a 2D or 3D spatial representation of the airport infrastructure. 
¢ Sometimes called Fast Time Simulation Models, these models are the most comprehensive in terms of 
their capabilities and output. They mimic the decision-making processes of the real world. The outputs are 
measures of performance, which we often call KPIs. 
¢ Fast Time Simulation Models that are not restricted to only airport surfaces (i.e., ground level or building 
floors). Several models exist for the analysis of airspace and air traffic control. 
e Very specialized 3D models also exist for simulating individual components of systems of the airport, such 
as the BHS, or detailed security checkpoint processes. 
While there are many vendors and simulation software in the market, three important considerations when 
choosing the simulation software are functionality, integrability and aesthetics. Most software can produce 
very nice, lifelike pictures of the models in 3D, but functionality in depth and scope of what the simulation can 
do is a more important factor. Integrability refers to the ability to transition across the boundaries of landside, 
terminal and airside with ease and without data issues. For a medium to large airport project, this is an 
important factor. Finally, esthetics implies making the appearance of models a realistic digital representation 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 411 

===PAGE 431===
Se a IATA iit Airport Development Reference Manual 
of the real world, which supports the common understanding of stakeholders. Much operator time can be 
spent in modelling airport processes with a high level of detail or making the models look nice by combining 
third-party software and static or moving illustrations. It is important to choose the too! with a suitable level of 
granularity or abstraction corresponding to the scope and objectives of a simulation project. An assessment of 
the tradeoff is, therefore, necessary based on scope, time and budget available. 
While this section has been a brief introduction to the types of simulation used in airport development, 
capacity planning and operations management, the remainder of this chapter discusses applications of 
simulation to airports and airspace in more detail. 
2.11.2 History and Evolution 
Simulation of airport operations has significantly advanced over the past 20 years. The use of simulation as a 
decision support system and communications tool has become an important and integral part of airport 
development, capacity planning and management processes. 
As computational power has become more available and affordable, simulation has become a tool to validate 
both the functional and the architectural design of airport terminal landside and airside facilities. Airport 
simulation has improved to address capacity issues of strategic, tactical and operational importance. Thus, 
simulation can be applied during the whole life cycle of airport systems and subsystems, from design to 
realization to operation. Once a simulation model is available, it can be regularly updated and used to test, 
monitor and enhance the capacity of airport facilities. Simulation is also the preferred tool when it comes to 
assessing the directly realized Level of Service (LoS)", from two of the measures of performance involving 
available space per occupant and maximum waiting times at terminal processing. 
The application of simulation covers the whole airport environment, including: 
e Airspace connecting airports to each other 
e Runway and taxiway systems 
e Aprons 
¢ Deicing facilities and temporary aircraft parking positions 
e Passenger terminals 
« Baggage handling systems 
e Landside access and car parking 
e Multimodal transport systems 
Using a computer model of the airport, all processes may be simulated, based on the scheduling of flights at 
the airport, itinerant flights such as cargo, GA, military, state, and flight training, and non-airport-related 
demand such as retailing, supply of goods and the use the airport roadway system. 
® Level of Service concept is for use with respect to passenger experience in the terminal. On the airside and landside, the variable to 
reflect a similar concept is the delay to a pilot or driver. 
412 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 432===
Tata il 4 Airport Simulation 
Areas of application for simulation range from checking layouts of newly planned airport facilities, validating 
redesigned airport facilities, and testing new operational procedures or regulations to assess their impact on 
existing airport facilities and to “maximize” or “optimize” capacity. An increase in airport capacity can be 
achieved without expanding the infrastructure by improving the operational concept, i.e. the way how airport 
resources are allocated and operated. 
The objective of simulation is to represent real-world processes in a computer model, so that the impact of 
inputs (decisions) on the output (consequences or results) can be analyzed and a number of “what-if” 
scenarios tested at a fraction of the cost of implementing in the real world and not achieving the target LoS or 
the cost-benefits necessary to make the project viable. Once a simulation model has been set up, it can be 
used as an experimental platform for various purposes. 
An advantage is that the simulated airport is virtual. Implementing new operational concepts, adding airport 
facilities, installing new equipment, expanding terminal buildings, constructing new taxiways and aircraft 
stands, or testing new operational procedures will not impact real operations. 
Exhibit 2.11.2a: Screenshot: Example of an Airport Simulation Model 
Source: Airport Research Center 
Experimenting in a virtual environment is far more cost-effective than implementing and testing in the real 
world. Planning parameters can be corrected quickly in a virtual model without causing major costs whereas, 
in the real world, significant cost could be incurred by changing or rebuilding existing infrastructure. 
Simulation enables informed decision making, helps avoid taking forward incorrect planning assumptions to 
construction, reduces the risk of making wrong decisions, enhances planning reliability, and attempts to 
ensure that all stakeholders concur with the decisions based on the simulations. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 413 

===PAGE 433===
we IATA Hn Airport Development Reference Manual 
How to simulate an airport? Following are some questions to ask: 
e How to model the reality? 
e What is the area of focus? 
« What are the KPIs? 
« What level of detail is really necessary? 
Reality involves an essentially unlimited amount of information and detail. Due to this complexity, it is not 
possible to replicate reality exactly. Thus, a simulation model is always an approximation of reality. It must 
focus on key aspects and be calibrated in order to match reality as closely as possible. 
Creating and calibrating a simulation model can be a labor-intensive effort; therefore, it is important to agree 
at the outset on the level of detail to be simulated (i.e., what point on the micro-model to macro-model scale). 
A suitable level of accuracy is required to ensure a valid model of reality to prevent incorrect decisions being 
made based on an incorrect model. 
Exhibit 2.11.2b: Transfer Reality into a Simulation Model 
Real Situation 
Source: Airport Research Center 
2.11.2.1 Use of Simulation in Traditional Airport Planning 
Traditionally, simulation has not been widely employed at the beginning of an airport design and planning 
project, but rather in later project phases. Capacity calculations, the main input for a design, were usually 
based on simplified rules of thumb. Thus, the number of required airport facilities was typically calculated by 
spreadsheet methods or handbooks with heuristic methods. 
In the preliminary design stage, a certain number of design alternatives might have been developed and 
analyzed. Then, in the detailed design phase only, one or two particular designs were planned in more detail. 
Simulation was mostly applied after a design alternative had been selected and planned in detail. The 
simulation study was carried out in order to test and validate the detailed design just before implementation. 
414 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 434===
Be py 
IATA Airport Simulation 
This traditional planning approach often showed that, at this late stage of the project, there was no time left to 
implement major changes (e.g., when operational bottlenecks were detected by simulation, it was usually too 
late to implement significant design changes). Thus, if simulation is only used in this late planning phase, the 
tool's full potential and value in supporting a target-oriented, well-balanced and optimized design cannot be 
exploited to its full extent. 
2.11.2.2 Use of Simulation in State-of-the-art Airport Planning 
Latest trends show simulation being used not only just before implementation, but in all life cycle phases of 
an airport in order to fully benefit from the many advantages of dynamic simulation modelling. 
Exhibit 2.11.2.2: Life Cycle Phases of an Airport Facility 
Source: Airport Research Center 
Initially, during the conceptual design stage, simulation can be used to assess the facility requirements in 
order to support and validate the initial results derived from the rules of thumb approach. The main input to 
this simulation exercise can a set of forecast schedules" for which an airport facility is to be designed. The 
basic operational concepts and process flows can be modelled on an abstract level taking into consideration 
the desired LoS and distributions“ of processing times as inputs. 
Later on in the planning process, when the design layout is being detailed and refined and when alternative 
designs are being developed, simulation is a very helpful tool to compare and assess the design alternatives, 
eventually identifying the most suitable design. As an ongoing process, simulation can accompany the design 
process by regularly testing the planned layout and simultaneously refining the operational concept for the 
facility. 
As the implementation and construction phase of an airport facility usually takes time, the requirements for the 
facilities may change (i.e., higher traffic growth than expected or a change in aviation regulations). During this 
phase, simulation is used to check the impact of changes which might support modifications to the planned 
design. A robust design, based on having tested several input scenarios, may often lessen the changes 
necessary during this stage of the process. 
Simulation is not only useful when developing new facilities, but also for LoS and quality assessment and 
“optimization” of operational processes at existing airport facilities. For instance, simulation is widely used to 
test modified runway usage concepts, new stand and counter allocation strategies and the introduction of self- 
*3 A forecast schedule is based on assumptions of the future and these assumptions can vary due to uncertainty about the future, 
individuals' perspectives and a host of other factors. Therefore, a number of schedules can drive the facility design. 
‘4 Processing times as well as other variables in the real world are random variables. The most realistic simulation models will use 
distributions rather than some standard time. In the absence of real data, some assumed distributions may be used, but should be 
based on educated guesses. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 415 

===PAGE 435===
& i Be 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
service facilities (i.e., check-in kiosks or e-gates for immigration). Moreover, simulation can support day-to-day 
operations by predicting the next few hours, although care is necessary in interpreting these short-term 
predictions’. This enables informed decision making when flight information and or other changes become 
available via the operational database on short notice. Information about a delayed departure at an originating 
airport can be used to predict the situation at the destination airport, and then to define the best measures to 
mitigate likely bottlenecks before they actually occur. 
To summarize, an airport has to be understood, planned and designed in line with what it is—a very complex 
system of processes where requirements and operational conditions are evolving continuously over time. It is 
a challenging task to plan and build a static infrastructure in steel and concrete, coupled with approaches to 
its management strategies, that is flexible enough to meet not only today's requirements, but also those of an 
unknown future. As many real-life examples show, infrastructure with significant flaws can still be operated 
with varying levels of creative management. The question is: how effectively and at what cost? With the trend 
towards more airport privatization, there is an increasing need for reliable planning and cost-efficient operation 
of airport infrastructure and processes. 
In recent years, airport simulation modelling has proved to be a valuable tool to validate designs and 
operational concepts with the objective of minimizing investments and optimizing operational efficiency. This 
chapter of the ADRM, Airport Simulation, is intended to outline the benefits of airport simulation, to give insight 
into the general process of simulation projects as well as to describe application areas and provide examples 
of simulation modelling that support airport planning and airport operations. 
2.11.3 Definitions and Basic Considerations 
2.11.3.1 Definition of Simulation 
Simulation is a methodology used to analyze dynamic systems by representing real-world systems with a 
computer model and analyzing the model's output. 
The model itself is an abstract representation of the original system and provides an environment for “what-if” 
experiments. The system may be an entire airport or part of an airport. By changing the set-up and input 
parameters (operational decisions or demand variables) of the model, the user may gain insights into causes 
and effects, thereby gaining an understanding of the dependencies between the simulated entities. The goal 
of the simulation model is to predict the behavior of the original system under varied inputs and future 
conditions. These predictions can then be related to reality and used to support the decision making process. 
A simulation model is a simplification and an approximation of the real world. Required input data may be 
incomplete and estimated through “best-guess-assumptions”. Thus, a simulation model can never be identical 
to the real system, but it can provide a tendency, an order of magnitude, and a best estimate of the system's 
behavior. 
*8 Since this simulation is based on probabilities, no future can be guaranteed. It can only predict a distribution of possibilities. For 
example, it could be said that 95% of the time, we will see a particular LoS, but 5% of the time a much different LoS may be observed. 
416 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 436===
SoS &, IATA rll Airport Simulation 
Before drawing conclusions based on the simulation's results, the model has to be evaluated and cross￾checked carefully to make sure that the model's behavior really reflects reality. In summary, it has to be 
verified and validated. 
Simulation on its own does not produce solutions. Rather, it is a tool to identify problems to be solved, and 
then to re-test solutions, if necessary. 
2.11.3.2 Simulation Techniques 
Many different kinds of simulation modelling approaches and techniques exist. The most common include the 
following: 
e Analytical Models. Representation of the system (closed-form solution) with equations and mathematical 
formulations that describe relationships between the different system variables. Many financial simulations 
and some airport simulation models are analytic models 
¢ Continuous Simulation. System states are changed and tracked by a set of differential equations over 
time. Examples of these include airflow over a wing's surface or the flow of heat in metals 
¢ Discrete-Event Simulation. A discrete event simulation is applicable where the change of state of the 
system occurs at discrete points in time and space, (e.g., when a passenger enters the terminal, a bag 
enters an x-ray machine, or the time a passenger occupies at a check-in counter). The choices made and 
the processing time selected are based on probability distributions, from which a selection is made based 
on random numbers. Monte Carlo techniques generate random numbers and from the sequence of 
random numbers, successive selections are made, and the simulation system recalculates the system 
status whenever an event occurs. The sequence of the system states describes the process flow and 
interaction of flow objects in the system. These models imitate the behavior of entities in complex discrete 
event systems by using discrete event simulation approaches to track system resources and activities. 
This kind of simulation modelling technique is widely used to simulate airport operations 
¢ Multi-agent-based Simulation. The system consists of several autonomous interacting agents and their 
environment. The agents represent actors, acting and reacting to given situations according to their 
individual characteristics. Every agent has individual properties that determine the agent's behavior (i.e., 
in similar situations, an agent's behavior can differ as agents have differing beliefs, desires, and 
intentions). Multi-agent-technology can be applied to all simulation flow objects (e.g., passengers, 
baggage, aircraft, landside access vehicles or ground service equipment and vehicles). An agent's 
behavior is dependent on its current environment and adapts dynamically under changing conditions. 
2.11.3.3 Simulation Animation 
Some simulation models have a visual component, which is an add-on to the simulation. In these, 
visualization can be turned off or on. In other models, the visual component is integral to the task of inputting 
data and, as such, the layout and animation is a natural byproduct of the simulation. The visual representation 
may be simple or complex. Many functional models eschew sophisticated visualization (working at the 
technical level), while other simulation models incorporate a sophisticated 3D environment, showing exact 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 A417 

===PAGE 437===
= 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
geometry and visualization. These animations can be quite close to the real appearance of the original entities 
(e.g., colors, textures, shapes, moving actors). 
Animations in 2D and 3D with time as the fourth dimension are quite effective at showing congestion, 
visualizing potential areas of concern, and providing an understanding of the model to stakeholders. 
3D models will not necessarily bring better simulation results, but will assist modelers in constructing the 
model and non-modelers in understanding the model and make the simulation a better communication tool. 
Results can be visualized in a realistic representation, thus making analysis, evaluation and interpretation 
more effective. 
The visualization facilitates communication between stakeholders as it helps with an understanding of cause 
and effect better than a pure numerical model or simple graphics. 
Although a 2D or 3D model with animation has a lot of advantages, it is not necessarily required. A 
mathematical process model may be a valid representation of a simple system that can deliver suitable 
analytical results without the need for layout and visualization aspects. For instance, more abstract process 
flow models are typically used for requirement analysis of airport facilities. 
Therefore, for the analysis and evaluation of a planned design of an existing airport, the layout should be 
incorporated (i.e., the exact geometry accounted for) to assess the spatial conditions regarding space 
standards, analysis of local occupation levels and the impact of possible cross-flows. For such analyses, one 
of the fast time simulation models with animation is recommended. 
2.11.3.4 Benefits of Simulation 
Simulation has a broad field of usage and generally comes into play if: 
Itis very difficult, to determine the impact of decisions and changes in the real world for many different 
variables without disruption to the system and the clients (e.g., passengers, baggage, aircraft, vehicles). 
This is especially important where major alternatives are considered 
¢ There are too many influencing factors and parameters with varying values, thus analytical formulas 
cannot be applied effectively 
e The impact of events over time and the interaction of different interdependent processes is important to 
consider 
e The visualization of the situation to be analyzed is requested 
When a system reaches a certain level of complexity, analytical calculations may not be efficient, sufficient or 
even possible anymore. Simulation allows analysis of complex systems with many input parameters”, 
processes and interdependencies while keeping the users' workload at a manageable level. 
18 Note that the input parameters for airports and airspace may be continuous or discontinuous, monotonic or non-monotonic (multiple 
peaks), deterministic or stochastic, limited range or infinite range. Therefore, mathematical formulation is extremely difficult and 
optimization in the classical sense is impossible.

2.11.3.4.1 Managing Complexity: Simulation vs Analytical Calculation Methods 
Analytical calculations for airports are rather limited due to the nature of the variables and because the 
abstraction level is relatively high and the level of precision is variable. In contrast, a simulation can deal with 
a large number of input parameters in order to establish and verify the model, and then validate and calibrate 
it to match reality as closely as possible. 
Because analytical formulas can only provide a high-level estimate in terms of defining facility requirements, it 
is common practice to calculate with a safety margin. Where only a low level of detail about the facility 
requirements is needed and, if the complexity of input data is limited, the handbook method and analytical 
formulas can be considered an acceptable approach as a starting point. 
In comparison, fast time simulation allows a narrower safety margin as well as more accurate and realistic 
balancing of facilities to the expected demand. Thus, to examine a process in more detail and to achieve 
more precise results over many observations, fast time simulation is the approach of choice. 
Generally, a specific airport facility is a subsystem of a more complex process with interrelationships and 
dependencies with other facilities and processes. Static analytical formulas cannot reflect the dynamics and 
interrelationships of such a complex system. Simulation can create a model that includes dynamic 
interrelationship and feedback effects; these allow visualization and analysis of the interdependencies within 
the process chain. 
2.11.3.4.2 Reducing Workload 
Even if analytical formulas for the model are available, they all have to be executed manually. Furthermore, if 
the formulas required to solve the problem are not available, they have to be formulated by the user. In 
contrast, some simulation tools can be easier to handle compared to an analytical calculation model because 
the construction of the model is more intuitive and visual. 
Airport simulation models often contain several simple predefined elements, ideally close to the real-world 
entities (i.e., runways, taxiways, aircraft stands, check-in counters, security controls), thus making the 
readability of results and configuration easier. It is easier, faster and cheaper to plug simple elements together 
than to handle the abstraction without guidance. 
Another beneficial aspect of these fast time simulation tools is that they allow definition of simple rules for 
individual entities or a collection of entities or mobile elements. These rules replicate very complex situations 
that would be very difficult to reproduce or calculate in analytic models. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 419 

===PAGE 439===
rors 
Be |! IATA aol Airport Development Reference Manual 
2.11.3.4.3 More Intuitive—“What You See Is What You Get” 
A simulation reflects processes in ways that approximate reality. This is easier and more intuitive to 
understand. Many different input parameters are considered and reflected in the simulation, in the same way 
that real elements have many influencing factors. The user can build a complex system using basic elements, 
feeding various input parameters into the model and observing what is happening. It is like undertaking 
experiments using a computer model. Often, the user might have a “gut feeling” of what the results may be, 
but simulation helps to quantify and confirm these assumptions. In addition, there may be surprises 
uncovered by the simulation. 
Simulation helps to track results easily and to understand the relationship between cause and effect in the 
model, and thus in reality. By varying input parameters, “what-if” scenarios can be investigated easily. 
When a simulation offers a good visualization and animation function, the verification and debugging process 
of the model is more intuitive. Invalid or unexpected behavior of the simulation entities can be tracked easily, 
thus speeding up the modelling process. 
2.11.3.4.4 Convincing Stakeholders 
Visualization in 2D, 3D or 4D is an excellent method to make processes and interdependencies between them 
understandable. When a queue can be seen forming in a model over time, it is easier to understand how the 
queue grows, the space required, and how it causes congestion. Of course, the aspect of visualization is not 
as realistic when applying analytical formulas which just give numerical or graphical output at instants of time 
rather than over time. 
A visual representation of the analyzed situation is the easiest way to generate a common understanding 
among parties with different backgrounds and modeling knowledge. The simulation results can be used as a 
“round table” where different stakeholders may sit together and discuss, based on a common understanding 
of the “virtual” reality.

2.11.4 Areas of Application 
2.11.4.1 Overview 
Analyzing a complex system such as an airport, consisting of many subsystems, the use of simulation 
software allows the replication of most of the interactions and dynamics that take place between the different 
processes and entities (i.e., aircraft, vehicles, passengers, baggage, visitors and other elements). 
Exhibit 2.11.4.1a gives an overview of airport subsystems, entities and their interfaces, which might be 
modelled and analyzed by means of a simulation. It also illustrates the actors and stakeholders of each of the 
major areas of the airport and airspace system. 
An airport simulation model may consider several interconnected subsystems or focus on a particular 
sub-system or even only parts of this subsystem. When a subsystem is modelled, it is important to consider 
the boundary conditions for interdependencies and interfaces with other connected subsystems.

Before a simulation model is set-up, it has to be decided which airport components and entities should be 
considered. This includes decisions about the simulation model's boundaries and its interfaces with other 
sub-systems. The recommended scope of the model depends on the question to be answered and the 
desired level of detail. The choice will have an impact on the quality of the simulation results, the time 
required to conduct the study and the input data. As a result, the efficiency and cost of the simulation study 
will also be affected.

Preceding or subsequent processors are analyzed in order to assess their respective impact on the 
sub-system being analyzed. These interdependencies may affect the demand at the facility of interest or its 
achievable service quality (e.g., because of interfering queues of various processors). For example, the 
dimensioning of a security checkpoint depends on passenger demand at the check-in process. 
422 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 442===
vr IATA Wi Airport Simulation 
Often, it is not required to model all processors. If the system boundary or interface to preceding processes 
can be described with sufficient level of detail, an explicit simulation of such secondary processes is not 
necessary. For terminal processes, for example, it is often sufficient to describe the passenger “show up” at 
the airport through a passenger reporting profile and modal split. It is not usually necessary to model the 
whole landside access of passengers on trains, cars, taxis and busses, etc. 
Changes to the analyzed process may also affect subsequent processes. If a bottleneck at one subsystem is 
resolved, this might lead to another bottleneck at one of the subsequent subsystems as demand is shifted 
and the processing capacity of the subsequent processes may become constrained under a higher demand. 
Also, the process of interest itself can be simulated at various levels of detail. For example, a security control 
can be modelled as a single process (“a black box”) with only one process time definition. Alternatively, it can 
be modelled as a sequence of various sub-processes (i.e., passenger and bag processes with tray 
preparation, x-ray scanning, collection of items, body search, secondary bag search, etc.) and their entities 
(i.e., passengers, staff, bags and trays). This level of analysis is called “micro-modelling”. Exhibit 2.11.4.1b 
illustrates two detailed example of micro modelled security. 
Exhibit 2.11.4.1b: Detailed Security Micro Models

Each question requires an individual definition of model scope and boundaries. As described in the 
Introduction, a model should be considered an abstraction from reality. It should be as comprehensive and 
detailed as necessary, but at the same time, as abstract and simple as possible to answer the question with 
the required quality and efficiency.

The objective of a terminal simulation is to support:

2.11.4.3 Baggage Handling Simulation

a baggage reclaim belt or to a transfer connection. 
Elements of the simulation model consist of, for example, conveyors, bag scanners, sorters, Explosive 
Detection Systems (EDS), make-up conveyor and early baggage storage. 
The simulation supports the planning and design of new or enhanced BHS in terms of decision-making for 
capacity and layout by quantifying the benefits of changes and additions to the system through new 
technology as well as existing technologies.

2.11.4.4 Landside Access Simulation 
Landside access simulation analyzes the airport's access infrastructure and processes regarding roads to the 
airport, the curbside traffic flows with drop-off and pick-up zones for departing and arriving passengers, 
checkpoints, toll booths as well as the parking utilization and requirements. 
Furthermore, train access and its airport station can also be part of the landside access simulation, either by 
simply adding another drop-off point or line in the life of a departing passenger and a pick-up point or line in 
the life of an arriving passenger, or by modeling it as part of the terminal system. 
All kinds of vehicle flows (i.e., cars, trucks, busses, taxis and trains) and person flows (i.e., passengers, staff 
and visitors) as well as the interaction of all traffic participants can be included. 
The main objective is to analyze the landside access system, which may include parking facilities, traffic 
controls, access roads to the terminal, maintenance hangars, general aviation, airport factories and employee 
parking, etc., for smooth, efficient operations with minimal delays and congestion.

2.11.4.5 Airside Simulation 
Airside simulation analyzes the aircraft processes and flows at and around an airport considering relevant 
components such as surface and airspace infrastructure, air traffic control as well as airport management 
rules, procedures, restrictions and operational modes. 
In terms of aircraft traffic, the relevant infrastructure will normally include runways, taxiways, taxilanes and 
aircraft parking stands (apron system). Furthermore, the nearby airspace, including final approach, holding 
and departure routes can also be part of the system. Specific facilities like deicing and isolation pads could be 
considered as well, if relevant. 
A complete airside model would include GSE traffic to model their interaction with aircraft and to analyze the 
ground service operations (see 2.11.4.6 Ground Service Equipment Handling Simulation), including 
requirements and routings for GSE to minimize the possibility of incursions. 
The main objectives of an aircraft simulation are to plan, assess and optimize an airside system's capacity, to 
plan infrastructure resources as well as to evaluate and optimize operations. 
Below are some examples of typical questions that can be answered with an aircraft simulation: 
e Does the airside infrastructure provide enough capacity? 
« Where are the bottlenecks in the system? 
e What will be the demand for contact and remote aircraft stands in the coming years? 
e What capacity does the runway system have under specific operational conditions? 
e Which operational concept leads to the best punctuality? 
« What does the optimal stand allocation concept look like? 
¢ How should the infrastructure be developed in order to meet the demand in forecast years? 
e What is the most efficient deicing strategy? 
e What should an optimal traffic guidance concept look like? 
* What is the most efficient operational concept? 
e How will construction measures influence operations?

e Aircraft taxi times and travel distances 
e Delays and waiting times for different phases of the aircraft turnaround 
e Capacity as a function of throughput and acceptable level of delay 
e Stand utilization and stand demand 
e Number of conflicts (e.g. opposing traffic) or events (runway crossing)

2.11.4.6 Ground Service Equipment Handling Simulation 
Airside vehicle traffic is the subject of a ground handling simulation. All kinds of airside vehicles, including 
Airside Operations Vehicles (AOV) and GSE, such as fuel trucks, baggage carts, catering trucks and 
passenger busses, along with the aircraft, are objects that move in the airside infrastructure and must not 
collide or lose safe separations from one other and perform their required tasks. 
The relevant airport infrastructure in a ground handling simulation usually consists of the aircraft stands, 
vehicle depots, road network, apron areas, and taxiways, which may be used by GSE (with ATC permission). 
The main objectives of a ground handling simulation include: 
e Anassessment of the required infrastructure 
e Identification of the required resources and their most efficient allocation 
e Detection of possible bottlenecks in the road network 
e Estimating the risk of incursions from vehicles and aircraft from a given operations plan and layout
