2.11.5 Project Methodology 
2.11.5.1 Overview 
The approach to a typical simulation study can be described with the steps outlined in Exhibit 2.11.5.2. The 
process is of an iterative nature (i.e., at some validation stages, it may be necessary to go back one or more 
steps and rework or improve that step). The beginning of each simulation project is the definition of the scope 
and objective of the project. 
While the simulation model represents a real-world system, the project objective will dictate the degree of 
abstraction and level of detail required. The model should only be as detailed as necessary and system 
boundaries have to be selected in an appropriate way. The collection of input data is a critical phase as the 
quality and suitability of input data highly influences the quality and usability of the simulation results. 
Usually, a baseline model is developed for the verification of the model's logic and for the validation of applied 
input data as well as the resulting output. This ensures that the model is a suitable representation of the real 
system and may be better suited for extrapolation into the future. 
After a suitable baseline mode! is available, the simulation model is used as a test bed for “what-if” 
experiments and sensitivity scenarios for future or changed conditions. 
The simulation output needs to be verified carefully before being interpreted and conclusions drawn 
therefrom. A report containing relevant textual, graphic and animation results summarizes the findings and 
recommendations with regard to the defined simulation objective. 
The following subsections provide more information and explanations regarding best practices for each step. 
2.11.5.2 Definition of Project Scope and Objective 
A simulation project starts with defining the questions the simulation study shall answer. In line with this 
decision, the system boundaries and the desired level of simulation detail are determined. 
Depending on the life cycle status of the airport facility to simulate (i.e., concept design, detailed design, 
facility under implementation, redesign of existing facility, optimizing operations of existing facility) and the 
time horizon of purpose (i.e., strategic, tactical, operational), either a high-level, time efficient approach or a 
more comprehensive, detailed approach might be chosen. 
434 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 454===
iy Twa 
Be IATA pull Airport Simulation 
The following questions will drive the model's intentions, the airport subsystems to model and the selected 
level of detail: 
* What are the questions to be answered with the simulation model? 
e What KPIs should be derived from the simulation study? 
e¢ Which part of the airport or airport subsystem needs to be modelled? 
e What are the system boundaries to consider? 
e Which time horizon does the project cover? 
Based on the answers given to these questions, the model scope can be formulated accordingly. 
2.11.5.3 Abstraction and Input Data Collection 
Once the model scope and objective has been determined, the level of system abstraction needs to be 
considered to define which input data, and at what level of detail, has to be collected. 
The goal of input data collection should not be to collect as much input data as possible. It is important to 
select the “right” set of data for the question of interest for the simulation. Based on the objective, a suitable 
abstraction level for the model and the input has to be chosen. 
In order to create a realistic and valid baseline simulation model, the input data for the model needs to be 
carefully compiled. Besides the geometric and functional layout of the airport facilities, behavioral 
characteristics of mobile elements or the entities (i.e., passengers, checked baggage, trolleys, aircraft and 
vehicles) are required. The following examples of questions will need to be answered: 
e What are the parameters that determine the entities’ behavior? 
¢ What input data needs to be collected? 
¢ Who are the relevant stakeholders whose input and collaboration is needed? 
e Which data is important and which data could be neglected or simplified? 
¢ When data is not available/known, which best-guess assumptions can be used (subject to scenarios)? 
Typical data sources are: 
e The airport and airline databases 
e Measurements and surveys at the airport 
e The manufacturers of certain equipment 
¢ Interviews with various stakeholders 
¢ Automated counting of airport systems 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 435 

===PAGE 455===
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
One should be critical and challenge all data. It might be useful to obtain and analyze raw data in comparison 
to aggregated data (e.g., on a monthly or annual basis). Caution is required as aggregated data might flatten 
out characteristics important for peak demand considerations. On-site cross-check measures are 
recommended to evaluate whether the provided data is realistic. 
When collecting input data for the simulation (e.g., processing times, distributions of checked baggage, 
numbers of visitors, types of passengers, distributions of choices such as number of passengers to full-serve 
check-in versus self-serve or web check-in, user shares, show-up profiles), it is important to ensure statistical 
relevance (sufficient sample size). Input data should be a statistical distribution or probability of occurrence 
rather than merely an average value”. 
If data is not known or available, the model has to be set up with “best-guess assumptions”. These can take 
into account the passenger behavior at similar airports, general knowledge, the modeler's own experience 
and expert evaluation, especially from airport operations staff. 
Assumptions that cannot be verified based on real data have to be handled with caution—one must think about 
the consequences on the model's results. Therefore, it is recommended to consider best case/worst case 
assumptions and simulate a variety of scenarios. These sensitivity tests illustrate the boundaries and 
robustness of the simulated situation. 
Regarding the amount and accuracy of input data, the following rule should be applied: the closer a simulation 
is intended to answer operational questions, the more accurate the input data should be. The better the input 
data is, the more certainty can be placed on the model results. When less data is available (i.e., further away 
from the operational question) the range of uncertainty is higher and more scenarios are likely to be required. 
For a greenfield airport it is recommended to refer to benchmark data of a reference airport in the same 
region of similar size and traffic structure. If just a terminal of an existing airport shall be replaced by a new 
one, data of the old one can be used as reference since passenger characteristics are stable and a large 
amopiunt of input data might be used based on the existing terminal. 
When input data is given by expert knowledge/best-guess assumption and not verified by real measurements, 
the data may not be accurate enough for the required level of detail. The older the input data is and the more 
uncertainty there is regarding their source and collection methodology, the more the data should be cross￾checked by actual on-site measurements. If large deviations are discovered between the input data and 
cross-checked measurements, a more comprehensive data survey is recommended. 
As stated, the suitable set of input data for a particular simulation is specific to its objectives; however, it 
generally consists of the following: 
e Demand for the airport, as defined by the flight schedule, itinerant and other traffic for the airside, and 
non-flight-related traffic for the landside 
e Infrastructure layout 
© Distribution of process times and throughput rates 
17 Averages should never be an input to a simulation as they will not allow the accurate determination or representation of the real-world 
phenomena and may be misleading. 
436 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 456===
IATA Airport Simulation 
e Resource allocation rules 
«Operational settings 
e Passenger, aircraft and vehicle characteristics 
e Process flow definition (flow charts or textual descriptions) 
It is recommended to base a simulation on a flight schedule as the main traffic demand input. Often, a 
24-hour schedule reflecting a “Typical Busy Day” or “Design Day” is used. This is the most realistic approach 
to model airport processes with the interaction and interdependencies of flight-driven events taking place at 
the airport and to capture all the peaks in the different airport facilities. Such a schedule is also referred to 
as the DDFS. (see 2.2.10.3 Design Day Flight Schedules for more information). 
If a past situation is to be modelled, it is recommended that the Airport Operations Data Base (AODB) or 
tower log for the last traffic year be analyzed to identify typical busy days that are suitable to be used for the 
simulation and its objective. !f a past situation is to be re-investigated, allocation (i.e., check-in, gate, stands, 
reclaim belts) and staffing information for the day to be simulated must be obtained for that specific flight 
schedule as well. (see 2.2.10 Peak Period Forecast for the selection of a past reference flight schedule and a 
representative busy hour rate). 
If a future situation is to be modelled and no forecast flight schedule is available, one or more flight schedule 
scenarios can be created as a baseline for the analysis. For this, historic flight schedules can be analyzed 
regarding their peak structures and characteristics of arriving, departing and transfer peak hours, which might 
occur during different periods. An assumption model for the airlines serving the airport, their fleet mixes, load 
factors and possible additional movements during peak times can be set-up. Based on these assumptions, an 
example scenario flight schedule can be prepared, discussed and agreed upon by the airport stakeholders. 
Sometimes, only peak hour numbers are given as traffic demand input for a simulation. Therefore, it is 
tecommended to build a realistic demand structure from arriving and departing movements that can be used 
as artificial traffic scenarios in the simulation. For certain very specific questions, a simulation can be 
conducted based on synthetic flows (e.g., continuous inflow to a security check-point). 
Process times describe the time spent in different activities required to be performed by a mobile element or 
flow object and, consequently, how long they are transacting there expressed in seconds or minutes per 
passenger. Throughput rates are measured in number of passengers per time interval (e.g., number of 
passengers per hour per security lane) can depend on the processor times, which in turn depend on the user 
characteristics (e.g., checking a resident passport is usually faster than checking a non-resident passport). 
When measuring process times, it is helpful to understand how the relevant process is modelled in the 
simulation so that the data collected includes the independent variables that lead to the processing time 
measurement. For example: 
e Are idle times of counters while waiting for a passenger walking from the common queue to the counter, 
included in the specified process time or modelled explicitly? 
*8 Many airports in the world operate across midnight as the busiest period of the day. Therefore, in those cases, it may be useful to 
consider a three day schedule, where the day of interest is the second day, thereby ensuring that the initial and ending conditions for 
the day of interest are correct. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 437 

===PAGE 457===
Se I IAT: wa Airport Development Reference Manual 
e Are several persons handled simultaneously at one processor, such as a security control lane, that 
consists of several sub-processes in reality? Here several passengers and their hand luggage are 
processes simultaneously at the same lane, but modelled one by one in the simulation with one 
transaction time. In this case, one usually measures and applies the throughput rate rather than individual 
process times per passenger. 
Resource allocation rules specify which service processor can be used by which passengers/flights/airlines 
(e.g., a check-in allocation or assignment of ground handlers to airlines). 
Further operational settings consider the airport characteristics (e.g., in terms of staffing levels in a terminal 
simulation or separation distances in an aircraft or vehicle simulation). 
Passenger, aircraft and vehicle characteristics determine the variety of users (mobile elements or flow 
objects) in the simulation. Examples of these characteristics are show-up profiles, check-in or passport types, 
number of bags, group size, aircraft size, and vehicle speed. 
Complete documentation of the input data and its sources is recommended to allow a well-structured 
approach, facilitate tracing of data and better understand the effect of each input data. The documentation of 
input data and assumptions must be reviewed with the relevant stakeholders to aim for a common 
understanding and agreement on the input data. This documentation can also be used for sign-off purposes. 
During the project, input data might be updated or extended. It is recommended to track these changes and 
keep the input data documentation up to date. 
See 2.3.6.1.9 Air Passenger Surveys—Scope and Best Practice for a comprehensive description which data 
are typically needed and how to collect them. 
2.11.5.4 Baseline Model Setup 
Decisions on very capital-intensive projects are based on simulation model results, thus the accuracy of the 
model is very important to ensure the results can be trusted. In order to assess the model's validity or to 
overcome remaining uncertainties, a baseline simulation of a well-known situation with many observations 
and input data available is recommended. The simulation output of this baseline model is compared to reality 
and the model is calibrated until it matches expectations. 
The following steps are usually required to set up a baseline simulation model: 
e Master plan and document the model: 
o What to model. 
o Level of detail. 
o Data required and used. 
o KP! reports to be output. 
o How to track changes in the input data. 
438 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 458===
we Al ; eae 
IATA + Airport Simulation 
o Results. 
o Workflow associated with the project. 
o Derivatives to be considered even though at the baseline model stage only the single, current model 
may be developed. Having thought out possible derivative points will facilitate the development of 
models based on changes to the baseline model. 
e Set up of the layout of the airport facility from an abstract as a process flow, or with its exact spatial 
geometry based on a CAD file, or from a table of geographic coordinates and spatial routes for the 
airspace structure 
e Implementation of operational rules (e.g., process times, allocation, operational concept) 
° Specification of characteristics of mobile elements or flow objects (e.g., passenger show-up profiles, bag 
shares, aircraft types, taxi speed) 
¢ Generation of mobile elements or flow objects from the flight schedule (e.g., passengers, bags, aircraft, 
GSE, landside vehicles) 
e¢ Modelling the logic of flows and processes as well as their interdependencies 
Once the model is set up, it has to be debugged to verify the model's logic has been implemented correctly. 
Afterwards, baseline simulation runs can be executed based on a well-known situation which is validated and 
calibrated in the next step. 
2.11.5.5 Baseline Model Validation and Calibration 
If a baseline model of an existing situation has been set up, the results of this baseline model can be 
compared to what has been observed during the simulated day. Based on the comparison, deviations can be 
detected and the reasons for the deviations researched. The applied simplifications/abstractions are reviewed 
and decisions made on whether the input data has to be corrected or refined. The identified model 
parameters should be adapted accordingly and the simulation run again. This process is iterative in nature 
and might take several iteration loops, depending on how good the initial input data was. 
Usually, a statistical data comparison is conducted to compare key simulation model results to data from 
actual operations. For the calibration, the baseline model should be run for multiple replications, just as all 
simulation analyses. Ideally, the model will be calibrated against data sources that are independent from the 
input data. 
Good data sources for calibration are, for instance, surveys, video/photo capturing and automatically recorded 
passenger data (i.e., taken at automatic boarding pass control). Next to that, expert calibration is used as well, 
which is rather a qualitative calibration method with the local operational airport experts. 
Exhibit 2.11.5.5a shows a comparison of simulated versus actual conditions of a base line model of part of the 
check-in hall at Birmingham Airport in the UK.

It is, possible to skip the calibration of input data and not set up a baseline model. In this case, it must be 
clearly stated that the model and the output will have a lower degree of accuracy and certainty. This approach 
may be applied when simulating greenfield sites where calibration is not possible. If the real system is not 
pre-existing, alternative means of validation with independent analytical cross-checks become more important 
(e.g., flight schedule analysis and estimation of order of magnitude). 
Once the baseline model is established, a complete analysis can be carried out, including an analysis of 
resource utilization and maximum queue times/lengths, based on processor variables and total time in 
system. With the insight gained from the baseline simulation, one might already gain a better understanding of 
the weaknesses of the operations. 
2.11.5.6 “What-If” Experiments: Scenario Simulation 
Once the model is regarded as being a suitable representation of the real system, the simulation of “what-if” 
experiments can start. This might comprise: 
e Layout changes (redesign or expansion options) 
e Changes in traffic demand (using other flight schedules) 
e Improvement of capacity by implementing more facilities or improved operational procedures/equipment 
e Allocation of flights or airlines to other terminal or gate areas 
e Changes to passenger behavioral characteristics (e.g., higher self-service share) 
e Changes in operational conditions (e.g., runway and/or taxiway usage) 
¢ Stress tests regarding extraordinary situation (e.g., runway closure, evacuation, pandemic) 
440 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 460===
aie 
Se i~—COL, 
IATA Airport Simulation 
Sensitivity analysis of certain important variables allows the analysis of a possible variety of results. This 
helps to obtain insight into the effect of parameter changes on system performance and capacity. It also 
evaluates the robustness of the model's result. For example, the throughput rate at security control might vary 
in future due to changing regulations. Therefore, it is wise to analyze a variety of realistic and “worst case” 
scenarios. 
At large airports with decentralized facilities, the allocation can have considerable effect on the demand at 
each checkpoint and corresponding service levels. Therefore, a simulation might consider a variety of 
allocation scenarios and not trust a “one-shot” situation. 
Simulations of airports are generally stochastic. Even when no input data is changed, they should be run a 
number of times to look at the range of outputs. The number of replications should be higher for new models, 
as the possible variety of results still needs to be identified. If the range of results is already known for existing 
models, it is easier to assess the output and the number of replications can be reduced. 
During a simulation project, there may be a very large number of “what-if” experiments and it is important to 
keep track of model changes and their effects. A well-structured approach to document intermediate models 
and their results must be followed. As with any project, management of the work flow, input data and 
variations should be part of the project plan of the modeling exercise.

demand in a scenario where one terminal has to handle the immigration demand of another terminal due to 
re-construction. The analysis analyses number of counters needed to ensure that “most” passengers wait less 
than 20/30/40/ or 60 minutes.

2.11.5.7 Result Verification and Interpretation 
It is essential that the simulation results be critically reviewed before they can be trusted due to the high 
number and variability of input data and settings. Diligent cross-checks are indispensable for result validation 
to ensure they are realistic. There are many variables that may be tested in a comparison of real versus 
simulated. For example, total daily passengers, total cars parked in a day, number of movements on the 
runways in a day, throughput per hour from a single lane of security are variables that can be easily 
measured in the real world. Therefore, these types of variables may be used for cross-checking. It is 
recommended to base these cross-checks on analysis of such variables, which may also include simulated 
flight schedule, including the total number of passengers or only the number of passengers of a subgroup of 
specific flights. 
When the simulation results are considered valid, implying that the model is validated, interpretation may 
begin. The simulation study is not finished just by extracting numbers for waiting times, queue lengths and 
occupancy levels, etc. In particular for stakeholders who are just partly involved in the topic, the numeric 
results have to be transformed into qualitative statements and recommendations, which can be impressed 
upon the stakeholders. 
The LoS Concept, for which IATA has established some recommended standards for Temporal and Spatial 
LoS for terminal facilities is a suitable way to evaluate the resulting waiting times and congestion levels. This 
will help determine whether they are acceptable or need improvement. The results for maximum queue time 
and the density level in terms of square meters per passenger can be used to assess the KPIs for the 
attainable LoS.

Numeric output of the simulation can be extracted as graphs which take into account the time component. 
Besides the maximum queuing times, the simulation analysis should also include average queuing times, 95" 
percentiles of the queuing time and waiting time distributions (quantifying the passenger shares who waited 
more than 5, 10, 15 minutes, etc.). With such differentiated analyses, the order of magnitude and frequency of 
occurrence of maximum queuing time can better be understood and interpreted. 
When applying dynamic, stochastic simulation models, they consider time-dependent and variable parameters 
and capture the fluctuations of traffic and other process or passenger characteristics. As a result, outliers 
might appear in these models as well and their occurrence must be considered when defining the analysis 
framework.

2.11.5.8 Report and Recommendations 
The final report of a simulation study should summarize the project's objective, applied input data, simulation 
methodology and generated results with interpretation and recommendations. 
Besides numeric outputs and charts, visual outputs (i.e., screenshots, videos and stress grids/heat maps) 
generate a good common understanding of whether the observed situation is acceptable or not. The visual 
output is key to sharing results with stakeholders who might not have sufficient background knowledge to 
evaluate numeric KPIs. Visual results can sometimes be required to gain stakeholder buy-in. 
It has to be emphasized that the input data is the basis for the observed simulation result. Thus, the applied 
input data should be carefully described in the report. Judging of scenario results is directly connected with 
the input data used. Also, the probability that the observed scenario results occur in reality is linked to the 
likelihood that the input data is representative of reality. Thus, a transparent report with assumptions and 
corresponding results, carefully explained, is fundamental. 
In the course of the study, the modeler will gain a lot of insights into the simulated situation. In fact, doing a 
simulation study may make people think about a number of unexpected questions and may bring various 
stakeholders together for discussion. This additional information often exceeds the initial question of the 
simulation project and supports the recommendation of mitigation measures. 
2.11.6 Best Practice Project Life Cycle Examples 
2.11.6.1 Overview 
A simulation model can be used for different planning horizons to answer strategic, tactical and operational 
questions during all life cycle phases of airport facilities. The application of simulation is a valuable decision 
support tool for: 
e New design and redesign of infrastructure 
e During the implementation and construction phase 
e Before going operational to support the ORAT of airport facilities 
e When optimizing or improving operational concepts of existing facilities 
¢ Supporting the operational management

In accordance with the life cycle of an airport facility, different simulation project types exist. For each of these 
types, the purpose, level of detail and accuracy of the required input and output usually varies. 
Types-Five Levels of Life Cycle Simulation Models 
1. Conceptual design: Rough estimation of needed resources and facility requirements 
2. Optimization of detailed design: Comparison of alternative layouts, rough capacity analysis 
3. Implementation/construction: Detailed and ongoing capacity and process analysis 
4. Optimization of operational concept: High detail capacity and process analysis 
5. Preoperational and operational planning and management: Real-time prognostic simulation 
Level of Detail of a Model 
As outlined before, simulation allows modelling at different levels of detail. A facility might be modelled 
aggregated as one process (‘black box") or very detailed consisting of several sub-processes (“micro￾modelling”). 
The same applies to input data that can be aggregated", or as average values or as a detailed distribution for 
several individual user groups. 
A suitable level of detail and accuracy for a simulation model depends largely on its purpose and where in the 
life cycle of an airport facility the project it is intended to support is situated.

result of a single object being divested, thus aggregating the processing times into one value whose distribution is the processing time 
of all items divested by a passenger.

Level of Uncertainty of a Model 
The level of uncertainty of a simulation model can be a factor of the current life cycle stage of the airport 
facility. In a conceptual design phase, before the facility actually has been built, not much detail or real-world 
data is available about the facility itself, and some questions may remain about the detailed processes and 
users that will use and operate the facility. This kind of information will usually become available at later stage 
in the detailed design stage before the actual realization of the facility. Therefore, the planning data input base 
is less detailed in early planning phases, which leads to a higher level of uncertainty. The simulation model 
can be refined at later stages when the information becomes available. 
Furthermore, this stage of a modeling exercise can be used to stimulate thought about the management 
processes that may in turn affect the initial design or the “optimization” process of the facility (i.e., a form of 
backward compatibility). Therefore, the involvement of professionals with operational knowledge is key to 
ensure that and the operational processes are modelled with maximum likelihood of a operationally 
acceptable design.

When input is high level, results have to be regarded as less precise. Therefore, it is recommended to 
consider a variety of possible scenarios where important input data is varied to reflect a variety of possible 
results. 
The more a simulation deals with an actual situation, the more details are known and can be considered in 
setting up the simulation model accordingly. This leads to more accurate results. 
To compensate for the higher uncertainty in early planning phases, it is recommended that some spare 
capacity (contingency) be considered when reserving areas for functions. In the course of the life cycle, when 
better knowledge is available, the areas can be optimized for further efficiency. 
In the following sections, the project types by life cycle stage are described and practical use cases show how 
simulation can be employed to gain the maximum benefit. 
2.11.6.2 1st Life Cycle Stage: Conceptual Design 
Situation for Application 
For airport development and infrastructure projects where new facilities are planned in a greenfield 
environment or to be integrated into an existing airport environment, the initial task is the dimensioning of 
facilities in terms of facility requirement numbers. 
In this facility development stage, usually not much information about the facility itself is readily available. 
Therefore, the simulation results are still vague and on a conceptual level. Furthermore, if planning for the 
long-term future (10 or 20 years), the main input reflects a set of assumptions derived from forecasting how 
this future might look. 
448 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 468===
ray 
oe, 
IATA Airport Simulation 
For many airport projects, therefore, the traditional approach has been to start with an annual demand volume 
that an airport facility is expected to process. Then, for an actual dimensioning of an airport, the peak hour 
capacity has been the driving variable. For any capacity calculation tool, whether it is a spreadsheet or a 
simulation, demand assumptions for peak hour volumes were essential. Frequently the driving input for a 
facility demand study is the flight schedule complementing peak hour volumes forecasts. DDFS or a set of 
forecast schedules, for which a new facility can be designed, are more often used. There is generally an 
attempt to marry the new methodology with the traditional approach by ensuring that the forecast schedules 
generate the same peak hour flow as would have been used in the traditional design. Nevertheless, planners 
need to keep in mind, that the further the planning horizon lies in the future, the higher the uncertainty unfolds 
regarding traffic demand as well as the future operational procedures and processes. For master planning 
purposes this uncertainty has to be taken into consideration to accept a higher level of variability and a lower 
level of detail in facility requirement planning (see 2.2.10.3 Design Day Flight Schedules). 
What is the Role of Simulation during the Conceptual Design Phase? 
Usually, the initial simulation deals with the calculation of the facility requirements and/or the assessment of 
capacities. At this stage, the simulation model is rather a process model without considering any detailed 
spatial layout or airport geometry. As input, a draft of the planned conditions for airport operations have to be 
discussed and defined in cooperation with the airport operator. 
The result of the facility requirement simulation is used as the main input by airport planners for the 
development of conceptual layout alternatives for which the facility requirements may come from the first level 
simulation in terms of resources and geometry. Typically, the number of stands, check-in counters, 
immigration positions, security lanes, length of curbside, etc. can be developed quickly based on the forecast 
schedule, and these specifications form the basis of the detailed design. 
Case Study Example: Initial Planning and Terminal Facility Requirement Analysis 
As no terminal layout is available in the beginning, functional facility requirement simulations can be used to 
determine the number of required facilities according to an expected traffic load (design flight schedule). 
Typical input: 
e Peak hour demand, defined preferably via a DDFS 
e Desired Spatial and Temporal LoS per facility 
e Assumptions for operational parameters (processing times, user shares, reporting, etc.) 
Typical results: 
(a) The number of minimum required processing facilities to meet the desired Temporal LoS. 
(b) The approximate space required for meeting the target Spatial LoS based on the maximum occupancy of 
queues or areas occupied by any mobile elements or flow objects. 
(c) Approximate sequence of processes to achieve some target system throughput per unit of time. 
(d) Probable bottlenecks that may be mitigated at this early stage of the design process by assessing the 
queue lengths, waiting times and spatial densities. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 449 

===PAGE 469===
IATA ‘a Airport Development Reference Manual 
(e) Facility requirements at the airside and landside interfaces to ensure the terminal design operates as 
planned without limitations from the interfaces with the airside (e.g., passenger busses, baggage carts 
interaction with the terminal) and landside (e.g., inadequate throughput to provide the demand as forecast 
for the terminal). 
The facility requirement model might be run with several future flight schedules. As a result, the number of 
facilities by planning demand level (i.e., number of passengers or operations) can be a basis on which to 
develop possible building stages. 
Case Study Example: Initial Assessment of Airside Facility Requirements 
It is important to recognize that the terminal demand requires only the commercial flight schedule. Airside 
demand, on the other hand, can include all the flights of the commercial schedule, all cargo flights, all general 
aviation flights, all military flights, and all training flights that may use the airport jointly with the passenger 
flights for the terminal. Baseline demand must be the forecast demand for all of these flight types, which 
define the demand for capacity of the runway system, the taxiway system and the aprons (aircraft stands) as 
well as the required GSE to service the aircraft. The goal of the initial planning is to define the number and 
dimensions of these components for passenger aircraft facilities, cargo aircraft facilities, general aviation 
facilities and military facilities, if possible, and investigate the planning options possible with this forecast 
demand of design demand, if a forecast is not available, particularly for military activity or training activity. 
Runway Capacity 
While considering the physical, social, environmental and political conditions, different options for the location 
and orientation of new runway(s) have to be developed and evaluated. Existing runways and infrastructure 
and possibilities for integration define the scope of potential configurations (distance and direction of the 
runways). Some simulation tools allow explicit analysis of runway capacity as illustrated in Exhibits 2.11.6.2a 
and 2.11.6.2b. 
For these options the runway capacity will be determined for different operational concepts defined by 
operational directions for different runways and the distribution of the movements to the runway. The 
conditions for using each runway as well as the interference between the runways have to be considered. 
This includes the connection to the airspace by arrival and departure routes, the arrival and departure 
procedures considering ATC dependencies, rules, restrictions and capabilities as well as the connection to the 
existing or potential taxiway and apron system.

In this initial phase of runway layout the taxiway and apron system often is only modelled in a simplified way 
(e.g., by using aprons with unlimited capacity). This eliminates bottlenecks, which might cause unwanted and 
potentially misleading interferences and keeps the model as simple as possible. 
The traffic samples used in general should represent potential options for the expected structure of traffic 
defined by distribution of arrival and departures, origins and destination of the flights and aircraft types. 
Regarding ATC procedure existing limitations might be removed and potential future technologies might be 
used in order to consider operational improvements enhancing capacity. In many areas of the world, airspace 
considerations must be taken into account as they will impact runway utilization and any capacity in excess of 
the limit imposed by the airspace would be wasted at a particular point in time. Some tools allow the 
accounting for airspace when considering the runway system planning. 
Aprons and Aircraft stands 
For the aprons and aircraft stands, options for potential locations, considering terminal development as well 
as their position relative to the runways, in order to consider taxi distances and taxi times are developed. 
The demand for apron space and parking stands is a function of the number of aircraft operating at any point 
in time on the airport and the duration each requires on the parking stands. Therefore, for an accurate 
estimation of stand demand, several design schedules and forecasts may be used to determine the minimum 
number of stands required, allowing for buffers between allocations, and this minimum pilus some margin for 
irregular operations would be the demand. If the available number of stands is less than this number, there is 
insufficient capacity. 
In order to see demand for different aircraft sizes (size categories) aprons with unlimited capacity can be used 
as a first cut in the analysis. A challenge to be considered is the fact that the maximum stand demand is 
sometimes the number of overnight aircraft and the requirements for accommodating overnight aircraft might 
be different from the operational requirements. For example, placing aircraft to remote positions might be an 
option in the night, but not during the ongoing operations during the day.

Taxiways 
The taxiway system as the connecting element between aprons and runways has to provide sufficient 
capacity and taxi options in order to facilitate smooth and easy traffic flow while minimizing the number of 
potential incursions or conflicts (e.g., crossings of runways and taxiways, opposing traffic and blocking due to 
push-back). In this planning phase, the general capabilities of the system are analyzed. Very important KPIs 
are the taxi distances and taxi times, which are main parameters for operational cost (e.g., taxi time, fuel burn, 
emissions) and cost of the infrastructure (e.g., building and maintenance). 
Typical Input 
e Peak hour demand or design flight schedule (including itinerant, general aviation, training and military 
traffic) with distribution of arrivals and departures 
e Aircraft types/categories 
e Origins and destinations (determining the use of runways and parking stands) 
¢ Configurations of runways and runway exits 
¢ Positions of aprons 
e Basic taxiway layout and relation to the runway exits 
e = Air traffic control separations 
e Aircraft flight and runway performance (e.g., approach, touchdown, liftoff, runway turnoff speeds, distance 
for roll out and takeoff) 
Typical Results 
e Matrix of layouts (number and position of runways) and options to use 
e Respective throughput and capacities of the runway system, including takeoff delays 
e Stand utilization/demand 
e Taxi distances, taxi times and taxi delays 
e Potential for taxi conflicts 
e Missed approaches due to aircraft on the runway

2.11.6.3 2nd Life Cycle Stage: Optimization of Detailed Design 
Situation for Application 
The initial conceptual design stage usually results in several alternative layouts for the airport facility. A limited 
number of concept designs will usually be selected and others eliminated due to some selection criteria not 
being met by that alternative. The alternatives selected foro further consideration will then be refined and 
planned in more detail. Based on a decision process, the preferred design alternative will be selected to be 
transferred into a more refined architectural layout in the detailed design. 
Depending on the design concept, the operational concept and process flows will be further refined as well 
(.e., centralized or decentralized facility layouts require different operational concepts). 
What is the Role of Simulation during the Detailed Layout Design Optimization Phase? 
The role of simulation is the assessment, evaluation and comparison of the initial layout alternatives as well 
as the stepwise refinement and optimization of the most promising alternative. 
The ultimate objective is to achieve a balance between an oversized terminal and an under-designed 
terminal. That is a choice between higher costs and insufficient capacity. In this way, excess capacity or 
under-performance can be identified and the layout can be optimized. 
In an ongoing process, the simulation can follow-up the design process by regularly testing the planned layout 
and simultaneously refining the operational concept for the facility. In this way, an ongoing/concurrent 
optimization of the design and the basic operational concept is possible at the early stages. Potential 
bottlenecks can also be identified and eliminated by means of improvement and testing under operational 
conditions. 
Typical input: 
e Layout alternatives 
e Design day flight schedule 
e Passenger, aircraft and, vehicle properties (e.g., passenger show-up profiles, user shares) 
e Detailed operational concepts (i.e., processing times, allocation rules) 
Typical results: 
e Impact analysis including reliable KPIs 
e Attainable LoS in terms of queue length at processing facilities, delay/waiting times, dwell time, and 
density of mobile elements in selected areas 
e Detailed visualization to see the density of mobile elements in selected areas and the interactions 
between the different flows

Based on the conceptual design details for all elements are analyzed. Access and line up locations and exits 
of the runways are optimized as well as the details of taxiway system. Operational concepts are developed 
including the taxiing concept and the rules for using the stands. For the aprons stands for the different aircraft 
sizes have to be developed considering dependency rules (MARS-stand), which often lead to complex 
optimization tasks.

2.11.6.4 3rd Life Cycle Stage: Implementation 
Situation for Application 
After the detailed design of an airport infrastructure project has been finalized, it takes a certain time before it 
is built and goes into operation. For instance, when it comes to a complete terminal realization project, the 
construction period can last one to three years or more. 
During this time, certain input data (i.e., traffic forecasts used in the initial planning) could become outdated. 
This might result in changed requirements for the facilities. If design changes can still be realized during the 
implementation phase, this can save considerable costs because the facility will not be built according to 
outdated requirements. 
What is the Role of Simulation during the Implementation Phase? 
Simulation can accompany the implementation phase and keep the planning and design up-to-date with 
regards to consolidated information or “last minute changes”. 
The same models that were used in the previous layout improvement or optimization phase can continue to 
be used. Also, the extent of input data does not necessarily need to be higher. With ongoing time, input data 
can become more accurate (e.g., the traffic demand forecast for the opening day gets more accurate as more 
is known about airline strategies, flight rotations and slot allocations at the airport). Thus, the technical level of 
detail of the simulation can often remain the same, but with more up-to-date and refined input data. 
There are two main tasks for simulation during the implementation phase: 
1. Continuous monitoring/updating of input data and main planning assumptions 
Resulting from the uncertainty during the general layout design, the previous phase still worked with a 
certain number of scenarios and a variety of results. Coming closer to the start of operations, the applied 
input data changes from assumptions to hard facts. For example, the actual schedule for the first day of 
operation becomes available, and resources and other operational procedures can be specified. The 
simulation can continuously pick up this enhanced data and update the results accordingly. 
Therefore, the situation when the airport or just the terminal goes operational can be analyzed in advance 
(operational readiness test). If the airport is close to capacity and fully coordinated, the simulation can 
also be used to support the definition of a declared capacity of the airport. The updated information also 
allows enhanced simulation of further forecast flight schedules to check how long the new facilities will 
offer sufficient capacity and when the next stage of expansion should be initiated. 
2. Last minute changes 
It may also happen during the implementation phase that ad-hoc changes have to be considered. An 
example is a changed regulation for security control: a security threat can trigger intensified requirements 
on short notice (i.e., different handling of liquids, aerosols and gels (LAGs)). 
Another outcome of this phase could be the consideration of technology leaps. Simulation can support the 
quick analysis of the implications and ensure changes can be triggered in a timely manner. 
456 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 476===
may 
Sae_ | IATA ii Airport Simulation 
The results of this phase are generally several iterative loops. Depending on the extent of input data changes, 
a step back to the layout design phase may be required. 
Case Study Example: Redesign of Security Checkpoints 
In this case study, a terminal realization project was faced with stronger traffic growth than expected while, at 
the same time, changes to regulations for the security process were introduced. Both triggered significant 
changes during the start of the implementation phase. 
The higher passenger loads were partly a result of the decision of one of the main carriers to develop a 
transfer hub at the airport under consideration. The other factor was caused by new EU LAGs regulation, 
which had an influence on throughput. 
The simulation showed that these changes would lead to capacity bottlenecks with the current planned 
design. A re-configuration of the security checkpoint prior to opening anticipated these changes and ensured 
smooth operation. 
Exhibit 2.11.6.4a: Example: Redesign of Security Checkpoint-Updated Processes and 
Change in Facility Requirements 
Source: Airport Research Center 
Case Study Example: Capacity Limit Assessment 
Once an infrastructure and its basic operational concept is fixed, the model can be stressed with different 
traffic loads to assess the maximum manageable demand. Adapted from a baseline flight schedule, the traffic 
loads are heightened either by increasing the number of passengers per flight or adding new flights. Based on 
KPIs like occupancy rates, waiting times and queue length, the capacity limits of the system can be evaluated. 
This knowledge is used to identify the capacity limits of the airport and predict how it will react in over-load 
situations. In this context, simulation is also a reliable tool to define the declared capacity of an airport.

2.11.6.5 4th Life Cycle Stage: Optimization of Operational Concept 
Situation for Application 
Once an airport facility is open and operational, and the layout is fixed, there may still be different ways to 
operate the available infrastructure. The attainable LoS and the efficiency of operations depends on the 
applied operational concept (i.e., management strategies). This refers to the operational rules and the 
resource allocation that govern how the facility is operated on a day-to-day basis. 
What is the Role of Simulation during the Life Cycle Stage of the Optimization of Operational 
Concept? 
Simulation with a focus on the operational concept is used to assess and optimize the capacity and attainable 
LoS with no or little changes of the infrastructure through construction or re-design. 
The time horizon for the simulation could be within the scope of tactical and operational planning, but also 
might be related to long-term planning. The time horizon could consider the flight schedule for the next year, 
the next season or even the next day. 
Simulation studies during this life cycle stage may also be triggered when: 
e Procedures/protocols change 
e Technology is being implemented 
e¢ Anew aircraft fleet mix evolves 
¢ The entire structure of the flight schedule changes (e.g., an airport becomes a transfer hub) 
The impact of such changes on the operations needs to be analyzed. If problems are detected, potential 
mitigation measures can be elaborated by means of simulation, preferably with little or no change to the 
building or airfield infrastructure. 
Case Study Example: Level of Service Assessment and Optimization 
Simulating one layout with different operational concepts helps to identify the most promising operational 
concept and maximum capacity. Changes can include: 
© Different strategies of resource use (e.g., common check-in vs. dedicated flight check-in) 
e — Introduction of self-service facilities (i.e., CUSS kiosks, e-gates, automated passport controls) 
e The use of centralized checkpoints instead of dedicated controls 
® Changed opening times of a facility (e.g., check-in counters) 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 459 

===PAGE 479===
= iil Se 
IATA ‘4 Airport Development Reference Manual 
A simulation study as a first step can assess the attainable LoS with the current operational concept, then 
focus on areas where the desired LoS is not met in terms of waiting times and/or reduced space standards. If 
simulation offers a 2D/3D animation, it can be used to visualize possible bottlenecks in a straight forward and 
transparent way. While testing the simulation model under different sensitivity scenarios, the behavior and 
sensitivity of cause-and-effect can be better understood. With the insight gained, possible operational 
mitigation scenarios can be tested and evaluated. This can help to identify hidden capacities. Quite often, a 
constrained situation can be resolved by changing operational procedures or the allocation of resources 
instead of building new facilities.

Queue length, waiting times and required resources are compared to find the optimum trade-off of passenger 
comfort and efficient operation. 
Case Study Example: Process Optimization 
Even without changing the infrastructure, it may be possible to increase the capacity of a security checkpoint 
by unlocking hidden capacity. A detailed simulation model is able to evaluate each sub-process of a security 
control (e.g., preparation of trays, passenger search and secondary inspection of hand luggage). Such a 
mode! can identify the impact of each parameter (i.e., trays per passenger, number of officers per lane) on the 
throughput capacity. 
In particular when facing new regulations like LAGs handling or shoe scanning, it is worth looking into the 
process in detail to test various “what-if’ scenarios to identify the most efficient and stable process. Measures 
for improvement can range from layout changes, changes to the process, or changes in the number of 
supporting staff and their operational procedures.

Case Study Example Airside 
One continuous task is to adapt the operational concepts for the airside to the changes in traffic amount and 
structure and others changes, like new terminal concepts or changes in the environmental or political 
conditions. The capacity has to be re-evaluated, sources of delay and bottlenecks have to be identified and 
mitigation measures have to be found without changing the infrastructure. 
Further objectives are the development of concepts on how to deal with extraordinary situations and bigger or 
smaller disruptions like drops in capacity due to weather, or how to manage the traffic during maintenance 
and construction. The optimal management of snow clearance and deicing are a challenge for many airports 
and simulations are done to optimize, or get the best performance from, the procedures.

2.11.6.6 5th Life Cycle Stage: Operational Management 
Situation for Application 
The previously described life cycle stages usually analyze a regular traffic day and base their 
recommendations on a predictable operational situation without irregularities. However, even the best 
planning will be flawed in the case of an airport that has to deal with unpredicted situations, like flight delays. 
Using simulation at this stage takes into account live information and supports decision making in the very 
short-term planning to allow real-time reaction, even in extraordinary situations (e.g., runway closure, strike). 
Todays digitalization offers a lot of possibilities to use real-life data in combination with a simulation model for 
real-time predictions during the day of operations. 
What is the Role of Simulation during the Life Cycle Stage of Operational Management? 
Usage of simulation in this stage has been less common, but there is a trend that airports applying predictive 
simulations not only for an improved situation awareness but also to optimize daily operations. 
462 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 482===
ie Se 
IATA Airport Simulation 
The previously described simulation tasks mainly focus on long-or medium-term and tactical planning 
questions. This means that the simulation is performed some time before the situation is expected to happen 
in reality. But it can also be applied to short-term operational management and real-time monitoring. 
If a calibrated simulation system is connected to an AODB or passenger counting system, the simulation can 
be used to anticipate and evaluate the potential implications of the actual passenger demand. 
Considering up-to-date information for all flights allows the assessment of the combined impact of the latest 
flight information on the operations of an airport. For instance, transfer security checkpoints or immigration 
control areas could be better operated when the simulation forecasts a critical bottleneck a couple of hours in 
advance. 
For the airside based on demand and predicted capacity runway throughput and resulting delays can be 
determined and mitigation measures can be triggered, if necessary. Expected on- and off-block times are an 
important input for passenger flow forecasting. If disruptions like weather, strike or accidents will reduce 
capacity, flights can be shifted, reallocated or even canceled. This typically happens in collaborative work of 
an operational control center (AOC or APOC), where different stakeholders jointly decide on suitable actions, 
possibly using the concepts of decision theory and not necessarily simulation over the next two or three 
hours. 
Simulation may allow the identification of time-critical operating conditions in the near future (0 to 4 hours in 
advance). Alerts can be triggered to enable intelligent on-demand staffing to ensure smooth operations. 
It is obvious that this kind of simulation has the highest requirement for input data (live data), but at the same 
time, the constantly performed recalculation and recalibration allows for results of the highest degree of 
accuracy. 
Case Study Example: Airside: Airport Performance Monitoring 
In the preoperational planning, determination of the stand utilization for next season, the next month, week or 
day or for special events, like a festival or football match is a typical use case. Stand capacity might be an 
issue as well as the allocation itself, which aims to fulfil the requirements of airlines and airports while 
considering several hard and soft restrictions. 
Especially for coordinated airports the capacity has to be evaluated considering the actual demand in detail. 
Mostly the runway is the relevant element but also stand capacity has to be considered to find a suitable 
scheme for the declared capacity. 
For short-term operational planning, the short-term forecast of registered traffic is the input for determination 
of throughput and delay, which may be exacerbated by runway or apron (stand) capacities. Predicted 
on-block and off-block times can be used not only as input for the planning of airside resources, but also for 
the passenger flow prediction and resource management in the terminal, and subsequently in the landside. In 
an AOC/APOC, this information will be used to jointly make decisions to mitigate unwanted consequences by 
shifting or even cancelling flights. By preparing scenarios (e.g., with a thunderstorm or snowstorm the next 
day, the involved parties can act proactively and coordinate with stakeholders at the airport and network.

Case Study Example: Avoidance of Safety Critical Congestion Levels 
A passenger flow forecasting simulation model can be used to look into the near future, even in exceptional 
situations. In a situation where the departing traffic is stopped (e.g., by a runway closure due to fog), more 
and more passengers accumulate in the gate area. When the number of passengers exceeds a certain limit, 
this can become safety critical in terms of evacuation. 
The simulation can be used to predict the passenger numbers in the gate area and answer when the 
passenger flow into the gate area should be stopped to avoid overcrowding. A triggered action may be to 
close the security control to make passengers wait in the check-in hall.

In most simulation models, a capacity may be set for the areas where the numbers are restricted to a fire 
safety limit. In those models, the results indicate at which point the areas become safety critical and mobile 
elements, such as passengers and visitors, may be held back or metered into the safety critical areas. 
Case Study Example: Reorganisation of Terminal Operations due to a Pandemic 
A pandemic triggers a drastic change how airport facilities are operated and allocated. The requirement for 
social distancing, disinfection as well as additional checks of health certificates and health declaration forms 
of all passengers have a considerable impact on airport operations. See 2.8 Pandemic Resilience and 
Healthy Buildings for further information on related measures. 
If an airport has access to a simulation model of its airport facilities, the model can be used to assess the 
impact of measures and support the decision making process of how the airport facilities are used to meet the 
special requirements. 
Although in absence of a pandemic situation, a planner might check a terminal layout by simulating a “what-if” 
scenario to assess the robustness of the planned terminal layout and operational concept. 
An example is the test of changed allocation rules for check-in areas or the reduction in throughput capacity 
and increased queue space requirements at all checkpoints.

2.11.7 General Considerations and Lessons Learned 
2.11.7.1 Effort, Duration and Cost 
Based on the previous simulation projects, the time and budget requirements of a typical simulation study can 
be allocated to its different phases as follows: 
e 10%: Definition of the project objective 
¢ 30%: System abstraction and input data collection 
e 20%: Model setup, validation and calibration 
¢ 30%: Scenario simulation (effort depends on the number of scenarios) 
* 10%: Result interpretation and report 
At the beginning of a project, it is essential to generate a common understanding of the agreed objectives that 
the simulation will deliver. A good project plan will result in a road map that all stakeholders and the modeler 
can not only understand, but follow, and against which work progress may be measured. 
Stakeholders often underestimate the effort required for system abstraction as they may not understand that 
input data collection is very time consuming. Frequently, airport stakeholders think that “all data for the 
simulation study already exists”. It is often true that the airport owns a comprehensive set of data, but this 
data usually has been collected for a different purpose than simulation. The identification of 
inadequate/unusable data and the collection of good replacement data can take a certain amount of time, but 
is essential for a successful outcome of the study. 
The required time for model setup, validation and calibration highly depends on the descriptive effectiveness 
of the project plan, the knowledge and experience of the modeler in the concepts of airport operations and 
planning, and with the simulation tool, as well as the ease of use of the simulation tool itself. The validation 
and calibration of the model can become a time-consuming task if a highly accurate model is required and the 
collected input data does not lead to a sufficiently accurate representation of reality in the simulation. In this 
case, time has to be spent to research where the deviations come from and debug the model. Also, where 
input data is being collected and refined, iteration cycles are required to calibrate the model until it is accurate 
enough to answer the question that the simulation is examining. 
The actual simulation phase and scenario evaluation is estimated to account for about one-third of the total 
project scope. However, new questions often arise once the first simulation runs are performed and analyzed. 
In particular, when the variation of the first results is very wide or the results are not satisfactory, there might 
be new questions and “what-if” scenarios to be simulated. Further simulation scenarios are often needed to 
gain a reliable understanding of the situation, but can also significantly extend this project phase. 
The main task of the interpretation and report generation phase is the aggregation of the multitude of results 
and their interpretation. Therefore, the amount of time spent on this phase is largely dependent on the initial 
scope of the project. The required time also depends on the amount and quality of the visual output 
(screenshots, videos) requested. Experience shows that it is worth taking the time to generate these visual 
466 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 486===
ae } 
IATA Airport Simulation 
outputs, as results are more convincing because stakeholders can actually see what is happening to better 
understand causes and effects. 
The actual time spent on a simulation project varies from days to months depending on the questions asked. 
Projects that involve the complete setup, validation and calibration of a comprehensive model take around 
three to four months, if all input data is suitable and available. However, simulations can take four to six 
months when the input data is not suitable and more time is required for data collection, validation, model 
calibration and feedback processes with the client. Due to the sequential structure of the project phases, 
feedback/iteration cycles and coordination with stakeholders, it is hard to reduce these time requirements, 
even when additional expert resources (simulation modelers) are allocated to the project. 
However, once a calibrated model is available, it can be used to answer recurring questions quite efficiently 
within a few days (e.g., testing a new flight schedule). Scenarios can also be tested by more than one user. If 
using such a simulation model regularly, it is important to keep it up-to-date. Therefore, the implemented input 
data should be cross-checked to verify that they are still valid on a regularly basis. 
The cost of a simulation study is driven by the required time and effort, the model complexity and the level of 
detail. A further driver is the number of scenarios to investigate. If using the too! in-house, the cost of 
acquisition and maintenance of the simulation tool, and training of staff members on the simulation tool, must 
be considered. 
2.11.7.2 Team for a Simulation Project 
Depending on the number of expected simulation projects in the future, the stakeholders, such as airport 
authorities or consultants in airport planning or operations, who aim to conduct simulation studies should 
decide whether to engage an independent specialist consultant or invest in purchasing their own simulation 
tool and training in-house staff to conduct their own studies. 
The team for a simulation project should be knowledgeable about airport planning and operations, and not be 
limited to only individuals who setup and work with the simulation models. The simulation tool is simply that-a 
tool. The prerequisites for formulating and solving airport and airspace problems include communication skills, 
knowledge of the subject domain, and creativity in generating solution alternatives that may be tested in a 
simulation model. In particular, during master planning and input data collection as well as the validation of 
baseline results, close cooperation with different airport stakeholders is essential. 
A simulation combines infrastructure layout with operational processes to “bring to life” the simulated airport 
and airspace facilities. Consequently, a simulation team needs expert staff members with both an 
infrastructure and an operational background. The infrastructure perspective is usually covered by facility 
planners (e.g., people involved in the planning, design and construction of the infrastructure). For the 
operational perspective, people are needed who know all the details of the day-to-day operations of the 
airport and its processes. Experts on traffic forecasting and flight schedule development complement a project 
team. 
The staff actually carrying out the simulation study is characterized by systems knowledge, analytical skills 
and the ability to structure and combine information into a coherent framework. Statistical knowledge is also 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 467 

===PAGE 487===
| py 
ae 
See_—C*“#“g IATA piu Airport Development Reference Manual 
necessary on the team to analyze the input data and the simulation output. Basic understanding of simulation 
modeling techniques is also desirable. Furthermore, experience in airport processes is key to focus on 
relevant aspects and guide other stakeholders through the project. 
The alternative option is to contract an external company specializing in simulation. This has the advantages 
that no tool has to be purchased and no dedicated staff has to be trained and allocated to perform the 
simulation study. There are currently numerous consultants with expertise in all of the required disciplines 
who own the simulation tools, and who have and can successfully support any stakeholder with objective 
analysis and report generation as well as support the growth and problem solution objectives of the airports. 
A third option is a combined approach, whereby the stakeholder (airport or consultant) acquires the tool and 
takes the training. The initial set-up of the simulation model, including data collection, validation and 
calibration is done by the external company. Then, the airport model is handed over to the stakeholder to 
conduct specific simulation scenarios. The external company can then support as and when required by 
internal resources. 
2.11.7.3 Stakeholder Involvement 
Simulation is a valuable tool that makes it possible to communicate results and problems with the various 
stakeholders during the entire pre-planning, planning and post-planning planning process. 
Ideally, stakeholders participate in the simulation project from the very beginning by defining the problem, the 
scope of the project, providing input data, which will ensure that the model is as accurate as possible, and 
reviewing and approving the work being done. The knowledge of persons who work on-site and know the 
actual operations is valuable to get a valid model and reliable results. Finding solutions for a future situation 
(i.e., defining simulation scenarios) is always a brainstorming task and various ideas from local experts are 
welcome. The early involvement and close cooperation of the airport stakeholders also increases the 
acceptance of the simulation results later on. 
Various graphical possibilities, above all the 2D/3D environment of the simulation system, enable a common 
understanding of future situations for all stakeholders. “What-if’ scenarios demonstrate the impact of certain 
decisions, enrich the discussion and support the negotiation of consensus for stakeholders with diverging 
objectives. 
2.11.7.4 Limitations of Simulation 
The transferability of the results of a simulated system to the real-world system has its limits and, therefore, 
must always be critically evaluated and cross-checked before being applied. 
Imperfection of a model: A simulation model is an approximated version of the real-world system. Thus, the 
simulation's output data will produce a likely estimate of real-world events. The simulation results are only as 
good as the input data and the model (garbage in-garbage out). Therefore, it is key to ensure that important 
system characteristics are modelled in a suitable way. 
468 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 488===
Airport Simulation 
Modelling capability of human behavior: Modelling human behavior is a very complex topic and often the 
modelling technical expert has to make many assumptions and define what the model will do (e.g., where 
passengers wait, what routes they take) when reality may show random actions from passengers not defined 
in the model. Therefore, some human behavior may not be modelled or simplified. 
Incorrect input data: Simulation models are generated from a set of data taken from a stochastic system. 
Collection and validation of input data is an activity that requires special attention. The data should be 
checked that it is statistically valid by fitting a statistical distribution®° and then testing the significance of such 
a fit. Deficits in data collection and incorrect assumptions lead to inadequate solutions and decisions. 
A main issue is that defective input data is often difficult to identify by the modeler. Therefore, it is 
recommended to verify input data and model validity by conducting a baseline simulation which includes a 
calibration of the model and input. A suitable amount of time and budget must be considered for data 
collection, validation and calibration. It is good practice to document all data input and review this with the 
relevant stakeholders before producing any results with the simulation model. 
Mistakes in mode! settings: The modeler can also be a source of error. With growing model size, complexity 
and the amount of input data to consider, there is the possibility of logical errors in the model set-up. 
Therefore, critical and diligent cross-checks of simulation results are a key activity before any conclusions and 
recommendations can be derived. It is recommended to use a second independent approach to verify 
stepwise simulation results. This can be based, for instance, on analytical cross-checks using a subset of 
assumptions for selected flights from the flight schedule and cross-check results for the right order of 
magnitude. 
Limits of computer power: Even with the advancements in computer hardware in recent years, the high 
number of interacting objects and parameters could cause the simulation to not be able to deliver results 
within an acceptable amount of time and effort. Therefore, a reasonable level of model abstraction has to be 
selected so that the simulation is still workable, but also includes all parameters that are relevant for the 
analysis. 
Time cost versus benefit: Even if a well-calibrated simulation model of an airport facility is available, this 
does not mean that all capacity-related calculations will be done with this model. Other models, such as 
spreadsheet models, can be used in parallel as well. Even if they are less accurate, they are faster to set up 
and run. Therefore, they are still being used for questions needing a fast evaluation. It must also be 
considered whether the question to be answered justifies the start of a simulation study, or would applying 
analytical formulas with a simple spreadsheet model result in a similar answer much faster and cheaper. 
There is no ultimate model to answer all questions: Usually, a model is set up for specific purposes and to 
answer specific questions. If the intention changes, the model logic and input might also need to be changed, 
if only in the level of detail and focus. Therefore, an ongoing simulation study always requires iteration cycles 
and changes to the model and input data. Other questions might also consider enlarging the system 
boundaries (e.g., model aspects of the BHS in combination with the passenger terminal) or even decrease the 
system boundaries (e.g., only model the security screening process in detail). Therefore, it is important to 
20 Fitting survey data to a curve implies that the nature of the distribution is known or suspected. This is rarely the case and, therefore, 
raw data may be used ‘as is’ in some models to reflect the real phenomena. This generally requires more data points.

===PAGE 489===
cay
