keep in mind that there is always some effort to using an existing model as it might need to be adapted to fit 
the question it needs to answer. 
2.11.7.5 Possible Pitfalls 
This section outlines some frequently observed mistakes that can occur when performing simulation studies. 
Inadequate Attention to the Input Data 
Mistakes may happen by simply using wrong input data. A simulation study with a poor database will produce 
faulty results, might lead to wrong conclusions and is not worth the investment. 
Usually, airports have comprehensive statistical databases from which input for a simulation study might be 
derived. Regardless of the source, the relevance of the data and the method of data collection might not be 
known or adequately documented. 
When using input data for important variables in the simulation, where the source is not clear, or if the data 
might be outdated, spot-checks should be undertaken on-site. A “spot-check” is not a comprehensive data 
survey, but rather a gathering of samples to check if the measured data is in the range and order of 
magnitude of the data obtained from the airport's database. When considerable deviation is detected, it 
should be researched why this difference exists. Reasons could include a change in handling processes or in 
passenger behavior (e.g., driven by a new regulation or airline rule). In this case, a more comprehensive data 
survey must be undertaken to collect a more current set of input. 
It is not recommended to use statistics aggregated to annual, monthly, weekly, daily or hourly averages. What 
is important for simulation and capacity studies are the traffic characteristics of the distribution of demand over 
time and not necessarily the aggregate for one hour as was done traditionally for the peak hour or peak 
periods. Therefore, an effort should be made to generate a realistic flight schedule with the correct flight mix 
and operating times and which generates the demand suggested by the peak hour or peak period. This could 
differ considerably from aggregated statistics because they might flatten out certain characteristics that are 
important to consider for a peak analysis. For instance, when using a general annual transfer share for all 
flights of an airline operating at a hub airport, and transfer is an important part of the traffic, a mistake could 
be likely. At different times of the day or on certain flight routes, the transfer shares might differ considerably. 
Transfer share is an important characteristic for demand at transfer security and at the O&D facilities. 
Compared to an average annual transfer share, a high variation of the transfer share for certain flights during 
peak times can have a large impact on facility requirements. Using averages can lead to wrong dimensioning 
of facilities that do not meet the requirements of the peak demand. 
Deficits in the Data Collection Method 
Before any data collection is undertaken, essential that the data collectors be trained to observe, interview 
and record data in a scientific way. The approach to data collection will depend on the data to be collected 
and this has to be communicated during training to the persons who will carry out the surveys and 
measurements. 
470 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 490===
any 
= TATA. al Airport Simulation 
Typical pitfalls of data collection are: 
Too low share of passengers measured (sample size): For some input data (e.g., process times), a spot￾check measurement of a few hundred passengers may be sufficient. Other kinds of data require a 
counting of close to 100% of passengers. For instance, assessing a passenger show-up profile is not 
really usable if just a small percentage of passengers of the flight of interest are counted in the relevant 
time period. The same applies for usage shares like passport types, etc 
Lack of reference to a flight: Passengers belong to different traffic segments (e.g., leisure/business or 
domestic/international). If the modeler is not aware of this and uses the same statistical data for 
passengers that usually behave differently (e.g., according to their show-up behavior or their processing 
times), such differences in passenger behavior are leveled out and not considered in the simulation. Data 
collection should consider this variety and choose relevant flights for the collection. Before doing a survey, 
careful selection of distribution criteria that considers a variety of different system parameters is 
recommended in order to abstract the data according to a meaningful grouping of statistical passenger 
behavior patterns. This is again covered in the survey design and training of the data collectors 
Position for counting: Errors in counting can happen because of a mistaken position of the measurement. 
If the passenger show-up behavior at the check-in is required, this cannot be answered by the check-in 
system data that is automatically recorded when a passenger checks in. When a passenger is only 
counted once he has transacted, this is too late and does not coincide with his show-up time (i.e., the 
moment he joined the-maybe long—check-in queue). A profile derived from check-in system messages 
will give a throughput for check-in, but not the actual show-up profile. The same error occurs if data from 
self-serve kiosks is used to represent kiosk service times. The actual time is the time the kiosk is 
occupied, which is more than the time recorded by the kiosk when the passenger first interacts with the 
kiosk to when the documents are all printed. 
Surveys versus data capture: The quality of data depends on the source. Often, surveys take place in the 
gate area, and passengers are asked when they arrived at the airport. This approach leads to rather 
rough results as passengers sometimes cannot remember the exact time. It is better to do actual 
countings at the various terminal subsystems. This can be done, for instance, by the “timestamp” method 
Measuring of wrong data type: At some services, such as security control, more than one passenger can 
be handled at the same time. However, security is modelled as one abstract process (black box) with only 
one process time in the simulation. In this case, we have the choice of two methods. The first one 
involves measuring the time a passenger spends in the security system, and the static capacity of the 
security area, then simulating the entire security area as “black box” which will generate realistic queues 
for the security area. A second method, which violates the rule that averages should not be used as an 
input to simulation, but which may be the only choice available, uses the throughput rate. For this, a 
continuous outflow of passengers during peak time is measured per lane and an hourly throughput is 
calculated. Then, an average process time is calculated (e.g., 180 passengers per hour results in an 
average process time of 20 seconds per passenger). In this method, variations in security queues or 
process times cannot be reliably estimated with any accuracy 
Lack of important variables: It is important to agree on what should be measured in detail. 
o Example 1: For the simulation, it makes a big difference if a process time at check-in is measured per 
passenger or per group. Ideally, process times could be made a function of group size and process 
times differentiated for group size (e.g., a distribution for singles, for doubles, for triples) etc. and use 
of that distribution which is applicable for that case. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 471 

===PAGE 491===
TATA i Airport Development Reference Manual 
o Example 2: If a service is fed by a common queue and passengers are processed one by one, it has 
to be decided if idle times at the counter should be considered in the measured process time or not. 
For detailed modeling, only the time that a processor is occupied should be measured. Then, idle time 
of the processor becomes an independent variable that depends on the walking speed and the 
source of the mobile element that must come to the counter or processor. This allows the 
development of the queuing configuration for maximum throughput allowing for privacy concerns, etc. 
Ignoring Important System Boundaries of Connecting Subsystems 
An airport consists of several sequential and concurrent processes. This is often neglected when only one 
sub-process is analyzed, leading to incomplete or wrong results. 
Interdependency factors not to be ignored include: 
The demand at one service depends on another service: If a sequence of processes is modelled 
(i.e., check-in, security and emigration), changes in one process can have an immediate effect on the 
other processes. An isolated view on only one process fades out the effect on subsequent processes and 
a newly created bottleneck can easily be overseen. 
Sometimes planners do not see the bigger picture and do not consider elements beyond the typical 
airport infrastructure (e.g., an airport train arrival has an impact on passenger show-up). 
Queues of various services interfere with each other: It is often not suitable to assume that the dedicated 
queuing area is sufficient during the peak period. Passengers might spread out and block other areas; this 
needs to be anticipated and consequences analyzed 
Handling of one process depends on another process: Besides the spatial interference, there might be 
technical interdependencies that can easily become out of focus. For instance, looking at a check-in area 
without considering the limits of the feeding conveyors into the BHS may fail if the BHS is the limiting 
element. This occurs frequently when substituting the slow full-service check-in by fast bag-drop solutions 
Furthermore, when testing an airport infrastructure, it is important not to forget typical “neuralgic” areas in a 
terminal, for example: 
Escalators ending up in a queue space 
Queue areas that interfere with narrow circulation corridors 
Unsuitable design of passenger routes resulting in cross-flows 
Areas where passengers get “trapped” (i.e., where a crowd develops because of congestion and cannot 
spread, thus resulting in a safety issue) 
Narrow arrival corridors from gate to immigration 
Not Using the Appropriate Level of Detail or Abstraction to Answer a Question 
The right level of detail or abstraction depends on the question to answer with a simulation. For instance, it 
can be wrong to use an existing model that has been set up in the scope of master planning for operational 
questions. 
472 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 492===
és 7 
Se IATA I Airport Simulation 
Example: If the number of required check-in counters is being calculated for short-term questions, it is not 
suitable to consider an all-common check-in, if that is not the way the counters are typically allocated, as 
individual flight check-in will lead to idle times at counters and allow a lower throughput compared to an all￾common configuration. 
On the other hand, too much attention is sometimes paid to irrelevant details. This may distract people from 
the important data (e.g., people may see one passenger behaving slightly strangely and ignore the general 
result showing that the facility is over capacity). 
Mistaken Selection of Flight Schedule 
The selection of suitable traffic loads in terms of passenger demand for the simulation model is key for the 
results. Even if well-known schedules of the past are to be simulated, it may happen that an incorrect 
schedule is selected. The following list gives some hints: 
¢ Risk of modelling one specific day: Often selected schedules are the typical Busy Day (as per IATA 
definition), the 30th busiest day of the year or the average day during peak month. Usually, these days 
are appropriate, but it can be dangerous to ignore the busier days, if the gap between these traffic 
volumes becomes too large. Furthermore, the busiest day may not be the worst in all areas due to daily 
differences in the flight schedule 
¢ Neglecting the peak structure: The typical approach is to select the Busy Day for a simulation by 
evaluating the total number of passengers per day. This approach does not look into the actual peak 
structure (i.e., the distribution of demand during the day or days) that may vary from day to day. High 
peaks of a varying distribution are more challenging to handle than equally distributed traffic throughout 
the day 
¢ Neglecting sub-peaks: Peaks for different user groups (e.g., arrival, departure and transfer passengers) 
do not necessarily occur at the same time. It is recommended to consider those individuals peaks rather 
than just looking at the total number of passengers per day or per hour 
When a scenario flight schedule reflecting a future situation is to be generated for a simulation, the peak width 
is very important, if facilities are stressed with a peak demand exceeding the capacity. If only the number of 
peak hour passengers is known, a realistic peak width should be assumed since assuming a constant 
demand of peak hour passengers for the whole time is as misleading as just considering it for one hour 
without assuming any traffic in the adjacent hours. 
Exhibit 2.11.7.5a illustrates two situations of the same aggregate demand in two different distributions. In both 
cases, the daily movements and number of passengers are the same. However, the hourly demand is very 
different and, therefore, for a given target LoS, the infrastructure and management strategies (operations 
concepts) have to be different for each case.

IATA Planning for Collaborative Decision-Making 
Understand Impact of Sub-optimum Staffing 
Simulation studies of a future situation usually do not consider staffing information with opening/closing times 
of facilities. Consequently, all available processing facilities are considered to be always open in the model, 
thus showing the infrastructure limit. This approach has to be kept in mind when the facility is stressed close 
to its capacity. A realistic staffing will rarely show “all lanes always open”. In reality, staff may only react ifa 
queue is already there. This means longer queues and may even need more facilities to resolve a massive 
queue if facilities are opened too late. Therefore, some facilities should be planned in reserve to cater for 
contingencies and staffing effects. 
Do Not Look at Only One Situation 
When it comes to long-term planning, it has to be understood that simulation always includes imperfection 
due to uncertainties in data forecasting. Thus, any expectation by stakeholders of a perfect model cannot be 
met, by definition. Trying to be as precise as possible does not necessarily generate any benefit. It can even 
be misleading, if one tries to only look at one set of input data and base results, and make decisions on that. 
In order to reduce this uncertainty, it is recommended to do scenarios and to test a range of worst case and 
best case assumptions. 
The same applies for replications. Simulations generally have stochastic variability based on their input data 
and various probabilities in the model logic. Thus, they should be run a number of times to look at the range 
of outputs. If a simulation has not been run for multiple replications, the results should be considered initial 
findings or draft results, and have uncertainty applied to the results. Recommendations or significant decisions 
should not be based on single-replication simulation results. 
Uncritical Transfer of Simulation Results to the Real System 
It is risky to trust model results without critical validation and verification of the results. The modeler and the 
stakeholders who are taking decisions should always be aware that a simulation is a prognosis of a possible 
behavior, not an unshakable statement. 
2.12 Planning for Collaborative Decision-Making 
2.12.1 Overview 
The increasing demand for airport and airspace resources has led to the need to identify more efficient ways 
to make use of existing infrastructure. Stakeholders agree that there is wasted capacity, and that aircraft 
operators are not able to operate utilizing their preferred trajectories. As multiple actors do not necessarily 
have visibility on each other's needs, preferences or constraints, numerous actors have attempted to address 
this issue through various approaches: 
Airport Collaborative Decision-Making (‘A-CDM’) involves the sharing of timely and accurate information 
among A-CDM stakeholders and utilizing a set of operational procedures and automated processes to 
benefit all airport participants in the process. A-CDM generally focuses on aircraft departure processes. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 475 

===PAGE 495===
== af IATA Biull Airport Development Reference Manual 
¢ Air Traffic Flow Management (‘ATFM’) is the use of processes, constraints, or regulations over air traffic, 
to avoid exceeding airport or airspace capacity. 
* Trajectory Based Operations (‘TBO’) is the air traffic management trajectory of a manned or unmanned 
vehicle, during all phases of flight, and the interaction of that trajectory with other trajectories or hazards. 
The goal is to achieve the optimum system outcome, with minimal deviation from the user-requested flight 
trajectory, whenever possible. 
* Total Airport Management (‘TAM’) is a developing concept without a single definition, but which generally 
includes the sharing of timely and accurate information between stakeholders at an airport, integrating 
multiple data sources such as surface access, in-terminal passenger processes, baggage, and ground 
handling systems. TAM will also include both arrival and departure processes, meaning that data sharing 
beyond the airport with ATFM systems becomes necessary. 
2.12.2 Achieving an Effective and Efficient Turnaround Process: A-CDM 
A-CDM will primarily require a program of cultural change at an airport. A-CDM is backed by a series of well￾defined processes and milestones, coordinated by the sharing of data between all stakeholders. Most A-CDM 
implementations have been done centered around improving the departure process. 
Overall, A-CDM is about making more efficient use of existing capacity and resources, as well as offering 
resilience and potentially better recovery from disruptions. A-CDM can optimize airport operations by 
enhancing the turnaround process and improving flight predictability through real time data exchange for all 
A-CDM stakeholders. A-CDM is also envisioned to improve gate/aircraft stand management, as well as 
reduce apron, taxiway and holding point congestion. A-CDM can, in some cases, reduce fuel burn operating 
costs, which will provide environmental benefits. 
Prior to A-CDM, stakeholders operated on the “first come, first served” basis in the start-up sequence of 
aircraft. A-CDM works on the premise of “best planned, best served”, whereby ATC will optimize the 
Predeparture sequence by using Target Off-Block Times (TOBT) submitted by aircraft operators. It is a 
collaborative approach, with its success ultimately dependent on the accuracy of TOBTs, which are managed 
by aircraft operators. 
The turnaround process encompasses the complete management of an aircraft from arrival at an airport, until 
its departure, and needs to be effective and efficient to contribute to a successful A-CCDM implementation. The 
A-CDM turnaround process involves stakeholders, operational services, data points and algorithms that are 
instrumental to the successful turnaround of an aircraft. Standardization of the turnaround process should be 
introduced. 
The maintenance of a Variable Taxi Time (VTT) is a key data point in A-CDM and helps determine other data 
points such as Estimated in Block Arrival Time (EIBT) and Target Takeoff Time (TTOT). The maintenance of 
the VTT process may be the responsibility of the airport operator, the ANSP, or a joint responsibility between 
the airport and ANSP. The A-CDM VTT should ideally be a dynamic value that reflects current runway, 
taxiway, and apron conditions. 
476 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 496===
wae IATA a Planning for Collaborative Decision-Making 
A minimum turnaround time (MTTT) can also be used in A-CDM implementations to predict early provisional 
TOBTs in advance of an aircraft operator's commitment to its TOBT. This is acceptable to the aircraft operator 
if the MTTT is accurate and that the airport operator uses this early prediction exclusively for resource 
allocation planning, and not for reporting to ATM, which may introduce unnecessary delays. Where MTTT is 
used, the airport operator may be responsible for its maintenance, or jointly with the ANSP. MTTT must be 
kept accurate for multiple aircraft types and flight types. Aircraft operators must be able to update MTTT as 
required. 
2.12.3 A Need to Rethink and Go Beyond A-CDM 
A-CDM has its roots in Europe and is the foundation for the European Single European Sky ATM Research 
(SESAR) concepts. SESAR seeks for the use of better data and technology to make aircraft and airport 
operations more efficient. The Eurocontrol implementation manual along with the IATA A-CDM 
recommendations are the foundations for many airports implementing A-CDM systems. 
As stated, A-CDM has been generally departure-focused, with implementation driven by the airport operator. 
While guidance material encourages following common, standard, and harmonized practices—most airports 
have implemented A-CDM in different ways. The result for aircraft operators has been a significant degree of 
complexity when flying to different A-CDM airports. Furthermore, while A-CDM systems often interface with 
the national ANSP or network manager, information is not shared with other ANSPs or airports. 
Consequently, while an A-CDM system may improve resource utilization at a specific airport, it does not 
always consider the impact at airports or airspaces further down an aircraft's flight path. 
There are potential opportunities for wider success, by integrating A-CDM implementations and information 
with ATFM systems to promote broader information sharing, while standardizing and harmonizing procedures 
and data standards. Coordinating data between all airports and ANSPs along an aircraft's trajectory, will 
ultimately deliver optimal performance. The wider benefits of A-CDM should be considered when considering 
local enhancements. 
In addition, both in the SESAR context as well as at the ICAO level, discussions are now turning their focus 
toward TAM-which will include the expansion of A-CDM into airport terminals and surface access systems. 
The ASBU block in the current A-CDM model that simply commences with a Start of Ground Activities 
timestamp and ends with an Aircraft Ready timestamp will develop into a highly optimized and automated set 
of activities. This will expand the philosophy of data sharing initiated in A-CDM, by delivering further 
integration of real time trusted source data from A-CDM stakeholders. 
2.12.4 A-CDM is Not for All Airports and Will Not Solve All Problems 
An A-CDM or TAM implementation is not only a significant investment, but also a major commitment and 
culture change albeit not appropriate for all airports. Notably, if there is limited resource contention, there are 
variations of the concepts which will reduce the scope while still enabling airports to contribute to an efficient 
traffic flow management without a full A-CDM implementation. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 477 

===PAGE 497===
Se G— ii | IATA Baul Airport Development Reference Manual 
The A-CDM concept may also not be applicable in all geographies and configurations. For example, in the 
United States-many surface movement areas are controlled by airlines themselves and the ANSP (FAA) is 
only involved once the aircraft enters the active apron. If the airline also performs their own ground handling 
activities or even manages the terminal-there is less of a need for information exchange between those 
parties. 
The most replicated model of A-CDM is the European version. This A-CDM version interfaces with a network 
manager, who controls most traffic management aspects in Europe. However, not all regions have such a 
centric ATM network, so the A-CDM application may be different in other regions. For the A-CDM concept to 
be successful, it must be adaptable to regional ATFM environments and, at the same time, comply with a 
substantial degree of harmonization to provide consistency for all stakeholders. 
One of the most important aspects of global A-CDM is the architecture. Where AFTM exists, the interface 
between an airport and a central airspace management system, is critical to ensure information is exchanged 
between A-CDM and ATFM units. Where an AFTM unit does not exist-the benefits of A-CDM 
implementations may be limited. Using A-CDM, industry is observing other facets of airspace management 
concepts. A-CDM is being used to provide the required data to fulfil continuity between major traffic flows and 
high-density airports. 
One such concept developed in Southeast Asia is known as the Distributed Multi-Nodal ATFM Network. 
Regional requirements, such as data exchange among different ATFM applications, requires appropriate 
system design and adaptation. The primary purpose of this concept is to mitigate airborne flow constraints 
that contribute to overflow in ATC sector capacities, which result in unanticipated en route delays. As ATM 
evolves and additional concepts are introduced, changes and adjustments to A-CDM may be required. This 
will most certainly contribute to the complexities of data exchange. A-CDM assists in the efficient 
management of airport operations; however, continuous improvement of the concept will be required to 
support the projected growth in air traffic demand. Current technology will continue to be harnessed to 
improve all aspects of the turnaround, as can be seen in the vision for the Aircraft Journey in IATA’s NEXTT 
program; however, the industry must not lose sight of the importance of A-CDM. 
2.12.5 General Guidelines for A-CDM Implementation 
The decision to implement any Airport-ATFM Network Integration solution should be subject to 
comprehensive consultation with all stakeholders at the airport. Both the local focus of operations at the 
airport and the wider focus of links to ATFM should ideally be within the scope of an A-CDM implementation. 
Ensuring early engagement with stakeholders and instilling a collaborative culture will support the success of 
an A-CDM implementation. This process should create clarity across A-CDM stakeholders on the objectives 
and timescales of the implementation, and the expectations from each party. With clear and agreed objectives 
across all key stakeholders, A-CDM implementation should yield projected benefits and prevent suboptimal 
operations or limited benefits. 
As A-CDM represents a change in procedures and culture for all A-CDM stakeholders, which ultimately can 
be a challenge to manage through an implementation. The human element of A-CDM and the impact it can 
have on an organization and its employees should not be underestimated; it is by far the most challenging 
478 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022

aspect of an implementation. Compliance and adherence to agreed processes will ultimately drive 
performance and efficiency for all the stakeholders in the A-CDM chain. Additionally, of paramount importance 
is to ensure all parties are aligned and understand the rationale and wider benefits of change introduced by 
A-CDM. 
2.12.6 Common Objectives and Performance Metrics 
A-CDM is designed to improve overall airport efficiency through improved sequencing, surface management 
and departure control, as well as integrating departure control data between airports and ATM systems. 
Airports that implement A-CDM have reported derived benefits from reduced fuel burn, carbon emissions and 
radio transmission (R/T) congestion as well as increased resource optimization, operational transparency, and 
availability of useful data. A-CDM brings a common operational picture to all parties via agreed and accurate 
shared information, which enhances the decision-making process from a common set of objectives. They are:

2.12.7 A-CDM Roles and Responsibilities for Airport Operators 
Beyond the common A-CDM roles and responsibilities shared by all stakeholders, the airport operator is also 
typically responsible for: 
e Establishing an A-CDM Steering Group, consisting of all relevant stakeholders. At a minimum, the airport 
operator, ground handlers, ANSP and aircraft operators to deliver a realistic implementation roadmap 
* Overall coordination of the A-CDM process during implementation and operations, including monitoring 
the performance of A-CDM operations

2.12.8 Stakeholder Access to A-CDM Data 
A-CDM requires airport stakeholders to exchange timely operational information to enable collaboration and 
the efficient management of operations at an airport. Data exchange speed is extremely important among 
stakeholder A-CDM systems and should support the individual airport's requirements. This is especially 
important for the distribution of Target Start-up Approval Time (TSAT) generation in a live operation. 
An A-CDM Information Sharing Platform (ACISP), or portal, typically provided by the airport operator should 
keep all stakeholders situationally aware through the provision of complete and timely A-CDM data. The 
ACISP should permit the input of TOBT by the aircraft operator, or its contracted ground handling agent. The 
TOBT update, which is critical to A-CDM, should be available to the local aircraft operator/ground handling 
agent, and remote locations such as at the aircraft operator Operations Control Center. 
The A-CDM Steering Group should ensure that access to A-CDM data is provided to all stakeholders, using 
optimal connectivity patterns and standards-based messaging. All interfaces and APIs should support A-CDM 
at the global level using standard interfaces/APIs. Using a standardized format would limit the costs system 
vendors would pass on due to multiple incompatible interfaces/APIs. 
Currently, two messaging standards are available to support A-CDM. The IATA Aviation Information Data 
Exchange (AIDX) standard is suitable for A-CDM messaging between all stakeholders at the airport and the 
Flight Information Exchange Model (FIXM). The FIXM messaging format recommended by ICAO, is the 
480 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 500===
=Be [i IATA rill Planning for Collaborative Decision-Making 
targeted standard for Air Traffic Management (ATM) messaging. An A-CDM extension for FIXM is being 
developed by ICAO to support A-CDM. 
Data exchanges, via standards-based interfaces, should support the complete A-CDM dataset of elements 
and milestones. Full-scope messaging will provide context to enhance situational awareness. Regional 
airports lacking an ATFM unit, but wishing to cooperate between A-CDM implementations, should enable a 
distributed version of the ACISP supporting standard interfaces. 
2.12.9 Airport Infrastructure Required to Support A-CDM 
e Predeparture Sequencer 
o A predeparture sequencer is a technical enabler. Typically, under the responsibility of ATC and 
potentially a component of a Departure Manager (DMAN) system. The predeparture sequencing 
concept used TOBT and VTT as input to calculate the TSAT and TTOT. The TSAT ensures optimal 
aircraft start-up timing, hence these times should be integrated into the A-CDM ACISP. 
e Visual Displays for A-CDM Data 
o A-CDM requires the display of A-CDM data to provide situational awareness to stakeholders. This will 
likely require the integration of A-CDM data with stakeholder-facing FIDS. Displays at head-of-stand 
will also require the display of at least TOBT and TSAT so that apron service providers and flight crew 
are aware of the timelines for a turnaround. Displays at on-pier stands may be easier to establish than 
off-pier stands, where cabling conduits may be more challenging. An alternative approach would be 
the provisioning of standards-based APIs, so that stakeholders can develop their own display 
solutions. 
2.12.10 Efficiency Benefits to be Expected from A-CDM 
Given that each airport is unique with its own set of opportunities and constraints, efficiency benefits derived 
from an A-CDM implementation will differ from airport to airport. However, it would be reasonable to expect 
benefits typically achieved by A-CDM. A study of European A-CDM implementations observed the following 
efficiency benefits: 
e Average taxi-out time savings of between 0.25 and 3 minutes per departure 
e Average schedule adherence improvements of between 0.5 and 2 minutes per flight 
e Reduction in push-back delays after start-up approval 
e Increased ATFM slot adherence 
e Improved ground handling resource utilization 
e Reduction in the number of late stands and gate changes 
e Improved management of and recovery from adverse conditions 
e Reduction in Flight Activation Monitoring suspensions 
* Increased peak departure rates at the runway

===PAGE 501===
Te GB lV IATA al Airport Development Reference Manual 
e Improved takeoff time predictability by 85% during adverse conditions 
e Reduction in the standard deviation of takeoff accuracy from 14 to between 5 and 7 minutes 
e Departures from A-CDM airports receive fewer ATFM delays than departures from non-A-CDM airports, 
through the same restriction, by an average of 1 minute per flight 
Each of these efficiencies may not stand-alone but may bring associated benefits to several stakeholders. For 
example, 
e A reduction in taxi-out times saves fuel costs for aircraft operators and reduces environmental pollution for 
the airport operator. With the addition of improved takeoff predictability, aircraft operators can optimize 
single engine taxi to improve both benefits. 
e A reduction in the number of late stand and gate changes improves the passenger experience and 
combined with the reduction in push-back delays, results in the greater availability of stands and gates for 
the airport operator. 
¢ The combination of increased peak departure rates at the runway, reduction in ATFM delays and 
increased ATFM slot adherence, may allow the airport operator to reassess capacity calculations. 
e Amore precise projection of expected benefits from A-CDM implementation may be created by a detailed 
examination of an airport to map the efficiency of current processes to the spectrum of improvements that 
A-CDM can deliver.

Section 3—Facilities Planning 
3.1. Introduction 
Once the forecast has been established and agreed to by all parties and all the key elements have been 
considered (See Section 2-Key Considerations for Airport Development), airport development enters the 
facilities planning phase. Logically, the planning process moves from the more general level of detail through 
to the more specific where the different elements that comprise the airport are examined together and 
separately. 
The update of the ADRM is structured to reflect this progression. The Facilities Planning Section follows the 
discussion of Master Planning (see 2.3 Master Planning for more information). 
And continues with a comprehensive chapter for each major element of the airport starting with Airside 
Infrastructure (see 3.2 Airside Infrastructure) followed by the Passenger Terminal (see 3.3, Passenger 
Terminal for more information). Passenger terminals are certainly one of the most interesting and complex 
elements at any airport. This chapter also addresses Levels of Service (LoS) from both a quantitative and 
passenger perception point of view. LoS continue to be of interest as airport infrastructure particularly terminal 
facilities, continue to be stretched by the overall growth in aviation. 
Other facilities described in this section address: 
¢ Cargo Terminal planning 
e Airport Support Elements planning (catering, maintenance hangars, ground equipment facilities, etc.); and 
e Surface access systems planning (roads, rail, etc.) 
e Utilities 
3.2 Airside Infrastructure 
3.2.1 Runways 
3.2.1.1 System Overview 
Runways and their associated taxiways serve as a starting point for consideration of airport layouts. Due to 
their spatial requirements, effects on the surrounding areas and their relation to airspace, runways are difficult 
and costly to relocate and hence affect the whole airport impacting all its elements, functions and facilities. 
The planning process for the runway system requires continuous reviews at planning stage in order to 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 483 

===PAGE 503===
Se @— i 
IATA pall Airport Development Reference Manual 
produce an airport configuration offering the maximum overall efficiency. Since runways and taxiways are the 
least flexible of the airport elements, they are considered first. 
3.2.1.2 Capacity 
The fundamental capacity constraint of any airport lies in the runway system. Runway capacity puts a natural 
limit on the expansion capability of any airport. When the runway system itself becomes the main constraint of 
the airport capacity, very careful consideration needs to be given to identifying and eliminating factors 
affecting the reliable maximum aircraft flow that can be processed by runways. Every attempt should be made 
to ensure that all other critical subsystems (i.e., taxiways, aircraft parking positions, gates, passenger 
terminals and landside access systems) are ultimately in balance with the maximum runway throughput. For 
example, an imbalance between runway capacity and gate capacity will result in significant aircraft delays and 
a reduction in the airport's overall sustainable capacity. Delays and throughput are the main runway 
performance indicators. 
Runway capacity is defined as the hourly rate of aircraft operations (departures and/or arrivals) that can be 
reasonably accommodated by a runway or combination of runways, under specified local conditions. 
The Terminal Maneuvering Area (TMA) and runway capacity largely depend upon: 
e Runway occupancy time 
e Approach and departure spacing between successive aircraft 
© Design of the airspace 
e Mode of operation 
e Meteorological conditions 
¢ Contiguous airports 
Delays (including where and why they occur, and what is an acceptable level) are a primary indicator of level 
of service, and demonstrate that capacity is being reached or exceeded for a given system for a given 
baseline schedule. 
3.2.1.2.1 Factors Impacting Hourly Capacity 
Maximum capacity is based on operating conditions and rules, but is also largely dependent on the particular 
demand profiles created by the mix of flights and flight sectors for a typical busy day. Factors effecting the 
hourly capacity of an airport include (listed alphabetically): 
e = Aircraft mix 
e ATC procedures and equipment 
e Electrical and NAVAID infrastructure 
e Noise abatement procedures. 
484 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 504===
eB, n TL 
Se | IATA Biull Airside Infrastructure 
e Operational mode—mixed or segregated 
e Ratio and sequencing of arrivals and departures 
e Runway configuration 
e Runway occupancy time 
¢ Standard Instrument Departure (SID) availability 
e Standard Terminal Arrival Route (STAR) availability 
e Wake vortex separation minima 
e Weather conditions 
Aircraft Mix: The separation between aircraft depends on the aircraft category. Therefore, the mix of 
successive aircraft operating will have an impact on overall separation and runway capacity. For example, an 
airport operating with a majority of medium-size aircraft will have an average arrival separation of three 
nautical miles (NM). The same airport serving a mix of small, medium and heavy aircraft will have a 
separation of 3 to 6 NM, depending on the sequence of arrivals, and will have a significantly lower runway 
capacity. Some very congested airports have introduced aircraft sequencing to optimize the separation 
between aircraft. 
ATC Procedures and Equipment: The performance of radar equipment and other ATC limitations 
sometimes imposes a separation greater than the minima shown in Exhibit 3.2.1.2.2a. These limitations 
should be dealt with prior to considering investing in new runways. ATC staff training also may result in lower 
separations. Possible ways for ATC to increase runway capacity include: 
Precision Runway Monitor: PRM is surveillance radar that updates essential aircraft target information 
four to five times more often than conventional radar equipment. PRM also predicts the aircraft track and 
provides alarms when an aircraft is within ten seconds of penetrating the non-transgression zone. Use of 
PRM helps air traffic controllers ensure safe separation of aircraft on parallel approach courses and 
maintain an efficient rate of aircraft landings during adverse weather conditions. PRM is also used to allow 
simultaneous instrument approaches in adverse weather. 
Simultaneous Offset Instrument Approaches: The FAA SOIA procedure would allow simultaneous 
approaches to parallel runways spaced from 230 m (750 feet) to 910 m (3,000 feet) apart. It requires the 
use of a PRM, a straight-in Instrument Landing System (ILS) approach to one runway, and an offset 
Localizer Directional Aid (LDA) with glide slope approach to the other runway. 
The SOIA concept involves the pairing of aircraft along adjacent approach courses separated by at least 
910 m (3,000 feet) with a designated missed approach point approximately 3.5 NM from the runway 
threshold. The pilot on the offset approach would fly a straight-but-angled approach until descending 
below the cloud cover. At that point, the pilot would have a period of time to visually acquire the traffic on 
the other approach before continuing to the runway. If the pilot does not see the other aircraft before 
teaching the missed approach point, the approach would be discontinued. 
Operational Mode—Mixed or Segregated: Airports with two or more runways sometimes dedicate runways 
to either departures or arrivals. However, the arrival and departure peaks rarely coincide, and the separation 
between successive arrivals and successive departures are different. This results in gaps on one runway 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 485 

===PAGE 505===
IATA yi Airport Development Reference Manual 
when another is at capacity. In these situations, mixing arrivals and departures on both runways as if 
operating with a single runway can increase capacity. 
Ratio of Arrivals and Departures: The distribution of arrivals and departures during busy hours has an 
impact on runway capacity. ATC not only needs to consider separation between successive arrivals and 
successive departures, but also gaps between arrivals preceded or followed by departures. 
Runway Configuration: The layout of an airport and its runway configuration are another factor having an 
impact on airport capacity. An airport requiring significant crossing of an active runway to get to or from a gate 
will experience more delays than an airport with a terminal concept minimizing runway crossing. 
Parallel runways with adequate spacing (1,035 m or more) can process independent arrivals. Interaction 
between runways is a constraint when the distance between runways does not meet the minimum 
requirement, or when runways intersect. Independent parallel runways are recommended for that reason. 
Runway Occupancy Time: A succeeding aircraft cannot touch down until the preceding aircraft clears the 
runway. Exit taxiways that are optimally positioned and configured to support an airport's unique traffic mix will 
ensure that the time an aircraft physically spends on a runway is kept to a minimum. A maximum runway 
occupancy time of 50 to 55 seconds is recommended for airports with high numbers of aircraft movements 
during busy hours. The spacing between successive aircraft increases and thereby runway capacity 
decreases with higher occupancy times. RETs allow aircraft to turn off at higher speeds than right-angled 
exits, thus clearing the runway more quickly. 
Wake Turbulence: Used to describe the effect of rotating air masses generated behind the wingtips of jet 
aircraft that can affect aircraft operating behind them. Heavier aircraft generally generate more wake 
turbulence. It is difficult to control an aircraft operating too close to a leading aircraft, which is why separation 
minima are recommended. Small aircraft are more effected by wake vortex than heavier aircraft. Vortices 
dissipate over time, depending on wind conditions. 
3.2.1.2.2 Wake Turbulences and Separations 
Maximizing the efficiency of the existing runway system is recommended by improving operations and 
exploring latent capacity, before considering investing in new infrastructure. Maximum runway capacity should 
be determined using best practices, proper infrastructure and equipment, good weather conditions under 
Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) and Visual Meteorological Conditions (VMC) and with the fleet mix for a typical 
busy day. Runway capacity calculations require careful observation of the actual traffic schedule at an airport, 
particularly during typical peak periods. Landing and departure delays should be analyzed separately. 
The successful implementation of proper procedures, equipment and facilities can result in reduced aircraft 
separation and increased runway capacity. ICAO wake turbulence separation minima are based on aircraft 
mass. Exhibit 3.2.1.2.2a shows basic provisions governing wake turbulence in use.

3.2.1.2.3. Runway Movement Simulation 
Delays, if regularly observed over successive peak days/hours, are a primary indicator that capacity limits are 
being reached or exceeded. Routine delays will detract from the level of service provided. 
Simulation models are effective in predicting the impact of projected airline schedules on airside infrastructure, 
passenger terminals and surface access systems. They can be used to identify the nature, location and 
degree of congestion and to measure delays. Planned infrastructure improvements can also be validated 
through simulation. Care must be exercised in the provision of accurate data. It must also be recognized that 
use of such software should be entrusted to highly skilled and experienced operators who fully understand 
airport operations. 
The sustainable runway throughput is determined by increasing the peak demand until the runway system is 
saturated, while maintaining the same hourly distribution of traffic and fleet mix. Unlimited gate supply should 
also be assumed.

3.2.1.3. Access and Egress 
Runway access and egress is provided by a system of Runway Access Taxiways (RATs), RETs and 
perpendicular taxiways used as exits only. For more information see 3.2.2 Taxiways and Taxilanes. 
3.2.2 Taxiways and Taxilanes 
3.2.2.1 System Overview 
The runway-taxiways system functionality and capacity depend on the efficiency of the taxiway system 
serving the runway(s). Taxiways and taxilanes should be designed (dimensioned) according ICAO Annex 14 
Standards and Recommended Practices for today's and future critical aircraft to be able to operate at the 
airport. 
Taxiways provide a defined path between one part of the airport and another (e.g., between gates/aprons and 
the runway system). As such, taxiways constitute a network of interconnected elements serving both arriving 
and departing aircraft. 
Exhibit 3.2.2.1 shows the network of taxiways, taxilanes, holding bays and RETs at the Munich Airport.

3.2.2.2 Functionality 
The taxiway network should be designed to optimize runway throughput and reduce delays to an acceptable 
minimum. Phased implementation of RETs, parallel taxiways and holding bays should be considered in order 
to increase system capacity in a cost-efficient manner as demand requires. 
3.2.2.3 Simulation 
Runways and taxiways are interrelated systems. The runway simulations described in 3.2.1.3 Access and 
Egress should include the taxiways from/to the parallel taxiway(s), or even the gate or aircraft stand if a full 
airfield simulation is warranted. Taxiing distance and delays should be carefully studied considering their 
significant impact on operational costs and performance. 
490 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 510===
Airside Infrastructure 
3.2.2.4 Parallel Taxiways 
When planning new runways, sufficient space should always be allowed for a dual parallel taxiway system to 
be located adjacent and parallel to all runways. Where availability of land does not permit dual parallel 
taxiways, the airport planner should note that this may reduce the efficiency of aircraft movements on the 
ground and that the capacity of the single taxiway could then be the factor that determines runway capacity. 
For smaller airports with low peak aircraft movements in the long term, a single parallel taxiway may suffice. 
Parallel taxiways can also allow separation of arriving and departing aircraft, thereby optimizing traffic flows by 
distributing bi-directional flows to two taxiways. The separation between parallel taxiways should conform to 
ICAO Annex 14 minima, and should be based on the forecast fleet mix at the ultimate development stage (the 
optimal maximum throughput that can be achieved from the airport's runway system). Taxiways designed for 
queuing multiple departing aircraft are recommended to maximize runway throughput and minimize delays by 
allowing sequencing or re-sequencing of aircraft. 
Dual parallel taxiways, unless constructed for replacement airports where existing movements are known, 
should be constructed in phases, as demand requires. 
3.2.2.5 Cross-over Taxiways 
Dual parallel links or crossover taxiways should be incorporated into a master plan to connect two widely 
spaced parallel runways. The number of crossover taxiways should be related to the ultimate development 
potential of the site and may need to be checked using a simulation model. 
See Exhibit 2.3.7.2.8: Capacity of Parallel Taxiways for broad guidelines on the range of hourly movements 
that can be achieved from taxiways. 
3.2.2.6 Runway Access Taxiways 
Should parallel taxiway(s) exist, at least one RAT should be located at each runway end to provide sufficient 
runway distance for departing aircraft relative to the aircraft mix and to allow efficient access to the runway 
from the terminal apron area. For runways with higher amount of traffic, a second or even a third RAT at each 
tunway end may be justified to enable efficient aircraft queuing and sequencing before take-off, thereby 
increasing runway capacity. 
RATs should always intersect the runway at a 90-degree angle to enable the pilot of an aircraft at a taxiway 
holding position to see an aircraft using or approaching the runway. 
3.2.2.7 Rapid Exit Taxiways 
RETs are constructed to minimize aircraft runway occupancy time in order to increase runway capacity. 
Construction should only proceed after a thorough cost/benefit analysis has been undertaken. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 491

Optimal exit locations should be determined after considering: 
¢ For which operational conditions runway capacity should be enhanced (i.e., peak period, special weather 
conditions, particular group of aircraft, mixed mode) 
e The representative fleet mix that the exit is intended to serve 
e The separation distance between the runway and taxiway (i.e., on non-instrument runways, the separation 
distances may not allow for the design of a satisfactory RET) 
e The characteristics of aircraft concerning threshold speed, braking ability and turn-off speed for differing 
wind conditions 
Should the above highlight more than one optimal exit location, it may be necessary to consider construction 
of two or more RETs. Note that a distance of approximately 450 m between exits should be observed. 
Reference should be made to ICAO's Aerodrome Design Manual (Doc. 9157) to determine the precise 
geometry required for: 
e The radii of turn-off curves and fillets 
e The straight distance after turn-offs 
e The intersection angle of the RET

3.2.2.9 Holding Bays/Bypass Bays 
At runway ends, a holding position allows queuing aircraft awaiting takeoff to be reordered as determined by 
ATC. This optimized re-sequencing of aircraft (with airline approval) can assist in relieving climb and en-route 
ATC constraints. The holding position should be designed to accommodate two to four aircraft and allow 
sufficient space for one aircraft to bypass another. The area allotted for waiting aircraft will depend on their 
size and maneuverability. Holding aircraft should be placed outside the bypass route so that engine exhaust is 
directed away from other aircraft. Runway end holding positions should be orientated perpendicularly to the 
runway to allow crew to see aircraft approaching to land. 
Oblique entrance junctions are not recommended. For aircraft operating at or near maximum takeoff weight, 
the entry point should be as close to the end of the runway as possible. Small and medium-size aircraft that 
do not require the full extent of the available runway's length may be permitted to access the runway at 
intermediate access points. This provides another means by which ATC can reorder departing aircraft. Such 
access points should also have intermediate holding positions with all the associated and required clearances. 
Peak traffic volumes at many airports may exceed the capacity of a holding position resulting in aircraft 
queuing on the taxiway leading to the runway end. Reference should be made to ICAO Annex 14 for holding 
bay marking and lighting standards and recommended practices. 
3.2.2.10 De-Icing Pads 
Where required due to meteorological conditions and the airport's off-stand de-icing policy, de-icing pads may 
need to be considered as an integral part of the taxiway network. It is important to locate and size de-icing 
pads such that they can accommodate peak demand and match the maximum runway throughput in winter 
conditions. See 3.2.4.4 Aircraft De-icing/Anti-icing for more detailed information.

IATA i Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.2.2.11 Sustainability Considerations 
Proposals to reduce emissions from aircraft during taxiing include the use of: 
* Special towbarless tugs that operate under the direct control of the pilot 
e Towbarless tugs which are remote-controlled by a ground handler 
e Electrically powered landing gear wheels with battery/APU as the energy source 
* Application of A-CDM minimizes excessive queuing as it aims at a just-in-time departure from the gate to 
allow an unconstrained flow to the runway with minimal taxi-out delays. This is all part of a timely delivery 
of the aircraft into the ATM system, which reduces emissions and aids fuel conservation. 
3.2.2.12 Taxilanes 
Taxilanes are aircraft taxiing routes on aprons directly accessing aircraft stands. It should be noted that the 
separation distances between the taxilane centerline and an object are less than those between the taxiway 
centerline and an object. 
Single aircraft stand taxilanes giving access to more than six high-turnover cul-de-sac gates should be 
avoided, as the resultant delays due to constriction of free movement would place inefficiencies on airline 
operations. A dual taxilane should be provided in those cases where a cul-de-sac arrangement cannot be 
avoided. Reference should be made to ICAO Annex 14 for taxiway and taxilane marking and lighting 
standards and recommended practices. 
3.2.3 Aprons 
3.2.3.1 Overview 
The apron is a defined area, separate but connected to taxiways and taxilanes, intended to facilitate the 
arrival, movement, unloading, servicing, parking, loading and departure of aircraft. Aprons can be further 
divided by specific functions into passenger-, cargo-, General Aviation- or hangar aprons depending on the 
airport design and layout. 
The apron is effectively an interface between the passenger and cargo terminals and the taxiways and 
taxilanes (i.e. where passenger/baggage/cargo flows become aircraft flows and visa-versa). 
This apron system should be carefully planned so as not to become the factor that restricts the overall airport 
capacity. The number of gates and their availability should be calculated to match the forecast runway 
throughput, and in the ultimate phase of development, the optimal maximum throughput that can be achieved 
494 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 514===
Tata, ie Airside Infrastructure 
from the airport's runway system. In addition, overnight parking requirements (both at contact and remote 
stands) should be factored in. 
At some airports, aircraft subject to an ATC departure delay will vacate their stands at their scheduled 
departure time and absorb the delay on specially designed remote parking areas near the runway. 
Running an apron aircraft flow simulation, including realistic gate assignment and pushback procedures, is an 
effective way to ensure minimal delays and identify potential/existing bottlenecks (see 2.11.4.5 Airside 
Simulation). 
Contact stands have a significant impact on the quality of service provided to users because they allow for 
more rapid and comfortable handling of passengers, avoid the need for buses, and enable better turnaround 
times. Contact gates are often essential in providing reliable MCTs in support of airlines’ and airport operators’ 
commercial objectives—especially at hub airports. Contact gates are required at airports with frequent adverse 
weather conditions. 
3.2.3.2 Aircraft Parking Arrangements 
3.2.3.2.1 Main Aircraft Stand Elements 
A typical aircraft stand consists of the following elements: 
e The aircraft parking area 
e GSE stillage area near the head of stand, delignated by appropriate markings 
e Passenger Boarding Bridges (PBB) 
e Fixed service equipment (“apron furniture”). 
These elements will be described in the following sub-sections.

IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.2.3.2.2 Aircraft Characteristics 
The apron geometry is driven by the dimensions and types of aircraft intending to use them. All aircraft 
manufacturers publish Aircraft/Airplane Characteristics for Airport Planning. 
These publications contain the minimum aircraft data required for general airport planning. The data 
presented on aircraft maneuvering represent maximum capability in terms of the geometry of each aircraft 
type. Since airline operational practices vary, it is always necessary to adjust this information in consultation 
with user airlines at the respective airport to determine values appropriate for the planned function of the 
apron prior to the start of detailed design. 
3.2.3.2.3. Clearance Requirements 
The application of adequate clearance margins in the development of apron layouts is essential to ensure 
acceptability by airport authorities and operability by GSE vehicles and staff. 
The apron and associated fixed equipment, as well as aircraft parked on the apron, are part of the total airport 
system which, in operational terms, is subject to the requirements for the safe conduct of flight operations. 
These requirements-in the form of Standards and Recommended Practices in \CAO Annex 14-have achieved 
universal acceptance as good aircraft operating practice. They recognize the need to conduct operations in a 
broad range of circumstances while achieving an acceptable level of performance and safety. 
Clearances in the following categories must be taken into account in the planning and design of apron 
layouts: 
Flight Operations: The practical effect of these requirements on apron planning is to provide adequate 
separation between apron areas, active taxiways and active runways. Other requirements are to restrict the 
height of fixed apron equipment and parked aircraft according to their distance from the runway and their 
position relative to it. These limitations are stated in ICAO Annex 14. If stand development is being considered 
at existing airports that could infringe on these clearance requirements, either by existing buildings or fixed 
facilities, the situation should be brought to the attention of the Airport Licensing Authority. 
Aircraft Ground Movement: The layout of apron areas must provide the clearance requirements for aircraft 
moving over the taxiway system between the runway system and the aircraft parking stands. 
Clearances should be provided for aircraft on the basis that they are capable of following the taxiway 
centerline. Due regard should be given to the ability of the aircraft type having the longest wheelbase to follow 
curved guidelines and the tendency of the wingtip on the outside of the turn to cover a greater area than when 
proceeding in a straight line. On apron taxiways and aircraft stand taxilanes, the minimum clearance between 
taxiing aircraft and parked aircraft, buildings or fixed obstructions should be as given in ICAO Annex 14. 
Where an aircraft taxies into a nose-in position in front of a building structure, a minimum clearance of 4.5 m 
between the structure and the nose of the aircraft is sufficient, provided an effective stopping guidance system 
is available. In such cases, sufficient clearance at apron level should also be allowed to facilitate the 
maneuvering of tractors and tow bars into position for the pushback operation. If a service road is located in 
496 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 516===
ay 
NG 
IATA 4 Airside Infrastructure 
front of the aircraft and can be used for tow tractor maneuvering, a distance of 15 m is required between the 
aircraft nose gear and the service road. 
The design of taxiways should include a minimal number of changes in direction. Where a change in direction 
is unavoidable, this should be accomplished by means of a large-radius transitional curve. Aircraft stands and 
taxiway layouts should not be developed on the basis of aircraft minimum radius turns. Where aircraft are 
required to turn from the taxiway or taxilane onto a stand centerline, a distance of at least half the length of 
the aircraft should be provided in order to achieve alignment following completion of the planned turn. 
Ground Service Equipment Operation: The type, quantity and method of operation of ground service 
equipment will vary widely from airport to airport (and widely within an airport), due to the range of aircraft 
types served, the equipment specifications and the procurement policies of the different ground service 
providers (GSPs). It is, therefore, essential that local requirements for space and clearances be established 
by consultation with the airlines. 
In favorable situations, the clearances required for the operation of GSE on the aircraft stand can be 
contained within the overall dimensions of the aircraft and the surrounding aircraft ground movement 
clearances (see 3.2.4.5 Ground Support Equipment Parking). 
In less favorable situations, additional space or clearances may be required when: 
* Transporters (e.g., buses, mobile lounges or other specialized vehicles) are used to convey passengers 
between the passenger terminal and aircraft on remote stands 
« Mobile tankers/bowsers are used in the absence of hydrant fueling 
* Other items of equipment, either individually or collectively, are exceptionally large or unwieldy 
¢ Large exchanges of baggage, cargo or mail are required during short turnaround or transit operations 
(this is particularly relevant with the operation of combi-aircraft) 
¢ The baggage sortation area and/or the cargo terminal is located remotely from the passenger terminal 
apron, with the distance and transportation times necessitating forward staging areas for baggage, cargo, 
or both 
e The overall aircraft size or wingspan is limited 
3.2.3.2.4 Multiple Aircraft Ramp System 
Aircraft stand layouts are dependent on many factors, both technical and financial. With respect to the 
financial objective, it is essential for an airport to be as efficient as possible so that stand layouts can 
accommodate an optimum number of parked aircraft combinations. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 497 

===PAGE 517===
w IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
Aircraft stands can be dedicated to a particular aircraft type, however, in so doing a degree of operational 
flexibility is lost. Alternatively, certain modes of operation can allow stands to be configured to permit the 
mixing of wide-body and narrow-body aircraft on a single Multiple Aircraft Ramp System (11) (MARS) layout. 
All layouts must be in accordance with ICAO Annex 14 stand and taxiway layout standards and 
recommendations. 
MARS entails a system that allows for handling of a mixture of aircraft types and sizes on a designated part of 
the apron, providing the airport with a certain degree of flexibility. 
MARS Stand Configuration 
A MARS stand configuration is most commonly defined as a configuration of three partly overlapping aircraft 
stands, enabling the airport to accommodate either one wide-body aircraft or two independent narrow-body 
aircraft simultaneously. However, other configurations are also conceivable. 
Within a typical MARS stand configuration, some constraints apply: 
e With the wide-body stand in use, both narrow-body stands are not available 
e With one of two narrow-body stands in use, the wide-body stand is not available 
e The two narrow-body stands can operate simultaneously 
Other aircraft stands adjacent to a MARS stand configuration are not affected by the mode of operation at that 
particular MARS stand configuration. 
Exhibit: 3.2.3.2.4a: MARS Stand Use-Example 
| {CODEE [CODEC 
MARS stand configurations lead to a more flexible and efficient use of apron and terminal infrastructure, and 
they increase airport resilience with respect to uncertainties tied to airport growth. However, it should also be 
noted that this additional flexibility can be limited by the added complexity impact on airport operations. 
Source: Jacobs 
498 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 518===
Se o.- IATA al Airside Infrastructure 
Fluctuations in Stand Demand 
Application of a MARS stand configuration enables the airport to better absorb short-term fluctuations (daily, 
weekly, seasonal) in stand demand in terms of aircraft size. When the terminal infrastructure is equipped to 
support swing operations at the MARS stand configuration, operational flexibility is further increased. 
Apron and Terminal Infrastructure 
Due to the flexibility of MARS stand configurations, an increased stand utilization can be expected, allowing 
the airport to handle the same volume of traffic with less airport infrastructure in comparison to a situation in 
which a mixture of dedicated single-use wide-and narrow-body stands is planned for. 
Application of MARS stand configurations, especially in a constrained airport environment, could contribute to 
a reduction of the total required pier frontage, resulting in a more compact airport design. Requirements with 
respect to apron area, terminal floor area and number of passenger boarding bridges can also be lowered. 
Futureproofing 
MARS stand configurations contribute to future-proofing the airport. Predictions with respect to future air traffic 
growth and fleet development of individual airlines always come with a degree of uncertainty. Application of 
MARS stand configurations helps ensure that various growth scenarios can be accommodated more easily by 
the airport. 
Airline Allocation 
MARS stand configurations introduce a larger degree of freedom with respect to airline allocation. Airlines are 
often assigned to designated areas of the airport. Airlines mainly operating flights using wide-body aircraft are 
typically assigned to areas with sufficient wide-body stands. Similarly, airlines mainly operating flights using 
narrow-body aircraft are typically assigned to areas with sufficient narrow-body stands. MARS stand 
configurations provide the airport with increased flexibility in terms of airline allocation, since the airport is no 
longer forced to designate airlines to certain parts of the airport infrastructure. 
Impact on Ground Support Operations 
GSE required to handle aircraft varies between wide-and narrow-body aircraft. Since the stand layout of a 
MARS stand configuration typically leaves very little free space for GSE parking when both wide-and narrow￾body aircraft stands are to remain available, frequent switching between wide-and narrow-body aircraft limits 
the ground handlers’ ability to park GSE at the stand awaiting the next flight. The added logistical complexity 
of having to move around GSE could, therefore, result in the operational decision to use a MARS stand 
configuration either as a wide-body or narrow-body stand over a longer period of time. 
Swing Operations 
Swing operation capabilities at MARS stand configurations allow the airport to handle a wide array of both 
wide-and narrow-body aircraft departing to or originating from destinations within various sectors, i.e. 
domestic or international. Typically, to facilitate swing operation capabilities at MARS stand configurations, a 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 499 

===PAGE 519===
IATA a Airport Development Reference Manual 
much more elaborate terminal infrastructure is required, ensuring segregated passenger flows (refer to 
Section 5 for further information). MARS stand configurations with swing operation capabilities should, 
therefore, only be considered when justified by current (or future) air traffic characteristics, in line with the 
strategic objectives for overall airport development. 
Take note that for a typical hub operation, with narrow-body aircraft for domestic traffic and wide-body aircraft 
for international traffic, the narrow-and wide-body aircraft peaks may coincide, facilitating fast transfers. Under 
these circumstances, application of MARS stand configurations will not be advantageous. However, in the 
case of a typical O/D operation, with narrow-and wide-body aircraft peaks likely to occur during different parts 
of the day, MARS stand configurations with swing operation capability could contribute to airport efficiency. 
Demand for MARS Stand Configurations 
The potential demand for MARS stand configurations is related to: 
¢ Subdivision of overall air traffic demand into relevant subsets 
e The demand for operational wide-and narrow-body stands during the overall aircraft stand peaks in 
relation to each relevant air traffic demand subset 
¢ The number of planned (or existing) operational wide-and narrow-body stands for each relevant air traffic 
demand subset 
¢ The ability to accommodate narrow-body aircraft on wide-body stands 
Stand Size 
The overall width of a Code E MARS stand is determined by the combined width required for two narrow-body 
stands, whereas the width of a Code F stand is typically determined by the Code F aircraft width. The depth 
of a MARS stand configuration is typically determined by the wide-body stand. 
Passenger Boarding Bridge 
The main objective of PBB planning and design at a MARS stand configuration is to ensure that each of the 
narrow-body stands can be serviced by a single PPB. The wide-body stand should be served by two (or 
possibly three for Code F) PBBs simultaneously. The MARS stand configuration should take into account the 
large variety of aircraft types and sizes to be accommodated. 
Apron Services 
When planning for the infrastructure of apron services for MARS stand configurations, fuel hydrant pits should 
be positioned in a way they can be used by wide-body and the narrow-body stands respectively. 
e Two independent PCA connections serving the narrow-body stands are to be provided. Take note that 
when a system is adopted where PCA units are mounted under/at the PBBs, each PBB serving a narrow￾body stand should be equipped with an independent PCA unit. 
* A Visual Docking Guidance System (VDGS) is to be provided for each aircraft stand that is part of the 
MARS stand configuration.

Terminal Infrastructure 
As previously mentioned, swing operation capability at a MARS stand configuration adds to the complexity of 
the required terminal infrastructure. Additional information can be found in 3.3.5.9.1 MARS Stand

3.2.3.2.5 Contact Stands 
Contact stands are aircraft parking stands that can be directly accessed directly from the terminal or satellite 
building without the need of a bussing operation. 
The contact stand can be used in conjunction with passenger boarding bridges, ground servicing vehicles 
(except buses), or apron stairs. However, it is recommended that contact stands should be accessed with 
passenger boarding bridges wherever possible to improve customer service standards. For further details on 
passenger boarding bridges, please see 3.2.3.4 Passenger Boarding Bridges. 
Contact stands are usually an integral part of the pier, satellite or main terminal, comprising: 
1. Fixed link bridge from terminal or pier structure to rotunda: 
(a) With segregated departure and arrival routes, or 
(b) With mixed departures and arrivals on a single route 
Rotunda 
Emergency stair node 
Stand area 
Passenger boarding bridge(s) 
on F YN
Optional chute/conveyor to move items that cannot be accommodated safely in overhead bins (e.g., child 
strollers, oversized bags, etc.) to the apron and aircraft hold 
Contact stands are the preferred solution for airlines, passengers and staff. They are more economical to 
operate than a comparably sized and served remote stand due their reduced requirement for vehicles, fuel, 
staff and time. The contact stand can also be configured to be used in conjunction with all three types of PBB 
(see 3.2.3.4.2 Passenger Boarding Bridges Types). 
Having established the mix of aircraft required to meet flight schedule criteria, it will be necessary to 
accommodate those aircraft types physically on the available apron area. It is essential that the correct 
number and type of aircraft be understood, with contingency consideration for late aircraft turnaround. Contact 
stands should be considered prime apron areas and should be allocated accordingly. Contact stands should 
be used to serve the majority of aircraft traffic as determined from the flight schedule.

IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
Where wide-body aircraft (Code E/F) are to be served, it is recommended that the gate be provided with two 
PBBs to facilitate quicker deplaning and boarding of passengers. A third bridge for A380 aircraft provides 
additional passenger convenience and faster embarkation/disembarkation times.

3.2.3.2.6 Apron-walk Stands 
Similar to contact stands, apron-walk stands are situated in close proximity to the terminal building. However, 
without the provision of a PBB, passengers access their aircraft by walking directly to the aircraft and embark 
via mobile stairs either just at the front or both front and back. Passenger comfort is reduced as they are 
exposed to the prevailing weather conditions. However, the airport operator saves capital and operational cost 
by not installing PBBs, which may reduce airlines’ fees and therefore ticket costs. 
To avoid conflicts with GSE vehicle traffic on the head-of-stand road or on the stand, dedicated walking areas 
to/from aircraft are recommended, safely segregating passengers from vehicles. 
3.2.3.2.7 Remote Stands 
Remote stands serve operational and non-operational purposes. Operational remote stands are accessed via 
passenger buses from the terminal building. Non-operational stands are typically used for long-term parking, 
or before and after maintenance procedures. 
When considering the introduction or extension of remote stands, the following factors should be considered: 
¢ The layout of remote stands must not interfere with apron taxilanes or runway clearance requirements 
e Aircraft maneuvering considerations for contact stands also apply to remote stands 
e Since remote stands are often located in close proximity to active taxiways, careful consideration must be 
given to entrance and exit procedures as well as the effects of engine exhaust velocities 
502 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 522===
Py 
2533, IATA Boul Airside Infrastructure 
Apron drainage must be in conformity with local building codes and environmental regulations (e.g., 
special treatment may be required for spills of aircraft fuel or de-icing fluid-see ICAO Annex 14) 
The economic viability of providing remote stands as opposed to contact stands must be established, 
including the cost of operating and maintaining buses/mobile lounges. 
Remote stands give more flexibility in assigning aircraft stands, especially for flights with long turnaround 
times, overnight stays, technical delays, or flights having special security requirements 
At the outset it must be clearly established what aircraft types will operate on the remote stands so they 
may be appropriately sized 
For a safe operation, it is important to have appropriate apron floodlighting 
3.2.3.2.8 Taxi-in/Pushback vs. Taxi-in/Taxi-out 
There are pros and cons regarding the choice between taxi-out and pushback parking configurations, as 
illustrated in Exhibit 3.2.3.2.8a:

Additional pier length is required for taxi-out at contact- or apron-walk stands 
Engine exhaust velocities and the effects from turning aircraft have to be considered 
Use of PBBs is easier to accommodate for taxi-in/push-out 
Taxi-out eliminates the need for push-back vehicles.
