In general, pushback configurations are favored at high-volume airports, and taxi-out configurations are more 
often considered at lower-volume airports, especially when using smaller regional-type aircraft (where 
maneuvering space is less restricted). In all cases, a study must be conducted considering present and 
foreseeable conditions that may influence aircraft parking configurations. 
The main advantages of the taxi-in/pushback configuration are: 
* Reduction in apron congestion due to the ability to position ground equipment immediately adjacent to the 
aircraft parking position 
e Aircraft parking guidance systems can be relatively simple 
° The effects of engine exhaust velocities on equipment, personnel and terminal facilities is substantially 
lessened and the requirement for blast fences is reduced or eliminated 
« Passenger boarding bridges can be easily deployed 
e The total area of the apron pavement and related costs are kept to the minimum 
A disadvantage of the taxi-in/pushback configuration is that it requires additional aircraft tow tractors and 
associated personnel to perform the pushback. Aircraft tow tractors are costly, especially those designed to 
handle wide-body aircraft. Procurement and operating costs, plus frequency of usage, must be balanced 
against the factors outlined above. 
3.2.3.2.9 Isolated Aircraft Parking Positions 
Aircraft stands or other suitable areas are required for accepting hijacked aircraft. These special stands 
should aid the anti-terrorist police force and reduce the risk of potential injury to passengers resulting from 
deliberate unlawful action upon the aircraft and its passengers and crew. 
The isolated aircraft parking position may also be located on a remote part of the taxiway network, but in any 
case should be located at the maximum distance possible from other aircraft parking positions, buildings, 
public areas, and the airport perimeter. If taxiways or runways pass within this area, they may have to be 
closed to normal operations when a ‘suspect’ aircraft is in the area. Planners should seek input on ideal 
locations for these positions from the security or law-enforcement agencies that would respond to such 
incidents. 
The isolated aircraft parking position may also serve as a ‘security parking area’, where an aircraft threatened 
with unlawful interference may be parked as long as necessary. In this special area, aircraft could be 
positioned to unload passengers, cargo, mail or stores during a bomb threat. 
Care should be taken to ensure that the isolated position is not located over underground utilities such as 
gasoline or aviation fuel networks, water mains, or electrical/communications cables. Consideration should 
also be given to the prevailing wind direction and aircraft landing and takeoff routing at the airport, so as to 
minimize disruption to airport operations and the surrounding locality in the event of an aircraft fire or release 
of dangerous substances from the aircraft.

3.2.3.3 Visual Docking Guidance Systems 
With the adoption of nose-in parking and PBBs, it is necessary to provide a guidance system to assist the 
pilot in positioning the aircraft accurately. The UK CAA Visual Aids Handbook (CAP 637) is a good reference 
to current best industry practice on AGNIS and PAPA installations. 
The following topics must be addressed during the planning and development of VDGS, and the appropriate 
positioning of the aircraft stop lines: 
Pilot Responsibility: The pilot should be provided with an unambiguous system that allows accurate 
guidance of the aircraft to the final parking position, and indicates the rate of closure with the desired stopping 
position. 
Accuracy: The system must recognize the aircraft type and provide the parking accuracy required on the 
particular airport or apron. This should be established by the airport authorities and airlines jointly. Points to 
be considered include: 
e The performance of the PBBs 
e The positions of fueling hydrants and dispenser hose lengths available 
e The space required for all aircraft ground servicing activities. 
3.2.3.4 Passenger Boarding Bridges 
The basic requirements for the passenger boarding bridge to aircraft interface can be found in the IATA 
Airport Handling Manual (AHM) 922. The AHM outlines the general functional requirements for the interface of 
either a passenger boarding bridge or a passenger transfer vehicle with aircraft passenger doors. The aim is 
to permit the safe transfer of passengers, avoid interference with protrusions on the aircraft fuselage and 
reduce the risk of damage. 
3.2.3.4.1 Objectives 
PBB are extensively used by airports worldwide and assist airport operations by: 
* Potentially reducing disembarkation and embarkation times by nearly 25% when compared to 
conventional steps and buses (when appropriate numbers of PBB are used) 
e Improving passenger and staff safety 
e Improving the passenger experience, particularly in extreme climates, since the transfer to and from the 
aircraft is in a controlled environment and away from adverse weather such as rain, snow, high humidity 
and heat 
¢ Improving access for PRMs and reducing staff injuries handling PRMs via alternative, non-automated 
means of access 
e Providing a means of escape from the aircraft in case of an emergency

3.2.3.4.4 The Rotunda and Link Bridge 
The rotunda is the main support mechanism for all PBBs. The location of the rotunda is the single most critical 
unit on the stand as every other component, including the aircraft, will be positioned around the location 
chosen for the rotunda. It is important to select a position for the rotunda that will permit the PBBs to: 
e Reach all aircraft likely to use the apron 
¢ Allow aircraft to be parked such that they do not clash with building structures or other aircraft 
e Create a link bridge clearance that permits vehicles to pass beneath them

e Parked position of all aircraft

e Apron slope characteristics

3.2.3.5 Stand Capacity 
The capacity of the runway, taxiway and apron systems are dynamic, as they relate to the ability to process 
traffic flows, which are in constant flux. The capacity of the aircraft stand system is related to the ability to 
accumulate aircraft, which is a static capacity. The number of aircraft parking stands for different types/sizes 
of aircraft is calculated to meet current and future requirements. This information is essential to develop 
realistic and cost-effective airport concepts, and to ensure capacity balance. 
The majority of airlines seek to minimize turn round times and maximize aircraft utilization. However, some 
schedules, particularly those for long-haul flights, may require aircraft to remain on the ground between early￾morning arrival and late-evening departure. Short to medium-haul aircraft may overnight at their home base or 
may be positioned at outstations to enable early-morning connections on return to their home base. 
Stand shortages can occur because: 
e Demand exceeds available capacity 
e There is a higher-than-expected large aircraft demand; or 
e Aircraft remain on stand for an extended amount of time 
This highlights that the key aspects of stand availability are: 
e The number of stands provided for different types/sizes of aircraft 
¢ The availability of these stands as influenced by occupancy times (possibly ranging from less than an 
hour to in excess of 10 hours) 
e Availability of multiple aircraft ramp system stands 
e The terminal(s) being served by the stands 
e Whether the stands are contact or remote.

===PAGE 530===

IATA ‘4 Airside Infrastructure 
3.2.3.5.1 Turnaround Times (TRT) 
Vision 
A fully coordinated aircraft turnaround processes, using the latest in automation, safety and environmentally 
friendly technologies to increase predictability. Refer to NEXTT aircraft journey. 
Stand occupancy time is an important factor in establishing capacity. When conducting a gate assessment 
study, the actual processing and servicing times should be observed and recorded. Airlines operating at the 
airport should be consulted to identify suitable TRTs for different aircraft types, traffic segments and business 
models. The use of swing gates and other flexible terminal solutions is fundamental to accommodate demand 
from multiple flight sectors. 
3.2.3.5.2 Capacity Enhancements 
Possibilities for flexible use of aircraft operational stands (e.g., two small aircraft on one large stand) should 
be kept in mind when assessing the maximum capability of a layout. The parking configuration adopted (e.g., 
taxi-in/push-back versus taxi-in/taxi-out) may not impact on-stand capacity, but could have a significant impact 
on the overall apron capacity. Availability of fixed servicing equipment such as hydrant re-fueling, which help 
to reduce TRT, should also be considered. 
3.2.3.5.3 Stand Assessment and Gate Assignment Studies 
While there is a physical limit on the number of aircraft that can be simultaneously accommodated at an 
airport, operational factors such as gate assignment policy, exclusive/preferential use, and handling of the 
aircraft by ATC impact the practical capacity of the system. The inputs required to conduct a gate assignment 
study include: 
e Busy day flight schedule 
e Apron plan indicating all contact and remote stands 
e List of all contact and remote stands by range of aircraft accommodated and sectors accepted/preferred 
e Policy regarding exclusive and/or preferential use 
e Operational parameters, such as: 
o Buffer time between flights using the same gate (either on a gate-by-gate basis or globally) 
o Minimum tow-on and tow-off time by aircraft 
o Minimum ground time before an aircraft is considered a candidate for towing 
© Potential separation of gates for international, regional or domestic traffic. 
Gate assignment study results (i.e., the number of gates by class of aircraft and by sector) and gate utilization 
can be shown in a Gantt chart.

3.2.4.2 Access 
3.2.4.2.1 Pedestrian Pathways 
Pedestrian pathways across service roads should be provided. Pedestrian walkways should be clearly 
indicated and located so as to keep pedestrians clear of hazards. 
3.2.4.2.2 Service Roads 
Basic planning requirements for airside roads are as follows: 
«The service roads between the cargo terminal and the aircraft must be capable of accepting ULD 
transporter equipment 
* Adequate bearing strength, height clearances and turning radii must be provided to accommodate existing 
and projected service and ground support equipment, including tow tractors, when applicable 
¢ Must comply with the requirements of ACI's Apron Markings and Signs Handbook 
e Recommended width of 10 m (dual lane) and a clearance height of 4.2 m (up to 4.5 m, depending on 
most onerous vehicles). The latter is of particular concern with regard to service roads that pass under 
sections of the terminal building and/or passenger loading bridges 
¢ Adequate separation must be provided from runways, taxiways or other areas where aircraft maneuver, in 
accordance with ICAO Annex 14 
e Where necessary, adequate roadway width to permit overtaking of slow-moving ground support 
equipment must be provided 
There are two possible locations for service roads accessing aircraft stands: 
¢ Behind the aircraft (referred to as back-of-stand or tail-of-stand road) 
* Between the front of the aircraft stand and the terminal building (referred to as head-of-stand road). 
Each type of road has its advantages and disadvantages. Since a lot of operational activity tends to occur 
around the forward portion of the aircraft, a head-of-stand road is required in most cases. However, the 
disadvantage with this type of service road is that the clearance height necessary to allow certain types of 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 513 

===PAGE 533===
we IATA - Hi. Airport Development Reference Manual 
service vehicles (i.e., aircraft catering vehicles) to pass underneath may create a major problem with the 
height or slope of the passenger loading bridge or the elevation of the departure gate lounge. 
When the service road is located next to the terminal building, adequate room must be provided for the 
aircraft pushback tractor to maneuver. 
Back-of-stand roads are often provided in addition to head-of-stand roads at busy airports. They are not used 
for through-traffic, but rather accessing the rear of aircraft and thereby alleviating congestion on the stand and 
on the head-of-stand road. When only back-of-stand roads are provided, it involves traffic coming off the 
service road and past the aircraft wings and engines when approaching the front of the aircraft. Movement 
around these areas must be done with extreme caution. 
3.2.4.3 On-stand Services 
3.2.4.3.1 Distributed Electrical Power 
Power required by aircraft can be supplied either directly through a fixed installation providing 400 Hz to each 
stand, or through 50/60 Hz industrial-type power that can be converted into 400 Hz by means of mobile 
converters. This latter solution has broader applications (e.g., heating or air-conditioning). A 400 Hz unit can 
be located in the head-of-stand area, feeding the aircraft by cable or through a pop-up supply unit next to the 
front of the aircraft. 
The justification for a fixed 400 Hz installation must be established versus the use of aircraft APUs, mobile 
diesel GPUs, or mobile electric converters connected to 50/60 Hz power outlets at each stand. Such 
justification may depend on the usage hours per day, calculated based on the average year, a typical stand 
will be occupied by an active (being serviced) aircraft. Other justifications are cost (higher installation cost, but 
lower operating cost), the reduction of GSE vehicles on the stand and, often as a guiding reason, an airport's 
sustainability targets. 
3.2.4.3.2 50/60Hz Systems 
An alternate solution to providing 200 V/400 Hz AC electric power outlets is to provide multi-purpose 50/60 Hz 
industrial power outlets on each stand. This solution frequently offers more flexibility and a lower mean 
operating cost. The same outlets, or a set of outlets on the same distribution system, may be used for a 
variety of requirements.

IATA Airside Infrastructure 
3.2.4.3.3. Preconditioned Air 
Fixed installations for supplying low-pressure, preconditioned (i.e., heated or cooled) air to aircraft include a 
variety of available technologies, such as: 
* Centralized systems distributing low-pressure, preconditioned air to a number of stands from a heating or 
cooling plant located in a central technical room. The plant may be independent technologies (e.g., 
electrical, ice storage, peak shaving, etc.) or based on heat exchangers fed by the terminal building's own 
hot or chilled water distribution system 
e Decentralized systems including a fixed air-conditioning/heating unit at each stand, with a heat exchanger 
fed by the hot or chilled water distribution system of the terminal building or an independent system (e.g., 
electrical, ice storage, peak shaving, etc.) 
¢ Decentralized systems including an independent fixed air-conditioning/heating unit at each stand 
Fixed, preconditioned air supply must be evaluated versus the use of aircraft APUs, or mobile diesel ACUs, or 
mobile electric ACUs at each stand. The decision usually depends on the combined result of: 
e How many hours per day in an average year a typical stand will be occupied by an active (being serviced) 
aircraft needing PCA 
¢ The desire to reduce the number of GSE vehicles on the stand 
¢ Sustainability considerations, since lowering the number of vehicles through fixed installations results in 
lower ground-borne emissions and noise.

3.2.4.3.4 Pneumatic Air 
Pneumatic generation and distribution systems for high-pressure air supply to aircraft are intended to provide 
the compressed air necessary to start jet engines on the stands when the APU pneumatic function is not to be 
used or inoperative. Due to the high peak of power consumption (flow + pressure) required, no decentralized 
alternative (except conventional mobile ASUs of either the diesel or turbine-powered type) has been made 
available. In general, installation of a pneumatic system is considered due to sustainability drivers, as noise 
and emissions are reduced through fixed units. 
3.2.4.4 Aircraft De-icing/Anti-icing 
Safe and efficient aircraft operations are of primary importance in the development of any aircraft de-icing 
facility, if dictated by prevailing weather conditions at the respective airport. The requirements for a de-icing 
operation will differ greatly for each airport. While remote primary de-icing may be desirable at one airport, 
gate de-icing (with or without remote secondary facilities) may be appropriate at others. Operational and ATC 
matters may be paramount at one airport, while environmental concerns may predominate at another. These 
are just some of the many options to be considered where de-icing operations are concerned. See 3.6.5 
Aircraft Deicing/Anti-Icing Facilities for additional information.

3.2.4.5 Ground Support Equipment Parking 
3.2.4.5.1 Introduction 
Ground servicing equipment must be parked in areas near the aircraft stands to be readily available when 
required. Such areas should be sized to accommodate all equipment used on a regular basis to support 
aircraft servicing for all types of aircraft usually served in a particular apron sector. Such areas should be 
clearly defined by appropriate apron markings. 
Long-term parking facilities must be provided for ramp equipment with convenient access to the apron area. 
At airports with harsh winter weather conditions, a heated ground equipment shelter will be required for 
parking certain types of ground-servicing equipment overnight. For airports with a high number of sun hours 
and excessive heat, shaded parking areas may be required. 
3.2.4.5.2 Equipment Parking Areas 
These are specific areas set aside for the parking of ground handling equipment, and include long-term 
parking, short-term parking and staging areas. 
When designing equipment parking areas, consideration should be given to coordinating the long-term, 
short-term and staging area requirements, including the size and type of equipment. Particular attention 
should be paid to the staging areas close to the aircraft. 
The size of each parking area depends on the types, numbers and dimensions of vehicles to be used at the 
airport. The number of ground handling agents also influences the area sizes, as with more handlers, 
additional equipment needs to be stored. The areas can be calculated by the planners and should include 
operational contingencies as well as expansion safeguarding.

3.2.5 Air and Ground Navigation Aids 
3.2.5.1 Visual Aids 
3.2.5.1.1 Introduction 
Visual aids are designed to increase the conspicuity of the runway, provide visual reference in the final stages 
of the approach and landing, and to expedite ground movement. Their importance increases as visibility 
becomes limited. There are three basic groupings of visual aids used by pilots for specific types of positional 
reference: 
4. Approach, runway centerline, and runway edge lighting and markings allow pilots to assess lateral 
position and cross-track velocity 
2. Approach and threshold lighting and markings provide a roll reference 
3. Touchdown zone (TDZ) lighting and markings indicate the plane of the runway surface and show the 
touchdown area providing vertical and longitudinal reference. 
The visual guidance derived from runway lights and/or markings should be sufficient to ensure adequate 
takeoff alignment and directional control for takeoff and stopping, whether after landing or in an emergency. 
Although additional instruments, such as head-up displays, may enhance the safety of the operation, 
reference to visual aids is a primary requirement even when some form of ground run monitor and displays 
based on the use of external non-visual guidance are being used. The criteria for approach lighting, runway 
lighting and runway markings are contained in ICAO Annex 14. Where appropriate, reflective beads may be 
added to the runway/taxiway paint to increase conspicuity. 
Visual aids are also important for the safe and expeditious guidance and control of taxiing airplanes. Special 
attention is required for taxiway lighting, stop bars and signs. ICAO Annex 14 contains specifications for 
markings, lights, as well as mandatory and optional information signs and markers. Requirements may vary, 
but they consist of markings and signs supplemented by taxi holding position lights to denote holding 
positions as well as taxiing guidance signs and markings on the center lines and edges of taxiways. 
ICAO Annex 14 also provides visibility standards in reference to lighting spacing as well as when taxiway 
edge lights and centerline lights should be applied. 
Runway Status Lights (RWSL) are an additional safety measure for pilots to prevent the risk of runway 
incursions. The lights consist of Runway Entry Lights and Threshold Lights. The lights are either ON (red) or 
OFF. When RED, pilots have to stop the aircraft. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 519 

===PAGE 539===
ox iil Se 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual

e Taxi-holding position lights, where there is a need to improve the conspicuity of the lighting of the holding

3.2.5.1.4 Precision Approach (CAT II/IIl) 
Approach, threshold, touchdown zone, runway edge, centerline, runway end and other airport lights are 
required in compliance with ICAO Annex 14, appropriate to the category of operation for which a runway is 
intended. Where the runway may, in future, be upgraded so as to be suitable for Category II and III 
operations, it is advantageous to provide the necessary improved lighting during the initial construction or 
resurfacing of precision approach runways. This would eliminate the need for extensive future modifications. 
For daylight operations, experience has shown that surface markings are an effective means of indicating the 
centerlines of taxiways and holding positions. A holding position sign is required at all Category II and Il 
holding positions. 
Signs may also be needed to identify taxiways. Taxiway centerline lights or taxiway edge lights and centerline 
markings providing adequate guidance are required for Category II and II! operations. 
Stop bars can also make a valuable contribution to safety and ground traffic flow control in low-visibility 
operations. The primary safety function of the stop bar is the prevention of inadvertent penetrations of active 
runways and Obstacle Free Zones by aircraft and vehicles in such conditions. Stop bars, when provided, 
should be used at least in visibility conditions corresponding to runway visual ranges (RVRs) of less than 
350 m (CAT Ill). They also may contribute, in conjunction with other elements of the advanced surface 
movement guidance and control system (A-SMGCS), to effective traffic flow when low visibility prevents ATC 
from effecting optimum flow and ground separation by visual reference. 
It may also be advantageous to partly automate the operation of selected stop bars so that the ATC will not 
be required to operate them manually every time, thus avoiding possible human errors. For example, manual 
switch-off of a stop bar after issuance of a movement clearance would be followed by an automatic 
te-illumination by the crossing airplane. A ‘limited visibility’ setting on the control panel would automatically 
illuminate stop bars across taxiways that are not to be used in limited visibilities.

Requirements and guidance on the design, maintenance and monitoring of lighting circuits is contained in 
ICAO Annex 14, and the Aerodrome Design Manual (doc 9157) Part 4. 
3.2.5.2 Non-Visual Aids 
3.2.5.2.1 Introduction 
The term ‘non-visual aids’ refers to the approved radio and radar aids used to assist the pilot in carrying out 
approach and landing under cloud or other visibility-impairing conditions. In conditions of moderate cloud base 
and visibility, the purpose of the aid is to establish the aircraft in a position from which the pilot can safely 
complete the approach and landing by visual means, and in such conditions a relatively simple aid may well 
suffice. In very low cloud base and/or visibility conditions, visual contact may not be available to the pilot and 
a much more accurate and reliable system will be required to effectively locate the aircraft. 
Specifications for radio and radar aids are given in ICAO Annex 10, Volume |. The criteria for terminal area 
fixes and information on the construction of instrument approach procedures are given in PANS-OPS 
(Doc 8168). 
The non-visual aids for which standards have been defined range from non-precision aids such as: 
e Very high frequency direction finding (VDF) 
e¢ Non-directional radio beacon (NDB) 
¢ Very high frequency omnidirectional range (VOR) 
¢ Surveillance radar 
¢ = Multi-lateration 
e Automatic dependent surveillance—broadcast (ADS-B) 
e Instrument landing system (ILS). 
3.2.5.2.2 Non-Precision Approach 
Non-precision approach aids provide azimuth and/or distance information only. When using a single non￾precision aid for an instrument approach, the position of the aircraft can only be fixed by over-flying the 
facility. Position fixes may also be obtained by an intersection of bearings or radials from more than one 
navigational facility, or by the use of distance measuring equipment (DME) or marker beacons in association 
with azimuth guidance. Air Traffic Surveillance (ATS) sensors generally may be used to provide fixes prior to 
the final approach fix. Terminal area radar may be used to identify any terminal area fix including step-down 
fixes after the final approach fix. 
It is essential that all non-precision aids be ground and flight-checked at the time of commissioning and at 
regular intervals thereafter. 
522 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 542===
x iil Ye 
IATA + Airside Infrastructure 
With the aid of GPS, or more generally termed Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), routes can be 
designed closer to each due to the fact that GNSS-equipped aircraft are able to fly the routes very accurately 
with the potential to free up airspace and/or create additional route capacity. 
Modern aircraft have GNSS avionics on board. Together with a properly designed airspace infrastructure, they 
are able to avoid, to a certain extent, populated areas through narrow route tracking, thereby reducing the 
noise impact. Ultimately, GNSS could replace all traditional ground aids like VOR, DME, etc. However, there 
will be a need to maintain a minimum ground network as a back-up in case GNSS fails. 
3.2.5.2.3 Precision Approach (CAT I) 
Precision approach aids provide vertical (i.e., glide path) information in addition to azimuth guidance and, 
possibly, distance information. The ICAO standard non-visual precision approach aid is ILS, which is 
commonly in use. 
Precision approach radar (PAR) is also recognized as a precision approach aid. ILS ground equipment 
comprises a localizer, a glide path and at least two marker beacons, or, where the siting of marker beacons is 
impracticable, a suitably sited DME, provided that the distance information so obtained is operationally 
equivalent to that furnished by marker beacons. ILS may be used for all categories of operations, but the 
beam structure specifications, monitoring requirements and continuity of service requirements are more 
stringent for Category II and II] operations (see 3.2.5.2.4 Precision Approach (CAT ll/IIl)). 
It is essential that all ILS installations be ground-and flight-checked at the time of commissioning and at 
regular intervals in accordance with the requirements of ICAO Annex 10, Volume I, Part | to ensure an 
adequate and uniform standard of non-visual guidance. In the event that a facility fails to meet the 
requirements for which it was commissioned, or if a routine flight test cannot be completed within the 
appropriate time interval, its status must be reviewed, and the facility downgraded as necessary. Users should 
be advised of changes in ILS status through the aeronautical information service (AIS). Guidance material on 
flight testing is contained in the Manual on Testing of Radio Navigation Aids (ICAO Doc. 8071). 
To ensure that the integrity of the guidance signal radiated by the ILS is maintained during aircraft 
approaches, all vehicles and aircraft on the ground must remain outside the ILS critical areas as described in 
ICAO Annex 10, Volume |, Attachment C to Part I. If a vehicle or aircraft is within the critical area, it will cause 
reflection and/or diffraction of the ILS signals which may result in significant disturbances to the guidance 
signals on the approach path. 
3.2.5.2.4 Precision Approach (CAT II/III) 
The ILS ground equipment must meet the facility performance requirements specified in ICAO Annex 10, 
Volume |, Part |. The guidance material in Attachment C to Part | of that document also provides information 
for the planning and implementation of the ILS. 
The Manual of Testing of Radio Navigation Aids (ICAO Doc 8071) provides guidance on ground and flight 
testing of radio navigation aids; Volume II of the manual is concerned with ILS facilities. The quality of the ILS 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 523 

===PAGE 543===
w& IATA wi Airport Development Reference Manual 
signals in space is not determined solely by the quality of the ground equipment. The suitability of the site, 
including the influence of reflection from objects illuminated by the ILS signals and the manner in which the 
ground equipment is adjusted and maintained, also have significant effect on the quality of the signal received 
at the aircraft. It is essential that the ILS signal in space is flight-checked in order to confirm that is meets in all 
respects the appropriate standards of ICAO Annex 10, Volume I, Part I. 
All facilities associated with the ILS ground equipment must be monitored in accordance with the requirement 
of ICAO Annex 10, Volume |, Part |. Guidance material on monitoring is contained in Attachment C to Part | of 
Annex 10, Volume |}. 
ILS critical and sensitive areas must always be protected if the weather conditions are lower than 60 m 
(200 ft.) cloud base or 600 m RVR (i.e., CAT II/III conditions) when instrument approach operations are being 
carried out. In the latter case, aircraft that will overfly the localizer transmitter antenna after takeoff should be 
past the antenna before an aircraft making an approach has descended to a height of 60 m (200 ft.) above 
the runway. 
Similarly, an aircraft maneuvering on the ground, for example when clearing the runway after landing, should 
be clear of the critical and sensitive areas before an aircraft approaching to land has descended to a height of 
60 m (200 ft.) above the runway. The protection of these areas when the weather conditions are better than 
the minimum specified above will facilitate the use of automatic approach and landing systems, and will 
provide a safeguard in deteriorating weather conditions and when actual weather conditions are lower than is 
reported. 
New developments in precision approach landing systems are underway in the form of Ground-based 
Augmentation Systems (GBAS) making use of GNSS. The Single European Sky ATM Research (SESAR 
Program) is validating the development of GBAS to support low visibility operations. FAA is working towards 
International GBAS implementation and interoperability by sharing technical expertise, operational experience 
and approval processes via the International GBAS Working Group (IGWG). 
The ultimate goal is to provide GBAS CATII/III services at airports for which ICAO is delivering standards and 
recommended practices (SARPS) and whereby ILS will be replaced by GBAS. It is expected that one GBAS 
is able to replace all the ILS installed at an airport with multiple runway ends. GBAS can be placed at an 
optimal location at the airport. The ILS-bound Safety and Critical Areas will not be applicable anymore and 
runway throughput during Low Visibility Operations will be improved.

3.2.5.3 Air Traffic Control Towers 
3.2.5.3.1 Overview 
Historically, control towers covered both ground and airborne aircraft, housing ATC equipment and staff. At 
busy airports today, tower ATC functions are more focused toward the control of aircraft on the ground from 
the point at which they physically touchdown. Tower ATC communication and control of aircraft in general 
covers the following: 
e Radio communication and control of aircraft on taxiways, runways and in the air 
e Runway and taxiway lighting systems control 
e Airport ILS control 
¢ Communication handover of the airborne aircraft to the neighboring Air Traffic Control Sector (APP/ACC) 
Apart from physical ATC towers, remote or virtual towers are being introduced at airports globally. These do 
not accommodate staff and hence are cheaper to design and construct that common physical towers. 
3.2.5.3.2 Design Characteristics 
The primary objective of a modern control tower is to permit the functions listed in 3.2.5.3.1 Overview to be 
completed effectively and safely. The following design characteristics should be observed by control tower 
and terminal building planners embarking on the design and placement of new or upgraded control towers at 
all code letter categories of airports: 
© Ability to clearly see without obstruction the stand perimeter of every stand on the apron (subject to the 
requirements of the national ATC provider and operator) 
e Ability to see and control all taxiways and runways systems 
e Ability to communicate with aircraft and remote ATC organizations 
e Provision of ground radar monitors 
e Provision of emergency services, dedicated crash/incident alert and security system communications 
e Provision of 360° anti-glare, anti-distortion ATC staff apron viewing glazing at the appropriate height 
¢ Provision of CCTV monitoring for the remote review stands or obstructed stands (subject to the 
requirements of the national ATC provider and operator) 
e Towers should not be placed too close to flight paths (see ICAO Annex 14) 
e Provision of suitable security fencing and access control systems 
e Provision of dedicated heating, ventilation and power transformer systems, which should be stand alone 
with provision of separate emergency back-ups for each of these systems (subject to the requirements of 
the national ATC provider and operator)

Designers should work closely with the ATC operator (private or national organizations) and obtain design 
criteria standards provided by the national ATC infrastructure provider pertaining to the country in question. 
The planners/designers should define the following building and ATC process requirements: 
Control tower height (based on line of sight requirements) 
Control tower placement within the airfield (line of sight requirements) 
IT systems provision and infrastructure

designers should consult national ATC legislative bodies for precise size and facility performance 
requirements.

The position of the control tower is vital for its functionality. The control tower staff must be able to provide

e Taxiways and runways are placed extra-long distances away from the terminal apron stand areas, which

e¢ More controllers will have a better vision of specific areas of the apron

3.2.5.3.4 Remote Tower Control (RTC) 
Recent developments in camera technology and the bandwidth of modern networks have allowed the 
virtualization of air traffic control towers. Although the wording in the industry still differs, commonly used 
nomenclature includes remote tower control, virtual tower or digital tower concept, which all describe the 
same basic principle. 
Instead of a traditional air traffic control tower, a mast or similar utilizable construction carries a set of 
cameras and additional technical equipment at the airport. The video stream and data received by the 
sensors is transmitted to the remote-control working position of the tower controller in virtual real time. The 
controllers can observe their area of responsibility by watching the video stream and data displayed as well as 
control the necessary equipment (e.g., radio and lighting) from a distance. 
Typically, a video panorama is used to replace the conventional line of sight out of a control room. As even 
modern cameras cannot fully reach the visual performance of the human eye, usually additional cameras 
support the main panoramic view. Use of pan/tilt/zoom (PTZ) cameras is recommended due to their spatial 
versatility, basically providing a digital binocular. 
The following are some fundamental motivations for implementing a RTC concept: 
e To avoid new and relatively expensive control tower constructions accommodating staff facilities 
* To ensure availability of service on remote airfields with typically low traffic, which need to be operated 
only on an intermittent basis 
¢ To protect critical staff in military scenarios and avoid their exposure in an area of conflict; and 
e In general, to use synergies resulting from centralized services (e.g., staffing and equipment), with the 
benefits of reduced cost of provision 
Modern camera and display technology used in RTC can also enhance the visual perception of a tower 
controller. Infrared cameras provide better vision through darkness and certain weather conditions (e.g., mist). 
Augmentation of video streams with additional information such as outlines of the runway and/or radar labels 
also support air traffic control in virtual environments and, in general, reduce “head down” times of the 
controllers, where their attention is distracted from the primary field of view of the airport. 
3.2.6 Jet Fuel Infrastructure 
3.2.6.1 Introduction 
Jet fuel supply is a critical part of airport operations and an important consideration in any successful airport 
design and planning project. Proper attention to jet fuel infrastructure needs to be given at the early stages of 
any airport development or expansion as jet fuel storage and delivery (above and below ground) occupies 
airport land and its location, capacity and necessary components impact the effective, efficient and safe 
operation of an airport. Retrospectively installing some parts of the infrastructure (e.g., fuel hydrant system) 
528 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 548===
& Hi Se | 
IATA Airside Infrastructure 
may be disproportionately costly, disruptive or technically difficult. It is therefore crucial that airport 
development projects be aligned with jet fuel infrastructure enhancements. 
This chapter describes key jet fuel system infrastructure design concepts to be utilized as reference for airport 
development plans. One of the most important recommendations is that airlines and fuel suppliers should be 
consulted on all fuel infrastructure developments and their commissioning. It is important to note that fuel 
infrastructure at an airport cannot be without first being inspected and approved by the airlines operating at 
the airport as having met the necessary fuel quality and safety standards. There are several key factors to 
consider for an efficient and effective aviation fuel system. These include: 
e Supply Chain Complexity 
e Airport Receipt and Storage 
e Delivery Systems to Aircraft 
The supply chain needs to have an adequate and preferably diverse supply of jet fuel from refineries in the 
area or elsewhere. The supply chain should also have well-established methods for delivery to the airport 
(e.g., pipeline, ship/barge, truck, or rail). 
The reliability of the supply chain directly affects the amount of storage that should be planned at the airport. 
The amount of storage should be based on the throughput used at the airport during peak periods, the 
constraints of the supply chain, the potential for natural disasters and political instability. It is recommended 
that a qualified engineering firm with experience in fuel supply chain dynamics performs a sensitivity analysis 
and makes recommendations concerning the amount of on-site storage required for each airport. 
Delivery of jet fuel from the 
on-airport storage to the aircraft can vary based on the demand schedule and volume. There are generally 
two types of delivery methods for civilian airports: 
e Refueller trucks that are loaded from a fill stand and transport the fuel to the aircraft 
e A hydrant fueling system that delivers fuel to aircraft stands 
Due to the much higher cost of a hydrant system, which requires extensive piping, more robust pumping, 
controls, and electrical supply, a detailed evaluation is recommended to be performed by a qualified fueling 
engineer to assist in determining the best approach for fuel delivery at each airport. 
It is essential that comprehensive procedures and practices are implemented and applied across the entire 
supply chain, from refinery to aircraft in an ideal arrangement, that safeguards aviation fuel quality and 
ensures safe fuel delivery into aircraft. The figure below depicts the various facets of a jet fuel supply chain 
from refining to aircraft, with various transportation and delivery options.

3.2.6.2 Components of Airport Fuel Infrastructure 
Jet fuel supply at airports is impacted by the supply chain that starts outside the airport perimeter, and for 
consistency, all elements of the supply chain need to be evaluated as one system. This concept is important 
when planning new facilities, but just as important when planning to enhance parts of an existing system. 
Airport developers should prepare a master plan that anticipates the long-term needs of the users with proper 
allocation of land, considering possible future expansion of fuel facilities. Planning for future expansion 
requires a high level of anticipation to ensure the airport follows a future-proof concept that accounts for 
electricity, water supply, tunnels, and any other aboveground and underground development to meet future 
demand. 
This section describes the key components of airport fuel infrastructure to better understand the 
interdependencies among them and with the overall supply chain. 
3.2.6.2.1 Fuel Receipt 
Fuel receipt infrastructure planning is critical to providing a sustainable, reliable supply of fuel to the airport. 
Available refineries, waterborne fuel delivery capability, existing or planned fuel pipeline networks, off-airport 
storage terminals, and truck loading terminals are all potential upstream factors affecting the strength of fuel 
supply to an airport. It is common to have multiple means of receiving fuel at an airport, such as one or more 
pipelines, potential connection to water receipt piers or wharves, and/or transport truck receiving. Off-airport 
storage terminals and refineries with their associated storage capabilities may be used to support required 
on-airport storage if the location is conveniently located and the fuel can be supplied without delay (e.g., no 
undue delays in supply occur due to prolonged testing, certification, or transport). 
530 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 550===
IATA Airside Infrastructure 
Pipelines 
When planning for airport supply by pipeline—existing pipeline networks, off-airport storage terminals, and 
supply origination (e.g., refineries, water or either both) and their availability need to be thoroughly 
investigated. Existing tanker berths and off-airport terminal storage tanks can be leased by airlines or airports 
for jet fuel receipt and storage. In some instances, dedicated off-airport storage terminals are constructed to 
serve an airport, with receiving capabilities from area refineries, pipeline networks or waterborne deliveries. If 
supplying pipelines are used for other purposes, such as for other vicinity airport deliveries or shipping of 
other products, pipeline “cycles” can reduce the frequency of deliveries. 
The logistics of the pipeline supply system can influence the delivery rates and required storage capacities 
both on and off the airport. Pipeline shutdowns are usually of relatively short duration (1-2 days) unless the 
outage is due to damage or intrusion into the pipeline. Planned (e.g., for routine maintenance) pipeline 
outages can be managed by having adequate reserve fuel storage capacity at the airport. However, 
significant planning and analysis might be required to accommodate non-routine pipeline outages. 
Transport Truck Delivery 
Truck receipts, although common at smaller airports where relatively smaller volume receipts by truck are 
practical, cannot normally replace a pipeline in the event of a pipeline shutdown. Significant numbers of 
transport trucks are not typically available to be used for jet fuel transport on short notice in an emergency. 
When planning for trucked fuel delivery, the number of trucks required per day and the duration of the daily 
truck delivery schedule (e.g., 8 hours, 12 hours, and 24 hours) can be analyzed to determine the number of 
required unloading positions at the airport. A typical transport truck is of 8,000-gallon capacity. Provisions for 
expansion and future additional truck unloading positions should be considered as well for airport growth. A 
significant site area may be required for trafficking, staging and maneuvering of transport trucks. 
Rail Delivery 
Receipt of fuel at an airport by rail is generally less common than other modes of fuel supply due to the 
logistical challenges of providing a railhead, as well as significant rail transport times, and associated 
scheduling concerns. Seasonal fluctuations in fuel usage at airports can have significant impact on the ability 
to adequately schedule rail deliveries. It is generally suited to relatively constant demand profiles if rail is 
provided. Consideration should be given to other modes of supply (e.g., truck) in cases where additional 
demand occurs due to seasonal or other factors. 
Waterborne Delivery 
Although jet fuel can be received directly into an airport fuel storage system, receipt of fuel by barge or tanker 
more commonly occurs at off-airport storage terminals, as described above under “Pipelines”. Typical 
high-volume receipt flowrates from a barge or tanker, and the enhanced fuel quality control measures (e.g., 
filtration, water removal, product certification) commonly utilized when receiving waterborne fuel, are more 
readily handled at an off-airport facility. Significant empty storage must be available for receipt from larger 
capacity barges and tankers, and the typical higher receipt flow rates tend to make incoming filtration 
upstream of receipt storage sizable, hard to maintain and uneconomical. Common practice is to receive 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 531 

===PAGE 551===
3% Gi IATA ll Airport Development Reference Manual 
directly into dedicated receipt tankage from the barge/tanker and then transfer fuel through filtration at a 
lower, more economical flow rate into airport “operating” storage. 
3.2.6.2.2 Airport Fuel Storage 
Issues that can affect airport fuel storage capacity include the method and frequency of fuel delivery to the 
airport, reliability and redundancy of the upstream fuel supply chain, and potential disruptions from external 
causes such as weather extremes, natural disasters, or political impacts. If fuel is not received at the airport 
every day, such as a weekly pipeline delivery, enough fuel needs to be stored on the airport to accommodate 
the airport throughput between deliveries, with a determined, additional contingency fuel volume. Determining 
the adequate level of minimum storage capacity at an airport is a complex task. The IATA Guidance on 
Airport Fuel Storage Capacity provides a framework and detailed process to determine what the optimum 
storage capacity should be, based on the airport's specific situation: at airports where there are multiple 
Tefineries or delivery methods available to supply the airport, a lower minimum on-airport storage would be 
acceptable compared to locations where the supply chain is vulnerable (e.g., with only one supply route that 
could be disrupted by inclement weather or where the single supply source is distant from the airport). 
The number of days of usage can be calculated for individual airports using the recommended evaluation 
process described in the IATA Guidance on Airport Fuel Storage Capacity which also emphasizes that it is not 
feasible to build facilities that can withstand all disruptions. While raising design limits (safety factors and 
margins) can lower the chance of events above such limits, the construction and operating costs would 
inevitably increase. 
The chart demonstrates that while the probability of a 100-million-liter disruption is limited to once every ten 
years, a five-million-liter disruption could occur six times a year. Similar relations between the magnitude and 
the probability may apply to any airport worldwide. Risk assessment and cost/benefit trade-off analysis are 
essential in striking a balance unique to individual airports. Different parameters yield strikingly different 
solutions. 
It is also physically infeasible and economically inefficient to protect airport fuel storage against all 
conceivable forms of supply disruptions. Hence it is prudent to determine a risk threshold that is reasonable 
and agreeable to all stakeholders in determining storage capacity and to put in place a fuel contingency plan 
to mitigate the risk of stock out. A qualified engineering firm should be sought to evaluate the storage 
requirements of the airport. 
A minimum of three fuel storage tanks are recommended for airport storage, such that with one tank out of 
service for inspection, maintenance or repair, the fuel system can adequately function with the other two tanks 
in service. For smaller airports with less than three tanks, a risk assessment should be undertaken to 
determine whether foreseeable outages could be accommodated by fewer number of tanks (e.g., with two 
tanks at a small airport, could tank cleaning of one be completed before the other tank is emptied). 
532 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 552===
Se 
IATA Airside Infrastructure 
At smaller airports or segregated areas of airports, such as general aviation, private corporate or government 
aircraft ramps, smaller fuel demands can result in a storage arrangement using factory-fabricated tanks, either 
aboveground or belowground, with a maximum practical size of 50,000 gallons, typically. This is because 
large volume tanks are not readily transportable down public roadways. Storage “banks” of four or more 
factory-fabricated tanks are not uncommon, connected to a common fuel receipt and issue system. 
Larger airports require field-erected tanks, with their inherent flexibility in size, number, and arrangement. 
Field-erected tanks, although some standard sizes may be available, are typically custom-sized with variable 
height-to-diameter ratios to provide the best fit for a site from economic, operability and clearance 
requirements, such as from adjacent properties, airfield operations or vertical airspace. 
Site selection for an airport fuel depot site should follow national and local regulations and consider locations 
that are outside of: 
e The ends of the runway(s), known as approach, takeoff and clearway funnels 
e Runway and taxiway side clearances 
e Aircraft parking aprons (taking into account any interaction between the depot and the aircraft during 
operation or possible calamities) 
If a hydrant system is considered, the distance between the on-airport fuel depot and the fueling area should 
be as short as practically possible. When it is not possible to locate the on-airport fuel depot near the fueling 
area, a satellite area should be considered with office and parking space for fueling equipment, hydrant 
services and, eventually, refuellers. 
Also, the location of supply methods (e.g., pipeline, road tanker, rail tank car or waterborne transport) should 
be taken into consideration in locating an on-airport fuel depot. The fuel depot location should also allow for 
easy access of emergency authorities to effectively respond to any incidents that may occur and the impact of 
security controls (e.g., by locating the road tanker receipt area outside of airport-controlled areas (landside) to 
facilitate access). The location of the fuel depot should also consider local or national requirements with 
regards to minimum distances (e.g., distance between center of runway, public roads, population centers, 
environmental hazards). 
3.2.6.2.3 Refueller Loading Facilities 
Refueller loading facilities, while required where no hydrant system exists, are also common at airports with 
hydrant systems. Not all aircraft parking positions may be provided with hydrant fueling due to a variety of 
reasons, such as remoteness from terminals served by hydrant systems (e.g., cargo areas, aircraft 
maintenance bases, remote parking aprons), and thus requiring tanker refueling. Refuellers may also be 
provided for redundancy in the event of a partial hydrant system shut down for maintenance/repair or hydrant 
system expansion and related construction outages. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 533 

===PAGE 553===
w IATA fi Airport Development Reference Manual 
A traffic study/analysis should be performed to determine truck driving routes and maneuvering areas. It is 
strongly preferred from a safety standpoint to not restrict refueller truck traffic in a manner that requires the 
trucks to back up. A spill-containment parking area for refuellers should also be planned for. The loading 
facility could potentially double as a parking area or be adjacent to it. Significant area can be required for 
Tefueller facilities and needs to be planned for. 
Where refueller loading is critical, a spare or redundant refueller loading position should be provided in the 
event one of the operating positions needs to be taken out of service for maintenance or repair. 
3.2.6.2.4 Fuel Hydrant Systems 
The planned or existing locations and arrangements of the airport terminals, concourses, related infrastructure 
and the relative location of the fuel facility can significantly affect the fuel hydrant system's layout, flexibility 
and cost. The farther away the pumping system is from the terminals, the more initial cost will be incurred to 
install lengths of piping and potentially larger pumping and supporting electrical power systems. Long-term 
pumping energy costs will also be affected. 
Planning of the fuel facility location, hydrant system supply pipeline corridors, and concourse hydrant piping 
systems should be included in overall airport master planning. Locating transfer pipelines and valve pits or 
vaults in locations where they can be adequately serviced without disrupting aircraft or vehicle traffic 
operations is ideal. Pipeline low points on the airport must be accessed monthly to remove any collected 
water. Valve vaults can also require frequent access for valve positioning, maintenance, or water removal. It is 
imperative that engineering companies familiar and experienced with aircraft fuel handling and quality control 
be employed in the planning and design of new hydrant fueling systems. 
Providing two transfer mains from the fuel facility to the terminal/concourse hydrant systems and providing 
“looped” hydrant systems as much as possible will allow redundancy in transfer piping and routing of fuel to 
the aircraft positions. See Exhibit 3.2.6.2.4 below. This arrangement also can allow for looped 
recirculation/flushing back to the fuel facility to initially clean the piping and promote fuel quality over the long 
term by performing periodic recirculation. 
Given the specialized nature of constructing hydrant fueling systems, it is highly recommended that hydrant 
systems only be designed and constructed by companies who are familiar with aircraft fuel handling and 
quality control.

Hydrant System vs. Refueller Trucks 
There is no simple rule of thumb to determine the optimum aircraft refueling system type for an airport. 
Typically, the number of aircraft gates or fueling positions and the size of aircraft play an important role in 
determining the feasibility of a hydrant refueling system. Less than 15 to 20 aircraft parking/refueling positions 
or gates can be an economic driver for a refueller tanker truck system. However, several factors such as large 
aircraft with associated large fuel uplift requirements, long potential drive routes for the refueller trucks, 
environmental concerns from truck usage, or even relative convenience can influence the decision to provide 
a hydrant refueling system. 
Any decision to install a hydrant system should be undertaken only after a robust cost-benefit analysis by 
experienced, capable industry experts has proven its cost efficiency. Input from the involved airlines, airport 
operations and management personnel as well as available fuel service providers can provide substantial 
assistance in developing the cost-benefit analysis and its successful implementation. 
Hydrant systems are typically employed at airports where daily fuel volume is relatively large and ramp space 
is limited (and at a premium). Annual airport fuel throughputs range from less than a few million gallons to 
several billion gallons. An airport can be small or large, but the airport must typically have a significant fuel 
throughput volume, between 160- to 200-million gallons, to justify the installation of a hydrant system. 
Furthermore, it is not only the number of gates at an airport that justifies a hydrant system, but also the size of 
aircraft and their length of flight upon departure. It depends on the amount of fuel that is uplifted and that 
depends on the range of the flights the airport hosts—the longer the flights, the greater the possibility or need 
for a hydrant system. 
Often, a fixed hydrant system can be justified as a safer, preferred means of fueling aircraft rather than 
utilizing large refueller trucks, which need to navigate congested aircraft parking aprons or ramp space. From 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 535 

===PAGE 555===
we IATA Wi Airport Development Reference Manual 
an environmental standpoint, arguments can be made that hydrant systems provide better protection, with 
less spill potential, less overall energy consumption vs. refueller trucks, and lower air emissions (no trucks or 
intermediate truck loading). With the employment of contemporary, automated leak detection systems, buried 
piping cathodic (corrosion) protection, quality external pipe coatings, and quality control testing and 
inspections during pipeline construction, hydrant systems are perceived to present less overall risk than 
refueller trucks. 
Refueling large aircraft with multiple refueller trucks consumes time, equipment and manpower. Truck 
refueling may not be a feasible mode of operation for the larger, long-haul aircraft, such as a Boeing 777 
(40,000 gallons +) or an Airbus A380 (70,000 gallons +). Normal large refueller trucks are of the 10,000-gallon 
capacity range, with the largest refueller trucks having a capacity of approximately 17,500 gallons. The 
logistics of filling a large aircraft with trucks could take longer than the aircraft is scheduled to be on the 
ground or also limit the availability of refueller trucks and personnel for fueling other aircraft during the same 
time. 
Other economic parameters that can affect viability of hydrant vs. refueller truck systems include: 
¢ The cost of refueller trucks vs. fuel hydrant dispenser vehicles or towable fuel hydrant dispenser carts. A 
10,000-gallon refueller truck can cost $400,000, a hydrant servicer approximately $200,000, and a 
towable hydrant cart less than $100,000". A refuel truck system bears lower cost of airport 
development as compared to hydrant dispenser system because the latter has added cost of civil and 
mechanical works for laying an underground fuel supply line network that extends from the fuel farm to 
airside of the airport reaching every aircraft stand. However, there are higher maintenance costs 
associated with refueller trucks when compared to fuel hydrant dispensers. 
e Ahydrant system is typically shared by all airport users and can be considered “centralized 
infrastructure”. System construction and maintenance costs can then be shared among the users. 
Refueller truck fleets can be individually owned and operated by individual users, with potentially less 
shared costs than for hydrant systems. 
e Flexibility in the layout of the airport is an important consideration. If there is great distance between the 
fuel depot (or existing hydrant) and the apron to be equipped with a hydrant system, the investment cost 
will also be higher in terms of pipe lengths, pipe sizes and underground construction. Refueller truck 
systems are more flexible if aircraft gate or parking position layouts (or aircraft type) are subject to 
significant change or variations. Hydrant fueling pits are installed in a fixed, permanent location, which 
would need to be physically relocated if the aircraft parking position moves or an aircraft type and relative 
fueling location is changed. Multiple hydrant pits are sometimes provided to accommodate multiple types 
of aircraft at a single gate. 
Retrofitting a hydrant system into an existing airport and aircraft ramp can be very expensive since concrete 
removal and replacement is required as well as extended disruption to existing aircraft gate operations while 
new piping and fueling pits are installed. 
21 Approximate costs for guidance only. These costs might vary as per the specification of each vehicle, and other factors such as the 
warranties and service support.

3.2.6.3 Jet Fuel Supply Design Requirements and Planning Considerations 
Every aspect of the jet fuel supply is ruled by standards and guidance material to ensure a safe product 
delivery. It is not possible to extensively explain every procedure in this document. However, this section lists 
the procedures or standards in use by the industry for a safe and efficient jet fuel supply. It is essential to be 
familiar with the following systems to ensure the jet fuel infrastructure incorporates best industry practices. 
3.2.6.3.1 Safety Issues 
(a) Safety Management System 
Every responsible organization involved in aviation fuel manufacture, supply, storage, transport, testing and 
aircraft fueling must have a robust Safety Management System (SMS). 
ICAO Doc 9859 defines a systematic approach to managing safety, including the necessary organizational 
structures, accountabilities, policies, and procedures. It has introduced harmonized requirements into its 
relevant Annexes to the ICAO Chicago Convention. 
(b) Quality Program 
Fuel vendors must have an established quality program to ensure safe receipt, storage and distribution of 
fuel, as well as an internal audit and surveillance function. This quality program shall be detailed in a policies 
and procedures manual that provides operational guidance to management and staff. 
(c) Fueling Safety Zone 
Fueling safety zones are areas with a radius of at least three meters, or as specified by local regulation, from 
filling and venting points on the aircraft, hydrant pits, fueling vehicle, and its hoses in use. No ignition sources 
are permitted within the fueling safety zone, when the refueling equipment is in the fueling position. 
(d) Fire Extinguishers 
Storage and refueling facilities must be designed to accommodate the requisite number of suitable fire 
extinguishers, so they can be readily available and easily accessible, in accordance with local requirements. 
(e) Fire Suppression Systems 
For fuel storage facilities, a more robust fire protection system involving fire suppression foam systems, 
cooling water, etc. may be required by local regulation or authorities having jurisdiction. Even if not required, it 
can be determined desirable to provide enhanced fire suppression systems for protection of assets and to 
mitigate the potential loss of the fuel system and the associated impact to airport operations. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 537 

===PAGE 557===
SS Ge IATA ‘a Airport Development Reference Manual 
(f) Bonding and Grounding 
Bonding is the process of connecting two or more conductive objects together by means of a conductor 
(bonding cable). Grounding is the process of physically connecting one or more conductive objects to the 
ground to safely dissipate any electrical charge. A grounding procedure is only necessary for older aircraft 
versions, particularly military aircraft. Ground points must be designed into all apron facilities at locations 
Tecommended by the respective aircraft manufacturers. All facility equipment, including the aircraft and fueling 
vehicles, must be bonded together prior to and throughout any fuel handling process to avoid potential 
differences and possible sparking. In view of potential damage to modern aircraft electronics, grounding of the 
fueling equipment is not recommended, unless specified by the Aircraft Maintenance Manual. 
3.2.6.3.2 Storage Facilities Design and Processes 
(a) General Design Features and Equipment 
Observance of certain fundamental practices in the design of airport storage facilities is considered essential 
to ensure that fuel quality is maintained. The following are general considerations regarding the design 
features and equipment for these facilities: 
e Any new installation or alteration/extension of existing facilities shall be designed and commissioned in 
accordance with recognized industry standards (e.g., El 1540, SAE AS 5789 Aviation Fuel Facilities, JIG 
publications, ATA 103, NFPA 407). 
e Accurrent schematic diagram identifying valves, etc. (e.g., piping diagram, computer display), must be 
available locally for reference by the persons operating the equipment. 
e All facilities utilized for handling aviation fuels shall be fully grade-segregated; there shall be no 
interconnecting lines between pipelines that handle different fuels. 
¢ No copper, cadmium alloy, cadmium or zinc-plated (e.g., galvanized) steel shall be permitted for piping, 
nor shall zinc-rich internal coatings be used for piping or tankage. 
«All pump start/stop switches at fuel receipt and refueling loading areas should be safely accessible and 
clearly identified in accordance with local regulatory requirements. 
e An emergency fuel shutoff system shall be provided; shutdown switches shall be safely accessible in 
close proximity to fuel handling activities and clearly identified in accordance with local regulations. 
e Fuel identification signs (per El 1542) and other applicable signs (e.g., “No Smoking”, “Flammable”, “No 
Vaping”) shall be prominently displayed. 
e An adequate number of suitable fire extinguishers shall be readily available, in accordance with local 
requirements. 
¢ Fueling vehicle parking, road/rail discharge and fueling loading areas shall be constructed of a low 
permeability material and have a positive slope and drainage to an oil/water interceptor or spill 
containment basin. 
538 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 558===
w& IATA‘ wi Airside Infrastructure 
(b) Storage Tanks 
The number and size of tanks should be sufficient to provide adequate working capacity, and consider peak 
period airport requirements, supply replenishment arrangements, and strategic stock coverage. Allowance 
should also be made for settling, testing and tank cleaning requirements. Typically, a minimum of three fuel 
storage tanks are recommended for airport storage, such that with one tank out of service for inspection, 
maintenance or repair, the fuel system can adequately function with the remaining two tanks in service. 
Industry standard fuel quality requirements, as addressed in publications referenced herein, indicate that fuel 
should not be received into and issued out of the same tank simultaneously as this may pose potential issues 
with verifying fuel quality prior to introducing fuel into aircraft. If multiple pipelines or other delivery modes 
allow receiving fuel simultaneously from separate sources, it is desirable to receive fuel from each source into 
separate tankage for fuel quality segregation reasons. This could lead to an additional quantity of tanks being 
needed. 
Aviation fuels should be stored in horizontal or fixed-roof vertical tanks (or fixed-roof vertical tanks with an 
internal floating roof/cover, if required by local legislation). Storage tanks can be aboveground (AST) or 
underground (UST) designed in accordance with the following standards: 
e AST-vertical, field-erected—API 650, EN ISO 14015, or equivalent 
« AST-horizontal, shop-fabricated—UL 142, EN ISO 12285/2, or equivalent 
e AST-horizontal, shop-fabricated, protected (fire, ballistics, impact)-UL 2085 
e UST-UL 58, or equivalent 
* UST-using reinforced fiberglass plastic-UL 13167 
ASTs shall be contained within bunds/dykes as required and constructed to meet local regulations for 
secondary containment. Shop-fabricated, double-walled ASTs may not require further secondary containment, 
depending on local regulations. Tank-top walkways should have non-slip surfaces, handrails, and kick plates. 
Tanks shall be: 
e Constructed and installed to avoid ingress of water and dirt, and to provide a positive low point to collect 
water and sediment for ease of removal. To achieve this, horizontal tanks should be installed with a 
minimum continuous slope of 1:50, and vertical tanks should have a cone-down bottom with a minimum 
continuous slope of 1:30 to a center sump. 
e Prominently numbered and marked with grade stored (see El 1542) and, as a minimum, show the date of 
the most recent internal inspection and cleaning.

e Completely coated internally, including the underside of the roof, with a light-colored epoxy material, 
approved as being compatible with aviation fuels (see El 1541). Existing tanks not fully coated internally 
must undergo a more frequent inspection cycle and shall, as a minimum, be coated internally on the

Tanks shall be fitted with: 
e Primary vent devices installed with coarse mesh screens (typically, with 5 mm or % inch diameter holes) 
to prevent the ingress of foreign bodies. Pressure/vacuum vents, if required, shall be suitably designed,

e A low-point sump with a drain line and suitable valve for the draining of water and sediment. The volume

¢ Separate product inlet and outlet connections. Inlet pipes should discharge near the bottom of the tank 
and be designed to minimize turbulence. 
e Access manholes to facilitate entry for gas freeing and cleaning. A minimum of two are recommended; 
one-meter or three-foot diameter access manholes are preferred (note: with horizontal shop-fabricated 
tanks, one access manhole is sufficient). 
¢ Gauge hatches to provide means of sampling and tank gauging/level measurement. 
e Anti-siphon valves, if required for installation (typical for horizontal tanks). 
¢ Floating suction arms, bonded to the tank shell, with position indicators and/or check cables bonded to the

contact with the tank shell. Position indicators are recommended for large aboveground vertical tanks 
(note: where legislation requires the installation of internal floating roofs/covers, it is critical to ensure that 
the floating suction will not interfere with the operation of the floating cover—and vice versa). 
e Automatic high-level alarm devices to prevent tank overflow. Low-level alarm systems are also 
recommended. At locations supplied by waterborne vessels, pipeline, or multiple simultaneous discharges 
of road tankers or rail tank cars, storage tanks shall be fitted with a high-level audible alarm and a 
separate “high-high” level system that shuts down the fuel flow when a predetermined level of fuel in the 
tank is reached. For locations supplied by single discharge of road tanker or rail tank car, an audible high￾level alarm or a single shutdown device is the minimum requirement. 
e Horizontal, shop-fabricated tanks shall be secured (tethered) to prevent movement in the events of high 
winds, seismic events, or severe flooding. 
¢ The use of non-metallic materials to plug or cap piping on aboveground tanks is not permitted. 
(c) Filtration 
Any fuel installation shall be equipped with the latest approved filtration system, as per El 1550.

(d) Pipework 
To ensure that aviation fuel requiring a recertification test is isolated from certified fuel in the airport fuel 
storage system until the fuel has been tested, airport fuel storage systems that receive aviation fuels shall 
have receipt storage tanks equipped with tank inlet and outlet valves that shall be physically and positively 
segregated using one of the following methods: 
¢ A double block-and-bleed (DBB) valve arrangement. This can be either a single DBB valve with two 
independent seals and a cavity between them, or two valves with a drain arrangement in a pipe spool in 
between. When the valves are in a closed position, the cavity or drain spool shall be checked to confirm 
no fuel is passing. 
e Aremovable distance (spool) piece. 
e A spectacle blind, pancake/skillet flange, or equivalent. 
e Wherever possible, all newly installed pipelines shall be routed aboveground. Where buried pipelines are 
unavoidable, they should be backfilled with appropriate material (select sand, typically) and protected from 
corrosion by a cathodic protection (CP) system. 
e Piping must be properly supported and supports must be designed in such a manner as to minimize the 
effects of corrosion, where contact with the product piping occurs. 
¢ Piping must be properly spaced, whether installed aboveground or belowground. 
e Buried pipework should have cathodic protection. Prior to installation, an external coating should be 
applied to provide additional protection from corrosion. Factory coating is preferred, with an acceptable 
field-applied coating used for weld joints and coating system repairs. 
* Single-valve separation is acceptable as tank isolation for dedicated and segregated systems, as the 
aviation fuel has already been certified and no additional certification testing is required after transfer into 
airport storage tanks.

facilitate the removal of water and sediment. 
e All exposed piping shall be clearly marked in accordance with El 1542, including fue! name and color 
coding, and with flow direction arrows. 
¢ Road transport (e.g., tank truck) and railcar receipt connections shall be fitted with selective couplings of a 
size and type chosen to give maximum practical degree of grade security. 
e Where more than one grade of aviation fuel is available at the airport, grade selective couplings or 
devices shall be fitted to truck bottom loading connections and hydrant pit valves. 
e For fuel applications, the use of Victaulic couplings is not permitted; joints must be properly welded for 
lines carrying fuels.

e Jet fuel without static dissipater additive shall require:

o A reduced initial loading/filling rate of a maximum of one meter (three feet) per second, until the inlet

(e) Hoses

Type C, or ISO 1825. Refueller loading hoses meeting the latest issue of BS 3492, or equivalent, rated for the 
maximum pressure of the loading system, are also acceptable. 
(f) Hydrant System Design 
The design of a hydrant system should take potential expansion into account by considering the size of pipe 
and provisions for future hydrant extensions. Factors like traffic forecasts, airport (and apron) development 
programs and trends in aircraft types, among other developments, will influence the design of a hydrant 
system and should be collected at the evaluation stage to ensure that feasibility and cost of future 
investments remain realistic. Where a new airport layout design or an anticipated airport extension or 
modification is still at the conceptual stage, but a hydrant design is required, ongoing close relationships with 
the airport development consultant(s) are of the utmost importance to ensure that, prior to any layout 
changes, the impact on the hydrant design is clarified. 
After completion of a new or extended hydrant system installation and before the system is placed into 
service, the structural integrity of the system shall be tested in accordance with El 1540. Each grade of 
aviation fuel must be handled in a completely segregated system. There shall be no interconnecting lines 
between pipelines handling different fuels. Where more than one grade of fuel is available, hydrant pits and 
couplers shall be clearly identified, selective, and grade-marked in accordance with El 1542. 
All hydrant systems shall be constructed using carbon steel (e.g., to API 5L Grade B or similar) as the piping 
material. All new hydrant lines shall be lined internally with an epoxy material approved as being compatible 
with aviation fuels. The interior of field weld joints and small-bore pipe and fittings are typically left as bare 
steel. 
All new hydrant systems shall have tightness control capabilities incorporated into the design to periodically 
prove their integrity. When significant modifications to an existing hydrant system are planned, consideration 
should be given to incorporating a tightness contro! system (leak detection). 
Hydrant systems and underground piping should have cathodic protection, and appropriate signs to warn 
against separation of system components without prior de-energization.
