3.2.6.4.1_ Cost Line Items and Definitions 
Receipt Systems 
Pipeline receipt systems can include significant valve manifolds, metering, filtration, and supporting controls 
and instrumentation. Transport truck receipt systems typically include offloading pumps, filtration, metering, 
associated valving, controls and instrumentation. Rail receipt systems include the railhead spur itself, 
offloading pumps, filtration, metering, associated valving, controls and instrumentation. Water receipt systems 
(barge or tanker) are commonly on shared piers or wharves that are also used for loading/unloading other 
liquid products, cargo containers or other freight. Therefore, the cost of the pier/wharf infrastructure is not 
included. These systems can include marine loading arms or hoses, connecting piping, valves, filtration and 
supporting controls and instrumentation. 
Storage Tanks 
Fuel received at the airport facility is stored in underground and/or aboveground storage tanks. Typically, 
storage tanks greater than 50,000 gallons are field-fabricated tanks. Field-fabricated tanks would have a fixed, 
cone roof, epoxy-coated interior surfaces, visual product level indicator, and a cone-down bottom with center 
sump and drain. 
Pumps and Filtration 
Pumps and associated filter vessels, valves, instruments, controls, electrical power and associated 
infrastructure are typically staged within the storage facility. Refueller loading positions can be utilized 
exclusively for aircraft or to supplement hydrant systems. Refueller loading systems are present at many 
airports with hydrant systems to service aircraft positions without hydrants (such as cargo) or provide a back￾up when portions of the hydrant system are not operational. 
Operations Building 
The fuel system controls, and system monitoring equipment are generally located within sight of the main 
pumping equipment pad in an operations building. Operators at these facilities manage and monitor day-to￾day system operations and site security, respond to control system alarms or notifications, and manage 
maintenance functions. System emergency shutdown functions are also typically centralized in the operations 
building. Depending on the size of the airport and fuel system, other potential functions of a central building 
can include fuel delivery scheduling, inventory accounting, other administrative management functions, a shop 
or maintenance garage, and a fuel testing lab. 
546 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 566===
Pay 
ae IATA pull Airside Infrastructure 
Hydrant Systems 
This portion of the hydrant system is comprised of one or more transfer pipes from the storage and pumping 
facility to the hydrant distribution system at the airport terminal apron. The piping layout is typically segmented 
with isolation valves to allow continued operation of a portion of the system when other portions are isolated 
for maintenance or due to emergency shutdown. 
3.2.6.5 Best Practice in Developing Requests for Tenders, Including Specific Models 
Producing a well-developed Request for Tender (RFT) is paramount to achieving a successful fuel system 
construction project and long-term satisfactory operation. Adequate preliminary scope development is a main 
key to allowing prospective bidders to provide consistent, comparable offers. A minimum 30% design 
completion is recommended for inclusion with an airport fuel system tender; however, a more developed and 
defined design, such as 50-60% complete, will potentially provide more accurate costing by bidders and 
reduce risk of additional, unforeseen costs as the final design and construction proceeds. 
Critical elements of an RFT can include: 
e Summary description of the tender scope 
¢ Bid form 
¢ Contractual/legal requirements and definitions 
¢ Regulatory and industry standards requirements to be followed in the design and construction of the fuel 
system 
e Engineering design drawings to the deemed completion level (30-60% or more) 
e Materials and equipment specifications 
3.2.6.6 Economic and Financial Best Practices 
Adopting economic and financial best practices in the development of airport fuel infrastructure ensures that 
the component of fuel costs associated with the use of the infrastructure can be kept to an optimum level. The 
following aspects should be taken into consideration when planning for new fuel infrastructure. 
3.2.6.6.1 Fit-for-Purpose Infrastructure 
The appropriate fuel infrastructure to be put in place at an airport needs to consider immediate fuel 
consumption as well as expected future consumption that is aligned with the traffic growth forecast for the 
airport. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 547 

===PAGE 567===
Py 
Se iC IATA al Airport Development Reference Manual 
Fit-for-purpose infrastructure refers to: 
¢ The right-sized infrastructure that allows optimum capacity utilization over the design period. Trigger 
criteria should provide the alert for timely investment in additional capacity. Right-sizing avoids 
overinvestment, which leads to higher cost from asset underutilization or underinvestment, which can 
increase the risk of supply disruption 
¢ The right type of infrastructure to meet the throughput volume at the airport over the next five to ten years. 
For low throughput volumes, construction of a hydrant fueling system would not be optimal and would 
unnecessarily increase the unit cost for fueling the aircraft 
3.2.6.6.2. Common-use Infrastructure 
To avoid duplicative investment and achieve the greatest cost efficiency, fuel infrastructure should be 
developed on a model of common usage. Suppliers of fuel should only need to pay a transparent and non￾discriminatory set of fees to use the common storage and, where it is present, a common hydrant system. 
Since blended Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF) must meet the same specifications as jet fuel from fossil 
origin (e.g., “drop-in’), SAF can be effectively and efficiently supplied at airports taking advantage of the 
common-use infrastructure-no SAF specific infrastructure is needed. 
3.2.6.6.3 Competition in Fuel Supply 
Open and fair competition contributes to a large extent in maintaining a higher quality of service, compliance 
with industry standards and competitive rates. Airport planning should ensure that open access to fuel 
facilities is promoted throughout the entire supply chain, including off-airport facilities. A cost-effective 
infrastructure at the airport could easily suffer from monopolistic practices at off-airport facilities, including 
pipeline, road transport and marine port facilities. It is, therefore, essential to involve regulatory authorities to 
ensure that owners of centralized infrastructure do not create barriers to market entry for fuel suppliers 
wishing to bring product into the airport. 
3.2.6.6.4 Pricing of Fuel Infrastructure 
Optimum pricing is achieved by implementing financial best practices that include setting a reasonable 
investment payback timeframe, a fair rate of return on investment and a transparent cost recovery 
mechanism. 
To ensure that infrastructure costs translate to reasonable fuel fees, it is essential to set a realistic 
depreciation period for storage tanks, hydrants, and other long-term investments that is tied to their useful 
lives. The depreciation time frame for a fuel farm, including its hydrant system, should not be less than 
30 years. 
For fuel infrastructure with a long useful life, to avoid front-loading of costs, which leads to high fees at the 
beginning, it is preferable to set fees based on the projected volumes for the entire life of the infrastructure. 
548 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 568===
ie 
Se IATA Pull Airside Infrastructure 
This practice allows a stable level of fuel fees to be applied throughout and avoids high fees paid by users at 
the beginning when utilization of the infrastructure is lower. 
3.2.6.6.5 Funding 
Funding of fuel infrastructure development could be from various sources, including the airport itself, an 
independent third-party investor, fuel suppliers, and even airlines. For example, in the United States and 
Canada, the airlines have formed independent consortiums where they lease the property and finance and 
build fuel facilities at major and medium-sized airports. This model has proven very effective in sharing the 
costs and giving the benefit of flexibility of supply as each airline arranges for fuel purchase and delivery to 
shared storage facilities. In some Latin and South American airports, the expansion or construction costs of 
the aviation fueling systems have been required by the airport to be part of the responsibility of the fuel farm 
operator that has the service contract to maintain and operate the fuel system. A throughput rate, charged in 
gallons or liters, is the predominant way to support the costs of fuel infrastructure. 
Investment by fuel suppliers, which have a vested interest in fuel supply, should be considered with caution 
and only allowed if safeguards are in place to ensure that fuel supply competition is not hampered and other 
suppliers can have unrestricted use of the infrastructure by simply paying a reasonable and transparent fee. 
Prefunding of fuel infrastructure investment (e.g., charging a fee to the user before the infrastructure is 
operational) must not be allowed as it would be unfair to make a current user pay for future infrastructure that 
the user is not using and may not be using in future. 
3.2.6.6.6 User Consultation 
© Consultation with fuel infrastructure users is essential during planning of infrastructure projects. It is 
equally important for the process to take place on a regular basis and, at least once a year, to evaluate 
the state of fuel facilities in operation. The objective of these meetings is to ensure that forecast demand, 
user needs, and financial requirements will be met during the lifetime of the project. One operating model 
used is to have an integrated management association comprised of the airport, fuel farm operator, fuel 
suppliers, home-based air carriers and foreign air carriers. Some of the key activities of the association 
that have to do with ongoing financial and operating activities would include reviewing policies and 
operational procedures. 
e Reviewing service standards. 
e Monitoring the performance of the fuel farm operator. 
e Reviewing and approving the operating budget prepared by the operator, including the throughput fee. 
The association would also evaluate future capacity investments to address anticipated demand. A 
knowledgeable regulator supported by industry stakeholders can also ensure that centralized infrastructure is 
cost-effective to meet the needs of the industry over the long term.

3.3. Passenger Terminal 
3.3.1 Introduction 
Airport passenger terminals must serve many different functions, accommodate a wide variety of stakeholders 
who frequently have diverging objectives, and respond to changes inherent in one of the world's most 
dynamic industries. Airport terminals need to be functionally and operationally efficient and resilient, 
commercially viable (for both airports and airlines), offer passengers as effortless and straightforward a travel 
experience as possible, whilst minimizing their impact on the environment. 
This chapter addresses the key requirements associated with typical airport passenger terminals and provides 
guidance on many of the specific challenges associated with airport facilities. 
Note: While the ADRM is an important guide for many key elements of the terminal, it is intended to be used 
in context where every airport will have particular needs and constraints that will warrant different outcomes. 
The ADRM does not provide a definitive guide on how to design an airport terminal and it is not intended to 
be used in that context. 
Some of the many varying parameters may include: 
e Volumes of passenger traffic in annual, busy (design) hour and peak hour numbers 
¢ Growth projections with different design and construction phasing requirements 
¢ Compositions of aircraft fleet traffic (e.g., wide-body/narrow-body/regional) 
¢ Mixes of passenger traffic (e.g., domestic/international, long haul/short haul, origin and destination, 
transfer, first-class/business class/premium economy/economy) 
¢ Types of airline operations (e.g., multiple carriers/dominant alliances, full-service airlines, NMAs, home￾based carriers) 
e Environmental and sustainability objectives 
* Local, regional, and national security/immigration/emigration/customs requirements 
¢ Level of Service standards (e.g., queuing times, space provision, seating provision) 
¢ Local customs with significantly different numbers of “meeters and greeters” and “well-wishers” 
e Cultural/religious behaviors regarding proximity, orientation and availability of amenities 
e Average number of checked baggage and/or cabin baggage 
550 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 570===
He Al , 
IATA‘ Passenger Terminal 
¢ Requirements for checked baggage screening 
e Demand and opportunity for retail and food & beverage offers 
¢ Perspectives on utilization of advanced technology/engineering systems, such as online or biometric 
processing; and 
¢ Kinds of intermodal connections to public transit, vehicles, rail, etc. 
¢ Cost and budget considerations 
Nevertheless, the challenges faced by each airport are frequently similar. Consequently, with reference to 
international best practices and targeted benchmarking, it is possible to gather a broad set of design guidance 
principles. These form the basis for the recommendations contained in the ADRM. 
3.3.2 Terminal Design Guiding Principles 
Airports, and the airport terminals in particular, play a vital role in the provision of aviation services, enabling 
mobility and exchange between regions, countries and continents. 
As terminals are the important interfaces where passengers transition from land-bound transportation modes 
to aircraft, special care needs to be given to ensure air travel is not only safe, but also accessible, and 
enjoyable. 
All terminal designs should aim to deliver optimum service to their passengers and airline partners, and 
should enable successful, commercially viable, sustainable and responsible operations. 
The planning and configuration of passenger terminals must be related closely to the runway/taxiway system, 
apron configuration and airport access (road and rail) systems. In design “FORM FOLLOWS FUNCTION”. So, 
the requirements of the airport operation and how the major airline users operate within the airport complex 
must be fully understood. The basic operational strategies and priorities of the major airlines need to be 
understood in order toto fully appreciate the terminal's required functionality. 
Whilst every passenger terminal planning process is different, and will need to be tailored to the individual 
requirements and constraints, it is recommended to always consider the following guiding principles: 
3.3.2.1 Provide a Safe and Secure Environment 
Safety and security are the highest importance in the planning, design and operation of terminal buildings. 
Passenger terminals provide a critical component in maintaining the safety and security of the global aviation 
system through the prevention of the passage of people and objects that can cause harm or lead to acts of 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 551 

===PAGE 571===
Se & 
IATA 4 Airport Development Reference Manual 
unlawful interference. This includes landside to airside, airside to landside and airside to airside. Passenger 
terminals, along with all other airport facilities, shall be designed to meet both international and national safety 
and security requirements. Threats to safety and security may be of malicious intent, such as terrorists or 
criminals, or unintentional, such as people carrying large quantities of batteries. Due to evolution of threats 
planners should work closely with authorities to determine appropriate solutions, including bringing in best 
practice emerging from the global aviation community. 
The terminal buildings can be high profile targets and will need to be designed to prevent harm to the 
occupants as well as damage to the facilities against threat. A wide range of solutions, such as physical 
barriers, air filters, digital solutions and operational procedures may be required to minimize the impact of a 
range of threats. It should be noted that threats do vary around the world and solutions will differ. Designers 
should also consider safeguarding space in case of an increase in threat. 
Terminal buildings also need to be safe for everyone to use and operate in both regular and irregular 
conditions and shall be designed to minimize the risk. The complexity of provision of fire life safety for larger 
terminal buildings should not be underestimated given the need to maintain segregation of different 
Passengers groups—such as inbound international arrivals, outbound security screened departures and people 
landside in the event of an evacuation. 
Airports and their terminal buildings are often used as a focus of activity in case of emergencies both on and 
off airport. Consideration should be given to the building purpose and design for resilient operations, for 
instance in the event of volcanic eruption, earthquake, flood, hurricanes and disease outbreaks. Discussions 
with local and national authorities on such matters should be undertaken at the earliest stage and should be 
included into the Concept of Operations. 
Solutions to safe and secure terminal buildings will be anchored in the building concept and layout, and will 
normally require a range of controls and surveillance with significant reliance on technologies such as access 
control, e-gates, CCTV, screening equipment, video analytics and communications. Technology can also be 
used to help minimizing the impact of such controls on the passenger journey and experience. 
3.3.2.2 Provide Optimum Level of Service to Passengers 
It is |ATA's primary objective to inform the planning process with recommendations to determine optimum, 
balanced capacity and level of service between facilities, operations, rules & procedures, and airline 
schedules. 
In providing the guidance and recommendations, the aim is to ensure that passengers are provided with 
terminal facilities that provide sufficient space to accommodate the necessary functions in a comfortable 
environment while offering acceptable queuing times. Each of the different functions that support the 
movement of passengers from the landside forecourt to from the aircraft and vice versa (as described and 
illustrated throughout this document) requires special attention. As a result, the balanced capacity should 
avoid congestion, and allow passengers to transition through the entire terminal process, from curbside to 
aircraft and vice versa, safely, with minimum delays and effort. 
552 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 572===
Ye ; IATA Passenger Terminal 
The IATA Level of Service (LoS) framework provides a set of industry guidelines for passenger terminal 
facilities, in terms of the space to be provided to passengers as well as the time passengers can expect to be 
queueing at individual facilities. These performance guidelines represent international best practice at many 
airports around the world. The guidelines balance the need for costly infrastructure provisions with passenger 
processing targets that allow for efficiently sized facilities. IATA strongly recommends that all parties involved 
collaborate to jointly provide terminal facilities with an “Optimum Level of Service”. 
Every reasonable effort should be made by airlines, airport operators, and involved governmental agencies to 
work towards a shared understanding of balanced terminal capacity and provided Level of Service. Please 
see 3.3.4.7 Level of Service Concept for further information. 
3.3.2.3 Provide Efficient, Consolidated Terminal Facilities 
Airports can be daunting places for passengers. Depending on the nature and volumes of traffic they serve, 
passenger terminals can be large, with particularly high demand in land take, especially airside, to serve 
parked aircraft. The need to provide multiple process points and the nature of aircraft operations can lead to 
large size and high degrees of complexity within the terminals, making navigation of these facilities not only 
difficult, but also stressful for passengers. 
Providing intuitive and efficient navigation and circulation throughout the terminal is a key planning and design 
objective. Intuitive planning and design support the natural circulation throughout the facilities with little 
reliance on wayfinding—-which supports efficiencies in operations and higher customer satisfaction. The 
architecture and layout of the facilities should strive to promote “intuitive” circulation throughout the terminal 
facilities. In striving for intuitive circulation, consideration should be given to the creation of “consolidated” 
processing areas. Consolidated processing areas are generally desired and typically provide a number of 
benefits, most notably for the passenger, and also from a reduced land use, operational efficiency, cost￾effectiveness, and sustainability perspective. 
Typically, consolidated terminal processing areas allows an airport to be more efficient in terms of its own 
resource deployment. This efficiency applies to its own staff, governmental agency staff, airline partners, 
ground handlers, and other stakeholders. Consolidated processing areas tend to reduce the complexity of 
operations, the amount and type of land use, and its environmental impact. In addition, consolidated terminal 
processing areas typically create the simplest and most efficient environment for passengers to navigate. 
Passengers generally benefit from the least amount of decision making required, over the shortest journey 
possible from landside transport to the aircraft and vice versa. Further, this concept tends to reduce the 
amount of interfaces for passengers. Consolidated processing areas traditionally afford a simpler security 
control operations concept: with one side of the screening area classified as “un-secured” (often referred to 
“landside” area); and the other side classified as “secured” (often referred to “airside”). A similar approach is 
applied for border control. 
Many of the most successful passenger terminal facilities employ these key design principles. The most 
intuitive decision is “no decision”. A good example is limiting the number of level changes, or where feasible 
consolidating operations into a single passenger terminal. As a guiding principle and for the reasons 
referenced above, IATA recommends the implementation of consolidated processing areas. However, under 
certain local circumstances, a centralized singular passenger terminal may not be the most appropriate 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 553 

===PAGE 573===
ee ii 
See IATA Baul Airport Development Reference Manual 
solution. A deep understanding of each airport's business goals and stakeholder requirements must be 
undertaken to determine the most appropriate passenger terminal concept/layout that is appropriate. 
3.3.2.4 Provide Seamless Passenger Journeys 
The best airport terminals are those that provide the most clear and direct path across all passenger and 
Public journey paths (domestic, international, and transfer traffic). Intuitive wayfinding, limiting decision points 
and level changes, the use of materials, lighting, outdoor views and other physical directional clues that 
enhance passenger orientation is significantly more effective than reliance on signage. Passenger orientation 
within the airport campus and more specifically within the passenger terminal can be greatly enhanced by 
adopting a transparent building philosophy: There is no simpler way to orientate passengers than to allow 
them to see their final destination. For departing and transfer passengers, this means views of aircraft. For 
arriving passengers, this means sight lines toward landside access systems and/or “meeter/greeter” areas. 
Directional information should only be needed to support ancillary facilities that may be away from the 
primary, clearly evident circulation routes (i.e., to information/transfer counters, CIP lounges, toilets and 
associated support services, etc.) or to confirm the route. Further detail is provided in 3.3.12 Wayfinding and 
Signage. 
When it is necessary to make a choice or change direction and/or level, the simplest way to maintain 
passenger flow and orientation is to limit the number of choices available. “Straight ahead” is always the 
simplest way to maintain passenger orientation which supports efficient flow and circulation. Convoluted 
circulation routes that include changes in direction or level negatively impact both orientation and the service 
level to the passenger. Passengers should not be subjected to changes in direction greater than 90 degrees 
and should not be made to perform repeated 90-degree turns within a short distance. Passenger routes that 
have to backtrack or cross other passenger routes should be avoided to limit confusion and congestion, 
promote efficient flows, and maintain a high service level. 
Planning movement flows must also include routes for people with disabilities and assisted vehicular 
passenger transfers. Further detail is provided in 3.3.9 Universal Design and Terminal Accessibility. 
Where it is impossible to avoid cross-flows, it is imperative to provide sufficient space to amply absorb the 
volume of people and factor congestion into journey time forecasts. 
Walking distances from the forecourt to the gate and vice versa should be minimized. Walking distances in 
excess of 300 meters should be augmented with moving walkways. 
Passenger flow routes should be clear and easily understood. Concession areas planned along the route from 
curbside to passenger boarding areas should afford convenient access and be available to Passengers 
without impeding direct access to gates or increasing the overall walking distance. Passengers who wish to 
make quick, easy and direct routings through terminals should also be accommodated balancing efficient 
flows and retail sales. Dedicated “fast-track” procedures, especially for commercially important passengers 
(VIP/CIP), families of passengers with disabilities, should be considered. 
If possible, departing and arriving passengers should not be required to change levels. In cases where difficult 
site conditions, existing operations or building structures leave no alternative, then level changes should be 
554 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 574===
Pas} 
IATA Passenger Terminal 
achieved by modes of conveyance (i.e., escalators and elevators) with an associated staircase and/or ramp 
as backup should the vertical circulation devices fail. Transfer passengers will arrive via one aircraft and need 
to navigate the passenger facilities to board a different aircraft for their onward journey. Intuitive design 
considerations can go a long way in assisting the transfer passenger circulation routes while providing a 
pleasurable experience. Further detail is provided in 3.3.11.3 Horizontal and Vertical Circulation. 
3.3.2.5 Enable Efficient Operations 
Before embarking on a major capital investment program, it is recommended that airports review their current 
operational processes and procedures to identify any opportunity to revise and update, with a focus on 
improving efficiency. Many airports continue to operate with outdated processes and procedures, whilst 
emerging technologies, new business models, and changing governmental regulations can generate 
improvements. By adjusting current processes and procedures—thus, better utilizing existing facilitiesthe 
airport can gain efficiencies, increase the level of service, and often add capacity with relatively small 
financial. Examples of process and procedure improvements can include, for example, extending the 
roller-bed lengths before and after the passenger security screening machine and walkthrough metal detector, 
or expanding the circulation path or queuing areas to afford a higher processing rate in key processing areas. 
Such exemplary actions can reduce costs, drive sustainable operations, and often defer major capital 
investments. 
Beyond process improvements, the planning and design of passenger terminals (including renovations and 
expansions to existing facilities) should be based on sound planning guidelines with a focus on efficiency. 
Efficiency should be a goal across all aspects of the terminal. The airport's ConOps plan (see 2.7 
Development of a Concept of Operations) should be a driver for efficiency and it should be reflected and 
incorporated into the design of the passenger terminal. Further, efficiency should underpin all sustainability 
goals, operations and maintenance programs, and be at the forefront of level of service considerations. 
Efficiency equates to higher levels of service, lower operations and maintenance costs, and a lower carbon 
footprint; three desirable outcomes for any airport. 
Determining the degree of centralization of the processing activity required is an important efficiency 
consideration when planning facilities. In centralized terminal concepts, all the major components (i.e., surface 
access systems, passenger processing, and BHS) are located in a single passenger terminal complex, 
independent of any particular traffic segment (i.e., domestic, international, or transfer). In a centralized 
terminal, airlines and airport operators can avoid unnecessary duplication of activities and processes thereby 
benefitting from economies of scale. Common facilities can be shared and the associated CAPEX/OPEX and 
resulting charges can be optimized to the benefit of the aviation community. 
It should be noted that a centralized passenger terminal concept may not be universally applicable. Each 
airport should review its vision, business plan, ConOps plan, and goals to determine the most suitable 
passenger terminal concepts/layout that best aligns with the airport's business plan and stakeholders needs. 
See 3.3.3 Terminal Planning Concepts for a detailed discussion on planning concepts and layout.

IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.3.2.6 Implement Sustainable Solutions 
There is heightened awareness and concern about the impact of aviation on the environment; therefore, 
sustainability has also become an important consideration in airport infrastructure (See 2.4 Airport 
Environmental Sustainability). Airports have been proactive in setting decarbonization targets as evidenced by 
ACI World establishing a global goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050 and implementing an Airport 
Carbon Accreditation Program to help airports assess and map out a strategy to reduce their carbon 
emissions, 
Airport planning and design decisions have a big influence on environmental and operational performance; 
therefore, passenger terminal plans should be developed with environmental considerations in mind. This 
includes making the best use of existing facilities to minimize the need for new build. 
Sustainability should be embedded across all phases of the passenger terminal infrastructure life cycle 
including the concept, design, development, delivery, and implementation. The use of sustainable building 
standards and design tools can increase energy efficiency, conserve resources, and minimize the co, 
emissions associated with materials and construction processes throughout the whole lifecycle of the 
infrastructure including maintaining and eventually demolishing it. 
The goal should be to create a structure that is flexible and can be adapted to different uses throughout its 
lifetime. Sustainability can be built into airport facilities through such concepts as a phased, modular building 
approach and the introduction of features such as the use of low carbon materials, natural and LED lighting, 
renewable energy, and alternative heating/cooling methods. How the terminal will be operated including its 
use of technology will influence its size, utilization, efficiency, and ultimately its environmental footprint. 
Passenger terminals are more intensively used than other similar buildings. They also have a lot of energy 
uses that other building types do not have-baggage handling systems, fixed electric ground power for aircraft 
at the gates, people movers and moving walkways. Therefore, energy strategies to sustainably source 
electricity, and increase efficiency are critical for limiting carbon emissions. Anything that will minimize energy 
needed to heat, cool, and light the structure will make it more efficient and sustainable in the long run. 
Terminal buildings that are designed to be in tune with their local climate, respond to solar impact, make 
efficient use of daylight, energy and water resources, rely on local materials and have robust waste 
management practices are set to use fewer resources in building operations. Focusing on the efficient use of 
land, energy, water and materials from the start yields the best results in building and operating efficiencies. 
Resource management that protects the local environment and optimizes the use of resources through the 
reduction and re-use of waste should be supported. Successful airport operators realize that partnerships with 
users, tenants and operators are essential to the successful implementation of any emission or waste 
reduction efforts. State and local requirements and airline/vendor goals also help support these efforts. 
3.3.2.7 Provide Cost-Effective Design Solutions 
Airports are heavily dependent on infrastructure and land. The need for land and costs of developing 
infrastructure can make any airport development an expensive undertaking. 
556 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 576===
whe IATA Passenger Terminal 
Airport developments should identify cost-effective solutions for terminal projects seeking to ensure that 
functional requirements are addressed efficiently and that design solutions are selected in order to optimize 
the long-term operating costs to the airport. 
Proposals to extend or construct new passenger terminal facilities should consider a detailed business case 
and cost-benefit analysis. The business case must demonstrate and quantify clear benefits in terms of 
increased capacity to satisfy existing and projected demand, improved passenger experience and operational 
efficiency, as well as providing sustainable design solutions. 
The business case considers not just the capital investment required (CAPEX) but where possible also the 
whole-life-cycle cost of the project. It is, as far as applicable, also recommended to consider operating and 
replacement costs (OPEX/REPEX), to achieve an optimum balance between initial investment and the need 
for ongoing maintenance. 
As outlined in 3.3.3 Terminal Planning Concepts, expansions and new construction should be conceived as 
additional modules to existing operational facilities and systems. Design, management and construction costs 
can be minimized by adopting a repetitive, modular approach that does not adversely impact existing or future 
operations. 
In order to facilitate future growth, airport owners, developers and designers should seek to ensure that 
airports can be expanded incrementally. As much as possible, and where it makes operational sense to do 
so, additional infrastructure should be added in an economically efficient manner on a “just in time” basis to 
meet increasing demand without negatively impacting investments in existing facilities. Furthermore, ongoing 
expansions and development must be planned so as not to negatively impact on-going airport operations. 
A comprehensive Master Plan that addresses all phases of the planned development is crucial. The aim of 
good terminal design should be that all incremental developments are consistent with the outcome shown in 
the Master Plan (see 2.3 Master Planning). 
3.3.2.8 Provide Accessible Facilities 
Globally, an estimated 1.2 billion people, or 15% of the population, have a disability (World Health 
Organization). According to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, persons 
with disabilities are defined as ‘those who have long-term physical, mental, intellectual or sensory impairments 
which in interaction with various barriers may hinder their full and effective participation in society on an equal 
basis with others’. 
Airports should follow the principles of Universal Design from the outset of all new projects. For brownfield 
projects where adapting legacy facilities can be challenging, every effort should be made to incorporate 
Universal Design principles, accepting that it might not always be possible to fully address the needs of all 
passengers with disabilities. Greenfield projects, on the other hand, can benefit greatly (and avoid subsequent 
costs) by incorporating universal design and inclusion early on as part of the planning process. 
A key objective of the ADRM is to ensure that airport facilities are planned and designed to be used by 
everyone, including those with disabilities, without the need for adaptation or specialized design. It also 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 557 

===PAGE 577===
Se 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
provides guidance on correct action and implementation, where appropriate, possible and practicable. Where 
legislated, national accessibility design standards should be complied with in full and it is strongly advised 
recommended practices are followed where provided. See 3.3.9 Universal Design and Terminal Accessibility 
for further information. 
3.3.2.9 Plan for Integrated Systems 
Airport passenger terminals are complex operational environments comprised of interrelated systems 
designed to ensure the safe, secure and efficient movement of people and bags. The development of new 
airports and the upgrade/expansion of existing airports requires careful consideration of the space and 
functional requirements of these systems. Their close integration is important factor in facilitating the 
seamless flow of passengers and bags and supporting an airport's resiliency. 
The systems environment of a terminal can be complex. An extensive variety of sophisticated mechanical and 
data systems support are used to enhance the operation of the airport and its partners (i.e., the airlines, 
governmental agencies, and others). These systems include, among many others, check-in systems, BHS, 
data management systems including AODBs, FIDS, CCTV systems, public address systems, fire alarm and 
evacuation systems, access control and intrusion Security systems, communication systems, building 
management systems, passenger monitoring systems, and staff management systems. 
Many of these systems exchange data information with each other in order to provide a comprehensive 
airport operational system. integrating and coordinating the input and output of these various data systems is 
an important part of comprehensive airport management. A key element of this system integration is to ensure 
that all systems, software, and data can be easily exchanged between the different systems in an acceptable 
and readable format. 
One of the most important systems, and the one that has the biggest impact on terminal design is the BHS 
system (see 3.3.8 Baggage Handling Systems). BHS are expensive to build, maintain and operate, and are 
an important factor in the footprint and cost of the terminal building. The BHS has a bigger impact on the 
design and spatial planning of a passenger terminal than other processing systems and can be difficult to 
tetrofit into an existing passenger terminal design. For new terminals, the BHS needs to be considered early 
in the design process and should be aligned with the terminal's planning assumptions including its traffic 
characteristics. The processing of passengers and baggage are fully interdependent therefore any constraint 
in the handling of baggage can limit a terminal's overall passenger capacity. 
The size, complexity, and requirements of the BHS can be underestimated (particularly in spatial 
requirements, circulation and staging requirements, cooling requirements, and electrical requirements). Care 
should be given early in the planning phase to ensure that there is adequate space and sufficient utility 
provisions allocated to the BHS to ensure success as the design progresses and more of these requirements 
are needed.

===PAGE 578===
IATA Passenger Terminal 
3.3.2.10 Design for Passenger Satisfaction 
Aviation is a service to move people safely and securely over long distances and the journeys through the 
airport terminal at each end of the flight are significant steps in that service. The passenger perception of the 
overall journey will be influenced by the quality of service provided in the terminal building and providing a 
good level of satisfaction, using the recommendations in the ADRM, is an important target for designers and 
operators. The target level of satisfaction will be influenced by passenger types, budgets and airlines and is it 
important to have targets that can be measurable and achievable using both quantitative service targets and 
industry wide benchmarks such as ACI's ASQ program and Skytrax. Designers should become familiar with 
these programs and the areas and means of measurement. 
Passengers will feel safe, supported and comfortable in an airport environment that meets their needs, 
enabling them to get to their chosen destination at their chosen time. Terminals should be designed to deliver 
all the core components consistently ensuring that everyone experiences a comfortable and enjoyable 
journey. 
Designing for passenger satisfaction should follow all the journey steps and for all different users including for 
staff and visitors as well as passengers. Particular attention should be paid to journey steps that can create 
higher levels of stress in passengers. Good facilities for staff are important in their delivery of service 
excellence whether front of house or in operations and maintenance. Designers should ensure that all the 
core components are resilient in their operation with necessary redundancy to enable maintenance to be 
carried out without affecting the journey and that all everything should be able to be kept rigorously clean. 
Design should embrace digital interfaces as a key component of the passenger experience, both visibly in 
wayfinding, entertainment and information but also behind the scenes to manage the journey to an optimum 
standard. There is increasing public interest in airports making positive interventions on important issues 
such as sustainability and inclusivity and clear demonstration of such values will likely add to the passenger 
experience. 
The commercial offerings, whether retail or food and beverage, airline or pay-in lounges are important 
features for many passengers. A good offering coupled with good levels of overall passenger satisfaction will 
likely lead to increased commercial performance, an important element in funding the facilities. 
3.3.2.11 Consider the Local Context 
Airports provide a gateway to the city, region and often country that they serve and will provide the first 
welcome and last goodbye to visitors as well as the leaving and returning home for residents. The journey 
through the passenger terminal provides an excellent opportunity for identification with the area that it serves, 
acting as a gateway with its unique culture and sense of place. The planning and design of the airport 
terminal should consider the local context through showcasing the culture, heritage, spirit, and amenities that 
can be expected. These can be through several media including art, branding, building finishes, events, food 
and beverage as well as the building form. Input from local communities is to be encouraged. 
The design of the terminal will also need to meet all local standards and regulations. This may result in 
different layouts for similar functional requirements, in particular for fire protection, security, seismic, religion, 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 559 

===PAGE 579===
=e 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
sustainability and climate conditions. As large terminal buildings are often not contemplated when local 
standards are developed it is often necessary to work closely with the authorities to gain approvals. The 
design should also be sensitive to cultural and religious needs of the location which may not necessarily be 
included in standards and requirements. 
If the local standards are lower than the recommendations of the ADRM, the designer should endeavor to 
meet the ADRM recommendations as this can also help to showcase good practice in the region. 
3.3.2.12 Plan for Flexible, Modular Expansion 
Each of the interconnected subsystems in an airport terminal will likely need to adapt as passenger traffic 
grows. Whether it is capacity enhancement (i.e., more security screening positions needed), a modification in 
operating protocols (i.e., more detailed search criteria) or the regulatory environment (i.e., changes in border 
control or Customs requirements), utilizing modular, expandable building designs, materials and systems 
facilitates accommodating such required changes over time. 
Terminal facilities must be designed so that they can respond to growth in a logical, phased manner. This is a 
fundamental need derived from the airport's Master Plan (see 2.3 Master Planning). 
It is recommended that, on an unconstrained “greenfield” or “bluesea” site, a plan be based on modular 
flexibility and expandability, starting from a single terminal complex or “campus” capable of accommodating 
the entire site's passenger handling needs for as long as possible before embarking on the implementation of 
further terminals. The goal is always to deliver excellent Passenger service and experience, and the most 
effective and efficient operations. To achieve this, the functions that drive airport and airline operations need 
to be fully understood and incorporated into the design and development. 
Each of the terminal sub-systems must be in balance with the others as there is no benefit in having surplus 
capacity in one sub-system if others are constrained. A modular design philosophy enables capacity 
enhancements to be added to individual subsystems and facilities without unnecessarily disrupting airline and 
terminal operations. In this way, new regulatory developments and changes in the nature and volume of 
Passenger flows can be readily and quickly accommodated. 
Designing terminal facilities that embrace flexibility is paramount. There are proven methodologies that 
enhance flexibility. For instance, large structural spans and “column-free” spaces improve flexibility. However, 
these solutions must also be cost-effective. Clustered siting of physical elements that are difficult, costly and 
disruptive to relocate (i.e., structural elements, vertical circulation and service cores) is effective. Another 
example is the use of vertical partitions that can be moved simply without extraordinary disturbance and 
expense. 
Building services also need to be designed to allow flexibility. The location of key aspects of the primary plant 
should be carefully considered with regard to future expansion. Distribution systems need to balance initial 
cost vs. the requirement for future flexibility. 
Airports must be designed to minimize the physical constraints each element imposes on future expansion by 
ensuring that all elements address flexibility. 
560 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 580===
—— 
we | . IATA Bul Passenger Terminal 
As previously outlined, it is preferable that new construction be viewed as an additional module to an existing 
but expandable operational system. Design, management and construction costs should be optimized by 
adopting a repetitive, low risk approach that should not adversely impact existing operations. Expensive, 
above-average cost solutions with unique “one off” architectural fixtures and fittings or engineering features 
should be avoided. 
3.3.2.13 Safeguard for Innovation and Future Operational Changes 
One of the most significant challenges for airports is adapting to constant change. As the aviation industry 
continues to be an extremely dynamic business, major changes will continue to affect the way airlines 
operate, passengers interact with airlines, and airlines and passengers use airports. In addition, changing 
governmental regulations, new industry standards, availability of user data and the constant search for new 
revenue opportunities will further drive change. These changes will, in part, continue to be supported by 
developments in technology which will change space utilization and processing at airports. 
Airlines and passengers will continue to challenge airports to optimize their processes and operate efficient 
facilities at the least cost generating efficiencies that can be passed on to the passenger. Given the dynamic 
nature of the aviation industry, future requirements for any airport cannot be predicted with absolute certainty. 
Airport owners, developers, and designers are faced with the challenge of providing cost-effective airport 
facilities that respond to airline requirements and changing business models, all while offering the greatest 
possible flexibility. The most successful airports can respond to changing requirements and adapt their 
facilities with minimal disruption. Terminal facilities and systems that are flexible and that safeguard for the 
future are essential for effectively adapting to change. 
Departing passenger processing has already changed dramatically, due to the increased availability of online 
off-airport processing. Increasing numbers of travelers no longer “check-in” under “traditional” norms (obtain a 
boarding pass and tag their checked luggage) at the terminal building. Many passengers today either check-in 
via their mobile phone or computer, and either self-tag and drop their baggage once at the airport or have a 
registered and secure RFID bag tag that supports direct bag drop. Indeed, future terminals are likely to 
feature more self-service bag drop units as passengers will arrive at the terminal with all processes previously 
completed off airport and will only need to introduce their self-tagged bags into the BHS. Only a minimal 
number of “traditional” check-in units will be required to resolve problems or assist passengers with special 
needs, such as groups, families and those requiring assistance. 
Other major terminal processing areas that are likely to see a considerable amount of evolutionary change in 
the coming years are security screening areas, due to introduction of new or improved processes and 
technologies, border control and customs facilities due to process automation such as “Trusted Traveler” 
programs, baggage claim areas, gate rooms (to process the on-boarding of passengers as a result of 
technology enhancements), retail and food & beverage facilities with the advent of direct delivery of 
purchases to gate rooms, and aircraft stands due to the need to accommodate changing fleet mixes and 
potentially longer length aircraft. Spaces and systems must be designed to be flexible to allow for simple and 
straightforward reconfigurations that can easily and cost-effectively accommodate the ever-evolving airport 
functionality requirements with minimal operational disruption. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 561 

===PAGE 581===
Se | IATA pif Airport Development Reference Manual 
To effectively adapt to these ever-changing impacts, airports are encouraged to adopt a mindset of 
innovation. This mindset of innovation translates into a culture and behavior whereby airport staff and 
stakeholders actively embrace the constant evolution of emerging products and services being developed 
within the industry. It is recommended that forward looking opportunities to improve safety and operations, 
increase efficiencies, reduce costs (all with a focus on increasing the level of service), should be a constant 
airport initiative. A focus on process improvements, the application of technology, and appropriate planning, 
design and construction of facilities will promote this mindset. Thought should also be given to the trialing of 
new processes and technologies with limited exposure/risk (see 2.6 Airport Technology). 
3.3.2.14 Champion Collaborative Partnering in Design and Development 
The process of collaborative partnering brings together all project development team members, including 
owners, architects, engineers, construction managers, and contractors, and all project stakeholders, including 
airport users, operations, maintenance, properties, environmental systems, security, inspections, 
concessionaires, airlines, and regulators, in a formal cooperative working environment. With collaborative 
partnering, common goals to achieve improvements in key project performance outcomes such as safety, 
quality, schedule, and cost, are established and agreed at the beginning of the project and steering 
committees measure performance throughout the life of the project. This formal model of shared success and 
common culture has been effectively applied by several airports in recent years to improve project outcomes 
in a number of key performance indicators. 
Consultation with stakeholders is a key component of a successful collaborative Partnering arrangement. A 
collaborative approach between airports and users is essential to the overall success of a project and, when 
managed correctly, will ultimately deliver benefits for all parties. 
Meaningful consultation requires identifying key stakeholders early in the planning process before irreversible 
decisions are made. See 2.3 Master Planning for related information. While there are many stakeholders who 
vary by location, airlines should be regarded as a primary stakeholder. In particular, a regular, structured 
dialogue between subject matter experts is beneficial, to ensure user requirements are captured during 
concept and options selection phases of design and development, taking their passenger, operational and 
financial needs into account. 
The benefits of consultation are considerable and typically include all or a combination of the following; 
sharing global and regional best practices; helping to align business strategies between the airline community 
and airport; agreeing traffic forecasts and investment triggers; aligning on the agreed Concept of Operations; 
assessment criteria to help select options; phasing strategies to minimize operational disruption and maintain 
Level of Service; ORAT to ensure a successful AOD.

3.3.3 Terminal Planning Concepts 
The ‘Terminal Planning Concept’ refers to the high level configuration of the airport terminal buildings. The 
configuration of the terminal buildings are often dictated by the available site, the layout of the runways and 
taxiways, and the locations of other existing terminal buildings, however the development of an appropriate 
terminal concept that fits within these constraints, is essential to successfully achieving an efficient and 
pleasant airport experience for all stakeholders. 
The requirements of the major airline users must be fully understood and incorporated in the functional design 
considerations. This will play an important role in the layout and flexibility of the airport facilities, now and for 
years to come. 
The types and categories of aircraft that will be operated by the airlines will dictate the required terminal 
concept layouts and relationship with the stands. The terminal concept will also relate closely to the types of 
airlines and passenger business markets that will use the facility. 
3.3.3.1 Key Functions 
The passenger terminal complex is fundamentally a series of interconnected subsystems. Ideally, each 
subsystem is capable of expansion as and when demand dictates. The interconnected sub systems for the 
processing of passengers and baggage include: 
e Ground transportation systems (e.g., vehicles, rail, etc.) 
* The main landside terminal spaces. For departing passengers, this comprises the departures forecourt 
and departures hall and any associated commercial (i.e., retail and food & beverage) offerings. For 
arriving passengers, this comprises the Arrivals Hall and Forecourt (for “meeters and greeters”) and the 
related commercial spaces) 
¢ Outbound (emigration) and Inbound (immigration) inspection services (i.e., security checks on departures 
and health checks, immigration and customs control on arrivals) 
¢ Primary and centralized lounges to accommodate airside waiting prior to boarding (i.e., the main 
departure lounge and the associated retail and food & beverage offerings) 
¢ Secondary and dispersed lounges (i.e., finger piers and/or satellites containing gate lounges). These 
zones can also contain associated commercial offerings; and 
* BHS to collect, screen, sort, store, transfer and deliver bags to aircraft on departures, and on arrivals to 
unload and deliver bags into the terminal for redistribution back to passengers

As developed further in this sub-chapter, certain basic criteria should be observed in the selection of a 
terminal concept and the planning of passenger terminals. The criteria include those considerations outlined 
below. 
3.3.3.2 Terminal Types 
3.3.3.2.1 Origin and Destination Terminals 
The Origin and Destination (O/D) terminal can be defined as a terminal that caters mainly to flights and 
passengers that use the airport primarily as their point of origin or destination. The O/D terminal generally 
does not facilitate transfer traffic. 
Dedicated O/D terminals are typically not large in scale and tend to serve a limited regional market. Typical 
examples of primarily O/D terminals are those that: 
¢ Serve a niche market (e.g., London Luton Airport, England; Toronto City Airport, Canada; Dallas Love 
Field, USA) 
* Serve regional communities (e.g., Cork Airport, Ireland; Cebu Airport, Philippines); and 
¢ Are located near a popular tourist destination (e.g., Marseille Airport, France; Phuket Airport, Thailand; 
Ibiza Airport, Spain; Aspen-Pitkin Colorado County Airport, USA) 
Some international airports with limited onward destinations that only cater to a small amount of local regional 
transfer traffic may also be classed as “predominantly O/D” rather than “dedicated O/D” (e.g., Cape Town 
Airport, South Africa; Geneva Airport, Switzerland). The primary passenger processing functions required for 
a typical Domestic/International O/D terminal are outlined in the illustration below. In its most simplistic form, 
an O/D terminal has no transfer facilities and only one centralized processing area. Baggage handling is only 
provided for inbound and outbound traffic and there is no capability of storing or transferring bags between 
aircraft.

meet internationally recognized passenger service standards. This operational situation should be avoided 
wherever possible.

3.3.3.2.2. Transfer (or Hub) Terminals 
A transfer terminal (also known as a hub airport) is where passengers and/or cargo are transferred between 
aircraft without a direct service from their point of origin to their point of destination. Delta Airlines pioneered 
the hub-and-spoke system for passenger aviation in Atlanta, Georgia in the 1950s. FedEx also adopted this 
model for cargo in the 1970s. In practice, most hub airports cater to both transfer traffic and O/D traffic in one 
terminal building, or in a system of terminals. This optimizes connection opportunities with minimal transfer 
times. 
A terminal designed for high levels of transfer traffic has a significant transfer infrastructure in the airside zone 
to cater to the transfer passengers. It may have reduced check in and landside facilities due to the lower 
proportion of O/D traffic. It should also be noted that this type of terminal will cater to transit passengers (i.e., 
those that are deplaning and reboarding the same aircraft en route to their destination for reasons of aircraft 
refueling, crew change, etc.). 
Airlines can build opportunities to transfer passengers across their own operation and that of their partners 
and alliances. This is often done through code sharing by scheduling flights into aircraft arrivals banks 
followed by aircraft departures banks to maximize connectivity opportunities. A hub strategy will impact the 
terminal design due to significant peaks in traffic around these arrival and departure banks. The profile of the 
schedule is a significant consideration during the initial scoping of any new terminal or redevelopment. 
For passengers the hub model includes stop overs on long-haul routes. The airside amenities for transfer 
Passengers must be carefully considered to cater to their needs. Extended waiting times between arriving and 
departing flights means that hotel rooms, retail outlets, food & beverage provisions as well as toilet and 
shower facilities should be amply provided. Hub airports are also able to maximize commercial revenue and 
augment/enhance the overall travel experience with extensive customer offerings. 
Terminals that accommodate transfer operations may over time need to also accommodate increased levels 
of O/D traffic due to changes in local or regional policies on tourism, industry, etc. Thus it is vital that 
transfer/hub terminals always incorporate the flexibility needed to adjust to changing demands over time. 
Current examples of a primarily transfer terminals are Dubai International Airport (DXB) in Duabi, United Arab 
Emirates, Hamad International Airport (DOH) in Doha, Qatar and Hartsfield—Jackson Atlanta International 
Airport (ATL) in Atlanta, United States. These airports all typically process a ratio of approximately 70 percent 
transfer to 30 percent O/D traffic.

As is the case for any terminal, transfer terminals must in all cases meet stringent international and national 
security requirements. Most large international transfer terminals require security screening for some or all 
transferring passengers in the airside zone. This can be accommodated in one central transfer area or in 
separate facilities specific to each pier or zone. To eliminate duplication of facilities, one central security 
screening facility for both O/D and transfer traffic may be considered. This will reduce staffing and equipment 
needs for typically “peaky’ traffic flows. However, the dramatic impact of transfer peaks needs to be taken into 
consideration during the design process. 
Some transfer facilities may allow arrival transfer passengers to bypass security screening if they are arriving 
from ‘trusted’ origins. This will be dependent on local security legislation and may require further segregation 
of arrivals passengers to separate ‘trusted’ and ‘untrusted’ arrival passengers. 
Similarly some facilities may allow passengers to bypass immigration checks if they will not be mixing with 
domestic passengers in the departure lounges. These passengers will all be subject to immigration screening 
at their final destination therefore can be exempt at the transfer point. 
Some transfer terminals may also have transit lounges to accommodate onward passengers who must 
deplane. Transit passengers without the proper visa to “enter” the transfer country should not mix with 
Passengers from other flights. These passengers may be escorted to and from their aircraft and, if 
segregation from other passengers is maintained, transit passenger need not be rescreened. 
Baggage facilities at a transfer terminal will need to accommodate a significant amount of transfer baggage. 
The transfer baggage storage facility can also need to be quite large and include an Early Bag Store. The 
BHS will need to process baggage from multiple inbound to multiple outbound flights simultaneously and will 
typically require a highly sophisticated level of automation. 
3.3.3.2.3. Small Airport Terminals 
A small airport is typically a facility capable of processing up to one million Passengers per annum (mppa). 
The airport facilities must still meet the same regulatory, legal and security requirements of larger facilities, 
and be in accordance with relevant ICAO regulations. However, processes are simplified wherever possible. 
At small airports, a single building typically serves all of the functions of a terminal and pier/concourse. Site 
Planning considerations for future expanded use must be considered even at smail airports. It is important that 
space for future development be safeguarded by creating a master plan. Demand analysis should align with 
the requirements of the airlines, the traveling public and the local community. 
Similar to larger airports, the small airport's master plan and associated business plan may provide for small 
scale non aeronautical uses such as training facilities, hotels, business parks and other commercial uses. 
Such development zones should be safeguarded accordingly. 
568 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 588===
IATA Passenger Terminal 
The design of small airport terminals often differs significantly from larger terminals: 
e The landside forecourt is likely to only require a single level 
e Many processes can be simplified due to the smaller traffic throughput 
e Ageneral departure lounge/gate area should be designed for optimal efficiency. Passenger wayfinding 
will be less complex given the smaller area. Retail, food & beverage, rest areas and toilets should be 
provided, in part to create parallel revenue streams to support the airport operation. It is also possible that 
smaller airports will incorporate business or private aviation functions (General Aviation) that may require 
CIP facilities such as lounges and dedicated passenger processing areas 
© Typically, a small terminal will have no concourse or piers. Passengers are often bused or walk between 
the gate and the aircraft using dedicated apron walk routes and staff-supervised protocols 
* Small airports usually operate remote stands that allow aircraft to power in/out (i.e., self-maneuvering 
stands) 
* Baggage handling facilities can be limited and geared around the processing of one flight at a time rather 
than multiple flights simultaneously as in larger airports. Baggage handling processes may also be mainly 
manual, but they must be designed in accordance with Health and Safety Regulations and industry best 
practices and all baggage safety and screening protocols must be accommodated 
¢ [tis not uncommon for a small airport operation to share its terminal building with a flying school, flight 
training facility or Fixed-Base Operator (FBO) 
Increasingly, there are situations where smaller airports will exploit a terminal space or equipment for multiple 
functions so as to maximize its utilization and optimize the use of space. For example, inbound transfer flight 
baggage may be processed with departures screening equipment using agreed upon protocols. 
3.3.3.2.4 Mixed Traffic Airport Terminals 
The most common form of terminal is one that serves a mix of different traffic modes and carriers. The 
primary passenger processing functions required for both small and large Domestic/International mixed traffic 
terminals are outlined in the illustration below. 
The most common approach is to design these terminals with enough flexibility to cater to all airline business 
models, while reducing operating costs as much as possible through efficient and simplified processes. This 
enables all carriers to benefit from lower airport charges. 
Although the small terminal will generally make use of the same high-level processes illustrated, they will 
have reduced capacity throughput requirements.

3.3.3.2.5 Dedicated Terminals for VIP/CIP or State Functions 
There are three types of “Important Passengers” to consider: 
4. Commercially Important Passenger (CIP): This generally includes business and first-class passengers 
who provide airlines with greater unit commercial revenues; 
2. Very Important Passenger (VIP): This can cover a range of passengers from celebrities to high-ranking 
officials and politicians; and 
3. Very, Very Important Passenger (VVIP): This usually refers to heads of state and royalty. 
Dedicated terminals or facilities for the above groups of passengers vary in configuration throughout the world 
according to local politics and protocols. CIP, VIP and VVIP dedicated terminals are common in the Middle 
East, but less so in Europe and the United States. CIP facilities in Europe and the United States are usually 
incorporated into the main terminal operation and include dedicated fast-track facilities and waiting lounges. 
3.3.3.3 Terminal Organisation and Flows 
Vision 
Passenger journeys and flow routes should be as simple and straightforward as possible. Terminal facilities 
must not impede the passengers’ progress. Interactions should always be at the passengers’ choice rather 
than imposed by others, thus making the journey simple and enjoyable. Passenger journeys should allow 
biometric capture and verification of the passenger's identity which will confirm that travel has indeed 
commenced (no check-in is required). This capture and verification may occur at a variety of airport entry 
points (car park, terminal etc.) Verification may be “on the fly” or “on the move”. The passenger's identity will 
continue to be verified throughout the airport journey and will enable “walking pace” passenger processing 
3.3.3.3.1 General Considerations 
Air terminals must be designed considering numerous different and functionally separate flow routes. These 
include 
e Passenger flows (i.e., departures, arrivals, transfer) 
Staff flows (i.e., air crew, retail and food & beverage support staff, airport maintenance and management 
staff, airline and agency ground staff, etc.) 
* Vehicle flows (i.e., private vehicles, public vehicles, delivery vehicles, service vehicles, ramp service 
vehicles, etc.)
