¢ Walking distances for passengers should be as short as possible. 
572 
Making the passenger's route to and from the aircraft as simple as possible will generate the most 
efficient travel path and help to manage walking distances. Means of assisting Passengers to manage 
their journeys (i.e., baggage carts, electric carts, moving walkways, etc.) should be an integral part of the 
terminal design process. 
Greater distances can be accepted, provided a form of mechanical assistance is readily available to 
Passengers. In all terminals where major expansion is envisaged, incorporation of a people-mover 
system, and due provision for the necessary right-of-way and other related factors, must be included in 
the original conceptual design. See 3.3.11.3 Horizontal and Vertical Circulation for more information. 
Separation of international and domestic passenger flows. 
In line with the requirements and regulations as described in the emigration (see 3.3.5.6 Emigration 
(Outbound Passport Control)) and immigration (see 3.3.6.2 Immigration (Inbound Passport Control)) and 
customs sub-chapters (see 3.3.6.6 Customs Processes), provisions must be made for the separation of 
international and domestic passengers on the airside of terminals. However, to address differential peaks 
between domestic and international flights, a flexible arrangement (“swing gate”) should be incorporated 
whenever possible. This enables all or specific gates to be used as required for either category of 
passengers, and allows for regulation evolution. 
Separation of arriving and departing passengers. 
In line with requirements from control authorities (e.g., Immigration, Customs etc.) international arriving 
Passengers must be separated from departing passengers. Facial recognition or other biometric controls 
may be useful to avoid such segregation. 
All level changes should be assisted. 
Level changes for passengers should be minimized. Along the passenger flow routes all level changes 
should be provided with escalators and/or ramps. Stairs may also be included as a contingency measure. 
The use of elevators to enable passengers (other than passengers with reduced mobility-see 
3.3.9 Universal Design and Terminal Accessibility) to change levels has the potential to limit capacity. The 
termination point of an escalator must not be in a confined or restricted processing area where “back flow” 
might occur 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 592===
Be 
IATA Passenger Terminal 
e Concessions should not interfere with optimal passenger flow. 
Special care should be taken to ensure that concessions are conveniently located and do not interfere 
with the passenger flow. While the need to generate additional revenue from commercial opportunities is 
appreciated and supported when this revenue is used to offset overall costs (“Making it Pay’), passenger 
flows should not be exclusively routed through concessions areas. Alternate direct routes should also be 
provided so that passengers have the choice to either avail themselves of commercial opportunities or 
move quickly and efficiently to their departure gate or specific destination within the terminal complex (i.e., 
CIP lounge, arrivals hall, etc.). See 3.3.10 Concessions and Retail for more detail. 
e Provide Airside CIP Lounges. 
In line with the functional requirements of business lounges, CIP lounges should be located airside and 
beyond immigration or security controls, either along or immediately above primary passenger routes 
(a Departing Passenger Flows 
e The forecourt represents the landside interface with the terminal building. Passengers approaching by 
private car or any other form of transportation should intuitively be directed to the terminal building's 
entrances. Wayfinding (signage), both vehicular and pedestrian, should be used to help orient 
passengers and facilitate access to the portion of the terminal from which their flight/airline operates. 
° The departures hall is usually the publicly accessible zone that marks the entrance into the terminal. It 
provides orientation opportunities and should therefore be designed as a generous and unobstructed 
space that allows an overview over the next steps in the passenger journey. The departures hall must 
also provide intuitive and logical access to these next steps. This zone is also typically the interface 
where passengers may obtain a boarding pass, if this has not been done already prior to arriving at 
the airport, and divest themselves of any checked luggage. This may be facilitated in different ways 
and the processes continue to evolve rapidly. 
« Passengers wishing to enter the airside zones of the airport need to pass security and additional 
authentication controls. These authentication controls should include boarding pass checkpoints, but 
can also include emigration and customs controls where applicable. Passengers should be processed 
swiftly and simply, with the least possible disruption and stress. 
* The departure lounge is a common space for passengers to wait comfortably for their flights prior to 
moving to the boarding gates. It provides the passengers with adequate facilities such as retail and 
food & beverage concessions, toilets, free seating and additional entertainment offerings. Departure 
lounges should provide ample views of the airside and utilize natural light to reduce passenger stress. 
There should also be clear visibility of routes to the gates. 
¢ Gate lounges and their associated circulation space are the main components of both finger piers and 
satellites. The gate lounge is an assembly area for passengers in transition between the main 
processor and the aircraft. Some concessions may be located within the pier or satellite. Gate lounge 
areas are designed to serve high-capacity aircraft boarded through more than one door and should be 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 573 

===PAGE 593===
%& IATA | wi Airport Development Reference Manual 
arranged so as to expedite passenger flow. Differentiation of passengers may also be accommodated 
(e.g., Business vs Economy, row numbers, etc.). 
Boarding gates are where passengers usually have access to the PBB or any other exit to aircraft. 
They pass through a security door after having their boarding pass checked, either self-served or by 
an agent. Ample space must be provided if escalators are used to access the PBB to avoid 
congestion problems at the foot of the escalators. 
(b) Arriving Passenger Flows 
574 
Upon arrival by aircraft, arrivals corridors can be provided to direct passengers toward immigration or 
baggage claim. Walking distances to the next steps of the journey should be optimized as much as 
possible. 
Where required, for example for international arriving passengers, immigration or other controls can 
be required. 
In baggage claim halls, passengers and their checked luggage are reunited. Baggage is usually 
delivered to passengers on reclaim belts, and special provisions might be in place for the delivery of 
oversized luggage. In some regions domestic reclaim can be landside accessible. 
Customs exits from baggage claim can be required (e.g., for international arriving passengers). These 
must be clearly visible to passengers and facilitate the passage from baggage claim toward the 
landside arrivals hall. 
The landside arrivals hall marks the exit of the passenger from the baggage reclaim hall into the 
publicly accessible landside airport environment. Here, the passenger can be reunited with waiting 
“meeters & greeters”, and must find access to the landside pick-up forecourt as well as onward travel 
opportunities. The arrivals hall must also provide facilities for the waiting “meeters & greeters”, such 
as retail, food & beverage outlets, toilets and free seating. 
From the arrivals hall, passengers proceed to the forecourt for pick-up or to the car parking location 
as well as toward other onward journey ground transportation (e.g., bus and coach stations, metro, 
tram or train stations or taxi ranks). The forecourt can also connect, where applicable, to landside 
airport city developments with hotels and offices. 
These passenger flow descriptions are general and require further detailed definition in each 
individual case. The flows of departing and arriving passengers must be detailed for international and 
domestic passengers separately, where required, or in any other manner that suits the individual 
airport situation. Passenger flow descriptions should be considered in conjunction with all other 
terminal flows required, and: 
° Be sufficiently flexible to permit the establishment of temporary channels that can be bypassed by 
other passengers (e.g., for individual heath control processing of a particular arriving aircraft 
Passenger load) or to permit regulation evolution. 
o Permit processing of passengers individually or in groups. 
Transfers Flows 
For a description of airside and landside transfer flows (see 3.3.7 Transfers Processes and Facilities).

3.3.3.3.3 Staff Flows 
Staff flows should be considered across all terminal facilities. Careful consideration needs to be given to 
different staff access rights to the various terminal facilities, including both front office and back office areas, 
as well as dedicated staff security checkpoints. 
3.3.3.3.4 Goods, Servicing and Vehicle Flows 
Dedicated routes must be provided or identified for the various delivery and servicing requirements to and 
from the terminal, as well as routes for vehicles that might operate within a terminal (j.e., electric buggies, 
cleaning and maintenance equipment, display vehicles, Segways or scooters, ambulance vehicles or 
stretchers). The requirements must be established for each airport individually.

14. Linear—long straight terminals usually parallel to runways with single or double sided piers.

3.3.3.4.1_ Linear Terminal Concept 
The linear terminal consists of a centralized passenger processor and an associated airside concourse. In 
linear configurations the airside concourse is often integrated and adjacent to the processor. Although the 
concourse generally has a linear configuration, the overall geometry is determined by landside and airside site 
conditions. Typically, aircraft parking positions are oriented along one side of the concourse. In many cases 
these positions may wrap around each end of the concourse. 
All originating and departing passengers and baggage flow through the central processing area and circulate 
to and from the aircraft parking positions on the concourse.

3.3.3.4.2 Pier/Finger Terminal Concept 
The pier/finger terminal concept consists of a centralized passenger terminal for processing passengers and 
linked piers (airside concourses) in single or multiple pier configurations. In large examples of this type, the 
main processor may consist of several semi-centralized areas such as passenger processing or baggage 
claim, sharing a common departures/arrivals forecourt. The geometry of pier/finger concourses vary and 
configurations can accommodate aircraft parking positions on one or both sides of the concourse. 
All originating and departing passengers and baggage flow through the central processing area and circulate 
to and from the departure lounges and aircraft parking positions located along the piers. In large terminals of 
this type, secondary baggage sorting areas may be located in the piers to facilitate processing and connection 
times. 
Subsets of this configuration include X-Type, Y-Type and H-Type. The possible advantages and

3.3.3.4.3 Satellite Terminal Concept 
The satellite terminal concept consists of a central processing building for passenger and baggage processing 
and remote concourses around which aircraft are parked. The remote concourses or satellites are connected 
to the main terminal by combinations of above- or below-ground links to facilitate the movement of 
passengers and baggage between the satellites and the main terminal. These connections may include 
monorail mass transit systems, Automated People Mover (APM) systems or underground walkways equipped 
with moving walkways. 
Satellite concourses typically include centralized concession nodes oriented around the APM stations, a 
circulation spine and departure lounges. However, this is dependent on the number of gates served from the 
satellite. 
Outbound baggage is collected at central passenger service counters, sorted and conveyed to the baggage 
makeup areas either in the central processor or in the satellite. Baggage is transported to the aircraft by 
mobile apron equipment or mechanical systems. This concept is often used in conjunction with pier/finger and 
linear configurations to provide additional aircraft contact stands.

3.3.3.5 Terminal Layouts 
3.3.3.5.1 Centralized vs. Decentralized Facilities 
A centralized facility is one that provides for processing of all passengers, and baggage where applicable, 
within the same facility, regardless of airline. Centralized facilities inherently provide many benefits to the 
operator, airlines and passengers, minimizing confusion and putting all service offerings together in one place. 
New airlines entering the airport market for the first time can be collocated with their alliance partners without 
the need to displace or move other airlines to other terminal facilities. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 581 

===PAGE 601===
Wr IATA i Airport Development Reference Manual 
For large airlines in a centralized facility, particularly if they are the base or a primary carrier, operations 
can be focused in a preferred operating zone that also accommodates operations of partners. The cost￾effectiveness of the terminal is increased by the optimal use of space. In centralized facilities passenger traffic 
can be directed past centralized concession offerings. This assists in improving concession revenue 
performance. 
Airport owners, operators and designers need to be aware of some of the challenges that need to be 
addressed when working with centralized facilities. Long walking distances to and between gates may need to 
be mitigated with an internal transportation system such as an Airport People Mover (APM). The complex 
nature of the terminal may also be addressed by providing different processing areas for different travel 
segments (e.g., International, Domestic, Schengen and Non-Schengen in Europe, and trans-border in 
Canada/USA). 
(b) Decentralized Facilities: Due to existing site constraints it may only be possible to provide additional 
capacity by creating a separate terminal facility within the airport site for processing passengers and baggage. 
These facilities may be separated by airline, alliance, departure, arrival or transfer, or any combination of 
these types, but the inherent difficulties in managing the different passenger flows usually creates potentially 
costly management challenges. 
The primary question during project definition and conceptual design is which of these two models is most 
appropriate. Considerations for decision making include: 
e Existing site conditions/constraints 
e The local market and the passenger types to be served 
¢ The level of service that can be achieved and maintained for both airlines and passengers 
¢ The need to accommodate the changing needs of airlines 
° The nature of the dominant base carrier(s) and ever-changing alliance partnerships 
* The economies of scale 
e Emerging trends 
e The integration of state-of-the-art technologies; and 
e Integrated IT systems 
582 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 602===
IATA Passenger Terminal 
3.3.3.5.2 Terminal Levels and Sections 
Minimizing level changes in the passenger journey can increase the footprint of the building and, therefore, 
walking distances; so a considered and balanced approach to the building design must be taken. Site 
constraints may impose further challenges and opportunities. 
Terminals can be split into two types for simplicity when considering level and design: 
(a) Complex multi-level terminals 
(b) Simple single-level terminals 
In order to establish the optimum arrangement of levels for a new terminal building, the following key factors 
should be considered: 
e Landside interface with forecourt, multimodal interchange and connection to adjacent terminals on the site 
e The size of the key processing spaces in relation to one another 
e Segregation requirements 
e Minimum level changes and optimum travel distance for passengers 
e The baggage system and space for expansion 
e Airside interface, configuration of piers and aircraft stands; and 
e Need for APM or light rail link through the site 
(a Complex multi-level terminals 
Large modern air terminal should have a significant landside “inter-modal” interface with local, national 
and international ground transport networks. These should prioritize public busses, metros, light rail, 
regional rail networks, high-speed national and international rail networks as well as providing private car 
access, and even maritime links. 
Intermodal connectivity requires careful planning to minimize level changes and segregate different flows 
(e.g., passengers, surface vehicles, rail links, etc.). The following diagrams are typical cross-sections for a 
complex multimodal interchange/terminal interface where the routes have been carefully planned to 
optimize the passenger arrival and departure experience and to ensure minimum crossover of passenger 
and vehicle routes.

Column spacing is an important consideration, as a floor plate with many columns disrupts the flow and

It is important that the departures and arrivals routes be maintained with minimum level changes. Often, 
the departures level is at the upper level and the arrivals is at a lower level. This tends to facilitate a 
quicker baggage route from aircraft to claim on the arrivals journey and offers the arriving passenger a 
route straight out of the terminal. 
« Segregation Requirements 
Segregation is best achieved through the use of different levels. This avoids the use of crossover 
points that can cause congestion and require additional staff. It also avoids perimeter circulation 
corridors that restrict gate utilization due to the need to maintain separation. Hence, in large terminals, 
it is common to locate the departures route on a different level from the arrivals route. A typical 
arrangement is indicated in the illustration below. 
Exhibit 3.3.3.5.2b: Example of Segregated Arrival and Departure Flows 
Source: NACO

with no level change. Arriving passengers travel along an arrivals corridor in the pier at a lower level, 
dropping to ground level inside the terminal building and leading directly out to the arrivals forecourt. 
This arrangement achieves the minimum number of level changes for both the departures and arrivals 
routes (only one level change for arrivals) and maintains full segregation of departing and arriving 
passengers throughout the terminal building. In most terminals, domestic departing and arriving 
passengers may not require segregation. In these cases, a single level pier may suffice. However,

terminal. Segregation of flows on a single level is likely inefficient as it could lead to cross-segregated 
crossover points that can severely limit floor usage and result in frequent operational disruption. 
e Minimum Level Changes and Optimum Travel Distances for Passengers 
Minimizing level changes is a key consideration for determining the internal organization of a terminal, 
and arriving ata compact and efficient terminal volume. It is to be seen in context of floor plan 
efficiencies and segregation requirements, as well as access to forecourts and aircraft stands. also

3.3.4 Terminal Capacity and the Level of Service 
The concept of Level of Service (LoS), as applied to airport terminal design, was originally developed by 
Transport Canada in the mid to late 1970s as the prevailing definitions of “capacity” were considered 
inadequate. In 1981, the Airport Associations Coordinating Council (AACC)-the precursor to ACI and IATA 
jointly published a study on airport capacity that resulted in the first edition of the Guidelines for Airport 
Capacity/Demand Management, which contained a tabular presentation of LoS guidelines by airport 
processing area, based on the Transport Canada concept. This guidance was further updated in 1990 and 
1996, after which it was incorporated into IATA's ADRM and remained largely unchanged through the 
9th edition (published in 2004). 
Over this period, the concept of LoS was applied in various ways for the design of new facilities, the 
expansion and monitoring of existing facilities, and as a benchmark that determines whether the contractual 
obligations of airport owners, operators and/or third party service providers are being met. It was also 
highlighted that the importance of the previous airport LoS guidelines was perceived to be higher in 
correlation with other key quantitative (e.g., waiting times, process rates) and qualitative (e.g., perceived 
service quality, information flow, wayfinding, walking distances) characteristics. These alternative key 
performance indicators are used in the industry, but often not with the same consistency as LoS guidelines. 
Taking some of these considerations into account, the LoS references were reviewed and refined in a way 
that incorporated waiting time aspects in addition to the spatial requirements. In this way, it is possible to 
determine a balanced LoS that neither under provides nor over provides and responds to a realistic design 
horizon for facility planning. This updated LoS methodology was released in the ADRM 10th edition and is 
now widely used. 
Terminal design and LoS should reflect the operating environment as well as the volume of passengers and 
baggage to be handled. Managing terminal capacity and designing with LoS in mind are key requirements in 
the development of cost-effective airports. These factors have long-term financial and operational implications 
for passenger facilities. 
Planners and decision makers must keep in mind that passengers visit an airport for one primary reason: to 
catch a flight. Passengers’ expectations and needs should be at the very heart of the planning process. The 
mark of a successful airport is its natural and unobstructed passenger flow between objectives, easy 
navigation through the terminal, simplicity and cost-effectiveness. 
It is important to understand and quantify the LoS currently being provided in order to establish an appropriate 
new LoS requirement. Existing LoS must be taken into account to ensure that the “stretch” to improve LoS is 
not as difficult or extreme as to discourage those tasked with making and managing the service 
improvements. 
588 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 608===
IATA 4 Passenger Terminal 
Smoothly managing airport peaks has been the subject of increasing concern by airlines and airport operators 
around the world. Extreme spikes in airport traffic can result in congestion and costly delays to aircraft and 
passengers. Bottlenecks and delays at airports are often the result of inadequacies in one or more of the 
airport system components. A balanced approach to capacity provision and enhancement is recommended to 
ensure one component of the terminal system is not causing a bottleneck when all other processes are 
adequately sized for the design throughput. It is important to also consider that all processing systems are 
interrelated and solving a capacity issue at one processing location may just move the congestion on to the 
next processing point. Solutions must be formulated holistically across the entire passenger flow. Oversized 
facilities for the current/design traffic LoS are unnecessarily costly. A management decision between the 
stakeholders and the airport must be made, which balances capacity provisions with economic and design 
objectives. 
The LoS concept is a way to ensure that considerations of demandand service quality are taken into account 
when defining airport service levels. The LoS can be expressed in terms of either the design target or what is 
actually achieved. LoS fluctuates during the day, week or month depending on traffic peaks. The larger the 
peaks, the more potential impact there is on LoS.

IATA + Airport Development Reference Manual 
Impact of COVID-19 on Terminal Capacity 
See Section 1.8 COVID19 Green Pages for additional explanation on how to interpret the Green Pages. 
Introduction 
As the world started to emerge from the initial stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, governments imposed new 
regulations to protect aviation employees and the traveling public as well as reduce the risk of transmission 
between countries and regions. These measures included introducing controls to ensure only allowed people 
were traveling, imposing minimum physical distancing, and instructing people to wear face masks indoors. 
Other measures, however, led to either changes in existing processes at airports (e.g., switching off 
self-service options) or resulted in the creation of entirely new ones (e.g., health temperature screening) and 
additional document checks prior to entering a check-in queue at departure or similar queue on arrival (e.g., 
verification of vaccine “passports” prior to entering an immigration queue or the baggage reclaim hall). 
Itis likely that these measures will not outlive the pandemic; however, while in place, they can have a 
significant impact on the capacity of terminal facilities in a number of ways. It is important, therefore, for 
airport and terminal operators to understand how the capacity of their facility has changed and consider 
appropriate action. 
While IATA strongly recommends these measures be phased out as the epidemiological situation improves, a 
quick move to enable advance automated “ready-to-fly” checks is required to limit the impact on passengers 
and airport capacity of any future pandemic. Adoption of digital processes and the establishment of a 
standard for testing and storing vaccination certificates is critical to reduce the impact of health credential 
checks on the capacity of terminal processes and to ensure aviation's restart is not brought to a halt by 
documentation requirements. 
New/Additional Process 
Some new checks that have been imposed form the basis of entirely new processes. For example, document 
checks made prior to being permitted to enter the queue zone for check-in and/or after arrival (e.g., prior to 
accessing immigration or baggage reclaim). Such processes can involve the passenger being required to 
show a range of documents: 
e Evidence of COVID-19 vaccination 
¢ Evidence of an authority to travel document being submitted and approved (e.g., passenger locator forms 
(PLF) and health declarations) 
e Evidence of a recent negative test 
e Evidence of travel insurance 
During the COVID-19 pandemic, some countries introduced testing on arrival at the airport as a temporary 
measure. Depending on the rules, certain flight(s) or certain passengers of a flight might need to be tested, 
the separation of passenger flows might be required, and the location and size of areas to be allocated as 
well as the associated logistics need to be planned accordingly. 
590 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 610===
%& IATA‘ wi Passenger Terminal 
In the event of a new or additional process being created, there are two considerations that airport operators 
should have in mind: 
¢ Facility Requirements: In the spirit of attempting to achieve a balanced capacity for all facilities, 
consideration should be given to providing adequate processing capacity for a new/additional process to 
avoid excessive queuing. It is possible that some form of temporary facility will need to be provided, 
utilizing space currently used for another purpose. When this is the case, it should be remembered during 
the design of the facility that it will be temporary and that, at some stage when the pandemic is over, the 
space will likely need to revert to its original use. 
e Area Provision: An assessment should be made as to whether there is adequate space readily available 
for the new/additional process and associated queue space. In the absence of adequate space, 
consideration should be given to ‘borrowing’ from areas already allocated to other processes. It is then 
important to assess what impact that will have on the capacity of the other processes. 
Increased Process Time 
Imposing additional document checks, in particular at check-in and immigration, will inevitably lead to 
increased processing times and a reduction in the capacity of existing facilities. It may well be necessary to 
suspend the stated (LoS) for a while. Longer processing times will mean that any given queue area will 
experience an increase in the holding demand of the area in terms of total passenger minutes, but the 
question remains as to whether adequate processing facilities exist to meet the demands being placed on 
them. 
For the security screening process, reduced throughput capacity per lane had been observed as well. Several 
passengers usually transact at the same time within dense handling areas. Due to physical distancing 
measures, a lower number of passengers are in the process at the same time, which reduces the throughput 
capacity of security checkpoints. This implies either the staffing of more lanes or an acceptance of longer 
waiting times, which would require additional queue space as well. 
Closure of Self-service Processing Facilities 
Self-service kiosks are fomites (surfaces that can carry infection and thus help spread disease). To keep 
passengers safe from infection, these facilities would either need to be cleaned between each use or a 
solution found to avoid passengers needing to touch them. Impact on capacity could be positive if the process 
is replaced by touchless self-service units. However, in many airports, the easier solution might be to consider 
switching off the equipment and requiring all passengers to use staffed facilities instead. However, this will 
have a large impact on airport capacity, resulting in very long queues and increased crowdedness in the 
areas, potentially resulting in an increased risk of transmission. In some countries, switching off the equipment 
has been required to integrate some of the documentation processes described in previous sections within 
the existing desk-based processes. On the other hand, increased cleaning of equipment can also result in an 
increase of the inter-process time, resulting in an impact on capacity. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 591 

===PAGE 611===
Bs | ara {ia} Airport Development Reference Manual 
To ensure aviation's restart is not brought to a halt by documentation requirements and increased processing 
times, adoption of digital processes and the establishment of a standard for testing and vaccination 
Certificates is critical to reduce the impact of health credential checks in processing times. 
IATA urges governments to work with the industry to implement effective standard-based solutions that can 
be operationalized while protecting public health. Where governments have decided to delegate the 
verification to airlines, there are a number of digital applications that have been developed. This includes the 
IATA Travel Pass, which is being developed specifically for the aviation sector. 
Change in Passenger Type/Journey Purpose 
Opening borders after the onset of a pandemic can lead to significant shifts in the types of Passengers 
traveling and for what purpose. Business trips may become less frequent (relying instead on videoconference 
calls) and visiting friends and family may become more prevalent. 
Differing passenger groups will exhibit differing characteristics and airport familiarization levels that are key to 
assessing the capacity of terminal facilities. For example, the time at which they arrive at the terminal may 
differ as will the group size, the time taken to be processed at the various facilities and the type of facilities 
required. Changes in how passengers get to the airport may also occur. 
Policies that reduce usage of overhead bins in aircraft might require passengers to check-in their usual 
carry-on luggage. This has an impact on a higher bag/passenger ratio for the check-in and BHS, and has 
implications for crowding in baggage reclaim halls. In addition, passengers may carry more hold luggage than 
usual in case they are affected by quarantines or changes in travel requirements before being able to take 
their return journey. 
Revised Staffing 
Another impact of a pandemic is a reduction of available staff due to illness or contact with someone who has 
tested positive. Reduced staffing will have a direct impact on the terminal capacity unless the process can be 
augmented by technology. It may also have a significant impact in terms of operations and amenities. 
Revised Capacity with Revised Demand 
Increases in processing times, spatial demands and reductions in staffing will likely reduce the capacity of the 
airport during busy periods. This may or may not be an issue depending on the level of demand suppression 
during the pandemic. It is recommended the airport/terminal operator review the resulting capacity from the 
changes in processes to better understand the ability of the terminal facilities to meet the demands being 
placed on them. 
592 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 612===
an 
Xo 
IATA Passenger Terminal 
Given there are likely to be ongoing changes in process, it is recommended a range of scenarios be 
developed with the analysis kept at a high level. For example, if check-in transaction time is 150% of pre￾pandemic levels and the number of desks that can be used is 75%, then the peak capacity will likely be 50% 
of the pre-pandemic level. If peak demand is 50% down, there will likely be no problem (as social distancing 
should be solvable). If peak demand is any higher, the impact on the passenger journey through queuing, 
delays, space, etc. should be assessed. 
Conclusion 
The COVID-19 pandemic offers several “lessons to learn”. The experiences and observations allow for the 
generation of a set of SOPs to be better prepared for the next pandemic. It is recommended an airport should 
have a plan ready that outlines all of the measures that need to be implemented. In this respect, it is also 
useful that an airport have knowledge of the impact on capacity and the new maximum levels of saturation 
that would result in another pandemic situation. 
This is also relevant for airports that operate several terminals, or several decentralized areas within one 
terminal. If traffic volumes decrease due to a pandemic, it is recommended infrastructure be planned to make 
it possible to consolidate the remaining traffic within one area or one terminal. Therefore, it is more important 
than ever to ensure flexibility in the configurations is one of the key design criteria. 
Testing, such capacity scenarios, to gain a better insight into saturation capacity under a pandemic situation 
can be supported by simulation modeling or advanced analytical tools, if an airport has a calibrated 
simulation/analytical model of its terminals available. 
Furthermore, larger accumulations of passengers in queuing or dwelling areas shall be minimized in general. 
Operational tools for forecasting and monitoring passenger flows and the density of passengers in areas can 
support situational awareness and trigger measures to alleviate crowded situations.

3.3.4.1 The “Optimum” Solution and Balanced Capacity 
A primary objective of the planning process is to find the correct, balanced capacity and level of service 
between facilities, operations, and airline schedules. Balancing capacity is primarily required to avoid 
displacing a bottleneck to another critical facility. It often means ensuring the terminal, gate and apron 
systems do not limit the overall airport throughput. The capacity of the runway system should always be 
regarded as the key capacity element. 
Every reasonable effort should be made by airlines, airport operators, and involved government agencies to 
identify airport capacity limitations and potential congestion problems during the design development process, 
long before problems actually occur. Coordinated efforts (i.e., design modifications, operational procedures, 
etc.) can then be undertaken to avoid such problems to the benefit of all concerned. This requires continuing 
and open communications and cooperation between all parties involved. Demand/capacity and LoS 
investigations at airports where congestion exists or is anticipated should be considered and discussed in a 
consultative manner in order to: 
e Establish the time, level and cause of congestion 
¢ Seek to agree on a methodology for determining the capacity of the airport, taking into account the LoS to 
be provided, and compare this with typical design peak demand in order to identify capacity limitations 
* Consider means of removing such limitations in the short term, at a relatively small cost, considering the 
effect of any related delay factor. It is often possible to increase capacities significantly through relatively 
inexpensive changes in procedures or personnel deployment 
¢ Where larger expansion is not possible, consider other temporary solutions, such as minor construction or 
lower service levels, 
Due to the dynamic nature of airports all terminal subsystems are interrelated. The operational performance of 
one processor impacts the demand for the subsequent one. In other words, the demand of a downstream 
facility usually corresponds to the capacity of the upstream one, unless there are amenities or other facilities 
diverting the flow of passengers from the main route. For example, the throughput of the arrival immigration 
facility will impact the accumulation of passengers in the baggage claim area. In order to reach an optimum 
design solution, it is desirable to obtain a balance in the capacity of all facilities. 
Determining a LoS for each facility in the terminal building, and for complete journeys (origin, transfer and 
arrival) will enable the assessment of capacity shortfalls for which corrective actions may be identified. A new 
LoS assessment will be undertaken to ensure that the solution is indeed appropriate and that the problem is 
not simply shifted to another facility. 
3.3.4.2 Airport Terminal Capacity 
The airport should undertake regular Capacity assessments to identify the source of any Capacity problems 
as well as the corresponding solution. The airport should also proactively anticipate where development and 
additional Capacity will be required. All stakeholders should work together to prevent Capacity limitations 
before they occur and minimize the risk of short-term reductions in LoS.

3.3.4.3 Capacity Definitions 
Capacity definitions and measurements vary from one subsystem to another. However, the term “capacity” 
generally refers to the quantitative measure for supply of service of a processing facility to accommodate 
sustained demand over a specified period of time, under given service conditions. 
Exhibit 3.3.4.3a: Queuing System not at Exhibit 3.3.4.3b: Queuing System Exceeding

Source: IATA Source: IATA 
In other words, capacity is a measure of throughput or system capability. Since an airport system is capable 
of operating at varying degrees of congestion and delay, the capacity must always be related to the LoS being 
provided. For example, a particular system might be able to process 1,000 passengers per hour at an optimal 
LoS, or 1,500 passengers per hour at a suboptimal LoS (i.e., with greater congestion). 
Comprehensive capacity assessments for the terminal building are based on several fundamental 
measurements. 
3.3.4.3.1 Dynamic Capacity 
Dynamic capacity refers to the maximum processing or flow rate of persons through a subsystem per unit of 
time. The actual time unit selected as the measurement index (e.g., minutes, hours) depends on the nature of 
the operation. Any excess in passenger demand over the dynamic capacity will lead to increased queuing. 
e Processing Capacity 
Processing capacity relates to the quantity of passengers and/or bags that can be processed over a 
defined period of time. The demand for a given process needs to be balanced against processing 
capacity. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 595 

===PAGE 615===
IATA ill Airport Development Reference Manual 
¢ Circulation Capacity 
Circulation capacity within a processing area or between processing areas is defined as the area between 
activities devoted to passenger movement within that space. Adjacent processes, services, zones or 
activities also need to be taken into account when considering circulation capacity. 
3.3.4.3.2 Static Capacity 
Static capacity is used to describe the holding potential of a facility or area, including queuing areas, and is 
usually expressed as the number of occupants that a given area will accommodate at any one moment. It is a 
function of the total useable space available and the LoS to be provided (i.e., the amount of space each 
occupant may occupy). Static capacity standards are stated as square meters per occupant for each LoS. 
3.3.4.3.3 Sustained Capacity 
Sustained capacity is used to describe the overall capacity of a subsystem to accommodate traffic demand 
over a sustained period within the space and time standards of a particular LoS. It is a measure of the 
combined dynamic and static capacities of the processors, lounges and links (e.g., corridor spaces). 
3.3.4.3.4 Maximum Capacity 
Maximum Capacity refers to the maximum traffic flow that can be achieved for the chosen time unit only, but 
not sustained for a longer period, regardless of delay or LoS. 
3.3.4.3.5 Declared Capacity 
Declared capacity refers to site specific limiting capacities, in numeric terms, of individual facilities and 
resources. The declared capacity is used as the basis for Airport Coordination parameters. 
When an airport system, or element thereof, cannot be developed further to increase capacity in the short, it 
may be necessary to manage demand to limit congestion and delay. This is referred to as Airport 
Coordination and the system uses numerical levels to aid in the management of the lack of capacity situation. 
IATA, ACI and Worldwide Airport Coordinators Group manage and publish the Worldwide Airport Slot 
Guidelines, which details the process of Airport Coordination for Level 2 and 3 airports.

3.3.4.4 Capacity Assessment 
The components of the passenger terminal building are made up of three basic types of facilities: 
4. Processing facilities, which involve a transaction with a passenger and/or a bag; 
2. Holding facilities, which consist of waiting or queuing areas; and 
3. Circulation facilities, or links, which allow the movement of occupants from one subsystem to another. 
Different methods are used for assessing the capacity of an airport as a complete system or of its individual 
processors. The most commonly used methods are: 
° Direct observations of the operation 
* Capacity formulas to determine theoretical Capacity and LoS given the traffic volume and area available 
e Simulation modelling 
Regardless of which method is used, there are three principal governing factors: 
4. The comfort and convenience of passengers is directly related to the Capacity and LoS provided by the 
facility; 
2. Capacity and LoS are interrelated and must always be considered together; and 
3. Designing to a Capacity and forecast level of activity that is too far into the future can result in overdesign 
and wasted capital resources, and will not necessarily result in a better service overall. 
The best outcome is one where a balanced capacity is provided at all steps of the passenger journey. Where 
possible, capacity can be further optimized by finding opportunities to share facilities between segregated 
passenger flows where peak demands occur at different times. These are referred as “swing” facilities. 
3.3.4.5 Factors Influencing Capacity and Level of Service 
The LoS may be expressed in terms of: 
© Queueing time per passenger for processing facilities, either as a maximum queueing time during the 
planning busy period or as a percentile target. (i.e., 90% of the design Peak Hour, or total busy day 
passengers queue for less than 7 minutes); and 
e Unit area per occupant for holding facilities 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 597 

===PAGE 617===
we IATA i Airport Development Reference Manual 
Several factors influence airport terminal Capacity. For processing facilities, capacity is influenced by three 
main components: 
* The passenger demand 
¢ The processing time (i.e., the time it takes to perform a transaction or other process for a particular 
passenger at a particular resource) 
These factors will have different values depending on the type of airport, its size and configuration. Passenger 
characteristics also vary according to the region they come from, the purpose of their travel and their flight 
destination. For example, a business traveler may travel with fewer bags and may arrive at the airport later 
than a leisure traveler. These two factors (amount of baggage and arrival time) will affect the space 
requirements for departure processes. Applying general rules-of-thumb (capacity formulas) for assessing 
capacity is an accepted method to estimate requirements. These methods are also useful in the preliminary 
planning phase to establish a rough order of magnitude for various facilities. Detailed design should make use 
of simulation modeling techniques to refine the space requirements and to assist with detailed LoS analysis. 
Demand also varies by the year, season, month, week and even by the time of day. Defining demand for the 
purpose of planning/designing airport subsystems is a complex exercise. It not only involves estimating the 
number of passengers who will need to complete a given process, but it must also address interdependencies 
between subsystems and how they affect the flow of passengers across the airport terminal facilities as a 
whole. See 2.2.10 Peak Period Forecasts for more information. 
3.3.4.6 Level of Service Concept 
The concept of Level of Service (LoS) is an aggregated framework for the design and expansion of facilities 
as well as for the monitoring of existing facilities. For processing facilities, both queueing time and space 
requirements must be considered together to provide a balanced LoS. For holding and circulation facilities, 
queueing time is not applicable and can be replaced by other service considerations, such as seat ratios. The 
general objective is to allow for a realistic design horizon for passenger facilities without over or 
underproviding. 
LoS is used to help determine facility requirements for a given design demand. Plans developed for a forecast 
busy hour will provide facilities that operate according to an optimum LoS aligned to an agreed future 
throughput. Until the airport reaches that forecast level of activity, the facilities will function at a higher LoS, 
falling in the Over-Design. Furthermore, because demand varies over time, the LoS will also vary. Planners 
should, therefore, consider targeting an optimum LoS in the knowledge that, during the busiest/peak traffic 
periods, the optimum LoS may not be achieved. Balancing investment decisions with LoS is a complex 
management and policy decision.

* If both axes show poor conditions (both LoS parameters fall into the ‘Sub-Optimum’ range), the resulting

airport management as well as with and within the overall airline/aviation community to ensure that the parties 
involved understand and support the inherent planning strategy. When an overdesigned subsystem will not 
reach its full capacity until well into the future (10+ years), the result of OVER-DESIGN is likely to be empty 
space, overprovision of resources and unnecessary costs. 
The boundaries comprising the optimum space allocation and the optimum queueing time represent the “not 
to exceed” limits that should be observed in order to reach an optimum solution. In some cases, due in part to 
very high demand peaks, an airport owner/operator may choose, together with the aviation community, to set 
agreed limits within the specified range to better fit the prevailing reality at that particular airport at that time. 
When planning/designing a major expansion or new airport, targeted LoS may be considered for initial sizing 
of subsystem areas. The target values shall be within the specified optimum LoS parameter range. The target 
should reflect the local realities and be responsive to passenger behavior and needs. 
An additional corollary can be applied to queueing times. In this case, target queueing times could be 
determined based on: 
¢ The operating cost of providing the service and the capital cost of providing the processing facilities, 
combined with the capital cost of providing the space per individual 
© The service level agreement between the service provider and the owner of the facility, as long as these 
targets fall within the optimum LoS range

gate lounges or departure lounges, passengers dwell until boarding starts, thereby requiring space for 
circulation, standing and seating. While the matrix space axis defines the overall average space per occupant 
(Space for seating and standing), the time axis is replaced by the seating rate axis (the proportion of seats 
provided). Like with processing facilities, both axes are required to define the resulting LoS. In the case of 
gate lounges or departure lounges, the availability of space and seating define the LoS.

3.3.4.7. Level of Service Guidelines 
Exhibit 3.3.4.7 provides the LoS guidelines for each airport terminal facility/subsystem. The table provides

include facilities involving self-service processing and customs control. 
The LoS guidelines have been adjusted to better reflect the current global aviation market. It is recognized, 
however, that different regions, countries and markets require adjustments to the airport environment to better 
equate with their service needs. The revised LoS benchmarks now include a range of values for space and 
time to better enable an airport to tailor its service level to the market and region it serves.

Impact of COVID-19 on the Level of Service Guidelines 
See 1.8 COVID19 Green Pages for additional information 
From the very early stages of the pandemic, one of the key protective measures that have been implemented 
across almost every country is a requirement to maintain a physical distance that reduces the risk of 
transmission. Physical distancing is an effective measure to limit transmission of SARS-CoV-2 and should be 
part of a comprehensive package of measures to limit the spread of COVID-19. 
However, one of the key challenges of the pandemic has been the lack of consistent application of the health￾related measures globally. In particular, where requirements have been applied different recommendations in 
terms of physical distancing have been proposed ranging between 1 and 2 meters. 
In an attempt to propose a harmonized approach to physical distancing both the WHO and ICAO established 
a recommendation to keep a distance of at least 1m which, in combination with other health related 
regulations (use of face masks, vaccination certificates, optimizing passenger flows etc), should provide the 
means for a safe and healthy journey. 
While there are different interpretations on how to measure the physical distance and how to apply it to 
queuing and holding areas of terminal buildings, it appears to be clear that the objective is to avoid potential 
droplets/aerosols from the nose and mouth of one passenger teaching the passengers standing immediately 
next to them. Therefore, it is fair to make the interpretation that a direct linear separation between two 
Passengers should suffice in order to comply with a physical distancing requirement of 1 meter. 
With all of this in mind, the current Level of Service Guidelines are perfectly able to accommodate those 
minimum requirements without any changes. Only minor adjustments to the layouts of queueing or seating 
areas should be required to accommodate the minimum requirements set by the WHO and ICAO. 
It should also be noted that while we recognize that regulatory mandates vary across different countries and 
regions imposing more stringent separation requirements than the minimum, it is IATA's view that these 
measures are likely to be temporary and will be lifted once the vaccination rates are high and consistent 
globally. This is also consistent with what has been observed in those countries with high vaccination rates 
and low number of infections where physical distancing requirements have been lifted in other public 
buildings, modes of transport and interior spaces. 
In addition, the Level of Service guidelines also address queueing times and seating availability. Both of these 
areas have also been impacted by some of the health-related restrictions (see Impact of COVID-19 on 
Terminal Capacity). While it is recognized that during times with additional processes or extra processing 
times the queueing objective defined in the LOS framework may not be achievable, the temporary nature of 
those restrictions should not have an impact on queueing requirements defined in the Level of Service 
guidelines. Similarly, current seating design makes it impossible to maintain the separation distances, but it 
should also be seen as temporary measure. Advancements in self check in and security screening will 
increase queuing efficiency. Other technologies exist or are being developed to flatten peaks using virtual 
queuing.” 
604 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 624===
G— | } IATA ii Passenger Terminal 
Asa conclusion, and taking all of the above into consideration, IATA does not see the need to change any of 
the recommended space, queueing time or seating requirements in the Level of Service guidelines. 
Note: Circulation and dwelling areas in passenger terminals have, in general, not been a capacity 
constraint. However, passengers are often less than 1m apart in these areas, in particular where 2-way flows 
and cross flows occur. Natural physical distancing of passengers may result in congestion occurring in such 
areas of conflict. Application of passenger guidance to create 1-way flows, such as using web barriers, may 
be appropriate to ease congestion as demand grows.

3.3.4.8 Service Quality Perception 
Service quality perception is a metric that relies on the direct input of passengers. It provides valuable input to 
the airport operator, especially in regards to aspects of airport operations that cannot be quantified (e.g., 
cleanliness, courtesy of staff, wayfinding, ambiance). Although some aspects may relate to the airport as a 
whole, some evaluation criteria may relate to aspects that are specific to a stakeholder. 
Since perceptions vary broadly between people, it will be challenging to determine a quantitative level to 
target without the appropriate references and benchmarks, but some underperforming criteria should at least 
be considered for further review in an attempt to enhance customer experience. 
3.3.4.8.1 ACI Airport Service Quality (ASQ) Survey 
In an effort to kick-start an initiative to measure and benchmark the service quality perceived by passengers, 
ACI launched the Airport Service Quality (ASQ) Survey in 2006. The airports participating in this initiative use 
the same self-completion paper questionnaire, translated into more than 40 languages. 
Passengers fill in the questionnaires while they are waiting for boarding at the gate areas, evaluating 34 
service quality indicators on a scale from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) related to the following aspects: 
e Access to the airport 
e Check-in 
e Passport and ID control on departure 
e Security 
e Wayfinding 
e Airport facilities and services 
e Airport environment 
e Arrivals services (based on previous experiences) 
e Overall satisfaction with the airport 
In addition to the service quality performance indicators, the questionnaire contains demographic fields that 
help to determine trends and analysis for specific groups of passengers depending on their needs, 
expectations and behavior. 
Currently, more than 320 airports worldwide participate in the ACI ASQ Survey initiative, which provide 
multiple benchmarking opportunities in terms of airport size, region, traffic patterns, etc. 
For those airports participating in the ASQ Survey initiative, it is recommended to include targets and 
performance references in the Service Levels Agreements related to those aspects that are influenced by the 
various stakeholders. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 607 

===PAGE 627===
Se IATA Bull Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.3.4.8.2 Airport Service Quality Awards 
The annual ASQ Awards recognize and reward the best airports in the world according to ACI's ASQ 
Passenger satisfaction survey. They represent the highest possible accolade for airport operators and are an 
opportunity to celebrate the commitment of airports worldwide to continuously improving the passenger 
experience. 
Since its creation in 2006, the ASQ Survey has become the world's leading airport passenger satisfaction 
benchmark with over 320 airports participating, across 84 countries. Its scientific methodology, strict quality 
control procedures and commitment to impartiality have won industry recognition and established the ASQ 
Survey as the global standard for measuring passenger satisfaction. 
For more information, please click on ACI ASQ Survey. 
3.3.4.9 Demand-Capacity Assessment 
In this section, the term “demand” relates to the quantity of users (passengers, visitors or staff, where 
applicable) that undertake a process (at processing subsystems) or just occupy terminal space (e.g., in 
holding/circulation subsystems) over a certain period. 
Demand varies by the year, season, month, week, and even by the time of day. The variability of demand, 
and in particular its peaking structure, will be significantly different from one airport to another. Besides 
estimating the number of passengers and other users who are required to complete a given process or who 
dwell within a certain area, the demand analysis may also need to address interdependencies between 
subsystems and how they affect the flows across airport terminal facilities. 
Within this context, “capacity” relates to the number users that a given number of facilities (processing units 
and/or areas) can process over a given period of time at a selected level of service (LoS); for example, a 
maximum queuing time (MQT) and/or a minimum space provision per passenger. 
When designing future airport infrastructure, providing capacity that is in balance with the forecasted demand 
is naturally a key aspect of the planning exercise. In the following sections, two different methods for 
establishing the future demand for a processing facility are presented. Afterward, capacity equations are 
defined to caiculate the necessary number of processing units and associated queuing area to process the 
demand. Finally, it is discussed how the demand-capacity assessment can also be applied when evaluating 
the performance of existing facilities. 
3.3.4.9.1 Demand Calculation 
To ensure future facilities are neither under-providing nor overdesigned, the selection of the initial planning 
level to be used for the demand-capacity assessment is an important first step. 2.2.10 Peak Period Forecasts 
discusses this in detail and this section builds upon the results and terminology established there. 
608 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 628===
Passenger Terminal 
Two distinct methods for calculating the demand are described in the subsections below: 
¢ Single Peak Method: This simple method uses the forecasted Design Hour Rate (DHR) (see 
2.2.10.1.1 Design Hour Rate (IATA Recommendation) and includes adjustments to account for 
passenger segmentation and presentation. However, it should be used with caution to avoid unintended 
results. 
* Multiple Peaks Method: This more advanced method is the approach that was introduced and 
recommended in ADRM 11" Edition. It uses both a DDFS, (see 2.2.10.3 Design Day Flight Schedules) 
and presentation profiles (also called show-up profiles) for multiple passenger segments. Calculations are 
then conducted for five different peaks of variable length (15 minute, 30 minutes, 1 hour, 2 hours, 
4 hours). 
It is important to note that there are many different use cases throughout the planning process that may 
require various levels of detail and accuracy in the demand calculation. For long-term master planning stages 
and initial conceptual designs (when planners are looking for order of magnitude results), a simple approach 
requiring limited amounts of data may suffice (Single Peak Method). This would significantly reduce the time 
and cost of producing a set of preliminary results. This choice may also be suitable for airports/projects that 
are not able to access the amount of data required for a more detailed study. 
For more detailed studies requiring a better understanding of the baseline assumptions and the implications of 
varying peaks and passenger behavior, it is recommended to investigate identifying the demand linked to 
multiple peaks and their structure (Multiple Peaks Method). 
(a) Single Peak Method 
This approach uses the DHR obtained as an output of the forecasting exercise (see 2.2.10 Peak Period 
Forecast) as the starting point for the calculation of the facility demand. DHR should be forecasted separately 
for each passenger segment relevant to the sizing of terminal facilities. As an example, if a security 
checkpoint for international departing passengers is being designed, the current DHR specific for the 
international departing passenger segment must be calculated and then forecasted to the future DHR. 
If the specific DHR for the processing facility in question is not available, the planner may use a more general 
DHR (e.g., for all departing passengers) and adjust it by applying a ratio relevant for the facility (e.g., the 
share of international passengers in the airport). The ratios used should (if available) be referencing the 
specific peak distribution. When data is not available, other more generic ratios may be used. However, using 
a ratio based on annual passenger figures may not be produce accurate results since the distribution of 
passengers during the peak may be quite different from the annual distribution. If data is available, it is highly 
recommended to analyze the relevant distribution in current peak situations and consider whether this 
distribution is also likely in a future scenario or should be adjusted based on expected market trends. 
It may also be necessary to further break down passenger segments where significant differences in 
processing times (PTs) warrant separate capacity calculations (e.g., separate check-in areas for individual 
carriers or airline segments). Similar care should be taken to identify the right distribution/ratios for the future 
peak situation. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 609 

===PAGE 629===
1 
Se a. iy —C*s . IATA Boll Airport Development Reference Manual 
The DHR (possibly adjusted as mentioned above) is calculated based on the arrival/departure times of flights 
during one clock-hour. However, the demand for specific terminal facilities is driven by the time when 
passengers show up to the subsystem in question and how long they dwell in the area. Using the DHR 
directly as the facility demand may significantly overestimate the facility requirements for subsystems where 
the relevant passengers are distributed across several hours (e.g., check-in). Conversely, the facility demand 
will be underestimated for subsystems where passengers show up during a very short time span (e.g., 
immigration) or if the demand is expected to be far from uniformly distributed across the hour (e.g., if most 
flights fall within the last half hour). For these reasons, the DHR must be adjusted to incorporate the 
passenger presentation at the specific facility and/or any significant flight distribution within the hour. When 
doing this, it may be relevant to shorten the initial time interval (At) of 60 minutes correspondingly to better 
reflect the demand characteristics. It is highly recommended to analyze the current correlation between the 
DHR and the actual passenger presentation at the facility in the corresponding peak periods. Data for this 
exercise may be derived from modern passenger flow monitoring (PFM) systems, boarding card scans at the 
facility entry, manual observations or passenger surveys. The analyst must further consider whether the future 
Passenger presentation at the facility is likely to change due to planned implementation of new processes or 
digital solutions (e.g., self-service, mobile options or biometrics). 
If historical data is available, the potential impact of the traffic during previous and following hours might also 
be analyzed to further refine the demand figure to be used. The output of this method is a single demand 
figure for the specific subsystem that is linked to the At selected. 
(b) Multiple Peaks Method 
Compared to the Single Peak Method above, this method provides a higher level of result granularity and 
captures different peaking structures of specific operations and passenger flows. It requires the development 
of a DDFS (see 2.2.10.3 Design Day Flight Schedules) as well as a thorough assessment of the passenger 
behavior via their presentation profiles. The following steps to obtain demand need to be repeated for each 
individual subsystem as presentation profiles may differ significantly and different segmentations of demand 
may be required. 
Note: The passenger groupings, presentation profiles and graphical/numerical representations presented 
below are only intended as examples. The indicative values shown in the examples should never be used as 
a reference. 
1. As an outcome of the forecasting exercise, the planner should obtain the DDFS (see 2.2.10.3 Design Day 
Flight Schedules). As it may not be possible to capture all passenger segment peaks (e.g., 
arrival/departure or domestic/international) in a single DDFS, it must be assessed that the selected DDFS 
includes the appropriate peak patterns and demand level for the facility in question. In some cases, it is 
advisable to construct multiple DDFSs to be used for the demand-capacity analyses of the various 
facilities. 
2. Current passenger behavior should be analyzed at each facility with the objective to obtain the passenger 
presentation profiles at each individual terminal departure/arrival/transfer subsystem. This should be done 
for each group of passengers that will be sharing the facility. Passenger presentation profiles can be 
different depending on many factors, such as the traffic segment (e.g., premium, economy), type of flight 
(e.g., international, domestic, scheduled, charter) or time of flight (e.g., early morning, afternoon). Given

profile can be used, or different groupings of passengers as shown below may be considered:

3.3.4.9.2 Capacity Equations for Assessment of Future Facility Requirements 
This section introduces capacity equations that can be used to calculate the future facility requirements based 
on the demand figures calculated in the previous sections. The equilibrium between capacity, demand and the 
selected LoS is expressed in the formulas described below. 
The formulas are simple to use and provide high-level results that can be suitable for initial capacity 
assessments, simple stand-alone processes, master planning purposes or long-term projects where the 
forecast uncertainty is high and a more detailed approach with additional assumptions is not expected to 
provide more accurate results. 
For short-term projects or detailed facility design where both forecasted passenger figures and other planning 
parameters are more certain, it is recommended to use more detailed planning tools. If a DDFS has been 
developed and presentation profiles have been established, using simulation tools to calculate detailed facility 
requirements is recommended (see 2.11 Use of Simulation for further details). Simulation also has the 
advantage of capturing the effects of interaction and interdependencies between other facilities upstream or 
downstream. 
In the end, the appropriate method for facility sizing should be selected considering factors like forecasting 
horizon, data quality, time and budget available. It must be emphasized that the capacity equations presented 
in this section employ some simplifications and approximations and are not intended as a substitute for the 
detailed evaluation of terminal capacity and LoS. Not all formulas will be applicable to all airports, since not all 
local factors are included. 
(a) For Processing Facilities 
Calculating the facility requirement for a processing subsystem requires two additional inputs in addition to the 
demand established in the previous sections: PT and selected LoS. PT is measured as the time between the 
start of subsequent transactions at each lane/counter and includes any time spent between the processing of 
each passenger (e.g., time spent for passengers to go from queue to counter). PT is, therefore, the inverse of 
the lane throughput capacity. For example, a PT of 20 seconds/pax is the equivalent of a throughput capacity 
of 180 pax/hour/lane (3600/180 = 20). 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 615 

===PAGE 635===
Se &, C=” 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
The current PTs at the facility should be measured (manually or automatically) and carefully analyzed to 
calculate an average that represents the observed PTs during peak hours. For instance, the check-in process 
for an individual passenger may take 60 seconds while the check-in process for a family of four may take 
120 seconds (30 seconds per passenger). The analyst must also consider whether the future PT is likely to 
change (e.g., due to the introduction of new processes or technology such as self-service, mobile options, 
biometrics). Any error in the selected PT will have an equally high impact on the output as an error of the 
same magnitude (in %) in the applied demand figure. Therefore, it is recommended to use the capacity 
calculations with different PTs to assess the sensitivity of the calculated facility requirements. Similarly, the 
selected LoS (as measured by the maximum allowed queuing time) has a direct impact on the facility 
requirements and the impact of different MQTs should be evaluated. See 3.3.4.6 Level of Service Concept for 
more details on selecting the appropriate LoS. 
The process for using the capacity equations is described below: 
1. Determine the design demand figures corresponding to the number of people using the facility in the 
different time increments. For the Single Peak Method there will only be one figure. Additional information 
will be provided in subsequent sections with some specific considerations relating to specific subsystems. 
2. Select the PT (in seconds) of the passengers and MQT corresponding to the target LoS 
Note: Steps 3, 4 and 5 are meant to be used sequentially without manually adjusting any of the outputs 
(.e., not adding additional units before calculating Qyay-see step 4 below). If additional units or queue 
space needs to be provided (e.g., to accommodate dedicated units or for redundancy), this should be 
done at the end of the process. When manually adjusting the outputs, planners should try to have overall 
balanced capacity in the system (i.e., processing capacity in the units should be matched with the 
correspondent queueing capacity). 
3. Calculate the number of facility units required to meet the target LoS using the equation below. If using 
the Multiple Peaks Method to calculate demand, repeat the calculation for each of the five time 
increments At. The most demanding result in terms of number of units should always be selected and 
then used as input of the following step. For the Single Peak Method, use the selected value of At after 
relevant adjustments have been applied. A conversion factor (60) is included in the formula to ensure 
consistency in terms of units as PT is defined in ‘seconds’ and MQT and At are defined in ‘minutes’. 
Demand - PT/60 #Units = ‘At+MQT 
4. With a MQT already defined as a design input and a known PT, calculate the number of passengers in 
the queue (Qyax) using as input the number of units computed in step 3.

Further capacity equations specific to each processing facility can be found in the following sections relevant

(b) For Holding Facilities 
1. Determine the arrival rate of occupants at the facility. 
2. Determine the processing (or departure) rate of occupants from the facility (this could be triggered by an 
event such as boarding call, call-to-gate, baggage pick-up or a discretionary dwell time). 
3. Using the arrival/departure rates collected above, calculate the maximum number of occupants at any one 
time during the period under analysis (see the sections listed below for additional details). 
4. Using the target proportion of seated versus standing occupants, calculate the number of people seated 
and the number of people standing. 
5. Using the target LoS space requirement, calculate the necessary effective holding area. The effective 
area is net of any obstruction or impediments such as walls, columns and amenities and does not cover 
circulation space or access corridors. This applies to holding facilities such as:

===PAGE 637===
IATA pull Airport Development Reference Manual 
(c) For Circulation Facilities 
1. Determine the design passenger flow per relevant unit of time for travel in one direction and convert into 
passenger flow per minute. 
2. Calculate the required effective width. 
3. Adjust the required effective width to account for edge effects. Total (net) width equals to effective width 
plus one meter on each side of the corridor. 
If circulation facilities allow movements in both directions, use total passenger flows for both directions for 
step 1 and adjust total width by adding half a meter for each side of the corridor plus another meter for 
counter-flow effect. 
Other considerations that need to be taken: 
¢ Provision of travellators should be in addition to the width required to accommodate 100% of passengers 
using the corridor. In other words, travellators are considered an aid to minimize walking distance and not 
to increase capacity. 
¢ The minimum width of the corridor should allow the use of buggies and other service vehicles plus an 
additional minimum width for passengers walking through. 
3.3.4.9.3 Assessment of Existing Facility Level of Service 
For assessment of the current LoS of an existing facility, it is recommended to monitor the process 
continuously using PFM systems or manual observations to capture queuing times and queue lengths. Actual, 
daily performance levels are typically highly influenced by operational factors such as delays, fluctuations in 
PTs, lane opening hours and staffing patterns. However, if operational data is not available, the capacity 
equations in the section above may be used to calculate the theoretical LoS provided by the airport in the 
current situation. Since the total number of units and the area are existing parameters, they can be used in 
the formulas to isolate the MQT and the SP. In addition, the equations can also be used to model “what-if” 
scenarios on the current infrastructure (e.g., by adjusting the PT, current demand or LoS). 
3.3.5 Departure Processes and Facilities 
3.3.5.1 Departures Forecourt 
Vision 
Airports should be highly connected to city centers. Locations to drop off or collect cargo and baggage will be 
numerous, secure, and convenient. Passenger can also commence their journey from secure entry gates 
within the city which provide access to multi-modal connections. The sector on an aircraft becomes an 
integrated component of a complete journey which may use several modes of transport (both traditional and 
new innovative modes). Refer to NEXTT Off Airport Activities. 
618 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 638===

IATA Passenger Terminal 
3.3.5.1.1. General Considerations 
The departures forecourt is accessed by the landside road system that serves the departing flight passenger 
flows only. It is the interface between the landside public traffic network and the terminal building. The 
landside departing traffic network encompasses the road systems, parking and public transit systems that are 
used to access the terminal building. 
The term “forecourt” is applied to the departures drop-off area, the road itself and the short-term parking 
system that interfaces directly with the terminal building. 
For the departures short- to long-term parking provisions, please see 3.4 Landside Access Systems. 
3.3.5.1.2 Departures Forecourt Drop-Off 
The departures drop-off function can be provided on a single-level forecourt or on a split-level forecourt.
