The departures forecourt usually reflects a multi-modal transportation system, with passengers using different 
modes of transport (modal split) to access the airport. Examples include: 
e Private cars 
e Rental cars 
° Taxis 
* Shuttles/coaches; and 
e Buses 
The order in which these different modes are accommodated (i.e., whether private vs. public vehicles get 
closest access to the forecourt) may be a function of regulatory (safety/security) requirements. The drop-off 
functions for the above-listed traffic modes should be located in close proximity to the terminal if they cannot 
be accommodated directly on the drop-off forecourt. 
Passengers that make their way to the terminal from vehicle parking areas, as well as those coming to the 
terminal by public transit systems, should ideally enter the terminal on a dedicated route that separates the 
passenger flows from vehicle flows using the drop-off forecourt. 
The departures forecourt is just one element of the entire landside access system. It must be considered 
holistically with the other elements of the landside access system (see 3.4 Landside Access Systems).

3.3.5.2 Departures Hall 
Vision 
The departures hall should be a welcoming first impression of the airport, with an open, unobstructed and 
well-organized space, easily accessible from landside. It should provide a calm, naturally lit environment that 
enhances passenger orientation and provides adequate space for passenger and baggage processing. 
Policy 
It is recommended that the departures hall should: 
* Create a connection between the facility and the geographical setting, city or region it serves 
e Communicate a sense of place 
¢ Provide ample orientation and circulation spaces for passengers to plan the next steps of their journey 
e Provide public facilities 
e Be public to support landside commercial revenues. 
3.3.5.2.1. General Considerations 
The departures hall is the entrance into the terminal building for departing passengers. Depending upon type, 
size and airport location, it can consist of various public and non public areas including circulation and waiting 
areas, orientation and regrouping spaces, public facilities and airline facilities. In some regulatory jurisdictions 
this space must accommodate a segregated zone for well-wishers.

Entrance, Orientation and Circulation Space 
The circulation, waiting and functional areas extend from the front fagade of the terminal up to the next 
Stage of processing, generally passenger security screening. The total area includes a general circulation 
area parallel to the fagade as well as functional processing zones. The area should be barrier free so that 
passengers arriving through the entrance doors have an unobstructed view of the circulation zone and the 
functional areas, and can easily locate where they go next. To assist with orientation the view should 
extend beyond the functional areas such that passengers can see the next step of their journey toward 
the departure gates, or in some cases their final point of departure and/or aircraft. 
To minimize the need for circulation inside the terminal that can potentially create bottlenecks, entrance 
doors should be multiple and lead directly to the appropriate functional areas. To facilitate passenger 
experience functional zones may be grouped by airline/alliances and these should be identified by 
signage on the forecourt and next to the entrance doors. 
Public Facilities 
Public facilities include, but are not limited to: 
¢ Concessions 
*® Communications facilities 
e Banking machines 
¢ Mail facilities 
*° Seating 
¢ Information desks 
¢ Toilets 
e PRM reception areas; and 
e Wayfinding Signage/interactive message boards 
e FIDS 
e Baggage trolleys 
Public facilities should be located in areas that do not conflict with functional areas in order to promote the 
most efficient and uniform utilization of the space. This policy will also assist in expanding the departures 
hall by adding further modules to either side of it. In countries with high visitor-to-passenger ratios, 
consideration should be given to controlling access to functional areas. Directional and information 
signage should be prominently located in the public areas (see 3.3.12 Wayfinding and Signage). 
Airline Ticket Sales and Service Counters 
These facilities are usually provided within the departures hall. Ticket sales and service counters are 
required for passengers who have not purchased tickets prior to arriving at the airport, and for passengers 
who wish to change reservations, flight class or pay for excess baggage. Such counters should be 
oriented along the normal line of passenger flow, but without inhibiting the flow of passengers. A good

location for ticket sales and service counters is parallel to the front fagade of the terminal between the 
entrance doorways, and on the same level within the terminal as the main departures hall. Unlike 
common processing counters, airlines usually require their own dedicated ticket sales and service 
counters. These counters provide each airline with a sales presence in the terminal. 
Airline Offices 
Airline passenger processing support offices are required in close proximity to that airline's preferred use 
area. The amount of space required by each airline and/or handling agency will vary depending on such 
factors as the volume of traffic or the type of handling service performed. Airlines will also require 
additional administrative offices, which may be located in other areas of the terminal but with convenient 
access to the passenger processing areas. Airline support offices are also required in the airside 
concourse close to the aircraft operation areas, usually at the apron level (ramp or apron 
accommodation). 
Baggage trolleys 
Baggage trolley and ample related storage areas need to be provided in and around the processing 
areas. 
Commercial areas 
Concessions can be incorporated into the landside departures hall as well as the airside departure lounge 
(see 3.3.10 Concessions and Retail for more information). 
Departure Flight Information Displays (FIDs): 
Such must be available within the departures hall. The FID monitors should show which airlines are 
operating from which processing areas (see 3.3.12 Wayfinding and Signage for more information). 
Ancillary Functions 
The departures hall can also accommodate additional functions, or might safeguard space for additional 
future functions. Such requirements should be determined with the relevant stakeholders. Local security 
protocols can change. Flexibility is important for potential implementation of additional passenger and 
baggage entrance security checks. 
3.3.5.3 Check-In 
Vision 
Check-in Processes should be quick and easy, making best use of automation and latest technologies 
tailored to passengers’ needs. Removing processing from the terminal building helps to smooth the flow of 
passengers and improves the passenger experience as a whole. 
Policy 
It is recommended that departure processes at terminals be provided in consolidated departures halls, ideally 
one single hall only, and that the spaces be: 
Flexible to adapt to future needs and safeguard for expansion or other changes

IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
e Adequately sized and to contribute to a stress-free environment; and 
¢ Intuitive, providing easily identifiable direction routings to allow passengers natural orientation 
3.3.5.3.1 General Considerations 
It is important for airport owners/operators and design professionals to understand that the “traditional check￾in” function at airports is evolving rapidly. As “form follows function”, understanding and accommodating the 
changing functionalities in this part of the airport can lead to innovative and cost-effective solutions that 
enhance the traveling experience. 
On the other hand, providing “more of the same” is no longer a viable option as automation and electronic 
features begin to modify the functions that have traditionally taken place in the departures hall. Airports that 
simply replicate existing counter configurations (i.e., linear, island, etc.) will soon find that they have wasted 
valuable resources creating facilities that are no longer needed or no longer function in the same way. 
3.3.5.3.2 The Process 
The departures hall represents one of the first interfaces of passengers with terminal equipment after entering 
the terminal. It also provides a link to the BHS, the largest specialized technical installation within airports. 
Traditionally, the “check-in” process encompasses the airline acceptance of passengers and their checked 
baggage, and the separation of checked baggage from the departing passengers in order to security screen 
the baggage, consolidate it in the BHS with all other checked baggage for a specific flight in order to 
eventually load it onto the aircraft. However, more and more frequently many of these processes are taking 
place prior to arrival at the airport, away from the terminal itself, often in the passengers’ homes or offices. 
The passenger and baggage processes can include: 
e Ticket purchase 
¢ Baggage weighing and overweight payments 
e Handing out of boarding passes 
e Issuing of bag tags 
¢ Tagging of baggage 
e Injecting checked baggage into the BHS 
e Validation of passenger identification documentation; and 
¢ Out-of-gauge (OOG) and super-OOG baggage acceptance 
The equipment at the airport terminal usually consists of self-service kiosks and bag drop positions with 
baggage conveyance facilities. Typically, these facilities are staffed by airline employees or sometimes 
subcontracted to airport handling agents. 
624 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 644===
IATA * Passenger Terminal 
Exhibit 3.3.5.3.2: Self-Service Kiosk (HAM) 
Source: SITA 
In recent years, the development and improvement of technologies has seen significant process 
enhancements. Many of the processes that were carried out at the terminal in the past are now taking place 
away from the terminal building itself. Process improvements are increasing the number of passengers that 
can be processed in a given area of the terminal building. These process changes will continue and, as a 
consequence, terminal departures hall functionality is changing quickly. Therefore, terminal departures halls 
must be designed to respond flexibly to future layout changes without negatively affecting the passenger 
experience. When designing and implementing passenger processing and baggage handling facilities, it is 
important to consider potential future alternative process scenarios with spatial flexibility within the terminal to 
grow or reduce the functional areas, depending on traffic development and deployed technology. The 
evolution of technologies and thus functionality cannot be underestimated by planners and operators. 
Airlines headquarters, operating departments and handling agents must be consulted in the design and 
equipment selection phases of the departures hall planning, as the layout will be influenced by the procedures 
they will use for passenger and baggage processing and on overall area allocations. 
The layouts have to provide fully segregated connections for baggage flows (typically conveyors) from 
processing positions toward the checked baggage screening, sortation and makeup positions that comprise 
the departures BHS. Specialist engineers should be consulted for the planning and integration of baggage 
screening and handling systems.

The layout of the departures hall is largely influenced by the functional concepts and the associated 
equipment planned by the airport authority. It is essential that the airlines and handling agents be consulted 
during the entire planning process to ensure optimal operational effectiveness and functionality. The allocation 
of equipment (i.e., desks, kiosks, bag drops, etc.) to the various airlines and alliances should be considered 
early during the planning process. There should be a logical flow for all passengers and particularly alliance 
passengers, from entering the terminal via the departures hall to the departure lounge and gate areas. 
The various different functional options that are available to airports, airlines and passengers are described in 
the following section. 
3.3.5.3.3 The Different Functional Options for Passengers 
Passengers have the choice between several different forms of processing, either assisted by handling agents 
or without assistance (passenger self-service). 
e Using online or mobile apps, remote from the terminal 
¢ Using self-service equipment at the airport, such as self-service kiosks, bag drops; and 
e Using agent-assisted processing at the airport 
The design intent of the passenger/baggage processing area is to provide the most seamless and efficient 
products for the many different types of passengers: 
¢ With or without checked luggage 
¢ Having used pre-airport or in-airport processing options; or 
e Traveling in economy or first/business class 
With mobile or online passenger processing becoming more prevalent, airports can provide specialized 
equipment to deal with passenger and baggage acceptance separately. 
Recent terminal developments have seen more and more self-service opportunities being provided. Bag drop 
units provide baggage acceptance processes, issue bag tags and inject the checked baggage into the BHS. 
Typically, the bag drop facility takes less process time than a full service passenger and baggage facility. As a 
result, throughput is increased, making the most efficient use of space-consuming and costly installations. 
Self-service kiosks are becoming well-established in many airports around the world. As the popularity of 
Internet and mobile processing increases, it is important to consider the longer term usage of self-service 
kiosks.

3.3.5.3.4. Types of Processing Equipment 
The processing options available to passengers can encompass the following: 
(a) Mobile services 
(b) Self-service kiosks (with or without staff support) 
(c) Self-service processing and bag drop facilities 
(d) Self-service bag drop belts 
(e) Over sized luggage processing units; and 
(f) Ticketing or assistance desks. 
(a) Mobile Services 
With mobile services, passengers can manage their processing from any remote location. The processes 
available via these channels/devices usually range from ticket bookings to boarding pass retrieval and 
changing of reservations. 
Passengers who have been processed this way will not require these services in the terminal. They might 
use self-service kiosks to print a boarding pass, and proceed to security search with hand luggage only, 
or use bag drop counters to hand over their checked luggage to the handling agents. 
(b) Self-service Kiosk (with or without Staff Support) 
628 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 648===
=e 
IATA + Passenger Terminal 
(Cc) 
Self-service kiosks can provide a variety of processing services, but are used typically to print boarding 
passes, check passenger ID and manage ticket payments. Kiosks provide space efficient solutions for 
these processes and are convenient to passengers. They can be deployed in numbers that allow for very 
short queues at each machine. 
Passengers traveling with hand luggage can use the kiosks to print boarding passes and continue toward 
government controls (i.e., security screening toward airside and other controls, as required) without 
having to use processing or bag drop desks. 
Passengers traveling with checked luggage can also obtain boarding passes at the self-service kiosks. 
For these passengers, the kiosks can be equipped with weigh scales and excess baggage payment 
functions (card readers). Bag tags can be printed at kiosks as well, relying on the passenger to attach 
them correctly to the bags. After finishing at the kiosk, the passengers continue to a bag drop counter, be 
it agent-assisted or self-service, in order to inject their bags into the BHS. 
Kiosks, whether organized in lines or in groups, need to be positioned logically within the context of the 
processing areas and flow of passengers. They can be accompanied by an agent desk with full computer 
equipment to aid with complicated bookings or to provide other assistance. 
Self-service Processing and Bag Drop Facilities 
Conventional processing facilities can be operated simply as bag drop desks. In this case, only the bag 
weighing, tagging and bag injection process are carried out by the agent. This option provides convenient 
and quick processing for passengers. Passengers using these facilities will have completed their 
processing by other means (i.e., online, mobile app or at a self-service kiosk at the airport). In this way, a 
time-consuming part of the process is removed from space-demanding facilities and provided via very 
space-efficient self-service kiosks or removed altogether from the terminal. 
Solutions are also available for airports whereby the traditional bag drop facilities are replaced with self￾service bag drop facilities. These solutions have a similar space demand as the conventional facilities, as 
they are usually connected to baggage collector belts in the same way. However, self-service bag drops 
do not provide an agent as a passenger interface. They rely solely on the passenger to carry out the bag 
tag printing, tagging and injecting process. Two aspects are vital to the successful operation of these 
facilities: 
41. Correct insertion of the bag onto the conveyor belts; and 
2. The correct attachment of the bag tag to the bag so that it can be read by the BHS. 
Several different solutions are available. Such solutions can consist of handheld devices that passengers 
use manually to scan an attached tag. Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology is currently being 
implemented by many airports, whereby an RFID chip is attached to each bag tag. 
Personalized bag tags may be used in the future, either based on RFID or barcode tag technology, 
whereby the tag is reused by the passenger for every individual journey.

===PAGE 649===

Both conventional bag drop processing facilities and self-service units are usually organized along 
baggage collector belts, with between 10 and 20 processing positions per belt, depending on predicted 
baggage volumes. Collector belts are typically organized in a linear layout. 
The unit may be arranged in an uninterrupted, linear layout or be spaced so as to allow passengers to 
pass between the positions after processing (pass-through layout). This type of processing layout may be 
suitable for small- to medium-size terminals or for site conditions requiring a minimal depth from forecourt 
to gate. 
(d) Self-service Bag Drop Belts 
Self-service bag drop belts enable the passenger to place the bag on a belt to inject it into the BHS. Such 
solutions are very space-efficient. The operation relies on the passenger tagging the bags, usually at self￾service kiosks. The passengers then proceed to the bag drop belt, where the bag tag is read by a tag 
reader before it is placed on the belt. In many cases, this tag reading process is carried out by a handling 
agent with a handheld scanning device. 
630 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 650===
Se g- if F 
IATA Passenger Terminal 
Source: InterVISTAS 
Usually, self-service kiosks and bag drop units are separated in order to increase the baggage throughput 
efficiency of the space-consuming counter positions. However, combinations are found where passengers 
are offered all the necessary processing elements by self-service equipment in one location. 
Payment for overweight or oversize checked baggage must be accounted for in the design of the bag 
drop process. This is being handled in a variety of ways and must be confirmed with the airport and airline 
operators. 
(e Oversized Luggage Processing Units 
Specially designed units are required for the acceptance of oversized, or OOG, baggage. This function 
must be located in clearly identified positions within the processing hall. These processing positions have 
wider baggage belts with a straight feed down to the outbound baggage hall. They usually also have 
access to a freight elevator or door that will allow large non conveyable items (Super-OOG) to be placed 
on a cart and taken to the outbound baggage makeup hall. 
3.3.5.3.5 Locations of Processing within the Terminal Context 
Processing equipment can be located in various different areas of a terminal and associated buildings, these 
can include: 
(a) Landside Locations 
e Centralized processing in a departures hall 
¢ — Split processing (i.e., decentralized processing in several halls or several other locations within the 
terminal). For example, recheck after customs exit on arrivals, or in VIP/CIP terminals

=e Wi ; 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
e Processing or bag drop at the forecourt 
e Remote processing in hotels; and 
¢ Remote processing in ground transportation centers or airport train stations. 
(b) Airside Locations 
* Bag drop (usually for hand luggage), ticketing and processing in departure lounges 
e Transfer facilities; and 
* Gate processing 
Equipment can also be provided in different locations for different flows of passengers (i.e., First/CIP/ 
VIP/Business Class passengers separate from Economy passengers). Passengers without checked baggage 
can be offered different routes through the departures hall than passengers with checked baggage.

Bypass routes to subsequent processes are provided for travelers who do not need to use the check-in 
facilities. Travelers with hand luggage only are presented with self-service kiosks and can bypass bag drop 
and conventional desks to continue their journey. Passengers with checked luggage can use self-service 
kiosks first and then proceed to bag drop desks. Passengers who require assistance for processing will find 
this provided at the sides or behind the bag drop desks. Queuing areas are highlighted in blue. Queuing areas 
can be organized in straight queue lines or in “snake” queues. Tensile barriers or other forms of queue 
management can be deployed. The queuing strategy is to be considered when laying out the processing 
areas. Yellow arrows indicate different passenger flows through the departures hall. Circulation widths 
between the various processing functions need to be sufficiently sized to allow for stable flows of passengers. 
3.3.5.3.7 Decentralized Processing 
Decentralized processing provides processing facilities such as kiosks in more than one location, be it in 
several departures halls or at “off-airport” locations, like an airport's train station, hotels, cruise ship terminals, 
public transport facilities, etc. It is important for passengers to know their processing options.. Connections 
between the processing zones have to be available. Decentralized processing can also include dedicated 
processing for specific user groups, such as first-class processing. 
3.3.5.3.8 VIP Processing 
First-class processing usually remains within a common departures hall. However, dedicated services can be 
provided as a VIP product, whereby specific passenger groups are served in a dedicated processing zone. 
These facilities may also be served by conveyors with members of staff performing the baggage weighing and 
bag labeling functions. Checked baggage is then injected either manually or automatically into the main BHS. 
3.3.5.3.9 Processing at Ground Transportation Centers 
Many airports offer processing opportunities at their ground transportation center or train station. This service 
is convenient to passengers arriving by train or bus as they do not need to carry their luggage into the 
terminal. 
These facilities adopt the same processes and technology as processing systems within the terminal complex. 
The main difference with these facilities is that they are remote from the terminal complex. Therefore, checked 
baggage screening is normally only completed once the baggage has been collected and transferred to the 
terminal BHS. This can be done via a conveyor- or vehicle-based transportation system. This might include 
bonded vehicles, where required. Some locations include screening facilities at the point of collection. Careful 
consideration should be given to the definition of airside and landside zones for such a process to ensure the 
integrity of the airport's security. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 633 

===PAGE 653===
w IATA Wi Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.3.5.3.10 Transfers or Airside Processing 
Transfer baggage processing facilities are typically located airside. The primary objective is to enable 
passengers who are in transit in the airport complex to be processed for connecting flights without having to 
go landside and be reprocessed through the departures sequence. 
Transfer processing in airside departures areas usually provides: 
e Ticketing services 
e New boarding passes 
e Flight changes 
* Bag drop opportunities, usually for hand luggage. This is a service that transferring passengers 
sometimes find useful, or in cases where hand luggage restrictions apply 
* Troubleshooting functions, be it for delayed or cancelled flights, rebooking or other forms of 
troubleshooting. Kiosk rebooking options may also be incorporated 
In the context of the baggage system, the objective of the airside processing facility is to confirm the 
+ connecting flight destination and tell the Departure Control System (DCS) how to process the transfer 
baggage.

For transferring passengers who are not yet security-controlled, similar facilities can be provided in dedicated 
transfer locations.

3.3.5.3.11 Enhanced Security Processing 
Processing areas that operate high-security protocols should use the main conventional conveying equipment 
and BHS interfaces. It is possible, however, to have high-security processing operations in remote processing 
facilities. The high-security elements can involve: 
e Passenger profiling 
e Security interrogation of passengers 
e Access to national and international security databases, including emigration and immigration; and 
* Biometric databases 
e Separate BHS Screening areas for hold luggage 
The operational protocols for high-security operations will vary greatly from case to case and need careful 
consideration during the planning process. All relevant stakeholders should be engaged early during the 
planning process. 
Although recent and significant security advances in self-service processing are evident, it is historically more 
common for high-security operations to use conventionally staffed desks. Baggage that has been checked in 
by high-risk passengers should be clearly identified within the BHS. The BHS should be able to link the profile 
data captured from processing and provide this information to the baggage control and security systems. 
As mentioned, high-security processing areas can be provided in remote or isolated locations. This can 
include physical barriers between traditional processing and high-risk processing. Additional baggage 
screening equipment might be provided near the high-risk processing desks to scan checked baggage before 
entering it into a centralized BHS. 
3.3.5.3.12 Remote Processing 
Baggage services that are provided before the passenger reaches the airport terminal are becoming more 
and more common. Examples include baggage services to and from a home destination, cruise ship or hotel. 
These facilities adopt the same processes and technology as terminal processing systems for both 
conventional and high-security processing. The main difference with these facilities is that they are remote 
from the terminal complex and that checked baggage screening is normally only completed once the baggage 
has been collected and transferred to the terminal BHS. This can be done via a conveyor- or vehicle-based 
transportation system. This might include bonded vehicles, where required, or screening facilities at the point 
of collection. Careful consideration is to be given to the definition of security-restricted and landside zones for 
such a process to ensure the integrity of the airport security. A dedicated baggage in-feed area might be 
required for baggage delivery trucks that access the terminal via the landside surface access systems. 
Checked baggage that has been profiled and deemed to be high-risk should be removed before transfer to 
the terminal complex and dealt with locally using secure protocols and equipment. This is not always practical, 
however, since some remote areas, such as hotel complexes are not versed in or equipped with the technical 
infrastructure required to deal with baggage threat issues. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 635 

===PAGE 655===
IATA pull Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.3.5.3.13 Baggage Makeup Hall 
The interface between the processing equipment and the BHS requires careful consideration and planning. 
On belted baggage systems, checked baggage is accepted at processing facilities and is then transported on 
dedicated routes toward the baggage handling area. These dedicated routes should be fully secured against 
public access, especially from the processing side, and are usually considered airside. Maintenance access is 
required along the full length of the baggage conveyors. The term “right of way’ is often utilized to describe 
the routing of baggage belts and refers to the fact that these have to be uninterrupted and segregated from 
any other terminal flows, be it services, passengers, staff or goods. See 3.3.8 Baggage Handling System. 
3.3.5.3.14 Considerations for Facility Sizing 
The departures hall is composed of different areas including kiosks and corresponding baggage conveyors, 
queuing areas and circulation areas. Circulation areas must be provided: 
1. Between the queue area and the service desks, to allow for easy access and egress to/from the process; 
and 
2. Between the entrance of the queue and any other obstacle in the public area, to allow for people to reach 
other destinations within the terminal building. 
It is common to see a single queue for multiple service desks. Also, airlines frequently operate under 
“common use” practices. This method of operation is proven to increase flexibility and capacity. Consequently, 
airlines are able to process multiple flights at the same time from one location for both customer facing (e.g. 
self-service kiosks, self-service bag drops) and agent facing (e.g. check-in desks, boarding gates) processing 
points using CUSS and CUPPS standards respectively. Please refer to the CUSS implementation guide and 
the CUPPS implementation guide for more information. 
The required footprint for initial processing (“check-in”) facilities and associated queuing areas depends on 
their geometrical configuration. A circulation area must be added to the queuing area. The circulation corridor 
width will vary with the flow of passengers. 
Queuing patterns will usually follow the airline's service frontage area. For example, if an airline uses a total of 
20 service desks, the total queue can spread over the width of the 20 desks and split into segments (e.g., bag 
drop, business-, first- and economy-class processing). The depth of the queue depends on the waiting time 
policy and queue management strategy. However, it is important for airports and designers to remember that 
the “traditional” process is under significant transition and the functions and therefore the form of these 
services areas will need to be modified to meet changing needs. 
Airlines often provide a more personal service to their premium class passengers. These may include 
business class, frequent flyers or any other type of passenger requiring special attention. A dedicated queue 
will be provided for them and many times the agents will serve premium passengers as soon as they arrive at 
the front of the queue. Additional desks will be made available to these passengers so that the maximum 
queuing time is kept to a minimum.

Sizing of the passenger processing hall depends on the number of passengers using the facility during the 
peak period, the proportion of premium passengers, the processing rate, the space provision per person as 
well as the maximum queuing time.

Variables influencing the sizing of self-service facilities are similar to those utilized for traditional check-in 
desks (see 3.3.5.3.17 Traditional Check-In Facility Sizing). The differences lie in the much lower footprint 
occupied by the facility and the reduced maximum accepted queuing time.

3.3.5.4 Boarding Pass Check (Access Control to Secure Areas) 
Airport and aircraft operators have responsibilities to meet certain security requirements related to access 
control. Among these requirements is the responsibility to prevent access by unauthorized persons to defined 
secured areas of the airport. Passengers require a valid boarding pass or equivalent electronic documentation 
in order to access the “airside”, or “security restricted”, or “security-controlled” portion of the terminal. Different 
terminologies and definitions exist. For passengers, the airside may be defined as: 
¢ Beyond immigration or customs controls 
* Beyond standalone boarding pass checkpoints 
© Concomitant to the entrance of the restricted security area, if the security screening checkpoint comes 
first 
Planners will need to consider the appropriate number of automated access points/gates and the required 
space for these. Depending on passenger flows, airports may consider a combined solution such that gates 
are used for the majority of passengers, with handheld or portable technology used to manage small peaks. 
Various options will need to be discussed during the planning process, taking into consideration current and 
future passenger flows. In some cases, this access control check may be combined with other processes, 
such as border control. The introduction of biometrics and other advanced technology may mean that 
passengers will no longer have to manually present the boarding pass or other electronic token (to a machine 
or person). 
3.3.5.4.1 Technical Requirements 
Access gates to the security checkpoint area usually involves several steps. Prior to accessing a security 
screening, a boarding pass check is usually required. The boarding pass check represents the first step in 
allowing a passenger to the airside, by validating a flight ticket. It also represents an interface to the airport's 
AODB. It should be equipped with barcode readers. Depending on the airport's and aircraft operators’ specific 
requirements, the boarding pass readers may also collect data from near-field communication (NFC), RFID, 
staff identification cards, frequent flyer cards, credit cards, biometrics, etc. The gates may also be equipped 
with a display and green/red lights to provide additional user guidance.

refurbishing or designing new screening facilities will need to understand the proposed passenger 
segmentation plans and ensure that the appropriate infrastructure, space and layout is considered.

3.3.5.4.3 Transaction Times and Throughputs 
Transaction times may vary depending on the information being processed. For example, simple boarding 
pass checks (to validate ticket validity) are likely to take less time than detailed background checks and 
biometric capture/validation. Passengers’ familiarity with the use of automated gates will also impact 
transaction times. Automated access gates reading boarding passes have average transaction times of only 
nine seconds per passenger. This translates to an average throughput for a 30-minute demand period of 200 
passengers per gate. 
3.3.5.4.4 Facility Sizing 
The number of gates will be dictated primarily by passenger volumes and how those volumes are segmented. 
Processes and procedures may vary greatly between jurisdictions. Planners and designers need to 
understand the locally applicable processes and procedures in order to provide adequate facilities. However, 
the installation of automated devices and redevelopment of existing facilities should also be seen as an 
opportunity to reexamine existing processes and modernize these processes, as appropriate. Many airports 
deploy a number of boarding pass gates that is in excess of theoretical capacity requirements, in order to 
guarantee the buildup of minimum queues at this process point only.

3.3.5.5 Passenger Security Screening 
An increasing number of airports are seeking to innovate within their checkpoints, not only to improve security 
outcomes, but also to improve operational efficiency and the passenger experience. Careful planning and 
innovative design can, therefore, support airports to effectively deliver on their vision for the future. 
Vision: 
The passenger security screening processes should aim to be as contactless and minimally intrusive as 
possible, using latest technology to minimize divesting and long transaction times. Enabled by risk-based 
screening and improved checkpoint design, the end to end security screening process will be seamless, 
secure, and fully optimized. Passengers will pass through an “on the fly” biometric control point. Identity will 
be verified to permit access to the security screening area and passengers will be directed to the next 
available lane. Screening equipment will dynamically adjust so that passengers and carry-on baggage are 
screened according to their individual risk score for that day/trip. 
Passengers’ belongings will pass through an advanced carry-on baggage screening system to check for 
concealed prohibited items or explosives. Electronics, liquids and other items will remain inside 
baggage-Passenger will proceed at walking pace through a walk-through scanner (there will be no special 
stance to adopt). The scanner will provide an instant message to operators who will advise the passenger if 
they are clear to go or if further screening is required. 
Policy: 
The design of security checkpoints should facilitate the efficient management of a necessary control process, 
with the objective to expedite clearance of persons or goods and prevent unnecessary operational delays. 
Checkpoint design should take into consideration the evolving screening processes and procedures, 
depending on regulatory requirements, changing risk levels and, last but not least, overall evolution of 
passenger handling.

===PAGE 666===
Passenger Terminal 
3.3.5.5.1 General Considerations 
Areas provided for screening activities should be expandable and adaptable, safeguarding for technological 
changes or increased screening requirements. Plans should also allow for an additional layer of screening 
that may be required at departure gates to comply with regulations of the State of destination, or during 
periods of elevated threat. 
Checkpoint design should support airport operators and screening authorities to maintain clear control of 
screened and non-screened passengers as well as cabin baggage at all times. 
(a) Future Proofing 
While a robust screening regime is important to deliver an efficient and secure journey to passengers, so too 
is operational efficiency and a reduction in the complexity and intrusiveness of security screening. Significant 
work has been undertaken by industry experts in recent years to implement new technology and processes at 
airports to achieve this balance. 
Foreseeable technological trends aim to increase the safety provided to passengers by deploying better 
scanning and detection technologies. In the longer term, it is anticipated that this will reduce the amount of 
divesting required by passengers. 
In the meantime, technology can be combined with process innovation to deliver significant improvements. 
For example, centralized image processing, where x-ray images are reviewed by the next available operator 
regardless of their location (similar toexisting hold baggage screening operations), provides greater flexibility 
in resource allocation and will likely become more commonplace. Many new solutions are being implemented 
and terminal planners/designers must investigate existing and upcoming technologies, in association with 
relevant security stakeholders, to ensure the appropriate facilities are provided for. This may include an 
Operator control room of appropriate size, or additional workstations and associated equipment networking 
infrastructure. 
In this regard, consideration should also be given to ensuring that surrounding facilities can be easily altered 
or incorporated into the checkpoint, as needed. For example, placing the checkpoint adjacent to complicated 
infrastructure elements, such as toilets/washrooms or structural, mechanicaV/electrical or vertical circulation 
cores (stairs, escalators, etc.), could make future expansion/modification difficult and costly. Expansion and 
phasing options must be thoroughly thought through during the design development phase to avoid 
unnecessary costs in the future. Checkpoints should be designed with flexibility in mind (e.g., additional 
electrical and other services, increased slab load capacities and expandable screening zones). 
Consideration should be also be made for evolving global developments and passenger trends (e.g., global 
harmonization of technologies and processes, passenger self-service, smart technologies, demographics). 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 647 

===PAGE 667===
x kdl Se 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
({b) Interoperability 
Consideration should be given to ensuring that various elements of the passenger journey are compatible, 
that infrastructure and systems are maximized, and that there is minimal duplication of effort, both on the part 
of the passenger and key stakeholders. For example, if there are plans to capture biometrics during the 
check-in process for subsequent use at the boarding gate, consideration should be given to how this 
technology can be used at the checkpoint. Related infrastructure and space requirements also need to be 
addressed. 
(c) Regulation 
While passenger security screening checkpoints make up part of the broader passenger journey, their 
purpose is extremely specific to “identify and/or detect weapons, explosives or other dangerous devices, 
articles or substances that may be used to commit an act of unlawful interference” (as defined by ICAO in 
Annex 17). Thus, although planners and airport operational teams seek to have passengers pass through 
security checkpoints as smoothly as possible, security outcomes must take priority and checkpoints must at 
all times remain compliant with regulatory requirements, both in terms of design and operation. 
National regulations may dictate screening point layout, minimum staff levels, in what order screening 
activities must be conducted and what screening equipment must be used. These considerations will all have 
varying levels of influence on the overall design of the checkpoint. 
Relevant national and international regulations (for example, ICAO Annex 17 and a State's National Civil 
Aviation Security Program) as well as local procedures have changed significantly over the past decade. As a 
result of future security threats, deployment of next generation screening technologies and process changes 
are increasing. These developments may result in different lane configurations and equipment than is seen 
today, as well as additional network connectivity and IT requirements. It is, therefore, critical that relevant 
government authorities are consulted early during the planning process to ensure all security risks and 
requirements (current and planned) are considered, and that the entire planning team has a clear 
understanding of the passenger process through the checkpoint. 
Airport operators and their consultants should engage in early discussions with authorities with jurisdiction to 
ensure that process simplification and improvement on the part of the regulatory agencies is also considered 
as a fundamental part of the airport development process. 
(d) Service Levels 
Often, airports are required to meet mandated services levels (such as those imposed by regulatory 
authorities) or may voluntarily enter into service level agreements with stakeholders (e.g., with the airlines 
directly). Examples of service levels may include maximum queue times and satisfaction scores, and when 
dealing with service providers may also include measures of transaction times and throughput rates. 
648 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 668===
Be IATA sal Passenger Terminal 
However, it is important to consider a wider range of key performance measures (KPMs) when designing 
checkpoints, particularly those that provide a more holistic view of checkpoint performance, including 
measures such as: 
° — Staff efficiency-sustainable passenger throughput per lane/number of staff allocated per lane 
* Surface efficiency-sustainable passenger throughput per entire checkpoint/m? checkpoint footprint 
¢ Sustainable throughput per lane-mean number of passengers processed by a single security lane per 
hour in a constant flow 
* Sustainable throughput per checkpoint-mean number of Passengers passing through the entire 
checkpoint per hour in a constant flow 
¢ Total transaction time—queue time plus screening transaction time 
Regardless of the measures used, airports need to ensure that checkpoint design will allow them to meet the 
service levels and collect the relevant data to substantiate this. Close cooperation between operational and 
planning teams is needed, therefore, to ensure that any current or future service levels are considered during 
planning, and that these agreed parameters form the basis of the design going forward. 
(e) Broader Security Process 
In addition to security controls applied at passenger and cabin baggage checkpoints, airports and their 
stakeholders may be asked to apply screening measures at other points in the passenger journey (e.g., in 
parking areas, at terminal entry points, at check-in or at the boarding gate). As already mentioned, queues 
and crowds created landside are potential targets for security-related attacks and should be minimized, where 
Possible. Planners should understand any additional passenger or baggage screening processes occurring in 
the airport environment and consider all solutions aimed at the reduction of such vulnerabilities, 
(f) Contingency Planning 
When designing or redesigning security checkpoints, planners and airport managers need to consider 
contingency plans for the following types of events: 
e Equipment outage 
e Power outage 
e Labor actions 
e Emergency situations 
Threat situation at or in the vicinity of the checkpoint (e.g., detection of an explosive devise during the 
screening, an attack in the non-restricted area of the terminal, unattended items). 
Increasing reliance on technology poses additional challenges. While increased automation and connectivity 
results in better and more convenient passenger screening, greater use of technology also makes the 
operation more susceptible to single points of failure. Planning should, therefore, take into consideration 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 649 

===PAGE 669===
ey IATA pull Airport Development Reference Manual 
protection of the digital network access points that could be connected with screening and associated 
screening equipment. Levels of redundancy need to be agreed and integrated into the system design. 
In addition to screening passengers and items, the checkpoint is a critical access control point. Therefore, its 
operation needs to be integrated into the emergency response procedures for the airport. Planners/designers 
should consult early with the relevant authorities to identify what emergency response technology and/or 
design features (e.g., CCTV, panic buttons, floor-to-ceiling barriers like roller doors) are required. 
3.3.5.5.2 Location Considerations 
(a) Influencing Factors 
There are a number of factors that will influence where checkpoints should be located and how many are 
required. At a minimum, design teams should consider: 
© Traffic type forecasts (e.g., point-to-point versus transfer, leisure/charter, general aviation/business, 
domestic/international) 
° Traffic and operations (staff) volume forecasts 
¢ The planned schedule of operations (day/night) 
* Space dedicated to commercial or administration activities 
In particular, airports and planning teams should consider: 
e The proximity of other critical infrastructure 
As far as practical, terminal designers should attempt to design security checkpoints that can be isolated 
in the event of an incident, without impacting other key airport processes and screening at other 
checkpoints. For example, locating checkpoints directly above elements of the baggage system may 
cause problems in the event of a serious security threat at the screening point. Ramifications could 
include the mandatory evacuation of both the security checkpoint and baggage processing areas, causing 
additional disruption. The same remark applies when centralized security screening checkpoints are 
adopted, as any security threat at that point (e.g., a bomb threat) may paralyze the entire flow during the 
resolution of the incident 
e Spatial requirements and flow 
In choosing screening point locations, careful attention should be given to the number (how many 
checkpoints), type (fully equipped or manual only), configuration (e.g., the number of x-ray machines 
versus the number of person-operated screening equipment, walk-through metal detectors (WTMD), or 
security scanners) and positioning of checkpoints so as to facilitate the flow of passengers through the 
terminal and the search area. Consideration also needs to be given to space requirements for queuing, 
physical search, and passengers requiring additional processing 
650 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 670===
O) Yara all Passenger Terminal 
(b) Centralized vs. Decentralized Facilities 
In determining the number and location of security checkpoints, there are three typical arrangements that 
airports adopt: 
e Decentralized (also called gate screening) security screening of passengers and cabin baggage takes 
place directly prior to entering the boarding area. There may be one checkpoint per gate, or a checkpoint 
serving a number of gates in a particular area. Gate screening may also be used for secondary enhanced 
security screening for specific destinations, as required by the State of destination 
e Centralized screening for all passengers is conducted in a single facility, in a consolidated location, at the 
border of landside and the security-restricted area, usually before the airside commercial area. It may be 
located before or after border control processing locations (depending on State regulatory requirements). 
Optionally, both outbound and transfer passengers may be screened through the same facility, although 
care must be taken to understand the impact of peak flows (outbound vs. transfer) 
e Semi-centralized. Several centralized checkpoints may operate across the airport and may cater for 
specific groups. For example, in a large terminal, there may be two or more dedicated outbound 
checkpoints, as well as one for transferring passengers and one for staff 
Specific considerations relating to the above models are detailed in the following tables:

(c) Transfer Screening 
As part of considering the checkpoint location, airports and planners need to agree on how transfer passenger 
flow and screening will be managed. 
Existence of transfer traffic, volumes (on the basis of airline estimations) as well as peak hours, together with 
airlines’ MCT and passenger presentation profile (arrival at the terminal via air bridge or bus), should be 
carefully analyzed to come up with the most suitable solution for these passengers. 
652 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 672===
IATA al Passenger Terminal 
Note: Airports with no or very limited transfer traffic might not see a business benefit of putting dedicated 
transfer checkpoint(s) in place, in which case passengers should be accommodated at the main outbound 
checkpoints. 
When analyzing the above factors and associated data, a distinction between transferring domestic￾international, international-domestic, domestic-domestic and international-international passengers, should be 
made. Separate pathways and transfer checkpoints may be necessary to accommodate different screening 
arrangements or border control checks. However, planners should seek to understand whether biometrics and 
other solutions may enable the combined processing of passengers, before developing any infrastructure￾based solution. 
Terminal planners should also understand current or planned “recognition of equivalence” (also known as 
“One-Stop Security’) arrangements between States that would allow for expedited transfer of passengers 
arriving from approved foreign airports. Provided passenger flows can be segregated, these passengers may 
be exempt from security screening. If the airport has plans to make use of such arrangements, planners will 
need to factor this in to transfer capacity calculations. 
(d) Screening of Staff, Crew and Airport Goods 
It is recommended that the screening of staff be separated from other screening operations. Screening 
requirements for staff may differ from those applied to passengers. Additionally, combining the two flows and 
processes in the same area can be difficult to manage, particularly during peaks, and may potentially divert 
valuable screening capacity when flows are combined. 
Similarly, planners should carefully consider the location for security screening of air crews. Where possible, 
dedicated checkpoints, or those combined with staff screening, will often make the most operational sense. 
However, in some States, crew are subject to border controls. Therefore, if there is a desire for crew to use 
dedicated staff screening checkpoints at these airports, careful consideration will need to be given to the 
location of these checkpoints in relation to border control facilities. In particular, planners and airport 
managers should seek to understand if the border agencies will want to segregate crew processing, or if crew 
will be processed in a common border processing area with passengers. This will be critical to understanding 
crew flow through the two processes. 
(e) Facilities for VIP Screening 
Most airports require some capacity to handle VIPs. VIPs may range from Heads of State and senior 
government officials (VVIPs), through to celebrities and sports stars (VIPs) and business people (CIPs), all of 
whom may be subject to a higher level of personal threat and/or require alternate facilitation/processing. 
Depending on the number and type of VIPs the airport is likely to handle, facilitation/processing may be done 
in dedicated standalone VIP facilities/buildings or handled through the passenger terminal, assuming that 
appropriate controls are in place. As with other passengers, VIP departing and arriving flows should be 
separated. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 653 

===PAGE 673===
we | IATA piu Airport Development Reference Manual 
Like other transfer passengers, transfer VIPs should be security screened before being accepted in the VIP 
departing facility. Careful consideration is required when planning these facilities and airports and planners 
should seek inputs from government and local regulatory authorities to better understand the possible threats 
and needs. 
(f) Processing via Dedicated Facilities (Standalone) 
Dedicated facilities, such as a dedicated VIP terminal, should allow for control of the VIPs and those involved 
with their reception and departure procedures. The facilities should be designed to accommodate a security 
checkpoint and any other processes the VIP will need to go through, including border control processing. 
While typically these facilities straddle the airside/landside boundary, the standard for access control should 
be no less than at other access points. Arrangements for the use of these facilities should ensure the integrity 
of the boundary between the landside and airside. Infrastructure must be in place to ensure these facilities 
can be easily segregated or secured when not in use. 
(g) Processing Via the Passenger Terminal 
Where no such dedicated facility is in place, VIPs will be processed through the main passenger terminal. 
Consideration should be given to access routes to/from the checkpoint and how VIPs could be processed 
discreetly. 
Discussions with local authorities (i.e., police, foreign affairs department, protocol agencies) may be useful in 
determining the requirements, which may include such elements as secure access from roadside drop-off 
points, dedicated screening lanes and private search areas associated with a dedicated lounge. 
3.3.5.5.3 Checkpoint Design—Features 
Checkpoint planners should give consideration to: 
(a) Information and Preparation 
Sufficient space should be allocated to set up passenger preparation areas, which may include such things as 
signage, waste receptacles and other infrastructure to support passengers’ awareness and preparation for the 
screening process. 
(b) Queuing Areas 
Consideration should be given to any non-standard lane or other spatial requirements. Airports may have 
agreements in place with airlines regarding LoS, often associated with dedicated facilities, or they may simply 
wish to segregate some passengers with special needs for operational efficiency reasons. It is important that 
654 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 674===
Be IATA a Passenger Terminal 
planners understand these commercial and operational segmentation plans, as they will have a direct impact 
on checkpoint layout and design. For example, lanes designated to accommodate families or PRMs may 
require additional passenger preparation infrastructure and space, and may even require a dedicated entry 
point, which should be considered as an integral part of the initial planning phase. 
Since the management of security queues will be an ongoing task, rather than designing a static queue 
management system with permanent infrastructure, terminal planners should liaise closely with the airport to 
understand how different queuing configurations can be accommodated to allow for maximum operational 
flexibility while optimizing operations. 
Consideration should also be given to accommodating an automated queue measurement system to assist 
with queue management and to augment current or future LoS obligations. 
As already referenced, queues and crowds created landside (e.g., because of the controls to enter the airside 
and security-restricted areas of the airport) are potential targets for security-related attacks, meaning that 
planners should consider all solutions aiming at the reduction of such vulnerabilities. 
(c) Divesting 
The divesting process will be largely influenced by regulatory requirements. However, planners/designers of 
new terminals should liaise with the relevant authorities to ensure they understand the existing and potential 
future requirements to ensure adequate space is allocated. Airports are encouraged to provide space to allow 
multiple passengers to divest simultaneously per lane in order to support efficient utilization of cabin baggage 
screening equipment and overall productivity of the lane. 
Planners should become familiar with new divesting solutions that impact design and operational processes. 
New systems have been developed to operate with increased automation and require additional space and 
connectivity within the checkpoint. Each system has its pros and cons, so it is critical that planners, airports 
and security service providers together investigate these options. It is important to note, however, that to 
achieve greater capacity, efficiencies and productivity, checkpoint designs should no longer be based on 
traditional lane design models. 
(d) Tray Return Systems 
Automated tray return systems can help reduce manual handling (by both staff and passengers) and ensure a 
constant supply of trays. While this facilitates enhanced overall productivity and increased passenger 
satisfaction, tray return systems tend to occupy more space than conventional X-ray roller beds and require 
additional technical support. The choice of tray return system is also closely linked with the divest options 
noted above, so they should not be considered in isolation. Automation in this regard should not be 
considered at all costs, but rather where it makes operational and business sense for a particular airport. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 655 

===PAGE 675===
ey Witt 
we fF IATA pul Airport Development Reference Manual 
(e) Cabin Baggage Screening Equipment 
These systems vary in size and weight as well as in technical and maintenance requirements. Terminal 
planners/designers must understand the specific detailed requirements of the equipment that the airport 
intends to install and ensure that, as a minimum, the manufacturer's instructions are considered in relation to 
technical and spatial requirements, including providing sufficient access for maintenance without unduly 
affecting the operation of adjacent security screening lanes. 
Today the majority of airports are operating with x-ray baggage systems for cabin baggage screening. 
However, other types of technology, such as CT are starting to replace x-ray scanners. Some of these newer 
machines are larger and heavier than their x-ray predecessors so planners should consider this when 
designing for the future. As an example a current x-ray may weigh in the order of 0.5T, whereas a CT 
machine could be up to 2T. In terms of floor space, the area required for such equipment may be as much as 
double what was previously required. 
In a traditional checkpoint, space is also allocated in the lane for the x-ray operator analyzing images. The 
introduction of centralized image processing (also referred to as multiplexing, matrixing or remote screening) 
now means that there is flexibility in where operators analyzing the images are located. With this arrangement 
the next image simply goes to the next available operator (as is currently the case with hold baggage 
screening). Some airports may elect to keep x-ray operators in the lane environment (to facilitate less 
complex staff rotations), whereas others may locate their x-ray operators at dedicated centralized image 
processing workstations, located adjacent to or remote from the checkpoint. Planners therefore will need to 
understand the airport's plans to use or introduce centralized image processing and ensure that appropriate 
image assessment facilities are accommodated when and as required. 
(f) Inspection Areas for Cabin Baggage 
For the foreseeable future, it is likely that manual passenger bag searches will remain an alarm resolution 
method. As such, space must be allocated to accommodate these searches, including the passengers whose 
baggage is being searched, so as not to impede the normal passenger flow at the checkpoint. In addition, it is 
recommended that designs allow for the search to take place at a dedicated bench, rather than on the roller 
beds. The image below is provided as an example only, as there are various search bench layouts depending 
on the manufacturer and lane design used. However, it demonstrates the additional space requirement at the 
back of the lane to accommodate the search bench. 
It is recommended that diverter systems and reject lanes are used to isolate bags that require search from the 
passengers by moving them directly to the manual search area. Such systems and dedicated benches 
support improved overall throughput, but the space requirement needs to be accounted for early in the 
planning phase. 
(g) Passenger Screening Equipment 
As threats evolve, the type of passenger screening equipment used at airports is changing. Increasingly, 
States are mandating the use of passenger security scanners in conjunction with, or in place of, WTMD (walk￾through metal detectors). For planners, this is an important development, as traditional checkpoint design 
656 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 676===
ray 
Soa IATA pull Passenger Terminal 
models will no longer be applicable. From a spatial perspective alone, passenger security scanners take up 
more space than WTMDs and the alarm resolution processes may differ. It is critical that planners discuss 
current and future equipment plans with the airport during the design phase in order to avoid costly 
retrospective installation of new equipment and the associated realignment of screening lanes. 
(h) Manual Search Areas for Passengers 
Despite advances in technology, it is likely there will be ongoing need for manual passenger searches. 
However, given that manual passenger search is often one of the critical limiting factors to overall passenger 
screening throughput, it is recommend that planners allow for sufficient space to conduct multiple passenger 
searches in parallel in order for overall passenger throughput to benefit from advances in automated 
screening technology. 
Cultural and/or regulatory requirements may demand manual search areas for passengers to be conducted in 
an enclosed area, requiring additional space either in the normal passenger screening flow route or 
separately in adjacent areas. Planners should investigate the use of temporary or “pop up” solutions, which 
support efficient use of space and improved passenger experience. 
Passenger privacy should be considered in the context of both passenger and bag searches. Therefore, a 
dedicated room for more private searches and follow-up resolution is usually required. Consideration should 
be given to the location of the search room, so that the passenger can be easily moved from the lane to the 
search room without impacting the screening status of the other passengers, or themselves, and allowing the 
screening authority to maintain positive control of the passenger and their divested items. In this regard, 
planners should understand the local regulatory requirements relating to screening areas. Dedicated facilities 
should be used, taking into account passenger privacy and comfort, during the process. Solutions that utilize 
a supervisor's office for private search should be avoided. 
(i) Additional Screening Equipment 
Depending on local regulatory requirements, additional measures may be required within the checkpoint. This 
may include screening via: 
e Dedicated shoe-screening technologies 
e Explosive Trace Detection (ETD) 
e Hand-Held Metal Detectors 
e Explosive Detection Dogs (EDD) 
e Liquid Explosive Detection Systems 
While individual equipment pieces may not be space intensive relative to primary passenger and cabin 
baggage screening equipment, the use protocol determines the quantity of equipment and its location at the 
checkpoint, which in turn impacts design and space requirements. It is important that planners take these 
protocols into account during the preliminary planning process. In relation to EDD, planners should also factor 
in handling facilities and kennels. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 657 

===PAGE 677===
Se 
ae 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
(j) Composure/Reclaim 
Planners must take into account the space required for the composure/reclaim activity. As overall security 
lane design continues to facilitate higher overall passenger throughputs, space for composure/reclaim may 
need to be extended to accommodate the protracted repack process, which usually takes longer than the up￾front divest process. Failure to address the variation in process times (divest vs. compose) will lead to 
bottlenecks at the end of the process, which will in turn negatively impact overall passenger throughput. 
Space should be provided to allow passengers to repack their carry-on bags and replace their divested items 
out of the main flow of screening lane. This space should be visible and close enough to encourage use, but 
also sufficiently far away that it does not impact other flows within the checkpoint. 
Overall, the space provided to accommodate the passenger screening process should remain flexible in order 
to accommodate both growth and, as processes and technology are improved, contraction of the space 
needed to accommodate the passenger screening process. 
(k) Security Staff Facilities 
Planners will need to consider both the operational practicalities of any such areas as well as any security 
requirements depending on where the facilities are located. Requirement discussions should be held early in 
the design process with the authorities with jurisdiction over these areas. Collaboration should address the 
need for break rooms, general accommodation, and special secure areas, and take into account local and 
national occupational health requirements. 
3.3.5.5.4 Checkpoint Design—Dimensions 
Lane configurations will vary considerably depending on the type of screening equipment to be deployed, the 
type of divest and composure system, and whether single or dual roller beds are used. Overall lane 
dimensions are an amalgamation of all of these variables. As a result, this document does not provide 
minimum or maximum lane dimensions. 
When determining dimensions of the checkpoint, however, the following elements should be taken into 
consideration: 
(a) Length (Overall) 
The length of security lanes needs to be tailored to the individual airport's functional requirements as well as 
the available space in existing facilities. Lane length needs to take into consideration passenger divest, cabin 
baggage screening equipment, reclaim space and any search benches. As airports increasingly automate 
many functions within the checkpoint, they are installing lanes of between 14 and 25 m in length, where space 
permits. More traditional lanes of less than 14m in length are unlikely to allow for all the necessary elements 
above, while delivering the range of operational and passenger experience objectives set by airports. 
However, airports should always assess their local needs before determining their lane requirements.

===PAGE 678===
IATA * Passenger Terminal 
(b) Width (for passenger movement) 
In addition to variations in lane length, planners should be aware that there are many passenger screening 
combinations that an airport, security authority or regulator may require that may differ from the traditional 
deployment layouts. For example, as passenger security scanners are increasingly adopted, more space may 
be required between lanes (compared to when walk through metal detectors are used in isolation). Planners 
should discuss the passenger screening requirements with the relevant airport authority and agency 
representatives, and base their calculations on the manufacturers’ spatial and installation instructions as well 
as on any regulatory building requirements. Particular attention needs to be paid to the space required to 
access equipment for cleaning and maintenance. 
More generally, as noted previously, threat levels and available technologies can change, as can passenger 
volumes. Therefore, security checkpoints should always be planned to allow for future adjustments, both in 
width and depth. Such flexibility can cater to potential increases in the size of screening equipment, increased 
screening requirements or updated technology that can impact screening processes. 
3.3.5.5.5 Checkpoint Design—Look and Feel 
While screening facilities have regulatory and functional requirements, they should also aim to keep the 
passenger and security staff as comfortable and relaxed as possible. Consideration should be given to the 
ambiance of passenger checkpoints. Cleanliness, noise and heat reduction, lighting and creation of a sense 
of space should all be included in checkpoint planning. 
While passenger information is important and contributes to the overall efficiency of the checkpoint, care 
should be taken not to overcrowd the area with signage or provide information not relevant to the passenger. 
In this regard, airports may want to consider dynamic signage that can be adapted to the time of day or to the 
changing passenger mix. Signage requirements should be discussed during the initial and detailed design 
processes as the resulting electrical and spatial considerations will need to be addressed.

The checkpoint must also be designed to be a practical working environment. Screening staff duties are 
largely repetitive and requiring constant alertness and concentration. Due consideration should be given to 
temperature, humidity, and lighting elements (i.e., avoiding glare). 
3.3.5.5.6 Technical Considerations 
(a) General 
In the selection of suitable locations for passenger security checkpoints at which WTMDs, security scanners, 
X-ray machines, and other advanced detection equipment are to be used, it is essential that sufficient reliable 
Power outlets be provided. It is also necessary to consider environmental factors that may have adverse 
effects on equipment performance. For example, some equipment can be susceptible to vibrations. 
Consideration should also be given to the space between machines for maintenance purposes. 
As noted above, flexibility should be built into checkpoints to cater to equipment and capacity changes. This 
flexibility can be addressed by: 
e Providing subfloor electrical capacity (e.g., raised computer flooring) to accommodate additional or 
relocated equipment. Similarly, mechanical systems need to be designed to accommodate flexibility

* Proactively addressing floor loading requirements, as more advanced detection equipment may require a 
greater floor loading than conventional screening equipment 
Planning should also take into consideration protection of the digital network access points that could be

(b) CCTV 
There are a number of reasons for using CCTV in screening areas, including but not limited to: 
¢ Quality control of the screening point process 
¢ General airport security procedures 
e Customer service monitoring 
e Emergency response 
e Criminality control 
CCTV requirements should be ascertained early in the design process to ensure appropriate facilities are in 
place to support CCTV implementation. 
3.3.5.5.7 Considerations for Facility Sizing 
Regulations, processes and procedures may vary greatly between jurisdictions. As a result, 
planners/designers need to understand the local security/passenger screening context in order to provide the 
most appropriate facilities. Authorities with jurisdiction should be encouraged to investigate new and improved 
technologies and processes as screening areas are redeveloped. 
Designers will also need to understand the impact of the juxtaposition of other passenger processing 
elements. For example, if departure emigration control is present and is located before the security 
checkpoint, the passenger presentation profile will be impacted by the throughput of the control. In such 
cases, domestic passengers will be processed in a separate checkpoint and demand on each traffic segment 
should also reflect that split. 
If regulations do not specify the location of the checkpoint relative to emigration, throughput modelling should 
be conducted to ascertain the appropriate location to minimize congestion created by throughput mismatch 
between the two processes. 
Important Note: See 3.3.4.9 Demand-Capacity Assessment for a detailed explanation of the methodology 
used and the steps to be undertaken. 
Calculations detailed in the following section should take into account the local conditions and considerations 
as well as technology applications (e.g., screening equipment types, passenger mix, seasonal load factors, 
local threats, cultural constraints).
