IATA * Passenger Terminal 
Where customs or security regulations stipulate transfer baggage be reconciled with passengers before being 
permitted onto the next flight, service desks can be provided in the direct vicinity of the customs exit. 
Passengers can recheck their baggage at the earliest opportunity without having to go to the departures hall. 
3.3.8 Baggage Handling Systems 
Baggage handling is an important consideration of airport terminal design planning. The quick and efficient 
movement of baggage to and from aircraft is critical for maximizing airport capacity and maintaining expected 
levels of service. A baggage handling system (BHS) consists of a sequence of processes to transport 
passenger luggage from departure check-in to arrivals reclaim. In between, the bags may undergo many 
steps including security screening, sortation, loading, transfer processing, and unloading. 
The layout of the baggage system is influenced by the type of airport and such factors as: 
e The location and size of the airport including the number of terminals 
e¢ The number and mix of passengers (e.g., domestic, international, origin and destination, transfer, etc.) 
e The type and business models of airlines (low-cost carriers, network carriers) 
e The chosen operating model for how to process bags 
3.3.8.1 Introduction 
The purpose of this chapter is to provide an overview of the principal aspects of the typical BHS and enable a 
better understanding of what needs to be considered in their design and specification. It does not seek to 
mandate particular technologies or suppliers. 
BHS are a critical part of passenger terminal infrastructure as they can be expensive to build, maintain and 
operate. The BHS has a bigger impact on the design and spatial planning of a passenger terminal than other 
processing systems and can therefore be difficult to retrofit into existing passenger terminal designs. Baggage 
handling processes and equipment require significant space, typically at least 25% of a terminal's gross floor 
area, and can be a major component of the overall capital costs of the terminal. 
For new terminals, the BHS needs to be considered early in the design process and should be aligned with 
the terminal's planning assumptions, including its traffic characteristics. As the processing of passengers and 
baggage are fully interdependent, any constraints in the baggage system, can limit a terminal's overall 
passenger capacity. 
Baggage handling quality, a critical issue for customer satisfaction, is mainly measured as a number or ratio 
of mishandled bags. There has been a steady improvement in performance in recent years. From 2007 to 
2019 the total numbers of mishandled bags fell by 45.8% from 46.9 million to 24.4 million (SITA, /T Baggage 
Insights, 2020). This progress reflects the greater use of automation and smart technology in baggage 
handling. Reducing mishandling has become an industry priority and the tracking of bags at key points in the 
journey (acceptance, loading, transfer, and arrival) is now an airline industry standard (IATA Reso 753). 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 707 

===PAGE 727===
cael Se 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
The introduction of large, integrated baggage systems can offer efficient handling of high volumes of bags, but 
system outages, whether caused by mechanical failures, IT issues or other factors, can have major 
repercussions. This may not only affect the baggage product but also, in some severe cases, it can lead to 
the cancellation of flights and highly visible disruption to passengers. 
Baggage handling is the responsibility of an airline or their appointed handler, albeit using infrastructure and 
equipment that is often provided and operated by an airport. If passengers experience problems or delays 
with their baggage, both airports and airlines will incur extra costs including damage to their reputations. It is, 
therefore, in the interests of both airlines and airports to deploy resilient baggage systems and processes that 
can reliably deliver the expected level of performance. This chapter provides guidance on how this can be 
achieved.

check-in, make-up, and reclaim functions, only hub airports will have significant transfer-baggage facilities. 
In addition to the usual range of activities and processes associated with the departure, arrival and transfer 
flows, emerging forms of operation should be considered which may include an end-to-end process such as 
home or off-site check-in and delivery.

3.3.8.3. Outbound Baggage System 
The outbound baggage system includes check-in and bag drop, security screening, baggage sortation and 
baggage make-up and loading. The types of systems vary from manual to more automated systems such as 
Individual Carrier Systems (ICS) which may be entirely passive on a track, or able to move independently in a 
designated space. The choice of system will depend upon the peak flow capacity required, the distance the 
bags need to travel, the desired level of service and the complexity of operations. Factors such as the cost 
and availability of a skilled workforce to operate and maintain the system should also need to be considered. 
3.3.8.4 Bag Drop 
The method of checking in bags has been changing as traditional check-in has been increasingly 
deconstructed to allow passengers to make use of the functions they require while bypassing others. Current 
check-in methods include: Web-based, Kiosk, Traditional, Curb-side and Off-site such as at an Air-Rail 
station. 
Hold baggage may enter the BHS via various types of bag drop including staffed bag drop counters, self￾service bag drops, and traditional check-in counters. Whatever options are used will depend upon the types of 
airlines and passengers that the airport serves and the outcomes it wants to achieve. 
The typical baggage drop consists of the following steps: 
¢ Confirming that the bag is acceptable (i.e., weight, size and condition) 
e Issuing a baggage tag that identifies the bag and the owner 
¢ Validating the passenger's travel itinerary and sending digital baggage messages so that the bag travels 
on the same itinerary 
e Accepting the bag from the passenger and sending it through the baggage system 
Upon acceptance, the bag tags of checked bags are activated and the information is fed into the departure 
control system (DCS) and is usually verified electronically through a Baggage Reconciliation System (BRS). 
Passengers selecting to use a self-service bag drop (SSBD) will be guided through document scanning and 
passenger questions, which will result in the SSBD printing a bag tag that the passenger must attach to the 
bag. In a one-stage process, the passenger will then press “go” and the bag will be conveyed into the BHS. 
In a two-stage SSBD process, the passenger will carry out the identification, bag tag printing and application 
at a kiosk and then approach the bag deposit location for baggage acceptance. 
At a manned check-in desk, the bags will be weighed and checked for length (ensuring the bag is not to be 
treated as Out-of-Gauge). If a bag is overweight, check-in staff will attach a tag that informs baggage handling 
staff that the bag weight is above the regular weight limit and ensure proper baggage handling. If the bag is 
inside the baggage allowance a bag tag is printed and attached to the bag. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 709 

===PAGE 729===
Be IATA pull Airport Development Reference Manual 
The time required for each of these processes is different and will vary according to regulatory and process 
requirements, the degree of airline assistance to resolve problems and whether or not such exceptions as 
payment for excess baggage are handled at the bag acceptance location. 
3.3.8.4.1 Bulk Inputs 
In some cases, bags are checked-in at a location other than the departure terminal. The off-airport 
acceptance of bags can reduce the number of touchpoints required at the airport and can therefore influence 
the size and scope of the terminal. This could be, for example, at a downtown location, a cruise terminal, a 
remote car park location, or via a bag collection service from another location such as home or office. 
These types of bags may either be security screened at the point of collection and transported, in a secure 
manner to the departure terminal or may be delivered to the departure terminal where they undergo hold 
baggage screening prior to joining the local baggage flow to bag stores, make-up positions, etc. 
3.3.8.4.2 Out of Gauge Baggage 
The volume of out-of-gauge (OOG) or oversized baggage can be a substantial at some airports. There are 
usually dedicated desks for the acceptance of articles (e.g., bikes, surfboards, golf clubs) that are too large for 
the baggage acceptance induction belt. 
Once checked-in, these items must be transported via alternate means, such as manually or via a dedicated 
oversized system to security screening and outbound make-up. Oversize items are typically screened 
manually using ETD equipment for primary screening. 
3.3.8.5 Manual Coding Station and Bag Traceability 
Baggage traceability is a key function in the baggage system, as it identifies where a passenger bag is at any 
given time. Scanners are installed at vital points in the baggage system to enable continuous tracking most 
commonly at check-in, early bag storage, loading, transfer, and arrival. 
The majority of baggage systems today support bag tracking through the use of bar code scanners, otherwise 
known as Automatic Tag Readers (ATR). Technologies like RFID or video identification can also be used. 
Sometimes bags are not able to be identified usually because either the baggage source message was not 
received by the system or the bag tag itself cannot be read because it is missing, damaged, or obstructed. In 
these cases, the bag will be moved to the Manual Coding Station (MCS) where the bag will be manually 
handled and scanned. 
New operations rely on cameras installed in the MCS area. The images are sent to an external operator with 
access to the baggage control system. The operator can use PTZ functionality and identify the bag (based on 
small images of the bag tag). The operator can then update the baggage control system so the bag can be 
routed to its correct destination. 
710 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 730===
he IATA + Passenger Terminal 
The Problem Bag Area (PBA), an extended version of the MCS, is where the tools available to the operator 
are more advanced and reach further into other systems where bag information can be retrieved. 
3.3.8.6 Hold Baggage Screening 
It is a mandatory requirement that all bags be security screened prior to loading into the aircraft hold. The 
ICAO, in Annex 17 ‘Safeguarding International Civil Aviation Against Acts of Unlawful Interference’, sets out 
security standards and recommendations. The implementation of these measures is defined by national 
governments or other responsible bodies some of which publish detailed planning guidelines, such as the US 
Transportation Security Administration's Planning Guidelines and Design Standards for Checked Baggage 
Inspection Systems. 
Itis important that the relevant requirements for hold baggage screening be clearly defined and understood. 
There may be additional requirements imposed from time-to-time, based on the security assessments of 
national governments. In some cases, where a One-Stop Security (OSS) arrangement between two states is 
in place, the flow of transfer passengers and bags can be expedited by eliminating the unnecessary 
duplication of security controls at the transfer airport. These bags can be fed directly into the sortation system. 
3.3.8.6.1 Hold Baggage Screening Technology 
Two basic methods are used to detect explosives in hold baggage: EDS, which use X-ray technology to 
create images of the contents of bags, and ETD, which uses such techniques as lon Mobility Spectrometry to 
capture and analyze the microscopic particles and vapors naturally emitted by organic substances. 
Developments in EDS technology have led to successive generations of equipment described as Standards 1, 
2 and 3. Although a simplification, the differences between the standards are as follows: 
e Standard 1-EDS equipment provides a view of the contents of a bag from a single angle 
e Standard 2-provides views from multiple angles 
e Standard 3-the latest, uses computed tomography x-ray to provide high resolution 3-D views of the 
contents of the bag 
The latest Hold Baggage Screening (HBS) systems are more capable and able to reduce the rate of rejected 
bags, but they are also larger and heavier than previous generations. The space and infrastructure required 
for these new units needs to be planned carefully with sufficient space around the screening equipment set 
aside to support maintenance and repair. In addition, their installation often requires structural enabling works 
and an upgraded power supply.

3.3.8.6.2 Baggage Screening Process 
Different levels of security are needed, depending on individual national requirements and agreements with 
other countries. Typically, these levels are: 
¢ Level 1: EDS screening is performed by a HBS machine. If the bag is cleared at this level, it is sent for 
sortation. 
¢ Level 2: Secondary EDS-a security agent inspects the image in a process called on-screen resolution 
(OCR). If the bag is cleared, it is sent for sortation. 
¢ Level 3: A more thorough screening (Level 3 HBS) or explosive swab testing (ETD) of the bag is 
performed. If the bag is cleared, it is sent for sortation. 
* Level 4: The bag is opened and inspected by a security agent-the passenger is usually called to assist 
the inspection. In the US, the TSA (Transport Security Administration) has the authority to search the bag 
without the passenger being present. This is performed in a secure area, where video cameras overlook 
the operation. In the US, a sticker is placed on the bag tag to notify that it has been inspected, or a 
disclaimer is placed inside the bag. In both cases, if the bag is cleared, it is sent for sortation. 
e Level 5: The bag is destroyed. 
3.3.8.6.3 Typical Baggage Screen Process Layouts 
There are four commonly used layouts for the HBS process each of which has its own throughput rates, 
benefits, and costs: 
¢ Centralized, in-line EDS screening 
* Decentralized, in-line EDS screening 
712 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 732===
=e A 7 TATA pris Passenger Terminal 
e Standalone EDS screening 
e Standalone ETD screening 
Centralized in-line EDS systems are generally used for large baggage throughputs where multiple EDS 
machines (each capable of 800-1,000 bags per hour) are required to meet demands. Bags will be routed from 
multiple inputs (e.g., banks of check-in desks and/or transfer inputs) to make use of one or more pools of 
shared EDS machines. This allows individually varying baggage loads from each input to be load-shared 
across the pool of EDS machines. In the same way, images from the machines for Level 2 decisions can be 
shared across a pool of security staff who will usually be accommodated in a dedicated room. With this 
system, providing redundant capacity to cope with a machine failure is more economically achieved-one 
spare machine being capable of providing cover for as many as five other machines. However, such 
arrangements involve the most extensive conveyor systems, both to route bags to and from the screening 
machines as well as to provide buffering and load-balancing capabilities. 
Decentralized in-line EDS systems can be used for moderate baggage throughputs. In contrast to the 
centralized arrangement, the decentralized configuration requires simpler conveyor connections and routing 
(fewer inputs and outputs) and, subject to the building layout, can lead to shorter in-system times because of 
more direct routings. Like the centralized arrangement, Level 2 decisions can be shared across a pool of 
security staff. However, given the need for physical access to bags to carry out ETD screening, staff dealing 
with the Level 3 process will be distributed to support each zone. This means that utilization of staff 
performing this function will be lower than seen in a centralized arrangement and, most likely, these staff 
would also deal with Level 2 OSR. Providing redundant capacity to cope with a machine failure will also be 
more expensive. For instance, if the demand for a zone is only 500 bags per hour (requiring a single EDS 
machine), a second, redundant machine would double the installed capacity. 
For situations with low baggage throughput demands (up to 200 bags per hour), a standalone EDS unit may 
be the most appropriate. No conveyor infrastructure is required beyond that of the machine itself. Screening 
staff will be deployed locally, so the machine and staff utilization will not be high. Consideration should be 
given to operations in the event of a machine failure. This might involve using another standalone machine at 
an adjacent location, perhaps requiring bags to be carried to the alternative machine. 
Standalone ETD screening (as distinct from the Level 3 process) can be used as the primary means to 
screen outsized bags and other items that cannot be screened using EDS. It may also be used at airports 
with very low baggage throughput demands (up to 70 bags per hour) that cannot justify an EDS machine. The 
equipment is standalone and, therefore, can be deployed easily, but the screening process is labor-intensive. 
3.3.8.7 Early Bag Storage (EBS) 
Early baggage arrives at airports from multiple sources. Typically, early baggage processing is most 
commonly found in airports with large volumes of transfer flights. The dilemma for airlines and airports is how 
and where to systematically store baggage which has arrived well in advance of the usual two- or three-hour 
window prior to flight departure time. When bags are checked in early they not only occupy space but are 
entrusted to the airport and airline in question for safekeeping. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 713 

===PAGE 733===
IATA Biull Airport Development Reference Manual 
At airports with primarily departing traffic, bags pass through the system and reach makeup positions where 
they are either temporarily buffered or loaded into ULDs or trailers. A separate bag store is usually not 
necessary. However, if the volume of early bags reaches a significant level (e.g., early check-in products) or 
there is enough transfer traffic, an early bag storage will often be needed not only to store the bags, but to 
manage and buffer the flow of bags to make-up positions. It is therefore important to agree with stakeholders 
and document the categories of bags and uses for which a bag store is designed. 
An important use of EBS is that it can help smooth out the flow of bags through the entire system which 
improves utilization and reduces bottlenecks by releasing bags at a steady rate that optimizes the utilization of 
sortation capacity. It also enables the use of compressed build which is where bags are held back in storage 
and then sent to the make-up at a set time prior to flight departure. This can optimize the make-up area by 
trimming down the number of required make-up positions as the amount of time that a position is occupied for 
a specific flight is reduced. Theoretically labor savings can also be achieved with compressed build as shift 
patterns can potentially optimized. 
In normal circumstances, the number of bags in a store will ebb and flow according to flight schedules within 
‘normal limits, although contingency planning should include spare capacity to absorb exceptional demands 
that may come from disruptions (e.g., cancelled or delayed flights, system outages, etc.). When designing the 
bag store, the “time to empty the bag store” and how to retrieve bags in times of disruption must be kept in 
mind. 
Bag stores can also be used for missed or problem bags. Rather than sending the bags to a re-flight station, 
the bag itself can be kept in a bag store and the baggage message associated with the bag can be updated 
remotely. The bag remains in the store until such time as the new flight is open for makeup, at which point the 
bag leaves the store. 
3.3.8.8 Early Bag Store Types and Considerations 
Early bag stores are a dedicated area which can take one of several forms. The type of store required 
depends on the peak number of bags that need to be stored at any one time as well as the expected baggage 
input and output rates. The following ‘rough guidelines’ give an indication of what type of bag store may be 
most appropriate: 
* Ad hoc storage within the bag hall footprint-less than 10 bags per hour 
° Dedicated manual store with simple transport to/from store-small to moderate amount of bags 
* Fully automated store with high-capacity input/output links—moderate to large volume of bags 
¢ Multiple fully automated stores—Very large volume of bags 
Bag store capacity is typically defined as the number of bags that can be stored, and there should be a buffer 
factored in to deal with operational situations and the fact that in many systems, performance degrades as the 
store reaches capacity. Equally important is the ability to get bags into and out of the store, therefore 
modelling should be conducted to ensure sufficient input/output capability, particularly for compressed and 
batch make-up operations that can generate surges of bag movements. 
714 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 734===
IATA Passenger Terminal 
Another consideration is the location of the bag store within the baggage system, in relation to where bags 
originate and where bags need to go. In the case of a simple conventional operation, the location is less 
critical. But, for compressed makeup, and certainly for batch makeup, latency (i.e., the time between 
requesting a batch and that batch being delivered) becomes an important design consideration. 
3.3.8.8.1 Manual Bag Store 
A manual store is the simplest type. This can involve not much more than lines painted on the floor or racks to 
accommodate the bags. Bags are grouped by departure time or flight and there may be a simple conveyor 
link to move bags to and from the space. The store is manually operated but can be equipped with scanners 
that can register when bags have entered or left the bag store. 
Exhibit 3.3.8.8.1: Manual Bag Store 
Source: IATA 
3.3.8.8.2. Automated Bag Store Types 
For higher volumes of bags, automated stores with integrated storage facilities are used. Bags inside the EBS 
can be either automatically sent to makeup or can be “called for’. When bags are picked automatically, it 
means that, when the flight opens for makeup, the control system will automatically ask the bag store to pick 
all bags for that flight and send them to makeup where they are loaded into a cart or ULD. Alternatively, in 
batch make-up, when the system shows enough bags are available in the bag store to fill a ULD, the bags are 
“called” or released from the bag store and sent to makeup. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 715 

===PAGE 735===
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
The designs of automated bag stores are continuously being improved in terms of resilience, space 
requirements, throughput, and maintainability. Some common types of automated stores include: 
(a) Lane-based Bag Store 
A lane-based bag store is composed of simple conveyor lines; each line stores bags for a specific flight until 
the bags are called for makeup. A lane-based system can provide simple and relatively compact storage, but 
it requires additional recirculation routes if it is to support access to individual bags (as distinct from a lane of 
bags). If a passenger's destination is changed, the bag must be moved to another location in the baggage 
system and all bags in the lane will need to be rotated to get that one bag out. 
Exhibit 3.3.8.8.2a: Lane-based Bag Store 
Source: London Heathrow 
(b) Rack-based Bag Store 
In a rack-based system, cranes move between the aisles and up and down the racks to place and retrieve 
any bag. Advantages including better resiliency and the ability to do sortation. Crane-based storage can store 
bags for one flight across a number of aisles, which enables the bags to be selected for the same ULD at the 
same time and delivered to the flight more quickly. If a passenger changes flight to a different destination, the 
bag system can simply assign the bag tag bar code to a different location.

an 
IATA * Passenger Terminal 
Exhibit 3.3.8.8.2b: Rack-based Bag Store 
Source: ARUP 
3.3.8.9 Baggage Sortation 
Once originating and transfer baggage has been cleared by security and/or retrieved from early bag storage, 
it is sent via the BHS to the make-up or build area for preparation and delivery to the appropriate departing 
flight. The system should provide the capability to sort bags by several criteria including airline, flight number, 
and destination. Sortation is usually assisted with automated technologies such as bar-code reading, and 
RFID but may be performed manually in the case of very small operations. 
The departure baggage sorting system should be planned on a flow basis with each element of the system 
being capable of handling the peak number of bags. The variables to be considered include the number of 
departing and transferring passengers, passenger flow rates and the baggage ratio per passenger. 
For low-capacity applications, simple conveyors and diverters may be used. For higher volumes, 
semi-automatic or fully automatic storing equipment, vertical sorting and merge units should be considered 
because these can switch sufficiently quickly to allow adjacent bags to be sorted to different locations. For yet 
higher capacities, tilt-tray sorters can be used. An alternative approach that reduces the risk of bag jams is to 
use an ICS which uses individual totes or carts to carry individual bags rather than a conveyor. These 
systems allow for higher speeds and makes baggage tracking and storage easier. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 717 

===PAGE 737===
ata lil Airport Development Reference Manual 
Sorters are installed at key decision points, such as whether the bag should go to make-up or EBS. Some 
common sorters include: 
e Vertical sorter unit (VSU) 
e Horizontal sorter unit (HSU), such as plows and pushers 
e Loop sorters (tilt tray, cross belt) 
e Automated Guided Vehicles (AGV) 
Vertical-sorter devices are used to separate or combine baggage flows, though the latter function is a less 
common. Baggage can be dynamically separated such that two bags travelling in succession can be 
separated to different destinations. Two bags can also be merged into a single output route. Vertical-sorter 
conveyors are useful where vertical space is more available than lateral space. 
Exhibit 3.3.8.9a: Vertical-Sorter Unit 
Source: IATA 
Horizontal sorter units such as plows and pushers are used to divert baggage horizontally into one of two 
directions. 
Exhibit 3.3.8.9b: Baggage Pushers and Plows 
Source: IATA

Tilt tray sorters are based on trays into which the bags are loaded and, when the sorter passes the chute 
where the bag must be offloaded, the tray tilts and the bag slides into the chute. 
Exhibit 3.3.8.9c: Tilt Tray Sorter 
Source: Beumer Group 
An ICS does not transport bags loose on a conveyor but instead transports each bag on a dedicated carrier or 
tote. These carriers may be entirely passive—essentially a tray transported by a conveyor-—or active with active 
controls and motive power. The active types can be either constrained or free ranging. The former are limited 
to following a set of routes pre-defined either by a track or by another guidance system (e.g., buried cables). 
Free-ranging carriers are able to move, in principle, anywhere within a given space, as they do not rely on any 
physical guidance infrastructure that defines a route, relying instead on sensors to navigate. 
All !CS share common characteristics that are relevant to planning: the need to ensure an adequate supply of 
empty carriers at points where bags are loaded into carriers to meet baggage appearance demands, and the 
need to redistribute empty carriers as bags are taken off. Consideration must also be given to where carriers 
are stored when the baggage system is powered down, and where carrier maintenance is performed. In the 
case of free-ranging carriers, an additional factor becomes relevant: where and how they are recharged. 
The primary benefits of using carriers include better tracking, improved handling, and higher speeds over long 
distances which is particularly useful at large airports. An added benefit is that, unlike a conventional BHS that 
uses continuous conveyor belts, an ICS splits the BHS into segments each with its own motor. This means 
that if only one baggage item is being carried by the BHS, instead of the entire conveyor belt having to move 
all the time to circulate that one object, only the individual segments move as and when the baggage item 
reaches them. Therefore, the systems are more environmentally efficient as there is no wasted energy from 
anything moving that does not need to move. The modular construction of ICS systems also make them more 
flexible as carts and tracks can be added as required.

===PAGE 739===

IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
Exhibit 3.3.8.9d: Individual Carrier System 
Source: Beumer Group 
3.3.8.10 Baggage Make-Up 
Departing bags are delivered via a system of carousels, chutes, or laterals to baggage make-up positions 
where they are loaded into baggage carts or unit load devices for delivery to the apron and loading onto 
aircraft. The number of make-up positions allocated per flight will depend on the expected volume of baggage, 
the flight-build time and the number of segregations into which bags must be sorted. This can vary from one 
or two positions for small aircraft to ten or more for larger aircraft with complex terminating and transfer 
products. 
The baggage make-up room requires parking positions for empty and filled containers, dollies and/or carts 
with sufficient height for easy maneuvering of vehicles. Properly sized multiple lanes are required to enable 
easy traffic movement and maintain a safe and efficient operation, including easy access to and from the 
apron. 
The overall efficiency of the baggage make-up area will be affected by how the facility is operated and 
utilized. Common use facilities that are shared by multiple airlines and ground handlers and used by flight are 
much more efficiently utilized than make-up areas that are dedicated to specific users. 
Baggage system interfaces with staff in the baggage hall should be ergonomically designed. Baggage off-load 
levels within the baggage halls should be designed to be ergonomically suited to the local workforce and 
should adopt best international working practices, such that the risk of off-loading injuries should be 
minimized.

There are several types and configurations of manual make-up devices each of which has different 
advantages and drawbacks: 
e Chutes: Can be arranged space efficiently and to ensure a one-to-one mapping between the chute and 
ULD and/or trailer. 
e Carousels: Offer a flexible means of distributing bags to a high density of makeup positions per square 
meter but require manual sortation before loading. 
e Laterals: Can be set at an optimal height and are compatible with modern handling aids.

The number of makeup positions allocated to a particular flight is generally a function of the number of distinct 
segregations into which bags are sorted and the expected baggage load for the flight. Segregations might 
include some or all the following types of bags: 
e Premium terminating 
e Economy terminating 
° Crew bags 
¢ Short-connect transfers (scheduled connection times > 2 hours) 
e Long-connect transfers (scheduled connection times < 2 hours) 
¢ — Inter-terminal transfers (by departure terminal) 
e Onward transfers (by transfer destination) 
In principle, bags from the same category should be loaded in the same cart and placed in the same hold 
area in the aircraft. Loading bags according to these types of segregation assists the speed and ease of 
handling at downstream stations, but the filling efficiency of ULDs generally will be poorer because some 
ULDs will only be partially filled. 
For a build area to work successfully, there needs to be good communication throughout the build process 
including notification from check-in when bags are starting to be delivered and once the last bag has been 
received for each flight. There should be a ground handler sweeper in the build area available to help during 
very busy periods. Bags that arrive at the build area after the build has closed, but before the flight departs, 
should be taken directly to the aircraft. Once the build has closed and the flight has departed, any left-behind 
bags must be re-flighted for a subsequent flight. 
3.3.8.10.1 Compressed Makeup 
The rate at which bags are checked-in for a flight varies over time; typically starting at a low rate, reaching a 
maximum, and then tailing off as the check-in close time approaches. This profile means that the work rate at 
makeup locations is also variable, which in turn means that makeup positions and staff are not always being 
fully utilized. To address this, compressed build concepts have been developed whereby bags are stored at 
times of low demand and then released later for makeup.

===PAGE 744===

The effect is to reduce the time that makeup positions (and staff) must be allocated to a flight, thereby 
increasing their utilization. This comes at the price of having to provide an automated bag store. In the 
example shown in the exhibit above, the conventional makeup opening is around 240 minutes before the 
scheduled departure time, while the revised makeup opening is only 135 minutes before the scheduled 
departure time. Of course, there is an increased requirement for early bag storage. In the example, at peak, 
around 15% of the bags for the flight have to be stored. However, a consequence is that compressed makeup 
delays the time at which bags are loaded into ULDs or carts, which means the impact of a system outage can 
become important: bags are left within the system rather than having already been packed into ULDs or 
trailers. 
The degree of compression needs to be examined critically. A modest amount of compression can yield 
savings in the space required for makeup positions without creating a demand for a very large early bag 
store. However, the actual trade-off between makeup positions and early bag storage depends on the bag 
appearance profile. With typical appearance profiles, it will be found that increasing levels of compression 
yield only modest reductions in makeup requirements while generating rapidly increasing bag storage 
demands. 
The overall benefit of adopting compressed makeup (whether the reduction in staff numbers or savings in 
equipment and space) depends critically on the profile of the departing flight schedule. Generally, the flatter 
the profile the more likely that staff and equipment savings can be realized. In contrast, a peaky schedule will 
create peak demands for makeup positions and staff that cannot be ameliorated through compressed 
makeup. Note too that employment shift patterns may mean that, even with compressed build, theoretical 
manpower savings cannot actually be realized.

===PAGE 745===
lil Se IATA } Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.3.8.10.2 Batch Makeup 
While compressed makeup represents a refinement of conventional makeup, batch makeup (in its purest 
form) is materially different in that resources (i.e., makeup positions and staff) are allocated to a batch of bags 
for a particular ULD or trailer, rather than to a whole flight. 
At its simplest, bags for a given flight (and a specific segregation) are routed to a bag store until such time as 
a whole ULD's or trailer's worth have accumulated, at which point the batch is released from the store and 
sent to a makeup position for loading into ULDs or trailers. The makeup position is allocated for this batch of 
bags and then released for subsequent batches, which need not be for the same flight and/or segregation. 
While batch makeup can be implemented with conventional makeup presentation devices, there are 
advantages in using partially and fully automated methods, specifically: improved manual handling and/or 
higher work rates. 
3.3.8.11 Unit Load Devices 
A baggage facility for a single airline is much simpler as there will be common pools of ULDs and trailers, and 
handlers at the makeup positions can make up bags for any flight. However, where there are multiple airlines 
and handlers in a single facility, the benefits will be harder to realize. In such circumstances, consideration 
should be given to a common handler to provide all ULD or trailer logistics and flight makeup for all flights. 
Each ULD has its own unique bar code, which is scanned at the start of loading with bags. Every bag that is 
loaded into that ULD will be bound to that ULD. This enables airlines to trace the bags and, when a bag 
needs to be offloaded prior to departure (i.e., passenger is not flying), the search for the bag can be narrowed 
down to the ULD. Hand-held RFID scanners can be used to identify where in the ULD a bag is located. Some 
airlines are separating baggage into ULDs based on different categories such as: 
e First and business class 
e Economy class 
e Direct or transfer bags 
3.3.8.12 Inbound Baggage System 
Once an aircraft has arrived at its stand, loose baggage or containers are unloaded and transported to the 
offload area of the inbound BHS. Usually, mail, light cargo, terminating and transfer bags are segregated in 
the aircraft hold to ease the handling process at the arrival airport. 
Baggage is taken to an off-load point for either transfer or arrival baggage where it will be off-loaded from 
containers and carts, scanned and then either put into the transfer process or onto inbound conveyors to 
baggage reclaim. 
726 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 746===
pay 
Se a 
IATA Passenger Terminal 
3.3.8.12.1 Offload Points 
Off-load points expedite the flow of arrival baggage and can be centralized or decentralized. Transfer input 
points provide a means of loading transfer bags back into the departure bag system for subsequent 
processing and sortation. Baggage conveyors or platforms should be installed at a comfortable height to 
facilitate unloading. 
For larger airports, mid-field input points can speed up the movement of bags and reduce the amount of 
vehicle traffic on the apron. If there are multiple input points a system should be in place to give ground 
handlers and indication of how busy each input area is so demand can be balanced during peak periods. 
Off-loaded final-destination bags are taken to a baggage breakdown area and then routed to the baggage 
reclaim system. Delivering baggage to the reclaim area at a rate that matches the passenger flow rate is an 
important element of the airport baggage operation so it is important to keep in mind that delays in arrivals 
baggage handling often occur at the offload point. For larger airports a sortation system for arrival bags may 
need to be considered. 
Access from the apron to the baggage delivery point should be unimpeded and the baggage breakdown area 
should provide space for off-loading baggage from containers or carts. This includes a passing lane for 
bypassing parked containers, space for maneuvering, and easy access to and from the baggage off-loading 
points. 
3.3.8.12.2 Hold Baggage Screening (Customs) 
Arriving international passengers are typically required to pass through customs control facilities and customs 
inspection of all bags may be performed. Regulatory requirements should be consulted. 
In-line embedded customs inspection machines may be installed between the off-load point and baggage 
reclaim. Bags which are suspected of containing illegal items may be invisibly marked, allowing the bag and 
passenger to be identified at the customs control facilities at the exit of the baggage reclaim hall. 
3.3.8.12.3 Baggage Reclaim 
As well as a means of presenting bags for collection, reclaim devices connect the inbound passenger process 
and the inbound baggage process. A reclaim device is usually allocated to a flight for a period of time that 
runs from the delivery of the first bag through to the appearance of the last passenger or bag. The most 
common baggage reclaim device is a carousel, of which there are two primary variants: 
« Flatbed carousels: easier for passengers to pick-up 
e Inclined carousels: can accommodate more bags per unit length 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 727 

===PAGE 747===
v& IATA i Airport Development Reference Manual 
Exhibit 3.3.8.12.3: Flat and Inclined Carousel Reclaim 
Source: ARUP 
Bags can be loaded directly onto the reclaim device or fed indirectly via one or more conveyor routes. 
Directly-fed reclaims are the most space-efficient arrangement and are typically (though not always) used with 
flat carousels rather than inclined. Indirectly fed systems allow reclaims and their in-feed lines to be more 
flexibly placed than is possible with a directly fed reclaim. Dual indirect feeds for baggage reclaim carousels 
should be considered to provide redundancy and limit the risk of bottlenecks from bag jams. 
Depending upon anticipated traffic volumes, at international airports, a claim presentation length of 60-70m 
should be provided for wide body aircraft and 30-40m for narrow body aircraft. The clear distance between 
adjacent claim devices for passenger claiming and circulation should be not less than 9m. 
The process of determining how many reclaims are required for a given scenario is similar to that of planning 
makeup positions: essentially determining allocation times and relevant constraints (e.g., long-haul flights on 
larger reclaims) and then creating a form of Gantt chart from which the peak number of reclaims (by type and 
location, as necessary) can be determined. Ideally, the passenger and bag journeys from aircraft to reclaim 
should be planned and coordinated at the same time. This will allow a more robust understanding of the 
reclaim allocations times to be designed for. 
728 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 748===
Se ea | | IATA al Passenger Terminal 
There should also be a means to transport oversized baggage to the reclaim baggage hall and a clearly 
marked space for customers to retrieve it. 
To ensure that passengers can easily locate the baggage claim unit for their flight, adequate information must 
be prominently displayed. The information system must also serve the airside unloading area to indicate to 
baggage unloaders which devices are assigned to a particular flight. 
Provision should also be made within the baggage claim area for the staging of self-service baggage trolleys 
for use by passengers and for other facilities such as space to buffer bags and secured storage for unclaimed 
bags. 
3.3.8.13 Transfers 
Arriving transfer bags are usually inserted, via dedicated transfers offloads, into the main departures security 
screening system, and then onwards to possibly be stored or sent to main sortation and make-up for loading 
onto an outbound container/cart. 
Large airports may be expected to have multiple transfer inputs, the number of which are determined by the 
demand and location. If distributed transfer inputs are planned (e.g., some in the main terminal, others in a 
satellite building), the geographical diversity of the inputs must be considered—an available input in one 
location may be too far away to drive to or its availability may not be known to the driver of a tug and dolly 
train. 
Multiple transfer inputs should result in shorter driving times between aircraft and system input. This can bring 
benefits in terms of handler and ramp equipment utilization and shorter end-to-end baggage processing times, 
which help support lower minimum connection times. This points to the importance of considering the 
proximity of transfer inputs to aircraft stands and the possible need for indicators, signaling and/or in-cab 
resource management systems to allow drivers to best use the installed infrastructure. 
Once delivered to the transfer input area, international transfer bags must undergo security screening unless 
the bags are coming from a state with which a one-stop security (OSS) arrangement is in place. This should 
be done as soon as possible and a dedicated HBS processing should be considered by airports that have 
significant volumes of transfer traffic. In cases where additional screening is not required, transfer bags can 
be directly inserted into the sortation system. 
Transfer bags can be delivered to an outbound baggage make-up area, early bag store or to a dedicated 
transfer area/facility. It is important that bags going into and out of an EBS be tracked. It is also recommended 
that all transfer bags have a brightly colored transfer baggage tag attached at check-in, so they can be easily 
recognized on the ramp. 
3.3.8.14 Importance of Baggage Concept of Operations 
Before designing a BHS, it is important to define the Concept of Operations (ConOps). A ConOps is a 
document that that describes the desired operational outcomes that the airport wants to achieve from the 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 729 

===PAGE 749===
Be @. [h | IATA Ball Airport Development Reference Manual 
perspective of the users of the system. It should be developed for all parts of an operational process and it 
should document all operational assumptions and characteristics of the proposed infrastructure. 
A ConOps should not detail the proposed solutions, the focus should be on defining and agreeing the 
outcomes that a solution will need to deliver. 2.7 Development of a Concept of Operations gives further 
guidance on the development of ConOps, including a specific sub section on processing bags which 
highlights issues to be considered. 
3.3.8.15 Baggage Demand Analysis 
A key design input is the definition of the demands that the baggage system and processes will need to 
handle. These demands are: 
(a) Those imposed externally at the system and process boundaries. 
(b) Those that are seen within these boundaries. 
The former are essentially unaffected by the system and process design, while the latter depend upon the 
system configuration and its operating mode. 
Traditionally, the external demands have been derived from a design day flight schedule for some future point 
in time based on traffic and growth assumptions. The following subsections describe how flight- and 
passenger-based schedules are converted to provide baggage demands, though the limitations of a traditional 
schedule-based approach need to be considered. In order to understand the internal demands on the system 
and processes, it is necessary to define the operating process. 
3.3.8.15.1 Schedule Analysis 
The approach, in summary, is as follows: 
* Convert design day flight schedule into passenger numbers by flight 
e Convert passenger numbers by flight into separate categories: originating and terminating, transfer, and 
by segregation (inbound and outbound) 
* Convert passenger numbers by flight and category into bag numbers, considering how bags per 
passenger might vary by airline or market 
e Using terminal reporting profiles, calculate the profiles of bags as they arrive at the airport, split by 
category and segregation 
e Aggregate demands by facility/process 
The starting point for this type of analysis is a peak day flight schedule for the design year. The schedule will 
include the following details for each arriving and departing flight, as a minimum: 
e Flight identifier 
e Aircraft type 
730 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 750===
& Hi : IATA Passenger Terminal 
* Number of seats 
e Passenger load factor (or number of passengers) 
¢ Scheduled time of operation 
While this primary information can be used to gauge the broad pattern of traffic, several secondary datasets 
or assumptions are needed to develop the detailed baggage demand picture. These are described in turn. 
3.3.8.15.2 Limitations of Schedule Analysis 
In order to size a baggage system and its associated processes, it is necessary to ‘predict’ 15-minute 
baggage demands, as much as 25 years into the future. Looking back 25 years, the changes in the airline 
business have been profound: low-cost carriers, major alliances, transformed security regimes, economic 
development in new regions, fluctuations in oil prices and taxation, to name but a few. While extrapolating 
current schedules for anticipated changes in a few years’ time may be reasonable for short-term planning 
purposes, it is hardly plausible that they will reflect actual demands in 25 years’ time with any certainty. 
While the detailed analysis of a given schedule (whether static or via simulation, etc.) can provide a possible 
demand scenario, such results should not, on their own, be used to define a design basis. It is not good 
practice to have demands that are quoted as single point estimates and those generating estimates should be 
encouraged to quote a range along with some estimate of the confidence limits. See 2.2 Forecasting provides 
further guidance on forecasting. 
3.3.8.15.3 Transfer Ratios 
For each flight, the number of direct departing or terminating passengers needs to be determined, since these 
passengers make use of check-in and reclaim facilities, respectively. The number of transfer passengers also 
needs to be determined for each flight. In this case, transfer passengers’ bags will use different facilities (i.e., 
transfer break on the inbound leg and departures screening; flight makeup on the outbound leg). 
Transfer passenger numbers may be given directly, or as a transfer ratio for a flight: 
where r,, is the transfer ratio, N,, is the number of transfer passengers on the flight and N,q. is the total 
passengers on the flight. 
Note that using a single transfer ratio for all flights is likely to give misleading results. There is generally a 
variety of transfer ratios for different carriers. Even for a single carrier, the transfer ratios may be expected to 
vary throughout the year, even within a day and by origin or destination. Transfer ratios can also vary on short 
notice: airlines can encourage transfer traffic through pricing as a way of increasing load factors. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 731 

===PAGE 751===
IATA 4 Airport Development Reference Manual 
Equally, it should be considered whether using current day transfer percentages is appropriate for designing 
new facilities. If the airport is striving to grow their transfer share, then this should be reflected in the transfer 
ratios to be used. 
It is recommended that, when designing transfer-related systems and processes, careful attention be paid to 
ensuring that there is sufficient system resilience and redundancy to accommodate peaks. Such an approach 
would be to consider a high transfer scenario to inform transfer facilities and a low transfer scenario to inform 
facilities for direct passengers. 
3.3.8.15.4 Bags per Passenger Ratios 
Having determined the number of originating, terminating and transfer passengers for each flight, this must be 
converted into the number of bags that passengers bring to be processed as hold baggage. The number of 
bags for each type of passenger for each flight may be given directly, or in terms of bag per passenger ratios. 
There is generally a variety of bag per passenger ratios for different carriers. Even for a single carrier, the 
ratios may be expected to vary by origin or destination, and whether or not the passenger is direct or 
transferring. The number of hold bags per passenger can also vary on short notice: airlines can change 
charging policies for cabin and hold baggage, which can lead to changes in passenger behaviour. 
In the absence of more specific information on local circumstances, the following bag per passenger ratios 
can be used as a starting point for planning purposes. Note that detailed analysis is essential and these 
figures are representative only as a high-level industry guide.

3.3.8.15.5 Presentation/Turn-Up Profiles 
The demand on inputs to the baggage system and related processes is dependent on their appearance times. 
There are three primary baggage flows to be considered: 
¢ Direct departing (i.e., check-in and bag drop) 
e Transfer (i.e., transfer bags arriving on an inbound aircraft) 
¢ Reclaim (i.e., terminating bags arriving on an inbound aircraft) 
732 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 752===
ay 
nts, 
IATA 4 Passenger Terminal 
Direct departing bags will typically appear progressively over one or more hours prior to the scheduled 
departure time. Appearance profiles (ideally based on measured behaviours) allow the anticipated number of 
bags for a flight to be distributed over time during the check-in phase. 
Note that using a single appearance profile for all flights is likely to give misleading results. There is generally 
a variety of profiles for different carriers. Even for a single carrier, the profiles may be expected to vary by 
origin or destination and by time of day. Examples are shown in the exhibit below. These are purely 
illustrative, but show typical trends: 
e Long-haul flights generally have extended appearance profiles, since there may be only a few flights to 
the destination and because travel to the airport is but a small fraction of the end-to-end journey time, 
passengers tend to arrive earlier. 
e Short-haul flights usually have more compressed profiles, reflecting the fact that there may be more 
frequent flights per day to a given destination. Short-haul appearance profiles can be very compressed. 
For example, an early morning check-in where passengers may only be able to get to the airport closer to 
the scheduled departure time. 
Transfer and reclaim bags appear in a more peaky fashion since they arrive on an inbound aircraft. The 
unloading process might be as short as 15 minutes, so all the bags appear within this, much shorter, window. 
Transfer and reclaim facilities, therefore, need to be sized to deal with these short-term peaks. 
Note that, while direct departing profiles are typically linked to scheduled departures times, the arriving 
profiles (transfer and reclaim) should be linked to actual arrival times. At the early planning stage, the 
distinction is usually overlooked with arrival punctuality being assumed to be perfect. However, in live 
operations, the impact of arrival punctuality can be very important.

3.3.8.15.6 Transfer Connections 
Transfer bags are linked to two flights (unlike direct departing and reclaim bags, which are linked only to one). 
To find the dwell time of transfer bags, a fully linked schedule would be needed. This has, for each inbound 
and outbound flight, not only the total number of transfer passengers, but also, for each transfer passenger, 
the inbound and outbound flight on which they travel. However, this level of detail is rarely provided in 
planning schedules. 
The inbound transfer loads can be used to size transfer input demands, since they are driven primarily by the 
incoming flights and do not depend on the outbound flights. But, once transfer bags enter the baggage 
system, they will be sorted and, if necessary, stored depending upon the outbound flight. In the absence of a 
fully linked schedule at a bag-by-bag level, approximations have to be made to deal with demands further into 
the baggage system. 
For each departing flight, it may be possible to apply an effective appearance profile for the outbound transfer 
bags. This is analogous to the appearance profile for direct bags. This may be sufficient to check demands on 
the downstream parts of the outbound systems (e.g., makeup). Of course, the accuracy of this depends on 
being able to obtain realistic ‘appearance profiles’ for the different categories of transfer bags. 
Combining these two approaches (i.e., bags entering the system according to the inbound flights, and bags 
leaving the system according to the notional appearance profile tied to outbound flights) is sometimes done in 
an attempt to estimate the number of bags within the systems, in particular the number of bags that will 
require storage. Great caution should be exercised when interpreting results obtained in this way. The 
calculated size of the bag store is, effectively, the result of subtracting one large number from another, and 
this makes the result very sensitive to small changes in the input assumptions. Furthermore, without the 
actual link between inbound and outbound flights, real-life correlations are lost in the approximation. This too 
can lead to large differences between the modelled results and reality. 
In all cases, a range of sensitivity checks should be made to explore how much results change with variations 
in input assumptions in order to be able to provide a sense on the uncertainty in the results. 
3.3.8.15.7 Exceptions 
While the majority of bags can be processed in automated systems and follow a predictable route, much of 
the complexity of typical baggage systems is driven by the need to handle exceptions. Though usually only a 
fraction of the total, these exceptions have the potential to affect performance adversely and, as such, have to 
be dealt with effectively.

===PAGE 754===
z rn 
IATA Passenger Terminal 
These exceptions typically include: 
¢ Outsize (also known as OOG) and non-system compatible baggage [10%] 
e No-read bags [3% direct, 25% transfer] 
e Level 3 or 4 bags [5%] identified as security threats 
© Customs inspection [% depends on jurisdiction] 
e Missed bags [1%] 
e Problem bags [0.1%] 
e Radiation detection [1 per 1,000,000 bags] 
Bags that are not handled through an automated system (such as OOG items) are generally at a higher risk 
of being mishandled. Furthermore, there are usually fewer tracking points, which can make tracing such bags 
more difficult than is the case with regular bags. Therefore, accounting for OOG processes at the start of a 
design will help to ensure that an efficient and effective operation is delivered. 
Not every bag's tag will be read automatically. The fractions vary: direct bags have a higher read rate (a well￾maintained system will achieve rates of around 97%). In contrast, inbound transfer bags may only achieve 
read rates of 75% as a result of variable quality printing at outstations as well as physical damage to tags 
through the loading and unloading processes. 
3.3.8.15.8 Example Operating Modes 
The total number of bags within the baggage system (and wider non-system processes) is a function of bag 
appearance and departure times and not the design or type of baggage system itself. Departing bags initially 
appear at a baggage input, typically a check-in or transfer input, and ultimately leave the airport on an 
outbound flight. Similarly, terminating bags arrive on an inbound aircraft and leave the airport having been 
collected by the passenger, typically at a reclaim device. In both cases, between these ‘arriving’ and 
‘departing’ events, bags must dwell somewhere within the baggage system and surrounding processes. 
Where bags dwell is influenced by the choice of operating mode. 
The exhibit below shows a number of different modes for departing baggage and highlights some of the 
characteristics of each. In this example, the dwell time of the bag is assumed to be 100 minutes in all cases. 
In the first case, although passengers arrive 100 minutes before departure, they spend 30 minutes of this time 
queuing before being able to drop their bags. While this is hardly an example of good passenger service, it 
does mean that the baggage system has to hold fewer bags at any one time. The second case improves 
passenger service by offering bag drop with negligible queuing time. In this case, in a conventional baggage 
system, the bags will spend more time at or near makeup. This may require more space for holding partially 
filled ULDs or carts.

In the third case, a degree of compressed makeup is used, which means that bags spend some time in a bag 
store before being sent to makeup. This can have the effect of reducing the space needed for makeup, but at 
the price of having to provide early bag storage. The fourth case uses batch makeup, which makes-up full or 
partial batches of bags as soon as they become available. This can significantly reduce the number of 
makeup positions required and, by storing bags in full ULDs, can reduce the demand for early bag storage. 
The type of diagram used in the above exhibit can also be used to make order of magnitude estimates of the 
number of bags that will dwell, at any one time, in each of the functional locations. This is a result of 
multiplying the design flow rate (in bags per minute) by the average dwell time (in minutes), which will give an 
estimate of the average number of bags dwelling. As an example, if the design flow rate is 40 bags per 
minute (equivalent to 2,400 bags per hour), the number of bags in transit within the system is 15 minutes x 40 
bags per minute = 600 bags. Using the same approach, around 1,200 bags might be in the store in the 
compressed build scenario, and around 800 bags (maybe 30 ULDs) in a ULD store in the batch makeup 
scenario. Coupled with benchmark figures for capital costs as well as equipment and effective bag densities, 
this type of analysis can provide useful preliminary estimates very rapidly and is especially useful for initial 
concept selection. The design of a baggage system is as much about apportioning dwell times to different 
functional areas as it is about ‘peak hour’ flow rates. 
Choosing an appropriate operating mode for the baggage system and process offers the opportunity to adjust 
where space and equipment is needed in a terminal, which can provide flexibility for terminal design. 
However, care must be taken to understand the total space and equipment required, together with the 
associated capital costs. Impacts (positive or negative) on operating costs must also be considered, when 
assessing the overall business case. Optimizing, in isolation, single parts of the end-to-end process risks 
creating an overall concept that is actually suboptimal.

At the concept stage, it is recommended that different operating modes are characterized and evaluated by 
breaking down the end-to-end baggage journey and assigning quantitative estimates of key parameters to 
each element, so that both the component parts and the totality of the design can be understood. Key 
parameters might include the following: 
e Space take (areas and volumes) 
¢ Capital cost of baggage handling equipment 
e Operational expenditures 
e Passenger experience 
e Operational resilience 
This will reveal whether apparent optimizations in one element are creating net benefits. 
3.3.8.15.9 Internal Processing Demands 
As noted earlier, the demands placed upon a baggage system are determined by the flight schedule and 
other external factors. The demands on transport and functional areas within the baggage system are driven, 
not only by these external factors, but also by the internal configuration and operating mode of the system. 
Progressively more detailed descriptions of the internal design of the baggage system are created. These 
levels of definition are as follows: 
e Black box with no internal structure 
© Process flow diagram (PFD), which shows the connections between functional areas and defines the 
operating mode. This is used as the basis for models or abstract simulations from which internal flows 
and demands can be determined (see Exhibit 3.3.8.15.9a below).

3.3.8.16 Facility Requirements Calculations 
This subsection provides guidelines for calculating the numbers of key components required within a BHS. 
The approach is appropriate for developing and scoping baggage system concepts. 
738 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 758===
= IATA al Passenger Terminal 
The accuracy of the results will depend on the accuracy of the input assumptions. We provide typical ranges 
for these assumptions, but recommend, where possible, making use of actual data, surveys, and/or trials 
related to the specific scenario. 
To calculate the required number of a given type of facility, there are two equivalent methods: 
1. Take the demand rate for a given class of facility and divide it by the processing rate per facility unit. 
2. Take the demand rate for a given class of facility and multiply it by the process (or occupation) time per 
facility unit. 
The first type of facility is where an appreciable dwell time is generally undesirable. This would include: 
e Check-in and bag drop 
e Hold baggage screening 
e Manual coding 
e Transfer inputs 
¢ Build cells 
In this case, expressing the capacity of each unit of a facility as a rate emphasizes the fact that, ideally, bags 
pass through these facilities quickly. 
In contrast, the second type of facility is where an appreciable dwell or occupation time is actually required. 
This would include: 
«Makeup positions 
e Bag storage 
e ULD storage 
e Reclaim carousels 
In this case, expressing the usage of a facility as an occupation or dwell time emphasizes the fact that bags 
are intended to accumulate at these facilities. 
In performing these calculations, it is important to clarify the degree of dedicated versus common usage 
expected. For example, if a bank of check-in desks may only be used by a single airline, the number of desks 
to be provided will be based on the demands generated by that particular airline and the processing rate 
achieved by their staff. More significantly, if these desks are permitted to be used by others, this calculation 
will need to be repeated for each distinct group of users. The total requirement for check-in, in this case, 
being the sum of the results for each group. 
While this will allow the basic numbers of components to be calculated, consideration must also be given to: 
° The effect of failures, which will reduce available processing capacity at times; and 
¢ Exceptional demands, which are demands that exceed the design basis for whatever reason
