3.3.8.17 High-level Baggage Control Systems 
While the design of a terminal involves the spatial planning of facilities-BHS being a key element-the 
effective operation of a BHS depends on the control systems. 
For the purposes of this description, the terminology used reflects a scenario in which the functional elements 
are separate components. This will typically be the case in legacy systems. With newer designs, baggage 
system suppliers can offer more integrated control systems. These, sometimes proprietary, systems 
nevertheless perform the same basic functions, though they may offer additional functionality. Complete 
control system solutions are also available from independent IT suppliers, who will integrate their controls 
systems with the electromechanical equipment from a wide range of suppliers. 
The choice of approach should be made explicitly. There are significant life-cycle cost implications inherent in 
the choice, which will vary from one situation to another. In this regard, it is worth noting that, while conveyors 
and other mechanical components may well have design lives of 20 or more years, controls and IT elements 
may have to be replaced two or three times during this period. This is not necessarily because they fail, but 
because they become unsupportable. This means that operating systems, databases, etc. are no longer 
supported by the suppliers and hardware may no longer be manufactured and available. The typical control 
‘stack’ consists of the following elements: 
¢ Sort Allocation Computer (SAC) 
¢ System Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) 
e Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) 
¢ Management Information System (MIS) 
Before describing the high-level functions performed by these elements, it is necessary to provide an 
overview of baggage messaging. 
3.3.8.18 Baggage Messaging 
Baggage messaging plays a vital part in most BHS. The reason is simply that the bar code on a bag tag 
(which is used by baggage systems to identify a bag) is just a ten-digit number, of which three digits are used 
to identity the issuing airline, one digit is reserved for special uses, and the remaining six digits are assigned 
to a single bag. Thus, the bar code itself does not contain any routing information. Routing information is 
contained in baggage messages (specifically, the Baggage Source Message-BSM) which are generated by 
airlines’ Departure Control Systems (DCS). These messages are sent worldwide via a Message Distribution 
System (MDS). BHS will receive and store messages for bags that are expected in the system. 
For the BHS to process bags correctly, the baggage system has to read each bag's tag and match the tag 
number with the corresponding baggage message, which will contain a range of information, including the 
departure flight. The baggage system is then able to process and route the bags according to defined 
business rules, delivering them to the correct makeup position for the flight. 
740 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 760===
Se By, sO IATA mul Passenger Terminal 
Baggage systems can generate Baggage Processed Messages (BPM), which are sent to an MDS. Airports 
and airlines can receive these messages from the MDS, allowing bags to be traced and changes in their 
status to registered (e.g., when a bag has been screened). 
A failure anywhere in the chain of DCS to MDS to the BHS can result in bags entering a system without a 
valid message. This will generally mean that the bag has to be ‘manually coded’: the bag is sent to a 
workstation where an operative will read the other data on the bag tag and manually enter the departure flight 
into the baggage system to allow the system to process the bag. 
For transfer bags, the message path is more involved. When the bag is first checked-in, the airline on whose 
aircraft the first leg is flown will generate a BSM from their DCS for reception by the local BHS. This allows 
the bag to be sorted and loaded for the first leg. The DCS also generates a Baggage Transfer Message 
(BTM), which is sent, via an MDS, for reception by the DCS of the airline on which the second leg of the 
journey is to be flown. This second DCS should then issue a BSM for reception by the BHS that will process 
the bag for loading on the second leg. In this case, more systems and communication legs are involved in 
successfully getting a message to the final BHS, which is one factor that contributes to a higher mis-handled 
rate for transfer bags than for direct bags. 
3.3.8.19 Baggage Reconciliation System 
The Baggage Reconciliation System (BRS) is an application that provides functionalities for loading, 
reconciling, tracking and managing baggage operations. The BRS provides real-time information on baggage 
status, enabling staff to increase operational efficiency and ensure a passenger's baggage is on the correct 
aircraft to the correct destination at the right time. 
The BRS solution should be compatible with IATA resolutions and recommended practices concerning 
baggage, such as Resolution 753 (Baggage Tracking) and RP 1800 (Automated Baggage Handling based on 
IATA License Plate Concept). 
The BRS can be deployed to address the specific needs of an airline for dedicated use, or of ground handlers 
providing services to multiple airlines, or as a shared solution deployed by an airport for multiple airlines. 
BRS are being added with new capabilities and features to help airlines meet their IATA Resolution 753 
obligations, and help staff locate any bag around the airport. The automated solution is comprised of ATRs 
using different technologies (e.g., laser, optical and RFID). Instead of users with mobile devices manually 
scanning each bag as it arrives or transfers, ATRs form an arch over the conveyer belt system and read the 
bag tag of every bag that passes through the arch. Data is sent to the BRS or a data repository to register 
and store the tracked bag number, its location and time of scanning. 
3.3.8.20 Baggage Reconciliation Operations 
Sometimes, the baggage system cannot receive BSM from the airline DCS system. In situations where the 
baggage control system is not able to add bags or retrieve bags from the system, there should be operational 
plans for how to: 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 741 

===PAGE 761===
Be e- WE | IATA At Airport Development Reference Manual 
¢ Get bags currently in the baggage system out 
¢ Get bags airside and screened when regular baggage check-in is not in operation 
e Ensure that transfer bags coming in are kept alive and connected to the departure flight 
e Handle “cold” bags and ensure re-flight 
If bags are not able to be routed to makeup, alternative means must be used. It is important to get bags out of 
the system as quickly as possible. This is done via the purge points designed into the system at critical 
locations. 
Wherever a purge point is located there will be floor space to offload bags and organize them according to 
destination. Bag are moved manually from the purge point to a location where they can either be moved into 
ULDs or to a Baggage Reconciliation Facility (BRF). The BRF should be created close to the terminal that it 
will support. 
The BRF is designed with two areas. The first is a ‘clean’ area where bags are screened, cleared and built 
into ULDs. The second is an ‘unknown’ area where bags, arriving via standard tub and dollies, are manually 
moved to a drop area and sorted by flight. When the flight build time opens, the bags are moved from the 
drop area to a screening machine where bags are screened and sent to the lateral for build. 
3.3.8.21 Sort Allocation Computer 
The Sort Allocation Computer (SAC) provides communications links with external systems, primarily baggage 
messaging (which can be via a MDS or directly with an airline's DCS) and the airport's flight information. 
Internally, the SAC is linked to the baggage MIS and to Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs). 
The SAC is where the ‘business rules’ are maintained and managed. An important example of this is the 
management and allocation of makeup positions. However, depending on the sophistication and complexity of 
the baggage system, the management of other resources (e.g., batch building cells, reclaims) may be 
included too. 
The SAC may also be linked to a reconciliation system, which is used to record which bags have been loaded 
into which ULDs or trailers, and also links this information to the passenger-boarded status. The SAC will be 
the primary source of bag search and tracking information. Operators and handlers will often need to locate a 
particular bag and, in general, the SAC will have information on where the bag was last read and based on 
tracking information, its current location. It is via the SAC that bags can be removed from the system on an ad 
hoc basis (e.g., to return a check-in bag to a passenger). 
Bags are identified by the system by means of a bar code or RFID tag. Although read rates can be very high 
(97% or greater for direct bags), a number of bags will inevitably fail to be read automatically. Manual coding 
stations will, therefore, be used to correct this. 
742 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 762===
abe 
IATA + Passenger Terminal 
3.3.8.21.1 Bag Traceability 
There has been increasing use of RFID technology for tracking bags. When installed correctly, RFID 
technology has a higher read rate than normal barcode scanners, resulting in fewer misdirected bags. IATA 
Resolution 753, which became effective on 1 June 2018, encourages airlines to further reduce mishandling by 
mandating that airlines be able to identify when bags are changing custody at four critical points: Check-in, 
Load, Transfer, and Arrival. 
It is important to underline that, while compliance with Resolution 753 lies with the airline, the baggage system 
must have the functionality to be able to deliver the required data to the airlines. There are no requirements 
as to how the identification is to be carried out; it can be done via technology or manually. 
Another trend related to traceability is the increased use of ICS. Bags are placed onto totes as early as 
possible, such as when the passenger is checking in their baggage. This ensures optimal bag tracking, as the 
system is not tracking the bags but the tubs. Each tub is RFID-enabled and, with a read-rate for RFID of close 
to 100%, the technology will support bag traceability. 
3.3.8.22 System Control and Data Acquisition 
The System Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) provides a control interface with PLCs. It allows control 
room staff to monitor the operation of the baggage system. This includes raising alarms when certain 
operational events happen, such as a jammed bag or a chute that is full. Control room staff can also directly 
control field equipment (e.g., turning off or resetting conveyors). The SCADA system can also be interfaced 
with the CCTV system. For example, if an alarm is triggered on a particular conveyor, CCTV images of the 
location can be viewed to help diagnose the issue. 
3.3.8.23 Programmable Logic Controllers 
PLCs are, in effect, robust industrial computers with specialized communication and interface capabilities. 
PLCs, supported by interface units, control equipment (e.g., motor warnings, beacons) and receive 
information from photocells, interlocks, switches, etc. They are programmed to perform a number of low-level 
functions autonomously, while also being able to signal to, and respond to, higher level instructions from the 
SAC and SCADA. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 743 

===PAGE 763===
uk pl Airport Development Reference Manual

management. Legacy systems generally have a set of predefined reports that can be produced, while modern 
systems make use of business intelligence tools that allow users to develop their own reports and 
dashboards, and to perform ad hoc explorations of information. An example dashboard-type display is shown 
in the exhibit below.

3.3.9 Universal Design and Terminal Accessibility 
744 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022

3.3.9.1 Introduction and General Principles 
Disability 
Globally, an estimated 1.2 billion people, or 15% of the population, have a disability (WHO). According to the 
United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, persons with disabilities are defined as 
“those who have long-term physical, mental, intellectual or sensory impairments which in interaction with 
various barriers may hinder their full and effective participation in society on an equal basis with others.” 
Disabilities can be visible or non-visible, permanent or temporary, and be situational, (i.e., fluctuating 
depending on the environment that someone is in). Regardless of the type of disability an airport passenger or 
staff member has, and the way in which that impairment presents itself within an aviation environment, they 
should be able to expect and experience an equitable level of support and service relative to their peers. 
Globally, the share of the population aged 65 years or over increased from 6% in 1990 to 9% in 2019. That 
numberis expected to be 1.5 billion by 2050, leading to a greater need for access and inclusion measures for 
all. This fact is already impacting the demand for assistive services in Europe and North America where the 
population 65+ has already reached 21% and 17% respectively. Japan, which leads the trend at 28%, is, not 
surprisingly, the world's foremost proponent of Universal Design (World Bank). 
Access and inclusion relate to how an environment isengaged by individuals, and how that user experience 
feels, respectively. As concepts, they can be improved physically (within the built environment of the airport 
itself), socially (through education, empathy and the creation of a positive attitude toward disability or other 
protected characteristics), and digitally (via websites, apps and other assistive technologies). Economically, 
this can also have a hugely influential impact on the airport as a whole; accessible environments benefit from 
the spending power of people with disabilities and their households, known in the UK as the ‘Purple Pound’. 
Universal Design 
Universal Design is a set of principles and process where built environment infrastructure, products, services 
and facilities as well as physical and digital communication and information may all be accessed, understood 
and used to the greatest practicable extent by all people. This should be achieved without the need for 
adaptation, assistive devices or specialized solutions. 
Universal Design is a fundamental condition of good design. If an environment is accessible, convenient and 
a pleasure to use, everyone benefits. By considering the diverse abilities and requirements of all throughout 
the design process, Universal Design and its human-centered approach also positively impacts a product or 
project's sustainability, durability and value. It results in more innovative, marketable and usable designs. It 
delivers on independent use, social participation, human performance, health and wellness, and increases 
safety and reduces risk. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 745 

===PAGE 765===
Ee 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
The seven principles of Universal Design can prove useful in ensuring access and inclusion. These seven 
principles are: 
¢ Principle 1: Equitable Use—Ensuring the design is useful and marketable to people with diverse 
abilities. 
¢ Principle 2: Flexibility in Use-Ensuring the design accommodates a wide range of individual 
preferences and abilities. 
¢ Principle 3: Simple and Intuitive Use—Ensuring use of the design is easy to understand, regardless of 
the user's experience, knowledge, language skills, or current concentration level. 
¢ Principle 4: Perceptible Information—Ensuring the design communicates necessary information 
effectively to the user, regardless of ambient conditions or the user's sensory abilities. 
¢ Principle 5: Tolerance for Error—Ensuring the design minimizes hazards and the adverse 
consequences of accidental or unintended actions. 
¢ Principle 6: Low Physical Effort-Ensuring the design can be used efficiently and comfortably and with 
a minimum of fatigue. 
¢ Principle 7: Size and Space for Approach and Use—Ensuring appropriate size and space is provided 
for approach, reach, manipulation, and use regardless of the user's body size, posture, or mobility. 
Source: The Center for Universal Design—Universal Design Principles (ncsu.edu) 
Airports should incorporate the principles of Universal Design from the outset of all new projects. For 
brownfield projects where adapting legacy facilities can be challenging, every effort should be made to 
incorporate Universal Design principles, accepting that it might not always be possible to fully address the 
needs of all passengers with disabilities. Greenfield projects, on the other hand, can benefit greatly (and avoid 
subsequent costs) by incorporating universal design and inclusion principles early on as part of the planning 
process. 
The purpose of this section of the ADRM is to ensure that airport facilities are planned and designed to be 
used by everyone, including those with disabilities, without the need for adaptation or specialized design. This 
section also provides guidance on the correct action and implementation, where appropriate, possible and 
practicable. Where legislated, national accessibility design standards should be complied with in full and 
recommended practices should be followed, where provided. 
Terminology 
It is recognized that disability is an ever-evolving concept and that differing language and terminology related 
to disability is used in different countries and regions. In line with both the UN Convention and IATA 
Resolution 700, the ADRM uses the term persons/people with disabilities. It is important that the term Persons 
with Reduced Mobility (PRM) is not used as it does not show an appreciation for personal identity or address 
the wide range of impairments and access requirements that people with disabilities have. 
746 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 766===
ay 
IATA 4 Passenger Terminal 
Considerations 
An accessible and inclusive airport should also consider and plan for the needs of its staff members with 
disabilities. Where possible and practicable, back-of-house staffing areas should mirror front-of-house 
passenger areas in terms of access and inclusion to ensure the staff experience is also positive for those with 
disabilities. 
Staff providing assistance, whether from the airport or airline, should be well trained in disability awareness 
and communication to provide a high standard of service appropriate to individual passenger and colleague 
needs. 
Unless otherwise stated, design elements and processes highlighted in this section of the ADRM should be 
considered equitably for both passengers and staff members with disabilities and integrated into both the 
front-facing and back-of-house areas of the airport. 
Standards and guidelines are typically used to demonstrate that buildings have been designed to be 
accessible. However, they are only part of the equation for effectively developing truly accessible and 
inclusive facilities. Superior design outcomes can be achieved by engaging with those who have a lived 
experience of disability. This could be achieved through a lived experience user group or airport advisory 
forum consisting of persons with a broad range of disabilities. 
3.3.9.2 Common Elements 
3.3.9.2.1. Desks 
Sightlines to all desks, including those for information and check-in purposes, should be clear from terminal 
entrances (with desks being on the same level as the terminal entrance), and access routes leading to the 
desks should be direct and clear of obstructions. 
Passengers and staff with additional requirements should be able to access desks, and the information 
related to them, at every stage of their airport journey or workday. This includes wheelchair users and those 
with mobility equipment who need to utilize space on and under desks and access lowered-height desks, as 
well as deaf passengers and staff who need to receive information at desks via induction loops, video remote 
interpreting (VRI), lip reading or other accommodation.

===PAGE 767===
IATA 4 Airport Development Reference Manual 
Exhibit 3.3.9.2.1: Airport Information Desks 
Source: Incheon Airport 
Any airport desk design should consider several factors, including but not limited to the: 
e Purpose of the desk 
e Length of time a passenger is going to utilize the desk 
e Interaction that is going to be required 
e Necessary safety and security measures that need to be in place 
¢ Ergonomic experience of the desk for an airport staff member, regardless of disability 
Desks that are specifically for the use of passengers requiring assistance should be signed with the 
international symbol of accessibility. 
Segregation of passengers and staff with disabilities should be avoided, wherever possible. Passengers 
should not have to go out of their way to access an adapted desk that caters to their requirements. Therefore, 
offering a dual height desk design at airports is an inclusive solution that could be of benefit to all; accessible 
adaptation is not required and segregation is not necessary.

3.3.9.2.2 Toilets and Changing Facilities 
Accessible and ambulant toilet facilities 
The provision of adequate toilet facilities at airports is absolutely vital, and a fundamental right for all 
passengers and staff members. For those with disabilities and older people, access to fit-for-purpose 
amenities is a crucial practical matter that can either significantly enhance or negatively impact their overall 
airport experience. The absence of suitable fit-for-purpose facilities can result in some people even avoiding 
drinking so they do not have to use the bathrooms in the terminal. 
There are generally two main types of accessible toilets with important differences between them: 
Accessible toilets 
Accessible toilets are specifically designed to provide sufficient space to accommodate access for wheelchair 
users, and assistance when transferring from a wheelchair to a toilet. 
Ambulant toilets 
In some countries, there is also a requirement to provide separate facilities for ambulant passengers. 
Ambulant toilets are specifically designed for individuals with ambulant disabilities such as arthritis, sensory 
loss, or who require the use of a walker. They do not require the extra space that is needed by users of 
accessible toilets. 
Ambulant and accessible toilets should be incorporated into all toilet blocks so they are easy to locate. Fit out 
standards should be to at least the same standard as all other facilities to avoid any perception that 
passengers with disabilities receive a lower standard of service. 
While nationally legislated design standards vary globally, the guidelines below offer general guidance on 
important design elements. 
General considerations 
Accessible toilets, changing facilities and accessible cubicles should be available for use by anyone who 
requires them, whether their impairment is visible or hidden. 
Inclusive wayfinding, door signage, level step-free access, and unobstructed turning and transfer space are 
critically important elements in the general provision of facilities, along with ensuring there are an adequate 
number of facilities provided. Minimum legislated standards (where applicable) should be considered the 
starting point with best practice being to exceed the stated number given the likely growth in future demand. 
There should be a clear path of travel. The entrance to the facilities for passengers with disabilities should 
ideally be directly accessible off main concourse areas for ease of access with entrance points off corridors 
avoided, where possible. Where the use of corridors is unavoidable, they should be wide enough to allow two 
wheelchairs to pass each other with a particular focus on wayfinding to the facilities. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 749 

===PAGE 769===
Py 
ee, 
IATA / Airport Development Reference Manual 
Additional features that should be considered within accessible toilets include: 
e Raised seat heights for easier wheelchair transfer 
* Toilet flush handles, door handles, locks and taps that can be utilized with limited dexterity and strength 
¢ Height adjustable basins large enough to facilitate basic washing and cleaning needs 
In addition, equipment expected in well-finished standard toilets should also be included, such as paper 
towels (electric hand dryers are not recommended as sudden, high-volume noise can be distressing for 
persons with cognitive impairments), wastepaper and sanitary bins (large enough to support the disposal of 
incontinence pads) and mirrors large enough and considerately placed to enable wheelchair users to view 
themselves in a seated position. 
Floors should have high slip resistance. Good quality lighting is another important safety element. It should be 
designed to avoid shadows with a high uniformity ratio. Any movable features, such as bins, should be 
considered at the outset to ensure the placement of such facilities does not become a barrier or impede use 
or toilet transfer in any way. 
The installation of assistance call points directly linked to the Airport Control Center should also be 
considered. Alarms must be able to be raised by passengers in need, wherever they may be located within 
the accessible toilet (i.., on the floor having fallen or on the toilet itself). Alarms should not require excessive 
force or dexterity, but should be visibly obvious to avoid accidental activation. If on cords, alarms should never 
be tied up out of reach. 
Where possible and practicable, all accessible toilet facilities should follow the same design and placement 
plans to make navigation and use as simple as possible for all users, particularly those with visual and 
cognitive impairments. 
Depending on their impairment, capabilities and whether or not they have assistance present, wheelchair 
users will use different methods to transfer onto the toilet seat. These transfer techniques include: 
* _ Lateral transfer onto the toilet using grabrails, with one or both rear wheels of the wheelchair backed up to 
the rear wall. 
* Oblique transfer using grabrails and leaning on the toilet, or just leaning on the toilet for full support. 
° Frontal transfer using grabrails that enable some users to pivot round and others to slide forward onto the 
toilet from their wheelchair and use the toilet in a forward-facing position. This may or may not involve 
standing as part of the transfer process. With this transfer technique, the toilet can be used as a urinal. 
* Transfer with the wheelchair at the front of the toilet and at right angles to it. 
Accessible adult changing facilities 
Standard airport accessible toilet facilities do not provide for the changing needs of non-ambulatory adult and 
child passengers with significant physical and/or cognitive disabilities. As a result, they are excluded from 
using the available toilet facilities and are often forced to use the floors of existing toilets as a changing 
facility. 
750 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 770===
IATA “4 Passenger Terminal 
An Accessible Adult Change Facility is a toilet and change facility that caters to users with high support needs 
and their caregivers where they require additional space, assistance, and specialized equipment to allow them 
to use toilets safely, comfortably and with dignity. 
Changing facilities should be inclusively signed throughout the airport and should, as a minimum, provide: 
e Automatic door with a large opening 
¢ Height-adjustable adult-sized change table 
¢ Constant-charging ceiling track hoist system 
e Centrally located peninsula toilet 
¢ Appropriate circulation spaces for wheelchair users and caregivers 
e Privacy screen 
e Shower 
e Sink and paper towel dispenser 
e Assistance call button connected to the Airport Control Center 
Fixtures and fittings should have a minimum 180 kg weight loading capacity. 
Changing Places is a UK-based non-profit with global affiliations campaigning for improved accessible toilet 
facilities. It is strongly recommended that adult change facilities are designed to the specifications outlined in 
the Changing Places design standards and formally certified as a “Changing Places” facility. This will ensure 
the already well-established global network of “Changing Places,” including many at existing airports, will 
grow, providing confidence to people with disabilities that the facility has been built and tested to a recognized 
standard. 
For small airports, an adult change facility located before security screening is recommended, enabling it to 
be used by both arriving and departing passengers. For larger airports and in particular those with 
international operations, it is suggested adult change facilities are also located in the departure lounge as it 
can be very difficult to backtrack to access landside amenities. All of the above should be considered for, and 
provided to, airport staff as well as passengers.

3.3.9.2.3. Nursing Rooms and Family Restrooms 
To meet the needs of parents with young children, airports should make available nursing rooms or family 
restrooms in the public and restricted areas of the terminal. These rooms offer a clean and quiet environment 
for nursing mothers who wish to nurse or pump in a private setting. 
When implementing nursing rooms and family restrooms within the airport, parents and children with 
disabilities should be considered, as both may require use of these facilities. There should be adequate space 
in both facilities for wheelchair users and members of their family to enter and make use of the rooms. 
Consideration should be given to the heights and adaptability of equipment that is installed within the space. 
For example, changing tables that can be adjusted in height are particularly beneficial as they are inclusive to 
all users and their requirements. Where possible and the space permits without encroaching on accessibility, 
a chair for feeding should also be present in both nursing and family rooms, along with a bin to dispose of 
soiled items and a sink to ensure cleanliness for all.

IATA Pull Passenger Terminal 
3.3.9.2.4 Induction Loops and Interpretation Facilities 
Audio induction loop systems (also referred to as hearing loops) are a sound system utilized by hearing aid 
users. The hearing loop provides a magnetic, wireless signal that is picked up by the hearing aid when it is 
set to the ‘T’ (Telecoil) setting. When in use, an induction loop is able to cut out background noise or difficult 
acoustics for the hearing aid user, not only providing clearer delivery of information, but also potentially 
reducing stress, anxiety or confusion when communicating in busy environments. Induction loops should be 
installed at all communication points within an airport environment, signposted inclusively and correctly, and 
tested often to ensure efficient use. 
Not all hard of hearing passengers and staff will be able to utilize induction loops. The opportunity to lip read 
should, therefore, be promoted, wherever possible, via universal product design. For example, desks should 
be designed to promote face-to-face contact that is not obstructed by computer screens or high worksurfaces. 
3.3.9.2.5 Wayfinding 
Wayfinding and signage used across airport campuses have a direct impact on the passenger experience. In 
terms of accessibility, signage can greatly support an independent journey for passengers with disabilities. 
Airport signage should be well considered in terms of its location, content and design. 
Well-located wayfinding systems should be validated by careful research, planning and strategy to ensure a 
connected end-to-end journey, as well as ease of identification and navigation for all. All airport wayfinding 
systems should provide an intuitive ‘breadcrumb trail’ that provides confirmation to all passengers that they 
are heading in the right direction. Wayfinding systems should also utilize a ‘sign family’ that includes lower 
level, tactile signage more appropriate for wheelchair users and visually impaired passengers, as well as 
overhead signs for more general navigational purposes. 
Signage content should include both written information and universally recognized iconography. Any written 
information should be concise and use straightforward language and a legible font at an appropriate size for 
its purpose. Graphical information will not only support international visitors, but will also support passengers 
who may have cognitive impairments or learning differences. Visual representations of facilities or directional 
information, such as toilets or elevators, will provide an extra layer of clarity for all passengers. Supergraphics 
(ie., large icons or graphics) are best applied in large, open areas to draw attention to facilities that may 
otherwise be hard to identify. These are particularly useful in busier areas such as check-in halls, departure 
lounges and baggage reclaim. Symbols, pictograms and supergraphics provide an opportunity to create a 
consistent look and feel that is easily recognizable by all passengers and may be particularly useful for 
neurodivergent passengers who thrive on consistency and familiarity. Wayfinding and signage should, 
therefore, be considered alongside the environment, brand and any existing information being provided within 
the airport network. 
Additionally, color has a large part to play in providing intuitive wayfinding systems. Color-blindness and other 
visual impairments may affect a passenger's ability to interpret information. Colors should, therefore, be 
chosen and tested carefully along with other important accessibility features such as appropriate levels of 
contrast between the signage materials and the surrounding environment. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 753 

===PAGE 773===
ue Se 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
Alternative tactile signage should also be considered for visually impaired passengers. Those who do not read 
Braille can still identify or be aided by tactile information, such as maps or embossed signage. The 
maintenance of tactile maps and information is important to ensure that the content is not distorted or become 
misleading through use over time. 
The use of digital application wayfinding systems is becoming more widely utilized within the travel and 
transport industries. If an airport utilizes such a system, those with assistance and/or accessibility 
requirements should be able to engage with the system in an equitable manner to their peers. The digital 
system should follow WCAG, or similar, and text font, size and color and contrast, in particular, should be well 
considered. Content should be written in easy-to-read and legible format. All multimedia should be able to be 
accessed visually and audibly, and video material should be captioned. Additionally, the digital system should 
offer pan and zoom capabilities, and any specific accessibility information should be signed with the 
international symbol of accessibility. 
For further information, see 3.3.12 Wayfinding and Signage. 
3.3.9.2.6 Seating, Assistance Lounges and Dwell Spaces 
Reliable, well-advertised and readily available seating is an important aspect of the passenger airport 
experience. Inclusive, comfortable seating should be available throughout the airport at regular intervals. This 
is especially important within circulation routes for both Passengers and staff who are unable to self-mobilize 
without adequate and frequent rest. 
Inclusive seating should provide a range of options. This may include a blend of seats with a variation of 
heights, with armrests for those who require extra Stability when sitting down and standing back up again, 
without armrests for wheelchair users to laterally transfer with ease and perched seating for those who may 
struggle to get up from a seated position. In addition to providing an adequate amount and range of seating, 
spaces should also be left clear of any seating or other obstructions to allow wheelchair users or families 
travelling with small children in buggies to sit together with their travel companions while not blocking any 
circulation or access routes. 
Consideration should also be given to where seating is provided, especially in areas such as circulation 
spaces. The seating experience may be much more enjoyable if a view can be seen out of the building from 
the seated position, or seating is thoughtfully placed and configured so users do not feel they are merely 
waiting in a busy corridor, for example. The time in which users are expected to sit and wait should also be 
factored into any seat height and width, space and material choices. 
In lounges, at gates, in staff break rooms and other similar designated seating areas, seating should be 
supported by appropriate entertainment facilities. Where possible, conveniences should not be far from all 
seating areas, be they vending machines, charging points, shops, accessible toilets or Changing Places. 
Seating areas should also include access to flight information at an inclusive height to ease anxiety or stress 
related to flight departure.

===PAGE 774===

Exhibit 3.3.9.2.6: Caring Corner in Hong Kong Airport

Assistance lounges should be clearly signed with the international symbol of accessibility so their intended 
purpose and use is clear to passengers with disabilities who are likely to benefit from utilizing them. Their 
entrances should be wide enough to offer a turning circle for wheelchair users. Sightlines to staff members at 
the nearest desk and provided information should be obvious upon entry. Accessibility features, such as the 
nearest accessible toilet or changing place, and the availability of induction loops, for example, should be 
inclusively signed within the assistance lounge. The ability to inclusively access information in varying formats 
should also be considered within assistance lounges to enable full engagement for a range of users who may 
have cognitive, hearing or visual impairments. Easy read, visual, audio and captioned formats should all be 
considered, as should information available in different languages. 
The environment that is created within the airport's assistance lounge(s) should also be an important 
consideration. A calm, welcoming atmosphere will be important for neurodivergent passengers, in particular, 
and if passengers with disabilities are likely to spend time in assistance lounges rather than other lounges, the 
pleasant element of ‘delight’ in their experience should be similar to one experienced by their peers. This may 
include comfortable furniture choices that are likely to make a longer lounge stay more appealing. As staff 
members are also likely to be spending a substantial amount of time within assistance lounges when they are 
hosting, their seating arrangements, and the ergonomics and inclusivity of this, should also be considered.

3.3.9.2.7 Lighting Design 
The way in which lighting is arranged and used can have a large impact on the overall passenger experience 
in both the way it looks and feels, particularly for passengers with disabilities. 
The increasing and innovative use of LED lighting rather than more traditionally engineered lighting solutions 
can be utilized as an effective wayfinding tool by differentiating routes for passengers with disabilities by color 
as an alternative to or enhancement of wayfinding signs. 
Within facilities for people with disabilities, well-designed lighting is particularly important, both to encourage 
safe identification and navigation for those with visual impairments, and to enable effective lip reading for 
those who are deaf or hard of hearing. Even lighting levels throughout an area should be designed, wherever 
possible and practicable, and elements of glare should be avoided. Strobe and flash lighting and other special 
lighting effects should also be avoided as this can have a detrimental effect for people with disabilities, such 
as those with epilepsy, tinnitus and autistic individuals. The use of light can create visual cues and focal 
points help to improve both the look and feel of the space and promote good safety in design outcomes. 
3.3.9.2.8 Evacuation and Emergency Considerations 
The safety and security of all passengers and staff must be of Paramount importance at any airport. A 
consistent, effective emergency and evacuation strategy that includes equitable processes and procedures for 
those with disabilities is vital. Passengers and staff members with disabilities must receive the same level of 
notification, instruction and protection as their peers, and their safety must not be compromised in the event of 
an emergency. Appropriate building codes and regulations must be followed to ensure safety. 
756 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 776===
IATA 4 Passenger Terminal 
Exhibit 3.3.9.2.8: Evacuation Chair Demonstration at Maastricht Aachen Airport 
Source: Courtesy of Escape Mobility International 
As most elevators cannot be utilized in an emergency, alternative processes and procedures must be 
introduced for airport passengers and staff members with mobility impairments. Refuge areas for these 
individuals must be available close to the egress point, and international, inclusive signage should be used to 
aid understanding. 
Alll fire and emergency alarm systems should have audible and visual features to enable equitable notification 
for those with visual or hearing impairments. Where possible, two-way communication devices should be 
available throughout the building to assist in any response required. 
Having knowledge on the whereabouts of passengers and staff with additional requirements will vastly 
improve the speed, safety and efficiency of an evacuation in the event of an emergency. It is recommended 
that, where possible, airport journey stages, such as check-in, security and immigration, act as checkpoints to 
monitor passenger and staff member locations.

3.3.9.3 Specific Supporting Facilities 
3.3.9.3.1 Vehicles and Equipment 
For larger airport facilities, in particular, transit trains, shuttle buses and mobility buggies/karts are often 
utilized to ease the strain of time and distance in a passenger journey. Transit buses are often used to take 
Passengers from the airport building to aircraft and back again, transit trains shorten the transfer time between 
airport terminals, and shuttles minimize otherwise lengthy walking distances. Mobility buggies specifically 
assist persons with disabilities and/or additional assistance requirements. 
Exhibit 3.3.9.3.1a: Mobility Buggies Available for use at Seoul Airport 
Source: Incheon International Airport Corporation 
While transit vehicles are intended to ease the airport journey, they can be difficult to utilize, and their purpose 
is not always easy to understand for less familiar or confident passengers. Inclusive signage, information, 
seating areas and available staff can all assist with easing this unfamiliarity and support passengers in 
Preparation for transit. Airport websites should also include any information relating to transit vehicles to aid 
this familiarity and preparation further. 
758 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 778===
Be fF IATA Passenger Terminal 
Mobility buggies may also be available to support passengers with additional requirements to navigate the 
airport campus. Primarily, mobility buggies are for internal use and should be beneficial for any passengers 
who may benefit from extra support and assistance, including those with temporary, situational or hidden 
impairments. 
Mobility buggies should be well-maintained, safe and comfortable for passengers and staff utilizing them. This 
includes providing comfortable and spacious seating, and adequate space should be available to store all 
passengers’ luggage as well as ensuring ease of access both into and out of the buggy. All mobility buggies 
should also include audio and visual alarms to alert other staff and passengers of their presence. It is not 
unusual for wheelchair users to be unable to utilize mobility buggies due to limitations regarding transfer onto 
the buggy, and its ability to store mobility equipment. If this is the case, staff should be available to 
alternatively assist wheelchair users, ensuring they have an equitable assistance experience through the 
airport. 
Sufficient space should be provided for parking mobility vehicles directly outside assistance facilities, and 
corners should be protected with bollards to reduce the risk of accidental damage.

3.3.9.3.2 Help Points and Assistance Services 
Help points should be available for those who require assistance, whether that be due to an impairment or a 
temporary or situational need, in which locating a member of staff face-to-face is not possible. Help points that 
have been activated by a passenger should be responded to by staff in a timely manner. 
Exhibit 3.3.9.3.2: Call Point Installation at Airport Entrance 
Medested 
Falck 
Source: Copenhagen Airport 
Help points should be provided at key points of the Passenger journey throughout the airport, both internally 
and externally. Help points will often be used by passengers in moments of worry, confusion or anxiety and, 
therefore, should be set away from main thoroughfares or direct access routes and avoid being complex in 
their design. Their appearance should be consistent and easy to spot in busy or visually cluttered 
environments such as departure lounges or arrival halls, and provide inclusive and accessible functions. 
Clear, direct and well-considered instructions should be available in written, tactile and audio formats, which 
760 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 780===
ae IATA Biull Passenger Terminal 
can be intuitively activated. Passengers should be able to talk to or send a written message to staff, for 
example through a text number, to ensure their needs are being understood. 
3.3.9.3.3 Sensory Rooms and Quiet Areas 
Multi-Sensory Stimulation Environments (MSSEs) and quiet areas support those with sensory and cognitive 
impairments or mental health conditions to de-escalate or better manage the effects of the busy airport 
environment. The facilities and equipment provided should aim to respond flexibly to the needs of individuals. 
The overall interior should be calming, soft and neutral with an aim to avoid triggering any further 
overstimulation. 
MSSEs can provide specialized equipment to promote emotional self-regulation and support a reduction in 
distress, disruptive behaviors, anxiety, and self-engagement behaviors. The key consideration for sensory 
spaces is to ensure all the equipment provided is age-appropriate, either for adults or for children. Features 
intended to stimulate or calm those using the room should be relatable and intuitive so as to not cause further 
confusion or frustration. While the majority of users may have cognitive impairments, such as autism, the 
needs and requirements of those using the space will vary greatly; therefore, multiple options should be made 
available to respond to each individual effectively. This includes providing a range of furniture, lighting and 
segregated spaces that can be adapted to suit the needs of the passengers or staff who require the MSSE. 
A quiet area or relaxation space is another way of providing support to people with profound, multiple, or 
long-term conditions as well as those with anxiety, depression, or related conditions. A designated space to 
allow passengers or staff the time and room to reflect and relax will benefit a much more diverse range of 
passengers outside of those who require an MSSE. Quiet areas should be easily identifiable, well placed 
within the airport and accessible to all those who may require them, regardless of whether they do or do not 
have a visible disability. Quiet areas do not need to be complicated spaces; they should be an oasis of calm, 
a safe and comfortable space for those who wish to escape and de-escalate from the hustle and bustle of the 
wider airport environments. 
3.3.9.3.4 Service Animal Relief Areas 
Service animals will be accompanying certain passengers with disabilities on their airport journey, including 
but not limited to, those with visual, hearing, mobility and cognitive impairments as well as those with mental 
heaith conditions. It is, therefore, important that relief areas are provided for service animals and located in a 
manner that is easy to access and utilize for their owners. They are recommended to be situated within the 
terminal building in a location that is ideally proximate to the check-in and arrivals concourses as well as in 
airside departure lounges. External locations can be difficult to find, unsuitable for use in poor weather and, 
therefore, not inclusive to passengers with service animals. 
The route to any and all relief areas should be inclusively signed, provide level access and be well lit. 
Assistance from staff members should be available upon request. Appropriate relief areas should be 
available, where practicable, both landside and airside to ensure a relief area can be found and used 
wherever the passenger and service animal may be within the airport facility. Providing relief areas both 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 761 

===PAGE 781===
Se iy IATA a Airport Development Reference Manual 
landside and airside will also ensure the animal can be relieved prior to departure and on arrival, as well as 
within areas where dwell time can be lengthy, such as when near departure lounges or in transit areas. 
All Service Animal Relief Areas (SARAs) should include, at minimum: 
e Astep-free, well-lit access route and entrance way with appropriate, inclusive signage. 
e An automatic or easy-to-open entrance door with large clear-width provision. 
* Clear, concise instructions for use in large print and Braille formats. 
e Ahard, flat and slip-resistant surface for use by wheelchair users. 
© Awell-drained softer area (usually including grass or gravel) intended for animal relief. 
¢ The ability to wash the area down after use, typically with an accessible hose and appropriate drainage. 
e Bags, scoops and bins to enable the disposal of solid waste. 
e A sink and paper towel dispenser. 
e A drinking facility for the animal. 
e A call button connected to the Airport Control Center for the user to summon assistance, if required. 
e Recessed fixtures and fittings to avoid potential injury to wheelchair users and visually impaired users. 
All facilities and features should be in reach for both seated and standing users. Where more than one SARA 
is provided at an airport, it is recommended that wherever possible a common layout is adopted. This is 
specifically helpful to assist visually impaired users, avoiding the need to familiarize themselves with different 
facility configurations. 
3.3.9.4 Pre-Journey 
The passenger journey begins prior to arrival at the airport and, as such, information on the airport's website 
(including access guides or statements), applications and in other forms should be accessible to all. This may 
be via easily read, visual (with captions), audio or alternative language formats, and by creating sites and 
apps that are compatible with assistive technologies that users may own, such as screen readers. Information 
should be clear, concise and encourage an understanding of the step-by-step airport process, as well as the 
wider aviation experience. 
The airport's website should conform to WCAG standards. In addition, manual user testing should be 
completed by those with lived experience of disability as compliance with guidance does not always result in 
inclusivity of use. 
Once at the airport, a consistent visual messaging should be used for all information points, enabling 
passengers to gain confidence in navigating the airport environment. These visuals should be utilized 
consistently throughout the airport. Visual messaging and information are likely to be even more important in 
confusing or anxiety-inducing areas such as security and immigration, and this information-where possible 
and practicable-should be supplied in advance to allow passengers to prepare.

Se . 
IATA Passenger Terminal 
The primary function of FIDS is to provide live flight and boarding gate information to passengers. FIDS. 
should be located throughout the departures and arrivals journeys, avoiding long distances where flight 
information is unavailable. Some FIDS displays should be installed at a lower height for wheelchair users and 
those of shorter stature. Font size and color contrast should also be considered to facilitate legibility for those 
with visual impairments. 
As is the case with physical access in the built environment, not all digital solutions will suit every passenger 
need and preference. Providing alternative pathways is always encouraged and digital features should not, 
therefore, be seen as a replacement for built environment services, as removing these could equally exclude 
some users. 
3.3.9.5 Processing Facilities 
Passengers with disabilities should have an experience at processing facilities equitable to their peers. This 
should be the case regardless of whether the individual has a visible or non-visible disability. Processing 
facilities should be designed to be accessible to all passengers and staff, regardless of their access 
requirement. Service desks and counters should be designed to allow access from a seated position by both 
passenger and staff member. Induction loops should also be available, inclusively and obviously signposted at 
selected desks, and regularly tested to ensure they are in order and available for use, when required. 
3.3.9.6 Passengers Journey—Outbound 
3.3.9.6.1 Arrival at the Terminal/Departures Forecourt 
Passengers with disabilities should be granted choice and autonomy in how they arrive at the airport: train 
stations, bus stops, car parking spaces and taxi drop-off points should all provide physical accessibility 
features and be inclusively signed. Furthermore, as far as possible and practicable, the airport should be 
inclusively signed from the nearest train and/or metro stations and bus stops. Regardless of how a passenger 
or staff member arrives at or departs from the airport, the aim should always be to provide a seamless, 
inclusive service and experience. 
As terminal forecourts and drop-off areas are likely to be the first impression many passengers with 
disabilities get of an airport, drop-off area signs should include concise, easy-to-understand and inclusive 
terminology, and be displayed in an easily identifiable and welcoming manner. The location of the reserved 
drop-off area should be located as close as possible to one of the front doors of the terminal building and 
should have sufficient space for mobility services to wait for pre-arranged drop-offs. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 763 

===PAGE 783===
Be IATA mull Airport Development Reference Manual 
Exhibit 3.3.9.6.1: Heathrow Airport-T5 Drop-off Point

All passengers will also benefit from flat, barrier-free access in which any curbs are either dropped or 
designed to a curb-free layout, where possible, visually contrast with their surroundings, and are easy to 
navigate. Passengers with luggage and small children will also be looking for a stress-free start to their 
journey. (see 3.4 Landside Access Systems for more information). 
Those who require additional support when arriving at the airport should also be provided with the ability to 
announce their presence and request assistance both inside and outside of terminal buildings, via a help point 
or similar. While it is understood that, in the case of public transport interchanges, the airport does not always 
have direct control of the environment and infrastructure, an arrival or meeting point should ideally still be 
provided for those who require it, even if this must be within the airport boundary itself. It is recommended that 
an agreement is made with the interchange operator regarding this.

3.3.9.6.2 Terminal Entrance 
All access routes leading to the airport, whether from the car park, drop-off points or other transport modes, 
should be spacious, flat and step-free. While it is understood that security measures may require the 
presence of bollards or similar, any ‘street furniture’ that is offered such as seating, help points or bins should 
not obstruct the clear width of the access route, which should ideally be wide enough for two wheelchair users 
to pass one another, at minimum. There should also be an understanding and appreciation that many 
passengers, regardless of disability, will likely be unfamiliar with their surroundings and prone to confusion. 
Therefore, signage should be well positioned, obvious and inclusive in its contrast, text size and font. Where 
possible and practicable, tactile and Braille signage should also be provided. In addition, an uncluttered 
environment will enable those with visual or cognitive impairments to traverse the airport forecourt with a 
lesser likelihood of accident, distraction or overstimulation. All terminal entrances should also be universal in 
their design and welcome everyone equitably. 
Once inside the terminal, passengers should also have a clear line of sight to the next parts of their journey. 
Intuitive wayfinding allows everyone, including those with cognitive impairments and anxious passengers, to 
plan for the next stage of their journey in advance. 
Where possible, assistance services should be as close as practicable to the entrance door. An example is 
shown below with tactile surfaces leading to the reception where passengers can be registered, transferred 
into airport-serviced wheelchairs and prepared for their journey through the terminal and onto the aircraft. 
Exhibit 3.3.9.6.2: Larnaca Airport Assistance Reception 
Source: Mott MacDonald

3.3.9.6.3 Departures Hall 
In terms of accessibility, it is via the departures hall that passengers can be guided through the step-by-step 
airport journey and informed of accessible toilet, sensory room and SARA locations, among others. It is, 
therefore, vital that obvious, well-placed and inclusive signage is available throughout the departures hall, and 
passengers with disabilities are constantly aware of the airport's inclusive features and facilities, while being 
able to have an equitable experience to their peers. 
While passengers should be encouraged to move through the airport and given ample opportunity to plan 
their journey through check-in, security and to the boarding gate, it is also important to create a welcoming, 
inclusive atmosphere throughout the airport, with multiple opportunities for dwell space and energy recovery. 
Airports can be vast in their nature, and even smaller airports can be overwhelming and confusing to 
unfamiliar passengers, leading to a need for recuperation. 
The design of a corridor or walkway should allow passengers and staff to find their way (be this to toilets, 
departure gates or security screening) easily and unimpeded. Each part of the concourse should be wide 
enough for two wheelchair users to pass one another. Floor finishes should be chosen carefully to avoid 
reflection for those with sensory or cognitive impairments. Strong patterns, such as stripes that could be 
mistaken as steps, should be avoided to ease navigation for visually impaired people. While visual 
distractions throughout the airport journey can be pleasant for many, these should always be carefully 
considered in terms of access and inclusion prior to implementation. 
Obstacles, protruding elements and obstructions in the path of travel should be avoided. Where this is not 
possible, they should be clearly detectable with a strong luminant contrast to the surrounding surfaces. 
Similarly, the installation of safety manifestation graphics to assist in the identification of glass or glazed 
screens is a very important feature to mitigate the risk of collisions or injury for those with a visual impairment. 
3.3.9.6.4 Check-In and Self-Service Facilities 
There should be opportunity for every check-in or self-service process to be accessed equitably and 
independently by passengers with disabilities. This includes ensuring that some self-service units, bag tag 
printers and check-in kiosks are lowered, have accessible touch screens, captioned videos, tactile and Braille 
information and information provided in easy-read, audio and visual formats. Infrastructure for requesting staff 
assistance should also be accessible to all, regardless of impairment or access requirement. Accessible 
self-service and check-in facilities should be inclusively signed with the international symbol of accessibility.

3.3.9.6.5 Emigration (Outbound Passport Control) 
All border control areas within an airport should be accessible to both passengers and staff with disabilities. 
Sightlines of passport control desks, or similar, should be possible from afar so passengers are able to 
prepare themselves and their documentation in good time. Passageways and aisles should be wide enough 
for wheelchair users to turn within, and obstructions should be avoided. Accessible lanes should be marked 
with the international symbol of accessibility. A priority lane should be available for any passenger with a 
disability, whether they are self-reliant or receiving assistance from the airline or airport.

3.3.9.6.6 Passenger Security Screening 
It is not unusual for there to be a hierarchy between security and accessibility in certain areas of the airport, 
and it is important for the security and safety of all passengers and staff to take precedence. However, all 
should still be done, wherever possible, to ensure the security screening process is inclusive for everyone. 
Equitable security checks should be carried out on passengers and staff members with disabilities, but these 
may need to be adapted, where possible and practicable, to ensure effective screening and the sensitive 
handling of the situation, simultaneously. 
768 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 788===
=e 
IATA Passenger Terminal 
Exhibit 3.3.9.6.6: Security Screening Checkpoint at Lisbon Airport 
Source: ANA Aeroportos 
Equipment and aisles at security screening areas should be wide enough for wheelchair users to pass 
through, and obstructions should be avoided. Accessible lanes should be marked with the international 
symbol of accessibility and open to any passenger with a disability, assisted or self-reliant. 
Security checks can be particularly anxiety-inducing for passengers with disabilities, and while they and their 
mobility equipment, if present, should undergo security searches as fully as the nature of their impairments 
allow, care must be taken to ensure this search is completed sensitively, safely and with consideration for the 
passenger and their dignity. A private area should be available upon request for physical searches (i.e., when 
a passenger has personal medical equipment that they do not wish to expose in public). 
Post-search, passengers with disabilities should be able to access bag, tray, repack and seating areas in an 
equitable fashion, and should have the autonomy to repack and continue their airport journey independently, if 
this is preferred. 
3.3.9.6.7 Departures Lounge 
In many airports, the departure lounge contains retail as well as food and beverage facilities. With several 
built environment and social awareness adaptations, these areas can prove welcoming to all passengers and 
members of staff, regardless of impairment or access requirement. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 769 

===PAGE 789===
& i Se _— IATA + Airport Development Reference Manual 
Departure lounges, restaurants and bars should all have inclusive seating provision. Access routes to desks, 
bars, order points and points of sale in all areas should be direct and obstacle-free, with payment options also 
being accessible via portable payment devices, or otherwise. Ideally, there should also be alternative routes 
provided for those who find bright, busy retail environments overwhelming or confusing. 
The layout of departure lounges, retail and food and beverage facilities should, as far as possible, facilitate 
communication between staff and passengers with disabilities. Airline Premium Lounge entrance desks 
should be designed to allow face-to-face communication, whether the passenger or member of staff is seated 
or standing and induction loops should also be available. 
While accessibility-specific assistance lounges are covered before, not all passengers with disabilities will 
require airport assistance, and may choose to utilize an airline, or conventionally more premium, lounge. 
These lounges should harbor all necessary equipment and facilities to inclusively welcome and provide for 
passengers with disabilities in an equitable way. 
3.3.9.6.8 Boarding Gates 
Boarding gate seating layouts should allow all passengers, regardless of where they are seated, to have sight 
of a nearby FID. Priority seating should also be provided close to the gate for passengers with disabilities and 
their travel companions. Priority seating areas should follow the same design and layout at each boarding 
gate to allow ease of identification for passengers and assistance staff alike. 
Aircraft PBBs are the most inclusive solutions for passengers with mobility impairments, in particular, as they 
provide opportunities for autonomy and independence up to the aircraft door with step-free access. Where 
possible and practicable, PBBs should be designed to promote manageable gradients (particularly at 
transitions), even flooring and continuous lighting levels. Accessible features such as continuous handrails 
should also be considered. Where aircraft are on remote stands, the transport links to and from these stands 
should also be accessible to passengers with disabilities. 
In terms of process, wheelchair users who are not ambulant will have to transfer from their personal 
wheelchair onto an aisle chair at either the boarding gate, on the PBB or on an ambulift or similar vehicle. 
However, they are usually provided with the opportunity to remain in their wheelchairs for as long as possible 
as this is likely to provide the most comfortable and inclusive experience. Personal wheelchairs and other 
pieces of mobility equipment are often the last items to be loaded in the hold and the first to be unloaded. 
Both processes have to be undertaken with great care, so as to avoid any damage to personal mobility 
equipment.. Where practical, airports should consider providing elevators or lifts in close proximity to gate 
areas to allow for safe and expeditious transport of power wheelchairs and scooters between levels.

3.3.9.7 Passengers Journey—Inbound 
3.3.9.7.1 Disembarkation 
Exhibit 3.3.9.7.1: Boarding and Arrivals Process at Lisbon Airport 
Source: ANA Aeroportos 
Under usual circumstances, from an operational perspective, passengers that require assistance are the last 
passengers to disembark an aircraft. Assistance on arrival is expected to be available with minimal delay, and 
suitable equipment present to assist the passenger(s) in disembarking safely and effectively, whether by PBB 
or ambulift. Mobility equipment carried in the cargo compartment of the aircraft is expected to be returned as 
soon as possible, either in the PBB or on an ambulift at hard stands. Unless specifically requested by a 
passenger, these pieces of equipment are not to be taken to the baggage hall. 
3.3.9.7.2 Baggage Retrieval, Immigration and Customs 
In a similar way to security measures at airports, the immigration process can prove anxiety-inducing for many 
passengers, particularly those who require assistance and support with physical, sensory or cognitive access. 
Information relating to the immigration process should be provided in a variety of formats, and available for 
passengers to access ahead of time. Easy read, visual, and captioned audio formats are recommended, as 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 771 

===PAGE 791===
Be IATA iW Airport Development Reference Manual 
are formats available in different languages. Orientation of the immigration area, and a description of the 
process, should also be available to visually impaired passengers, if required. Any apps or kiosks that 
expedite the process for passengers should be designed to accommodate all user needs. 
Well-signed and staffed assistance lanes can make a huge difference to passengers with additional 
requirements, as can noise-reducing materials within the immigration area, and adapted equipment for 
passenger and staff use when filling in forms or other documentation. All immigration processes and 
equipment should be set up to ensure staff members with disabilities are able to work in an equitable manner. 
Accessible restrooms, adult changing facilities and SARAs should be provided prior to immigration, wherever 
space and local security regulations allow. 
Post-immigration, inclusive seating and signage should be readily available to allow dwell space for over￾stimulated passengers and provide an ease of understanding and journey flow for those continuing onto 
baggage reclaim and arrivals. 
For passengers with checked baggage, the baggage reclaim area is a necessary part of their airport journey. 
This area is where passengers are likely to have to wait for their baggage to arrive via the carousel, and the 
first area that has the ability and space for restrooms and seating facilities. The inclusion of these in an 
accessible capacity is of paramount importance, as is the correct signage and communication facilities, should 
passengers need to contact staff or transport organizations for assistance with their onward journey. 
Passengers with disabilities, in particular, may require additional assistance within the baggage reclaim area. 
This may involve the removal of their baggage from a carousel, support in communicating with a transport 
organization or relative regarding their onward journey, or the pushing of their baggage trolley through 
arrivals.

3.3.9.7.3 Leaving the Terminal/Arrivals Hall 
The arrivals experience at airports should be as inclusive as the departures experience. The arrivals hall 
should provide the same level of accessible features and facilities to ensure a welcoming environment for 
arriving passengers. 
When leaving the terminal, passengers may be confused as to the direction of their hotel or vehicle, or where 
they have arranged to meet a relative or friend. Equipment such as public telephones should be at an 
accessible height, and with appropriate knee recesses, for wheelchair users and those of shorter stature, and 
have large, contrasting tactile buttons for use by those with visual impairments. A text number should also be 
available for deaf and hard of hearing passengers, as well as those with speech impairments who may not 
feel comfortable with using the phone. Accessible help points and payment machines should also be available 
in car parking facilities and at the airport boundary, wherever possible and practicable. 
3.3.9.8 Passengers Journey—Transfers 
Arrangements for transferring passengers should be accessible and accommodate those who require 
additional assistance and support. Walking distances and the time this is likely to take for a passenger or 
member of staff with a mobility impairment or experience of fatigue, for example, should be considered at 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 773 

===PAGE 793===
wae ; 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
every stage of the transfer journey. Inclusive seating and dwell spaces, as described in more detail earlier in 
this section, should be readily available and include spaces to be utilized by wheelchair users. Inclusive 
transfer information and signage should also be present at these dwell points, as well as throughout the 
transfer space itself. Where the distances to be covered by foot are too great, specialized accessible transport 
equipment or other assistance should be provided. 
Exhibit 3.3.9.8: Accessible Height Tables for Security Search Preparation 
Source: Mima 
3.3.9.9 Access and Inclusion for Staff Members 
Access and inclusion for staff members should be considered at every airport. Any airport back-of-house 
environment should be designed to be accessible to staff members with disabilities to promote an inclusive 
workplace and diverse workforce. 
Simply put, equal consideration should be given to staff members with disabilities, and their individual 
requirements, as is given to passengers with disabilities throughout the airport journey. This relates to clear 
width in corridors, the color contrast and tactile formats of back-of-house wayfinding systems and turning 
circle provisions for wheelchair users. It also includes accessible features and facilities in the built 
774 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 794===
He | ; 
IATA + Passenger Terminal 
environment back-of-house areas such as accessible toilets and Changing Places, availability of sensory 
rooms, dwell spaces, inclusive signage and digital facilities, and SARAs. 
Equipment such as desks, lounge information points and retail outlets should be designed for use by 
members of staff with physical, sensory and cognitive impairments. Staff should be made aware of the 
purpose and use of equipment and facilities, such as induction loops and quiet areas, to enable them to notify 
passengers of their presence and support utilization, wherever possible and practicable. All airport staff 
should be trained on the airport's evacuation procedures and processes, including the use of evacuation 
chairs. 
Consideration should also be given to the inclusive recruitment of employees with disabilities and their ability 
to complete a variety of interesting, flexible and challenging roles to the best of their ability. After all, staff 
members are an airport's most frequent visitors, so physical access within the built environment and social 
awareness and inclusion are both of paramount importance. Ultimately, involving those with lived experience 
of disability as a part of the airport's workforce will lead to a more empathetic, progressive and inclusive 
airport for passengers and staff alike to enjoy and appreciate.

3.3.10.1 Introduction 
Commercial activities are now an important source of non-aeronautical revenues for many airports, with 
income being generated from a wide range of activities.

Airports have evolved from pure transport infrastructure into businesses serving a much wider range of 
customer needs. Non-aviation activities can deliver a number of benefits, such as: 
° The additional revenues they generate can lower airport charges for passengers and airlines, incentivizing 
competition between airline stakeholders while providing additional funding for improving infrastructure 
and facilities 
e A good shopping offer, including F&B, retail and entertainment can help to differentiate an airport, and 
critically enhance the passenger experience and the airport's reputation on a local, regional and 
international scale 
e The airport city concept-the development of the airport as an urban node-can help stimulate local 
economic activity and can, if properly planned and executed, help make aviation more sustainable 
776 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 796===
ae ww , 
IATA Passenger Terminal 
A successful airport requires good quality and affordable retail and F&B outlets, which passengers now simply 
expect. Airport concessions can make an important contribution to an airport's success, but require careful 
and timely planning that includes keeping up with evolving consumer tastes. 
An important element to consider throughout the planning of airport retail areas are the operational 
requirements of the airport and its users (i.e., airlines). Planners should always take into account the needs of 
customers to deliver balanced solutions that include passenger experience requirements, a consistent Level 
of Service (LoS), and the operational needs of the airport and airlines to use the infrastructure efficiently. 
Discussing and agreeing to the airport's retail strategy with airport operational staff and key users is highly 
recommended from an early stage in the planning process, both for the overall strategy and on a project-by￾project basis. 
In this section of the ADRM, the term ‘airport retail’ is defined as selling goods and services to consumers or, 
more commonly, ‘shopping’. It is part of the ‘non-aviation business’ (also called ‘non-aeronautical business’) 
as opposed to ‘aviation business’ (everything related to the airport's core business of aircraft handling). This 
section is intended to help airport owners, managers, planners and their commercial partners develop an 
airport non-aviation business that meets customer needs and supports the bottom line.
