(a) Duty Free on Departures 
‘Duty-free’ has become synonymous with airport shopping ever since the first products were sold without tax 
at Shannon Airport in 1947. Technically, duty-free means free of excise duties on alcohol and tobacco, 
whereas tax-free indicates the absence of sales tax (e.g., value-added tax, or VAT). The distinctions have 
somewhat blurred over the years, and in many countries all shops situated airside at the airport are called 
duty-free. In this chapter, all of these shops are defined as simply ‘airside retail’. 
For most international airports, airside retail is an important contributor to net total income. Airside retail 
performance can be much higher than at a regular shopping mall or main street retail. Examples include the 
world's single biggest duty-free store at Tel Aviv Ben Gurion Airport and Seoul Incheon Airport, which in 2016 
had the highest spending per passenger. 
According to Generation Research, around USD 40 billion in gross sales was generated at airports around the 
world in 2016. However, it is important to keep in mind that the global industry always faces challenges and is 
subject to external demand shocks in the form of economic crises, currency volatility, terrorism, pandemics, 
and natural disasters. Any drop in passenger numbers can adversely impact airport retail. In addition, online 
retail competition and shifting consumer behavior pose further challenges to maintaining a successful airport 
retail environment. 
Despite this, global duty-free retailers have strengthened their position to grasp the opportunities presented by 
integrating horizontally and vertically. The world's current no.1 travel retail company, DUFRY (with 24% of the 
market) has built its critical mass by integrating through takeovers of World Duty Free and Nuance Group. 
Global duty-free sales growth from 2005 to 2016 outstripped passenger growth. Average sales per passenger 
(spend per head, or SPH) grew, especially between 2005-2010, but have stabilized between 2010-2016: 
Exhibit 3.3.10.2.1b: Global SPH Evolution in Duty-Free Shopping 
CAGR 2005-2016 2005-2010 2010-2016 
Pax +5.2% +4.1% +6.1% 
Sales +8.5% +10.6% +6.8%

(b) The Importance of Emotions 
There are a number of reasons why passengers are attracted to duty-free shopping: 
Bringing a gift to hosts 
Buying something for people left back home (the guilt feeling) 
Passengers have time available (‘dwell time’) between check-in and boarding the aircraft and nowhere to 
go-better to spend time browsing in shops and restaurants than sitting in a waiting room 
Lower airfares in real terms have left passengers feeling that they can spend their perceived travel 
savings on an airport purchase 
Airport shopping is not necessarily primarily about the cheapest price 
Flying can be both a thrilling and stressful experience, and while every effort should be made to provide a 
calm and well-planned environment for passengers, this can lead to a higher retail spend 
(c) Differences With Downtown Retail 
Airport retail is distinctly different from regular downtown retail or shopping malls, resulting in higher spending 
in airport environments: 
In shopping malls, people come to shop, whereas at airports they come to fly. So, an airport must go to 
greater lengths to entice a customer 
Shopping malls have multiple entrances and exits. Airports have one directional passenger flow to attract 
and convert passengers into buyers 
Unlike a shopping mall, potential customers cannot avoid an airport mail when airside 
Shopping malls have regular customers, airports generally have less frequent travelers 
Airport retail requires different techniques to attract time-constrained passengers. With limited time, 
offering too many choices, too many brands within a product or price category, competition for the same 
article in different shops can confuse airport customers 
Shopping malls can have multiple levels with food courts on the top floor or in the basement. At airports, 
retail works best when it is on the same floor as the boarding gates 
Airport retail contracts are also different. They usually have high concession fees in the form of a 
percentage of gross sales. Regular retail contracts are usually based on a fixed rent per m? but also 
sometimes include a percentage of sales Airport rents are often higher; margins can be higher too, but so 
are the operating costs (e.g., opening hours and staff) 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 779

(d) Planning 
The following recommendations are based on feedback from projects at small, medium and large airports 
globally: 
e Airport retail should be considered in the design stage of terminal projects. The involvement of an airport 
concession planner can ensure that the space is suitably designed. A balanced approach is required to 
identify the optimal mix of retail that should always be planned around operational priorities 
e Arectangular shape and a central airside market square, are well suited to retail. These market squares 
must have sufficient depth to make retail and F&B readily available to passengers. A central market 
square is needed to build maximum critical mass. Long, shallow terminals and concourses, straight or 
curved, are suboptimal because they lack commercial space, cannot accommodate facilities on two sides 
and ‘spread out’ the passenger flow too much 
e When exiting the security filter, passengers should come into a ‘decompression zone’ where available 
time, boarding information and directions should be immediately clear 
e The main duty-free store is either centrally planned across the exit from security, or is a ‘walkthrough 
store’ where all passengers must automatically walk through. However, care should be taken to ensure 
unimpeded traffic flow. Retail in an airport should always be “on the way” and not “in the way” to avoid 
hampering the natural flow of passengers 
e Luxury brand boutiques selling fashion and accessories should be near the central duty-free store 
e Airport retail stores need storefront width, not depth. Merchandising should aim to tempt passengers 
inside and the brand/category choices should be simple and clear

(f) Duty-free on arrival 
The customs authorities in many countries allow duty-free shopping on arrival. In fact, in airports such as 
Istanbul, Oslo, Zurich, Johannesburg and Sao Paolo, it is the main source of retail income. Residents do not 
buy on departure, but on arrival. A special case is the above-mentioned largest duty-free store in the world in 
Tel Aviv, where passengers do buy on departure, but pick up the goods on return. This form of duty-free 
shopping does not compete with domestic retail, but rather with the country/airport where the passenger 
returned from (one of the rationales for duty-free on arrival). 
In planning, duty-free arrival stores are best located in the reclaim area next to the central exit from customs. 
At the above-mentioned airports, they are sometimes larger than the departure duty-free stores. 
(g) Logistics 
Airport retail requires special logistics and it is of crucial importance that planning takes this into account. 
Changes after a terminal has been put into operation are much more expensive. Care must be given to: 
e Accommodate the duty-free supply process and separate product security screening 
Plan goods elevators in the terminal of sufficient size to allow large product carts 
e Plan a separate delivery corridor at the back of the stores 
e Integrate quick resupply storage spaces at the back of the stores (“hand storage”), as well as dedicated 
storage in close proximity to the stores 
e Plan employee pause rooms and welfare facilities 
e Design waste and recycling flows that comply with national health regulations and are out of sight of 
passengers 
e Plan shop shutters and/or product island screens to protect during shop closure hours 
e Design the shop spaces with sufficient utility and IT access points. Airports usually provide ‘core & shell’ 
units while the retail operator pays and installs the shop interior 
Airports are becoming more adept at understanding and accommodating F&B supply streams and operator 
needs in such areas as food deliveries and waste management. This can lead to remarkable reductions in 
space required for ‘back-of-house’ processes. Specialized companies exist that can assist with this process. 
3.3.10.2.2 Airside Food and Beverage 
(a) The Increased Importance of Airside Food and Beverage 
The importance of F&B has greatly increased at airports. It was once a neglected area with mediocre, 
generic-looking restaurants that served plain food. It is now a magnet rather than an afterthought in airport 
planning and customer expectation. Today, more than 50% of passengers eat and drink at airports. F&B 
concepts have become more modern and sophisticated. Local brands make the airport stand out and superior 
quality is expected. Celebrity chef-led restaurants are popping up at many airports. “Eating is the new

shopping”. In fact, in recent years, airside retail SPH has decreased in saturated markets such as Europe, but 
airside F&B has increased. 
Exhibit 3.3.10.2.2: Luxury Seafoods Concept 
Source: Market Square Consult 
(b) Trends in Airport F&B: Planning, Consumers, Operations, Logistics 
When F&B is needed closer to the gates. Generic seating space is converted into universal F&B spaces with 
tables and seats. It has been observed that having F&B on a mezzanine level may only attract 50% of the 
passengers than a facility at the same departure level. Whenever possible, consideration should be given to 
integrate F&B with retail, preferably on the departures level in such a way that it does not obstruct the 
passenger flow. 
Operator-driven trends for airside F&B provisions include celebrity chefs, pop-up restaurants, food trucks at 
the airport (mobile outlets), vending machines at gate and food delivery to gate via app ordering. 
Signs of the airport F&B market becoming mature include rising standards and increased competition. In the 
battle for attention (and the traveler's wallet) the ‘celebrity chef has entered the airport scene. This may be a 
local restaurant operator with a stand-alone contract with the airport or a regional “hero” with a wider audience 
who has franchised their concept to the master airport F&B concessionaire. 
Consumer-driven trends are the increased awareness of dining at the airport, the need to eat at airports 
where food is not offered on aircraft, especially on LCCs, increased pricing ranges and affordability, as well as 
the search for authentic regional food experiences.

An industry trend is the desire of consumers to be in control of their actions (e.g., online check-in). This trend

e Fear of missing a flight-consider FIDS inside restaurants 
e Fear of not having enough time for the entire meal process—Reassure customers 
Affordability 
The range and affordability of dining options are important factors in whether passengers decide to dine at the 
airport. 
Experiences and ‘trueness’ 
Consumers want experiences and stories; they can be ‘engagement driven’ and their F&B needs are shifting 
towards more ‘meaningful’ food. Driven by the drastic growth of social media self-expression and digital 
marketing opportunities, out-of-home restaurant food now has to fulfil more needs of customers: 
It is important for an airport to employ a mix of F&B concepts, including any of the following: 
¢ Trusted international brands in fast-food, conveniently grouped in a food court 
¢ Local F&B brands that help create an important sense of place

3.3.10.2.3 Airside Services 
A range of airside services appear at airports worldwide. 
(a) Currency Exchange 
Modern, well-managed, large international airports limit the number of currency exchange operators to one or 
a few, to develop consistency in service and avoiding customer confusion. There are, however, still airports 
(mostly in developing countries) that feature tens of small operators scattered around the airport, each with 
their own exchange rates and, therefore, creating maximum confusion with passengers—obviously something 
to avoid. 
The following are useful planning recommendations and trends: 
e Airside currency exchange counters are often open ‘pods’ without glass barriers and looking quite 
spectacular, blending in with the airport mall design 
e Landside currency exchange counters are often located in the baggage reclaim hall or in the form of an 
automatic teller machine (ATM) in the arrivals hall 
({b) Airside Hotels 
Transfer passengers or those with early departures are the target market for airside hotels. They offer 
sleeping rooms or pods (capsule hotels) on an hourly basis and separate shower rooms for travelers with a 
long lay-over or an early connection the next day. Many modern concepts appear at airports around the world. 
In planning these hotels, care must be taken in creating: 
e Comfortable climate control 
¢ Daylight (when not possible in rooms, then at corners where passengers can orient themselves) 
e High standard of cleanliness 
° Meeting fire/emergency regulations 
e Excellent noise isolation (transfer passengers are from different time zones) 
e Plumbing in the terminal allows a high volume of waste and water flows 
e Convenient wayfinding to/from the hotel 
(c) Spa and Wellness Centers 
Another trend in international travel is spa and wellness centers, which exist in many formats: 
¢ International chains with a full menu of services (e.g., massage, hair, manicure/pedicure) 
e Individual local operators of wellness and massage services 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 785

IATA vill Airport Development Reference Manual 
e Beauty parlors focusing on hair, make-up and nails 
e Sauna and hammam centers 
e Fitness centers 
e Pop-up kiosks with a chair and a masseur 
e Automatic massage chairs with coin operation 
(d) Information Centers 
Even with good signage, it is still important to have a clearly visible, centrally located information center where 
passengers can seek a wider range of information. 
Help staff should ideally be dressed in bright colors, have excellent communication skills, and possess the 
necessary information to answer a range of possible questions. 
(e) Airline and Commercial Lounges 
Many full-service airlines have their own lounges for their business and/or first-class passengers. These 
lounges are a critical part of their product strategy. Airports also have commercial lounge operators who may 
offer access to both airlines and individual customers. These types of lounges include: 
1. VIP Meet & Greet-including personal assistance to and from the gate, baggage handling and delivery, 
limousine transfer and buggy service 
Transit hotel-airside rooms and showers 
Business center—reception, meeting and conference rooms, and secretarial services 
Exclusive airport restaurants 
gy F ON 
Spa, massage and beauty services 
(f) VIP Center 
VIP centers often cater to diplomatic/political customers as well as CIP and usually have their own security 
and passport contro! channel, car parking positions, plus direct access to the apron to deliver their guests to 
the aircraft door by car. 
The cost of operating a VIP center is usually very high and its economics depend on the likelihood of national 
governments paying the VIP center bills for diplomats and politicians they dispatch or receive (in some 
countries, governments refuse to pay). It is, therefore, often a cost center and eats into the airport's profits.

(g) Children's Play Area 
A very useful convenience, particularly for airports with a large volume of holiday travelers, is a dedicated 
area for children to play. Play areas can be supported by sponsors or even operated commercially. Safety, 
cleanliness and maintenance are obviously key demands. 
(h) Smoking Lounges 
In many locations, smoking is not permitted in public buildings, while others allow smoking lounges in 
dedicated spaces. 
(i) Fast-Track 
Fast-track passenger services are now available at many airports. Amsterdam Airport Schiphol has packaged 
it in a wider set of services called Privium, which gives you premium parking, lounge access and dedicated 
security and passport control. The service can also be of interest for airlines to service their premium and 
frequent-flyer customers. 
(j) Personal Shopper 
Some airports have Personal Shopper services. At London Heathrow, for example, customers are contacted 
after booking to discuss what the passenger is looking for, the budget and the time available. If the passenger 
commits to buying more than GBP 250, the Personal Shoppers (a team of 24) will arrange where to meet the 
passenger after security. 
(k) Limousine Service 
Limo service remains a valued service for some passengers. Some airlines offer to pick up and deliver their 
premium passengers at both ends of their journey. 
(I) Other Airside Services 
Other commercial airside services at airports include airside business/conference centers, casinos, swimming 
pools, cinemas, tropical gardens, golf practice boxes, landside city tours for transfer passengers, live music 
performances, shoeshine services, and delivery services of food to your gate.

3.3.10.2.4 Landside Retail 
The retail and F&B requirements of the landside area also needs to be considered. The customer segments 
include: 
e Arriving passengers 
e¢ Meeters & greeters 
e Departing passengers (in the check-in area) 
e Well-wishers. 
¢ Airport staff (e.g., handling agents, security, immigration, police, customs, cleaning staff) 
e Airline crews 
e Airport visitors 
e Taxi drivers 
e Public transport transfer passengers (if the airport is a public transport junction) 
e¢ Nearby community inhabitants 
There are airports with nothing more than a news stand and a coffee shop, and there are airports with large 
landside shopping malls. Hong Kong International Airport and Frankfurt Airport have impressive landside 
malls.

Many considerations come to mind when planning landside retail services, including staff requirements: 
e Are the non-flying customer segments large enough to warrant substantial retail? 
How far is the airport away from the city? If far away, it won’t attract a lot of non-flying visitors for 
shopping (contrary to eating and drinking, which happens everywhere) 
Does the airport have a lot of landside offices and tenants (i.e., an airport city)? 
Consideration for a supermarket 
Convenience stores, news and book kiosks, drugstores/pharmacies, telecom stores and luggage/travel 
gadget stores usually do well in landside retail 
Operating margins are lower at airports because costs are higher. Therefore, landside retail concession 
contracts tend to have lower fees and longer contract periods 
(a) Landside Food & Beverage 
F&B is the dominant player in landside retail areas. Recommendations and considerations include: 
Meeters & greeters, airport staff and airport city workers are key target customer segments. To a lesser 
degree are well-wishers with their departing friends or relatives, non-flying visitors and other groups 
Airport staff and airport city workers typically come in peaks during lunchtime or when work shifts change 
To attract visitors to the airport, it may consider offering combi packages of free parking when money is 
spent landside, or vice versa (the parking ticket provides a discount) 
Because it is a public area, the landside F&B facilities may be more prone to misuse and may have to be 
supervised and cleaned more rigorously than airside facilities 
Opening hours may be around the clock at large hubs, which means higher operating costs than 
restaurants in the city 
Many landside food concepts change their menu according to the time of day 
Airport F&B units of large international food chains can be the busiest of the entire company 
The bigger the airport, the more opportunity exists for full-service and even celebrity chef-led restaurants 
A consideration to make for the airport's commercial management is always: do we want passengers to 
spend money landside or airside? Typically, the bulk of the income is made with airside retail. F&B simply 
ears less, so airports want their departing passengers airside as soon as possible. However, desired 
behavior cannot be forced and this equilibrium should be gently and carefully sought 
(b) Landside Services 
Airport Information Booth 
Just as with the airside information center, many people require additional information. Therefore, having 
a Clearly visible information center centrally located in the arrivals hall is a necessity.

e Luggage Wrapping 
This service is growing in popularity. More people fly and there are many first-time flyers among the new 
middle classes. Many of these people want the added security of having their luggage wrapped. A 
luggage wrapping unit is best positioned close to the check-in counters. The business model is usually 
fixed rent per position. 
e Dry Cleaning 
At larger airports, airline crews and airport staff find it a convenience to have a dry cleaner close to their 
work. For the business model, such a service concession requires a percentage fee on gross sales and/or 
fixed rent per m?. 
e Shoe Repair 
This vital service for airline crews is often combined with the dry cleaning service or a shoe shop in the 
landside terminal area. 
e Bag Storage 
Indispensable at major airports with large amounts of transfer traffic, either with a manned counter or 
unmanned wails of deposit boxes. Usually located in a basement or remote corner because this is not an 
impulse service and does not earn a lot of income. 
e Bank and Currency Exchange 
Currency exchange operators would rather have an airside booth because the cost of securing the booth 
(i.¢., glass walls) is lower than landside. Therefore, there are more ATMs in the arrivals hall than full 
counters. 
Full-service banking offices are getting scarcer at airports because banking is becoming more electronic. 
In many countries, however, there is a lot of cash traffic at the concessions and other business partners, 
who would like to deposit that cash at a bank close by. This is typically a concession with fixed rent per 
m, 
e Ticket Sales—Taxi, Limousine and Other Private Transport 
Airports should inform their passengers in the arrivals hall before they are confronted with the variety of 
private transport possibilities: taxi, limousine and TNCs such as Uber, Lyft, etc. Information can be in the 
form of a taxi dispatch office (inside or outside the terminal), counters for limousines, counters for private 
buses (many LCCs offer such deals) and clear signage pointing out the taxi prices and location. 
Sometimes this information is provided in the baggage reclaim area, so that passengers can prepare 
better. 
e Ticket Sales—Public Transport 
An information counter and facilities to provide assistance for the purchase of tickets to the public 
transport system are important. Visitors to a new country may not know how to operate a ticket-selling 
machine. The resulting irritation affects the airport's reputation, so preventing this is worth the investment. 
e Travel Agent 
With so many travel bookings (e.g., flights, hotels, car rentals) taking place on the Internet, the travel 
agent's use may seem dwindling in some countries. However, passengers may still prefer human contact 
at the airport. The business model is usually a fixed rent per m? of counter and back-office space.

* Tourist Office 
A regional tourist office is sometimes present at a counter in the arrivals hall, and could be considered

¢ Hotel Reservation 
This service is becoming outdated. It is typically a bank of telephones or a separate hotel reservation

3.3.10.2.5 City Tours 
An interesting service offered at larger hub airports, city tours offer transfer passengers with a layover of four 
hours or more a fully-serviced tour to the city center, with return service to the airport. At some airports, 
passengers who pre-booked this trip get welcomed and picked up airside. 
3.3.10.2.6 Landside Passenger Lounge 
Some airports have airline or independent lounges located landside in the terminal arrivals hall for their 
preferred customers to spend their layover or take a shower and a nap. Economically, such a lounge takes a 
vast amount of space and should be carefully balanced against the benefits by airport management. 
3.3.10.3 Other Non-Aviation Business 
3.3.10.3.1 Car Parking 
(a) World regional comparison 
According to the latest ACI Economics Report 2019, car parking revenue and other non-aeronautical revenue 
follow retail concessions as the second and third sources of revenue at 20.9% and 17.8%, respectively. 
There is significant variation in the infrastructure designated for car parking across regions. In North America, 
most airport users commute to airports using their own automobiles, but in other parts of the world, 
passengers are typically dropped off at terminal buildings or use public transit as the preferred mode of 
transport to and from airports. As a result, it is not surprising that a key revenue generator in North America is 
car parking and related concessions. 
(b) Self-operation or Outsourcing 
Airports have the choice of operating the car parks (parking lots or garages) themselves or outsourcing the 
business. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 791 

===PAGE 811===
iil we 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
When self-operating, airports require thorough knowledge of the business and a department of people 
dedicated to the sector in operations, security, maintenance and management. Parking systems are evolving 
and, in order to stay on top of their game, airports must have real specialists in house. Furthermore, these 
airports must have the capacity to finance and develop new parking facilities, renovations and systems. These 
can be huge investments. Another consideration is the need to compete with off-airport car parking because 
many business people have car parking lots close to the airport. Whether an investment in car parking by the 
airport pays off also depends on the environment-driven substitution trend of cars for public transport and 
shared TNCs (e.g., Uber). 
When outsourcing the parking business, a range of specialist companies can help including: 
e Full-service car parking operators (develop, finance, build, own, operate and transfer) 
¢ Car parking management companies (managing car parks for a fixed management fee and a percentage 
of the returns) 
e Car park system providers (barriers, signage, payment processing) 
¢ Online parking specialists (managing a portal for pre-booking and payment) 
¢ Investors (develop, finance, build and own car parking garages) 
3.3.10.3.2 Car Rental 
As tourism and business grows, so does the demand for car rental. This business is very mature and 
competitive. Airports usually have a minimum of five global car rental brands on their premises. In many 
countries, there are plenty of local companies with a small operation competing with the big brands. They are 
either also at the airport with a counter or just outside the airport. 
Car rental is very common, particularly in North America, where it represents 16.3% of total non-aviation 
fevenues, against a world average of 6% (see Exhibit 3.3.10.2.1a). 
A typical airport car rental service is located at a customer reception desk in the arrivals hall, after which the 
customer walks to a dedicated car parking facility or is driven there by a shuttle. Car drop-off after use by the 
customer is often made very easy and without any delay. Proper wayfinding to find the car rental service is 
essential. 
Sometimes arrivals hall space is so scarce that airports locate the car rental service points in portable cabins 
near the car parking lots. Or, a car rental company may not have a customer service point at the airport at all, 
but instead has powerful website marketing and succeeds in shuttling its customers to a location far away 
from the airport premises. 
At a lot of large airports, however, the opportunity to materially improve the airport's car rental product offering 
and revenue can only be delivered by providing a consolidated car rental center.

===PAGE 812===
Se Sy IATA al Passenger Terminal 
3.3.10.3.3 Advertising 
Another specialist industry is the airport advertising business, which is part of the ‘out-of-home media’ world. 
Its worldwide share of airport non-aviation business is 2.3% in 2019 (see Exhibit 3.3.10.2.1a). Some very 
large outdoor advertising companies have dedicated airport departments. 
As with car parking, airports can operate their own advertising or outsource it. The preferred model for large 
airports is to outsource. However, some larger airports manage advertising in-house to earn the full 
advertising income and to be in control of their critical digital and analog media infrastructure, being part of the 
all-important customer journey through the airport. 
More digital media is the trend, allowing more flexibility and personalized messaging. Copenhagen Airport 
was the first to go 100% digital. Elsewhere, closer partnerships between airports, retailers, brands and media 
companies are the trend. 
3.3.10.3.4 Terminal Office Rental 
If office space is available, it should not be in the premium areas. Ground floor space is consumer business 
terrain and can generate income growing with traffic and entrepreneurial inventiveness, which office rent 
cannot. 
Many airport partners would like to, or have a need to, rent a terminal office: 
e Handling agents 
e Airlines 
« Security companies 
e Police 
e Immigration 
e¢ Customs 
e Airport operational management 
e Airport commercial management 
This list excludes concessionaires and consumer service providers with their service units, back-of house 
space, offices and storage space. Typically, terminal office rent goes per square meter per month and 
includes arrangements for cleaning, utility, security and maintenance services.

3.3.10.3.5 Taxis and Transportation Network Companies 
(a) Taxis 
It is important to carefully manage taxi operations, including the taxi line. Arriving passengers should not be 
exposed to aggressive solicitation for taxi services. Most airports have licensed the right to pick up 
passengers to one or more taxi companies against a fee per transaction. It requires the taxi companies to 
clearly identify their taxis so as to prevent non-licensed ‘spontaneous’ taxis from getting passengers. In 
addition, a proper queue is organized and very often a taxi dispatch office is located inside the arrival halls or 
at the taxi queue. In some cases, passengers can pre-pay for the taxi at the taxi dispatch office and avoid the 
fear of being overcharged. 
Airports should have clear taxi information (prices, destinations, pictures of the taxis, reassurances) in the 
baggage reclaim area where the arriving passenger is still relatively at ease. A chaotic taxi business creates 
an unwelcome negative image for the city and the airport, and that is why airports should devote strategic 
attention and money to making the taxi experience as pleasant as possible. 
(b) Transportation Network Companies 
TNCs are private car-sharing companies such as Uber and Lyft. TNCs are increasingly popular and here to 
stay. The impact of accommodating TNCs at an airport can be large: 
e Increased curbside congestion 
e Increased number of dead-head trips 
e Increased vehicle emissions 
¢ Inability to require use of alternative fuel vehicles 
e Need for new or expanded vehicle staging areas 
e Enforcement required, but less than taxicabs 
* Obtain technology to track vehicles/document number of trips 
However, where local regulations allow TNCs, airports must find a way to embrace the operations. The 
current practice is that local/state agencies regulate vehicles and drivers. Airports can supplement local/state 
regulations by requiring the TNC to: 
¢ Comply with airport rules 
© Obtain airport permit 
e = Maintain insurance while on airport 
e Limitations on vehicle staging, drop-off and pick up 
e Use of geofence to limit where rides are accepted 
e Enforcement/auditing provisions

we i . 
IATA Passenger Terminal 
3.3.10.4 Landside Real Estate 
Airport landside real estate development has become an important focus for airports as a means to develop 
additional non-aviation business revenues. Besides increased revenues, the development of the airport as a 
business location can drive traffic growth. 
When planning landside commercial real estate, the following recommendations are made: 
No airport city will be successful if the core processes of the airport are impacted adversely. 
3.3.10.4.1 Recommendations 
(a) Phased and flexible Development 
Similar to a master plan, landside real estate should be developed in phases, with enough flexibility built-in to 
allow for new kinds of developments and functions. As the economy of a region or country develops and 
transforms, new strategic opportunities will present themselves. If there is no current demand for prime office 
space in the short or medium term, there might be in the long term as cities get saturated and/or as the 
service sector of a country develops. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 795 

===PAGE 815===
Tata ie Airport Development Reference Manual 
Exhibit 3.3.10.4.1a: Phase One of Coeur d’Orly 
Source: ADP 
(b) Ensure multi-modal accessibility 
The airport should be accessible by multiple modes of transport. In the context of landside real estate 
development, this serves two purposes: 
1. It will increase the attractiveness of the airport location to prospective office tenants. 
2. It will ensure that the airport will be able to cope with the additional traffic generated by office workers and 
visitors. 
(c) Activities should enhance and add value to the airport location 
A strategic focus should be kept on attracting activities that strengthen the function of the airport and add 
value to the airport location; that is, companies with activities that drive air traffic growth (i.e., consulting 
company). 
To be avoided: the location of large-scale retail outlets or even furniture stores, whose customers have no link 
to the airport function and just help congest the roads. Here, airport management must take the long view 
toward the airport's development. 
796 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 816===
Hy he i . 
IATA Passenger Terminal 
Exhibit 3.3.10.4.1b: Good Real Estate—-Lufthansa and KPMG's Offices at Frankfurt's Square

(d) Prime locations for commercial tenants 
The best office locations—those closest to the terminal building and the ground transportation center—should 
be set aside for commercial tenants. It is neither desirable nor necessary to have non-critical activities, such 
as the airport administration, occupying prime office locations. 
(e) Ensure stakeholder collaboration 
Stakeholder management is of the utmost importance. For on-airport real estate developments, for example, it 
is important to involve financial institutions, investors, possible tenants and lessees in order to develop 
successful and bankable projects. This is all the more important if the airport cannot finance the projects on its 
own. Also, it is important to involve the city and surrounding municipalities to make sure that developments 
are aligned and facilities are not duplicated, leading to competition and waste of resources. An aligned 
approach between stakeholders, such as the airport, the urban planning departments of all municipalities 
involved and the major transport providers of the region, is necessary to define the future vision and make 
sure that different land use zones support the overall goals.

(f) Involve the right expertise 
Most, if not all, firms engaged in airport master planning claim to have expertise in the development of airport 
cities. Their airport city development strategies tend to be generic/‘out of the box’ in nature. It is recommended 
to involve niche firms or individuals with highly-specialized (local) expertise on urban planning, economics, 
marketing, transportation planning and real estate planning during the feasibility and planning process. 
(g) Deliberative and Strategic Planning 
Similar to the importance of airports preparing master plans for aviation facilities, the landside real estate 
development also needs long-term strategic planning and vision. 
3.3.11 Supporting Facilities and Design Principles 
3.3.11.1 Security, Safety 
3.3.11.1.1 Terminal Security Zones 
Airports and airport terminals deploy security measures to mitigate the risk of a security threat to the airport 
itself as well as to aircraft and passengers. Most commonly, passengers and their luggage are security￾controlled (see 3.3.5.5 Passenger Security Screening) within the airport terminal before entering the airside 
Zone, if security is located before immigration, then the security restricted area right after security screening, 
and subsequently, the aircraft. Once security-screened, passengers and their baggage are considered 
“sterile” or “clean” depending on different terminology used around the world. 
798 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 818===
IATA Passenger Terminal 
Airports generally utilize a zoning concept to manage security within the terminal and the entire airport. 
Access and egress to and from these zones is managed and controlled in order to maintain their secured 
integrity at all times. Different security concepts and terminologies exist; however, the most common and 
internationally recognized security zoning is the following: 
(a) Public Area and Landside 
Access to the public area is not security controlled and is granted at the discretion of the airport. Examples for 
publicly accessible terminal areas include the arrivals and departures halls. It should be noted that access to 
public areas of an airport could be restricted because of local regulations; for example, in the case of 
demonstrations or safety evacuation concerns, under the authority of the local airport or police entities. 
Landside is defined in the ICAO Security Manual (Doc 8973) as the parts of an airport, adjacent terrain and 
buildings, or portions thereof, that are not airside, as identified by States and relevant entities in their security 
programs. As queues and crowds created landside are potential targets for security-related attacks, additional 
security measures could be imposed by regulators with the aim of mitigating the risks associated with such 
vulnerabilities, in accordance with risk assessments carried out by the relevant authorities or entities. 
Depending on the nature and magnitude of these additional security measures, landside portions of the 
airport could become airside, or even a security-restricted area, for a specific period of time or even 
permanently. 
Private offices, locked storage rooms, maintenance bays, etc. could be located in public areas even if the 
access is limited to their users or owners. They are not considered as “security” or “secured” zones in the 
sense of aviation security. 
Terminal design should take into consideration measures to mitigate the effect of explosives in public areas. 
For more information, please consult the ACI Landside Security Handbook or the Aviation Security in Airport 
Development (ASIAD 2017) issued by the UK Department for Transport. 
(b) Airside 
The number of security checkpoints should be optimized to meet real needs. This can be achieved by 
centralizing screening points at one or more spots where the passenger and baggage flow routes converge. 
When possible, adoption of ‘recognition of equivalence’ agreements resulting in one-stop security for transfer 
operations should be incorporated in any new design or major restructuring to enhance total flexibility. 
Differentiation of passenger flows at transfer points could also mean additional security measures for specific 
destinations only (elevation of threat level). 
The number of points where pedestrians can have access to airside areas should be minimized. This can be 
done after a rigorous analysis of ground personnel flow routes and by applying the basic principle of 
developing an overall plan for the permit system. The more entry points, the more recurrent operational costs 
for operators and the more difficult deployment of sustainable high-quality security systems. 
The following considerations should be given to any landside observation deck/terrace or viewing area that 
overlooks aircraft parked on the apron or passenger handling operations: 
e Terraces or viewing areas should be totally secured against direct attacks 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 799 

===PAGE 819===
ray 
Se IATA vif Airport Development Reference Manual 
e The area should be enclosed, or contain barriers to prevent unauthorized access or the throwing of 
objects at parked aircraft or into security-restricted areas 
e Access control features should enable the area to be secured and closed to the public when required 
Each baggage storage facility to which passengers and the public have access should be constructed in such 
a way as to minimize the effects of an explosion occurring in an item being handled or stored, and should be 
capable of being secured when not staffed. 
The airside and security restricted areas should be designed and constructed to prevent the passage of 
unscreened articles from non-secure areas. For example, links or connections between plumbing, air vents, 
drains, utility tunnels or other fixtures from security-restricted area restrooms to restrooms in non-sterile areas 
should be avoided to limit the possibility of articles being passed from one area to the other. When planning 
the construction of non-restricted or public access suspended walkways or balconies over or adjacent to 
security-restricted areas, it is critical to ensure that they not facilitate the passing of items into the security￾restricted areas. 
The integrity of passenger area security can be enhanced by designing built-in fixtures (i.e., railings, pillars, 
benches) to prevent concealment of weapons or other dangerous devices. This could help reduce the 
difficulties and costs associated with monitoring such areas (i.e., closets, utility rooms, restrooms, lockers, 
storage areas, stairwells, recessed-housing fire extinguishers, and fire hose storage cabinets). Such areas 
should be capable of being locked when not in use. Natural line of site should be considered to assist with 
surveillance. 
Design measures for protecting and facilitating escape from a marauding armed assault (active shooters) or 
reducing the risk of an improvised explosive device (IED) attack should be deployed in landside. This 
underscores the importance of a local risk assessment to inform the design. 
The objectives of fire safety and crowd control provisions may sometimes appear contradictory to those of 
security provisions. Optimum safety aims to enable people to be evacuated in the event of danger, while 
security aims to control people's movements and limit their access to certain areas. Means of safety egress 
should be distributed evenly throughout the airport. The means of egress need to be considered together with 
the security strategy. Where feasible, occupants should evacuate to an area of equal or higher security level 
to prevent secondary attack targeting evacuating flows. Security rescreening may be necessary when the 
incident or crisis is resolved. A security search of all security-restricted areas infected by the evacuation, as 
well as security screening of all passengers, are required. 
Where safety or emergency exits are accessible to the public and lead to the airside or security-restricted 
areas, this poses a vulnerability to the terminal security and operations. Where unavoidable, this should be 
mitigated using door access control and/or delayed egress hardware and CCTV for monitoring. Such door 
hardware systems may require special approvals from authorities having jurisdiction. Where the public 
evacuate to the airside, there should be designated assembly points for the public to assemble during an 
emergency. These assembly points should be marked by signage and/or ground marking, so these areas are 
obvious and intuitive. Means of egress systems (i.e., exits, exit door hardware, exit signage, emergency 
lighting and evacuation zones) should also be coordinated with the fire alarm system, public address system, 
and fire compartmentation/smoke control system, where applicable. 
800 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 820===
=e 
IATA 4 ; 
Passenger Terminal 
Consideration should be given to the displacement of risk and the vulnerabilities generated by the crowding of 
people at predictable times—a characteristic of safety incidents. This consideration includes the location and 
security clearance of mustering points. A known attack tactic is the detonation of a second device at the same 
location targeting first responders or along the route of evacuation as people evacuate following the initial 
explosion. 
Surface access should be designed based on the findings of a local risk assessment. Consideration should be 
given to controls that prevent the parking of vehicles along the forecourt for longer than the time needed to 
offload passengers. 
It is recommended that the parking positions reserved for private vehicles be separate from those reserved for 
buses and taxis. Bus and taxi parking positions should be placed away from their maneuvering lanes to permit 
them to load and offload their passengers along the curb. 
Goods delivery direct to the passenger terminal building should be minimized. 
All security posts, offices and premises should be located so as to minimize the response time to an incident, 
thus ensuring maximum security service efficiency.

3.3.11.2.1 General Considerations 
Toilet provisions play an important role in airport facilities for passenger and staff convenience and passenger 
perceptions regarding their overall experience at an airport. Passengers and staff should be provided with 
adequate toilet facilities near all main waiting zones and workplaces, at all main terminal facilities. 
The design, as well as the sizing of toilet facilities, should recognize international best practices since the 
facilities will be used by many nationalities with varying perceptions. Design parameters should also address 
the service levels that a specific airport wants to provide to its passengers and an assessment of the peak 
traffic volumes that are expected for the various zones where toilets are to be provided. 
Sufficient facilities should be provided to allow temporary closure of some facilities for cleaning. Ample width 
in toilet circulation areas should be provided. Trolley provisions should be considered for the sizing of toilet 
blocks, particularly in landside areas where use of trollies is prominent. Toilet facilities should be easy to 
locate for passengers. Signage should support passenger wayfinding where required. Please see 3.3.12 
Wayfinding and Signage for more information. Special attention should be paid to the sizing of cubicles and 
circulation spaces for toilets where checked luggage and/or hand luggage may be taken into the toilets.

Toilets should always be planned in a way that prevents views from the public concourses or lounges into the 
toilet area. Doors are not a mandatory provision at entrances to toilets as long as the entrances are designed 
to completely obscure views into the facilities.

3.3.11.2.2 Special Needs Provisions 
Passengers with disabilities, or passengers with small infants, should be provided with toilet facilities designed 
to suit their needs. Toilet layouts should consider the various different forms of reduced mobility and provide 
accessible solutions to all passengers. See 3.3.9 Universal Design and Terminal Accessibility. 
3.3.11.2.3 Religious and Cultural Considerations 
Where required, toilet details should consider religious and cultural aspects, such as the orientation of toilet 
facilities, or the provision of specific toilets types, lavatories, wash basins and/or urinals. Privacy between 
appliances should also be considered. 
3.3.11.2.4 Distances between Toilet Blocks and Areas without Toilet Provisions 
Distances between toilet blocks should take maximum walking distances into account. Passengers should 
have easy access to the nearest toilet block. Where applicable, local regulations for distances between toilet 
blocks need to be considered, but practical levels of comfort should always be taken into consideration as 
well. 
Where toilet provisions are restricted to certain areas only, with minimum provisions only in other zones such 
as boarding gate areas, signage should clearly inform passengers that they are entering zones where no 
toilets are provided. This situation should be avoided as much as possible as groups with children, the elderly 
or disabled passengers may not be able to manage long periods without access to facilities, such as may 
occur with delayed flights, even with prior warning. 
3.3.11.2.5 Cleaner's Rooms 
Cleanliness and maintenance of toilet facilities is a key aspect of positive passenger perception of the 
terminal's facilities, and larger toilet blocks should be provided with dedicated cleaner's rooms, for storage of 
cleaning equipment and a cleaners’ sink. 
3.3.11.3 Horizontal and Vertical Circulation 
Vision 
Terminals should be configured to provide the shortest possible walking distances with as few changes in 
level and direction as possible. Passengers should be able to move freely without obstruction. In cases where 
distances exceed walking parameters, the passenger journey should be facilitated by automated transit 
systems.

===PAGE 823===

IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
Policy 
Minimize level changes wherever possible 
e Any walking distance in excess of 300 meters should be provided with moving walkways that reduce 
unaided walking distances; and 
e Where level changes are unavoidable, a combination of ramps, escalators, elevators and stairs will 
provide the passenger with the most comfortable journey. 
3.3.11.3.1 Level Changes and Vertical Circulation 
Not only should terminals be configured to provide the shortest possible walking distances, they should also 
feature as few changes in level as possible. 
Ramps should be at gentle gradients and wide enough to enable PRMs and passengers with wheeled 
baggage and/or children in strollers to move freely and pass each other. 
If possible, departing and arriving passengers should not be required to change levels. The use of ramps to 
facilitate such level changes is encouraged where the overall walking distance is not increased excessively. 
In cases where difficult site conditions, existing operations or building structures leave no alternative, then 
level changes should be achieved by modes of conveyance (i.e., escalators and elevators) with an associated 
staircase and/or ramp as backup should the mechanical devices fail. 
(a) Elevators, Stairs and Escalators 
Any change of level that cannot be achieved by gentle ramps must be provided with satisfactory modes of 
mechanical vertical circulation. 
Escalators are the preferred method for moving most passengers quickly from level to level, but they must be 
accompanied by elevators to ensure that PRMs and passengers with wheeled baggage and/or children in 
strollers are provided with an equivalent, speedy and straightforward method of making the level change. 
Wherever mechanical vertical circulation is provided, contingency measures are needed to address both 
planned and unplanned (breakdown) maintenance. 
Combinations of elevators, escalators and stairs (as an alternate and least preferred contingency) will provide 
passengers with the quickest, most resilient journeys. 
804 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 824===
IATA Passenger Terminal 
3.3.11.3.2 Horizontal Circulation 
(a) Horizontal Circulation Spaces 
Passenger journeys should be as straightforward as possible with clear sightlines to approaching decision 
points. Simple direct routes are preferred, with adequate width for passengers to move freely. Walking speeds 
vary considerably so ample space is required for individuals and small clusters of people to pass each other. 
For passengers traveling through airports frequently and/or passengers with wheeled baggage and/or children 
in strollers, ample space is required to enable them to move freely and pass each other. PRMs should also be 
provided with ample circulation space and with rest areas at appropriate intervals. The circulation route also 
needs to provide ample space for electric vehicles (passenger electric carts, etc.) to move freely, back and 
forth. 
Space should be provided for passengers to rest at all major decision points through their journey (e.g., 
wherever they are provided with flight information displays, or FIDs). These resting areas should be located to 
the side of the main circulation zone so as not to obstruct the main flows. 
Wherever passengers are provided with a large number of options, for example at the entrance to a 
departures lounge with many different shops, food & beverage outlets, toilets and other facilities, Orientation 
Zones should be provided. 
Walking distances from the forecourt to the gate and vice versa should be minimized. Convoluted circulation 
routes that include changes in direction or level negatively impact orientation. Walking distances in excess of 
300 meters should always be augmented with moving walkways. 
At all times, where departing and arriving passengers must transport their checked baggage they should be 
provided with freely accessible baggage trolleys. Terminal conveyance systems (i.e., elevators, escalators 
and moving walkways) should permit passenger movement without the need to off-load and reload trolleys 
when changing levels. Circulation routes should also permit passengers to pass one another, with or without 
baggage trolleys. 
On the airside of the passenger terminal complex, baggage trolleys should be smaller to assist with permitted 
cabin baggage, and they should be easily accommodated within all concession outlets. 
Changes in direction should be avoided wherever possible. Wherever unavoidable, they should be as shallow 
as possible with ample maneuvering space for all passengers and, where provided, electric vehicles. 
Unsegregated piers (where departures and arrivals flows are not separated) need to be wider than 
segregated piers in order to accommodate not only the larger total passenger flows, but also to recognize that 
there are counter-flows. Similarly, wherever circulation flows are not direct, for example in departures lounge 
retail areas, the general circulation areas need to be more generous. 
Cross-flows should always be avoided. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 805 

===PAGE 825===
2 [ff IATA paul Airport Development Reference Manual 
(b) Moving Walkways 
Wherever there are lengthy walking distances, and certainly where they are in excess of 300 meters, 
passengers should be provided with moving walkways in addition to the general horizontal circulation space 
requirements. 
Moving walkways should be sufficiently wide to enable passengers to pass each other. 
Appropriate attention needs to be given to planned, and occasionally unplanned, maintenance requirements. 
Contingency measures include duplicate parallel moving walkways and/or electric vehicles (see below). 
Moving walkways should also be reversible to allow for the potential of dual directional flows during 
contingency operations. 
(c) Electric Vehicles 
The need to satisfy an ever-increasing percentage of PRMs is leading to increased demands for assistance 
through the terminal. In general, this is a shared responsibility between airports and airlines. 
Particularly in large airport terminals, electric vehicles are increasingly used to help passengers cover the 
longer distances. Additional circulation space is required to enable the electric vehicles to move freely without 
obstruction from other passengers, or to passengers. 
(d) Trolley Provisions 
Trolleys, or luggage carts are vital at terminals, due to the amount of luggage that passengers bring with 
them. Baggage trolleys should be provided for passengers to transport unchecked luggage from landside 
transport areas, such as the forecourts or ground transportation centres, to the check-in or bag drop halls. 
Trolley should also be provided for arrivals passengers, once it has been retrieved from the baggage claim 
belts. 
Storage areas for trolleys should be located near the transportation interfaces, vehicles drop offs, and on the 
reclaim belts, adequate in number and size to suit the projected numbers of trolleys, bags and passengers. 
Trolley storage areas should be clearly marked and should not obstruct passenger circulation routes or 
waiting areas. 
A trolley management strategy should be in place to determine the operational requirements of handling the 
trolleys. Dedicated trolley recirculation routes should be provided, allowing trolleys to be restocked in the 
landside surface access areas, as well as the baggage claim hall. 
Provision of trolleys should be free of charge.Many airports still have coin-operated carts. However, this can 
be problematic and irritating for passengers who may not have a coin. The perceived benefits incentivizing 
trolley logistics do not generally outweigh the trade-offs in negative passenger perception. 
A porter service can be provided where required. Porter staff numbers are to be considered for the sizing of 
the baggage claim facilities. Porter access to the baggage claim hall is to be considered in line with the 
terminal's security strategy.

3.3.11.3.3 Automated People Mover Systems 
As new airports are developed and existing airports are expanded, the distances that passengers must travel 
within the airport tend to increase. Conventional pedestrian modes such as moving walkways are acceptable 
over shorter distances, but these support systems do not provide a sufficient level of service to passengers 
when greater distances are involved. 
Automated People Mover (APM) systems have become common solutions to moving large numbers of 
passengers quickly within airports. An APM system is an automated, driver-less vehicle or train operated at 
frequent intervals on dedicated tracks or guide-ways. APM systems are designed to carry large numbers of 
people at high frequency within high-density activity areas. 
APMs offer lower cost solutions compared with traditional rail offerings, both in terms of reduced operating 
and capital costs. Drivers are rarely needed (APMs can be operated in manual mode with a driver on-board 
as an option). Track infrastructure is both cheaper and easier to install, with fewer track-placed signals, than 
most other systems. 
The term “APM” applies to a diverse group of technologies with a wide range of physical and operating 
characteristics. New technologies are constantly being developed and marketed, and existing technologies 
are refined with each new application. 
Technologies vary in size, performance, propulsion type, suspension type, appearance, and numerous other 
aspects. For planning purposes, the key characteristics are as follows: 
e Size. Technologies vary in vehicle size and train length, from single vehicle personal rapid transport 
(PRT) with four-passenger capacity to four to six vehicle trains of 60 to 80 passengers per vehicle 
* Speed. The nominal operating speed of various APM technologies ranges from 25 to 80 km per hour. In 
applications where the distances between stations are very short, the differences in speed make very little 
difference in overall travel times. In layouts with longer distances between stations, the higher speed 
technologies can reduce the travel times significantly 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 807 

===PAGE 827===
x kil Se | 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
¢ Propulsion type. APM technologies can be classified into two general groups: self-propelled and cable￾propelled. Self-propelied technologies include those propelled by convention electric traction drawing 
power from trackside power. PRT vehicles, using electric car technology, can be battery-powered, 
removing the need for electrical pick-up along the guide-way. Cable-propelled technologies use passive 
vehicles attached to a cable that is propelled by drive equipment at a single point along the guide-way 
¢ Guide-way type. Three primary types are commonly used: rubber-tired on a direct-guided track, rubber￾tired on an indirect-guided track (with no side contact) and steel-wheeled on a steel rail. The direct-guided 
track, including monorails, can have the most complex switching arrangements as the whole concrete 
guide-way and trackside power has to be moveable. The indirect-guided track, where electronic guidance 
is used, results in simpler and less expensive systems

The basic building blocks of APMs are:

e CCTV systems

e Emergency exits and firefighter access 
Typical characteristics of Airport APM systems may include: 
e The travel distance between stations typically less than one kilometer 
e The service frequency requirement is high to minimize waiting times 
e The drop-off and loading points for passengers are limited in number, often fewer than five destinations 
on a single track (commonly, only two destinations are provided)
