These combined factors support the implementation of APM technology rather than manned services, such as 
full gauge rail and/or buses. Long-term plans for large airports should include for the implementation of an 
APM system at some point in the development strategy. Adequate space and rights-of-way should be 
reserved so that APM systems can be accommodated in the master plan. 
(a) APM Applications at Airports 
APM systems can be planned to satisfy several different transportation requirements at airports. The principal 
applications for APM systems are: 
* Terminal-to-gate connections-APM systems connecting main terminal processing areas to aircraft gates 
in satellites or piers 
¢ — Intra-terminal connections-APM systems serving as connections between aircraft gates within one 
terminal or satellite to facilitate the movement of intra-line transfer passengers 
e Landside connections—APM systems connecting unit terminals and landside airport functions such as 
remote parking and car rental facilities 
(b) APM Planning Considerations 
After identifying the need for moving large numbers of passengers over long distances at an airport, and an 
APM has been identified as appropriate, the demand characteristics of the airport are analyzed to properly 
specify the APM solution. Often, simulation studies are the most reliable way to ensure all operational and 
design elements have been taken into consideration. 
Sizing of station waiting areas and circulation areas, and the area per passenger on the trains will also be 
target service level-led design criteria. All categories of potential APM car occupants should be identified. It is 
important to identify each category separately so that different demand, peaking times, and other 
characteristics can be applied to each category. Categories vary for each airport and application; however, 
typical categories include the following: 
e Passengers with check-in baggage 
e Passengers with carry-on baggage 
e Passengers with reduced mobility (including escorts, wheel chairs, etc.) 
e Airport staff 
e Airline crew 
e Well-wishers 
e Airport visitors 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 809 

===PAGE 829===
We IATA fi Airport Development Reference Manual 
For each category of APM car occupant, the demand should be analyzed, including peak traffic requirements, 
based on airporv/airline operational forecasts and aircraft types/configurations. The APM car occupancy 
demand analysis should be performed on a consistent basis with the other airport forecasts and analyses. 
The overall design goal, as with all airport systems and processes, is “balanced capacity”. The APM car 
occupancy analysis should account for the possibility of varying peak times for different categories of APM car 
occupants, such as international vs. domestic peaks, and peaks within airlines or groups of gates. If airport 
design hourly demand forecasts are used, a surge factor should be applied to account for the uneven 
distribution of passengers throughout the design hour. 
The APM car occupancy demand numbers can be applied later to alternative system configurations to 
determine the optimal capacity requirements of the APM system. Particular consideration should be given to 
the effect of high peak flows on multi-station APMs that can lead to trains filling to capacity at early stops, 
leaving passengers unable to join the train further down the track. This condition can lead to increased MCTs 
and a poor perception of the level of service. Careful airline allocation, both during planning and operations, 
can help to minimize this problem, but not necessarily eliminate it. Passenger flow peaking profiles are a 
vitally important design input. 
Difference scenarios for growth of domestic or international flight sectors, different airlines and different 
schedule characteristics should be considered to ensure the chosen APM system. 
(c) APM Configurations and Operational Modes 
In early planning, alternative APM configurations and operational modes should be developed, analyzed, and 
evaluated. These early planning analyses will ensure that adequate rights-of-way and space provisions are 
made for the APM system, and that the selected airport and APM configurations are compatible. Numerous 
variations and combinations of APM configurations can be developed. Some systems use multiple 
overlapping routes with off-line stations, or switching and crossovers between shuttle systems. Added 
complexity can increase the cost and reduce the reliability and availability of an APM system. 
APM configurations and operational modes can be different for each airport layout. The most appropriate 
configurations should be determined by detailed analysis and evaluation of alternatives performed by APM 
specialists. 
(d) APM Airport Security Considerations 
APM systems at airports operate either security-screened, unscreened or both. 
Outbound security-screened, inbound unscreened airside operations. 
Segregation between screened and un-screened passengers needs to be maintained, with screening facilities 
located in the areas that facilitate the most efficient passenger flow. When APM carriages switch between 
carrying screened and unscreened passengers they require a physical sweep at each end of the run for 
security purposes. This time needs to be incorporated in the headway and capacity calculations for the 
system. 
810 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 830===
== IATA mul Passenger Terminal 
Unscreened airside operations 
This configuration carries passengers to their destination station following outbound emigration controls, 
where applicable. Once at the destination station passengers go through central search security or gate 
security, as applicable. 
This system is simpler to operate as there is no need to search the cars at the end of each run. It also 
provides an anywhere-to-anywhere connectivity, in particular when coupled with gate security. APM systems 
can more easily be configured as an unscreened loop, improving the system redundancy. 
However, this configuration has potential disadvantages where there is centralized outbound search at each 
station due to the increased space, facilities and staff required for the multiple check-points. 
Carriage of unscreened passengers on APM systems can be considered an enhanced security risk, due to 
the essential nature of such systems as well as the high concentration of potential targets on each carriage. 
Fully screened airside operations 
This is possible where passengers from all inbound flights using the APM system are subject to the same 
security performance and oversight, such as domestic flights within the USA. A fully screened APM system 
can be simplified in its operation, avoiding a number of the issues of the partially or wholly unscreened 
options. 
Unscreened landside operations 
These operations for connecting terminals, connecting car parking and other landside activities provide a 
simple operation similar to light-rail systems, provided that they are not required to traverse the airside 
boundary. 
(e) APM Evacuation 
Evacuation requirements will vary based on national regulations and requirements, but is it common to find a 
maximum distance between evacuation points of approximately 1,000 meters. As APM systems often run 
through both airside and landside environments, evacuation of passengers in case of an emergency can 
provide security or cross-border complications. APM Technologies. 
(f) APM System Resilience and Maintenance 
APM systems operating over any significant distance at airports become a primary component of the 
integrated passenger movement system and are known as a “must-ride” system. Although APM technology is 
now very reliable, failure of part of the system remains a possibility. To avoid substantial delays to airport 
operations, the overall transport system needs sufficient resilience to maintain a good level of service at all 
times. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 811 

===PAGE 831===
Be 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
A number of options are available, including the provision of alternative walking or bussing routes. 
Planned preventative maintenance is critical for APM systems with vehicles running in the range of 50,000 to 
150,000 km/year. Maintenance will range from daily inspections to planned outages. While many airports will 
have a period of the day or night with little or no traffic, many airports have full 24-hour operations. Therefore, 
allowing for ongoing and emergency maintenance in the initial planning of the APM system is very important. 
This is especially true where facilities for alternative modes of travel, such as bussing, need to be 
accommodated in the context of the overall initial (master plan) facilities planning. Vehicle maintenance may 
also require alternative locations for light maintenance and stabling away from the main depot. 
(g) APM System Integration Into Facilities 
Specific APM facilities to be integrated into the overall airport and terminal facility design include the following: 
e Passenger stations 
e Guide-way 
¢ Maintenance and stabling facilities 
e Insertion and extract pits to accommodate single APM cars 
e Central control facility 
e Propulsion power substations 
e Equipment rooms 
¢ Emergency escape routes 
Well-integrated systems allow convenient passenger flow and access to stations, and allow good visibility of 
the system, improving passenger awareness and understanding of the use of the system. 
3.3.12 Wayfinding and Signage 
3.3.12.1 Introduction 
Wayfinding and signage systems shall be designed to ensure that passengers complete their journey through 
the airport without getting lost and missing their flight or landside connection. They shall also ensure that 
escape routes are clear and effective. 
Good application of wayfinding and signage should make an airport easier to understand and navigate, taking 
into consideration all user groups while supporting the functional needs of the airport operation. The 
experience of getting to and around the airport contributes significantly to the overall impression of the airport. 
Its effectiveness reflects directly on the public image of the airport operator and the ‘host’ city/country. 
812 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 832===
IATA * Passenger Terminal 
A disciplined, well-executed wayfinding system will allow its users to navigate with confidence, reduce stress 
and increase passenger experience levels for all its user groups. It also contributes to the overall efficiency of 
the day-to-day operation. 
Wayfinding and signage are an integral part of normal, irregular and emergency operations planning, closely 
linked to the Concept of Operations (see 2.7 Development of a Concept of Operations) supporting all journey 
routes. Priority should always be given to operational wayfinding to ensure all passengers are able to pass 
through airport facilities in a time efficient manner. Wayfinding shall be provided for all passenger types. 
Particular consideration shall be given for passengers with accessibility needs (see 3.3.9.2.5 Wayfinding). 
Wayfinding 
Wayfinding is the action of navigation throughout a journey. For almost all passengers, that journey now starts 
and ends outside the airport, at home, at work, or at a holiday destination. Journeys are experienced through 
a sequence of orientation and navigation points that take place on the way from A to B as well as navigating 
through complex areas. 
Wayfinding is used to guide passengers along their journey in the most effective manner and for much of the 
journey can be accomplished through natural architectural wayfinding without signage or formal information 
through the use of visual and sensory features. 
Throughout the journey wayfinding information may be required to understand and experience a place and to 
help inform travel decisions as well as confirming arrival at interim destinations, such as the gate. Wayfinding 
information is particularly important at decision points or where natural wayfinding cannot be accomplished. 
Wayfinding information is provided through a variety of communication channels, including web-based 
information, mobile technologies, printed products, on-route signs and people services. 
Signage 
Signage encompasses all visual or contextual signs that inform about navigation requirements and provide 
wayfinding information, both static and dynamic. 
3.3.12.2 Principles of Good Wayfinding 
By focusing on consistent basic elements, a restrained approach to providing information, and creating 
moments of delight, these principles can ensure an exceptional wayfinding experience. 
1. Brilliant Basics 
Wayfinding content and design should be based on international standards and best practices. It must be 
clear, comprehensive, consistent, conspicuous, and contextual. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 813 

===PAGE 833===
w TATA Gi. Airport Development Reference Manual 
2. Less is more 
The key to successful wayfinding is a streamlined, easy-to-perceive environment. It should be free of 
visual clutter to allow optimal balance of architecture, art, interior, branding, and commercial activities. 
Wayfinding elements must be carefully designed and integrated into the architectural design and scale. 
Do not place more signs than necessary to provide the right information at the right time. 
Keeping wayfinding up-to-date is crucial to providing a reliable, enjoyable experience. Often this means 
limiting and removing information, rather than adding new information. 
3. Surpass Expectations 
Getting the basics right ensures that passengers are relaxed, clear minded, and well informed. This 
unlocks the opportunity to introduce delightful, only-in-my city “wow” experiences 
3.3.12.3 General Considerations 
Many airports face the challenges of being complex, multi-function destinations, not just a location to catch a 
flight, but also a place where there are commercial offerings on display. Commercial considerations will 
influence the airport design and layout as modern airports try to provide a distinct offer as well as new and 
attractive experiences. While recognizing this is the case, operational wayfinding should always take 
precedence over commercial elements, with the location of wayfinding information taking priority over 
advertising and commercial offerings. 
New-build airports can plan for both present-day requirements and plan ahead for future increases in 
capacity, such as extensions to piers or satellite hubs. Existing buildings will often be extended, refurbished or 
new terminals or satellite structures added. This often provides the greatest challenge for wayfinding that 
must adapt to these changes while maintaining a coherent strategy for the passenger. Smaller airports often 
face the challenge of fitting in functionalities and aspects expected of a larger airport in ways that could leave 
less space to provide adequate wayfinding however due to their smaller size and more human scale natural 
wayfinding can be easier. 
Planning 
Development of wayfinding should commence from an early stage in the architectural design process, after 
the initial terminal plan has been proposed, to review the proposed passenger flow routes before the position 
of lifts, escalators and travellator's are fixed. Consideration should be given to ensuring logical flows, 
removing any unnecessary, complex turns or routes and preserving sightlines that support intuitive 
wayfinding. Early identification of wayfinding locations is recommend to support the terminal design and 
budgeting process; for instance, to identify where services should be located or where larger items of signage 
may be provided to inform structural considerations. 
814 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 834===
IATA Passenger Terminal 
Wayfinding input should be included within the concept design to communicate to the client how signage 
could be integrated (i.e., in visuals/renders), but details of the appearance or structures need not be 
developed at the point. Aspects such as initial user flows should be included to demonstrate how the building 
will work. This is especially important for any complex flows, such as those for transfer passengers. Detailed 
wayfinding planning and design should commence during the ‘Schematic Design’ stage as soon as area 
layouts and detailed floor plans have settled, working closely with the architect to ensure coordination within 
the building, through to ‘Detail Design’ stage, when final planning, graphics and signage products are detailed 
and ready to tender, supply and install. 
3.3.12.4 Strategy and Users 
A detailed strategy should be developed that includes for the following elements: 
« Passenger journey (i.e., arrivals, departures, connections, including transportation options) 
e Irregular operations, such as off-gate services 
« Emergency evacuation 
e Airport operational requirements 
e Airlines as the primary users and customers of airports 
° Staff and back-of-house use 
e Emergency responders (e.g., fire, police, medical services) 
e Security requirements 
e Landside roadways 
e Public transport access 
© Car parking 
Wayfinding should be consistent across the airport with other service providers, such as car park operators 
providing information to support the journey. 
Wayfinding is fundamental to the successful operation of an airport, as it not only guides passengers through 
their journey in terminals and concourses, but also through various procedural and processing points along 
the way. In addition, wayfinding and signage also need to be understood by passengers that come from 
various diverse cultures and backgrounds and, therefore, should not be underestimated.

3.3.12.5 Architectural and Planning Considerations 
Intuitive wayfinding 
Architecture that supports natural and intuitive wayfinding will rely less on directional signage, and will ensure 
the most efficient passenger flow. Once this has been achieved to best affect, the wayfinding planning can be 
simpler and more effective. A vision with open spaces and clear lines of sight as well as limited level changes 
and turns will support an intuitive and linear passenger journey to the greatest extent possible. 
Architectural integration 
Large graphic pieces can often replace a trail of smaller signs and be ‘beacon’ elements that draw 
passengers to areas and zones, adding to the character of larger spaces. This must be an early consideration 
in the design of new buildings so that areas are safeguarded early on in the design to ensure clear views are 
maintained. 
Illuminated graphics, including sign boxes that are required to sit flush with the wall finish, need to be taken 
into account by the architect when designing wall linings during detailed design to ensure the depth of the 
product is accommodated at all locations. 
Suspended items need to be designed so that they will fit within the building, or be installed while they can be 
moved into position. Structural issues, such as the weight of large suspended and floor-mounted items should 
also be considered. 
Sign placement 
A number of factors should be considered by airport planners regarding sign placement: 
e Ensure that there is a consistent approach to locating signage wherever possible 
* Provide spatial distancing to separate of signage from other features such as advertising, retail, and art 
and branding features and creating a wayfinding zone on the journey 
e Ensure signage is positioned at a frequency that suits the required viewing distances for the particular 
terminal design and environment 
e Consider the frequency of positioning to suit the architecture and other design criteria; for instance, to 
identify departure gate locations or confirm routes between travellator locations 
¢ Care should be taken to avoid placing signs against bright backgrounds such as windows or large, 
brightly lit advertising because of silhouetting/background glare 
e Ensure sight lines are kept free and clear of obstructions and features 
¢ Consider the aesthetic design works within the overall (visually competitive) environment 
e Ensure sign placement is compatible with CCTV cameras to avoid blocking views 
e Ensure placement of advertising displays and retail do not detract from signage 
¢ Consider safety requirements; for instance, attention should be paid to the location of escalators and lifts 
so they are clearly visible and easily accessed 
816 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 836===
B= 
IATA 4 Passenger Terminal 
Architectural models are recommended to aid the review of locations. Building Information Modelling (BIM) 
software is recommended to review the design from a 3D and volume perspective. 
Exhibit 3.3.12.5: Example of Architectural BIM Model to Inform Building Design

Headroom clearance and fixing heights 
The optimum headroom clearance in single height spaces is 2.3-2.4 m with an absolute minimum of 2.1 m, 
although larger height areas may require more clearance to suit the proportions of large-scale signs. It is 
important to check local health and safety requirements and regulations to ensure compliance. Ideally, 
planners should establish consistent datum heights. 
Consider, for instance, that passengers may carry small children on their shoulders who may reach out and 
touch signs, to ensure that sufficient height exists to avoid injury and damage. With all new buildings, it is 
recommended to check the final finished floor-to-ceiling heights, and where signs may need to be fitted below 
other services/ducts. 
Information such as detailed maps should be positioned to facilitate close study, and take into consideration 
wheelchair users. Planners/designers should reference relevant international architectural and/or accessibility 
standards for applicable criteria. 
Human factors-movement and crowding 
Within the architectural design and layout of areas, consideration should be given, within the architectural 
design, not just to capacity of spaces for queuing and seating, but how users react and behave when they 
move through a building or enter an area. Is there sufficient space to stop and decide on which route or 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 817 

===PAGE 837===
x dil SBS | 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
queue line to take? Is there sufficient space to stand back and view flight information without disrupting others 
using a walkway? 
In particular, attention should be paid to intuitive architecture when locating escalators and lifts, with the lifts a 
visible and safer option if passengers are to be encouraged not to take heavy bags on escalators. Adding 
signage at escalators directing to the lifts can be difficult to achieve, especially if the lift is hidden from view. 
In large airports, it is recommended that ‘time to gate’ information be provided (based on operational 
parameters agreed with airline users). This gives the reassurance to passengers as to how long they have to 
shop or eat, and helps ensure passengers arrive at the gate on time. Solutions can be static or electronic 
signs and/or noted on summary screens when the gate is allocated. 
Flight connections should be as stress free as possible, both in the provision and processing facilities and 
routes, especially at airports with more than one terminal. Connecting passengers are travelling through 
different time zones and arrive tired and anxious. Clear information should be given about where to go for the 
next step of the journey and the status of onward flights. 
Movement between terminals should also be considered for those who will ‘land’ themselves at their 
connecting airport and depart from another location after arrival (i.e., customs regulations in some locations 
dictate passengers collect their hold luggage, pass through Immigration & Customs, and re-check in from 
landside). Signs to other terminals should be provided for those passengers who may have gone to the wrong 
terminal or for contingency, in case of flight changes. 
3.3.12.6 Airport Operational Considerations 
The end user client may consist of a number of key stakeholders, all with different requirements or priorities 
for their focus area. The main client groups include: 
e Airport operator (including Passenger Services)-The functional movement of passengers through each 
step of the passenger journey, ensuring associated passenger satisfaction. Specialist departments may 
be responsible for different areas, such as Baggage Services or Airport Security. The requirements of 
government agencies, such as Border Control, Immigration or Customs, are usually managed via the 
airport operator. Specific note should be taken for key passenger service focus areas, including: 
o PRMs with respect to accessibility (e.g., tactile, braille and audible messages) 
co Flight transfers 
e Airline operator—Airlines are the primary customers and users of airports and, as such, airports should 
consult and agree the passenger wayfinding and signage strategy with the airline community. Other 
specific elements include airline branding and wayfinding (e.g., directions to airline lounges or branded 
flight transfers desks) 
e Airport commercial operations (advertising, retail, F&B)-Coordination with wayfinding is critical. It is 
recommended that advertising be sited after wayfinding is placed. Signage should be carefully 
coordinated within retail layouts so that routes to gates are visible

3.3.12.7 Airport Wayfinding Design 
For the wayfinding designer, joint consideration is required for both the graphics and signage products, as 
well as functional requirements. For new-build airports, close collaboration with the architect, interior designer 
and other consultants (e.g., those responsible for advertising, retail or lighting) will also be required. 
Best practice airport design should combine creativity and functionality in a single package. 
The three primary criteria in signage design are: 
1. The font/color/pictogram 
2. Use of digital components 
3. Decision on predominant illumination—either internally or externally 
Careful selection of these criteria will heavily influence effectiveness and quality of the wayfinding. 
Planning and content 
Consideration must be given to the: 
e Terminology and what needs to be signed 
¢ Number of messages or information required at a given point 
e Viewing or reading distance of signs 
e Number of languages required on signs 
e Longest message (this will inform sign sizes and proportions, while the choice of typeface will also 
influence this) 
Planners should aim to avoid information overload. Too much information results in hesitation and confusion. 
Only give as much information as is needed to get to the next stage of the journey. Consider progressive 
disclosure of information, adding more detail when needed. 
Graphics, color, illumination and appearance 
For wayfinding to be effective, the graphics must be functional and legible. To achieve this, the appearance of 
signs should be considered separately from any airport branding and follow the best practice design principles 
described below. 
Font and Typeface 
Typeface selection should be based the letterform shapes and proportions. Sans serif fonts with large 
lowercase to capital letter size proportions and good open letter shapes are typically easier to read. For 
example, compare the spaces inside letters such as the letter ‘e’ or ‘g’. The styling of letters will also differ 
and affect readability, with the traditional shape of a letter ‘a’ or ‘g’ being more complex than more modern 
fonts. Very bold or condensed typefaces should be avoided. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 819 

===PAGE 839===
Se By IATA pil Airport Development Reference Manual 
Arrows should clearly indicate the direction to be taken. The favored arrow of many international standards 
documents is sometimes referred to as a ‘Belgian arrow’. This has even proportions, a clearly defined arrow 
head and an arrow stalk that is slightly longer than its height. It is important to see how an arrow looks for all 
directions when seen alongside messages in the chosen typeface. It should be drawn to be visually balanced 
with the chosen typeface and not appear to be too heavy or too weak. 
Reading distance is directly influenced by the choice of typeface. The more complex the letter shapes, the 
shorter the reading distance. There are various viewing distance tables that can be used as a guide to letter 
size, based on the height of the lowercase or uppercase letter size. As proportions of uppercase to lowercase 
letters vary by typeface, it is recommended to check viewing distances based on the lowercase letter. Where 
possible, test the chosen typeface at actual size. Allowance should be made for color and illumination, which 
will also affect reading distance. 
Legibility is also influenced by the layout style and appearance of the messages (typography) and the spacing 
of the words and individual letters. Adjustments to spacing can make some typefaces easier to read, although 
this must be done with care and checked for various letter combinations so that the spaces between straight 
and curved letters, when seen together, are not too wide (e.g., an ‘I’ next to a ‘c’). 
Color 
Color choice for foreground (text) and background is critical to develop contrast needed to provide clarity. To 
be successful, color in the use of wayfinding must: 
e Stand out from the environment 
¢ Be inclusive as possible to all users regardless of ability, including color blind and low-vision passengers 
e Avoid trends to ensure a timeless system 
e Be adaptable to a range of environments and evolving technologies 
e Reflect airport and regional sense of place 
Color choice should be influenced by the environment(s) in which the signs are to be placed. The color choice 
should be consistent across the airport. Color choice for externally illuminated signs are more sensitive than 
internally illuminated as there may be less contrast with their surroundings. 
Panels should be easily identifiable in their surroundings. If there are many darkly lit areas, dark panels are 
best avoided unless internally illuminated. Again, for legibility, there should be good contrast between the text 
and the sign panel. Consider any optical effects. Lettering on a dark background will appear bolder than on a 
light background. Dark lettering on a light background will appear thinner if the background is illuminated. 
Illumination 
Internally illuminated signs will normally provide superior visibility and be more effective than alternatives. 
Internally illuminated signs will normally be more expensive but do not normally require external illumination 
and will not be affected in the same way by changing ambient conditions. 
820 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 840===
many 
ae 
TATA Passenger Terminal 
Externally and internally illuminated panel in mock-up form should be compared before a decision on signage 
form is made. 
Language and terminology 
Multiple language signs can be provided where appropriate to the passenger profile. Priority should be given 
to the language seen by the majority of airport users, with English often seen as the common language of air 
travel. Other considerations may apply to the design of layouts. Arabic, for example, can produce long 
message lengths and may be better produced at a slightly smaller size below any English texts. Non￾European language typefaces should be selected according to what is most legible to the native reader, while 
still sitting comfortably alongside other fonts. 
Terminology should use straightforward wording that international readers can easily understand. Local 
phrases or airport jargon and acronyms should be avoided. 
Pictograms 
Pictograms for airports are often designed to complement the overall look of the design panel and can add 
character. It should be remembered that the pictograms are there for those who may not understand the 
languages used on a sign or as an easily visual reference, without the need to read each message. It is 
recommended that the basic content of pictograms reference International Standards (ISO) as these have 
been tested for ease of understanding by an international panel. Additional pictograms will be needed to 
support requirements within an airport context. These should be kept as simple as possible and designed to 
work together as a set. 
Local context and passenger profile may affect how signs are seen, used and understood by travelers (e.g., 
regular vs. infrequent airport users). Signage will need to work for all. Left-to-right or right-to-left reading of 
messages in different languages will influence sign layouts. Also ensure that there are no items that may 
offend. Some colors may have local cultural meaning. Pictograms, especially those with human figures, may 
need to be adapted to be acceptable. 
Operational information, staff and back-of-house signs should be differentiated in scale and design so as not 
to be confused with primary passenger flow information. It should be ensured that the overall aesthetic design 
works within the overall (visually competitive) environment. 
3.3.12.8 Sign Product Design and Fabrication 
There is much to consider in the design of signs prior to manufacture and installation. The following points are 
provided as guidance. Design considerations include: 
e Are the product design and graphics proportionate to the environment and do they meet the overall 
interior client brief? 
e Is the wayfinding and product functional in form and aesthetic? 
e Does the containment and supporting product design distract from the wayfinding message/content? 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 821 

===PAGE 841===
wr IATA ii Airport Development Reference Manual 
* Does the design allow the product to be procured locally (that may be a requirement of the client brief)? 
e Is the product fit for purpose and easily maintainable in the event of damage, so as not to disrupt 
designed information flows? 
e Is the product made with reflective finishes, which can distract from the messaging as well as mirror 
wayfinding messages? 
e Are sign locations chosen carefully to avoid confusion with reflection? 
Other considerations 
The airport planner should also consider the following important elements: 
e¢ The design should allow the use of practical component assembly. Generally, this may be of aluminum or 
steel, however, composites may be used if they meet construction fire/material standards 
e Ensure face panel materials meet all project control criteria and fire regulations, both local and national 
e Ensure the project lifecycles are considered in the component selection 
e Ensure Ingress Protection (IP) ratings have been met. Products mounted externally or within polluted 
environments will have higher ratings to maintain their appearance and function 
¢ Check if the project requires any security and ‘bomb-blast’ compliance. Does the product meet these 
requirements, if positioned in particular positions? 
e Ensure wind-loading and seismic activity have been considered for the airport location 
¢ Does the design accommodate access to any component parts that require servicing? 
e Ensure construction design enables an effective and professional finish; for instance, there should be no 
sharp corners within reach of passengers or staff 
e Ensure consideration is given to engineering requirements where products are on overhead passenger 
routes and walkways, including approved coordination with support or structural services 
© Consider if the design allows for the product to be procured locally (that may be a requirement of the 
client brief), noting the quality of manufacture can vary substantially between markets 
e Ensure that the key aspects of the design proposal are not compromised 
Product maintenance considerations 
Check the following elements: 
¢ Can the product be maintained locally? If not, consider the provision of temporary signage systems to 
maintain changes to passenger or information flows 
e Does the design consider interchangeability (e.g., to replace content panels with minimum disruption)? 
* Does the design accommodate access to any component parts that require servicing? 
e Ensure sufficient spare parts and replacement components, especially if the product was not procured 
locally. This applies to both static and digital forms of signage 
e Ensure manufacturers issue all component warranties, as well as cleaning and maintenance manuals

aie

Environmental responsibility/sustainability 
Planners should carefully consider environmental and sustainability elements as part of the core signage 
strategy. Only suppliers and manufacturers that use sustainable components and offer recycling should be 
considered in the procurement process. Other key elements to consider include: 
e Does the product conform to the project LEED standards and other environmental initiatives? 
e Are components easily accessible and spare parts in stock to maintain replacement parts over the 
designed lifespan, for both static and digital signage 
e Product lifespan is a key element to consider. Does the specification meet the project objectives for end 
user lifespans, and minimize maintenance costs? 
Materials coatings and finishes can have varying lifespans when used internally or externally as well as in 
different environments in different countries (e.g., extreme heat, cold, wet, Ultra Violet-UV). Has the effect of 
UV light been considered in the material finishes? Ensure coatings can endure external conditions, where 
applicable. 
IMumination 
All signs will require illumination, either internal or external, for day and night-time operations. Consider the 
form of illumination needed. Check if the wayfinding graphic design stands out effectively against the variable 
backgrounds of the architecture, media and retail installations. Also note that the level of lighting should be 
consistent throughout all wayfinding products. 
Planners should test product and color temperature within the airport environment (live or mock up) for 
effectiveness and consider illumination levels so as to not create glare and ensure legibility criteria are met. 
Certain locations, such as ceiling mounted signs with a low headroom are normally very difficult to make 
effective without internal illumination. 
Lighting products should use LED to reduce energy demand and maximize service life. Products should be 
maintained to ensure even illumination and that there is no light leakage to ensure effective appearance. 
Supply and manufacture 
Consider if the chosen product supplier meets the project and end user expectations, and whether all the 
specifications been adhered to. Also, check if product mock-ups and prototypes have been produced and 
signed off for quality and visual effect. Colorfastness of display materials is important to maintain contrast and 
definition.

=e IATA pull Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.3.12.9 Technology 
Dynamic information 
Dynamic information refers to any element designed to deal with a process or system, characterized by 
constant change, such as to keep people informed and up-to-date or to manage the activity of process. 
The use of technology in airport wayfinding includes all categories of flight information (e.g., flight (FID), gate 
(GID) and baggage (BID) information displays). These are often seen as the ‘traditional’ airport applications 
that all passengers expect to find. 
Recommendation 
Dynamic signs should be considered where uses and routes (passenger, staff and vehicles) may need to be 
altered e.g.: 
e Assignment of desks, gates, belts etc. in a common use environment 
e Update on status of flights 
* Optimization of capacity—e.g., where there are two passenger search areas are in operation, use of 
frontage roads etc. 
° Differing operating conditions—developed in conjunction with ConOps 
e Augmenting public address announcements 
Dynamic signs have the ability to provide branding, advertising, destination information when not in 
operational use which can add to the airport revenue stream. Dual use (scrolling between wayfinding and 
advertising) should be avoided where this can delay passengers seeing the information that they need. 
Supporting technology: Websites, Apps, Beacons, and Augmented reality. 
New technologies can now support passenger service by providing information in advance of their planned 
travel, and on the day, through to the point of departure, on arrival, and during the onward journey. If required, 
the experience at the airport can also be ‘personalized’ to the user. These technologies enable the airport 
operator, for instance, to measure dwell times and queue lengths so that resources can be allocated to meet 
the agreed service levels. The information can also be used to support dynamic wayfinding, pushing maps 
and coupons to travelers, where appropriate to do so in order to support passenger journeys. This can help to 
improve the passenger experience and, where appropriate, support non-aeronautical revenues. 
Future technologies 
New technologies are continually being developed and automation within the airport is gradually being 
introduced worldwide, where it can facilitate more efficient passenger processing to reduce queue times. 
There are now numerous points at which the passenger may interact with new technologies; for example, 
self-check in facilities, boarding card readers and e-visas/passports. This has a direct influence on both the 
airport design and its operating model. The design and layout of functional spaces can change considerably 
824 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 844===
IATA * Passenger Terminal 
where the need for desks and counters is reduced or removed. Wayfinding and supporting information, 
however, will still be required to help passengers navigate through these new processes. 
Safeguarding or adapting to change 
New technologies and processes will continue to be introduced, with some products specifically aimed at the 
aviation sector. To incorporate such change, area layouts and associated signage will need to change, 
especially at passenger processing locations that still use conventional methods. Conventional, static 
wayfinding, however, will still be required. Reliance on handheld technology will always carry with it the risk of 
lost or stolen devices, low battery or limited Wi-Fi-access. 
Consider what can be done to avoid ‘redundancy’ in the design and planning of wayfinding. The design of the 
wayfinding system should allow for signs to be relocated, content changes to be made, and/or new items to 
be introduced. A supporting temporary wayfinding system should also be considered, when required. It should 
be noted that, while nothing can be fully ‘future-proofed’, consideration can be made to planning ahead for 
future airport expansion (e.g., expansion of piers or phased introduction of new facilities for new-build or 
refurbishment projects) to ensure the seamless introduction of new signage and wayfinding. 
Whichever or however many technologies are selected, the considerations should be consistent for best 
practice planning and product assessment. 
Digital information should be of a scale appropriate to viewing distance and screen size.

Maintenance of dynamic items 
Ensure sufficient spare parts and replacement components are available, especially if the product was not 
procured locally; for example, if it is necessary to swap out a failed display screen. Items provided for use in 
fire and emergency evacuation and management may require a back-up system to ensure illumination of all 
items. 
Fire, emergency and safety signage 
Fire and emergency signage should ideally be considered as part of the overall airport wayfinding strategy 
and carefully coordinated with the architecture and interior design. Emergency egress route signage must be 
viewable from any position within the building, including signs within back-of-house areas. 
Often, fire and emergency signage may be progressed separately, and not by the wayfinding specialist. 
Therefore, it is important that all items are coordinated for optimum placement. The planner must also ensure 
that sightlines are not interrupted and there is not a conflict where both types of sign are required at the same 
location. 
Coordination with the architect can allow for even more detailed consideration, with the option for signs to be 
recessed into wall linings rather than surface fixed. Fire and emergency signage should not look like an 
after-thought. 
Fire and emergency signage can either be standalone or designed so as to sit with other wayfinding in the 
same sign panel or on the same structure. This may or may not be permitted, depending on location. The 
relevant international and building codes applicable to the project and incorporation of any local codes should 
be checked. The approving body should also advise on requirements as their own recommendations and 
interpretation of any standards may differ and will influence approvals. 
Be aware that, occasionally, one code document may request something that conflicts with another, especially 
when both international and local codes are to be applied. In some instances, a policy directive may not work 
in practice as many standards are designed to suit smaller public buildings. When there is a ‘code clash’, this 
should be bought to the attention of all responsible for final handover to agree on resolution. 
Supporting safety notices (Fire, Statutory, Mandatory and Warning signs) should follow the relevant codes 
and may incorporate more than one language, where required. 
Other types of airport signage 
There are two other areas of airport signage that require specialist design and planning expertise: 
1. Approach roads (local highway and on-airport)-Signage requirements on roads will need to comply with 
the relevant transport standards and legislation for the airport location, and will need to be developed by a 
specialist in this area. The airport should be indicated on major motorways/highways, usually using the 
approved symbol and named, where a city may have more than one airport. On approach to the airport, 
routes to different terminals will need to be indicated as well as cargo, airport service areas, airport 
parking and/or car rental facilities. Usually, the latter are within the airports operator's boundary, with 
brand names and logos required to be shown to ease of recognition; however, it is recommended that the 
826 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 846===
Pay 
Se IATA Pull Landside Access Systems 
principles of the local transport standards be maintained. Dynamic signage may be required to optimize 
road and forecourt capacity. 
2. Post-installation—-Review and assessment—Many large airports include wayfinding as part of their service 
quality management review process. While objective quantitative measurement is preferred (e.g., 
regarding the availability of FIDs), regular periodic reviews can help to gauge passenger reaction and 
experience of using the signage and the applied wayfinding principles, also taking into account 
multicultural considerations. Checks should be made to ensure that content is correct and updated when 
area or operational changes are made and that any updates do not compromise the applied wayfinding 
principles. For example, type size should not be reduced to fit extra messages. In addition, the design 
aesthetic should be maintained. Temporary changes such as patches fixed over panels do not give users 
confidence in the system. 
3.4 Landside Access Systems 
A coherent surface access strategy is vital to the success of an airport. Efficient travel to and from an airport 
greatly contributes to the overall efficiency of air transport and supports end-to-end passenger experience, 
accessibility for employees, and functionality for cargo and goods. 
3.4.1 Introduction 
Airport users have varying requirements and purposes to use surface access. It is therefore essential to 
accommodate a wide variety of needs and to provide an accessible, efficient and resilient surface 
transportation system. For instance, sufficient robustness should exist to enable reliable airport access for 
operational staff during adverse weather conditions to mitigate the effects of different conditions (e.g. snow, 
floods, power outage) on airport activity. Other factors that need to be considered range from dealing with 
peak traffic congestion and emergency situations to planning for maintenance and redundancy requirements 
and changes in access modes/services. 
3.4.1.1 Importance of Surface Access as Part of the Total Journey 
Journey time reliability to and from an airport is a key factor in planning a surface access strategy. A large 
proportion of trips to an airport are time critical, with passengers wanting to arrive at the right time prior to a 
flight, or for staff arriving in time for work. The surface access system should therefore provide enough 
resilience to support the demand and enable reliable journey times, even when transport system disruptions 
may occur. Stakeholder engagement with transport providers, rail and highway authorities, and the cities and 
other communities the airport serves is important to ensuring a reliable surface strategy. Early engagement 
with stakeholders, resilience, and future proofing are key elements to success. 
Journeys to the airport not directly related to flying also need to be considered. Airports tend to generate good 
multi-modal transport links. These links can attract additional trips to the area solely to use the airport surface 
transport hub as an interchange for their onward surface journey. Surface access strategies must ensure 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 827 

===PAGE 847===
== pti 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
capacity on the transport network can accommodate this background traffic as well as time-sensitive airport￾related trips. 
Poor surface access systems that lack a clear and well-thought-out strategy adversely affect the passenger 
experience and restrict the efficient and timely operations of an airport. It is increasingly common for airports 
and their stakeholders to develop a surface access strategy that considers the services and infrastructure for 
all airport access methods and the entire end to end passenger journey from home to gate. These plans, 
combined with airport operational plans, interface with both the airport master plan and the local transport 
plan. 
3.4.1.2 Key Influences of Surface Access 
Key influences that drive an effective surface access strategy are based on operational requirements, local 
and national transportation and environmental policies, as well as cultural behaviors. Surface access to and 
from an airport should accommodate the needs of many diverse groups with differing objectives; from 
passengers traveling to catch a flight during the early hours, staff commuting daily during peak hours, taxis 
looking for their next fare, and freight vehicles needing to drop off or pick up goods. 
Efficient surface access must take into consideration the airport type, size and needs to support an overall 
strategy in particular: 
e Master plan strategy 
e Potential airport or city development 
e Intercity connections 
e Future expansion without disrupting existing access to the airport 
¢ Potential development within the area immediately surrounding the airport, but not within its control 
* Future proof the surface access strategy in anticipation of changes in technology and passenger behavior 
e External policies and actions 
As mass transit projects and ground infrastructure development are not only an airport matter, the surface 
access strategy shall engage non-aviation stakeholders such as local governments, metropolitan and regional 
planning organizations, and transit agencies. It should be coordinated with the relevant city, metropolitan, 
regional, and sometimes even national transportation plans. 
3.4.1.2.1 Airport Function 
Cost, comfort, and travel time to and from an airport can have an impact on passengers’ decisions regarding 
their end to end journey, timing or potentially which airport they use. Surface access modes should not only 
provide a reliable opportunity to travel to and from the airport but should also be cost efficient for users. 
Providing efficient and affordable surface access can influence airport development as an essential element of 
master planning, that should be taken into account to enable and not constrain growth. Airports should identify 
and engage with off-site transport service providers to optimize services and infrastructure from an early stage 
828 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 848===
ye 
IATA Landside Access Systems 
in the planning process, and ensure developments are affordable, realistically achievable, and delivering a 
service that meets the needs and expectations of the public. 
A key driver for the surface access strategy is to ensure operational staff as well as passengers can access 
the airport on a reliable basis. Without this essential element, the airport cannot function effectively, potentially 
resulting in delays and congestion among other factors. For many airports, this may also mean discouraging 
the use of on-airport roads for through traffic by vehicle, that can be less resilient than other modes of 
transport. Multi- and inter-modality are alternatives to increase the resiliency of surface access through the 
diversity of transportation modes, technologies, and operators. 
3.4.1.2.2 Cultural Behavior and Regional Specificities 
Cultural behaviors and regional trends must also be considered as there is no single global or regional 
strategy that will work in all cases. For example, private cars may be the predominant mode of transport in 
one country or region whereas public transport may be the main mode in another. In some regions the 
number of people accompanying passengers may greatly outnumber the number of people flying and require 
longer duration short-term parking. 
Airports that typically cater to short-haul business flights typically cater forpassengers traveling alone with little 
or no luggage. This type of traveler has very different needs from those traveling in larger groups, or for those 
with long haul destinations who are likely to have hold luggage and arrive at the airport earlier. 
The type of destinations the airport serves should also be taken into consideration. For example, an airport 
serving predominantly tourist destinations could have a higher than typical share of car rentals or high￾occupancy vehicles serving tour groups (e.g. vans, coaches and buses), a higher number of passengers 
carrying multiple pieces of luggage, and likelihood of irregular-sized luggage such as skis, bicycles, and golf 
bags. 
3.4.1.2.3 External Policies 
The strategy that drives the airport's surface access system should reflect airport specific goals and policies 
as well as local and regional policies and priorities. Local and national policies guide the vision, objectives and 
targets of the surface access strategy. These policies and ensuing actions may not always fully align with the 
airport's needs. Therefore, ongoing consultation between airport and governing authorities is required to 
ensure development of an airport surface access system that balances needs and policies. 
It is recommended the airport have active engagement with local and national policymakers on matters that 
may affect the airport, airlines and other stakeholders at the airport informed of changes that may have a 
material impact on the airport access system.

3.4.1.3. Recent Changes in Surface Access Approaches and Emphasis 
Recent trends and evolving technology have had an impact on airport surface access. Various airport 
innovations as ride-hailing applications have affected surface access staging requirements and parking 
demand. Changes in social behavior, demographics, policy developments and attitudes towards” 
environmental responsibility “and easy access to online resources environmental responsibility should all be 
considered and carefully balanced as part of the strategy. Advancing technology is enabling more efficient 
and sustainable movement of greater numbers of people to and from an airport. Airports should design in 
flexibility and adaptability their surface access strategy to enable further changes in technology and 
passenger behavior. 
3.4.1.3.1 Contribution of Surface Access to Airport Environmental Impacts 
The latest technologies should be considered to promote surface access solutions that are safe and 
sustainable. There are many examples of improved awareness of environmental impacts. In general, policies 
and technologies consistent with reducing environmental impacts are those that reduce the number of vehicle 
trips per passenger (and per employee) and/or reduce the emissions of vehicles accessing the airport (either 
through cleaner vehicles, more mass transit, or by reducing delays and related emissions). In some countries, 
emission calculations to support environmental assessments with and without surface access improvements 
are an important part of substantiating the emissions impact. 
3.4.1.3.2_ Benefits to Local Public Transport of Airport-Related Services 
Airport-related transport services can have a large influence on the transport characteristics of the 
surrounding area. The relationship between airport-induced trips, their impact on the local area, and 
conversely the impact of background traffic on airport-related journeys need to be considered. Surface access 
to the airport must integrate with the wider transport network. Good integration promotes capacity gains and 
service improvements across the airport and throughout the surrounding region. Airports often act as major 
multimodal connecting hubs, enhancing mobility in their surrounding communities. 
Efficient intercity airport surface access connections, and connections between the airport and local city can 
also have a positive impact on airport growth by enlarging an airport's catchment area.

3.4.2 Preplanning 
3.4.2.1 Setting the Vision and Objectives for Surface Access 
All airports should establish a vision and set of objectives for its surface access strategy, in active 
collaboration with the broader airport stakeholder community, that links to and aligns with national and local 
policies. The agreed vision and objectives shape the priorities of the surface access strategy going forward. 
3.4.2.2 Modes to be Considered and Setting Mode Share Targets 
Targets are vital to achieving the surface access vision and meeting objectives, and provide quantifiable 
performance measures that move the strategy forward. Due to differing geographies, cultures and many other 
socio-economic factors, different airports have different priorities. However, all airports should set mode-share 
targets that shift users away from less efficient modes to those that are more consistent with achieving the 
objectives of the airport and its surrounding communities. 
Mode-share targets should align with: 
e Airport vision and objectives 
e Local and national policies 
e Direct interests of local communities 
e Airport operational requirements 
e Social and cultural behaviors 
e What is practical and affordable 
Mode-share targets, therefore, need to be ambitious, but realistic taking the above factors into account. 
Targets need to be challenging, but not beyond what is achievable within a given timeframe. Targets that are 
too aggressive can be counterproductive. Targets should be SMART: Specific, Measurable, Attainable, 
Relevant and Timely. 
3.4.2.3 Integration with Airport Master Plan 
The airport surface access is a key element of the airport master plan. During the airport master planning 
process, the role of surface access must be integrated into the overall planning process. Master planning is 
described in more detail in 2.3 Master Planning. Some terminal developments are placing an emphasis on 
integrated surface access with a ground transport center (GTC) as a key feature of the terminal plan 
consolidating multiple modes of transport in one place. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 833 

===PAGE 853===
Soe IATA ia Airport Development Reference Manual 
Air transport demand is one of the key drivers behind surface access provision, noting the greater the 
transport capacity available, the more potential the airport has to accommodate future passenger demand. 
The airport master plan needs to consider who will be using each facility, where they are coming from and 
going to, and how they will make the journey. At major hub airports, the campuses can be vast. The location 
of key facilities must be considered during the master planning process so integration of facilities with surface 
access modes, including public transport links, is taken into consideration and designed into the master plan. 
Key considerations: 
¢ What is the land use? 
¢ Who and what is traveling to a particular land use (e.g. staff, passengers, goods)? 
e How will the users get there? 
e Will the land use generate a high number of trips during peak periods? 
¢ How does this surface access project include and serve the different airport facilities, consider the various 
users, and connect to other public transportation services? What mode(s) of transport is most suitable to 
travel to this land use? 
e What are the social and environment impacts and benefits? 
e Consider the level of resilience required in the transport network to accommodate the development as 
part of the planning process. 
3.4.2.4 Prevailing Regulations 
Surface access modes should always take into consideration the prevailing standards and regulations 
applicable to the airport, including: 
¢ Local planning controls 
e Safety and security standards 
e Quality and design standards 
e Land-use policies 
¢ Local/regional transportation plans 
e Environmental policies and standards 
e Relevant transportation (non-aviation) regulations that pertain to the surface access mode(s) 
e Laws and regulations on transportation markets (economic regulation, fair access, etc.) 
e Industry standards and best practices 
In some cases, the requirements of airport surface access systems may lead to modification of existing 
standards and regulatory frameworks, or specific approvals. An example would be introduction of access 
charges for departure forecourts where the airport may not have an automatic right as a private entity.

3.4.2.5 Consultation 
As part of the wider airport strategy, airports should consult relevant stakeholders, when planning and 
discussing surface access. 
Airlines, integrators, tour operators and other handlers of cargo, goods and passengers 
Operational efficiency is vital at an airport. Therefore, airlines, integrators and tour operators should be 
consulted. The many varied needs of these groups must be reflected in the surface access strategy. 
Good neighbor imperative and best practices 
Airports should consult with local groups to ascertain their concerns and how they can work together to 
improve surface access in the area surrounding the airport. 
Planning authorities and transport authority liaison 
As part of the surface access strategy, there needs to be alignment with government and regulatory policies. 
The access strategy should also be integrated with the wider transport network. Consultation with national, 
regional, and local planning authorities on policy issues should lead to aligned planning and development 
strategies. 
Communications Strategy 
Depending on the stakeholder and level of decision being taken, the line of communication must be suitable. 
Use of focus groups as well as formal and informal consultation should be considered. 
3.4.3 Data Collection and Site Evaluation 
3.4.3.1 Existing Conditions 
Establishing the existing surface access conditions at an airport as a baseline is essential when devising a 
surface access strategy. Available transport and travel data that can quantify and qualify these existing 
conditions enable better understanding of how people travel to and from an airport. 
Data on existing conditions will help to identify: 
e Any spare capacity on the network 
e Problems on the existing transport network, both in capacity and supply 
e Location of facilities 
* Choices of modes to catchment areas that generate high airport demand 
* Opportunities for future capacity use and development

===PAGE 855===
we IATA fi Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.4.3.2 Passenger Characteristics 
Passenger characteristics can vary widely from airport to airport, terminal to terminal and even from flight to 
flight. A wide range of factors impact passenger characteristics (e.g. origin and destination, journey purpose, 
journey length, demographics, cultural and social behavior). Surface access modal choice can be influenced 
by numerous factors including arrival times before a flight (lead/lag times), group size, amount of luggage. 
Often, passengers may also be escorted to and from the airport by family and friends. These “well-wishers” or 
“meeters and greeters” will make return trips to and from the airport. The modal choice for the group will often 
be different from that of a passenger flying alone. As a result of certain cultural and social behaviors, airport 
visitors may well outnumber the actual traveling public. Understanding the number of additional trips to and 
from the airport generated can have a substantial impact on the surface access strategy and the required 
capacity of different surface access modes, as well as space provision within the terminal. 
3.4.3.2.1. General Aviation 
General aviation passengers are usually handled through a separate facility removed from the commercial 
passenger terminal and operations. Adequate services in line with the needs and expectations of the GA 
community, as well as different security requirements from those applicable to commercial service operations 
should be provided. Separate, dedicated access provides for safety, security, and privacy, and mitigates the 
impact of VIP trips on the overall airport capacity and delay as well as public safety. The mode of access is 
usually by road and a dedicated access is often provided. 
3.4.3.2.2 VIP and Protocol Passengers 
VIP and protocol passengers may be on dedicated flights or on commercial flights. Although usually small in 
number, transport for VIP and protocol passengers may often require segregation from the main road 
operations, either through temporary road closures or through dedicated access routes. In addition, there can 
be a significant number of people who travel to and from the airport as part of the local protocol delegation. 
The demand for VIP and protocol passenger services differs from airport to airport but is more prevalent 
atairports serving capital cities and other metropolitan areas hosting seats of institutions. 
3.4.3.2.3 Seasonal Charters and Religious Traffic 
Some airports include passenger terminals designed for specific events opened for limited times of the year 
(e.g. large sport events such as Olympic Games, Football World Cup, SuperBowl, music events, winter sports 
or the Hajj). The characteristics of surface transport for these airports is likely to be unique to the location. 
Increased use of charter coaches could be a characteristic of such facilities. Where such facilities do exist or 
where there is a significant presence in the main passenger terminal, it may be necessary to consider how 
passengers are handled. An example would be an airport with both a winter sports season and a significant 
summer tourist peak requiringflexible drop-off and pick-up areas for cars, taxi's, car rentals or buses. 
836 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 856===
Se By, IATA i Landside Access Systems 
3.4.3.2.4 Commuting of Airport Employees 
It is important to ascertain how all workers travel to and from an airport. Understanding staff transport 
requirements provides the airport management team with an opportunity to better manage staff travel 
demand. Airport employees represent everyone working at the airport, including those who may be based 
elsewhere, but need to travel to the airport. Consolidating travel characteristics from all stakeholders can help 
to justify public transport services on routes and at times that suit staff travel demand in an effort to reduce 
dependencies on private cars. 
3.4.3.3 Freight and Mail 
Freight and Mail journeys can account for a substantial proportion of an airport's surface access especially by 
road and needs to be managed carefully to avoid surface access congestion. It is important to understand 
and address how all types of vehicles access the airport for delivery and pick-up of freight and mail. 
Technology can help collect data about length of stay and processing times at the airport, for example, GPS 
tracking systems can monitor variables such as where vehicles are going and how long they are spending in 
collection facilities. Freight and mail facilities can also generate other airport trips (e.g. to pay import customs 
duties, personal deliveries, and collection of live animals, human remains and high-value goods). 
3.4.3.4 Goods and Other Deliveries 
As with freight and mail, goods and other deliveries such as fuel, catering and retail, as well as waste 
removal, also generate airport trips. The size of delivery, shuttle vehicles as well as their frequency can vary 
widely and should also be considered. Collecting data regarding these trips can be done similarly to freight 
and mail. It is important to look at the types of deliveries. 
3.4.3.5 Ground Access for Construction Projects 
Airports are likely to undergo significant development over time. This may add significantly to the surface 
access demand at an airport. Construction activities should have their own transport impact assessment and 
travel plans to minimize the impact on normal operational activities. 
Large construction projects can generate substantial vehicular traffic with the delivery of materials and 
equipment, as well as construction worker commuting. Construction activities should be carefully planned 
from a roadway and ground access perspective to provide adequate access for construction operations, and 
mitigate the impact on passenger and cargo surface access.

IATA / Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.4.3.6 Volume Surveys 
The analysis of survey data can aid the process of future surface access planning. For example, identifying 
the most and least popular modes of transport can help pinpoint user preferences. Understanding the reasons 
for current preferences can help planners establish priorities, such as travel time/duration and efficiency 
versus costs. 
Different types of users may prefer different modes of transport. Traveling passengers prefer different 
transportation modes than terminal operations staff, while freight and cargo staff have another set of 
transportation priorities. 
Volume surveys should be carried out at different times of the year and times of the day in line with peak and 
off-peak travel seasons and conditions. While the tourist peak demand may be in the summer or winter 
months, typical peak demand may be reduced at that time due to school vacations and fewer business trips. 
Volume surveys can be collected by several techniques: 
e Automated vehicle counts 
e Classified counts for different vehicle types 
¢ Cordon surveys (by number/license plate) 
e Parking occupancy 
e Pedestrian counts and surveys 
e Passenger and employee surveys 
«Dwell time by mode surveys 
e Vehicle occupancy by mode surveys 
e Acquisition and analysis of network Wi-Fi data, which are increasingly used over conventional techniques 
due to increased coverage and onward data analysis capabilities 
3.4.3.7 Surface Access Safety, Resilience and Security 
The surface access road network should be assessed for safety and security. This could include: 
e Accident locations 
e Areas of non-compliance with design regulations 
e Pedestrian and cyclist segregation from vehicle traffic 
e Road junctions, signage, and controls to prioritize traffic 
e Availability of alternate routes and variable signage in case of an incident or congestion 
e Actual record and potential for flooding (e.g. in underpasses, parking areas) 
e Proximity of surface access to the airside/landside boundary security fence and security-sensitive 
buildings 
e Vehicle speed and size constraints
