o Assignment of existing trips to the existing network to create a network validated against surveys 
o Assign future traffic scenarios to future network models to create a range of unconstrained demand 
for the design years (subject to interim and time dependent policy/facility provision introductions) 
e Facility requirements 
o Develop facility requirements based on demand | 
e For large area networks, consider the use of macro models that are better at distributing vehicle 
assignments 
e Undertake microsimulation if required, for critical elements of the network that are likely to be close to 
capacity to determine the level of delays and queuing that may be expected. These are likely to be at 
forecourts, junctions, pedestrian crossings, and areas of merging and weaving 
e Adjust the facilities following simulation, as necessary 
3.4.5 Forecasts 
3.4.5.1 Aircraft Arrival/Departure Profiles 
There is a direct relationship between the daily traffic profile of flights and the number of trips generated by 
arriving/departing passengers, freight, and mail at different times of the day. Surface access flows are 
typically driven by a combination of the design flight schedule, staff rosters and background traffic. 
Departure flows at the terminal entrance tend to be less “peaky” than equivalent flows within the terminal 
building processing facilities due to variances in the departure passenger profiles. Conversely, arrivals profiles 
can be consolidated into dense peak periods. These variances need to be evaluated and understood to 
840 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 860===
Se & IATA a Landside Access Systems 
accurately forecast and design the necessary departures and arrivals vehicle interface facilities (e.g. 
departures/arrivals curbs, parking facilities). Surveys, including passenger, vehicle and digital, can provide 
significant insights into the relationship between passenger presentation at the gate and on the curb. Once 
profiles are known, simulation modelling to test variances in demand within the model can be useful, 
depending on the complexity involved. Through this, the output information is an assessment of all scenarios 
to ensure the arrival/departure zone is capable of managing peaks within peaks. 
Consideration also needs to be given to the proportion of transfer or connecting passengers that, unless 
transferring landside, will not require surface access modes. The proportion of connecting traffic often varies 
by time of day and air carrier. A terminal with a large transfer volume may require fewer surface transport 
facilities than one with a high proportion of origin and destination passengers. However, at hub airports the 
timing of large transfer volumes may not coincide with the timing of origin and destination peaks. It is 
therefore important to consider the impact of the different passenger peaks on surface access. Hub airports 
often have higher origin and destination peaks in the early morning and late evening, resulting in peak curb 
requirements at that time even through the busy hour rates may be higher in the middle of the day when 
transfer rates are higher. 
3.4.5.2 Mode Share 
Baseline mode share 
Forecasting the future share of transport modes for all the airport users is a critical element of forecasting. For 
existing airports, the current mode shares should provide a cornerstone to the baseline of the forecasts. For 
new airports or new facilities, research into mode share from other similar airports or other facilities at the 
airport will help inform the mode share. Care should be taken to ensure exiting mode share is represented for 
difference times of the day and that variations are not just taken as evidence, but are also explainable; for 
instance, a low public transport mode share in the morning could be due to lack of service availability. Mode 
share should be disaggregated, where possible by journey types (e.g. passengers guided to different 
destinations if the number of escorts is significant). The baseline mode share should have a high degree of 
correlation across a range of surveys. 
Future mode share. 
Future mode share forecasting risks planning for solutions that may not be realistically deliverable or 
affordable for airports to finance or airport users to fund. Changes to the existing mode share are either 
evidenced through historical changes in behavior or through the introduction of new modes, interventions, or 
technologies in the future. 
An example of modal share change would be for the introduction of a new rail link connecting the airport to 
the city center. Some of the key pieces of information that would be important in development of the market 
share could include: 
e Proportion of passengers that make the journey on existing modes (in peak times) 
* Existing transport modes that the rail link will compete with 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 841 

===PAGE 861===
IATA piu Airport Development Reference Manual 
* Characteristics of the rail link (cost, time, connectivity, reliability, and frequency) that will persuade 
passengers to change mode 
¢ Potential for route substitution where people who would not normally route via the city center will change 
their route, based on cost, time and reliability 
e Competitive response from the other modes to retain market share 
e¢ Good communications of the benefits of a new service are important to ensure the facility captures the 
forecast client/passenger base 
* Evidence from other airports on the change to modal share for a similar service 
It is recommended that changes to an existing mode share to different traveler types should be considered as 
scenarios and a range tested to understand the impact on future facility requirements. Any change to the 
existing mode share assumptions should be properly tested and documented as part of the concept of 
operations. 
3.4.5.3 Airport Passenger Arrival Profile Forecast 
It is important to understand what drives passenger mode choice, the length of time passengers arrive before 
a flight (the presentation profile) and how long after a flight has landed passengers leave the airport. This 
allows for suitable transport capacity to be provided at relevant times to align with passenger requirements 
and movements. 
The timing of passenger arrivals at the airport via surface access can vary from airport to airport due to a wide 
range of factors, including: 
° Reliability 
© Reliability is the primary concern of passengers regarding available transport modes to airports due to 
the consequence of missing a flight 
o Departing passengers who choose a potential unreliable access mode, typically allow for a buffer 
which sees them arrive well ahead of their flight's scheduled departure 
o Improvements to surface access reliability could result in later passenger turn-up profiles, which 
requires coordination with airport planning parameters to ensure service levels are met at processing 
facilities such as check-in and bag drop 
° Trip purpose 
o Business and leisure passengers are likely to have a different arrival pattern, with business 
passengers often arriving at the airport closer to departure time 
o Whether a trip is international or domestic 
m Passengers who frequently use the airport and those without checked baggage (e.g. domestic 
travelers) often arrive at the airport closer to departure time than infrequent travelers (e.g. 
international travelers)

3.4.5.4 Freight and Mail Forecasts 
The movement of freight and mail to and from the airport can lead to the presence of large goods vehicles 
with differing requirements compared to passengers or staff. These vehicles travel at different times on 
different schedules, via different routes, and, potentially, to different destinations. 
Key considerations when forecasting freight and mail traffic include: 
e Types of goods being shipped (e.g. potential time sensitivities) 
e Existence of a dominant integrator/handler that requires its own facility (versus shared facilities) 
e Types of vehicles that deliver/pick up goods at the airport 
© Typical load weight/volume carried per vehicle 
¢ Origins and destinations of the freight vehicles 
° Vehicle access routes and impact of possible restrictions on local roads 
e Existence of off-site consolidation centers 
* Locations of existing or potential loading/unloading areas 
e Vehicle waiting areas 
¢ Dwell times and facility efficiency 
e Security and customs requirements 
© Dwell time that loading bays are occupied and space required 
¢ Prevalence of landside-to-landside and airside-to-airside transshipping activities 
Freight traffic management planning is essential to ensure goods vehicles arrive and depart according to an 
agreed program. This allows for better management of loading/unloading space, time, and trips on the 
network. 
3.4.5.5 Employee Numbers, Job Mix and Shift Profiles 
Employee travel can account for a significant proportion of trips to/from an airport. It is important to note that 
employees have different travel preferences from passengers arriving for a flight. Key considerations and 
influencing factors include: 
e Cost and availability of staff parking facilities 
e How and if staff travel and parking is subsidized by employers 
© Trip origin location (home address or district), work location (job role) and shift profile 
¢ Variations in shift profiles (how often shift profiles are adjusted) 
e Proportion of travel cost vs. salary 
e Availability of public transport services near employee residences and transit schedules during airport 
employee commute times (especially shifts that may begin before or end after transit operating hours)

IATA Landside Access Systems 
3.4.5.6 Background Surface Access Growth (All Modes) 
Background surface access demand around the airport across all modes can fluctuate due to circumstances 
beyond an airport's control, such as population growth, new developments near the airport, and provision of 
additional transport links (e.g. road, rail). 
3.4.5.7 Air—Rail Substitution 
Air-rail substitution is the provision of rail services in-lieu of air services between cities, either independent of 
the airports and airlines or as an integrated service using the airport rail station, with or without airline￾connected ticketing. 
Development of high-speed rail networks can create viable substitution options to air travel over significant 
distances and may be particularly attractive for passengers who have a city center as their ultimate 
destination. The effectiveness of air-rail substitution will depend on the level of accessibility between the rail 
station and the passenger terminal, service frequency, pricing, journey time and service availability. For many 
air-rail substitutions, the journey to the airport would no longer be necessary. This can have a substantial 
impact on demand and mode shifts and the potential impact should be considered in the planning of airports, 
even if only a scenario. 
Air-rail substitution can also free up airport capacity for routes that do not have a viable surface transport 
mode. There are several examples of airports with fully integrated high-speed rail and inner-city services, 
including Frankfurt, Shanghai Hongqiao and Paris Charles de Gaulle (CDG). Air-rail substitution can also be 
imposed by governments as part of sustainable transport policies where the rail journey is within one country 
or economic bloc. 
3.4.5.8 Development of Busy Hour Demand Flows for Terminal Landside Access 
The busy hour for landside access may look significantly different from the busy hour profile at the gate due to 
factors described in 3.4.4 and 3.4.5. A similar methodology to the one described for the terminal facilities 
should be considered (see 3.3.4.9 Demand-Capacity Assessment to understand how to develop demand 
profiles). That methodology should be adjusted to identify specific criteria applicable to the specific landside 
subsystem. Some important considerations related to landside access have to be noted: 
e Asegmentation of passenger types will be required where or if there are different modal choices

e Planners should take into consideration that terminal access and forecourts are typically not designed as

e Different modal splits may need to be applied to the specific flow rates noting that those may vary at

e Vehicle passenger occupancy rates need to be applied in order to determine the vehicle demand figures 
3.4.6 Development of Options 
3.4.6.1 Design Criteria 
Surface access design criteria mirror that of other elements of an airport including capacity, level of service, 
safety, security, sustainability, and resilience. However, there is an additional need for the airport to work with 
external providers of infrastructure and services to integrate the access needs of the airport with the landside 
capacity and future developments. 
The design criteria need to work with current and future local and regional transport plans to ensure the 
capacity constraints are fully understood, and that on- and off-airport surface transport infrastructure is 
developed in a coordinated manner. This may include safeguarding on-airport zones for future transport 
systems (e.g., metro, rail) that may not be available on the initial opening of a new facility. 
While the airfield and terminal design criteria tend to follow international standards or best practices, the 
landside infrastructure needs to meet local regulations as a minimum and should accommodate appropriate 
local behaviors. However, the airport's approach to capacity, level of service, safety, security, sustainability, 
and resilience can often result in a higher level of design criteria than would be found off-airport. 
In development of new facilities or new airports, there is normally an obligation on the airport to deliver at 
least a portion of the surface access infrastructure. The extent of this investment will depend on number of 
factors, including airport ownership, land ownership, available financing as well as the rights and obligations 
of off-site transport operators and infrastructure providers (e.g. governments). 
3.4.6.2 Capacity 
The capacity of the surface access system needs to consider a value range within the modal split. This 
ensures changes in policy to promote one mode over another (e.g., subsidized rail travel to offset road 
journeys, thus reducing environmental impact) can result in significant changes in modal split. Changing 
policies on staff travel or off-site cargo consolidation can also make significant changes to demand for surface 
access facilities. 
846 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 866===
ie IATA | Landside Access Systems 
The overall capacity must be sufficient to ensure all journeys are on time, reliably and avoid delays with 
sufficient capacity. Staff arriving late for work can be as operationally problematic as passengers missing 
flights. 
The capacity of a given airport road link is typically less than its equivalent off airport, as on-airport roadways 
have a higher proportion of drivers unfamiliar with the road layout, junctions, and pedestrian interactions as 
well as more buses and trucks on some links. Planners should recognize this lower capacity, and both include 
it in the analysis and aim to simplify the journey to improve the capacity. The landside system needs to 
consider the impacts of downstream and upstream facilities to accommodate passenger demand and levels of 
service. 
When considering the capacity of the surface transport system, the planner needs to recognize there is a 
close relationship between the ratio of demand and capacity to delays. This is due to natural variability in the 
regularity of vehicles arriving in any given flow rate. 
For each country or region, there are differing local characteristics that need to be accommodated, including: 
e Vehicle dimensions and capacities 
© Vehicle mix 
e Shared versus personal transport 
e Driver performance (speed and headways) 
¢ Impacts of geometric and physical constraints (e.g. ramps, gradients, curvatures, junctions) 
e Impacts of traffic patterns, such as excessive recirculation within the airport 
e Impact of commercial vehicle behavior and its interaction with private vehicles 
Capacity of terminal forecourts can be complex to evaluate due to the various factors, such as maneuvering in 
and out of spaces, variable dwell time, effective length versus full length available, passenger/vehicle 
interactions, through traffic, recirculation traffic, pedestrian crossings as well as variability of the flow within the 
peak period. 
A simple static model would follow the following principles as the basis of calculation: 
e Use a peak demand rate (vehicles per hour) split for each transport mode. Specific dwell time and curb 
length requirements for each type of vehicle need to be identified Consideration for some additional 
allowances for disabled spaces and law enforcement will provide an indication of the net curb length 
e The total curb length required will be a function of the net curb length and the target level of service. 
Additional factors to adjust for the irregularity of flows and dwell times during the design period may be 
applied (e.g., Poisson distribution factor) 
¢ The curb length required for each vehicle type will vary depending on the country and commonly used 
vehicles. Dwell time for vehicles should be derived from existing operational data or tailored surveys. 
Consideration should be given to active curb management and no “waiting” vehicles during busy periods. 
Dwell times are likely to vary depending on vehicle type and time of day

e Pedestrian crossing patterns from offside frontages will influence vehicle progression; therefore, 
operational assistance technology may be necessary to achieve the desired outcome 
3.4.6.3 Safety 
Airport surface access services a wide number of road users, primarily categorized in vehicles and 
pedestrians. Interaction between the various users presents many safety risks. These risks are heightened 
because, for many users, visiting an airport is an infrequent occurrence that is often associated with time 
pressures. Drivers and pedestrians who are not familiar with the airport surface access systems and routes 
will be distracted from normal transport behaviors. Therefore, local regulations and recommendations for the 
layout of the surface transport interchanges should be adopted at airports. 
Safety should be enhanced by carefully considering: 
e Early wayfinding (signage) with clear and limited choices at each junction; ideally, only a choice of two 
directions (either “A” or “B”) 
e Clearly planned routes for each mode from the inbound transport links to the face of the building or 
secure perimeter 
e Use of physical devices (e.g. ramps, speed bumps, traffic circles, traffic lights, rumble strips) to control 
toad vehicle speeds 
e Points of pedestrian/vehicle interface are protected with minimized speed, clear priority signage and 
adequate capacities 
e Segregation of staff, deliveries, cargo, VIP, and passenger access vehicles 
e Avoiding the ability to double or triple park vehicles on forecourts to ensure passengers have direct 
access from curb to vehicle 
e Avoiding short merge and weaving areas 
e Where necessary, provide active and visible enforcement staff to ensure smooth flow, avoid unattended 
vehicles and excessive dwell times 
¢ Utilization of CCTV to monitor safety 
3.4.6.4 Security 
The increasing prevalence of threats targeted at airport landside facilities targets means that appropriate 
measures need to be considered to control and, if possible, interrupt the effect of any attack. Methods may 
include: 
e Full CCTV coverage of access roads and parking with video analytics to warn of suspect behaviors (e.g., 
unusual driving or parking) 
e Interception areas to enable law enforcement to block access to vulnerable areas 
e Segregation of public and private vehicles to prevent higher risk vehicles passing close to vulnerable 
areas 
848 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 868===
IATA Landside Access Systems 
e Separation of forecourts from the face of terminal buildings. Where a threat is considered credible, a 
minimum distance is commonly imposed from the nearest curb to the building facade. In some countries 
this applies to all vehicles and in others to only private vehicles. The purpose of this is to reduce the 
impact of a vehicle-born explosive device on the fagade and passengers inside of the building. The 
requirements are often determined following a risk-based assessment and can vary across a country 
(such as the US) and also by vehicle type 
¢ Separation of car parking facilities from terminal building facades of a minimum distance also applies. For 
instance, in the US, the TSA may require 91m or the ability to close parking that is within this distance 
during periods of alert 
¢ Provision of bollards or other barriers to prevent vehicles from breaking into vulnerable areas (sometimes 
known as hostile vehicle mitigation (HVM) measures) 
e Provision of blast-resistant facades 
As the nature of threats is constantly changing, mitigation measures must also continue to evolve. 
Development of the landside access facilities needs to include early consultation with the national aviation 
security regulator. While there are best practice examples at several airports around the world, these may not 
necessarily be appropriate due to the nature of the threat profile. 
An example of a change introduced as a result of evolving threats is the physical separation of the forecourts 
and building facades to reduce the risk from blasts. An offset has been found to also benefit the passenger 
journey, providing orientation space for passengers having alighted their vehicles as well as for passengers 
exiting the terminal and finding their onward connection. Airports have also made use of this space to create a 
plaza feature.

When planning landside facilities, the designer should consider the consequences of additional space being 
required in the future and allow for such space in the initial design. 
3.4.6.5 Sustainability and Future Systems 
In keeping with the aviation industry's stated goal to decarbonize, and with the increasing availability of 
electrically powered transport and the forecast availability of autonomously driven vehicles, there will be 
increasing opportunities for airports to restrict access to vehicles with internal combustion engines, in 
particular those vehicles related to passenger and staff access. 
As airports usually have a high level of influence over the ease of access for different modes and user types, 
they play an essential role in the aviation industry's efforts to decarbonize. As airports can be centers with 
high resilience in energy supply, they can also play a key role in providing charging stations for electric 
vehicles. Design of future surface access should, therefore, consider changes to the connected electrical load 
(e.g. provision of vehicle charging infrastructure). By analyzing an airport's goals on sustainability, the surface 
access plan can integrate with the available technologies. This enables an airport to consider and adapt its 
sustainability plans and reduce its carbon by adopting new technologies

3.4.6.6 Resilience 
Surface transport systems must be designed with a significant and reliable level of resilience. Without this 
resilience, surface access disruptions can have consequential impacts on airport and airline operations. 
Airports should work closely with local transport authorities to ensure there is sufficient resilience in each 
surface access system. A risk assessment of the surface access infrastructure should also be provided. This 
study should look at the frequency and severity of each risk and recommend measures that maintain 
adequate capacity and be an input in the Concept of Operations. These measures should eventually form part 
of the airport's SOPs. 
Major risks (e.g., rail disruptions, traffic accidents, floods) may require an alternative mode or route with the 
necessary capacity. Minor risks (e.g. vehicle breakdowns, traffic signals out of order) should be managed 
through additional width and bypassing capability, redundancy systems, or human intervention. “must ride” 
systems need resilience within their own capacity. Enhanced service level maintenance/response agreements. 
can be implemented to ensure the timely rectification of faults. 
3.4.6.7 Access Modes 
3.4.6.7.1 Private Vehicles 
Speed restrictions should be in place for all vehicle types to improve safety at all drop-off and pick-up areas 
due to the nature of the environment, with pedestrians and moving vehicles in close proximity to each other. 
Travel to and from the airport by private car continues to be a popular means of surface access for airport 
employees as well as travelers and escorts. This mode of surface access often provides the most flexible 
mode of travel for many, particularly for travel outside the operational hours of public transport systems. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 851 

===PAGE 871===
we IATA - Hi. Airport Development Reference Manual 
Planners should consider trends in car ownership for the country and region. High quality alternatives such as 
mobility as a service (MAAS) where available can provide a viable alternative, whereas at many airports the 
cost of parking and travel time are still the prevalent factors to consider. 
3.4.6.7.2 Taxis 
Taxis can account for a significant proportion of trips to and from an airport, particularly for passengers. Most 
taxi trips are likely to be to and from terminals, and consideration needs to be given to the routing of taxis, 
where they will pick-up and drop-off their fares, and the location of taxi staging areas. Taxi pick-up and drop￾off areas should be close to the terminals. 
3.4.6.7.3. Transportation Network Companies 
Transportation network companies (TNCs) such as Uber, Lyft and Grab are more commonplace at airports 
and provide a service similar to taxis with the exception that they operate on a pre-booked basis and are a 
non-hail service. They cannot be flagged down in the street for hire or queue at a taxi rank and pick up 
passengers without a contracted ride. Instead, passengers request rides directly from private drivers under 
contract with a TNC, usually with a smartphone app rather than using dispatch centers. TNCs are considered 
competition to traditional taxis and mini-cab companies who have progressively lost market share. Therefore, 
it is common practice to provide separate pick-up areas for TNCs and taxis. 
At larger airports, TNCs will generally need a holding area while waiting for new rides. This is to avoid TNCs 
parking on road verges or congesting the road network around the airport by circulating. Where space 
permits, these holding areas can be located away from the terminal area. Passengers can connect with their 
TNC rides at a designated area of forecourt or GTC. Technologies are now enabling TNCs to queue in a 
similar manner to taxis with passengers receiving a “short code” or PIN after making their ride request. The 
passenger then enters the first vehicle in the queue and provides the PIN to the driver. TNC allocation can be 
“geo-fenced” to ensure vehicles enter the desired holding area. 
3.4.6.7.4 Private Hire Vehicles 
In recent years, the number of private hire vehicles (e.g., mini-cabs, limousines) has increased in many cities, 
most notably where on-demand private hire services are available. Holding areas for taxis and private hire 
vehicles should be incorporated in the overall surface transport master plan. These holding areas should 
provide controlled parking areas away from curbside areas to reduce curbside dwell time. 
3.4.6.7.5 Rental Cars 
Rental cars provide a major mode of surface transport at many airports. While many passengers will 
prearrange their car rental, there is still demand for bookings to be made on arrival. Multitenant rental car 
reservation and vehicle staging facilities, either within the GTC itself or nearby in remote parking areas served 
852 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 872===
Pay 
TATA Landside Access Systems 
by buses or other means of surface transport (e.g., light rail), should be included in the airport's overall 
surface access master plan. 
On-airport rental car operations include various processes that will add traffic to the airport road network 
depending on the location of the rental car agencies. In addition to the rentals and returns, traffic resulting 
from car jockeying operations and quick turnaround areas should be taken into consideration. 
3.4.6.7.6 Buses 
Buses at airports provide a convenient public transport service in the vicinity of the airport for staff, 
passengers and through traffic. Bus services provide more frequent stops than local rail service and can 
access local residential areas, thus providing an attractive surface access service to people living near local 
bus routes. A night bus service can also provide valuable public transport for staff working night shifts or for 
passengers traveling to early morning/late night flights. Key considerations for bus services include: 
e Route requirements 
e Service demand/frequency 
e Layover facilities for service regularity 
¢ Stop locations 
e Interchange with other surface access modes (é@.g., rail, coaches) 
3.4.6.7.7 Coaches 
Coaches provide a longer-distance service than buses, typically calling at larger towns and stopping at key 
public transport hubs enroute to the airport. At some locations, passengers can purchase tickets for coach 
transfers to and from the airport as part of an air vacation package. Other users include: 
e Courtesy vehicles operated by hotels/motels 
e Off-airport parking companies 
e Off-airport rental car providers 
e Shuttle buses carrying passengers to/from remote on-airport parking facilities 
e Charters 
e Non-public-transport buses, such as those serving resorts 
Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) systems are large capacity, high level of service buses operating, as far as 
practicable, on reserved lanes. Transit fares are typically paid at the station in order to minimize the boarding 
time. BRT provides enhanced bus services with the level of service of light rail and the flexibility of the bus.

===PAGE 873===
IATA zal Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.4.6.7.8 Water Transport 
Water transport to and from an airport is applicable for several of the world's airports. Ferry transport provides 
surface access services either in the absence of or in addition to other access modes other surface transport. 
Airports serving cruise terminals may have operational features for handling baggage, customs clearance and 
connecting passengers. 
For airports that are accessible over water, barge transport can significantly reduce the impact on local roads 
for delivery of bulk construction materials, large construction and operational equipment, as well as fuel. 
Barges can also be useful for the removal of waste. 
3.4.6.7.9 Employee Shuttles 
At larger airports, where there is significant demand, airline operators run employee shuttles to move staff 
around the airport campus. Shuttle services are typically provided when walking distances to the terminals 
and operating centers from the staff parking areas are too long. These shuttles usually run in a similar fashion 
to a local bus service, with stops covering key locations on the airport campus. Typical shuttle services 
operate between employee parking lots, operations centers, airport terminals, offices, and public transport 
stations. Key considerations for employee shuttle services mirror those of local bus services: 
¢ Route requirements 
e Service demand/frequency 
¢ Stop locations 
e Interchange with other surface access modes (e.g. metro, rail, local bus, regional coach) 
¢ Contingency plan for when regular shuttle services are not available (e.g. strikes, adverse weather 
conditions) 
3.4.6.7.10 Emergency Services 
It is vital that access for emergency vehicles be included in the airport surface access master plan to ensure 
quick and effective response times. Adequate emergency vehicle access may require providing multiple 
routes to the same key locations. Where route options are limited, space should be provided for emergency 
vehicles to pass potential queueing traffic, that could be achieved in part with select vehicle priority 
infrastructure. 
It is important to consider the types of emergency service vehicles that require access to the transport 
facilities, airport terminal and other key installations (e.g. cargo, aircraft maintenance, general aviation). 
Infrastructure design must consider the dimensions of emergency vehicles, turning circle radii, weight of the 
vehicles, and any limitations for traversing gradients to upper or lower-level platforms. Designing emergency 
access must balance the need for easy access (e.g. gates with breakable sections) with security needs.

IATA Landside Access Systems 
3.4.6.7.11 Goods Vehicles 
Goods vehicles for the transport of supplies at the airport, for construction or airfreight will drive the geometry 
and design of many of the roads at an airport. Planners should arrange the road layout to separate goods 
from passenger vehicles before entering the terminal area. 
Where goods vehicles need access to terminals for delivery purposes, these should be routed to avoid the 
use of passenger forecourts. Goods vehicles for cargo and support services may also include those for freight 
forwarding facilities located off-airport. Sufficient road and parking capacity should be available to avoid 
impacts to local communities. 
3.4.6.7.12 Rail 
There are several different types of rail access: 
e High-speed 
e Regional/intercity 
* Commuter rail and metro (subway) 
e — Light rail 
e Dedicated airport express 
High-speed rail 
High-speed rail provides a fast, efficient, sustainable, and high-quality rail service connecting major city 
centers. For some short-haul air journeys, high-speed systems may provide a competitive alternative service 
whilst also supporting sustainability goals. 
Airports with integrated high-speed rail services, including Paris CDG, Baltimore-Washington International, 
Frankfurt, and Shanghai's Hongqiao, are directly connected into the nation's high-speed rail network. These 
airports act as hubs for cities in the region and increase the respective catchment areas. 
Regional/intercity 
A regional rail service is valuable for increasing the airport catchment area. Frequency may need to be 
adjusted to be compatible with the classic hub-and-spoke airport operation with waves of inbound and 
outbound connecting flights. 
Commuter and metro rail system 
The most common types of metro rail system are subway/underground, including extensions on a local 
commuter network. These are particularly suitable for employee access because their services are part of a 
public transit network serving residential areas, and the fare structure is geared to frequent travelers. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 855 

===PAGE 875===
ra OWirt 
LSS IATA ja Airport Development Reference Manual 
An advantage of airport access to the railway operator is that many employees and some air passengers 
travel outside of the local peak rush hours, and therefore make good use of spare capacity inherent in a 
commuter operation. However, some commuter rail variants that only have a few peak trips in the peak 
direction are not suited to airport traffic. To adequately serve an airport, an expansion of service to 
multidirectional, reverse commute, and regularly scheduled trips throughout the day should be considered. 
Commuter and metro rail systems are typically not as convenient as other surface access modes for air 
passengers, especially those traveling with baggage. Accommodation of large pieces of baggage in stations 
and on trains is often an issue. In addition, the airport needs to be kept aware of operational disruptions on 
the system and to be ready to liaise, if necessary, with the transport provider. 
Light rail 
Light rail is increasingly becoming a solution for airport surface access, although as with commuter and metro 
systems, it is more suited to employees than air passengers due to the types of railcars provided and their 
ability to deal with baggage. An example of successful integration of light rail into an airport is London City 
Airport where nearly 50% of passengers use the Dockland Light Railway for its speed and convenience. 
However, most of these passengers are business travelers who tend to travel without large bags. 
Light rail can also commonly be used to connect terminals to the main airport rail station as well as a 
distributor of passengers, staff, and meet/greeters around the airport campus as part of the overall ground 
transport system. 
High-speed dedicated airport express 
The high-speed dedicated airport express will usually provide the best service to passengers traveling from 
the city center to the airport. There are several examples such as Shanghai (PVG) and Toronto Pearson, 
characterized by high-speed limited stop services and trains with a relaxed ambience and purpose-built 
luggage accommodation. In some cases, these systems also provide in-town check-in. Some systems offer a 
commitment to punctuality and reliability. In a number of cases, the timetable is such that there is always a 
train waiting for passengers. 
The downside of dedicated airport rail systems is that the operating cost per passenger is usually high. The 
service needs to maintain a high frequency throughout the operational period with frequencies in the order of 
every 15 to 20 minutes for a 20 km service distance or 20 to 30 minutes for a longer service, otherwise road 
or metro options can be more attractive. 
3.4.6.8 Emerging Modes and New Developments in Surface Access 
New technologies allow for the just-in-time ordering and pick-up of passengers, which can reduce waiting 
times making the curbside more efficient.

3.4.6.8.1 Journey Information Services 
The provision of personalized journey information services through several technology companies, such as 
Google, Waze, Apple as well as many transport service providers, has transformed landside transport 
information. Journey ti me certainty has improved with routes that avoid congestion, leading to potential 
network optimization. Working with these service providers can significantly help in the provision of improved 
experience for normal journeys as well as during irregular operations (both on and off airport) and if major 
changes are being made to the landside road network. 
3.4.6.8.2. Advanced Urban Air Mobility (AAM) 
While currently in the prototype phase, the introduction of E-VTOL aircraft connecting airports to city centers 
or other destinations such as resorts at a price point between taxis and helicopters are expected to become a 
reality for some major airports. This is particularly so where the journey to the onward destination, would take 
more time by surface transport resulting from congestion or where road connections do not exist. These 
services are likely to provide connectivity for air passengers over short distances, and while unlikely to make a 
significant impact on surface access demand as a substitute mode, could make the airport more accessible 
and be a net generator of trips. E-VTOL facilities will require ground and air space, electrical power and 
connectivity to passenger terminals at airports. 
Vehicles used for delivering AAM services can have different performances to operate from traditional airside 
facilities (CTOL-Conventional Takeoff and Landing), short runways (STOL-Short Takeoff and Landing), and/or 
vertiport facilities (VTOL-Vertical Takeoff and Landing). 
Most E-VTOL operations are likely to be on the landside of an airport, and operations are likely to be 
classified as helicopter operations with helipads and final-approach-and-takeoff (FATO) areas as described 
under ICAO Annex 14 Volume 2 until specific regulations are approved. Approach and departure procedures 
will need to be coordinated with the surrounding airspace users, not interfere with existing operations and 
should be planned to minimize impacts on the long-term development of the airport. 
The development of AAM services at airports will provide both challenges and opportunities for airport 
operators. While they may create fast connections by air that are not impacted by the congestion on the 
ground, they might warrant, due to their operational specificities and facility requirements, the creation of new 
infrastructure, either they are VTOL, STOL ports, or separate terminal facilities. The planning and design of 
such facilities, and their integration into the airport setting, will need to balance the needs of the AAM-related 
operations, aviation safety and security requirements, efficient transfer from AAM vehicles to conventional 
aircraft, and the capacity, delay, and land-use aspects for the overall airport 
Consideration for E-VTOL operations include the amount of space required due to the need for recharging 
bays, which could conflict with other infrastructure such as car parking, potentially with a lower net yield. The 
main differences between helicopter operations and E-VTOL are the need for an electrical energy source 
instead of hydrocarbons. The amount of spare electric load capacity will also influence the initial 
attractiveness of E-VTOL operations at an airport. Power supply and smart power management for supporting 
AAM should be developed with considerations for the broader “Electrification of Everything” from the landside 
to the airside, noting costs and the need for a viable business case.

IATA al Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.4.6.8.3 Clean Fuel Vehicles and Corresponding Fueling/Charging Points 
Supporting the use of zero-emission ground transport is important for the aviation industry in its endeavor to 
decarbonize. Electric vehicles (EV), sustainable diesel (biodiesel) and hydrogen fuel cells are the three most 
likely technologies for the future. Electric power is likely to be the future for smaller vehicles with lower 
utilization, while hydrogen and sustainable diesel are likely to be more appropriate for larger vehicles with 
higher utilization. Many countries are planning to ban the sale of cars that burn fossil fuels so there will be a 
transition period as EVs generally take over, which provides opportunities to make positive interventions for 
users of zero-emission vehicles. Such interventions could include reduced or zero parking charges for EV's. 
3.4.6.8.4 Autonomous Vehicles 
An autonomous vehicle (AV) does not have a driver, but AVs have the potential to have a significant impact 
on landside transport by providing transport services with little human interaction and are likely to operate on 
their own segregated network. 
Digital connectivity between AVs could reduce separation and increase capacity of existing infrastructure. 
Vehicles are more likely to be provided by technology transport companies than private users, such as an 
extension to TNC operations with potential disruption to car rental, car parking and other driver-biased modes. 
Autonomous vehicle operation can also be provided by airports to enable easy connection between facilities. 
Introduction of AVs may ultimately change vehicle ownership from private to car sharing through vehicles-as￾a-service models, a potential disrupter/opportunity for car rental companies. To provide an on-demand service 
for arriving passengers, consideration should be given to safeguarding for consolidated storage, charging and 
pick-up, either in proximity of the arrivals forecourt or in a consolidated rent-a-car (CONRAC) facility. 
3.4.6.8.5 Off-Site Freight Delivery 
Certain logistics companies are already operating a just-in-time operation of their landside fleet, which has 
significantly reduced the dwell time for trucks around integrator/e-commerce operations. However, as many 
deliveries are likely to remain by third parties, the opportunity for slot delivery or pick-up for all commercial 
vehicles has the potential to realize additional capacity especially where the airport is space constrained. 
Interventions to prevent overspill of early arrivals into the local community would be required; for example, 
provision of common early arrivals trailer parking, similar to cellphone lots for cars may be needed. 
3.4.6.8.6 Consolidation Centers 
Several airports such as San Diego International Airport (SAN) have consolidation centers located on the 
periphery of the airport acting as hubs for deliveries to and from passenger and cargo terminals. These 
centers provide a number of opportunities to increase the efficiency of the airport, including: 
e Use of consolidation centers to store goods and cargo until needed by the terminal/cargo terminal, 
reducing storage required in the terminals

===PAGE 878===
x dil Se 
IATA - Landside Access Systems 
¢ Provision of consolidated outbound security screening/inbound customs, reducing the requirements on the 
terminals 
e Reduction in third-party vehicles on airport roads and use of bonded/secure trucks for deliveries 
e Reduction in the size and number of truck docks 
e Reduction in security risk as on-airport trucks can be restricted to known/approved providers 
3.4.6.8.7 E-Cycles/E-Bikes 
Electric power-assisted cycles/bikes have the potential to transform commuter traffic. 
Their extended range and reduced physical effort required compared to traditional cycles/bikes make it an 
increasingly attractive mode of transport. Cycling/biking is often encouraged, and many cities are investing 
heavily in cycle networks as this can free up capacity on public transport or general road space and provide 
health and environmental benefits. For this to be an attractive mode for staff travel to airports, it is important 
that suitable cycle/bike routes are developed that are as continuous as possible. There should also be 
storage, charging and changing facilities at places of work. 
3.4.6.9 Airport “Front Doors” and Mode by Mode Guidance 
3.4.6.9.1 Road Hierarchy of Access 
Airports of all sizes have a hierarchy of access to meet the needs of all users. The arrangement of the 
different “front doors” needs to be supported by clear wayfinding and a resilient road (and entire surface 
access network). As airports grow in size, the surface access requirements may become more specific for 
each “front door.” Therefore, the airport master plan needs to consider the long-term requirements for the 
development of the surface access infrastructure, in particular where grade-separated structures are needed 
now or in the future.

3.4.6.9.2 Highway Access Systems and Design Considerations 
The highway network should be free flowing with the main access and egress roads being segregated 
highways (e.g. either one-way or with a central reserve/median strip). The primary circulation of travel should 
reflect the side of passenger egress from private vehicles, taxis, and coaches/buses (clockwise for right-hand 
drive systems and counterclockwise for left-hand drive systems). 
Distributor roads are generally designed as two-way elements. Junctions should be either free-flow or 
prioritized (with traffic control signaling), and be kept as simple as possible with ideally just two available 
choices for the motorist. Clear and consistent signage is essential to ensure the road-space is used efficiently. 
860 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 880===
By 
IATA Landside Access Systems 
Roundabouts can be considered as an alternative to traffic signals or junctions to support free flowing traffic 
and where necessary recirculation of traffic. 
Access road systems should be designed to support the needs of all road users, including cyclists and 
pedestrians. Footpaths/sidewalks should be provided on primary access roads and distributor roads. 
While access to and from the airport may be on high-speed road network systems, the on-site roads normally 
have lower speed restrictions. Slower operating speeds not only improve safety, but also give the driver more 
time to follow the wayfinding. The highway design can also assist in the wayfinding for drivers by giving strong 
visual clues for the primary vehicle flows. 
While highway design is normally based on the appropriate national standards, these should be considered 
as minimal requirements and be supplemented with specific airport-related requirements (e.g. wayfinding, 
lane control). 
3.4.6.9.3 Wayfinding and Signage 
Clear wayfinding across the surface transport system is essential. Signage should be clearly visible and 
simple as much as is practicable. It should be compliant with the local codes for roadway signage, as well as 
the recommendations and best practices specific to airport roadway signage. Dynamic signage is 
recommended to also be used to manage flows, especially lane control during peak periods. With increasingly 
accurate onboard vehicle and mobile navigation systems, airports can provide dynamic wayfinding information 
to drivers. Wayfinding also needs to provide for route recovery and recirculation. In locations where rental car 
use is prevalent (e.g., leisure destinations), wayfinding and signage needs to be particularly clear. Traffic 
management plans should include all wayfinding methods and considerations. Electronic wayfinding and app￾based wayfinding are opportunities to support and easily implement multi-language information, local minority 
languages, and special needs with customized information to enhance accessibility, inclusion, and equity. 
3.4.6.9.4 Car Parking 
Parking facilities are associated with most of the airport front doors. Parking signage should commence from 
the earliest point of entry to the airport property and should give clear routing to short-term and long-term 
parking, as well as to car rental drop-off and pick-up locations. Displays with available car spaceswill help to 
optimize the use of large parking lots. 
Any height limitations should be displayed well in advance of the entry into the parking lot and height 
restriction/clearance bars should be installed prior to vehicles entering the restricted area. Where parking lots 
are served by shuttle buses, there should be sufficient maneuvering space forthe type of vehicle used. 
Suitable lighting and CCTV should be installed for the safety and security of the airport and its users. 
Parking for people with reduced mobility (PRM) should be clearly signposted, be conveniently located and 
appropriately sized. Some of these facilities may need EV charging infrastructure. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 861 

===PAGE 881===
Be G= | IATA all Airport Development Reference Manual 
Within public parking lots, there should be clear pedestrian routes that guide people to the intended 
destinations with sufficient space to separate pedestrian flows from parked or moving vehicles. The use of 
curbs should be limited to avoid trip hazards and to make the passenger journey as easy as possible, 
particularly when moving baggage or carts with luggage. Elevators or ramps should be provided to access all 
floors of multistory parking lots and should be sized to handle passengers with baggage/carts, based on the 
peak passenger demand. 
Most airport parking will have some form of use restriction in place. This should be clearly displayed at the 
entrance and as necessary throughout the parking lot. Public lot demand can be reduced where barrier 
systems are used on entry with payment required on exit, however depends on the available choices. Car 
parking strategies should aim to utilize capacity efficiently through competitive pricing. 
Parking facilities should also facilitate the charging of electric vehicles to encourage use of carbon neutral 
vehicles. Airports may wish to promote further use of EVs and other cleaner modes/technologies by 
passengers through a number of incentives such preferential parking locations and free of use charging. 
Given changing trends some airports may observe a decline in car parking demand. It is therefore important 
to consider the long-term use of parking structures in their design and engineering, allowing for future 
repurposing of these structures as offices or retail spaces. Car parking lot designs are typically at 
grade/surface-based or multistory. Sub-surface parking is another option however is less desirable due to 
higher costs. Provision of at grade parking is significantly less expensive; however, passenger walking 
distances can become an issue. Covered walkways should be considered to protect customers from the 
elements including shaded parking in hot climates. Spaces should be sized for different vehicle types, and 
sufficient separation should be provided to enable easy access for passengers and luggage, which may be 
larger than minimum standards used in the region. 
Multistory car parks are commonly provided for premium parking when close to the terminal building to 
minimize walking distances. This is predominantly for short-term parking, however depending on pricing 
strategies may also be attractive for longer-term parking. Parking management systems that provide visual 
and dynamic wayfinding to vacant parking spaces increase user convenience, reduce vehicle circulation times 
and emissions, and maximize capacity. For large multistory car parks, the vertical circulation of vehicles is 
recommended to be segregated from the parking lanes (e.g. ramps external to the building) to allow vehicles 
to exit the car park as soon as possible and avoid parking on sloped floors. This also provides flexibility for 
future options concerning AV parking developments. 
Various parking pay systems are available with payment methods becoming progressively more user-friendly 
by using electronic payment systems. Many airports also encourage pre-booking car parking with discount 
incentives to manage the overall parking lot capacity and maximize yield. Key considerations for airport 
parking include: 
e Proximity to terminals 
* Multistory vs. surface (or sub-surface) 
e Long stay and/or short stay provisions 
° = Staff parking 
e Wayfinding and signage

3.4.6.9.5 Access Control and Control Gates 
3.4.6.9.5.1 Vehicle Access Controls 
Data analytics is commonly used to help detect unusual or suspect behaviors. The airport should have overall 
control of the access onto the airport property and adjacent access roads. The airport should maintain a 
continuous consultation process with stakeholders to discuss control aspects, and to manage peak demand 
and incidents taking into account national security interests, border control and local policing. The access 
control and screening procedures at an airport (e.g., physical checkpoints) will have a considerable impact on 
the design and capacity of the related infrastructures. For instance, an airport practicing systematic, detailed 
screening of vehicles, drivers and passengers will require wide checkpoints and large waiting areas, while 
other airports using digital surveillance may be invisible to the road user. 
{t is common practice for all people working at an airport and their vehicles to be issued with identification that 
includes their security-related level of access (e.g. landside, airside). Access control is normally integrated into 
the airport-wide security system to detect not only security threats, but also civil issues (e.g., theft and 
vandalism). 
Wherever possible, the access control data and Closed Circuit Television (CCTV) information should be made 
available to all airport management teams on a real-time basis for the purpose of ongoing secure surveillance 
and flow management. Control Gates For Airside Access 
Control gates segregate general road users from those with permits to access and park in the non-public 
areas of the airport e.g. airside access. Where necessary, weather protection should be provided to 
security/operational personnel staffing these gates. 
Control gates are put in place to manage the flow of vehicles from landside to airside and to perform the 
necessary security screening processes. The number of landside/airside control gates depends on the 
airport's operational requirements however should be minimized as much as possible to optimize the cost of 
staffing and equipment. The capacity of control gates should be determined using the same methodology as 
terminal building capacity, as the capacity of control gates is integral element of the overall airport operational 
performance. 
Control gates should include a roof structure covering the length of the vehicles to be inspected and 
incorporate inspection lighting. CCTV cameras, including those recording the license plate of each vehicle are 
required, as are control barriers preventing unauthorized crossing by vehicles or pedestrians. To prevent 
tailgating through a control gate checkpoint, a control barrier may be necessary at the rear of each entry lane 
to enclose each vehicle.

Seo sg IATA aul Airport Development Reference Manual 
Control gates need to include equipment to support the search of all people and vehicles. The type of 
technology and level of screening typically depends on both the requirements stipulated in national legislation. 
Sufficient signage must be provided in advance advising authorized entry only, and exit points should be 
provided before control gates at a sufficient distance to enable unauthorized vehicles to turn around 
preventing delays, 
3.4.6.9.6 Passenger Terminals Road Access 
Passenger terminals have several “front doors,” including those used by: 
e Arrival and departure passengers 
° Goods delivery and waste collection vehicles 
e — Staff and flight crew 
e VIPs and commercially important passengers (CIP) 
The layout of the road system should accommodate the requirements of each of these users. Depending on 
the airport's requirements, some of these users can be combined (e.g., passengers with flight crew). For each 
front door, there will be different interface requirements. 
Passenger flows will be served by a range of modes and, for larger airports, at different levels on the landside 
face of the terminal building. An intuitive and safe journey from the terminal to the chosen transport mode is 
important. When a particular mode (e.g. car rental) is not within short walking distance, a shuttle bus or light 
rail link is normally provided. 
Dedicated access for VIP passengers is often a requirement at multilevel terminals, to access lounges or 
even separate terminals that provide VIP passengers with personalized services to facilitate their departures 
and arrivals processes. While VIP passengers could be handled through a general aviation terminal, the 
security screening requirements change if VIPs are travelling on a scheduled passenger flight. Some airlines 
may also want a separate entrance for their frequent flyers or those traveling in premium cabins (CIP 
passengers). 
Goods deliveries are normally handled at a truck dock to support the efficient unloading of goods. 
Waste handling includes controlled and uncontrolled waste that may also be pre-sorted for recycling or 
compost. Suitably segregated and contained facilities are required for waste transfer, which may be collected 
by a range of vehicle types.

3.4.6.9.7 Curbside Vehicle Access and Design Considerations 
Airport forecourts are one of the most complex areas of passenger/vehicle interface. The curb is the point of 
transition where travelers move from vehicle user to pedestrian and vice-versa. 
Security requirements may impact the stand-off distance between the curb and the building facade and vary 
by region. Some regulators stipulate a minimum separation distance and/or a requirement for bollards or other 
vehicle barriers to be provided along the terminal building frontage. All forecourts require a degree of 
segregation and active management to provide the required capacity. Defined areas could include the 
following for both departures curb drop off and arrivals curb pick up: 
e Public bus, airport shuttle 
e Regional coach 
e Private vehicle, taxi, TNC and private hire 
¢ Passengers with reduced mobility 
The curb area consists of a sidewalk, covered or partially enclosed, bordering the terminal road system with 
an adjacent paved area to permit vehicles to drop off or pick up passengers. The road in front of the terminal 
should include drop-off/pick-up lanes, maneuvering lanes to enter and exit the drop-off/pick-up lanes, and 
through traffic lanes. The curb system is a destination and should not be used by any other vehicles. Further, 
the system should be designed to allow through traffic to pass stationary vehicles uninterrupted.

Pedestrian crossing points, signalized or with other traffic management measures in place, should be

with baggage and PRM.

The hierarchy of curb capacity is defined by the number of vehicles that can be processed in the drop-off/pick￾up lane, supported by traffic lanes providing access through the forecourts. Congestion is usually the result of 
an inadequate number of drop-off/pick-up positions (e.g., curb length) that results in double parking (or more). 
However, the number of traffic lanes is also important to carry the traffic through the forecourt area. Provision 
for dedicated drop-off areas should be made for PRM, which should be coordinated with the PRM lounge in 
the terminal. 
Terminals with a high demand for curb space may lead to forecourts that start before and stretch beyond the 
terminal building. As passengers prefer to be dropped off close to the terminal; therefore, this can lead to the 
ends of the forecourts being underutilized and the area close to the terminal being congested by demand, 
resulting in vehicles parking two, three or four deep. In addition to creating a dangerous and very poor 
passenger experience, this behavior will also negatively impact curb circulation and the access road system. 
An even distribution of traffic over the entire curb may be assisted by technology, adequate signage or 
physical infrastructure enhancements. 
Where insufficient curb length is available on the terminal side of the curb road, the use of multiple curbs 
could be considered. While near-side curbs are preferred, the use of off-side curbs is used increasingly. With 
off-side curbs, vehicle speeds need to be strictly controlled, which can be achieved with raised pedestrian 
crossing points that act as wide speed bumps. Pedestrian crossings can be either priority or signaled 
depending on demand and safety assessments. When pedestrian profiles attain a certain threshold, they will 
influence vehicle progression and induce the risk of low levels of frontage discharge. At these thresholds, 
signal technology should be the preference.

Saw tooth—This layout provides for discrete bays for cars, vans and buses. It is commonly used for pick-up 
rather than drop-off areas as passengers can be directed to a particular bay for the onward ride. When used 
for vans and buses with near-side doors, only the near-side curb should be used.

3.4.6.9.8 Cargo Vehicles 
Inbound and outbound cargo is generally managed through freight forwarders or integrators. Cargo 
delivery/pick-up facilities and surface access routes need to be able to adequately service the product being 
handled as well as any time sensitivity. While security screening is normally undertaken for outbound cargo, 
customs inspections for inbound and outbound international freight may be carried out at the airport or off￾airport, provided that delivery/pick-up vehicles are secure and bonded. Inbound non-perishable cargo often 
require significant parking for freight forwarders or integrators waiting and paying for the goods to be released. 
Fresh produce and live animals require time-sensitive processing. Parking and maneuvering requirements for 
the cargo facilities depend on factors such as dwell times as a result of customs procedures and easy/direct 
access for time-sensitive cargo. 
3.4.6.9.9 Support Elements-Vehicles 
Support elements include a wide range of buildings and operations. They all have unique operational 
tequirements and make use of a range of surface access solutions for different types of vehicles. The location 
of support elements will range from landside, the landside/airside boundary to airside. For a complete list of 
support facility requirements See Section 3.6-Airport Support Elements.

===PAGE 888===
Be | 
IATA * Landside Access Systems 
3.4.6.9.10 Connection Between Terminals and Support Facilities-Vehicles 
Cross-connectivity between the different airport facilities is essential for the efficient operation of the airport. 
This may require additional distributor roads, both airside and landside, to ensure timely servicing of aircraft. 
Where distances are significant, remote holding/processing facilities may be required close to the point of use. 
3.4.6.9.11 Landside Development—Further Considerations 
Landside development is an important feature of many airports. The extent of some landside developments, 
such as hotels, fuel stations and car rental facilities are directly related to the level of activity of the airport. 
Other facilities, such as offices and warehouses, operate more independently based on the local level of 
economic activity. All these facilities require suitable surface access in the overall surface 
access/transportation master plan for the airport. Airports often set sustainability targets for to landside 
development under their control to encourage users to take public transport or use vehicles with a lower 
carbon footprint. 
3.4.6.9.12 Road Network Capacity 
The on and off-airport surface access network capacity should be modelled throughout a design day, using 
dynamic simulation tools if needed for complex systems or for detailed evaluation metrics. Off-airport capacity 
will be affected by local and regional fluctuations, especially daily commuting traffic and peak holiday traffic. 
These traffic peaks, however, may not necessarily coincide with the airport peak hourly/daily demand. 
If the local off-airport network is saturated, access and egress from the airport can become congested. This 
can lead to queuing back onto the airport egress roads, which can compromise airport operations. Secondary 
distributary road systems can help to insulate airport operations from off-airport congestion. 
It is also highly desirable to have at least two (or more, if considered necessary) primary means of access to 
the airport to provide operational redundancy. Primary access routes should have segregated roadways and 
sufficient width on each roadway to allow for vehicle breakdowns. 
Flow management techniques may also be required to manage and optimize road infrastructure capacity in 
certain areas of the airport. These could include: 
° Vehicle height control to restrict access for heavy vehicles 
e Vehicle operator control, such as taxis and TNCs, for access to exclusive waiting areas and frontages 
e Toll road pricing is discouraged and is unlikely to be an effective means of flow management 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 869 

===PAGE 889===

IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.4.6.9.13 Intermodal Stations 
Rail and bus stations at airports usually serve both passengers and airport staff. However, as airports may 
have premium rail service into the city center, this may attract customers who are not actually using the 
airport to use the premium rail service from the airport station. This can bring benefits in additional revenues 
however may also result in the need for additional car parking and drop-off areas. See Rail Services and Rail 
Stations for further details on key design considerations. 
3.4.6.9.14 Bus and Coach Stations 
The bus and coach stations at an airport need to be functional for both staff and passengers. Keeping in mind 
that both staff and passengers use these stations, the station's location, proximity to terminals, and wayfinding 
elements need to be carefully considered. 
Bus stations should be located at ground level or below ground in centralized, easy accessible locations for 
pedestrians. The proximity of a bus station to the terminals is important as a shorter walking distance will 
encourage usage. This is also the case with wayfinding, as poor signage will lead to a lower uptake of bus 
users. 
It is important that bus and coach stations provide comfortable waiting areas with adequate seating, 
appropriately sized to accommodate travelers with luggage. 
Planners should understand the busiest bus and coach destination and passenger volumes to minimize 
walking distances and ensure easy access to terminals and other modes of transport. 
Bus and coach stations should provide real-time information of services. This should be available in the 
waiting area as well as in the terminal arrivals area. 
3.4.6.9.15 Car Rental Facilities 
The space requirements for car rental vehicles are considerable. Car rental facilities require space for a 
customer lobby, ready/return spaces, fuel/wash facilities, and vehicle storage. Consolidated rental car 
facilities, either as part of the GTC or as a remote standalone facility, may provide the most appropriate 
solution as they reduce the overall space required for rental car facilities as well as delivering operational 
efficiencies for rental car companies by reducing land take. Shuttle services, using buses or light rail, should 
be provided where walking distances are beyond reasonable. A limited number of parking spaces at walking 
distance from the terminal may also be provided to enhance the customer convenience, both for rental car 
pick up and drop off. 
870 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 890===
ai Be IATA aol Landside Access Systems 
3.4.6.9.16 Taxi and Holding Facilities 
Automated call-forward systems should be considered as part of the overall taxi management system at 
larger airports where traffic volumes justify these facilities and the associated investment. Provisions for a taxi 
marshal at the terminal interface should also be considered as part of the overall management system, 
particularly during peak periods. Provision of facilities for taxi drivers at the holding areas, such as toilets and 
a café, should be considered to assist with the well-being of the drivers. For large airports, additional forward 
holding areas adjacent to the terminal may be required to ensure a constant flow of taxis during peak periods. 
3.4.6.9.17 Mobile Phone Lots 
Mobile phone lots can assist with the curb management of private cars, TNCs and hire cars. Private cars, and 
hire cars can access a designated remote parking area and wait until they are contacted by their 
passenger/customer on their mobile devices. They can then effectively coordinate a meeting time/place and 
make an approach to the arrivals area that minimizes waiting time at the pick-up point. 
Holding and mobile phone lots can also be considered for use by TNC's. 
3.4.6.9.18 Remote “Park and Ride” 
To reduce vehicular demand peaks in the immediate vicinity of an airport, remote “park and ride” facilities 
provide a solution. These facilities operate as satellite airport parking or drop-off areas. Typically, a 
bus/shuttle or light rail service provides transfers from the park and ride site to the airport terminal area at high 
frequencies. Key considerations for park and ride sites include: 
e Demand characteristics 
e Distance from the terminal 
e Wayfinding and signage requirements 
e Flight Schedule information 
e Available locations 
3.4.6.9.19 Freight and Mail 
Cargo handling facilities as well as their aprons are generally located away from passenger facilities. Where 
possible, cargo handling facilities and aprons should be consolidated in a limited number of zones of the 
airport to simplify access.

3.4.6.9.20 Goods and Other Deliveries 
A strategy for goods delivery and waste collection should be part of the planning and concept of operations. 
Delivery of consumables to terminal facilities and collection of waste should take place away from the terminal 
curbside in a segregated zone with dedicated security measures in place if and where required. Ideally, 
delivery and waste collection vehicles should not use the passenger curb roads. If this is not possible, goods 
deliveries and waste collection should be planned in off-peak passenger periods and preferably using smaller 
vehicles. 
3.4.6.10 Rail Services 
3.4.6.10.1 Goods and Other Deliveries 
Offer will vary from airport to airport and depend on several factors, including financial feasibility, geography, 
demand, capacity, and preference. 
3.4.6.10.2 Generic Factors at the Planning Stage 
A full analysis of the airport rail access system is required. The planned system capacity needs to match the 
terminal and airside capacity, however, the peaks used to calculate capacity for airport rail are measured in 
shorter periods of time. Close coordination between airport planners, local planning authorities and local 
transportation providers is necessary to ensure the current and projected requirements are fully understood 
and imbedded in local/regional transportation plans as well as in capital expenditure programs. 
The demand for rail-based surface access between the airport and the metropolitan area it serves is 
generated by: 
e Originating and terminating passengers 
e Meeters and greeters and other visitors (including those shopping or doing business at the airport) 
e Airport and airline employees 
e Aviation fuel suppliers and other specialized cargo, depending on the location 
3.4.6.10.3 Ticketing and Information 
Ticketing and train information is a major obstacle for inbound travelers when compared to the simplicity of 
using of taxis and well organized TNCs. Easily accessible ticketing and information on train times and 
destinations is essential to increase its attractiveness. This should include multilingual signage, information 
panels, ticket machines and announcements. The ticketing process is changing significantly, however, with 
transactions and ticket delivery being undertaken on passenger mobile devices. 
872 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 892===
Landside Access Systems 
3.4.6.10.4 Baggage Facilities 
On most rail journeys to and from airports, passengers self-handle their baggage. This can place additional 
burden on space within the carriages/railcars. Provision of baggage hold areas near doorways should be 
discussed with the rail service provider. 
A limited number of rail service providers enable remote check-in at rail stations, allowing for standard size as 
well as oversize (or out-of-gauge) bags. Containers with checked luggage are loaded onto the passenger 
trains, allowing for segregation and quick onward processing on arrival at the airport. 
3.4.6.10.5 Operational Times 
Airport operational hours usually extend beyond the traditional operating window of public transport, for 
instance night closure of rail systems might be necessary for inspection and planned maintenance. Effective 
coordination to minimize operational disruptions taking staff access into account is essential. 
3.4.6.11 Rail Stations 
3.4.6.11.1 Rail Stations 
Rail stations at airports are used for different types of journeys and by different groups of travelers. The 
stations can be considered as an origin, destination, or interchange point as part of a multi-legged journey. 
Key considerations for rail stations at airports include: 
e Proximity 
° Stations should be ideally located within reasonable walking distance of the terminal building, thereby 
avoiding the need for passengers to ride a shuttle bus or other transfer vehicle 
© Stations should also be located within easy access of baggage claim areas 
© Accessibility 
© Stations and the routes to and from them should be designed to minimize the need for passengers to 
change levels 
e Design 
o Effective accommodation of passengers with luggage 
o Wide platforms, smooth walking surfaces, and minimal level changes 
o Passenger amenities (e.g., sheltered waiting areas, seating and toilets) must be included in the

e Wayfinding and signage 
° Clear wayfinding and signage are essential to ensure passengers travel between terminals and
