Consider including flight departure information in the rail station; this will assist rail passengers in 
finding the correct terminal building 
3.4.6.11.2 Terminal Proximity and Walking Distances 
The station should be considered an integral part of the airport, either within the terminal building or linked 
directly to it. The main purpose of effective integration is to minimize walking distances as passengers will 
often be carrying luggage. Underground rail stations directly below passenger terminals are becoming more 
popular at airports as one option, enabling easy access via elevators to and from the rail station into the 
terminal with short walking distances. 
Where a rail station serves multiple terminals, a decision needs to be made regarding location and the 
number of stations taking into account: 
e Multiple stations 
° This is possible with a metro system or a dedicated airport express system, but generally undesirable 
for national rail networks. This is due to restrictions in headways (e.g. the distance and time between 
trains in transit) and extended journey times unless the airport is at the end of the journey 
London Heathrow, Toronto, and Kuala Lumpur are examples of multi-terminals served by dedicated 
airport express rail. Shanghai Hongqiao and Tokyo Haneda are examples of multi-terminals joined by 
a metro system 
e A ssingle central station with pedestrian links to each terminal 
° This may be the least expensive option and allows the development of the rail infrastructure 
separately from the terminal. A central station can also integrate other transport modes, such as light 
rail and coach/bus stations. In such cases, the rail station forms part of the GTC. See 
Exhibit 3.4.6.11.2. 
e Station at one terminal with walking, vehicle, or APM link to other terminal(s) e.g. such as Orlando 
International Airport (MCO), and Toronto Pearson Airport (YYZ) 
° Station remote from all terminals with APM or light rail links to all terminals. This is particularly 
advantageous where there are multiple terminals.

3.4.6.11.3 Orientation 
Rail platform requirements can be between 250 m and 400 m long depending on the train sets used. It is, 
therefore, desirable to either orientate the platforms parallel to the face of a terminal building especially for 
above ground station, or provide the main platform entrance/egress at the center of the platforms to minimize 
the on-platform walking distances and assist with train loading times. A train can easily carry the equivalent of 
a large aircraft in terms of passengers, resulting in a very high surge factor when exiting the train. Transport 
links need to accommodate these peak demand flows with minimal queuing. Pedestrian modeling tools, such 
as STEPS, Legion, CAST and Mass Motion others, can determine pedestrian movement patterns/flow 
requirements during the planning process. 
3.4.6.11.4 Level Changes 
The airport rail station platform level should be flush with the floor of the train to facilitate passengers with 
luggage, buggies and accessibility needs. Facilities for PRM are to be provided, and where assistance is 
required this needs to be appropriately resourced with trained staff. Rail station designers should also 
minimize the vertical and horizontal gap between the platform edge and the train. 
Level changes need to accommodate passengers with baggage as well as PRM. The use of escalators, 
elevators and ramps is preferred over stairs due to convenience factos. Vertical transport systems need to be 
designed with sufficient resilience and backup redundancy.

3.4.6.11.5 Waiting Facilities 
The demand for waiting facilities will depend on train frequencies. Passengers departing by train need 
Platform-level waiting facilities that are protected from the weather only in case of putdoor station platforms. 
Waiting facilities can also provide information and catering for passengers. 
3.4.7 Levels of Service 
3.4.7.1 Introduction 
Due to the different characteristics of landside access systems, vehicles, occupancy and driver behavior the 
levels of service can vary substantially from terminal facilities. 
3.4.7.2, Demand 
While the busy hour rate for a terminal building is driven directly by flight schedule, the landside busy hour 
demand is likely to occur at a different time than the gate peak due to reporting profiles, modal choice, 
connecting traffic as well as non-passenger activity that can vary throughout the day. Road traffic does not 
arrive in a uniform flow and a Poisson adjustment factor should be used to replicate random vehicle arrival 
times and the microburst in traffic patterns. Using robust data, in particular from surveys, will help to develop 
the peak landside demand criteria. 
3.4.7.3. Capacity 
Unlike capacities of terminal systems that are highly process oriented and typically operate at their quoted 
capacity, the maximum capacity of landside road systems is affected by high levels of delay. Reduction 
factors are needed to account for unfamiliar drivers, heavy vehicles etc. Planners need to assess the impacts 
of delays and additional resilience required to ensure reliable free flowing operations with sufficient capacity. 
3.4.7.4 Access to a Curb 
Sufficient capacity shall be provided for all vehicles to be able to access a curb when picking up or dropping 
off passengers to avoid passenger/vehicle interaction, improve safety and customer experience. Where 
vehicles, such as buses, have passenger access on one side, the parking position shall provide direct access 
from the curb to the passenger door(s). 
A curb with sufficient loading/unloading spaces, but with only a single travel lane, can be just as inadequate 
as a curb with insufficient drop-off/pick up positions. The number of traffic lanes needs to be sized 
appropriately 
876 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 896===
roxy 
wt 
IATA Landside Access Systems 
3.4.7.5 Car Parking 
As a tule of thumb, the peak occupancy-to-space ratio for car parking should be limited to 90% for the design 
day. Use of yield management systems to optimize use of car parks during peak periods should be 
considered to ensure people who wish to park are able to. 
3.4.7.6 Journey Time Reliability 
The reliability of landside journey times for departing passengers is critical to the performance of the airport. 
While responsibility for landside roads outside the airport usually does not lie with the airport, it should still 
undertake measures to mitigate risk. For example, the airport can encourage passengers to leave extra time 
to get to the airport when traveling during the afternoon peak or inclement weather. 
3.4.7.7 On-Site Roads 
Where queuing occurs during peak periods, it should be contained within the area designated for a particular 
function (e.g., queuing for departures curb drop-off should not back up and delay vehicles arriving to pick up 
passengers). 
3.4.7.8 Mobility-Impaired Passengers 
Drop-off and pick-up positions should be provided for PRM on the closest curb to buildings, subject to any 
security requirements. Similar priority should be provided to parking of vehicles. 
3.4.7.9 Walking Distances 
Journey distances should be kept as short as practicable. Acceptable walking distances landside will be 
significantly shorter than in the terminal as passengers will often have luggage with them. Where possible, an 
alternative walking route should be provided in case of service failure. Additional options such as shuttle 
buses or covered walkways/travelators should be considered. 
3.4.7.10 Canopies 
Consideration should be given to canopies to protect passengers from inclement weather at waiting areas or 
other areas of significant foot traffic. Canopies provide an opportunity to mount photo voltaic cells. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 877 

===PAGE 897===
we IATA mull Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.4.7.11 Pedestrian Crossings 
At grade surface crossing of busy roads should be minimized, where practicable, unless it is shared space, 
such as car parking lots and forecourts where the vehicles are traveling at low speeds. Pedestrian crossings, 
whether priority or signaled, should be as short as possible to reduce the interaction distance and timing. 
3.5 Cargo Terminal 
3.5.1 Introduction 
Although air cargo facilities may differ in design, the basic function of every cargo facility should be to ensure: 
¢ Ahigh level of safety, security, efficiency and technology in all aspects of its handling procedures 
* The accommodation of customer needs through reengineered ground processes 
This chapter of the ADRM addresses the key requirements of a typical cargo terminal and provides guidance 
on many of the challenges associated with cargo facilities. 
Note: The ADRM does not provide a definitive guide on how to design an airport terminal and it is not 
intended to be used in that context. 
IATA's Cargo Handling Council (ICHC) is comprised of airlines and ground handlers. To address the lack of 
consistent quality in cargo handling, ICHC and the Cargo Operations Advisory Group (COAG) developed a list 
of capabilities against which a cargo facility could be measured, now called the Smart Facility Standards. The 
purpose of this matrix is to enhance cargo handling capabilities to a consistently high standard and identify 
possible non-compliance in critical areas such as safety and security. 
The Smart Facility Standards have been endorsed as a Recommended Practice in 2018 and the Smart 
Facility Operational Capacity (SFOC) audits is now launched. The SFOC audit will assess a facility's 
infrastructure, equipment and the procedures to operate them in accordance with [ATA Regulations and 
Recommended Practices. Its main goal is to create transparency in cargo handling services and to enhance 
basic cargo operations capacities to a consistently higher baseline level across the industry. 
3.5.2 Cargo Operations 
The purpose of a cargo facility is to enable safe and efficient cargo operations. The following areas should be 
considered when building a cargo facility: 
¢ Cargo safety, including the safety of people and the environment 
* Cargo security 
o Unknown cargo

3.5.2.1 Cargo Security 
3.5.2.1.1 Overview 
The term air cargo, in the context of aviation security, includes the following shipped as cargo on passenger 
or all-cargo aircraft: 
e General cargo 
° Consolidations 
¢ Transshipments 
e Unaccompanied courier items. 
¢ Diplomatic mail 
e Company stores 
e Unaccompanied baggage 
Air mail (postal mail) is sometimes considered in this same context, as it is often processed through the air 
cargo operation, however, it follows specific security regulations and procedures, which differ slightly from 
other air cargo. 
Shippers/consignors, account consignors and regulated agents frequently use civil aviation as an expedient 
method of transporting cargo from point to point around the globe. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 879 

===PAGE 899===
Ey v 
Se —C IATA pull Airport Development Reference Manual 
Cargo can be tendered for carriage by: 
e Another airline 
e Aregulated agent 
e Acourier service company 
e An express parcel company 
e A freight forwarder 
¢ Adirect shipper (either as a known consignor or an unknown consignor) 
Whichever source tenders the cargo for carriage, security measures need to be taken to prevent acts of 
unlawful interference (i.e., the introduction of explosives or incendiary devices into air cargo). Airlines reserve 
the right to examine, or cause to be examined, the packaging and contents of all cargo, including courier and 
express parcel consignments. Airlines may also enquire into the correctness or sufficiency of information or 
documentation tendered in respect of any consignment. The right to examine the contents of consignments 
does not extend to post office mail. 
ICAO Annex 17 requires (Standard 4.6.2) Member States to establish a supply chain security process, which 
includes the approval of regulated agents and known consignors. This is achieved through the provision of the 
National Security Program, the Regulated Agent Security Program and Known Consignor Security Program. 
3.5.2.1.2 Regulated Agent Status 
Certain organizations, such as freight forwarders, cargo handling agents, airlines or any other entity who 
applies security controls in respect of cargo and mail may be designated as a ‘regulated agent’. That status 
must be obtained through the appropriate State authority where the business is conducted. 
Unless otherwise specified, the appropriate authority requests that the regulated agent produce and continue 
to comply with a security program. 
These programs may be a: 
(a) Regulated Agent Security Program: written by the freight forwarder, courier service company, etc., with 
compliance acknowledged by the appropriate authority. 
The security program details methods of meeting the provisions of Annex 17 and the appropriate authority 
requirements. When meeting set program standards, freight forwarders, courier service companies, ground 
handling agents, airlines, etc. may be registered/listed by the appropriate authority as ‘regulated agents’. 
Although reference is made to cargo, it should be understood that cargo also includes within its definition 
unaccompanied baggage as well as courier and express parcels. Cargo consigned directly to an airline and 
not via a freight forwarder needs to be dealt with by virtue of the provisions of the Regulated Agent Security 
Program. In the case of airlines, they will also be bound by the provisions of the National Civil Aviation 
Security Program (NCASP). 
880 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 900===
=e | IATA Cargo Terminal 
3.5.2.1.3. Known Consignor 
Unless otherwise specified by the appropriate authority, a known consignor is the originator of property for 
transportation by air for its own account, and whose procedures sufficiently meet the minimum security 
requirements and standards approved by the appropriate authority to allow the carriage of cargo on any 
aircraft. 
A known consignor must have an established and registered business with a permanent address from which 
to conduct its business. It must also be able to provide proof of an implemented security program that is 
recognized by the appropriate authority. The security program may be in either of the two forms listed below. 
The security program must meet the minimum requirement of ICAO Annex 417. 
(a) A known consignor's own security program approved by the appropriate authority and implemented within 
the known consignor's business processes 
(b) A security program mandated by the appropriate authority and implemented by the known consignor 
The objective of the known consignor model is to ensure that there are adequate security controls on the 
entire logistics chain while the consignment is under the control of the known consignor so as to preserve the 
integrity of the shipment and to prevent any unlawful interference. 
3.5.2.2 Valuable Cargo 
Valuable cargo is defined in IATA Cargo Services Conference Resolution 012. Generally, it includes gold 
bullion and other precious metals, precious stones, bank notes, valuable securities, works of art, etc. 
Valuable cargo, by the nature of its contents, should be subject to a close inspection on the part of the airline 
and checked against the details on the air waypill. The airline should adopt security measures for handling 
valuable cargo in cargo terminals as well as during aircraft loading, unloading and ground transportation. 
Insurance companies may require the use of specific equipment such as a vault or specialized transport 
vehicles designed to specific standards. 
Local security regulations should be instituted as the result of a review carried out by the chief security officer 
of the airline, airport security and cargo terminal management. This review should be ongoing and take into 
consideration various levels of threat in and around the airport. As a general rule, valuable cargo must be 
booked with the airline and any special arrangements made for it prior to its acceptance. Details of value, 
contents, routing and storage must be kept confidential. 
3.5.2.3 Post Office Mail 
Mail carried on passenger aircraft and/or all-cargo aircraft shall be subjected to security controls by airlines 
and/or designated postal operators before being placed on board an aircraft. Global postal services are 
members of the Universal Postal Union (UPU). The UPU is a specialized agency of the United Nations which 
has the same status as ICAO. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 881 

===PAGE 901===
ee | 
Se IATA ja Airport Development Reference Manual 
The UPU Convention sets security standards for the protection of mail services and specifies the standard 
forms to be used for the purpose of mail transport. Such forms will be completed by the post office. 
A designated postal operator regulated by the UPU Convention shall: 
¢ Deliver mail to the airline in a prescribed UPU mail receptacle 
¢ Such mail receptacles will be tagged with airmail bag labels and secured with the prescribed secure ties 
¢ A delivery bill will accompany all airmail shipments 
¢ A ccopy of the delivery bill will be signed by the airline and returned to the postal authority; other copies of 
the document will be retained by the airline as a form of quittance (proof of payment/receipt) 
Where there is agreement between the designated postal operator and the airline, the delivery bill may be 
provided and receipt acknowledged electronically. 
A designated postal operator, as a member of the UPU, when conducting business with an airline, shall 
provide security controls that are acceptable to the appropriate authority. The appropriate authority may 
increase the levels of security involving the carriage of mail where there is a heightened threat assessment 
involving the applicable State, the airline or civil aviation authority. 
Airlines should take certain actions to ensure the integrity of the mail delivered to an airport mail center before 
loading onto a flight. These actions are: 
e Ensure the number of mail receptacles stated in the delivery bill or electronic transport message coincides 
with the number of receptacles received from the designated postal operator 
¢ Make a visual inspection of the mail receptacles to ensure they have not been subjected to tampering 
¢ Ensure that the integrity of the mail receptacles and seals has been verified upon the receipt of the mail 
* Store the mail in a dedicated secure area 
¢ Ensure that only persons with the necessary form of ID and a valid reason for access be permitted into 
the mail storage area 
Documents handed to airlines by post offices should be stowed in the flight portfolio or where other flight 
documents are kept. They should be extracted immediately upon arrival of the aircraft at its destination. 
Although the airline or its agent does not normally have the right to examine the content of items in the mail, 
the airline may refuse the shipment and return it to the designated postal operator during times of increased 
threat or when the airline or its agent reasonably suspects the mail may contain unauthorized content or pose 
a safety threat. The mail, which also includes registered parcels and registered letters, is attractive to people 
intent on dishonesty and should be subject to special security handling from the point of acceptance to the 
point of delivery. 
Airlines involved in the movement of time-sensitive mail should not provide booking details to shippers unless 
they are known shippers/consignors or regulated agents.

3.5.2.4 Courier and Express Parcel Companies 
Courier and express parcel corporations should become regulated agents with a registration number issued 
by the appropriate authority. If there is no regulated agent regime in that country, the courier and express 
parcel company must have a security program implemented within its business operations. The security 
program must meet the minimum standard of ICAO Annex 17. 
3.5.2.5 Unknown Cargo 
All unknown consignments are to be subjected to enhanced security screening to ensure that they do not 
contain any device, material or substance that will pose a safety or security threat to the aircraft or to anyone 
handling the consignment at any time.

3.5.2.7 Unaccompanied Baggage 
Unaccompanied baggage is defined as baggage that is transported as cargo and is not carried on the same 
aircraft with the person to whom it belongs. There are obvious dangers in transporting unaccompanied 
baggage on passenger aircraft. Stringent standards must be implemented to overcome these dangers. The 
shipper/consignor of the baggage will be considered as an unknown shipper. As such, the procedure for 
acceptance of unaccompanied baggage shall be the same as that for unknown consignors described above in 
3.5.2.6.

3.5.2.8 High-Risk Cargo and Mail 
High-risk cargo and mail is defined as follows in ICAO Annex 47: a cargo or mail consignment is considered 
high-risk when it is presented by an unknown entity or showing signs of tampering, and, in addition, meets 
one of the following criteria: 
© Specific intelligence indicates that the cargo or mail poses a threat to civil aviation; or 
e The cargo or mail shows anomalies that give rise to suspicion; or 
e The nature of the cargo or mail is such that baseline security measures alone are unlikely to detect 
prohibited items that could endanger the aircraft (i.e. IEDs). 
Regardless whether the cargo or mail comes from a known or unknown entity, a State's specific intelligence 
about a consignment may render it high-risk. 
High-risk cargo and mail should be subjected to appropriate procedures, including screening, to effectively 
detect an Improvised Explosive Device (IED) or mitigate the specific threat associated with it. This should 
include other detection methods or robust security measures that are not part of baseline security measures. 
Such additional screening methods and measures should be determined by the appropriate authority. 
The airline, regulated agent and other supply chain stakeholders should adopt appropriate security measures 
for high-risk cargo and mail in their premises, during aircraft loading, unloading, transfer, transit and ground 
transport. 
Local security regulations should be instituted as the result of a review carried out by the appropriate 
authorities, chief security officer of the airline and the cargo terminal management. This review should be 
ongoing and take into consideration various levels of threat in and around the airport. As a best practice, high￾risk cargo and mail must be booked with the airline and any special arrangements made for it prior to its 
acceptance. Details of value, contents, routing and storage must be kept confidential. 
3.5.2.9 Live Animals 
Live animals are defined in the IATA Live Animals Regulations. 
Live animals, by their nature, should be subject to close inspection on the part of the airline and checked 
against details on the air waybill. The acceptance process must be done in accordance with the IATA Live 
Animal Regulations. Any items accompanying the animals are subject to the applicable security screening 
regulations. 
Physical space to handie the cargo may include warm rooms and dedicated animal-handling facilities such as 
horse or livestock stalls. Whether or not these facilities are required should be decided in consultation with the 
airline and the handlers who perform the service. Multi-user versions of these types of facilities can be 
developed at an airport to maximize efficiency. 
Driven by industry standards, the Center of Excellence for Independent Validators (CEIV) for Live Animals 
Logistics establishes baseline standards to improve the level of competency, infrastructure and quality

management in the handling and transportation of live animals throughout the supply chain. 
www.iata.org/ceiv-animals 
3.5.2.10 Perishable Cargo 
Perishable cargo is defined in the IATA Perishable Cargo Regulations. 
Perishable cargo, by its nature, should be subject to a close inspection on the part of the airline and checked 
against details on the air waybill. The acceptance process must be done in accordance with the IATA 
Perishable Cargo Regulations. 
Physical space to perform the handling may include locations for controlled room temperature, cold rooms 
and/or freezers for both loose cargo and cargo in ULDs. Whether these facilities are required or not should be 
decided in consultation with the airline and the handlers who perform the service. 
Some commodities require segregation, including for short-term storage and transport, as they may be 
incompatible. These considerations should be taken into account for the design and operation of the 
perishable cargo facility. 
3.5.2.11 Pharmaceutical Cargo 
Pharmaceutical and healthcare cargo is defined in the IATA Perishable Cargo Regulations and IATA 
Temperature Controlled Regulations. 
Pharmaceutical cargo, by its nature, should be subject to a close inspection on the part of the airline and 
checked against details on the air waybill. The acceptance process must be done in accordance with the IATA 
Perishable Cargo Regulations. The entire distribution and transport process should follow the Good 
Distribution Practices (GDP). GDP is a quality management system that provides guidelines for the 
proper distribution of healthcare products and includes requirements for the purchase, reception, storage and 
distribution of these products. 
Due to the importance and value of much of pharmaceutical cargo being transported by air, all parties must 
follow the GDP. Adequate facilities include those validated by the Center of Excellence for Independent 
Validation—Pharma (CEIV-Pharma). www. jiata.org/ceiv-pharma 
Physical space to perform the handling may include locations for controlled room temperature, cold rooms 
and/or freezers for both loose cargo and cargo in ULDs. Whether these facilities are required or not should be 
decided in consultation with the airline and handlers who perform the service. 
3.5.2.12 Dangerous Goods 
Dangerous goods are defined in the IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations.

IATA Cargo Terminal 
Dangerous goods, by their nature, must be subject to a close inspection on the part of the airline and checked 
against details on the air waybill and shipper’s declaration for dangerous goods. The acceptance process 
must be done in accordance with the IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations. 
Physical space to perform the handling and acceptance may include locations to facilitate the separation of 
incompatible goods, for both loose cargo and cargo in ULDs. Whether these facilities are required or not 
should be decided in consultation with the airline and handlers who perform the service. In addition, local fire 
codes may impose more stringent requirements for certain types of dangerous goods being handled or 
temporarily stowed in a cargo facility. 
3.5.3 Digital Cargo 
Vision 
Data is shared across the supply chain in digital shipment records, creating full transparency and optimizing 
people, systems, and assets. Any status changes and outcomes of control processes are interactively shared 
up and downstream via connected devices, master data and a common backbone. An increasing array of 
data is used in a variety of ways (digital twins, big data analytics, artificial intelligence and machine learning) 
to improve decision making, risk mitigation, contingency planning and enhancing customer satisfaction. Air 
cargo enables a connected, smart and highly efficient supply chain, to facilitate new business models and 
distribution models of the air cargo customer. Refer to NEXTT Cargo vision. 
Transporting cargo by air is information intensive. The industry still relies largely on paper. Where electronic 
processes are in place, they suffer from many limitations (e.g., poor data quality, incomplete coverage, lack of 
common data standards, use of legacy technology and standards). 
Driving efficient operations will require the use of electronic processes such as the electronic air waybill 
(eAWB), ONERecord, Interactive Cargo and others incorporated into a well-designed warehouse or 
transportation management system. 
3.5.4 Air/Rail Cargo 
For General Cargo, trucking remains the most affordable and flexible mode of ground transport for connection 
with air. However, with increased road congestion and the environmental benefits of rail service, some 
changes are beginning to be felt. 
In Europe, the CAREX Project aims to connect cargo airport terminals at Amsterdam Schiphol, Liége Bierset, 
London, Lyon-Saint Exupéry and Paris-Roissy CDG with the high-speed rail network. The expected 
opportunity is to replace the Road Feeder Service (RFS) with more fuel efficient freight trains and reduce 
carbon emissions. 
Other examples include rail and air services connecting from Asia to Europe/USA. Also, Gulf countries are 
investing in rail connectivity with ports and airports. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 887 

===PAGE 907===
Seo iy 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
The success of air cargo and rail will depend in part on the airport's capability to provide railport 
infrastructures that facilitate interoperability and ULD transfers. Therefore, vehicle flows to and from the cargo 
facility need to be taken into account in the terminal design. 
3.5.5 The Cargo Apron 
The following requirements must be considered when planning cargo aprons: 
Size and Location 
Cargo aprons must be considered a continuation of the cargo facility. The apron should be immediately 
adjacent to the cargo facility and should be used by all-cargo/freighter aircraft. This will provide short 
transportation distances and easier access between aircraft and the facility. On the apron, cargo service 
roads should be separate from the apron taxiway. 
An analysis of the peak-hour stand requirements and the related volume of air cargo to be transported and 
processed is necessary in order to determine the size of the apron and adjacent areas. 
Expansion 
The cargo apron must be expandable in order to accommodate increases in peak hour demand for aircraft 
stands or increased aircraft sizes. Parking configurations depend on local requirements and constraints, and 
must allow for necessary ground handling equipment. 
Staging 
The cargo apron design should provide for, at each aircraft stand, adjacent staging areas for the equipment 
needed for loading and transportation of arriving and departing ULDs and bulk cargo. The size of the staging 
space should be at least twice the capacity of the largest aircraft type intended operate on the stand in order 
to stage departing ULDs and bulk cargo as well as receive arriving cargo. Storage can be either on fixed 
racks or in the form of parking space for equipment supporting ULDs. Where aircraft are self-maneuvering, 
the staging areas must be protected from jet blast. 
Parking 
Space for parking of handling equipment should be planned between the airside cargo road and the apron, 
and/or along the outer edges of the apron. Parking areas must not impede aircraft maneuvering on or off the 
apron. Parking for power-in/power-out aircraft requires more space for each stand and extra precautions 
against jet blast. 
888 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 908===
i IATA Hi : Cargo Terminal 
Loading Bridges 
Several factors must be considered when fixed loading bridges are planned to connect all-cargo/freighter 
aircraft to Elevating Transfer Vehicle (ETV) storage systems within the cargo facility. Justification for loading 
bridges will depend on utilization potential, staffing requirements, processing/turnaround time, and frequency 
of extreme weather conditions. As with passenger loading bridges, cross-utilization between wide-body and 
narrow-body aircraft, as well as within certain types of narrow-body aircraft, may be limited. In addition, 
aircraft cargo door configurations (nose, side-forward, side-aft) will impact utilization potential. 
The cargo carrier's fleet mix, types of cargo and other operational factors will weigh heavily in the decision to 
use specialized loading bridges or flexible mobile loading systems. 
Servicing Equipment 
Fixed aircraft servicing equipment (i.e., hydrant refueling and power) are only appropriate to aircraft stands 
with high utilization. 
Lighting 
Lighting on the apron should provide sufficient illumination to permit the reading of cargo documents and 
labels at the aircraft parking stand. However, such lighting should not be allowed to adversely affect crew 
visibility when taxiing aircraft. 
3.5.5.1 Lower Deck ULD Sizes 
Baggage and cargo containers are important airline assets and subject to stringent airworthiness regulations. 
A damaged container may not be loaded aboard an aircraft. Accordingly, their storage and handling must use 
only roller equipment with vertical restraint to avoid containers falling off due to wind. This is especially true 
given the trend toward lighter ULDs for fuel savings. 
The use of lower deck-sized containers is practiced by many airlines to protect the aircraft and improve the 
loading and unloading of baggage and cargo on the apron. Baggage is better restrained when using lower 
deck containers, and is less likely to fall out and become damaged on the road way while being driven to and 
from the aircraft. The following lower deck ULD specifications are commonly used.

3.5.5.2 ULD Operational Storage 
The design of aircraft parking stands should provide sufficient space to accommodate the temporary storage 
of empty or loaded baggage or cargo ULDs in the immediate vicinity of each aircraft position, but entirely 
outside the Equipment Restraint Area (ERA) limit. 
The size of the ULD storage space should be at least twice the capacity of the largest aircraft type intended 
Operate on the stand in order to be able to stage departing ULDs and receive arriving ones. Storage can be 
either on fixed racks or in the form of parking space for equipment supporting ULDs. Where aircraft are self￾maneuvering, the ULD storage areas must be protected from jet blast. 
ULD storage facility and equipment standards can be found in the IATA ULD Regulations (ULDR).

3.5.7 Forecasting and Sizing 
3.5.7.1 Cargo Traffic 
Cargo traffic may be carried on all-freighter aircraft, on ‘combi’ aircraft (where the main deck is shared 
between passengers and cargo), or in the belly holds of Passenger aircraft. Since this traffic mix affects the 
requirements for apron facilities, IATA forecasts differentiate between these transport methods. 
Other considerations in the forecast include the combined number of tons of freight and mail handled at the 
airport. Usually scheduled and non-scheduled cargo traffic are considered together as both are handled in the 
same Cargo terminal area. 
Since most cargo and mail today are carried in or on ULDs, weight alone is not usually the most appropriate 
factor to evaluate space requirements. The forecast should also be expressed in terms of the number of 
ULDs. For translation into space requirements, the reference size usually taken is size M (2.5 m x 3.2 m). 
Two size K or P units can fit into one size M space. One size G or R pallet occupies two size M positions. 
3.5.7.2 Necessity for Cargo Traffic Studies 
The handling of increased amounts of cargo in larger terminal facilities entails complex physical and 
document handling systems (for both airlines and handling operators). Comprehensive studies are an 
essential basis for such systems and will maximize handling efficiency at the lowest cost. 
Based on forecasts, the project can then be planned by representatives of both authorities and operators and, 
if required, with the assistance of external experts. 
3.5.7.3. Cargo Transfer Areas 
Not all import cargo will terminate at the station. The methodology for handling on-line transfer cargo must be 
determined in the plan, and space must be provided for cargo returning to the warehouse for reprocessing. 
This may require additional bulk cargo breakdown space, an export bulk cargo staging area and/or a build-up 
work area. For ULDs transferring intact (no breakdown or build-up required), additional staging and storage 
space may be required, and cargo transferring to and from other airlines must be evaluated. 
When transfer cargo is not governed by customs requirements and same day transfer routing is possible, it 
may be possible to establish a transfer function at the Passenger terminal. This function captures transfer 
cargo at the arrival of an inbound flight and delivers it directly to the outbound departing flight. The degree of 
892 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 912===
or il Sa IATA Cargo Terminal 
transfer will depend on staffing and the facilities available at the passenger terminal. The impact on cargo 
facility sizing can be significant if transfers account for a sizeable proportion of total cargo boarded. 
Proposals should take into account the need for a rapid turnaround without compromising security measures. 
3.5.7.4 Planeside Cargo Traffic Forecast 
Planeside volumes are normally the most commonly available. They represent enplaned and deplaned cargo 
for all aircraft and over-the-road movements. The planeside forecast generally represents the “big picture” of 
cargo types that are processed through the warehouse (e.g., general freight, priority freight, small packages, 
company material, mail, etc.). The forecasts must correspond with, or be converted to, the prescribed peak 
facility design volume (e.g., cargo processed on the peak day of the average week of the peak month, or the 
maximum volume occurring on 95% of the days in the peak month, etc.). Where there is a distinct difference 
between processing requirements for domestic and international shipments, planeside volumes should be 
computed separately. Planeside volumes should be further categorized to reflect how much is carried in 
containers versus how much is carried as bulk, in both narrow-body and wide-body bulk holds. It is also 
necessary to ensure volumes for all third-party handling arrangements are quantified. 
The planeside cargo forecasting methodology technique relies on determining the average historical cargo 
carried by an aircraft equipment type (e.g., A330, B747, B777, A320, B757, etc.) and by market (e.g., Atlantic, 
Pacific, Latin America, North America, etc.). These averages are then applied to future aircraft schedules. 
When new aircraft types are included in future schedules, estimates based on available cargo capacity and 
range will need to be determined. 
Exhibit 3.5.7.4a and Exhibit 3.5.7.4b provide survey forms to quantify planeside volumes and describe a 
growth rate approach to forecasting.

3.5.7.5 Operational Cargo Forecasts 
Operational cargo forecasts are intended to translate the previously developed planeside forecast into 
volumes that correspond with each function or operation in the material handling process. 
The level of statistical detail for each airline cargo operation may vary significantly. As a result, the source and 
availability of data to define each cargo operation may differ. However, the need to quantify each function 
temains the same. 
3.5.8 Sizing Parameters 
Besides cargo volumes, there are several other cargo handling characteristics that impact the size of a cargo 
facility. This section will address many of the factors that will be required by cargo facilities planners to 
determine the sizing requirements. Since there are several methodologies applicable to cargo facility sizing, 
the task of quantifying the space requirements will be left up to qualified cargo facility planners, their 
designers and consultants. 
Before actual facility sizing can begin, the planner must first take several key steps: 
* Understand the current operation(s) 
e Define operational objectives for the future 
¢ Determine present constraints that need improvement 
* Decide on common objectives and policies to be realized in the new or extended area (e.g., faster 
handling, function as a transfer center for international cargo, more efficient air/road transfer, etc.) 
° Establish processing requirements and applicable standards of handling with the airlines and operators 
concerned 
* Determine the extent to which each operating function will be performed outdoors on a routine basis. This 
will have a direct effect on the size of the facility required. It is common for most material handling 
functions to be performed indoors, however some staging and storage functions can be managed outside 
depending on space, security and weather issues 
Once the above factors have been evaluated, the planner will have an idea of the functions that will need to 
be sized. The ultimate objective of the facility planner will be to convert each operational cargo volume 
defined earlier into space requirements through the development of various conversion factors and processing 
tates. Some of these are discussed below. 
3.5.8.1 Cargo Terminal Building 
The size of the cargo terminal building facility is derived from total annual cargo movement estimates. The 
space required is a function of the facility's proposed processing capability. The planning ratios shown in the 
following table can be used if no site-specific information is available.

3.5.8.2 Cargo Ramp Area 
As a general rule, the ramp size for all cargo facilities lies in the range of four to five times that of the cargo 
terminal building area. This includes aircraft stands, internal taxi lanes, airside roads, ground service 
equipment parking as well as processing zones on the apron. 
If more defined data is not available, the following procedure can be used to size the ramp area. The tonnage 
per annum is used to derive the number of aircraft per day and the ramp accordingly. The annual tonnage = 
250 (days) provides the daily tonnage. The average load per aircraft (all cargo) is 50 to 55 tons. The typical 
fleet mix for an all-cargo operation is as follows:

Source: IATA 
Two other important factors in facility sizing are the hours of operation and the average turnaround time per 
aircraft. Cargo facilities typically operate no less than 20 hours per day and have a turnaround time of 
between four to seven hours per aircraft. Facility planners should seek operational confirmation of the 
expected turnaround times 
3.5.8.3 Dwell Time 
Dwell time is a term used to reflect how much time import and export shipments remain in the facility. Dwell 
time will need to be quantified for each of the operational staging and storage functions. It is important for the 
planner to remember that the volume estimates developed earlier generally represent those processed during 
the peak design day. If international import shipments dwell for three days on average, the facility will need to 
be sized to manage three days of temporary storage. 
Dwell times for specific types of cargo will also need to be considered to ensure adequate facilities are in 
place.

3.5.8.4 Average Weights 
Average weights are required generally whenever a processing rate or sizing conversion factor is defined in 
terms other than weight. For instance, the processing rate to determine the number of ULD receiving and 
pick-up docks may be ULDs per hour. As a result, the volumes representing the amount of cargo received or 
picked-up will need to be converted to ULDs received or picked-up. This would be accomplished by 
determining the average weight per originating and terminating shipper-loaded ULD. 
Typical average weights that may be required include: 
¢ Weight per terminating domestic bulk shipment 
© Weight per originating domestic bulk shipment 
© Weight per terminating international bulk shipment 
¢ Weight per originating international bulk shipment 
© Weight per terminating domestic ULD shipment

3.5.9 Cargo Design Considerations: Scope of Evaluation 
The guidelines contained in this section should be considered in the planning of multi-tenant cargo terminal 
complexes under any of the following three development scenarios: 
1. Entirely or substantially new cargo terminals to be built at an airport where it is expected that both all￾cargo/freighter aircraft and cargo-carrying passenger aircraft will be operated. 
The chosen cargo complex site should include provisions for later expansion of all facilities to avoid them 
becoming obsolete in the future. However, the cargo facility should not be planned to immediately fulfill 
the ultimate planned requirements. These should be defined for the long term and space provisions 
should be made to accommodate them if and when the need arises. 
Extensions or modifications of existing cargo facilities that do not entirely meet guideline 
recommendations. 
The layout and design guidelines stated in this chapter should be considered insofar as is practicable 
given the existing constraints, even if the existing constraints do not permit full compliance with the details 
of the guideline recommendations. 
The planned cargo complex expansion or modification should include provisions for later expansion to 
avoid them becoming obsolete in the future. However, the cargo facility should not be planned to 
immediately fulfill the ultimate planned requirements. These should be defined for the long term and 
space provisions should be made to accommodate them if and when the need arises. 
Build or extension of a shared, or potentially shared (i.e., multi-user, multi-agency), cargo terminal. 
Although these guidelines may also be useful when designing a dedicated single-user facility, it is obvious 
that in such a case only one of the flexibility requirements (modular expansion to keep in line with traffic 
development) applies. The other requirement (handling agencies/space sharing flexibility) does not apply. 
Hence, the designer of a single-user cargo facility may find it advantageous to occasionally deviate from 
these guidelines. 
In this section, cargo terminals within the typical size range (from 1,000 to 10,000 m? and from 10,000 to 
50,000 m? covered space) are primarily considered. These ranges refer to the total covered space 
involved in a project or a set of buildings jointly planned and developed. These size ranges cover most of 
900 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 920===
Se Sy IATA al Cargo Terminal 
the foreseeable requirements for international multi-user cargo terminals. Smaller or larger buildings may 
require different design or layout solutions, but the basic objectives should remain the same. 
Planners should keep in mind that, even where a significant portion of the total cargo volume is carried by 
all-cargo/freighter aircraft, the majority is usually carried on passenger aircraft. Hence, although it is 
recommended to retain space provisions for the nearby handling of all-cargo/freighter aircraft (even if 
there are none foreseen at the time of planning), all aspects of moving cargo to and from the passenger 
terminals should be fully integrated in the building design at all times. This will usually require a 
preliminary assessment of the variety of means of transportation to be used (refer to JATA Airport 
Handling Manual AHM 960/966 and 967 for details of the various types of dollies and cargo transport 
vehicles available). 
3.5.9.1 Design Consideration Objectives 
In compliance with ICAO Annex 9—Facilitation, Recommended Practice 6.4, and the IATA Cargo Facilitation 
policy, the design, layout and/or access of buildings should in no way be detrimental to the possibility of any 
aircraft operating on the airport to have choice of self-handling. Alternatively, the aircraft may be handled by 
another airline, or by a handling agent, or by a common-user/co-operative type of handling agency, as 
appropriate for the handling and storage of the cargo. 
The direct commercial impact of cargo warehouse handling makes it an essential factor of cost/quality-of￾service competition. Therefore, in addition to common world-wide facilitation objectives, any restriction on the 
choice of handling organization, dictated by the cargo building layout or otherwise, would have an adverse 
effect on airline competitiveness and, ultimately, the shipping public's interest. 
The general building layout should consequently leave all possibilities open for the choice of handling 
arrangements. The space and installation requirements in a cargo facility usually vary considerably between 
the airlines operating at a given airport, and for airlines individually over a period of time (e.g., evolving 
development and changes in schedules, aircraft types, traffic patterns, etc.). For instance, some airlines may 
operate all-cargo/freighter aircraft whereas others may not. Some may be totally ULD-oriented whereas others 
may operate only with bulk cargo. Some may wish to improve productivity with a high degree of 
mechanization or automation, whereas others may be satisfied with the most simple terminal-and-dollies 
arrangement, etc. 
Keeping this in mind, it is essential that any common-user cargo terminal layout offer maximum flexibility, 
including space provision for development of infrastructure, facilities and offices. These may be utilized for 
different applications depending on the extent to which any individual airline's or handler's cargo activities 
have developed at a particular point in time. 
Experience demonstrates that the physical division of customs areas (i.e., import/export/transit) inside 
warehouses is significantly detrimental to space utilization and flexible cargo-handling methods. This results in 
prolonged dwell times in the facility, thereby adversely affecting building costs, cargo-handling efficiency, air 
cargo competitiveness and the shipping public's interests. 
Design of the cargo facility should therefore be based on prior agreement with local customs authorities that, 
preferably, will permit a free flow within each facility or section of the facility. Import and export cargo should 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 901 

===PAGE 921===
== IATA rll Airport Development Reference Manual 
be controlled by customs staff at the boundary of the bonded area and the landside acceptance and delivery 
area) and use the WCO Framework of standards for a data-driven approach. 
3.5.9.2 Siting 
In choosing a site for the cargo facilities/terminal and support facilities, the following should be taken into 
account: 
902 
The site should be in accordance with the long range master plan for the entire airport, which should be 
reviewed and updated periodically keeping in mind both passenger and cargo facilities expansion 
Sufficient land area should be provided for future expansion over the specified planning period 
A high-quality airside road is required for transportation of cargo directly between aircraft on the 
Passenger terminal apron and the cargo facility 
The site should include adequate space for a cargo apron adjacent to the main cargo facility for direct 
cargo access. This cargo apron should be adequate for: 
o Existing and projected aircraft types 
o Related loading and transport equipment 
o Future expansion 
The area adjacent to the cargo apron should be designated only for cargo processing facilities, with each 
facility having its own expansion capability 
Other cargo-related facilities (i.e., agent/forwarder facilities, bonded stores, free-trade zone facilities, 
customs offices and other office blocks) should be accommodated on the landside of the terminal 
complex, without impeding cargo flow, traffic and parking 
When insufficient area is available in the cargo terminal complex for these functions, space should be 
reserved on a conveniently located site, with direct access to the cargo terminal to facilitate transfer 
operations 
If a railway or underground link to the airport is foreseen or already exists, an intermediate station or an 
extension to the cargo terminal area should be considered for staff transportation 
When a cargo terminal area is separated from the passenger area by a taxiway or runway, or otherwise

© Using palletized roller bed trucks (refer to the IATA Airport Handling Manual AHM 960) to expedite 
airside transportation. 
o Providing an adequate tunnel in order to shorten the airside distance

= The clear height at any point in the tunnel should exceed 4.6 m in order to allow the use of trucks

3.5.9.3 Infrastructure 
The infrastructure (i.e., roads, loading areas, parking) should be designed for the planned capacity and allow 
for future expansion. The airside and landside road systems should accommodate all vehicle sizes expected 
to require access to individual facilities and the total cargo area, with particular consideration to large vehicle 
access. 
The roads in the cargo terminal complex must be integrated with the public road system and the airport road 
system, and include adequate (possibly separate) access to the existing and future road network. 
Although moving cargo to and from the passenger terminal(s) is a basic consideration, it should be only a 
secondary objective when selecting the cargo terminal location. Experience indicates that ground 
transportation of cargo is much more sensitive to the quality of the roadway used, in terms of duration, 
potential damage to pallet contours and economics, than to its length. 
3.5.9.3.1 Airside Roads 
At least one airside, fully customs-bonded, two-lane roadway must be provided between the cargo terminal(s) 
area and any of the passenger terminals. This road should meet the following criteria: 
® Minimum usable width of 10 m, preferably 12 m, to allow crossing of wide-pallet dolly trains and/or over￾width ULD transfer vehicles 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 903 

===PAGE 923===
Se B, q IATA ul Airport Development Reference Manual 
¢ Strong vehicle-grade pavement, designed to withstand up to 1,500 kPa (15 bar) local footprint pressure 
with a typical load of up to 10,000 kg per axle, to withstand the worst cases encountered with 
transportation of air cargo pallets on dollies 
e Up and down gradients should be avoided, if possible, and should never exceed 4% at any location, 
including any necessary tunnels or underpasses 
© The number of turns should be minimized and ample turn radii, in excess of 20 m at any location, should 
be provided where a turn is necessary 
e Crossings that include a STOP signal, and particularly any crossings of an aircraft taxiway, should be 
avoided wherever possible 
e Apaved shoulder, three meters wide and of sufficient bearing strength, should be provided on each side 
to allow for an emergency stop by unserviceable transportation vehicles without impeding other traffic 
3.5.9.3.2 Landside Roads 
At least one, two-lane public roadway of at least 10 m in width must be provided to give access to each part 
of the cargo terminal complex on the landside (i.e., the truck docking area). It is also recommended that, in 
order to accommodate the frequent occurrence of standby trucks having to wait for clearance or rest, 
additional parking spaces at least 18 m deep be provided across the public road, along the cargo terminal 
facade. 
A customs and security-guarded gateway should be provided in the immediate vicinity of the cargo facility to 
permit direct access to the apron of customs-bonded or oversized shipment trucks whenever necessary. 
Appropriate loading or unloading equipment may then be required on the apron. 
3.5.9.4 Cargo Terminal Concept 
A cargo terminal designed in a linear or modular plan layout, with the possibility of allocating parts or modules 
to as many airlines/nandling agents as necessary, and with the potential for expansion at preferably both, but 
at least one, end(s) of the building, will have many advantages, particularly in view of the following objectives: 
e A free choice of handling organization 
e Acargo terminal is essentially a physical transitory sorting facility, between airside and landside 
e A large number of vehicles need to have free access as close as possible to the essential warehouse 
portion 
e Later phased development/extension, which should not necessitate destruction or significant change to 
the parts already built 
It should also be noted that offices, technical service areas, and special storage facilities should be positioned 
without detriment to normal cargo flow and future expansion. 
904 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 924===
Se ey IATA al Cargo Terminal 
In order to provide each user airline with the required possibility of conducting its own commercial cargo 
activity (i.e., customer contact, document handling and processing, etc.), it is essential that the cargo terminal 
complex design provides proportional office space in each individual section or module allocated, including, in 
the event of later expansion or reassignment of the modules to other operators, a re-arrangement capability. 
The easiest way to provide this flexibility, without detriment to normal cargo flow and future expansion, is to 
design continuous office space at a mezzanine level above the landside dock area (i.e., import delivery and 
export acceptance) over the whole terminal transverse width. 
3.5.9.4.1 Transverse Layout 
A cargo terminal complex building should be designed so the module proportions (i.e., width and depth) 
provide sufficient linear facades and doorways for trucks and vehicles to dock, and sufficient area to perform 
all other cargo processing and storage functions. 
The space allotment to the various operators and handling agents should be via modules that are as flexible 
as possible, with dimensions defined, for example, by the pitch of columns in the construction. Each allotted 
module should have access to both airside and landside. Permanent dividing walls should be avoided in favor 
of a system of demountable partitions that can be relocated when the need arises, thus facilitating changes in 
space allotments within the terminal complex. The partitions should provide adequate security between 
airlines. 
Where customs regulations make it mandatory for each warehouse to have separate import and export 
storage, this requirement should be taken into account to define modules, space allotment and partition 
systems for each operator's warehouse. 
3.5.9.4.2 Depth Layout 
The building depth should be established only once the operational requirements of all tenants have been 
defined. In general, the building depth should be as short as practicable, but the dimensions should be large 
enough to accommodate all areas and processing functions in a natural and direct flow between the landside 
and airside faces. Points to note include: 
* The objective of operational flexibility 
e The requirement to plan for phased development through various stages, allowing space utilization and 
capital spending to increase in step with the operator's expanded activity 
e Provision for the space and functional requirements of the Boeing 747F all cargo/freighter aircraft as well 
as the latest high productivity mechanized cargo handling systems 
e In order to avoid potential obsolescence, adequate space should be protected in the overall plan for future 
wide-body operations

3.5.9.5 Facilities 
3.5.9.5.1 Doors and Entrances 
The following points should be considered when designing access to and from the cargo warehouse: 
e Access from landside and airside should be direct through large doors of a size compatible with the 
equipment used. Airside doors must allow passage of forklifts, dollies and vehicle traffic; doors five meters 
high and five meters wide are typical. Landside truck dock doors are typically four meters high and three 
meters wide 
¢ Doors are the most vulnerable item in a cargo facility. Doors and frames should be well protected against 
damage by vehicles and cargo. Ease of replacement should be a design consideration 
¢ Proper locking mechanisms on all doors are required for security purposes 
¢ Canopies are typical for weather protection, but special curtains or high-speed folding doors in open 
doorways may also be required under severe inclement weather conditions. The design should include 
such provisions without imposing undue constraints on cargo flow 
° In the case of two-way traffic through one door, a one-way flow route or traffic light may be required 
e Appropriate door signs or numbers, clearly visible and similar both inside and out, will facilitate efficient 
customer and cargo handling 
* Manual operation of large doors is both slow and cumbersome. Mechanical or electrical drives improve 
the operation, but should always incorporate required manual override and safety provisions 
¢ Normal and emergency exits for personnel should meet local requirements 
¢ Adirect interface between airside transport equipment or landside shipper vehicles and a container 
handling system may be included in the design 
e Airside doors should not be located so that traffic entering/exiting the building would impede or interfere 
with aircraft parking or aircraft interface 
3.5.9.5.2 Column Spacing/Obstructions 
Fixed obstructions such as utilities, special facilities and offices should not impede cargo flow and processing. 
For the same reason, the building column grid should be as large as economically possible. A free span for 
cargo handling would be ideal. However, this is only possible occasionally and in special cases. Construction 
costs and beam considerations generally make columns necessary. In such cases, the widest column spacing 
achievable is most desirable; generally the spacing should be in excess of 15 m. The planned operational and 
storage systems, and the main aisles and entrance doors, should be considered when designing the column 
grid. Another basic consideration is future flexibility. 
When a six meter ULD depth is used, with related storage and transfer vehicles in a ULD storage system on 
airside, the free span should be a minimum of 22 m from the outside wall containing the storage system. 
906 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 926===
& p Se IATA al Cargo Terminal 
To protect columns from damage by vehicles and cargo, strong surrounding protection is required in the 
operational maneuvering areas. 
3.5.9.5.3 Free-Height Requirements 
Depending upon the cargo terminal layout and size of the future storage area, provision for various heights 
must be incorporated in the terminal design. Utilities, lighting, beams, fire protection, etc., must be installed so 
as to clear calculated free heights. 
In order to arrive at the most acceptable design decisions, it is essential that ‘trade-off studies, which evaluate 
various storage systems versus the required facility size and efficiency, are carried out in conjunction with the 
airlines and handling operators. 
In the basic cargo operation, bulk shipments are normally moved from place to place with forklifts. The 
minimum clear height where forklifts operate should be five meters to allow for normal lift capacities. As forklift 
extension depends on the model and manufacturer, the cargo facility planner should verify equipment 
utilization with the airline or cargo operator. 
When storage systems are utilized, the clear height will be defined by the number of storage levels, the 
distance between each level, and the clearance requirement above cargo stored on the top rack. 
3.5.9.5.4 Storage 
As most cargo is delivered to or received from clients in bulk, to be consolidated into or broken down from 
aircraft load units at another time, interim storage by shipment or destination is required in the cargo facility 
along the planned lines of flow. Some facilities will focus on shipper-loaded ULDs, requiring instead adequate 
ULD storage and automated/semi-automated truck-to-ETV interfaces. 
Floor storage will require more space than vertical storage systems if comparable circulation is provided. 
Whereas storage systems provide an adequate constant space between racks for lift vehicle maneuverability, 
the tendency with floor storage is for aisles to decrease in size and number as cargo volumes increase. As a 
consequence, multiple handling of shipments increases and inventory control becomes more difficult. At this 
point, vertical storage may not significantly enhance space utilization, but it will improve productivity and 
customer service. 
Use of high storage systems can reduce the required storage floor space, but investment in equipment and 
systems is necessary in both the primary and subsequent development phases. When designing the cargo 
terminal facility, floor space should be planned to permit later expansion and constructed with the correct 
height, floor strength, etc. in the appropriate areas in which storage installations will be located. 
Automated Sort and Retrieval Systems (AS/RS) will limit the need for large spaces between racking systems 
that allow for human-driven forklifts. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 907 

===PAGE 927===
rie IATA Airport ae Development Reference Manual 
Bulk Freight Storage 
Bulk freight is often placed on industrial wooden skids, euro pallets or the equivalent. The skids provide an 
effective way to transport and store bulk shipments within the facility. The typical stacking height on a skid is 
approximately 1.5 m, allowing a shipment on a skid to be placed directly into lower deck containers. Stacking 
height may exceed this for shipments placed in main-deck and high-stack ULDs. If the preponderance of 
cargo is received in lower deck containers, then a reasonable distance between bulk freight storage racks 
would be 1.5 m. 
Typical storage racking for a forklift operation is three levels. Mechanized lift equipment may permit additional 
levels. The actual mix of freight stored should be evaluated and racking systems should be developed to 
accommodate the specific height requirements. If the racking system can only provide for storage of the 
smallest shipment received, it will be necessary for cargo personnel to reduce the shipments heights or use 
floor space. 
There are options in unit level or piece level systems that should be evaluated based on the proposed and 
predicted traffic flows. 
ULD Storage 
ULD storage capacity sizes and locations are critical to the effectiveness and productivity of a cargo facility. 
They should be assessed through: 
e Calculation of the estimated mean and peak cargo flows expressed in individual ULD modules. Refer to 
3.5.10. The reference size usually taken is size M (2.5 x 3.2 m) 
e Identification and optimization of the ULD circuits, including empty storage, build-up and breakdown 
positions, as well as loaded ULD storage and transportation 
All empty or loaded ULD storage positions should be on roller equipment and meet AHM 911 and AHM 942 
requirements. As an exception, storage of empty pallets can be on fixed supports, providing each pallet is 
stored individually and can be retrieved with its net, where attached, without friction with others (e.g. empty 
pallets racks). 
When an ETV and two or more tier pallet/container storage system is planned, the distance between stacking 
levels will depend on ULD height. The ULD height generally to be taken into account is: 
e Lower deck: 1.7 m 
e Main deck: 2.4 m 
e Full-contour: 3.0 m 
Overall clear height will depend on the mix of 1.7, 2.4 and 3.0 m storage requirements. For example, three 
tiers of 3.0 m storage will require a clear height of 12 m. 
908 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 928===
ae 
IATA Cargo Terminal 
In addition, overall clear height should include: 
e 0.5 m additional height wherever the ULD is to be handled on mobile equipment (dollies) or forklifted with 
a slave pallet 
e 0.8 m additional clearance over the roof of lower deck containers to allow for container door deployment 
(3.0 m minimum overall ceiling height, including 0.5 m support equipment height) 
Building height should be considered as an economical method of achieving future expansion. Initial 
construction of a tall warehouse may allow a tenant to expand vertically to meet storage expansion 
requirements before it is necessary to expand transversely. 
Long-Term Storage 
On occasion, lengthy storage times for cargo may occur as a result of slow clearance, inefficient handling 
and/or lack of aircraft capacity. Such storage is detrimental to fast and efficient space utilization. To combat 
this problem, higher storage charges for longer periods can be implemented, together with mandatory transfer 
of the cargo to secondary storage spaces. Reserve capacity in the terminal facility, or in an agent's building, 
should be used for this purpose whenever possible. 
3.5.9.5.5 Illumination 
The following factors should be taken into consideration regarding the lighting of cargo terminal facilities: 
* Outside area lighting should be sufficient for safe vehicle movement and operations at nighttime 
*® On the apron, lights should not blind crews in aircraft cockpits 
e Lighting at dock areas and entrances should allow normal reading of marks and labels on cargo and 
ULDs handled. It should also be adequate for security surveillance requirements 
«Inside the terminal, general lighting should be adequate for normal handling operations and traffic flow 
e Extra lighting is required at work stations and storage areas to facilitate document and label reading 
* 200 to 300 lux at floor level should be available 
¢ All lighting shall allow true color reading 
e Offices and control areas require the applicable standard light intensity 
e The layout of the lighting system should allow for the special requirements of PC/CRT operation 
e Offices should have windows to admit daylight. Where possible, work areas in the terminal should also 
have access to daylight either through windows, along the tops of walls or in the roof. This will reduce 
energy costs and improve working conditions

3.5.9.5.6 Facilities 
Staff Facilities 
Staff facilities such as washrooms, toilets and canteens should be available for all staff working in terminals 
and offices, and should be easily accessible to persons with reduced mobility. Public conveniences, light 
tefreshment concessions, etc., can be provided centrally or per terminal facility, on the landside. 
Technical Facilities 
Technical areas for the repair or overhaul of equipment and systems, including battery charge or change 
facilities, should be located in or near the cargo terminal(s). 
Special Facilities 
Special facilities in the cargo terminal{s) to handle particular commodities require specific positioning and 
construction according to their particular standards. The size and location of special facilities will depend on 
the type and quantity of special cargo that will be handled. The most important special facilities are: 
e Vaults and safes to store valuable shipments 
¢ Coolers, refrigerators and freezers for perishables 
* Animal and house pet storage, with quarantine facility if required 
e¢ Human remains storage 
¢ The dangerous goods storage and handling area, including provision for the holding of radioactive 
materials, should be located well away from work stations 
3.5.9.5.7 Bypass 
Large and special shipments of valuables, perishables and livestock should bypass the cargo facility and be 
transferred directly between aircraft and road vehicles on the apron. Access to the bypass must be restricted 
and meet all airport security requirements. 
910 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 930===
=e iW . 
IATA Cargo Terminal 
3.5.9.5.8 Unit Load Devices 
ULD Build-up and Breakdown Space 
ULD build-up and breakdown positions should meet AHM 911 requirements. In addition, they should provide 
adjacent free floor space, not to be used by vehicles, to allow full deployment of pallet nets for the detailed 
inspection required by airworthiness regulations. Based on the most commonly used size M (2.5 x 3.2 m) 
module, this space, which can be common to several positions, should be located alongside one long (3.2 m) 
side of the pallet, and should be at least 6 x 6 m where only lower deck units are handled, or 9 x 9 m where 
main deck units are handled. 
Free height requirements for ULD build-up and breakdown positions should be in accordance with 3.5.9.5.3 
Free-Height Requirements. Where pallet fire containment covers (FCC) are to be used at local Airline Users 
Group request, lifting means such as gantries may be required to install and remove the FCCs, and will 
require additional vertical clearance. 
ULD Handling Maneuvering Space 
Mobile equipment maneuvering space should be planned alongside any ULD transfer position, consistent with 
the foreseen handling means. Maneuvering space provisions should be taken into account where handling is 
foreseen to be allowed by forklifts equipped with a slave pallet (e.g., at truck loading docks), ULD build-up, 
breakdown and storage positions, or on the air side. 
Spare ULD Accessories Storage 
Enclosed storage space should be planned for spare ULD accessories storage, including pallet nets, tie-down 
straps, FCCs, and various other accessories to be determined with the local Airline Users Group. Since textile 
items (i.e., nets, straps, and FCCs) are sensitive to ultra-violet light, their storage space should be enclosed 
and protected from sunlight. The planner should also provide means for separate storage by sizes, types, and 
owners.
