3.5.11 Cargo Communication Controls 
Provision for good communications, both between and within cargo complexes and terminals, is essential for 
efficient operations. The scope and types of communication facilities must, therefore, be included in the 
planning. These will include cables, ducts, conduits etc., as well as facilities for the transportation of 
documents. At one time or another, in addition to telephone and telex, any of the following systems may be 
required: 
¢ Ground-to-air radio 
¢ Two-way personnel radio 
e Public address system 
¢ Data processing and sharing with handheld or portable devices 
¢ CCTV 
All offices and terminal areas should have access to the communications tools required for process control. 
* To ensure that the cargo processing time matches the speed of air transport, an efficient, integrated 
system of communications is required. This involves the interrelation of the following functions in all 
communications and documentation systems related to the dispatch of air cargo Customs, including 
customs brokers 
e Airlines or handling operators 
e Freight forwarders 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 913 

===PAGE 933===
x iil a Si 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
e Trucking companies 
e Security agencies 
In the planning of communications systems that may be required in relation to local situations (i.e., company 
procedures, larger cargo volumes, etc.), it is recommended that only those systems required for immediate 
use in the early years of growth be installed at the outset. However, it is also essential to ensure that due 
provision is made for the subsequent installation of more advanced systems, including their related 
connection requirements. 
3.5.11.1 Dynamic Communications 
The rapid developments in communications, data processing and automation have made it possible to 
establish direct connections locally and world-wide via Local Area Networks (LAN) and Wide Area Networks 
(WAN) for all parties concerned with cargo processing. Coordination and transmission of information using 
these connections results in faster handling and clearance of cargo. Tracking of items dynamically has 
become a reality with users accessing cargo inventories via the web and monitoring real time progress of 
goods through the cargo process. 
3.5.12 Cargo Control Regulations 
Compliance with all government (i.e., Customs), safety and security regulations must be included in the 
terminal design, layout and cargo terminal operations to ensure approved cargo handling in all facilities. This 
compliance should be without detriment to the facilitation of cargo handling procedures. 
In the planning phase, approvals must be obtained from all authorities concerned, particularly customs 
officials, with respect to cargo processing as well as combined control and checkpoints on the established 
customs boundary. 
3.5.13 Cargo Security Controls 
Security is one of the aviation top priorities and the safeguard and transportation of air cargo remains a key 
part of the aviation security system and a key concern for the industry. 
Security responsibility lies with the civil aviation authority, airport authority, other authorities (i.e., law 
enforcement bodies, customs and border protection, etc.), airlines and terminal operators to safeguard the 
landside, airside operations, the aircraft, and the cargo and mail stored and processed in the designated and 
914 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 934===
IATA 4 Cargo Terminal 
secured areas. The necessary controls, procedures and provisions must be incorporated in the development 
strategy and plans as well as the SOPs of accredited secure operators. Air cargo is made up of a large 
percentage of high-value goods and valuables that require special attention during transport, storage and 
ground handling by airlines/operators in order to avoid tampering. Besides special storage in vaults in the 
terminal facility, additional escort and guard services to protect against theft and fraud should be considered. 
In order to prevent acts of unlawful interference, access to the operational section of the terminal facility, and 
to the adjacent airside area, which is under the control of the terminal operator and subject to approvals by 
the appropriate authorities should apply appropriate screening and security controls before entering the cargo 
security restricted area. Entry to this area should be restricted to airline, terminal operator and customs 
personnel. In certain cases, due to the risk of theft, continual surveillance of the total cargo terminal area may 
be necessary. 
There are various aviation security standards and recommended practices applicable to cargo transportation 
and storage at airports. Specific solutions pertaining to the infrastructure will depend on the location of the 
cargo terminal and the regulatory requirements in relation to the transport and carriage of the cargo. 
The cargo terminal itself could be located within the airport boundaries, adjacent to the airport or be an off￾airport facility. 
When determining infrastructure\ solutions and terminal design, consideration should also be given to the end￾to-end cargo process from the moment it is accepted until it is loaded onto the aircraft. This shall also include 
requirements for the protection of secured cargo and screening of unknown or tampered cargo. Planners 
should be aware that the treatment of cargo once it arrives on airport premises is largely determined by the 
processes that take place off airport. Therefore planners must understand the variety of processes that need 
to be accommodated once the cargo reaches the airport and ensure facilities are designed appropriately. For 
example, some cargo may need to be screened, whilst cargo received from known shippers or screened 
upstream in the supply chain need to be protected and may be cleared without the need to apply additional 
screening measures. 
Designers should consult cargo warehouse operators, appropriate aviation security authorities and the airport 
operator (where applicable) to understand security standards for cargo protection and screening that should 
include approved screening methods. The route and/or methods by which cargo is moved between the cargo 
secured facility and the aircraft, whether or not cargo facility is on the airfield or adjacent to it, needs to be 
secure and protected to ensure that the security status of cargo can be maintained to ensure facility and flight 
safety. 
More details regarding security precautions and procedures can be obtained from the ATA Security Manual. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 915 

===PAGE 935===
Be ft IATA al Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.5.14 Cargo Safety Controls 
Fire prevention and protection for the terminals, the handling systems and the goods stored therein, as well as 
the staff, must be incorporated in the terminal design in compliance with local regulations. 
Dangerous goods such as flammable liquids, explosives, corrosives and radioactive materials should be 
handled and stored in accordance with IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations as well as local or national 
dangerous goods regulations (e.g., issues related to fire extinguishing systems for certain dangerous goods, 
specifications for storage facilities, etc.). High-rise cargo storage systems generally require additional, 
integrated, fire protection (i.e., sprinkler system). 
Working conditions for the staff and safety provisions for the facilities, systems and equipment used must 
comply with national standards and industry practices. All mechanical systems must incorporate built-in 
safeguards. Vehicle exhaust should have minimum toxic contents, or special ventilation must be provided 
where exhaust problems can arise. Battery-powered vehicles should be used in all working areas in the 
terminal. 
3.5.15 Cargo Government Controls 
For international cargo, and sometimes for domestic cargo, customs control of import and export is required. 
The airline/operator/shipper must provide Customs with the goods and related documents at established 
checkpoints. 
All cargo handling in the cargo facility, and on the airside of the airport, must comply with specific customs 
regulations (i.e., relating to the safeguarding of goods in an operator's custody, records of the air transport, 
transfer to other airlines, or delivery to consignees). 
3.5.16 Cargo Facilitation 
Efficient handling, with minimal obstruction by government control checks and short storage time in the airport 
terminal facilities, can only be achieved through facilitation agreements and with the approval of the facility 
design by Customs and other authorities. 
3.5.16.1 Cargo Customs 
Often the modification of long-standing customs regulations will need to be obtained to facilitate operations in 
a new situation. These may include: 
¢ Delegation to the airline terminal operator of control over the process area behind a customs boundary, 
inside the cargo facility, and the adjacent apron area, based on good in-house inventory control and 
security. Spot checks can be made by Customs in this area at any time 
e An agreed customs boundary between the landside area, open to forwarders and shippers for acceptance 
and delivery of cargo, and the airside processing and operating area which is only open to operational 
916 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 936===
lil Se 
IATA Cargo Terminal 
staff. Appraisal space for customs checks in the boundary area provides required control of cargo flows. 
Operational customs offices should be located in this area 
* Temporary enclosed storage of import cargo, if required. This should be arranged in an area adjacent to 
the import flow in the cargo facility 
e Aseparate bonded warehouse, on the landside of the cargo handling facilities, if complex clearance 
procedures result in import cargo being stored longer than one or two weeks at the airport. All goods to 
be held longer than operationally acceptable can be transferred to this warehouse, and thus free the 
cargo facilities for their main function of fast cargo processing 
3.5.16.2 Automated Customs Clearance/Communication 
In the wake of advances in technology and integrated databases, customs clearance is becoming more 
automated. A few governmental agencies have developed automated customs clearance programs. 
Connection or integration with systems for airlines/handling operators and agents will significantly improve 
processing and clearance of cargo. 
3.5.16.3 Other Customs Areas 
Where the airport master plan foresees duty-free zones for the handling of international transfer cargo, these 
areas should be developed adjacent to cargo facilities and the related expansion area. In conjunction with 
Customs, a common bonded area can then be designated to facilitate cargo movements between areas. 
3.5.16.4 Additional Controls 
Other government controls to be expected, with their separate requirements, are animal quarantine for all live 
animals as well as food and plant control for produce shipments. Additional controls may be instituted to meet 
other requirements which may arise. 
The processes developed and adopted by the cargo systems designer should permit international and 
domestic cargo to be processed efficiently and in accordance with the above legal instructions and 
recommendations.

3.5.17 Express Cargo Processing 
3.5.17.1 Introduction and Scope 
Express processing facilities are, in many ways, closer to a passenger terminal in function than they are to a 
cargo terminal. The concepts presented within this section are intended to provide guidance for the planning 
and design of future express cargo processing facilities. The focus will be on common processes, facilities 
and services that are necessary to support this activity. The content addresses the international movement of 
express cargo and is thus involved with the complex variations of: 
e National economies 
¢ Commercial and legal considerations 
e Local infrastructure 
e Regulatory requirements and standards 
In some cases, a facility may be designed to accomplish both express and normal cargo flows with some 
need for transfer between the two areas. 
3.5.17.2 Express Cargo Development Philosophy 
Each express operator has a unique processing system—there is no market for ‘speculative’ facilities. The 
only source of requirements is from individual companies and are determined by them. The questions to be 
considered in determining the scope of any facility include: 
e Will the facility be a hub, gateway or O&D point? 
e What relationship will it have to surface transportation? 
e What kind of volume will be processed? 
e What functions will be performed on-airport and what will be performed off-airport? 
e What are the processing times required (sort windows)? 
e How many destinations are involved (splits)? 
e What processing procedures are required by the local authorities? 
e Is it part of a secure freight supply chain? 
It is important to keep in mind that the express company is directly responsible to the customer and is held 
responsible for any failures. It's therefore important that the express company be able to exercise ‘custodial 
control’. 
918 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 938===
= IATA al Cargo Terminal 
3.5.17.3 Pre-Design Considerations 
Airports should understand the needs of the express industry and must not treat such facilities as just another 
cargo warehouse. Because the express industry is relatively new, quite often express must be made to fit 
within the parameters of the traditional air cargo system. 
It is not only critical to have specific express facilities, it is also important that specific clearance and handling 
procedures be instituted. It is pointless for an express company to invest in an express handling facility if the 
custom authorities will treat the express product as regular cargo. 
Determining who will build the facility and how it is to be financed is often subject to more debate than the 
facility itself. Parties that need to be involved with facility development are: 
e = The airport 
¢ Government agencies concerned with bilateral and self-handling rights 
e Customs 
e Security agencies 
e Government agencies concerned with commercial trucking and delivery 
e Government agencies concerned with business and operating licenses 
¢ Slot coordinators 
3.5.17.4 The Express Cargo Process 
The role of the express operator vs. the cargo operator can be quite different, although some of the processes 
for express operations are similar to those of traditional air cargo. The express company is solely responsible 
for the early phases of the following: 
e Data collection 
e Analyses and studies 
e Decisions on the scope and role of the operation 
One aspect of data collection that differentiates express from other operations is that volume figures for 
express operations are not considered as single source per airport. Critical in the consideration of the scope 
and impact of an express operation on an airport is the regulatory flexibility of both the airport and relevant 
government agencies. 
There are many kinds of specific operations within the express industry, and in some cases within the same 
company. Express is generally divided into four types of operations: 
1. Ramp or O&D point: serves a metropolitan area and its immediate surroundings. 
2. Gateway: a point serving a larger area. Arriving express is trans-loaded into other feeder aircraft or 
commercial line haul, or into trucks for shipment to other cities. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 919 

===PAGE 939===
Sa e- Ff IATA Biull Airport Development Reference Manual 
3. Hubs: Major facilities where the bulk of express is not destined for the local area. These are major sort 
facilities with heavy aircraft activity. Tracking and sorting are major activities. Custom clearance cannot be 
an issue. 
4. Co-location: It is common to find a ramp located adjacent to a gateway or hub. These would be separate 
operations located under the same roof, but independent from each other. 
3.5.17.5 Typical Express Cargo Product Flow at Express Cargo Facilities 
Each express company should take the minimum requirements described below and add onto them according 
to their needs. The processing facility must be able to accommodate redesigns and changes as they occur 
over time. 
3.5.17.5.1 Express Item Arrival 
The arrival process needs to begin before the shipment arrives. Arrangements should be made with Customs 
to pre-clear any arriving shipments. Arrangements should be made in advance to guarantee that Customs can 
advise which shipments they want to examine before the plane lands. 
When the aircraft arrives, the shipments are separated into their respective channels for processing. Those 
that need to be cleared are identified, scanned and sent to the inspection area. Customs will insist on having 
the right to inspect any shipment, even those that were pre-cleared. 
Some ULDs will come off an airplane and be loaded immediately onto another. This transfer needs to be 
done quickly, therefore there is no need to bring these ULDs inside the facility. A canopy would be desirable 
in rainy and snowy climates. 
Other ULDs will be off-loaded from the aircraft and loaded onto large trucks. This practice is especially 
popular in the Americas. The trucks are allowed on the ramp and receive the ULD directly from the aircraft. In 
other airports, ULDs have to travel through the facility to be loaded on a truck waiting at the dock. 
For a hub, most ULDs must be brought into the facility, broken down, sorted and rebuilt before being sent to 
their next destination. The time this takes is known as the “sort window’. It is vital to the express companies’ 
operation to have customs procedures in place that allow through shipments destined for another country to 
proceed without impediment. In airports that restrict the express companies’ rights to self-handle or require 
common clearance, it can be very difficult to do adequate tracking. 
3.5.17.5.2 Express Item Departure 
In a sort-transfer operation, arrival and departure is the same process. The airport processing facility is not the 
point of origin of the shipment, it is merely a waypoint on its journey. 
920 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 940===
he ha . 
IATA 4 Cargo Terminal 
Departure customs requirements are usually much simpler than on arrival. The important documentation is 
the manifest for the next arrival destination. There may be many different final destinations on a single aircraft 
and thus different manifests required. This complicated task can be simplified if a standardized pre-selection 
manifest is not used. 
3.5.17.6 Express Facility Design Parameters 
3.5.17.6.1 The Express Ramp 
Usually, the express operator will share a ramp unless the operation is large enough for a single operator. All 
express operations operate at approximately the same time; therefore, the ramp needs to be built for peak 
operations. Express operators consider the airport as a waypoint and not a destination, therefore they will be 
interested in having the shipments moving quickly. Accommodating trucks on the ramp as well as using racks 
and dollies will contribute to faster shipment movements. 
Three additional items need to be considered when designing a ramp: 
1. Tether pits are now being used in most cargo terminals to avoid having aircraft sitting on their tail. Most 
modern cargo planes have their main loading door in front of the wing, which means that the rear of the 
plane is loaded first. Tail stands used to be the norm, however they've been known to cause structural 
damage to aircraft, and require inspections to be performed which can delay aircraft departure. Airports 
are encouraged to install a tether pit at each cargo aircraft parking position. Specifications must be 
followed exactly, otherwise the pit will be rendered useless. If tether pits are refused, an alternative is a 
weight cart. Usually a reinforced dolly stacked with steel, it can be a good substitute provided it does not 
have to be moved often. If an aircraft needs a pushback, the weight cart will have to be moved. Its very 
small wheels and heavy weight may damage the ramp quickly. 
2. When considering drainage, two factors have to be kept in mind: 
(a) The slope for drainage cannot exceed 1%, otherwise it might impede the loading and unloading of the 
ULDs on the aircraft's roller deck floor 
(b) Provisions need to be made for the containment and routing of runoff and spills 
3. Lighting designs need to be very sensitive to adjacent properties, taxiways and ATC. On the other hand, 
since a majority of ramp operations occur at night, lighting should be strong enough to allow efficient 
work. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 921 

===PAGE 941===
ue a Se IATA { Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.5.17.6.2 Express Processing Facility Considerations 
The following factors need to be considered when planning an express cargo processing facility: 
¢ The site needs to be in accordance with the airport master plan and the plan needs to allow for the unique 
requirements of an express facility 
e Remote location from passenger and cargo operations 
¢ Sufficient land for future expansion, in line with forecasts which should take into consideration the strong 
historical growth rate of express shipping 
¢ Ground transportation network capable of accommodating large trucks 
e Airside access road to passenger and cargo complexes for commercial line haul transfer 
e Ramp should be dedicated to express aircraft with exclusive or preferential rights 
* The ramp needs to be conveniently located close to the runways and taxiways in accordance with ICAO 
Annex 14 
* The area adjacent to the ramp should be reserved for express operations only 
¢ Sufficient land for employee parking and dedicated bus or train stops, if applicable 
¢ GSE and ULD storage facilities located airside 
e Easy access to electricity and telecommunications services as heavy usage is the norm in express 
operations 
3.5.17.6.3 Express Processing Facility Structural Considerations 
The functional capability and flexibility of the express processing facility building is more important than the 
architectural details. The following characteristics must be considered: 
e Assimple, functional building with no elaborate decor or design 
* Kept, as much as possible, on a single level, but mezzanine levels are commonly used for locating sorting 
equipment 
¢ Located at ramp level on the airside so tugs and dollies will have easy access 
e Adjacent to the ramp and adhering to the apron planning requirements of ICAO Annex 14 
e Truck docks and ramps on the ground-side of the facility 
e A vventilation system designed for the building type, size and usage (all of which differ from conventional 
cargo facilities which often have much higher ceilings and very different usage) 
e Lighting LUX levels designed to provide staff with suitable levels of light in the different areas of the 
building (i.e., working areas and rest will require different LUX levels). A specialist should propose the 
correct LUX levels for the various building functional areas. 
¢ Due to the high number of staff working in the express processing facility, the provision for rest rooms, 
toilets and showers.

e The telecommunications requirement is much greater than in a typical cargo facility, therefore attention 
has to be paid to the number of lines coming into and out of the building 
¢ The proportion of office space should be 20 to 25 m? per 100 m* of processing floor space 
e It is better to have the office space on the same level as the operations instead of using the traditional 
cargo approach of putting office space on a mezzanine level 
3.5.17.6.4 Express Facility Sizing and Functional Considerations 
The size of the facility will be determined by the expected volume of express the facility will handle. The sort 
window will determine how many shipments can be handled within a specific time frame and will subsequently 
determine the size of the facility needed. The amount of bypass that can avoid the system will also greatly 
affect the size of the facility. 
Once the sort operation has been determined and designed, there must be accommodation provided for other 
necessary functions: 
e Customs, immigration, quarantine (CIQ) 
e Oversize shipment handling 
e Dangerous goods processing 
¢ Aircraft line maintenance facilities 
e GSE maintenance 
e Traditional air cargo processing and storage 
e Pilots and crew 
Clarification: Shippers/integrators tend to use multiples of 3,000 parcels per day, particularly when designing 
sorting systems. However, cargo forecasts and aircraft load information are expressed in tonnage.

3.5.17.6.5 Express Apron Area 
As a general rule of thumb, the apron size for express facilities lies within the range of 8 to 10 times the size 
of the express building. This includes aircraft stands, internal taxi lanes, airside roads, ground service 
equipment parking as well as processing zones on the apron. 
If more defined data is not available, the following procedure can be used to size the ramp area. Again, as. 
with all cargo facilities, express facilities can use tonnage per annum to calculate the number of aircraft per 
day. This will enable the planner to size the ramp accordingly. 
The annual tonnage = 250 (days) provides the daily tonnage. The average load factor per aircraft (express) 
varies according to the classification of the facility. A regional hub/gateway has average loads of 20 to 25 tons 
per aircraft, with two-thirds of all aircraft being Code D. A reliever hub has average loads of 15 to 20 tons per 
aircraft, with two-thirds of all aircraft being Code C. 
Important issues when planning express facilities are: 
e Understanding the type of operation; the hours of operation; as well as the turnaround times. An express 
operator typically operates between two and 12 hours per day, with two hours being the low end for a 
reliever hub and 12 hours being the high end for a regional hub. Aircraft servicing the facility arrive and 
depart in a wave with the majority of aircraft on the ground within a short time period. The typical 
turnaround time for these aircraft is between one and two hours

3.5.17.7 Express Cargo Project Management and Control 
3.5.17.7.1 Design Approval 
The express company needs to approve the final designs of both the building structure and the interior system 
and fit-up. Design details cannot be finalized until customs clearance procedures are known. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 925 

===PAGE 945===
wr IATA +4 Wa Airport Development Reference Manual 
Recommendations: Design Approval 
The following organizations and persons should be consulted throughout the design process for a new or 
extended express processing facility: 
e Airport operator 
¢ Government agencies concerned with bilateral and self-handling rights 
e Customs 
e Security agencies 
e Government agencies concerned with commercial trucking and delivery 
¢ Government agencies concerned with business and operating licenses 
© Slot coordinators 
3.5.17.7.2 Express Cargo Project Management Structure 
A simple building that is flexible and leaves room for expansion is best. The structure must have the sort area 
enclosed and useable power provided before installation of the sort system can begin. It is important to note 
that the developer should allow four to six months for the installation of the sort system and three months for 
offices, the bulk of which going to the installation of telecommunications tools. 
Recommendation: Expansion Capability 
The express sort system designer should ensure that, upon opening, the provided space and systems can 
cope with the following conditions: 
¢ Meet the operational protocols defined in the agreed building user requirement specification 
¢ Meet the throughput expected for the forecasted final design year for the facility, plus provide a further 
25% contingency express processing hall space to account for any potential abnormal growth in traffic 
e Future ramp expansion requirements 
* Operational express cargo infrastructure IT systems should have a redundancy capability as agreed in 
the building user requirement specification 
Recommendation: Development of a Building User Requirement Specification 
Express cargo facilities have unique operational attributes. The operational needs of the user(s) should be 
fully explored and understood. Bespoke facilities should be provided to ensure appropriate processing 
capability. It is recommended that a building user requirements specification be developed and endorsed by 
the user(s). The specification should detail and capture the specific operational and building requirements 
and contingencies. 
3.5.17.7.3 Express Cargo Project Management—Apron 
It is preferable that the apron be built by the airport, since they will normally insist on controlling the apron. If 
the apron is exclusive and part of the leased area, the developer may have to be the project manager. It is 
important that the connectors between taxiways/runways not be overlooked. 
926 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 946===
any 
IATA Cargo Terminal 
3.5.17.7.4 Project Management—Sort System 
The sort system will typically belong to the express company and should be managed solely by the express 
company. The airport needs to allow the express company the freedom of choice of supplier when it comes to 
building the sort system. 
3.5.17.8 Testing and Trials 
Once the express facility and systems are installed, they need be subjected to testing and trial runs before 
being considered fully operational. Using real aircraft and real cargo, the elements to be included in trial runs 
are: 
e The apron, including tether pits 
e Lighting 
e Fueling equipment and procedures 
e Handling equipment and procedures 
e The structure, including all utilities and HVAC 
* The sort system, including all belts, readers, rollers and lifts 
* = Telecommunications 
e All personnel, including the CIS personnel involved with the clearance operation 
A trial run must be a live run, not a dummy run involving only a few staff members and packages. The facility 
needs to be able to function as if it was a peak period. A minimum of three trial runs should be performed 
before declaring an express facility operational. 
3.5.18 Perishable Cargo 
3.5.18.1 Types of Perishable Handling Facilities 
There are two main types of handling facilities for perishable cargo: 
1. Transit 
2. Total distribution 
These facilities are usually designed and constructed to perform specific functions to meet the needs of 
airport users. The most recent information about perishables and perishable handling facilities is contained in 
the IATA Perishable Cargo Regulations, which is updated by the IATA Live Animals and Perishables Board. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 927 

===PAGE 947===
ee 
TATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
A transit facility can be defined as a processing center with established infrastructure and operational units 
that: 
* Facilitate the loading and unloading of perishable shipments to and from the aircraft 
e Enable swift connections within the airport handling facilities 
e Interface with surface transport 
The process may also include import formalities such as health inspection and customs control. The primary 
function of a transit facility is to move perishable goods quickly and efficiently with the coordination of all 
parties involved and supported by modern technologies and tracking systems. 
A total distribution facility provides the same services as a transit center with additional value-added services, 
such as: 
e Repackaging 
e Pre-cooling

3.5.18.2 The Essential Component of a Perishable Handling Center 
There are two essential components found in most perishable handling facilities: 
1. Processing area 
2. Working area 
3.5.18.2.1 Processing Area 
Different kinds of products are categorized and processed separately. Fruits and vegetables are processed 
separately from other products such as seafood, fish and meat. Although flowers may be processed in the 
same area as fruits and vegetables, they should be separated wherever possible. 
928 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 948===
w IATA fi Cargo Terminal | 
3.5.18.2.2 Working Area 
Working areas are specifically assigned locations within a perishable center with controlled environments for 
specific loads. Each working area has its own temperature control and is large enough for ULD build-up, 
goods sorting, repackaging and quality control. The area protects the goods from exposure to harmful 
conditions. 
Wherever possible, the processing of flowers should be separate from the processing of vegetables, fruits and 
meats. The processing and working areas should have temperature and humidity controlled environments to 
suit the products being processed, as defined below. 
(a) Fruits, Vegetables and Flowers Working Areas 
The ideal working temperature for these products is from 4 to 6°C with humidity of about 85%. 
Considering that the products may stay inside a working area for a couple of hours, special attention 
should be made to minimize condensation on the products. It is a known fact that any load exposed to 
near-zero temperatures is susceptible to condensation on its surface. Condensation causes irreversible 
damage to sensitive products such as berries. A well contained working area can prevent condensation. 
Short exposure to low temperatures does not affect products such as tropical fruits. 
There is increasing concern about ethylene contamination on products. New technologies, such as the 
use of potassium permanganate or ozone in the ventilation system to help prevent ethylene, are being 
evaluated for commercial application. 
(b) Seafood and Fish Working Areas 
A suitable working area for seafood and fish should have high humidity (near 100%), but a very low 
temperature (near 0°C). This type of controlled environment ensures no dehydration of the product and 
keeps pathogen growth as low as possible. Repackaging and re-icing should be handled in separate 
working areas to ensure sanitary control. In some cases, using ozone in the ventilation system may be 
considered to remove bad odors. 
(c) Meat Working Areas 
Meat must be handled in accordance with the health regulations of the countries of origin and destination. 
There are also other requirements that are more stringent than those for general perishable products. It is 
strongly recommended that the national health authority and the local government be consulted prior to 
the planning of a perishable center, especially its meat working areas. 
3.5.18.2.3 Loading Areas and Trucks 
Most perishable products are transported from the shipper's premises to the perishable center at the airport 
(or from the airport to the consignee's premises) in refrigerated trucks. These trucks are equipped with 
refrigeration systems that are designed to maintain certain temperatures within the cargo compartment. In 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 929 

===PAGE 949===
an 
RZ 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
most cases, however, these mobile systems are not capable of cooling (i.e., lowering the temperature of) the 
product inside. If the temperature of the perishable loading and unloading area, as well as the working area, is 
set to align with the product, condensation will not occur and the quality of the product will be maintained. 
Curtains should be used between the loading area and the working area in order to prevent drafts. Excessive 
air movement can be caused by imperfect interface between the truck and the loading dock. 
3.5.18.2.4 Transit Areas for ULDs 
Prolonged exposure to sun, wind, rain, snow or extreme temperatures are known factors that cause damage 
and loss to perishable shipments. The key to a successful perishable center depends on its temperature￾controlled storage/holding capacity for palletized and containerized perishable loads. When the transit area for 
ULDs is not fully temperature controlled, it should provide the load with adequate protection from extreme 
weather conditions. Well-packed loads are unlikely to deteriorate rapidly when they are kept in a temperature￾controlled environment. The critical path is between the transit area and the aircraft, where exposure to all 
kinds of weather conditions can expedite the deterioration of the product. 
3.5.18.2.5 Inspection and Customs Areas 
Inspection by local authorities is a routine part of the process for all perishable shipments. Ideally, specific 
inspection teams and facilities should be assigned to inspect specific commodities. The inspection of fruits, 
vegetables and flowers should take place in a dedicated area isolated from seafood, fish and meat. An 
inspector working in one specific area should not be allowed to enter another specific area without going 
through a thorough sanitary treatment. 
3.5.18.3 Other Features of Perishable Cargo Facilities 
3.5.18.3.1 Cold Rooms 
(a) Fruit and Vegetable Cold Rooms 
Two different kinds of cold rooms for fruits and vegetables should be used in a perishable center: one at 
Q- to 2°C and the other at 12 to 15°C, with humidity in both near saturation. These temperatures will meet 
930 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 950===
aie 
Se IATA Pull Cargo Terminal 
the requirements of all kinds of fruits and vegetables. The control of ethylene levels using prescribed 
technologies will further reduce the rate of deterioration of the products. 
(b) Flower Cold Rooms 
Flowers should be stored at low temperature (near 0°C), and high humidity (near 100%). As well, control 
of ethylene levels is essential. However, in the case of tropical flowers, the room temperature should be 
maintained at around 15°C. 
(c) Seafood, Fish and Meat Cold Rooms 
Generally, the cold room temperature for these commodities should be set at 0°C. If they are frozen, deep 
freeze coolers designed to maintain a temperature of at least -18°C are required. 
3.5.18.3.2 Pre-Coolers 
Maintaining the appropriate temperature for fresh fruits, vegetables and flowers can be difficult during 
transportation, primarily because they produce their own heat. Even with appropriate packaging and handling, 
these products can raise their own temperatures significantly. Since higher temperatures can shorten the shelf 
life of these products, it is imperative to cool down the products immediately upon arrival at the perishable 
center. 
(a) Fruit and Vegetable Pre-Coolers 
Many facilities use vacuum pre-coolers to cool products. The technique is to drop the atmospheric 
pressure until the water inside the product starts to boil at near-zero temperatures.: This technique is only 
suitable for products with large surface areas and small volumes such as lettuce. The disadvantage of this 
technique is too much water being evaporated from the product while it is cooled. For a long journey and 
exposure to various weather conditions, further loss of water from the product can significantly reduce its 
marketability. A method broadly used by growers is to shower the product prior to vacuum cooling. But 
this technique can hardly be applied within a perishable center. 
Another technique that has been commonly used is forced air cooling. This technique employs a forced 
air system to send cool air through the boxes. This technique is affordable and works for any kind of fruit 
or vegetable. 
(b) Flower Pre-Coolers 
The technique used to cool flowers is similar to the forced air cooling method. Vacuum cooling should 
never be used for flowers because it decreases their shelf life significantly. 
3.5.18.3.3 Treatment Rooms 
Different kinds of treatments should be available at the perishable center as a service to customers: 
(a) Quarantine Treatment Rooms 
Some countries require that imported products be quarantined prior to distribution. Two common 
quarantine treatments are fumigation and the use of high temperatures. Both forms of quarantine should 
be performed in a closed, ventilated room to avoid possible contamination of the rest of the building. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 931 

===PAGE 951===
=, de [i IATA aul Airport Development Reference Manual 
(b) Ripening Treatment Rooms 
Many products such as tomatoes, bananas and tropical fruits are shipped green and need to be exposed 
to ethylene in order to start the ripening process. This ripening treatment can be performed in a forced air 
pre-cooling room with injection of ethylene and an increase of temperature. Any leak of ethylene must be 
controlled in order to avoid contaminating the facility. 
3.5.18.3.4 Repackaging Rooms 
When perishable loads are delivered to the airport, some customers may need a service to remove or 
repackage damaged packages prior to departure. Modern perishable facilities should be capable of providing 
such services. 
(a) 
(o 
(c 
3.5. 
Fruit and Vegetable Repackaging Rooms 
Poor packaging often results in the loss of a certain percentage of the entire shipment. Repackaging the 
damaged packages will unavoidably reduce the content or weight of the shipment, but will certainly help 
reduce further loss and contamination of the remaining stock. This service should be performed in a 
special sanitary room. 
Flower Repackaging Rooms 
Flowers can benefit from repackaging, however in most cases, flowers must be packed in a specific way 
by trained and highly qualified personnel only. 
Seafood and Fish Repackaging Rooms 
Repackaging marine products usually requires re-icing and the application of strict processing standards. 
Re-icing a fish that has undergone extreme temperatures may be in breach of food safety laws in some 
countries. Therefore, only highly trained personnel should be allowed to perform this service, in a special 
sanitary room. 
18.3.5 Quality Control 
Quality control helps to determine what kind of treatment (i.e., re-icing, pre-cooling or fumigation) is necessary 
for tl he load. It provides advisory service to customers for maintaining consistent standards. Quality control 
sometimes includes monitoring the temperature of loads and the environments of the various facilities inside 
the perishable center. 
3.5. 18.3.6 Tracking Systems 
A reliable tracking system is an essential service to customers. It enables customers to obtain real-time 
information about their shipments. Customs can also access the data to perform advance clearance of 
shipments. Typical tracking systems use barcode technology and many are now accessible through the 
Internet.

3.5.18.3.7 Distribution Services 
Many customers demand this type of service. It allows the customer to assign the entire transaction to the 
perishable center, which includes collection of a shipment, transportation, and delivery to its final destination. 
In essence, the perishable center provides total logistics that includes both ground handling and storage.

3.5.19 Mail Facilities 
3.5.19.1 Introduction 
Airmail is a valuable goods flow, requiring fast airport processing and air transportation with last-minute close￾out times for acceptance. Depending on the agreement with the postal authority, it can have very high priority 
for loading. Routings are decided bilaterally with postal authorities in a tender process based on the first 
scheduled airline to destination, Payments to the airlines are based on the documents proving carriage over 
particular route segments. Such documents are essential for billing the mail departments concerned. 
Airports processing mail shall require a secure means to accept mail into the airport, allocate the mail to the 
correct aircraft (flight/country sortation), and in some instances, screen the mail and then dispatch it to the 
aircraft. Where screening of selected mail for explosives or toxic substances is required by the country or 
province/state in question, this should be conducted in facilities designed, fitted-out and operated by the 
national mail processing organization (e.g., Royal Mail (U.K.), United States Postal Service, etc.) or a licensed 
and authorized agent. 
3.5.19.2 Pre-Design Considerations 
The following criteria will decide the need for an airport airmail facility: 
¢ Volume of airmail (import/export/transfer) 
e Safety, speed and service requirements for airmail categories 
e Airmail distribution function for several national mail centers 
e Efficiency requirements 
Siting of the mail facility is optimized by providing: 
e Fast airside connection for mail with scheduled (mostly passenger) flights on the apron 
* Good landside access and docking facilities for mail trucks 
e Positioning on the customs boundary between airside and landside with minimum customs control 
e Flexibility for future expansion and additional services

===PAGE 954===

IATA Cargo Terminal 
3.5.19.3 Mail Processing Facility Objectives 
The main objectives of an airmail facility are: 
Fast and accurate processing of mail and documents at the airport 
0 First-class mail within two to three hours after delivery 
o Second-class mail within 24 hours after delivery 
Minimal duplication of sorting/manifesting at the airport by using segregated mail delivery and 
documentation between postal centers, where possible 
Efficient sorting by destination, flight and category, with bypasses for special and pre-sorted mail 
Checking and recording of outgoing mail weight for aircraft safety and billing 
Optimal use of pre-information regarding shipments between airports, and with related community mail 
centers 
Implementation of automation involving national postal communication and documentation to improve 
handling speed 
Maximum security in view of the valuable nature of most airmail. Vaults should be provided for high-risk 
mail (i.e., gold bullion, precious stones, etc.) 
Facilities must be provided for the screening of items for explosives and toxic materials to aid security. Also, 
all facilities will take into consideration the protection of the mail from prevailing weather conditions. 
3.5.19.4 Mail Processing Requirements 
The main functions to be performed in the mail facility are: 
Landside acceptance and delivery of mail from trucks, in units or in bulk 
Airside acceptance and delivery of mail in airline carts or in ULDs on dollies. Checking, sorting, weighing 
and distribution, per flight or truck, of the various categories of mail 
Temporary storage of mail prior to dispatch, preferably in airline or postal transport units 
Documentation and communication of shipment data, re-routing, and tracing of mail 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 935 

===PAGE 955===
ie Se 
IATA - Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.5.19.5 Mail Handling Systems 
Depending on the volume of mail, availability of labor, and the transport equipment used by postal authorities 
as well as airlines, processing varies from manual handling to mechanized handling. However, fast handling 
remains the major objective. 
Where unitized delivery from mail centers exists, special unloading provisions are required on the landside. 
Mechanized equipment to unload transport units onto a sorting system will speed up sorting. Adequate space 
around the sortation devices is required for ramp carts and dollies to fill the units for departing flights. 
Adjacent space is required to store lower-priority mail leaving later. Incoming mail is normally received after 
the outgoing mail has been processed, and can therefore be sorted on the same sorter. Large volumes 
require more complex sorting systems. 
Outgoing mail on carts should be weighed to verify the total weight, by mail category, leaving per flight. 
Where it is necessary to automate the processing of mail handling within the confines of the airport perimeter, 
the designer should work closely with the mail processing companies to ensure that system demand profiles 
are fully understood and that adequate flight carrier sortation facilities are provided. Organizations that should 
be consulted include airlines and customs authorities, as well as traditional mail processing organizations. 
3.5.19.6 Locating the Mail Facility 
After completing the study of the proposed physical handling, flows and volumes of mail, as well as the 
required space for communications facilities and documentation, a decision can be made as to site and size 
of the mail facility. It is important to always have regard to future expansion. The location and design of the 
facility must ensure that no unauthorized persons have access to the mail. 
936 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 956===
ay 
Se 1 IATA a Airport Support Elements 
The mail facility can be situated in one of three locations: 
1. Next to the baggage handling area, with mail truck access to the airside for delivery and acceptance. 
Since most priority mail is transported on passenger aircraft, integration with fast, last-minute baggage 
transport will contribute to efficient mail transportation on the apron. 
2. In the cargo complex, adjacent to a cargo terminal which normally provides adequate space for 
processing inside and around the facility. In this solution, special airside transportation of mail to the 
passenger apron is required in view of the last-minute delivery requirement. If a large volume of transfer 
mail is to be handled in a short time period, a secondary mail section in the passenger area may be 
required. 
3. A-separate mail facility with its own infrastructure situated between the passenger and cargo areas, with 
optimum distances to both. This will mainly apply to the handling of large volumes of airmail. However, 
integration with other surface mail handling should be discouraged in view of extra landside traffic not 
related to the airport. With a separate location, special airside transportation is required between the 
aircraft and the mail terminal. 
3.6 Airport Support Elements 
3.6.1 Aircraft Maintenance 
3.6.1.1 Introduction 
Aircraft maintenance capabilities are required at most airports, using various degrees of sophistication, to 
support aircraft flying safely in accordance with appropriate maintenance service standards. Maintenance is 
comprised of general routine servicing and major overhaul servicing activities. 
Virtually all airports are required to permit routine maintenance activities. Routine (“A” Check and “B” Check) 
maintenance can be completed on an aircraft stand, at other apron areas or within dedicated aircraft hangars. 
Major servicing of aircraft is usually carried out at major airports, often where airlines are based, and it is 
common for multiple alliance partner airlines to share maintenance facilities. Hangars are generally used to 
accommodate major maintenance activities of aircraft, which can include, but are not limited to, activities such 
as: 
e Wiring investigations and modifications 
* Software checks and upgrades to aircraft control systems 
e Main thrust and APU engine replacements 
e — Interior refit 
e Control surfaces servicing 
e Aircraft surfaces (i.e., impact damage) servicing 
e Hydraulic systems servicing 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 937 

===PAGE 957===
she S— i |) Tara al Airport Development Reference Manual 
e Lubricant replacement 
e Landing gear tire and brake replacements 
e Aircraft utility systems 
Routine servicing activities can include, but are not limited to: 
e Lubricant topping up 
e Hydraulic fluid topping up 
e Fuel line checks 
¢ Control surfaces operational checks 
e Turbine starter unit replacement and checks 
Hangars provide protection from the elements under carefully controlled conditions and house specialized 
maintenance equipment and tooling. Dust filtration ventilation systems are commonly provided and are 
particularly useful when the local environment presents servicing problems. 
3.6.1.2 Functional Requirements of Maintenance Hangars 
The space contained within maintenance hangars is used to accommodate certain functional requirements 
needed to maintain single aircraft or multiple aircraft. The overall size of the maintenance facility will depend 
on the fleet mix to be serviced and the depth and frequency of servicing to be done on site. 
The aircraft bays need to accommodate the aircraft in the fleet with adequate clearance for staging and traffic 
around the perimeter. Consideration should be given to the routing of tugs and other maintenance equipment 
after positioning the aircraft in a bay. 
The internal clearance and overall height of the hangar should consider the following: 
© Tail height of the design aircraft 
° Clearance to allow the overhead crane to pass over the top of the aircraft tail 
e The need for the aircraft to be jacked for undercarriage removal 
e Ensure that any deflection resulting from the use of long spans in the structure do not infringe on the 
overall functional internal height of the necessary clearances (aircraft tail, overhead crane) 
e Clearance for hangar services (e.g., HVAC, exhaust, lighting) 
The hangar doors need to be appropriately sized for the largest aircraft in the fleet to be maneuvered simply 
and safely into the bay. 
In addition to the aircraft bays, major maintenance facilities usually include the following functional areas: 
e Landside to airside security facility to process staff accessing the hangar 
e Fixed or demountable staging for access to the aircraft frame, doors and engines

3.6.1.3 Aircraft Maintenance Aprons 
Aircraft maintenance aprons are sized to accommodate peak overnight aircraft parking stand demand for 
aircraft requiring maintenance, excluding those aircraft receiving minor maintenance on terminal stands. In 
addition, maintenance aprons may need to be used as remote aircraft stands to supplement terminal apron 
capacity. Engine run-up pens are typically provided and blast fences may be required in some areas to 
protect adjacent facilities and operations. Adequate space should be provided for the maneuvering of aircraft 
into and out of the hangar(s). 
3.6.1.4 Location of Maintenance Hangars and Aprons 
Maintenance hangars and aprons should be included as a key element of airport master plan layouts. The 
overall height required for the facility in relation to obstacle limitation surfaces and radar clearances needs to 
be investigated. Access for delivery of large aircraft components and spares should also be addressed. 
Airlines will typically request locations that are close to terminal aprons in order to reduce aircraft travel times 
and distances. Due to the fact that aircraft need to be serviced and maintained as quickly as possible, it is 
common for hangars to be used 24 hours a day, which can present noise problems for airport neighbors. 
Appropriate care and attention should be taken to ensure that locations are correctly selected and planned to 
avoid or minimize such issues. 
It is important that these stands are not included in the overall terminal stand provision count. The 
maintenance apron aircraft stands have a significantly different function than the terminal aircraft stands. 
3.6.2 Airline Administration Buildings 
Airlines require operation and administration offices within the passenger terminal building to efficiently 
manage day-to-day operations at the airport. See 3.3.5.2.1 General Considerations for guidance. 
In addition to space provided within the passenger terminal building, base carriers may also have 
supplemental needs related to their broader network operations, including: 
940 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 960===

Se 
IATA Airport Support Elements 
© Corporate headquarters 
e¢ Operations Control Center (OCC) 
e Flight crew, cabin crew and customer service training 
e Ancillary facilities (i.e., conference centers, record/data centers, museums) 
A separate building on the airport can provide a corporate presence for a major airline, allowing it to 
accommodate a wide range of administrative and support facilities in addition to those required to support 
essential services in the passenger terminal. Airline administration facilities can range from a single office 
building to larger campus developments. 
While it is not necessary to locate these facilities at the airport-there are some notable examples of airline 
offices located in downtown areas (e.g., the former landmark Pan Am building in mid-town Manhattan)-tt is 
generally considered preferable to consolidate facilities in the immediate area of an airline's principal hub 
airport to take advantage of the proximity to other airline facilities. 
The development of airline administration facilities on airport property is dependent on the availability of real 
estate for development. Nearby “Airport City’ developments may provide a convenient location for airline 
administration facilities. 
The development of new airline administration facilities is typically driven by the replacement of aging 
infrastructure, new airline entrants, airline mergers, and the development of new greenfield airports. 
3.6.3 Airport Authority Administration 
Airport authority administration includes a wide spectrum of personnel, including the executive management 
team and their administrative staff as well as departments for legal, finance, planning, operations and other 
disciplines. 
Airport authority administration can be accommodated in a variety of ways depending on the size and layout 
of the airport and the organizational structure of the airport authority. 
At smaller airports, it is common for all airport authority administration staff to be accommodated within the 
passenger terminal building. At larger airports, the authority may elect to build a separate building to 
accommodate the majority of their staff, and to locate only operations staff in the terminal. The authority may 
also provide staff canteens, restaurants, training facilities, recreation and other staff welfare facilities in 
conjunction with their offices. 
Facility sizing for planning purposes is typically based on benchmarking against comparable airports and 
establishing representative sizing ratios (e.g., square meters per million annual passengers). Detailed design 
requirements should be determined through comprehensive discussions with the appropriate airport 
authority/organization. 
Where separate airport authority administration buildings are developed, employee access, which includes 
proximity to public transportation and travel between the administration building and passenger terminal,

should be considered in site selection. Airport authority administration buildings should not be located in an 
area that will limit expansion of terminal, apron, airfield and other critical airport functions. 
3.6.4 Airport Maintenance and Logistics 
3.6.4.1 Introduction 
Airport maintenance and logistics are the responsibility of the airport authority/operator. Facility requirements 
will depend on the size and location of the airport and its operational framework. Facilities typically include: 
e Airfield maintenance 
e Building maintenance 
e Vehicle maintenance 
° Central stores 
e Waste collection 
¢ Consolidation/logistics center 
e Garden/landscaping center 
e Wildlife management facilities 
e Snow and ice control 
e Airport staff access 
e Locker rooms 
3.6.4.2 Airfield Maintenance 
Airfield maintenance buildings are typically equipped with drive-through bays for equipment storage and 
heavy equipment repair, vehicle repair, and equipment/vehicle washing. The building should include 
workshops for welding and painting, and administrative, storage and staff facilities. Separate storage will also 
be required for materials for seasonal maintenance (i.e., runway sand and dry chemicals), depending on the 
location of the airport. 
These buildings have accommodation for administration personnel, but will be primarily industrial in nature, 
comprised mainly of workshops and maintenance bays. These bays are provided to accommodate the 
storage and maintenance of airfield signage, navigational aids, lighting systems and lightweight airport GSE, 
and will be fitted with hydraulic lifts, access pits and over-head cranes. 
Sand blasting rooms capable of removing material from small items such as airfield signage as well as paint 
shops for painting such items should be provided. Additional secure storage for equipment, hazardous 
material and flammable liquids should be provided. 
942 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 962===

IATA Airport Support Elements 
3.6.4.3 Building Maintenance 
Building maintenance facilities (workshops) can be centralized in terminal buildings to respond to demand and 
preventative maintenance requirements. Centralized workshops should accommodate all facilities 
maintenance activities (i.e., mechanical, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, painting, carpentry, and welding). 
3.6.4.4 Airport Vehicle Maintenance Building 
A building for the maintenance of vehicles is required to accommodate servicing of a wide variety of airport 
maintenance vehicles and equipment, including staff shuttles and transport buses. The facility should provide 
sheltered service bays along with supporting infrastructure (i.e., triturator, wash rack, body shop, paint booths 
and sand blasting rooms). 
3.6.4.5 Central Stores 
The central stores shall function as the airport operating company's central storage and warehouse facility for 
all airport-related supplies, including: 
e Electrical, mechanical and plumbing supplies, hardware and replacement parts 
e Cleaning supplies 
e Office furniture/supplies (i.e., desks, computers) 
Special facilities, in compliance with local regulations, should be provided for the handling and storage of 
hazardous materials, which can include paints, cleaners, lubricants and gases. 
Central stores are typically comprised of high and low bay warehouse areas, vehicle loading docks and 
administrative areas. In addition, outdoor storage areas (covered or uncovered) may be required to 
accommodate the handover of construction materials and bulk materials. 
To minimize the number of controlled airside access points, the central stores may also serve as, or be 
collocated with, a central receiving facility to provide screening of landside deliveries. 
3.6.4.6 Waste Collection Facility 
Airport waste management plans will vary based on the size and complexity of the airport operation and the 
availability of regional facilities for recycling and composting. 
Waste will need to be collected (in varying amounts) from all airport facilities, including tenant facilities. Larger 
airports may have dedicated waste collection facilities which function as a central collection point for all 
domestic and international waste streams generated by the airport. These facilities shall be equipped with 
loading docks along the building's periphery and equipped with: 
e Collection bins and containers 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 943 

===PAGE 963===
ae IATA iw Airport Development Reference Manual 
e Paper, cardboard and plastic presses 
e Wood compactors 
Special provisions for the storage and handling of hazardous materials and specific protocols for the disposal 
of international waste need to be provided for in the waste management plan and associated facilities. Airport 
waste control facilities should be designed to support and located to aid airline users meet their sustainability 
strategies which include minimizing waste and its environmental impact. 
3.6.4.7 Consolidation/Logistics Center 
Retail concessions and terminal supplies generate a significant amount of goods movement at an airport, with 
a large proportion of those goods destined for airside facilities. Regulations regarding the screening of airport 
supplies entering secure areas vary by country and can include random inspections, known supplier programs 
and pallet/vehicle screening. With many countries adopting 100% goods screening policies for all airport 
supplies, the logistics of providing screening in an efficient way is an important consideration in the planning 
and design of facilities. 
The objective of a Consolidation/Logistics Center is to promote security, improve operational efficiency and 
reduce the total volume of traffic and storage areas required in the passenger terminal. A 
Consolidation/Logistics Center requires landside access for goods deliveries, screening facilities, as well as a 
storage and staging area. Following security screening, inbound goods are loaded onto a dedicated internal 
fleet of delivery vehicles and delivered to the passenger terminal or other airside facilities served by the 
Consolidation/Logistics Center. This type of operation allows greater flexibility in the management and 
scheduling of goods deliveries. 
Consolidation/Logistics Centers should be located outside of the space safeguarded for future terminal and 
apron expansion. The airside road network and facility siting should provide for the efficient movement of 
goods between the Consolidation/Logistics Center and the passenger terminal. 
3.6.4.8 Garden/Landscape Maintenance Center 
This facility shall function as a nursery for all flora associated with the passenger terminal and other airport 
buildings, along with the overall airport landscaping. The scope and scale of the landscape center vary based 
on climate and the extent of internal and external plantings. 
3.6.4.9 Wildlife Management 
The goal of a wildlife management plan is to promote aviation safety for passengers and flight crews by 
reducing risk to aircraft and airport operations caused by wildlife activities on the airport. 
Birds, mammals and reptiles can pose safety issues at airports. Wildlife management techniques are diverse, 
ranging from habitat manipulation, use of predators to repel wildlife and lethal control. Facility requirements 
944 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 964===
Be &, IATA ull Airport Support Elements 
vary based on the type of wildlife and specific techniques employed. Infrastructure can include facilities for 
wildlife control officers, patrol vehicles, aviaries and other facilities. 
3.6.4.10 Snow and Ice Control 
Airports in geographical areas that historically have been subject to icing conditions or annual snowfall should 
have snow removal equipment provided on site. A winter snow and ice control plan is critical to maintaining 
operations and limiting service interruptions. The plan should identify critical aircraft movement areas and 
supporting facilities that require priority snow clearance. 
Equipment requirements should be calculated based on an estimated snow depth, the area of pavement to be 
cleared in the priority area and target clearance time. The FAA recommends a target of 30 minutes to clear 
the Priority 1 area and provides guidance (see below) on calculating snow clearance vehicle fleet and 
associated facilities requirements. 
Snow and ice control equipment can include: 
¢ Displacement plows and scrapers 
e Rotary plows or snow blowers/throwers 
¢ Snow swath sweepers/brooms 
¢ Gritting and deicing fluid vehicles 
These vehicles are very large compared to common airside vehicles, and direct access to taxiways and 
runways should be provided. Facilities for the storage of snow and ice contro! equipment include: 
e Vehicle parking bays 
° Vehicle washing bays 
e Vehicle maintenance workshops 
«Materials storage (e.g., heated sand, liquid deicer, dry deicer and urea) 
© — Staff accommodation and administration 
It is very important that the airport designates areas for contaminated snow storage to reduce environmental 
impacts from snow melt. Where space is constrained, mobile or fixed snow melting units may be used to 
manage the buildup of snow. Wastewater generated by snow melting should be controlled. 
Recommended reference manuals: 
Reference should be made to the following documents when assessing the planning requirements for snow 
and ice control facilities: 
e FAA Advisory Circular AC 150/5220-18A “Buildings for Storage and Maintenance of Airport Snow and Ice 
Control Equipment and Materials” September 2007 
e FAA Advisory Circular AC 150/5220-20A, “Airport Snow and Ice Control Equipment” September 2014

3.6.4.11 Airside Gates (Control Posts) 
Controlled access to the airside is required for staff, goods and vehicles. The number of access points should 
be minimized to the extent that is practical. Airside gates should provide areas and facilities for screening and 
inspection. The demand and processing capacity at each location should be considered in the planning and 
design of access gates (control posts). Control post processing capacity can impact the overall effective and 
efficient operation of the airport, particularly where crew access via control posts is an integral part of the 
airline operational strategy. 
While minimizing the number of access points is important, the need for timely movement of vehicles and staff 
from landside to airside is vital to the efficient operation of the airport. Introducing a Level of Service (LoS) 
metric to identify and monitor acceptable queuing standards and continue to inform capacity and demand 
planning is recommended. Sufficient control post facilities need to be provided to eliminate any potential 
operational bottlenecks. In particular, peak vehicle and staff flow periods (e.g., shift changes) need to be 
considered as part of the requirement analysis. 
In some locations, a single consolidated access gate is employed, which provides access for all airside staff, 
goods and vehicles. Landside parking and access to an airside shuttle bus network are required. The overall 
peak flow requirements need to be taken into consideration as an important part of the overall analysis when 
establishing the appropriate number of access points. 
Terminal employees are typically screened in dedicated facilities located in the passenger terminal building. 
However, depending on the overall airport layout, airport employees working on the airside, including air traffic 
controllers and airfield maintenance staff, may also be screened at airside gates (control posts) where 
alternate transport methods (e.g., employee busses) are in use. 
3.6.4.12 Location Considerations 
Airport maintenance facilities are generally located in areas designated for support facility development in the 
airport land use plan. They require convenient landside access for the delivery of parts and supplies, waste 
temoval and staff access. Direct access to the airside service road network is required for maintenance 
vehicles and large equipment including snowplows and grass cutters. 
The various airport maintenance facilities noted above may be consolidated where there is an opportunity to 
achieve facility or operational efficiencies. At smaller airports, maintenance facilities are sometimes included 
in a “combined services building”, which typically includes a fire station as well as vehicle maintenance 
facilities, equipment storage, workshops, and materials storage. 
For planning purposes, preliminary facility sizing is typically based on representative sizing ratios established 
on the basis of existing operations and comparable airport benchmarks. Detailed design requirements should 
be developed based on the Airport Operations Plan and through comprehensive discussions with 
stakeholders. Where feasible, space should be reserved for future expansion, in line with traffic growth 
forecasts in the airport master plan.
