3.6.5 Aircraft Deicing/Anti-Icing Facilities 
3.6.5.1 Introduction 
Safe and efficient aircraft operations are of primary importance in the development of any aircraft de/anti-icing 
facility. The requirements for a deicing operation may differ greatly for each airport. While remote primary 
deicing may be desirable at one airport, gate deicing (with or without remote secondary facilities) may be 
appropriate at others. Operational and ATC matters may be paramount at one airport, while environmental 
concerns may predominate at another. These are just some of the many options to be considered where 
deicing operations are concerned. It is important to keep in mind that each airport will have varying priorities, 
and that many factors will need to be weighed before responsible, safe and efficient deicing operations can be 
arrived at. 
The manner in which the ATC system operates during icing conditions is critical. If the ATC system imposes 
significant delays before takeoff, the deicing problem is increased, not only because of the need to deice 
again, but also because of the extra taxiing required. Keeping safety concerns in the forefront, airlines and 
airport authorities must work with ATC to minimize delays. 
It is important to recognize that the requirements for, and economics of, recycling and reuse vary widely. The 
environmental circumstances, ranging from the proximity of the airport to rivers and water sources, the runoff 
patterns to be expected, the types of receiving water, and the movement rates of water bodies, all impact the 
problem. Another variable is the type of soil and the potential for soil contamination. 
The first and most important task for designers contemplating the development of deicing facilities is to 
evaluate the type of facility best suited to the airport needs. This evaluation will entail an assessment of the 
actual physical layout, the operational requirements and the environmental sensitivity of the airport. 
Considerations include: 
e Aircraft movement flows 
e Frequency and severity of icing events 
e Realistic capacity requirements in snow/ice conditions 
e Physical space available 
e Length of routes to the departure points 
e Available and potential drainage 
¢ Kinds of fluid in use 
e Fluid collection/retention/recycling options 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 947 

===PAGE 967===
we ff 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
e Local codes and natural resource requirements 
e Recycling and reuse 
3.6.5.2 Types of Deicing Operations 
In general, there are four types of deicing operation options: 
1. At passenger terminal gates, where aircraft are deiced just before departure after passengers and 
baggage/cargo are loaded 
2. At designated deicing areas at or near the passenger terminal ramp 
3. At designated remote deicing areas en route to the departure runway, or integrated with the runway 
holding area 
4. Ata specially designed centralized deicing center 
Facilities for these operations progress in level of complexity from (1) to (4), although they all must satisfy the 
airport considerations noted above. Because option (1) does not typically entail additional facility 
development, but principally relies on mobile equipment, only options (2) to (4) are discussed below. 
Historically, the principal method of deicing has involved the application of heated freeze depressant fluids. In 
recent years, new thickened fluids have been implemented which offer extended protection times (fluid 
holdover times). Other new developments should be taken into consideration, including the application of 
. infra-red heat. 
3.6.5.2.1_ Designated Deicing Area at or Near the Terminal Ramp 
For some airports, decentralized deicing facilities at or adjacent to terminal ramps can adequately meet the 
demands of the airlines, while still allowing acceptable taxiing time to the departure runways under varying 
weather conditions. Improvements to, or expansion of, the facilities at terminal stands should include apron 
drainage areas that collect glycol runoff for proper disposal or recycling. Alternatively, deicing runoff should be 
collected on the spot by sweeper/vacuum cleaning vehicles. The collected runoff is either stored or directly 
transported to disposal/recycling contractors. 
3.6.5.2.2 Remote Deicing Facilities 
Remote deicing facilities located near departure runway ends or along taxiways are recommended when 
taxiing times from terminals frequently exceed holdover times. Under changing weather conditions they can 
compensate for icing conditions or blowing snow expected to occur along the taxi route taken by the aircraft to 
the departure runway. These facilities can improve flow control by permitting retreatment of aircraft without 
having the aircraft return to a more distant deicing pad. Remote deicing facilities have the following 
components: 
e Aircraft deicing pads for the maneuvering of aircraft and mobile deicing vehicles, or deicing gantries 
948 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 968===
Be 
IATA Airport Support Elements 
e Bypass taxiing capability 
e Environmental runoff mitigation measures 
e Permanent or portable lighting systems 
3.6.5.2.3 Centralized Deicing Facilities 
Centralized deicing facilities located off-terminal are recommended when terminal deicing facilities experience 
excessive gate delays, taxiing times, or suffer from severe weather conditions conducive to aircraft icing 
conditions. Terminals whose deicing gates lack permanent environmental runoff structures are candidates for 
off-terminal deicing facilities, as the construction costs for runoff mitigation is not cost-effective. Centralized 
deicing facilities usually have the following components: 
¢ Aircraft deicing pads for the maneuvering of aircraft and mobile deicing vehicles 
¢ Bypass taxiing capability 
e Environmental runoff mitigation measures 
¢ Permanent or portable night-time lighting system 
e Support facilities that include: 
© Control center 
© Storage tanks and transfer systems for aircraft de/anti-icing fluids 
© Deicing crew shelters 
o Deicing vehicle maintenance facility 
© Deicing vehicle parking 
3.6.5.3 Siting Considerations 
The following is an overview of the planning and design considerations for deicing facility siting locations 
recommended in SAE ARP 4902A. Thoughtful siting of deicing facilities is critical in order to maximize the 
benefits of the de/anti-icing process while minimizing the potential adverse impacts on airfield efficiency, 
safety and operations. Certain considerations in siting deicing operations facilitate compliance with the ‘clean 
aircraft’ concept. Foremost among such considerations is the need to site deicing facilities so that the 
maximum time interval between the start of the last step of the de/anti-icing process, subsequent taxiing, and 
the start of takeoff does not exceed the estimated holdover times of the applied fluids. Other major 
considerations include the need to site deicing facilities so that aircraft, deicing facility structures, and mobile 
deicing vehicles or fixed deicing equipment do not penetrate the object clearing criteria or airway facility 
critical areas. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 949 

===PAGE 969===
See By, IATA eiulf Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.6.5.4 Deicing Facility Design and Construction 
A deicing facility has to be properly planned, designed and constructed to perform as intended. Elements of 
these preparations include such elements as: 
e Facility siting 
e Number and size of deicing pads 
e Pad configuration and layout 
e Visual guidance considerations 
¢ Construction materials 
° Drainage facilities 
e Other related components 
e Access to deicing fluid connections 
Most of the design criteria for these components are addressed in FAA advisory circulars and other accepted 
industry design guidelines and standards. A deicing facility is intended to provide an area for parking of 
aircraft to receive de/anti-icing treatment. To perform this function, the deicing pad requires a pavement 
system that supports the anticipated loads and a positive drainage system to collect runoff containing spent 
deicing fluids. 
3.6.5.5 Environmental Considerations 
Since de/anti-icing fluids are chemical products with environmental consequences, deicing facilities shall have 
runoff mitigating structures. The recommended structures collect and retain runoff for proper disposal or 
recycling. In terms of structural best management practices, this approach to ‘control the source’ offers airport 
managers an effective and economical means to comply with storm water permit requirements. 
3.6.5.6 Operational Considerations 
Operational issues should be addressed prior to the design of the facility to insure that the intended benefits 
will be achieved in an operationally efficient and cost-effective manner. 
Typically, deicing facilities are common use facilities available to any user of the airport, and thus must be 
designed and operated to ensure equal access to the facility by all airport users. A coordinated approach to 
facility operation and use is necessary to ensure that the deicing facility accommodates expected airfield 
capacity during a de/anti-icing event, as well as mitigating ground congestion that may impact aircraft 
operations.

3.6.6 General Aviation 
General aviation (GA) can be defined as all civil aviation operations other than scheduled air services, and 
non-scheduled air transport operations for remuneration or hire (i.e., charter operations). GA flights range 
from gliders and powered parachutes to helicopters and corporate business jets. 
GA facilities at airports typically include a fixed-base operator (FBO), defined as a commercial business 
granted the right by an airport to operate on the airport and provide aeronautical services (i.e., fueling, hangar 
space, aircraft tie-down and parking, aircraft rental, aircraft maintenance, flight instruction). 
Other facilities can include private hangars for large corporate jets with associated apron areas and T-hangars 
for small single-engine fixed wing aircraft. 
The assessment of facility requirements should determine the number, size, location and ownership of GA 
hangars, aprons and tie-down areas. In addition, the number of FBOs and the number/mix of based aircraft 
should be determined. 
The sizing of GA facilities are airport and demand specific. Detailed requirements should be based on 
discussions with potential operators and tenants. 
3.6.6.1 Location Considerations 
GA facilities are typically located away from the passenger terminal and apron areas, and provided with 
independent landside access. Direct airside access to the runway and taxiway system should be provided, 
however, potential conflicts with airline operations should be minimized. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 951 

===PAGE 971===
ue SoS 
IATA +4 Airport Development Reference Manual 
The separation of helicopter and fixed wing GA facilities is recommended to avoid operational conflicts. 
3.6.6.2 Runway Capacity 
Airports with a mix of commercial and GA operations need to consider the impact of GA movements when 
assessing runway capacity. GA operations require greater wake turbulence separations and can have longer 
Tunway occupancy times than commercial aircraft. 
At larger airports, where runway capacity presents a constraint, it may be necessary to restrict or manage GA, during peak periods in particular, in order to minimize impacts on runway capacity and to avoid conflict with 
commercial aviation. Similar considerations are necessary regarding air terminal gate occupancy. Generally, 
air terminal gates and stands are allocated primarily to large commercial aircraft operations. 
3.6.7 Ground Service Equipment Maintenance 
Airport authorities, airlines and ground service providers Operate a wide range of vehicles and ground service 
equipment (GSE). The majority of GSE operates on the airside, servicing passenger and cargo aircraft 
operations. GSE is critical to daily aircraft operations. The Purpose of a GSE maintenance program is to 
Provide safe, serviceable, reliable equipment with minimal downtime. 
Depending on the airport, ground handling services may be provided by a number of different handlers or by 
a single ground handler contracted by the airport. A reasonable level of open access should be provided to 
favour competition at the airport and ideally avoid service provision by only a single handler. Typically, GSE 
maintenance is provided by airlines, ground handlers or independent maintenance companies. 
Maintenance programs and facilities should accommodate scheduled preventative maintenance as well as. 
unscheduled maintenance and repair. The number and size of the maintenance workshops is related to the 
scale of the airport operation, the number of ground handlers and the number of vehicles being maintained at 
any one time. 
Vehicle maintenance should be performed in workshops. Drive-through service bays provide for efficient 
vehicle movements and double-height service space with an overhead gantry crane can assist with vehicle 
servicing. In addition to the main vehicle servicing and repair area, functions may also include ULD repair 
workshops, light vehicle overhaul, paint booths, sand blasting booths, battery charging, stores, as well as 
administration and staff accommodation. Staff facilities can be accommodated on mezzanine levels. Facilities 
should also be provided for vehicle washing, waste collection, and parking or staging for vehicles waiting for 
maintenance. 
3.6.7.1 Location Considerations 
GSE maintenance is generally undertaken in the support facilities area of an airport and in close proximity to the terminal apron area. Airline GSE maintenance can be colocated with an airline's aircraft maintenance 
facilities, for convenience and economy of operations. 
952 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 972===
ae IATA ii Airport Support Elements 
Depending on the airfield size, it may be advantageous to provide a series of smaller GSE maintenance 
facilities around the airfield to reduce the distances and time taken to travel between the apron areas and the 
facilities. 
Facilities should be located on the secured airside to allow efficient circulation between the apron and the 
vehicle maintenance and parking areas. 
3.6.8 Aircraft In-Flight Catering Facilities 
3.6.8.1 Introduction 
Catering facilities provide prepared in-flight food and beverage items for most departing and some transfer 
flights from airports. The size and capability of these catering facilities will be based the requirements of the 
airlines, and on their flight schedules. 
Aircraft catering facilities should be separate from, but located as close as possible to, the terminal building, 
with ready access to both airside and landside zones. It is important that the locations of the catering facilities 
not infringe on areas reserved for future expansion of the terminal and apron areas. It is common for airports 
to have multiple flight catering companies serving different airlines. Flight kitchens can also be located offsite, 
with a smaller logistics facility on airport to facilitate the transfer of meals to flight catering trucks for delivery to 
aircraft. 
3.6.8.2 Design Requirements 
The design requirements for in-flight catering facilities are generated from airline flight schedules. Building 
sizing is based on the peak daily demand for airline meals, taking into account the type of: 
© Aircraft and number of seats 
e Airline (e.g., full service or low cost) 
¢ Flight (e.g., short or long haul) 
Buildings should be designed for incremental expansion, in line with traffic growth forecasts in the airport 
master plan. Initial construction is typically sized for the first five years of operations. 
The typical in-flight aircraft catering facility will, as a minimum, contain the following functional facilities: 
* Vehicle maneuvering space for catering and supply trucks 
¢ Catering vehicle loading and unloading bays 
* Fully equipped industrial quality food and beverage kitchens 
e Food preparation areas 
e Wares and utensils cleaning areas

¢ Refrigerated and freezer storage 
¢ Aircraft galley equipment staging/storage

3.6.9 Airport Security/Controlled Access 
3.6.9.1 General Principles 
ICAO Annex 17 to the Chicago Convention requires each Contracting State to establish a national civil 
aviation security program and to adjust it on the basis of a risk assessment. This, therefore, requires security 
measures implemented by operators that are risk based and compliant with the national civil aviation security 
program. Specific to airport development, ICAO requires that architectural and infrastructure requirements 
necessary for the optimum implementation of civil aviation security measures be integrated into the design 
and construction of new facilities, as well as into any alterations to existing facilities at airports. 
To provide for efficient and effective security outcomes in all new or redeveloped airport infrastructure, a local 
risk assessment should be conducted and used to inform the design of security measures and other 
infrastructure in the event that the latter introduces or alters the security risks at the airport. The risk 
assessment should be conducted according to the national risk context and threat level, taking into account 
local or regional environments. 
When conducting a risk assessment for the purpose of informing design, consideration should be given to 
potential changes in the risk context, including existing vulnerabilities and changes to the threat level or risk 
acceptance/appetite expected in the years to come. This risk assessment should identify how operations and 
infrastructure need to perform in these circumstances, in turn influencing the design (i.e., the steps that may 
become necessary to upgrade buildings/facilities and their operation to meet an increased threat). A simple 
example is the design of surface transport should the drop-off and pick-up points at a terminal be closed. 
When undertaken early in the design process, this risk-based approach provides a number of advantages, 
including: 
e The ability to design out some risk (through reduction of vulnerabilities) 
e Avoiding conflicts between security and other design disciplines 
e Avoiding expensive retrofits 
¢ Allowing for expenditures commensurate to risk 
¢ Providing architects and designers with the opportunity to identify innovative approaches 
Allowing for more options to achieve the desired security and design outcomes 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 955 

===PAGE 975===
oz il ye 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
Moreover, a risk-based approach will address the risks and vulnerabilities that are unique to an airport, which 
may not be addressed through a purely compliance-based design. This latter benefit is becoming increasingly 
relevant as appropriate authorities move to outcome-focused regimes and less prescriptive requirements are 
available to designers. 
In addition to the local risk assessment, consideration should be given to design guidance or requirements 
established by the appropriate authority and any legislative requirements. 
In establishing any security design criteria based on a risk assessment and national compliance requirements, 
it is essential that the security requirements focus on vulnerabilities, risks and economically viability. The 
security requirements must allow for an appropriate balance between the needs of aviation security, safety, 
operations and facilitation. The criteria should also include Provisions to ensure that the airport design 
facilitates the implementation of contingency measures. 
3.6.9.1.1 | Planning and Design 
Effective airport security planning should be risk-based and an extension of nationally conceived and adopted 
aviation security criteria. Once the criteria are established, it is essential that they be made available to 
planners and designers. They also need access to specific risk information to be able to integrate solutions 
that address the identified security risks, including future contingency requirements, into the structural and 
operational parameters guiding the development of an airport's passenger systems and other infrastructure. 
For example, structural security considerations should be informed by the area pressure created bya 
potential explosive device or the identification of protective materials to prevent firearm damage. 
While outcomes of the local security risk assessment and national compliance requirements will be the final 
determinants of the local design, the following are guiding principles for planning, design and enhancement of 
an airport's security: 
* Preventing the introduction of weapons, explosives or dangerous devices by any means into the airport or 
aircraft by: 
o Deterrence 
° Detection 
© Ensuring the segregation of passengers who have been screened from those who have not 
° Controlling access to and movement within the airside and security restricted areas. 
© Ensuring the security of channels by which Passengers, baggage, personnel, vehicles, cargo and 
other goods are screened 
* Facilitating implementation of the airport emergency plan during an act of unlawful interference (i-e., bomb 
alert) 
* Minimizing the effect of an explosive or incendiary device on persons or facilities by incorporating design 
features to limit casualties and damage 
956 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 976===
Tata x 4 iil Airport Support Elements 
e Providing for the protection and escape of persons in the event of a marauding armed assault (e.g., active 
shooters) 
3.6.9.2 Site Evaluation and Layout of Facilities 
When designing or redesigning airport facilities, there are many factors that could influence site evaluation 
and the layout of facilities. When designing or redesigning airport facilities, the security considerations and 
implications should take into account the: 
¢ Airport location 
e Size and topography of the airport site 
¢ Location of adjacent transport and support facilities 
Layout and relative location of vulnerable points 
¢ National, regional and local risk contexts 
Role of the airport in terms of airline operations (i.e., point-to-point or transfer hub) 
3.6.9.2.1 Landside Development 
In deciding the layout of the terminal building landside area, special security consideration should be given to 
the following: 
e Road layout 
e Access control posts 
e Vehicle parking 
¢ Landscaping and boundaries 
° Terminal forecourts and egress pathways 
e Lighting and signage 
e Emergency services access 
¢ Local risk context

3.6.9.2.2 Airside Development 
Airside development should provide for the following security measures: 
e Airport perimeter and security restricted areas 
¢ Perimeter roadways and other access roads for patrol purposes 
* Security and apron lighting 
* Perimeter and security restricted area vehicle and pedestrian access points, including automatic access 
control systems 
¢ Isolated aircraft parking positions for searching aircraft subject to a specific threat or an act of unlawful 
seizure 
* Blast containment area for suspect explosive devices 
¢ Cargo security, including access to security facilities for transfer cargo and secure cargo storage 
¢ Facilities for the kenneling and training of explosive detecting dogs 
¢ Airside and Landside boundaries in tenant facilities 
* Relative location of vulnerable points 
e Emergency Services access 
¢ Emergency Operations Center location 
* Hostile vehicle mitigation measures 
If the installation of an automatic access control system is envisaged at a later stage of airport development, 
provision should be made at the earliest stages of runway and taxiway construction for an automatic access 
control system power supply and data transmission trenches/conduits. Similar provisions for the future 
installation of intrusion detection systems, electronic alarms, and video/data transmission networks should 
also be made in terminal buildings and at vulnerable point locations. 
3.6.9.3 Perimeter Security 
In deciding what form of perimeter or restricted area security is required, many factors need to be taken into 
account. First and foremost, the local risk assessment and compliance requirements along with topography of the site, the life expectancy of any materials used and access control requirements. It is important to note that the physical components of perimeter security (e.g., fences, perimeter intruder detection systems, CCTV) 
should not be viewed in isolation, but rather as an integrated whole. For example, the impact on resources for the surveillance of CCTV rooms and intervention teams. 
The following perimeter detection technologies might be considered and their merits evaluated as a minimum: 
° Radar-based systems 
¢ Infra-red systems 
* Microwave systems

===PAGE 978===
i IATA Hi ! Airport Support Elements 
e° Thermal imaging systems 
e CCTV systems 
e Taut wire detection systems 
The following fence types should be considered: 
e = Chain link 
e Welded mesh 
e Vertical pressed or rolled steel (painted or galvanized) 
Where airport perimeters are close to public walkways, roads or rivers, the perimeter should be under 
surveillance either by patrol or by automated detection systems. Signs should be placed at intervals to clearly 
advise the public that perimeters are under surveillance. Signs should be visible from any point along the 
length of perimeter. Airport perimeters should be complete and provide consistent security protection 
throughout the whole perimeter. This might require different standards depending on vulnerable points and 
topography. Areas within the terminal complex that border vulnerable areas (i.e., vehicle and staff gate posts) 
should be monitored, with data recorded 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. 
The local risk assessment will identify those operations/locations that require additional surveillance, which 
may include: 
e Airside/landside gate post positions for vehicles and staff 
e Rivers penetrating the perimeter 
e Power plants 
e Fuel farms 
e Control tower 
© Centralized air conditioning facilities 
e Aircraft approach lighting 
e Emergency access routes 
¢ Drinking water reservoirs within the perimeter and serving the airport terminal/infrastructure 
When designing security systems for airport perimeters, the detection systems should have full redundancy 
capability. If a single component fails, the system's overall integrity should remain intact. Field devices such 
as fence detectors should provide an indication to the central control room that a failure has occurred and 
where the failed field device is. 
Waterways that intersect the perimeter boundary should be protected. Unauthorized access should not be 
possible beneath runway or terminal complexes.

===PAGE 979===
=e IATA lh Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.6.9.4 Access Control 
Maintaining the integrity of security restricted area boundaries (including sterile landside and airside areas) 
Plays a critical role in deterring, detecting and delaying unauthorized access to, or attacks on, an airport or aircraft. Effective security relies heavily on the integrated application of technical measures (e.g., barriers, 
identification and access control systems, surveillance and detection equipment), along with the effective 
implementation of security procedures based on security awareness, training, supervision and security 
culture. 
Consideration should be given to reducing to a minimum the number of access control points to airside and 
other security restricted areas. Effective access control can be achieved by: 
* Having plant and maintenance facilities landside, but with controlled access, especially where ducting, 
piping, cabling and other plant or inspection panels pass through the security restricted area boundary 
* Planning kitchen and catering facilities carefully. Increasingly, airports are planning a single catering 
facility to serve airside and landside. Where this is so, the facility should be situated either totally landside 
or totally airside, with the means to service the other area via security airlock hatches rather than having 
staff move between landside and airside. If the facility is located on landside, additional security on goods 
might be required to avoid introduction of prohibited items 
* Providing adequate facilities for staff within the security restricted area in order to reduce the number of 
times they need to pass control points in the course of their duties, in particular if security controls are 
also applied on staff 
* Coordinating landside non-public access and airside security restricted area access control. This can be achieved by minimizing the number of, and Strategic placement of, access control points to the apron, 
elevators to plant rooms on the roof, and by the use of parallel corridors (one landside, one airside) 
¢ Having a single, suitably located access point for deliveries. For larger operations, having a single delivery 
point landside from which deliveries are screened, secured and shuttled in dedicated vehicles into the 
security restricted area or airside. This arrangement would also facilitate the introduction of additional 
security measures should the threat increase 
* Wherever possible, avoiding locating landside toilets back-to-back with security restricted area toilets. If this is not avoidable, ensuring that they are designed and constructed so that it would be difficult to 
penetrate the airside boundary through the walls or roofs 
¢ Having baggage reclaim areas outside the security restricted area to reduce the risk of Passengers 
backtracking through the exit doors. To meet customs requirements for international reclaim areas, these 
should be non-public areas and serve as a buffer to protect the security restricted area 
* Planning a means of baggage trolley return (i.., security airlock) which eliminates the need for staff to 
move between the landside and airside security restricted area 
960 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 980===
i IATA Hi ! Airport Support Elements 
Maintenance areas, service areas, miscellaneous activities areas, and buildings or controlled areas are 
usually located landside with controlled access to airside. Duplication of such facilities airside should be 
studied in order to limit the volume of airport supplies to be controlled on a daily basis. 
To prevent unauthorized access, doors, windows or gates leading from landside to security restricted areas, 
and to controlled areas that are not under surveillance, should be equipped with locks and/or alarms. This 
includes securing pipes and drains running from landside to security restricted areas. 
Buildings and other fixed structures may be used as a part of the physical barrier and be incorporated into the 
fence line, as long as measures are taken to restrict unauthorized passage through them. Care should also be 
taken to ensure that roofs, ceiling cavities, parked equipment or other structures do not provide an easily 
accessible route for unauthorized access to airside. 
3.6.9.5 Security Lighting 
Security lighting can offer a high degree of deterrence to a potential intruder, in addition to providing the 
illumination necessary for effective surveillance either directly by the security guards or indirectly through a 
CCTV system. Security lighting can make an important contribution to physical security but, incorrectly 
applied, it can assist intruders more than guard forces. Good security lighting should: 
¢ Allow guards to see intruders before they reach their objectives 
e Conceal the guards from intruders 
¢ Deter intruders or hinder them in their purpose 
Security lighting acts as a particularly good low-cost deterrent. Even a low level of illumination will act as a 
deterrent to potential intruders and vandals. Airports should provide for aircraft parking positions to be 
especially well-illuminated. If CCTV is installed, the lighting level and uniformity must be such that it helps to 
present a clear monitor picture to security guards. 
Where facial recognition technology is used, or may be used in the future, specific lighting requirements 
should be considered. 
3.6.9.6 Closed Circuit Television 
The use of Closed Circuit Television (CCTV) for surveillance can save manpower, especially when used in 
conjunction with intruder detection and automatic access control systems. CCTV may also supplement, 
extend and make more effective an existing security system. CCTV enhances the effectiveness of perimeter 
security, particularly if used to verify the alarms signaled by a Perimeter Intruder Detection System (PIDS). It 
can also lead to improved working conditions for security guards who may not need to be exposed to danger, 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 961 

===PAGE 981===
ry 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
inclement weather or other inconveniences of routine patrolling and related tasks as frequently. The 
Operational false alarm rates of PIDS should be carefully studied before deployment to avoid unnecessary 
costs and lack of confidence in technology. 
If CCTV is to be used, clear operational requirements should be developed and CCTV systems should be 
commissioned. Once installed, the CCTV system should be audited, using appropriate methodology and 
trained staff. 
3.6.9.7 Vulnerable Points 
A vulnerable point is any facility on, or connected with, an airport, which, if damaged or destroyed, would 
seriously impair the functioning of the airport. 
Airport vulnerable points include: 
* Control towers 
* Communications facilities 
° Radio navigation aids 
¢ Power transformers 
¢ Primary and secondary power supplies 
¢ Water and fuel installations, both on and off the airport 
¢ Additional vulnerable points are identified by the local security risk assessment 
The risk assessment will identify where physical security measures must be supplemented by operational 
security measures (i.e., patrolling). Physical security controls (¢.g., control rooms) should have strict access 
control. 
3.6.9.8 Support Operations 
A precise inventory of support operations and other non-aviation activities should be drawn up at the initial 
planning stage so that a decision can be made concerning the location of each of these activities, The 
following basic principles should govern this decision: 
* The role, responsibilities and accountability of tenants should be considered for access control 
¢ Except for those which have a direct and Permanent link with air transport operations, the number of non￾aviation activities located airside should be restricted as much as possible (e.g., hotels and freight 
forwarders' buildings/facilities should not be located airside) 
¢ When facilities for support operations and other non-aviation activities do have to be located airside (e.g., 
to enable them to have access to the runways), they should: 
© Be located away from the airport's Passenger and cargo buildings and other vulnerable points 
o Whenever possible, be isolated within the airside area 
962 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 982===
Be | IATA Airport Support Elements 
Private airside access points through non-aviation buildings/facilities should: 
o Be kept to the minimum required for pedestrians and service vehicles 
© Be controlled 
3.6.9.9 General Aviation Security 
General Aviation (GA) operations need to be segregated from the main air terminal areas in order to keep the 
movement of persons and vehicles to a minimum and subject to security restricted area arrangements. These 
movements relate mainly to fueling operations, meteorological services and the airport control reporting office. 
GA may be subject to the same level of access control as others at the airport at all times, or only during 
periods of heightened threat. This should be taken into account when considering airside transport planning 
and the location of access control points. 
3.6.9.10 Isolated Aircraft Parking Positions 
An isolated aircraft parking position should be located at the maximum distance possible from other aircraft 
parking positions, buildings, public areas, and the airport perimeter. Planners should keep in mind that the 
isolated aircraft parking position can be used in the event of an aircraft hijacking or bomb threat. If taxiways or 
runways pass within this area, they may have to be closed to normal operations when a ‘suspect’ aircraft is in 
the area. Planners should seek input on ideal locations for these positions from the security, law enforcement 
and meteorology agencies. 
The isolated aircraft parking position may serve as a ‘security parking area’, where an aircraft threatened with 
unlawful interference may be parked as long as necessary, or positioned for the loading or unloading of 
passengers. It may also be necessary to remove and examine cargo, mail and stores from an aircraft during 
bomb threat conditions. 
Care should be taken to ensure that the position is not located over underground utilities such as gasoline or 
aviation fuel networks, water mains, or electrical/communications cables. Such parking areas should ideally 
be located so as to eliminate the possibility of unauthorized persons physically reaching or being able to 
threaten the security/safety of the aircraft. Consideration should also be given to the prevailing wind direction 
and aircraft landing and takeoff routing at the airport, so as to minimize disruption to airport operations and 
the surrounding locality in the event of an aircraft fire or release of dangerous substances from the aircraft. 
Consideration should also be given to communication requirements for the Emergency Operation Center (i.e., 
CCTV system and/or unobstructed line of sight). 
3.6.10 Vehicle Refueling and Recharging Stations 
Refueling and recharging stations are needed to serve a wide variety of vehicles and GSE operated by airport 
authorities, airlines and ground service providers. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 963 

===PAGE 983===
IATA ‘al Airport Development Reference Manual 
The majority of airport vehicles operate on the airside. The movement of vehicles between the airside and landside should be minimized for reasons of security and operational efficiency; as such, the provision of both airside and landside refueling and recharging stations may be required. 
3.6.10.1 Alternative Fuels 
Historically, airport vehicles and GSE has been fueled by diesel or gasoline. More recently, airports have begun to incorporate alternative fuel vehicles in response to increasingly stringent emissions standards and broader environmental, economic and operational concerns of airports and their stakeholders. 
The use of alternative fuel vehicles can provide the following benefits: 
¢ Reduction in greenhouse gas emissions 
* Improved air quality on the apron and in buildings 
¢ Reduction in operating costs (i.e., fuel, maintenance and repair) 
There are a number of alternative fuel options for surface vehicles, including: 
* Natural gas (CNG/LNG) 
¢ Propane (LPG) 
* Electricity (battery or hybrid) 
e Ethanol 
¢ Biodiesel 
e Hydrogen 
The use of natural gas and electric vehicles is most common, while the development and adoption of hydrogen fuel cells is more limited and not expected to be widely adopted at airports in the short to medium 
term. 
The type and role of alternative fuels will vary by airport and are influenced by the cost and availability of different fuel sources, the scale of operation and future fleet development plans of the airport, airlines and other ground service providers. 
The planning of fueling/electric infrastructure and refueling/charging stations should take into consideration 
future trends and, where practical, Preserve flexibility to accommodate expansion or diversification in the future. 
Facility requirements and siting considerations vary for refueling and recharging stations, as well as between airside and landside facilities.

===PAGE 984===

3.6.10.2 Airside Stations 
Airports have large vehicle fleets operating airside, including: 
¢ Airport operations and maintenance vehicles (e.g., rescue and firefighting vehicles, airfield maintenance 
and snow removal equipment, buses, delivery vehicles) 
e Airline GSE (e.g., baggage tugs, belt loaders, cargo tractors, aircraft tugs, cabin service/catering trucks, 
hydrant trucks) 
e FBO vehicles 
3.6.10.2.1 Refueling Stations 
Airside refueling stations are typically collocated with airfield equipment maintenance and GSE maintenance 
facilities, as well as at convenient locations on passenger terminal aprons. These facilities are often 
supplemented with mobile tankers that supply fuel directly to some larger diesel- or gasoline-powered apron￾based GSE (i.e., container loaders) in order to minimize travel distances. 
Planning and design of refueling stations should consider the following: 
e Aviation and non-aviation fuel storage and refueling stations may be provided in separate locations or 
collocated 
* Landside access for fuel delivery is preferred 
¢ Maneuvering clearance for the largest vehicle in the airport fleet 
¢ Provision for queuing and/or staging 
¢ Dispensing pumps should be protected against physical damage (e.g., raised platforms, bollards or posts) 
e Pumps should be fitted with remote shut-offs and be color-coded to distinguish different types and grades 
of fuel 
3.6.10.2.2 Electric Vehicle Charging Stations 
Airside charging stations should be located to minimize Electric Vehicle (EV) travel requirements. They 
require convenient spaces for parking that do not interfere with airside operations and, in certain climates, 
may require weather protection for vehicles being charged. Indoor stations will be needed to protect vehicles 
in extreme climactic conditions. 
The provision of adequate space for charging stations and vehicles can be an issue and needs to be 
investigated. A number of recharging technologies exist, including: 
° Cable—Level 1, Level 2 and Level 3 (commonly known as “fast” or “quick” charge) 
* Wireless induction

===PAGE 985===

IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
Fully recharging an EV may take between four and eight hours. Even “quick charges” can take 30 minutes or 
more. The ability to charge electric vehicles in an efficient and systematic way is critical to a successful 
operation. 
The following locations should be considered when Planning for EV charging: 
¢ In the passenger terminal building. For health and safety reasons, vehicles that enter confined areas of 
a passenger terminal (i.e., baggage areas) are required to be electric powered. Many electric GSE 
vehicles travel relatively short distances airside and usually return to the same locations, which should be 
considered in determining where charging points are needed. Electric baggage tractors, for example, may 
be charged in outbound baggage rooms 
¢ At the gate, the majority of GSE is associated with the servicing of aircraft. The incorporation of charging 
Stations on the fixed links (gate houses) can provide an efficient option for aircraft service vehicles and 
should be considered in the planning and design of aircraft stands and GSE staging areas 
° Atcentralized facilities. In some instances, larger consolidated recharging facilities may be preferred or 
Provided in conjunction with other distributed charging points. To cut downtime to a minimum, some 
airports operate a battery change system, avoiding the need for vehicles to remain at a charging station 
for up to eight hours to fully recharge 
¢ In the vehicle maintenance area 
Electrical loads associated with vehicle charging should be modeled. An electrical service upgrade may be 
required to support the loads. Strategies such as trickle feed and charging during off peak times may be used 
to reduce the impact of electric vehicle charging on the airports peak power requirements. 
3.6.10.3 Landside Stations 
Demand for refueling and recharging landside typically include, but are not limited to: 
¢ Rental car companies 
¢ Airport shuttle buses 
¢ Private vehicles (passengers and employees) 
Landside stations tend to be distributed by the specific fuel needs and location of landside facilities and 
operations. For example, individual rental car companies will often incorporate a refueling point as a part of 
their vehicle detailing and maintenance area. 
In some instances, consolidated facilities may offer certain advantages where an individual operator's demand 
is limited and it is more efficient and economical to supply a number of users from a single facility. This 
approach can be seen with the introduction of alternative fuels. Airport shuttle buses can be good candidates 
for CNG fuel. Providing public access to the associated CNG fueling station can provide additional incentive 
to other users (i.e., taxi and shuttle van owners) to convert to CNG. 
Provision of public gas stations is typically met by off-airport commercial facilities where space can be at a 
premium; however, some airports are providing them as an additional source of revenue. Many airports, 
966 EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 986===
Wats itl A Airport Support Elements 
however, have started to offer EV charging stations and preferred parking spaces for alternative fuel vehicles 
in their on-airport parking facilities. Such provisions are aimed at enabling/encouraging the use of alternative 
fuel vehicles for airport access as a component of an airport's overall sustainability objectives. 
3.6.11 Airport Fire Services 
3.6.11.1 Fire Services Overview 
The main objective of rescue and firefighting services is to extinguish fire and rescue people within the 
confines of the airport boundary where the risk of an aircraft accident is the greatest. The rescue and 
firefighting service should be under administrative control of airport management, which should be responsible 
for ensuring that the service is organized, equipped, staffed, and trained appropriately. Some airports rely on 
local or regional fire stations and vehicles for building (structural) and non-aircraft fire incidents, whereas 
others may provide this service on-site, and may, in addition, provide fire protection services to local 
communities. 
Regarding survivable aircraft incidents, the most important factors bearing on effective rescue are: 
¢ Training 
° The effectiveness of the equipment 
e The speed with which the rescue personnel and equipment can be put into use 
The rescue and firefighting services will typically also perform other important tasks: 
¢ Handling hazardous materials 
¢ Vehicular incidents 
¢ Other types of emergencies that threaten life, safety, property or the environment 
e Fire and safety prevention programs and education 
© Building code enforcement 
3.6.11.2 Airport Category and Level of Protection 
In accordance with ICAO Annex 14, Section 9.2, airports should be categorized for rescue and firefighting 
purposes and the level of protection provided should be appropriate to the airport category. The category level 
is based on the aircraft size and volume of traffic operating at an airport. 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 967 

===PAGE 987===
she | 
IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
For the purposes of clarifying the airport category for fire services, ICAO Annex 14, Section 9.2, Table 9-1 should be used. 
Having established the airport Category, it is then necessary to establish the fundamental equipment 
requirements. This should be done in accordance with ICAO Annex 14, Section 9.2.41, where the minimum 
number of rescue and firefighting vehicles to be provided is noted. 
3.6.11.3 Response Time and Airport Fire Station Locations 
ICAO Annex 14, Section 9.2.19 sets the operational objectives of the rescue and firefighting services on the airport: to achieve response times of less than two minutes and not exceeding three minutes to the end of each runway, as well as to any other part of the aircraft movement area, in optimum surface and visibility conditions. The response time is considered to be the time between the initial call to the rescue and firefighting service and the time when the first responding vehicle is in position to apply foam at a rate of at least 50% of the specified discharge rate. 
The location and number of fire stations needed is dependent on the required response times, the equipment provided, and the geometry of the airfield. At some airports, it will be necessary to provide more than one station. Stations should be located to ensure that the access to the runway system is direct and clear, 
requiring a minimum of turns. Wide radius turns should be used at intersections of access roads and runways, 
to maximize vehicle speeds. Satellite fire stations should be provided whenever the response time cannot be achieved from a single fire station. 
Simulation may be employed to assess travel times and routes of emergency vehicles on complex airfield 
geometries to assist in determining the number and location Of fire stations. 
To achieve the recommended response time, the airport should have emergency access roads capable of 
supporting the heaviest vehicles where terrain condition permits, and be equipped with suitable rescue 
vehicles where areas to be covered include water, swamps or other difficult environments that cannot be fully served by conventional wheeled vehicles. Airports adjacent to large bodies of water, such as rivers or lakes, 
or located on coastlines, should establish special provisions to expedite rescue, based on ICAO 
recommendations. 
A coordination program between the rescue and firefighting services at an airport and the local public 
emergency agencies (i.e., local fire brigade, police force, coast guard and hospital) is also a key element in the success of a rescue mission. The division of responsibility between the various agencies needs to be established, as this will impact the facility requirements program. All communications links should be in place 
to provide quick and direct access to the airport grounds for the local and other external emergency services. 
The implementation of permitted vehicle access cards, which can be fitted to selected local fire brigade 
vehicles and ambulances, should be considered. Access for these types of vehicles should only be permitted in situations when the external emergency services have been specifically called to assist the airport fire services.

===PAGE 988===

3.6.11.4 Vehicle and Equipment Requirements 
The number and type of aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicles should be capable of meeting the specified 
response times, as well as delivering the principal and complementary extinguishing agents at the discharge 
rates specified in ICAO Annex 14, Chapter 9, Table 9.2, in accordance with the listed airport category. 
Suitable rescue equipment and services should be available at an airport where the area to be covered 
includes water, swamps or other difficult environments that cannot be fully served by conventional wheeled 
vehicles. The airport must select the right vehicle types to suit their needs and airfield topography. Rescue 
and firefighting vehicle types may range from conventional wheeled trucks to boats and helicopters. 
Rescue equipment commensurate with the level of aircraft operations should be available on the rescue and 
firefighting vehicles, and should include: 
e Highly efficient firefighting agents, preferably foam 
¢ Lighting equipment, preferably operating from a portable power source 
¢ Power tools, operated from a portable power source, for cutting operations 
e Hand tools (e.g., wire and bolt cutters, hammers, axes, crowbars) 
¢ Forcing equipment, usually hydraulically operated, for lifting and bending operations 
e Respiratory equipment (e.g., self-contained breathing apparatus) 
*® Communications equipment 
¢ Equipment capable of providing water spray within an aircraft fuselage 
e Equipment capable of providing fresh air supply 
e Medical first aid equipment 
Airport specific fire and emergency equipment requirements, including any requirements for fighting building 
(structural) fires, should be assessed in consultation with local fire brigades, using specialized advisors. 
3.6.11.5 Fire Station Types and Facility Requirements 
As documented in FAA Advisory Circular AC 150/5210-15A, several types of fire stations may need to be 
provided, depending on specific airport requirements, including: 
e The headquarters station typically houses the airport fire chief and administrative staff, as well as aircraft 
rescue and firefighting vehicles 
¢ Satellite stations work in conjunction with the headquarter station to maintain maximum responses times 
on larger sites. Satellite stations house aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicles and staff facilities 
¢ Combination stations that house both aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicles as well as building 
(structural) firefighting vehicles from a single facility 
© Multifunction stations that house other services that support airport operations (e.g., snow removal 
equipment, medical/first aid facilities, security offices, emergency operations center)

3.6.11.6 Firefighting Personnel Training 
All rescue and firefighting personnel should be Properly trained and equipped to respond quickly and perform efficiently in an emergency. Suitable training facilities should be provided so the personnel can perform live fire drills commensurate with the types of aircraft and the types of rescue and firefighting equipment in use at the airport.

Some larger airports develop dedicated training facilities with the objective of providing a safe training

3.7 Utilities 
3.7.1 Utilities Master Plan 
A comprehensive Utilities Master Plan is a planning document that is required to guide foresight and 
investment in the critical utility systems that sustain an airport's operations. The Utilities Master Plan should 
include an inventory of existing and required utilities, including capacity determination, age, remaining useful 
life, and any possible future constraints. The benefits of developing and maintaining a Utilities Master Plan 
are: 
* Ability to monitor capacity, condition and replacement/upgrade cycles for utility systems and their 
associated budgets 
¢ Early identification of interfaces with municipal utility suppliers 
¢ Understanding of the costs of maintaining and upgrading airport utility systems, allowing the 
establishment of dedicated budgets 
Identification of the future needs for utility systems to support airport capital investment projects, and the 
associated load demand growth that expansion brings 
Identification of primary utility corridors and methods (e.g., direct-bury, utility tunnel or above ground) to 
support airport expansion projects and ensure that these remain free from conflicting land uses 
establish reliability criteria to improve the performance of critical systems (i.e., power and water), 
minimizing outages and failures along with their associated impacts on airport operations 
Identification of the opportunities for renewable energy and water conservation measures to be 
implemented 
e Establish a protocol for reporting utility usage and trends 
* Establish a Planned Preventative Maintenance (PPM) regime to support the cost-effective maintenance of 
assets 
e Reliability and resilience 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 971 

===PAGE 991===
Soe By 
IATA 4 Airport Development Reference Manual 
A Utilities Master Plan is a planning tool that needs to be maintained and updated to respond to changing 
codes/standards, the sustainability objectives of the airport, and load growth associated with airport 
expansion. As a minimum, a Utilities Master Plan should provide a framework for the following systems: 
* Power, including Uninterrupted Power Supply (UPS) for critical facilities 
* Chilled and hot water distribution 
e Potable water and recycled water systems 
e Firefighting water 
¢ Communications 
e Natural gas 
¢ Wastewater treatment 
¢ Storm water drainage 
e Jet fuel 
3.7.2 Centralized Utilities Distribution 
A Central Utilities Plant (CUP) should be a consideration when planning a new airport or expanding an 
existing airport, due to the mix of facilities and the size/profile of the energy loads. On-site energy generation 
and distribution provides a higher level of resilience and control to the facilities served, and the use of 
cogeneration processes (combined heat and Power) will improve energy generation efficiencies and can realize significant energy cost savings over grid connectivity.

Key considerations when planning a CUP include: 
* Sufficient space to construct a CUP and the associated cooling towers

* Climate and the associated chilled water/heating needs (both current and future/projected) 
e Consideration of load profiles for the airport and the lifecycle costs of a CUP, to determine whether it is 
the right commercial investment 
¢ Availability of fuel source to drive a CUP's power and heat generation 
e Experience and availability of skilled staff to operate the facility and systems 
3.7.3 Electric Services 
As airport passenger terminals increasingly become centers of commercial activity, with higher passenger 
demand and associated retail, commercial and hospitality facilities, there is a corresponding impact on 
electrical load demand. Additionally, to facilitate the reduction in greenhouse gas emissions around airports, 
electrical GPU and PCA are replacing portable diesel GPUs and PCAs, increasing airport terminal electrical 
load densities. Utility master plans should, therefore, review and consider the impact of these changes, and 
determine the optimal distribution voltages and power densities. 
The following table provides guidelines for electrical utility services for airport terminals and associated 
buildings, based on recognized sustainability and energy efficiency standards. 
Exhibit 3.7.3: Airport Electrica! Utility Provisions

An airport should consider the provision of centralized standby power. Where gas is available locally, and the 
airport has a good base load, a cogeneration plant should be considered as a cost offset. A cogeneration 
plant can provide the standby power required on loss of utility power, and provide redundant power without 
being subject to the utility's transmission and distribution failures. Additional benefits include high energy 
conversion factors when the airport has a large hot water demand, and overall lower energy costs for airport 
operations. A life cycle assessment of potential fuel sources, power capacity, demand, and resell rates should 
be developed to determine feasibility of a cogeneration process. 
Wherever centralized facilities are in place, redundancy/backup plans should also be included to ensure 
ongoing uninterrupted operations in the event that a central plant goes down.

3.7.3.1 Airport Terminal Sustainable Measures 
Airport terminals handle passenger traffic. Hence, they have higher electrical load densities than other airport buildings. To reduce terminal electrical energy consumption, the following measures should be considered: 
¢ BHS-consider Linear Induction Motors (LIM) and Linear Synchronous Motors (LSM) 
* _ Lifts/elevators—consider machine room-less elevators with regenerative power 
¢ Escalators and moving walkways-consider variable speed drives 
* — Lighting—consider high efficiency LED lighting, and maximizing daylight control 
¢ UPS systems-consider provision of eco-mode ‘N’ UPS systems for telecom rooms in lieu of 2N UPS 
systems 
3.7.4 Water 
Airports are significant water users. An airport's water infrastructure includes potable water, firefighting water, 
wastewater, recycled water and storm water. Historically, these systems were considered in isolation, 
however, there are many synergies and conservation opportunities when they are considered together. 
3.7.4.1 Potable Water and Firefighting Water 
These critical systems need to function at all times and, where possible, should be separately operable 
systems since firefighting water often needs to Operate at higher pressures than potable water and typically 
requires larger pipes. The following should be considered when planning these systems: 
¢ Layout and flexible operation-loops with regular isolation valves are preferred to add redundancy and 
allow individual parts of the system to be taken out of service for maintenance or repair 
¢ Pipe material-careful selection of pipe material to meet the design performance criteria and soil 
conditions is very important 
¢ Conservation-specification of water saving fixtures in buildings, metering to monitor use and improve 
billing, and opportunities to reduce Potable water demand by supplementing it with recycled water 
3.7.4.2 Wastewater and Recycled Water 
The following should be considered when planning wastewater infrastructure: 
* Maximize the use of gravity systems wherever possible 
* Consider on-site wastewater treatment and a recycled water network to redistribute treated wastewater to 
serve non-potable demands 
* Provide regular access to the systems to facilitate access for maintenance and inspection 
* Consider options such as relining for pipe bursts in aging systems to avoid total system replacement and the accompanying impact on operations 
974 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 

===PAGE 994===
= IATA Utilities 
The use of recycled water at airports is becoming more prevalent in response to more aggressive water 
codes, sustainability objectives, increasing potable water costs, and the need to reduce consumption of 
potable water. Recycled water can either be sourced from the municipality (if available) or from on-site 
wastewater treatment. Non-potable water uses at airports include: 
e Cooling towers 
e Landscape irrigation 
e Non-potable uses in buildings 
e Aircraft/vehicle washing operations 
e Dust contro! 
Significant reductions in potable water demand can be realized through on-site wastewater treatment. 
When planning a recycled water network, the following will need to be considered: 
© Horizontal and vertical separation from potable and firefighting water infrastructure 
¢ Location of points of connection and working pressures if connecting to a municipal supply 
* The quality of the wastewater and where it can be used 
e Clear identification that the network is recycled water to avoid cross-connections 
¢ Pipe material-PVC and HDPE are recommended for most applications 
e Sizing of the system to meet current and projected demands 
¢ Clear and secure separation of potable/non-potable water 
3.7.4.3 Storm Water 
The management of storm water is often governed by local codes. If storm water is not properly managed, the 
consequences for an airport include flooding and pollution. Where possible, the following hierarchy should be 
followed for the management of storm water runoff (with the understanding that open storage areas are not 
desirable for most airport applications as they attract wildlife): 
Infiltration close to source—use of infiltration devices (e.g., underground tanks, dry wells and filter strips) to 
return water back to the ground as close as possible to where it falls 
¢ Where infiltration is not feasible (e.g., due to ground conditions or the need to drain large expanses of 
pavement), consider applications where storm water is captured, treated and reused on site (e.g., to 
supplement an irrigation supply source) 
e Where infiltration and capture-and-use are not feasible, flow-through treatment devices (i.e., bioswales 
and mechanical separators) should be considered to manage the downstream flow rate and water quality

IATA / Airport Development Reference Manual 
3.7.4.4 Flooding 
Flooding has the potential to seriously impact airport operations and needs Proper consideration. The FAA 
Advisory Circular 150/5320-5D provides flood risk guidance for an airport's facilities, however, airports are 
often planned to more stringent criteria, such as the following, to ensure operational continuity and resilience: 
* 1:200-year storm event for critical infrastructure (e.g., power generation facilities, central utilities plants, 
wastewater treatment plants) 
¢ 1:100-year storm event for terminal buildings and facilities that experience high passenger traffic volumes 
(@.g., access roads and emergency vehicle routes) 
* 1:50-year storm event for runways and taxiways 
A site-specific evaluation is recommended for each airport prior to the selection of flood risk criteria.

IATA Glossary 
Glossary 
Aircraft movement: An aircraft takeoff or landing at an airport. For airport traffic purposes, one arrival and 
one departure is counted as two movements. 
Airfield: The network of runways and taxiways at a given airport, the configuration of which is selected based 
on a wide range of criteria, including future development considerations, the direction of prevailing winds, 
average monthly temperatures, altitude from sea level, natural obstacles, local surface transportation 
networks, neighboring airport facilities, etc. 
Airline capacity: Seats available, often referred to as Available Seat Kilometers (ASKs) operated by an 
Airline. 
Airline Operators Committees (AOC): Committees concerned with the day-to-day operation of the airport 
for which they are established. Usually, information concerning a proposed airport development is first 
received from the airport authority at AOC meetings. 
Airport catchment area: The geographic region where the majority of originating passengers (or goods for 
cargo) begin their journey prior to arriving at the subject airport. 
Airport Consultative Committee (ACC): A committee developed by IATA in the event of an airport 
expansion proposal or new airport development. The purpose of the ACC is to consolidate the views of those 
airlines who use or will make use of the facility in question and provide a focal point for consultation with the 
airport authority. 
Airport Operational Database (AODB): The central repository for all flight-related operational data to feed 
various real-time functions that support the operation. 
Airside: The aircraft movement area of an airport, including adjacent terrain and buildings or portions thereof, 
access to which is restricted to operational employees and (in specific enplaning and deplaning areas) 
members of the traveling public who have been security screened. 
Apron: A defined airport area intended to accommodate aircraft for purposes of loading or unloading 
passengers, baggage, mail or cargo, fueling, parking or maintenance (ICAO Annex 2,4, 11, 14, Vol. |, 
PANS-ATM). Synonymous with ramp and tarmac. 
Available Seat Kilometers/Miles (ASK)/(ASM): A seat kilometer or seat mile is available when a seat is 
flown over the distance of one kilometer or one statute mile. Available seat-kilometers/miles are equal to the 
sum of the products obtained by multiplying the number of passenger seats available for sale on each flight 
stage by the stage distance expressed in kilometers or statute miles, based on airport-to-airport great circle 
distances. Seats not actually available for the carriage of passengers because of the weight of fuel or other 
EDITION 12 - MAY 2022 977 

===PAGE 997===
IATA rll Airport Development Reference Manual 
load should be excluded in the calculations. Synonymous with capacity passenger-kilometers/miles 
(CPK)(CPM) and seat kilometers/miles available (SKA)/SMA). 
Available Ton Kilometers/Miles (ATK)(ATM): A metric ton of available payload space flown over the 
distance of one kilometer or one statute mile. Available ton-kilometers/miles are equal to the sum of the 
Products obtained by multiplying the number of metric tons of capacity available for the carriage of revenue 
load (i.e., passengers, baggage, freight and mail), on each flight stage by the stage distance expressed in 
kilometers or statute miles, based on airport-to-airport great circle distances. The same method of calculating 
available payload capacity is used for both scheduled and charter flights for statistical reporting purposes. 
Synonymous with capacity ton-kilometers/miles (CTK)(CTM) and ton-kilometers/miles available (TKA/TMA). 
Note: The term production ton-kilometers/miles (PTK)(PTM) normally refers to the total number of metric 
tons of capacity available on both revenue and non revenue flights. 
Baggage, Cabin: Baggage that the aircraft Passenger retains custody of and carries aboard an aircraft 
(IATA RP 1008). This covers personal belongings, such as briefcases, handbags and other non bulky 
baggage conforming to specified dimensions to permit stowage aboard the aircraft. Synonymous with carry-on 
baggage. 
Baggage Check: Those portions of a ticket which provide for the carriage of a passenger's checked baggage 
and which are issued by the carrier as a receipt for same (IATA RP 1008). 
Baggage, Checked: Baggage of which the carrier takes sole custody and for which the carrier has issued a baggage check (IATA RP 1724). 
Baggage Handling System (BHS): A BHS is a system used to collect, screen, sort, store, transfer and 
deliver bags to aircraft on departures, and on arrivals to unload and deliver bags into the terminal for 
redistribution back to passengers. 
Biometrics: The systems and ideologies associated with a form of passenger identification which utilizes the 
measurement of exclusively self-identifying physical attributes. Examples of biometric devices and systems 
include but are not limited to facial recognition devices, fingerprint scanners, iris scanners, and the software 
Programs developed for same. Any one of these types of systems may be used alone or in conjunction with 
other forms of biometric, electronic or documentary identification for purposes of Passenger security and 
customs screening and/or passenger facilitation. 
Bluesea: See Greenfield/bluesea airports. 
Brownfield Site: Previously used land. 
Busy Day: A forecasting measure, IATA defines the ‘busy day’ as the second busiest day in an average 
week during the peak month. 
Capacity: The variable measurement of a specific airport system or subsystem's throughput, or the system's 
Capability to accommodate a designated level of demand. Comprehensive capacity assessments are based 
on five fundamental measurements: Dynamic Capacity; Static Capacity; Sustained Capacity; Maximum 
Capacity; and Declared Capacity.

Se 
IATA Glossary 
Capital Expenditure Plan: The long-term financing and expenditure plan pertaining to the acquisition, 
construction, or improvement of fixed assets such as land and buildings. 
Charter services: Flights performed for remuneration on an irregular basis, including empty flight stages 
related thereto and inclusive tours other than those reported under scheduled services. 
Common Use Passenger Processing Systems (CUPPS): Describes the range of services, specifications 
and standards enacted to enable multiple airlines, service providers, or other users to share physical check-in 
or gate podium positions whether simultaneously or consecutively. It is the modern development of the CUTE 
concept. 
Common Use Self-Service (CUSS): Refers to systems such as self-service check-in kiosks. It is a shared 
kiosk offering convenient passenger check-in whilst allowing multiple airlines to maintain branding and 
functionality. 
Common Use Terminat Equipment (CUTE): See Common Use Passenger Processing Systems (CUPPS). 
Delanti-icing: De-icing is the process which removes ice, snow, slush or frost from airplane surfaces for flight 
safety purposes. Anti-icing is a precautionary measure which prevents frost, ice or snow from forming or 
accumulating on the protected surface of an aircraft. Standard safety procedures usually involve proper and 
adequate de-icing, followed by an application of appropriate anti-icing freezing point depressant (FPD) fluids 
to create a protective film that delays formations of frost, snow or other types of ice. 
Demographic data: Covers population related statistics. 
Departures hall: The entrance into the terminal building for departing passengers. Depending upon type, size 
and airport location, it can consist of various public and non public areas including circulation and waiting 
areas, orientation and regrouping spaces, public facilities and airline facilities. 
Designated Postal Operator: Any governmental or non-governmental entity officially designated by a 
Universal Postal Union (UPU) member country to operate postal services and to fulfill the related obligations 
arising from the acts of the Convention on its territory. 
Destination Coded Vehicle (DCV): A baggage handling system that uses carts to move bags, normally at 
high speed, to an individual point in the airport. The carts move on rails and allow bags to travel large 
distances at high speed, as well as providing rapid routes to specific functional areas of the system. ADCV is 
also an excellent system to link baggage facilities in different terminals to provide redundancy and flexibility. 
Facilitation (FAL): A general term reflecting the action being taken by governments, airlines, airports and 
other organizations involved in civil aviation to standardize, simplify and reduce government-imposed 
formalities and procedures at airports. The main objectives are to improve efficiencies and services to 
passengers and users of cargo services, and to reduce relevant waiting times and costs. See IATA Guide to 
Facilitation.

IATA Airport Development Reference Manual 
Fixed-Base Operators (FBOs): Provider of support services to general aviation operators at an airport. 
Flight Information Display System (FIDS): A computerized airport, airline and baggage claim information 
display. 
Forecourt (formerly curbside): That area of an airport terminal facility dedicated to the safe and efficient 
transfer of passengers and meeters/greeters to and from road-based surface transport systems (cars, buses 
and taxis). 
Fractional ownership: With fractional jets, customers buy a “share” of a plane, rather than an entire plane. 
Greenfield/bluesea airports: ‘Greenfield’ or ‘bluesea’ are terms used to describe what most planners would 
consider to be ‘ideal’ airports or (alternately) airport locations. In general, greenfield or bluesea airports are 
mega facilities that have benefited from planning decisions whereby designers and ACCs have opted to 
create large, modern facilities on hitherto “undeveloped” land, incorporating many of the latest ‘best-practice’ 
airport planning guidelines. Current greenfield/bluesea airports include facilities such as Hong Kong 
International Airport, Denver International Airport, Kuala Lumpur KLIA, and Seoul Incheon, which all became 
operational between 1995 and 2000. These new airports are generally sized in the 400,000 sqm range and 
have operating capacities upwards of 30 mppa. They're usually designed to be hub facilities, are capable of 
adapting to service currently-envisioned larger aircraft, and incorporate a detailed master plan that will allow 
them to grow in a modular fashion to capacities up to 100 mppa. 
Gross Domestic Product (GDP): is the market value of all Officially recognized final goods and services 
Produced within a country in a year, or other given period of time. 
Hub: Any airport having numerous inbound and outbound flights and a high percentage of connecting traffic. 
In the context of scheduling and marketing from a hub-operating carrier's perspective, hub denotes an airport 
where many of its inbound and outbound schedules are Coordinated with the aim of producing the most 
convenient connections and/or trans-shipment for Passengers, freight and/or mail. The same airport may 
serve as a hub for more than one air carrier although this is exceptional. Currently, most hubs have been 
designed for passenger traffic but the Concept is also used for the development of cargo and mail traffic. 
Intermodal transportation: Intermodal Passenger transport involves using two or more modes of 
transportation in a journey. 
International Industry Working Group (IIWG): IIWGs bring together IATA, Airports Council International 
(ACI) and the International Coordinating Council of Aerospace Industries Associations (ICCAIA). The IIWG 
was founded in 1970 and its main goal is to review airport/aircraft compatibility issues which might improve 
the development of the air transport system. 
Landside: Those areas of an airport to which the non-traveling public has free access. Sometimes referred to 
as the public side. 
Latest Check-in Acceptance Time (LAT): Latest time prior to departure when a Passenger can check-in for 
a flight.
